Was the first school worth four hundred dollars of pure uncertainty, or was she in love with a building? Her mother's voice drifted up from downstairs, complaining to Gran that nothing in the house stayed where you put it, and Keira thought, not for the first time, that entropy was a family condition.

She typed a sentence at the bottom of the document: I don't know if I want it more, or if I just want to be wanted. Then she deleted it, then she typed it again, because it was true even if it was embarrassing. The honest position, she decided, was this: she would pay the deposit, because a bird in the hand was not a cliché when the hand had earned the money one onion-scented shift at a time, and she would stay on the waitlist, because wanting something did not become disloyal just because she'd bought insurance. Both things could be true. She would not pretend the four hundred dollars didn't sting, and she would not pretend she'd stopped hoping.

In May, after deposits everywhere had settled and the colleges counted their openings, she refreshed the portal at 3:14 on a Thursday, purely from superstition. The wheel spun. Dev appeared behind her with two forks and a bag of leftover pasta, which he offered without a word, held out like a peace treaty or a wager. The page began to load.

The trail climbed out of the pines into a clearing where the whole valley opened up, gray-blue and hazy, and Mr. Okonkwo's voice finally gave out behind them. He had insisted the debate team practice outdoors, saying that a change of venue extenuated the staleness of their arguments, whatever that meant, and so eight of them had followed him up the switchbacks with water bottles and printed evidence packets sweating inside their backpacks.

Coralie walked beside Dennis, who had drawn the skeptic's position in tomorrow's scrimmage. That was the assignment, to argue that the case for carbon dioxide was overstated, and Dennis took assignments seriously, which was the trouble with him. For two miles he had been rehearsing his opening under his breath like a prayer he didn't believe in.

"Water vapor," he said suddenly, aloud this time. "There it is. Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas. That's my whole first rebuttal. If water vapor traps heat, and there's more of it than anything else, then CO2 is a side character. That's the argument. That's what they use."

"That's what who uses?" Coralie asked, though she knew. She had seen the clip he'd found, some man in a suit holding up a graph.

"Everyone who says CO2 doesn't matter." Dennis stopped at the trail's edge, where a wooden sign with a faded map showed their elevation in peeling numerals. "Look, I'm not saying I believe it. But I have to argue it tomorrow, and I don't actually know why it's wrong. Do you?"

She didn't, she realized, which galled her, because she was the one on the team who cared about this. She had given a speech in April about the Keeling curve, the sawtoothed line of carbon dioxide climbing across a century, and she had described it beautifully without understanding what made the sawtooth, why the line dipped each year and rose again, always higher than before. She had said "seasonal respiration" and moved on quickly, hoping no one would ask.

They sat on a flat rock below the sign and she pulled out her phone, which had one bar. Dennis leaned over her shoulder, smelling of sunscreen and trail dust. She found the graph first, the full record, and they looked at it together, the little wobbles riding on the long climb. Then she typed water vapor into the search field and started reading, slowly, out loud, stopping whenever she hit a sentence she couldn't say like she meant it.

"Okay," she said after a while. "So it's true. Water vapor really is the most abundant greenhouse gas. Your clip isn't lying about that part."

"Ha," said Dennis.

"But listen. Warmer air holds more water vapor." She read the line twice because it seemed too simple. "So when something else warms the air, the air pulls in more water vapor, and that traps more heat, which warms it further. It's not the trigger. It's the amplifier." She looked up. "It's a feedback. That's the word they use."

"Feedback," Dennis repeated. "Like a microphone next to a speaker."

"Kind of. The point is the warming starts with something else. With gases like carbon dioxide. Water vapor just makes whatever CO2 starts into something bigger." She scrolled down, checking, because she wanted to be sure before she said it to him. "So your whole rebuttal is true and it doesn't matter. It's the most abundant, and it's still not the cause."

Dennis was quiet for a moment, watching a hawk tilt over the far ridge. "That's actually a better argument against me than anything Priya's going to say tomorrow," he said. "She'll just call me a denier."

Below them on the switchback, Priya herself came around the bend, red-faced and cheerful, with Marcus behind her arguing about whether their coach counted as a mentor or a tormentor. Priya flopped onto the rock beside Coralie, looked at the graph still glowing on the phone, and said, "Is that the CO2 curve? God, it's so ugly when you zoom out. Like a hockey stick having a seizure."

"That's the sawtooth," Coralie said, and then, because Priya was actually asking, she tried to explain it, the breathing of the northern forests, and found she could almost do it now, the way you can almost play a song you've only heard while trying to teach it.

"You two are disgustingly sagacious for a Thursday," Marcus said, dropping his pack. "Meanwhile I got lost twice and Mr. Okonkwo called me a navigational embarrassment."

Coralie smiled, but she was still turning something over. She thought about how she'd built her April speech, all that certainty, that rising line, and how she'd stood in front of the room and implied she understood things she'd only memorized. There was a kind of consanguinity between her speech and the man in Dennis's video, she thought, an actual family resemblance: both of them using a true number to say something the number couldn't carry alone. She hadn't lied. She had just never gone down into the basement of her own facts and checked the supports.

"So what do I do tomorrow," Dennis said. He wasn't joking now. "I still have the assignment."

"Argue it. Argue it the best you can, that's the drill." She paused. "But when they counter you, don't fight the water vapor thing. Concede it fast and keep moving. If you fight it, you'll lose the room."

Mr. Okonkwo's voice floated up from below, calling them onward to the overlook. They shouldered their packs. Dennis lingered a second, zipping the packet away, and said, quietly, "For the record, I made my cousin send me that clip. I wanted a rebuttal I couldn't beat, so I'd know I'd beaten everything."

She stared at him. "You've known the answer since Tuesday?"

"I knew the answer. I didn't know the why until just now, up here, from you." He tightened a strap and started up the trail. "That's why I asked you and not Google."

She stood a moment in the clearing, phone warm in her hand, uncertain whether she'd been taught something or used, and then she followed him toward the overlook, where the rest of the team was already shouting at the view.

The last box in Nicolas's room was labeled MISC, which his mother said was a way of admitting you had no idea what you owned. He sat on the bare mattress and texted Devon: you coming or what. Devon replied with a thumbs up and, three minutes later, appeared in the doorway holding two energy drinks like an offering.

They spent the afternoon doing nothing much in a room that was already nobody's. Devon peeled the labels off the cans in long strips. Nicolas stacked the boxes by size and then restacked them by weight, which made no difference to anything. When Devon left, he said, "It's only two hours away," and Nicolas said, "I know," and neither of them said the thing that underpinned the whole visit, which was that two hours was far enough to turn friends into memories you scheduled around.

The new town revealed itself in stages: a highway exit with three gas stations, a main street that pretended it hadn't been designed for cars, and a library built of pale brick with a plaque from some civic club nobody had belonged to since the seventies. They had no internet hooked up yet at the apartment, which was his mother's excuse and his reason. On the third day he walked there with his laptop and no real plan.

He chose a table near the periodicals because it had a window behind it and an outlet underneath, the way a hermit crab chooses a shell. A girl was already at the next table with a textbook open to a diagram of a cell, highlighting it in a color he had never seen used for anything, a kind of acid green. She looked up once, looked down, and that was the extent of their diplomacy for an hour.

He came back the next afternoon. And the one after. The girl was there both days, always alone, always highlighting as though the diagram would eventually confess something. On the fourth day a man with a beret and a chessboard set up at the table by the magazines and waited, and within ten minutes an older woman arrived, unzipped her own board, and they argued over whose to use. This happened every day. Nicolas began to feel like a wildlife observer.

"You're the table guy," the girl said on Friday, when he dropped his charger cord and she caught it before it hit the floor.

"I'm the table guy," he said. "You're the cell girl."

"Mitosis, actually." She capped the highlighter. "My grandmother does the chess thing too. She calls this her office. She retired and couldn't stand the house."

"It's not an office."

"She means it like that. Not home, not work." She shrugged, as though the rest were obvious. "Some sociologist wrote a whole book about it. The Great Good Place, 1989, guy named Ray Oldenburg. He called them third places. Cafes, libraries, wherever people meet outside home and work."

"Third places," Nicolas repeated, and the phrase settled somewhere with the satisfaction of a key fitting a lock that he hadn't known was locked.

He thought about Devon then, about the two of them orbiting a convenience store parking lot for four years, and about how the parking lot had never mattered and had mattered entirely. He had been mourning the wrong thing. It wasn't Devon specifically, though it was also Devon specifically. It was that in the old town he had never once had to build a place to stand; the standing places had been handed to him, pre-made, underpinned by other people's routines. Here nobody's routine included him yet. That was the actual problem, and it was, he noticed with some surprise, a solvable kind of problem, or at least a workable one.

"You want to know something embarrassing?" he said. "I've been telling my mom I come here for the wifi."

"Is that not true?"

"The wifi is bad. The wifi is a lie we tell each other." He felt the grandiose version of the speech forming in his head, something about loneliness and architecture and how cities fail their eighteen-year-olds, and he let it die unspoken, because she had a cell diagram to finish and he had, he realized, a small and sufficient errand. He got up, walked to the magazine table, and stood over the chess game.

The man in the beret glanced up. "You play?"

"Badly," Nicolas said.

"Sit down, then. Ludmila here needs humbling."

"From a child," Ludmila said, already sliding the board to make room.

The girl with the highlighter watched from her table, and Nicolas thought about texting Devon later: found a third place, there's this old woman who trash talks in two languages. His phone stayed in his pocket. He sat, took the white pieces without ceremony, and moved a pawn into the center of the board.

Brayden found the printout folded in his jacket pocket during fourth period, where it had been since his uncle Ray had pressed it on him in the clinic waiting room on Tuesday. His mother was there for her blood pressure, and Uncle Ray had come along because he liked the free coffee, and somewhere between the vending machines and the examination rooms he had produced the article from his coat as though handing over evidence in a trial. "Read that," he had said. "Twelve kids. Twelve, and they wrote it up in that Lancet paper like it was the word of God." Brayden had taken it to be polite, and now, in the back of Ms. Ferreira's classroom, he smoothed it flat under his chemistry binder and looked at it properly for the first time.

The room smelled like the ethanol Ms. Ferreira used to wipe the whiteboards, and the radiator under the window ticked in its slow, patient way. On the front table sat the day's materials: a folder of journal abstracts she had photocopied for their unit on how scientific knowledge actually gets made. Brayden had taken the class because it counted for his last science credit and because the alternative was physics, which he had already survived once. He had not expected the unit to have anything to do with his uncle.

"Okay," Ms. Ferreira said, pulling a stool to the front. "You've all got the abstracts. Three different studies, same question. Talk to each other. I'm going to sit here and drink my coffee and say nothing, which will be harder for me than for you." A few people laughed. She held up her mug as if taking an oath.

Brayden's partner was Priya Raman, who wanted to be an epidemiologist and said so to anyone who would listen, and to several people who would not. She had already spread her three abstracts in a row like playing cards. "So these two find the same thing," she said, tapping two of them, "and this one finds nothing. But it's a bigger sample, so I trust it more, but the other two agree with each other, so." She spread her hands, palms up, the gesture of someone offering a problem rather than a conclusion.

"One study finds something and two don't," Brayden said slowly. He was still thinking about the folded article. "What if there's just one study? Just the one, and it's the only one anybody ever reads?"

"Then you're in trouble," Priya said. "Unless somebody repeats it. That's the whole point, right, that's what she keeps saying. It doesn't count until somebody else does it and gets the same answer, and then somebody else after that." She pulled her sleeve over her wrist, a habit of hers. "Why, do you have a one-study situation?"

He almost said no. Instead he unfolded the article on the table between them, and she leaned in, and he watched her eyes move down the page. "My uncle gave me this at the doctor's office," he said. "It's about that Lancet thing. The vaccine thing. It says twelve children."

Priya sat back. "The Lancet retracted it," she said. "In 2010. Fully retracted. That's not a small thing, they don't do that lightly."

"It doesn't say that in here anywhere."

"No," she said. "It wouldn't, would it."

Brayden turned the page over, then back, as if the retraction might be hiding on the other side of some fold. Twelve children. He had a sudden clear memory of Uncle Ray's face in the clinic's fluorescent light, certain and generous at once, a man handing his nephew a shield. And it occurred to Brayden that he had been halfway to believing it, not because the science was convincing but because Uncle Ray was, and that these were two different kinds of trust and he had been sliding between them without noticing.

He raised his hand, which surprised him. "Ms. Ferreira. What happens to a paper that gets retracted? Does everyone who read it find out?"

She took a long sip of coffee, visibly wrestling with her vow of silence, and lost. "That, Brayden, is one of the best questions in this whole unit, and I'm going to answer it with another question. You found that article somewhere. Is the retraction easier to find or harder to find than the article was?" Then she set the mug down and pointed at the abstracts. "Priya, keep going. You two are circling something."

They worked through the rest of the period. Priya explained peer review the way she explained everything, fast and with her whole face, and Brayden listened while a suspicion assembled itself in him piece by piece: that Uncle Ray was not a liar and not a fool, that he was something harder to be angry at, an apologist for a story he had needed once and could not now put down. Brayden had seen him on the family group chat, patient and then suddenly vitriolic, defending the article against cousins who sent him links. Brayden had scrolled past all of it. He had never once asked where any of it came from.

When the bell rang, Priya packed her cards of abstracts and said, "Look it up tonight. The retraction. Then text me what you find, because if your uncle's version is out there, other people's uncles have it too." She shouldered her bag and was gone into the hallway noise before he could answer.

He walked home the long way, past the clinic, and stood outside it for a minute with his hands in his pockets. His uncle had sat in that waiting room drinking free coffee and being wrong in a way that felt, to him, like love. Brayden could not disabuse him with a fact the way you'd take away a sharp object, and he did not want to ambush him with a link the way the cousins did. He took out his phone and opened a message to Uncle Ray and typed, "Can I ask you something about that article," and then sat on the low wall by the clinic steps, thumb hovering, watching the automatic doors slide open and shut for people going in.

The folded notice sat under the cashbox all morning: debate camp tuition due by five o'clock, and Clara forty dollars short. She had until the afternoon heat died to sell enough lemonade, and between customers she rehearsed the thing that had sunk her interview last week, the question she would get again when she called the camp director at five. How does a central bank raising interest rates slow inflation? She knew the words. She could recite them like a poem and, like a poem, they dissolved the moment anyone looked at her expectantly.

"You're mumbling again," her grandmother said from the porch, shelling peas into a blue bowl. "Your elocution was better when you were eight and charging a quarter."

Clara reset the pitcher, sliced another lemon. "When rates go up, borrowing costs more, so people buy less, so prices stop climbing." She said it to the street, to the mailbox, to a boy on a skateboard who rolled past without stopping. "That's the whole sentence. Why can't I make it land?"

"Because you don't believe it yet," her grandmother said, which Clara thought was unfair, because she did believe it, the way she believed that ionize meant to strip electrons off an atom, a fact she could hold without being able to feel.

At noon Mr. Aldous came down the sidewalk, the retired economics professor from two doors over, impecunious in his frayed canvas shoes but never too poor for a cold drink on a hot day. He counted out coins and then lingered, because he always lingered. Clara braced for a lecture. Instead he pointed at her hand-lettered sign, which read COLD, and asked why she sold only lemonade and not iced tea as well.

"Too much work."

"Suppose it weren't. Suppose you could make both better than the kid on Maple Street makes either one."

"Then I'd outsell him at everything."

"Would you?" Mr. Aldous settled onto the curb. "When you spend your afternoon making tea, what do you give up?"

Clara started to say nothing, then stopped. Lemons. Lemons and time and the customers who wanted lemonade, who were most of them. If she made tea, she gave up a lot of lemonade. If the kid on Maple Street made tea, he gave up very little, because nobody on his street bought lemonade from him anyway. "He loses less by making tea than I do," she said slowly.

Mr. Aldous smiled at the curb.

"So even if I'm better at both, I can't have the advantage in both," Clara said. "It's called comparative advantage, isn't it. A lower cost for one thing means a higher cost for the other, so it evens out." She stood very still, holding the pitcher, and something shifted, not in the facts but underneath them. Being better at everything wasn't the same as being better off doing everything. Everyone was giving something up, always, and the price of what you chose was the thing you didn't.

"Grandma," she called to the porch. "When the central bank raises interest rates, what does borrowing give up?"

Her grandmother looked up from the peas. "It gives up being cheap."

"No, I mean the borrower. What does a person give up when they take a loan now instead of waiting?" The answer assembled itself as she spoke it. The money they would have saved. The cheaper price later, the interest not paid, the other uses of their cash. Borrowing had an opportunity cost too, and the central bank, whatever else it was doing, was turning that dial. Raising rates made the thing people gave up bigger, so more of them waited, and she could see it now as a street of small decisions rather than a sentence to memorize.

"Rate," Mr. Aldous said, raising his paper cup. "One more, and put nothing in the tip jar but your own conviction."

She poured it, and poured three more in the next hour as the heat peaked, and at four forty she counted the cashbox with her grandmother's cool hand steadying her elbow. Forty-six dollars and change. She had enough, barely, if the camp would take cash dropped at the office before five. She also had a question she couldn't answer: whether cooling prices was worth the neighbors who wouldn't borrow this year, and she decided she would say that on the phone, out loud, as part of her answer rather than as a weakness in it.

She carried the cashbox up the porch steps and reached for the phone.

"Dial," her grandmother said.

The book came from the college library downtown, three weeks before Olivia's summer class ended, and she read it in the living room because it was the only room with air conditioning. Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five filters, and Olivia had copied that sentence into her notebook on the bus, the pen jolting against the page. The first filter, the book said, was the ownership of media by large corporations. She had underlined it twice, then felt embarrassed by the underlining and tried to erase one of the lines, which only smeared the paper gray.

Her assignment was to take one local news story and trace it through two outlets. She had chosen the story about the mill closing out past Route 9, four hundred jobs, because her uncle Denny had worked there for eleven years and because both papers had covered it. On the living room carpet she spread the clippings side by side. The Clarion's version ran three paragraphs and led with the company's statement about restructuring. The other paper, the Valley Courier, ran nine paragraphs, named the union rep, printed the number of jobs in the headline. Olivia wrote these observations down. Then she turned the clippings over and looked at the mastheads, and found the Clarion's parent company listed in small type, and looked that company up on her phone, and found that the same corporation also owned the plant's mortgage holder. She sat with that for a while. The ceiling fan clicked on its third rotation, a sound she had never noticed before.

Marcus came over at four with his laptop because they were supposed to draft the piece together. He was the kind of student their teacher called a polymath, the one who had taught himself to suture a wound at fifteen after a cycling accident, and who now kept a first-aid kit in his backpack for other people. He dropped onto the couch and read her notes upside down.

"So you're saying they buried it because of who owns them," he said.

"I'm not saying that," Olivia said. "I'm saying the book's first filter is ownership. I can't prove why the Clarion ran three paragraphs."

"That's a weak thesis."

"It's an honest one."

They argued through the crepuscular hour, the windows going from gold to gray, Marcus tapping the arm of the couch, Olivia refusing to write the sentence he wanted, the one that said the paper had protected its owner. She could not know that. She could only know who owned what, and that the coverage was different, and that the difference had a shape to it.

Across town, in a kitchen that smelled of burned rice, Denny read his niece's text twice. She had sent him the Clarion clipping and asked what he thought of the coverage. He thought about the union rep the Clarion never called, the way the photographer had come to the gate on the last day and taken pictures of the sign and not the men. He thought about telling her all of that. He typed instead that the story was fine, deleted it, typed that the story was fine, and sent it before he could change his mind again. Some things a man carried on his own. His wife watched him set the phone face down next to his plate, and she did not ask, because in eleven years she had learned which silences to leave alone.

Back in the living room, Marcus had given up on the strong thesis and was formatting the citations while Olivia held her phone, her uncle's message open on the screen. "Fine," he had written. Nothing else. She read it the way she had read the mastheads, looking for the small type.

"Marcus," she said. "Two-sentence conclusion. One: the outlets are owned by different companies. Two: the coverage differed. Three: the book's first filter says ownership can shape news, and this story is consistent with that, but it doesn't prove it."

"That's three sentences."

"Fold two into one." She picked up the clipping with the mill gate in it, the workers small in the background, and set it on top of the stack. "I'm keeping the picture, though. The Clarion didn't run this one."

He looked at the photo, then at her, and started typing.

Victor's mother left on Sunday night for a week of night shifts at the hospital, and on the kitchen table she had set down a bank card, a pad of yellow paper, and a sentence she clearly considered sufficient instruction: "Feed yourself." He was sixteen, and until that moment his contribution to the household's food had been locating things in the refrigerator that other people had cooked. The pad of paper looked back at him with the blank patience of an exam he hadn't studied for.

He stood at the counter and tried to introspect, which was a word his English teacher used and which Victor privately suspected meant "staring at a wall with your eyes open." It didn't work on meals. What worked was a list, and what made the list survivable was a plan his mother had once mentioned in passing: cook in batches, eat the same thing twice, buy everything at once so you weren't in the store every day losing money to impulse. He wrote Monday through Sunday down the side of the paper, then, because seven distinct dinners felt like seven separate defeats, wrote "chili" beside two days and "pasta bake" beside two more.

The grocery store on Tuesday afternoon was a landscape he had never properly visited. He had been in it a hundred times, but always downstream of the decisions, grabbing bread his mother had phoned ahead about. Now he stood where the decisions were made. He bought dried beans because they were cheaper than canned, a fact he discovered by standing in the aisle doing arithmetic on his phone, and cumin because the recipe said so, and an onion, and a block of dark chocolate because the same shelf held it and because Saturday was Delia's birthday and he had, three weeks earlier and in a moment he preferred not to examine, volunteered to make her chocolates.

The chili took four hours, mostly because of the beans. He had not known that dried beans needed soaking, and the bag had told him this only after he had already begun. He soaked them overnight, cooked them Wednesday, and ate chili Wednesday and Thursday, and by Thursday he had formed a considered position: batch cooking was less like cooking than like logistics, and logistics rewarded the person who thought ahead and punished the person who merely responded. His mother texted a photo of hospital vending machine noodles at 3 a.m. and the words "you're eating better than me," which he chose to take as a compliment.

The chocolate was the part he had not planned honestly. He had imagined himself Saturday morning pouring neat squares into the silicone mould he'd ordered online, and the mould arriving in a padded envelope with a small insert that said, in four languages, nothing useful. He broke the chocolate into a bowl over simmering water, melted it all the way, stirred in cream because a video had said ganache, and spooned it into the little heart-shaped cavities with the focus of someone defusing something. Then he put the tray in the fridge and went to read about pasta bake.

Two hours later he turned the mould over and tapped it, and nothing happened. He tapped harder. One heart broke at its waist and stayed in the mould, half in, half out, like something alluvial deposited there over geological time. He dug at another with a spoon and it came out smeared, dull, and wrong, its surface bloomed with pale streaks. He stood at the counter holding a ruined heart and felt the specific embarrassment of a person who has claimed a skill in public that he does not hold in private.

He did not call anyone. He looked it up himself, and the looking up was a small humiliation of its own, because the answer was everywhere, and the fact that he hadn't known it made him feel like the last person to arrive at a meeting everyone else had left hours ago. Somewhere in the forums, in a thread from 2017, someone with the username cocoa_mum had written the whole thing in one line: properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould. Victor read it twice. His batch had been melted and poured and never tempered at all, whatever that consisted of, and it had sat in the mould like a tenant who refused to acknowledge the lease had ended.

Finding out what it consisted of took most of Friday evening. He learned to melt most of the chocolate, then take it off the heat and stir in the reserved unmelted chunk until that melted too, and to test a smear on his lower lip, which was cool enough to tell him something, though he wasn't entirely sure what. He worked the bowl with a spatula longer than seemed reasonable. At some point his friend Marcus texted asking if he was coming out, and Victor answered "making chocolate," and Marcus replied with three crying-laughing faces, and Victor put the phone face down without holding a plebiscite on whether it was funny. It was, a little. That wasn't the point.

Saturday morning he filled the mould a second time, set it in the cool of the garage because the kitchen was warm, and waited with the particular discipline of a boy who had already lost once. When he turned the mould over and flexed it, the hearts dropped out one after another onto the plate, glossy and exact, each with a soft click against the ceramic. They had shrunk, just slightly, just enough. He picked one up and turned it in the light. He still couldn't have said why the method worked, only that it had, twice in a row now, the second heart-shaped batch and the fact of it, and that somewhere between the ruined first tray and this plate the difference had been patience he hadn't known he could operate.

Delia arrived at four. He gave her the box, and she opened it, and she said, "You made these?" and Victor, who had prepared several modest and self-deprecating answers, heard himself say, "They're in temper."

"What?"

"The chocolate," he said, and turned the plate toward her. "Listen." He tipped it, and they clicked again against the rim.

Sara spread the towel flat on the sand and weighed its corners with a cooler, a sneaker, and a paperback copy of the oceanography text she was supposed to have finished by now. The morning was already warm, the kind of warm that made the parking lot shimmer, and she had until four o'clock to learn how to explain, out loud, to an actual audience, how greenhouse gases trapped heat and how to read a century of carbon dioxide measurements off a single line. On Monday she had to stand in front of her seminar and teach it for eight minutes. Teaching it was the assignment. Faking her way through it was not allowed.

Marcus arrived with his board under his arm and a folded map in his teeth, which was typical, since he had one want all summer and it was the water. He dropped the board, spat the map into his hand, and knelt beside her.

"Read this to me," he said. "Quiz is Tuesday. If I fail again I have to retake the unit, and my dad said he's not paying for summer school twice, that the first time was supposed to indemnify him against me being lazy. His word."

"You can't be insured against yourself," Sara said, and he laughed, though neither of them was entirely sure it was a joke.

He smoothed the map across the towel. It showed the Atlantic with arrows threading across it, some red, some blue, a few fat and short, some long and skinny. Marcus tapped a long red arrow off the eastern coast.

"So this one's fast," he said. "Red's fast, blue's slow. That's why they're colored like that, right? Like a speedometer."

Sara looked at it. She had been staring at graphs all week, a rising line of carbon dioxide climbing and sawtooth-ing across a hundred years, and she had learned the hard way not to assume what a picture was telling her. Her eyes moved over the arrows. There was a red one crawling down the western side of Africa, slow and wide. There was a blue one running fast up the eastern coast of North America, narrow as a pencil stroke. If red meant fast, the map contradicted itself.

"Wait," she said. She held her finger over the red arrow near Africa. "This one's huge and it's going south. If it were speed, it'd be flying. But it's labeled with temperatures, look, at the edge. Degrees."

Marcus squinted. "So what's the color for?"

"I think it's temperature. On current maps, red arrows are warm currents and blue arrows are cold ones." She said it slowly, testing it against the shapes on the page, and the whole map reorganized itself in her mind like a sentence she'd been misreading. "The colors aren't speed at all. They're warm and cold."

He sat back on his heels. "So I've been studying it wrong for two weeks."

"You've been studying it wrong for two weeks."

"That's why I failed the practice questions." He dragged his hand through his hair, leaving it salty and crooked. "I kept answering how fast the water moved. Okay. Okay, warm red, cold blue. Say it again so I get it stuck."

She said it again, and he repeated it back, and then he made her quiz him, pointing at arrows while a gull screamed over the dunes and the tide chewed steadily at the slope below them. He was quick when he wasn't wrong, which Sara thought was the most frustrating kind of smart.

"Okay, your turn," he said finally. "Teach me the greenhouse thing. I'll be your practice dummy. But make it good, I want to actually get it, not just nod."

Sara took out her printed graph, the long sawtoothed climb, and flattened it on the towel beside the current map so the wind couldn't take it. She began where the book began, that sunlight came through the atmosphere and warmed the ground, and that the ground gave heat back as a different kind of light, and that certain gases let the sunlight in but were much less willing to let the heat out, so the heat lingered. She used the word physiology once, by accident, saying the planet's physiology was the way heat moved through its skin, and then stopped, because it wasn't quite right, and she was honest about that out loud. "Scratch that. It's more like a blanket than a body. I have to pick one and stick with it Monday."

"With the graph," Marcus said, leaning over the printout. "Why does it sawtooth like that, up and down every year, but always climbing?"

"I don't fully know yet," Sara said. "There's a yearly cycle, the teacher said so, something about seasons and plants, but I couldn't explain the mechanism if someone paid me. I'm going to say that part carefully." She traced the long rise with her finger, the line going up and up across the decades. "The main thing is the trend. Whatever the wiggles are doing, the whole thing climbs. It's not flat, and it's not coming down."

Marcus looked at the graph for a while, then out at the water, which was blue and glittering and, she now understood, crossed by currents whose colors on paper had nothing to do with their speed. He stood, picked up his board, and waded in, and Sara stayed on the towel with the two maps side by side, the rising line and the red and blue arrows, rehearsing under her breath. When he caught his first wave and stood up on it, she held the graph above her head so he could see the line climbing even from the water.

Mr. Osei had left the classroom door propped open with a wedge of folded cardboard, and the corridor smell of floor wax drifted in and settled over the desks. Noah sat near the window, where the afternoon light made a long rectangle across his worksheet, and on the worksheet was a chart he did not understand. It was a profile of Kenya, printed from some atlas, two columns of horizontal bars standing back to back like shoulders pressed together, and beneath it the question: Will this country need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years? Explain your reasoning.

He had a reason, and it was wrong. He had decided the wide bars at the top of the chart meant crowds of children, so the answer was schools, plenty of schools, and he had written half a paragraph before Priya leaned over from the next desk and said, "You've got it upside down." He looked at her, then at the chart, then back. "It's a pyramid," he said. "The point goes up."

"Flip it," she said. "Youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top." She tapped the wide base of the shape. "All that is down here. That's the young ones." She was eating a cereal bar in small bites, holding it in her left hand so the fingers of her right stayed clean for her own worksheet. "And males on the left, females on the right, by the way. That part matters if the imbalance is at one age."

Noah erased his paragraph. The rubber smeared graphite into a grey bloom across the paper, and he turned the sheet over and started again on the blank side, because the front was no longer trustworthy. He copied the bars with his pencil, quickly, to feel their shape in his hand: a broad base tapering steeply to a narrow tip, a country stacked with young people at the bottom of the chart and thinning out toward the old ones at the top. Schools, then. Still schools. But now the answer felt different, because he had arrived at it by a road he could see rather than a guess he had dressed up as a guess he hadn't made.

His phone buzzed against his thigh, and he angled it below the desk. A message from his sister Amara, who was on a gap year in Warsaw and owed him letters she never sent.

"Visited a travel agency today to book a bus ticket," she had written. "They had country profiles on the wall, little charts, and I stood there reading one upside down for a full minute before the agent laughed at me. Bars are ages, apparently. Kids at the bottom, grandparents at the top. I felt like an idiot. Also I met a girl who works at a care home and she says they can't fill the jobs. Love you, learn something."

He typed back, "I'm literally learning that exact chart right now," and put the phone face down on his knee. He noticed that his own first mistake, made twenty minutes ago in a classroom, was the same mistake his sister had made in a travel agency in Poland, and that this comforted him in a way he didn't examine too closely. People misread the same things everywhere. The bars ran the way they ran regardless of who was looking.

Priya was working on Japan, her chart an almost perfect rectangle with a slight pinch in the middle. "Nursing homes," she said, not looking up. "Obviously." Mr. Osei passed between the desks with his hands behind his back, paused at her sheet, and said only, "Consider what you might be leaving out," and moved on. Noah watched Pria's jaw tighten. She hated being told to consider things. She began writing fast, and he could see the word migration appear twice, underlined.

That word sat in Noah's mind while he drew his own Kenya again. The bars showed the population as it stood today, stacked youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top, males on the left half and females on the right. But the question asked about thirty years from now, and thirty years from now the children at the base would be the adults in the middle, having or not having children of their own, leaving for Dubai or London or not leaving, and no chart on the page could tell him which. He thought of the care worker in Warsaw who couldn't be replaced, and of his uncle, furloughed from the cement plant two winters ago, who had said at dinner that a man who loses his shift loses his whole shape. He thought about how a population, unlike a fact, was ductile; you could bend it with work or war or a new highway, and it would hold the bend.

He wrote his answer in careful sentences. The base of the pyramid was broad, so schools first, certainly schools. But he added a paragraph beginning "What I cannot know from this chart is," and in it he put migration, and policy, and the possibility that the whole shape could be bent in a decade by decisions nobody had made yet. He did not pretend this was a failure of the chart. He wrote that the chart was honest about the present and silent about the future, and that a person reading it had to admit which half of the question was arithmetic and which half was weather.

When the bell rang, Priya was still writing, and Mr. Osei stood at the doorway collecting nothing, watching them file out. Noah stopped beside him with his worksheet folded once. "I got it backwards at first," he said. "The whole thing. Read it like a tree, oldest rings inside." Mr. Osei took the sheet, glanced at the paragraph that began with what Noah could not know, and handed it back. "Keep that part," he said. "Most people abrogate the uncertainty the moment they find a number that looks solid." Noah slid the paper into his folder, between a history handout and the permission slip for Thursday's trip, and followed the others out into the corridor, where the wax smell was already giving way to rain coming through the open doors.

The classroom above the strip mall smelled of old carpet and burnt coffee, and the radiator had desiccated the air until even the posters on the walls, DRIVING IS A PRIVILEGE NOT A RIGHT, seemed to curl at the corners. Landon sat in the back row with the enrollment form in front of him, reading it more closely than a form probably deserved. Waiver of liability. Terms and conditions. Consent to participate in behind-the-wheel instruction. At the bottom, a line for his signature, and beneath it, a line for a parent or guardian, which his mother had signed that morning in the kitchen, pressing hard enough that the pen had gone through to the counter.

He had never thought about how much of driving school was paperwork before you touched a wheel. You could not simply learn to drive; you had to agree, in writing, to what driving was. The instructor, a dour man named Mr. Reyes who wore his laminated certification badge like a piece of evidence, collected the forms one by one and checked each signature against a roster. When he reached Landon he paused, tapped the guardian line twice, and said, "Tell your mother the ink bled through." Then he moved on.

Under the desk, Landon's phone buzzed. A message from Deshawn: got the lease, read page 6, tell me if I'm crazy. Attached was a photograph of a lease agreement, the apartment on Fairmount where Landon and Deshawn and Priya had planned to live starting in September, if they could sign by Friday at five, because the manager had two other groups asking. Landon had skimmed it once at Deshawn's kitchen table, mostly looking at the rent number, which had seemed fine when divided by three.

Mr. Reyes dimmed the lights and began the first module, right-of-way, but Landon turned his phone sideways under the desk and enlarged the photograph. Page six. He read the paragraph twice. Each tenant shall be jointly and severally liable for the full amount of rent and any damages. He mouthed the words. Jointly he understood. Severally was the one that snagged, and he looked it up on the dictionary app with the brightness turned low, feeling faintly like he was cheating at something.

He read the definition, then the clause, then the definition again, and felt the rent number change shape in his head. It was not divided by three at all. Each of them could be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share. If Deshawn lost his job, or Priya's transfer fell through, the landlord could come to Landon for the whole rent, every month, alone.

"Now," Mr. Reyes said, and the lights came up. "Who can tell me what a waiver actually waives?" Nobody raised a hand. "You signed one this morning. You agreed to it. Did any of you read it?" A boy in the second row said he had read most of it. Mr. Reyes studied him. "Most of it. Interesting. The parts you skipped are the parts that matter to the person who wrote them." He said it without heat, the way someone says something they have said four hundred times, and Landon found himself raising his hand, which he almost never did.

"The liability part," he said. "If something happens in the car, the school's saying we agreed not to hold them responsible for certain things. We consented in advance." Mr. Reyes considered this, then nodded once. "Contracts are just promises with teeth," he said, and moved on to right-of-way at uncontrolled intersections, and Landon wrote nothing for a while because he was thinking about teeth.

He was thinking, specifically, about two pictures of the same idea that did not quite match. His mother signed the school form in one second, trusting the school, trusting him, trusting the general decency of institutions. Mr. Reyes's whole manner, and the paragraph about waivers, suggested the opposite: that institutions prepare for people to fail each other, and that the paper exists because someone, once, did. Which picture was truer? He did not know. Maybe both, depending on the institution, depending on the person. During the break he texted Deshawn and Priya a single question: can we meet at the apartment before five?

They sat on the floor of the empty Fairmount unit because the manager had no chairs yet, the lease between them on the hardwood. Priya had done her own reading on the bus and had the same expression Landon suspected he'd had, the expression of a number rearranging itself. "So if one of us bails," Deshawn said slowly, "the other two could get stuck with everything. Not two-thirds. Everything." Landon said that was how he read it, and that he was not a lawyer, and that they should probably ask somebody who was, except it was four-forty and the manager was tapping her pen at the door.

"We could ask for separate leases," Priya said. "Or a cosigner. Or we could sign it anyway because we trust each other, and that's a nice thing to do, and it's also exactly what the clause is for, people who trusted each other." Deshawn laughed once, without much humor in it. The manager called from the doorway that she needed an answer. Landon looked at the signature lines, three of them, blank and evenly spaced, and picked up the pen, and then set it down again.

Brandon spread the textbook on the picnic table and pinned it open with two rocks from the flowerbed, because the August wind kept flipping the pages back to glycolysis as if the chapter itself wanted him to start over. Tomorrow was the placement exam, the one that would decide whether he entered freshman biology or spent a semester in remedial science, and though he had told his mother it didn't matter either way, he had not believed himself when he said it.

He read the pathway aloud, half to the yard and half to nobody: glucose, broken in the cytoplasm, pyruvate carried inward, the citric acid turning and turning and yielding almost nothing he could hold onto. The words slid past him the way names did on the first day of a job. Somewhere in there, at the end of all of it, sat the mitochondria, and inside them a thing the book called the electron transport chain, and beyond that a molecule called ATP, and the exam expected him to trace the whole route from sugar to energy without once getting lost.

The problem was that he had never been good at this and had chosen it anyway. Last spring, when his counselor asked why he wanted to switch from the vocational track to pre-med, he had said something about liking science, which was only partly true. He liked the idea of it, the way it dichotomized the world into things you could verify and things you merely believed, and after his junior year, when his father's diagnosis had come and gone in a blur of words like "idiopathic," he had wanted to live somewhere that words had to prove themselves. Whether that was a real reason or an extrinsic one, a story he told to make the choice look noble, he still couldn't say.

A screen door banged and Deja came out carrying two glasses of lemonade, ice already melting fast in the heat. She had been his lab partner in the one honors class he'd risked, and she was starting at the state university in nine days, and she had agreed to quiz him today mostly, he suspected, so they would have one more afternoon before everything scattered. She sat on the table's edge, set the glasses down, and said, "Okay. Glucose goes in. Then what."

He got as far as the inner membrane and stalled. Deja didn't prompt him. She watched a june bug crawl along the table's splintered rim with the patience of someone who had learned, in a year of shared labs, to let him find his own way out of a silence. And in the silence he was suddenly not in the backyard at all but at the science museum in sixth grade, the one field trip his father had chaperoned before the diagnosis, standing in front of a giant plastic enzyme with a rotor in the middle. The placard had said ATP synthase. A guide had spun the rotor with his hand, and the other kids had gotten bored and wandered toward the dinosaur hall, but Brandon had stayed, and his father had stayed with him, reading the little sign twice through his glasses.

"Protons," Brandon said now, slowly. "Protons flow through it, through ATP synthase, and they make part of the enzyme spin. Like a motor. It actually spins, and the spinning is what builds the ATP." He heard how it sounded, like a claim a person should be embarrassed to make about something smaller than a cell, and Deja laughed, but not at him. She said, "Yes. It's literally a rotary motor. That's the part everyone gets wrong on the exam, they think it's just a metaphor." She drew it on a napkin with a pencil stub from her shirt pocket, a lollipop shape with a hole through the stem and an arrow showing the protons pouring through, and the rotor turning, and the ATP coming off the top.

What struck him, sitting there with the wind riffling the napkin's edge, was that his two versions of the world, the one he wanted to save for and the one his father had stood beside him in, had stopped being opposites the moment he said the sentence out loud. He had spent a year trying to dichotomize them less, and here the work was already done for him: the motor was real, verifiable, and it was also the most beautiful thing he had ever been asked to memorize. His discernment, such as it was, told him that the first thing he'd loved about science was not the rigor but the spinning model with his father's breath fogging the glass case, and that both of those could be true, and that he could not yet tell which one would still be there in November.

Deja was saying something about the shuttle proteins, and he turned the napkin over and asked her to start again from glucose, and he went through the whole path twice, all the way to the little motor at the end. When she left at dusk, she took the textbook but left him the napkin, folded into his shirt pocket without comment. Later, in the kitchen light spilling across the grass, he unfolded it by the picnic table and looked at the lollipop shape, then noticed, for the first time, in his father's handwriting in the bottom corner, small and faded, three words he had no memory of the man putting there: held up fine.

Adam had commandeered the corner table by the periodicals at three-fifteen, before the after-school crowd could claim it, and he spread his notes across it like a general planning a campaign he did not yet understand. The assignment sheet sat at the top: a historiographical essay, two thousand words, tracing how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. He had written the word historiography on a sticky note and stuck it to his laptop, partly as decoration, partly as a threat.

"You're in my spot," said Priya, arriving with a stack of books and an expression that suggested she had been rehearsing the line since second period.

"There are no spots. It's a library. There's just furniture."

"There are spots, and this is mine, and you know it." She set her books down on the far edge of his territory and sat, which was as good as a treaty. She was writing about the Haitian Revolution for the same class, and for weeks they had been conducting a low-grade competition over who could find the more obscure source, a competition neither of them had acknowledged aloud.

His real problem was simpler and worse: the essay required him to identify the moment when historians first seriously challenged the Marxist view of the Revolution, and he did not know when that was. He knew the Marxist view well enough, the bourgeois revolution against a feudal order, the class engine underneath the politics. He knew people had argued against it. He did not know who had fired the first real shot, and without that, his whole structure collapsed into a list of opinions arranged by date, which was the thing Mr. Okonkwo kept warning against. "A list is not an argument," Mr. Okonkwo had said, with the weary patience of a man who had read four hundred lists.

Adam pulled the stack of photocopied journal articles toward him and began skimming for names that recurred. Lefebvre appeared everywhere, Soboul almost as often, both cited as the orthodoxy, the social interpretation, the classic account. Then a footnote in a 1980s article caught his eye: it referred back to "Cobban's celebrated inaugural lecture," and when Adam checked the citation at the bottom of the page, the details assembled themselves like a combination lock giving way. Alfred Cobban, 1954, University College London, delivered as an inaugural lecture and published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution. The article called it an attack on the Marxist social interpretation, and suddenly every later revisionist essay he had skimmed made sense as an echo of that one moment.

He sat back. On the other side of the table, Priya was squinting at a map of Saint-Domingue and mouthing dates to herself. He watched her draw a small frustrated circle around a plantation name, cross it out, and try again.

"That table lamp's flickering on your side," he said. "Want to swap seats?"

"It flickered once. In September." But she gathered her pens and moved around the table anyway, and he noticed she took the article he had just finished, the one he'd set aside, and squared it into her pile without asking. He let her. He understood the code: an exchange of small courtesies licensed an exchange of larger ones.

"Did you know," he said, "that the first serious challenge to the whole Marxist reading was one lecture?"

Priya looked up. "Whose?"

"A guy named Alfred Cobban. 1954, his inaugural lecture at University College London. It got published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution. He attacked the Marxist social interpretation right there, in front of everybody, at his own inaugural."

"Bold way to start a job."

"Right? You get the chair and immediately you torch the field." She laughed, a real one, loud enough that the librarian glanced over with a look that seemed almost atavistic, some ancient ancestral displeasure at noise near books. Priya apologized with a wave.

From where she now sat, closer to the window, Priya watched Adam work differently than he had worked all week. Earlier he had hunched over summaries, hoarding facts. Now he was building, moving articles around the table like pieces, writing in the margin of his outline a line that read, in his cramped hand, "Before Cobban: social explanation dominant. After: questions of politics, culture, contingency." He stopped, crossed out "dominant," and wrote "persuasive," then crossed that out too.

"What's wrong with persuasive?"

"Nothing's wrong with it. It's just doing too much work. Saying one view was persuasive isn't the same as saying it was the only one." He turned the outline so she could see. "That's the thing I keep almost getting. Cobban broke the automatic link between class and event, but that doesn't mean class stopped mattering. It means historians had to argue for it instead of assuming it. So my essay can't be 'Marxists wrong, revisionists right.' It has to be, the ground shifted, and here's what each side saw that the other missed." He tapped the page. "And I still don't know what I think about the Terror. Whether it was inherent in the Revolution or a response to war. I've read four people and they all sound right."

"That's going to be a short conclusion."

"It'll be an honest one." He said it lightly, but he kept the sentence.

The library was emptying. Priya packed her bag, then slid the borrowed article back across the table to him, aligned with his stack, and pointed at his cold coffee. "Bin's behind the biography shelf," she said. He carried the cup over, and when he came back he wrote a new opening line at the top of his outline: In 1954, at University College London, Alfred Cobban stood up to deliver his inaugural lecture and dismantled the ruling interpretation of the French Revolution. He underlined "stood up" twice, then sat down himself and kept writing.

The trail climbed out of the parking lot through a stand of boreal spruce, dark and resinous, the kind of woods that held its cold an hour after the fields below had warmed. Alexis walked behind his father and ahead of Marcus, who was telling them, again, about the house he'd closed on two days ago. "Three bedrooms, and the yard goes right down to the water," Marcus said. "You can hear the river from the porch."

Alexis had his tablet zipped into the front of his pack, and in his head he had the deadline. The city council had opened a comment period on the riverside rezoning, and it closed at five o'clock tonight. His geography teacher had not assigned it; she had merely mentioned it, and Alexis had decided that if he was going to learn to use the mapping software properly, he ought to use it on something real. By noon he had pulled the floodplain layer over the parcel map of the city, color-coded so that anything with a yearly flood chance of one percent showed up green. Then Marcus had called, wanting company on the hike, and Alexis had brought the tablet along with the plan of finishing his comment at the summit, where there was supposed to be signal.

"How far to the top?" Marcus asked, ducking under a dead limb.

"Forty minutes, maybe," Alexis's father said. "Less if you stop narrating the house."

Marcus laughed, but Alexis noticed how he described it. The river as an amenity. The porch. The price per square foot, which was, Alexis had thought even then, suspiciously good.

They stopped at a granite shelf where the trees opened. Wind moved through the spruce with a sound like distant surf, and Alexis took out the tablet, shielding the screen glare with his jacket. The overlay was all there, the layers cached offline: parcels, flood zones, and a third layer he'd added himself, median income by block, because he wanted to see not just where the water would go but who would be standing in it. He worked the zoom with two fingers until the map found the river's southern bend, and there, outlined in green, was the new subdivision. He tapped the parcel records and read the owner's name. He read it twice.

"What are you doing up here, anyway?" his father asked, crouching beside him. "You've been staring at that thing since the car."

"School thing," Alexis said. He angled the screen away, casual, though his pulse had picked up. The parcel database was public, but it still felt like reading someone's mail. He pulled up the comment draft and typed fast, the cold making his fingers clumsy. One bar of signal flickered at the top of the screen and then vanished, like something surfaced from deep water and gone again.

"Let the boy breathe," Marcus said, dropping onto the granite with a granola bar. "Tell me about this school thing, though. You're mapping floods? They teach you that in tenth grade now?"

Alexis looked at him. Marcus was forty-three, had spent his savings on the down payment, and was unwrapping his granola bar with the untroubled contentment of a man who believes his luck has finally turned. Alexis thought about what his grandfather used to say, that school should inculcate not just facts but the habit of checking them. He had always found the phrase stiff. Now he understood it as a kind of mercy, or a kind of cruelty, depending on which side of the check you were standing.

"It's not really floods," Alexis said. "It's odds." He turned the tablet so Marcus could see the green polygons riding the river. "A home with a one percent yearly flood chance has about a twenty-six percent chance of flooding at least once during a thirty-year mortgage." He said it evenly, the way you'd read a weather report, and watched Marcus's jaw slow on the granola bar.

"Twenty-six," Marcus repeated. "That's over the whole mortgage."

"That's over thirty years. And you got a thirty-year, right?" Alexis didn't wait for the answer. He pulled the signal meter up again. Nothing. The comment box sat on the screen, cursor blinking after the sentence about the southern bend, which he had not yet typed. He could submit it without the parcel name. He could submit it with it. His father was watching him now too, having gone quiet in a way that Alexis recognized from arguments at the dinner table, the way his father went quiet when he wanted Alexis to arrive somewhere on his own.

Alexis typed the name of the subdivision. He typed that the city's own data placed it inside the one percent zone, and that the people buying there were, on the block-level income layer, measurably poorer than the people on the hillside two miles north. He did not type Marcus's name. He did not know yet whether that was honesty or cowardice, whether the veracity of a public record was worth more than the privacy of a friend, and the comment box waited under his hands like a question with more than one right answer. Two bars of signal appeared, held. His thumb hovered over submit. Marcus leaned over and read the screen upside down, and after a long moment, in a voice Alexis hadn't heard from him before, said, "Press it."

The laminated menu at Marisol's had a coffee ring on it shaped, Rebecca decided, like Portugal, and she kept rotating it while she read the article for the fourth time. The article was Spanish, from a paper in Seville, about a city council debating whether to grant amnesty to shopkeepers who had occupied an abandoned market building for six years. Her college required a language placement test in August. Her debate coach had told her, more or less, that reading aloud was the only way to make a language live in your mouth instead of your head, so here she was, at the corner table by the window, muttering at a newspaper.

"¿Más café?" The waitress, Doris, was maybe twenty-five and had already corrected Rebecca's pronunciation twice, once with great gentleness and once laughing so hard she had to hold the coffee pot with both hands.

"Sí, por favor. And also." Rebecca turned the paper around. "I have to summarize this. Out loud. In Spanish, then in English, without looking. For my placement prep."

"Then you will need more than coffee," Doris said, and poured.

The trouble was that Rebecca could summarize in English forever. She had spent four years on the debate team building arguments like walls, brick on brick, and she knew exactly how a wall went up. She could still hear her coach at the state semifinal last spring, leaning over the flow pad: "You've got the logic, Reyes, but you're arguing at a jury made of computers." In the flashback she'd rolled her eyes at him. Now, seven weeks from a campus where nobody knew her, the memory sat differently, the way a song you skipped in June becomes, by August, the only one you can hear.

She tried the summary anyway, staring at the sugar dispenser as though it might prompt her. "El consejo, uh, debate. The council debates amnesty for the shopkeepers, porque the building, la edificio, is..." She lost the thread, found it, lost it again. "They are not destitute, exactly, but the article says some are. The reporter says the city should not, no debe, historicize the occupation, should not treat it like a piece of the past in a museum, because people still work there."

Doris set down the pot and folded her arms, which was either judgment or interest. "That part was good. The last part."

"The grammar or the idea?"

"The idea. The grammar was a crime scene."

Rebecca laughed despite herself, and something about the laugh loosened the knot she'd been carrying since she'd opened the paper. Because she realized, mid-chuckle, what had been bothering her about the summary. She had explained what the article said the way she always explained things: reasons, evidence, a clean line from claim to conclusion. If the shopkeepers had stood up at that council meeting and argued the way Rebecca summarized, listing clauses like ingredients, nobody would have moved. But the article quoted one shopkeeper, a woman named Pilar, who had only said that her daughter had learned to walk between the stalls. That was the sentence the reporter had chosen to end on. Not the zoning law. Not the six years.

"Okay," Rebecca said slowly, "this is going to sound like a class I'm not taking yet. Aristotle. Three means of persuasion." Doris raised an eyebrow and said nothing, which Rebecca took as permission. "Ethos, that's the speaker's credibility. Pathos, the audience's emotions. Logos, the logic of the argument." She tapped the newspaper with each word like she was dealing cards. "My whole summary was logos. Just logos. Pilar's one line was pathos, and it probably did more than the council's whole file of documents."

"And ethos?" Doris said. "You said three."

"I don't know. Hers, maybe. Six years in the building. You can't fake six years."

Doris considered this while wiping a table that was already clean. "So for your test, you will say the facts, but also you will say the woman's daughter learned to walk there."

"Maybe." Rebecca turned her cup in its saucer. She wasn't sure, honestly, whether a placement test wanted Pilar or wanted clauses, whether a summary was supposed to have a heartbeat or just a skeleton. Maybe both. Maybe the summary in Spanish would be clumsy no matter what she did, her accent a crime scene for another month, and the best she could hope for was that the ideas arrived dented but recognizable. What she did know, with a certainty that surprised her, was that the next time she built an argument, she would count the walls and find only one, and she would look for the other two on purpose, even if she couldn't always tell where logic ended and feeling began.

She spread the paper flat, took a breath that fogged the window for a second, and started over, slower this time, saying the woman's sentence first: "Su hija aprendió a caminar entre los puestos."

"There," Doris said. "Now more coffee."

The signup table stood between a folding chair and a dumpster, which struck Eve as either ironic or efficient, depending on how charitable she felt. She had chosen the neighborhood cleanup because the email said food bank volunteers were needed, and because her mother had said the words "college applications" twice in one dinner. She was honest enough with herself to admit that this was the reason she had come. She was honest enough to admit that she didn't know yet whether it would stay the reason.

The basement of the community center smelled of cardboard and disinfectant. A woman named Doris handed her a hairnet and a box cutter and put her to work sorting dented cans, which turned out to have rules: bulging out, throw away; dented seam, throw away; dented side, fine. Two teenage boys, Amadou and his brother, worked the conveyor beside her, and Doris's nephew Dev took photographs for the center's newsletter, an acolyte of good works with a camera around his neck. Eve found herself enjoying the rhythm of it, the small verdicts, each can guilty or innocent of something she could actually see.

Around eleven, a woman came down the stairs carrying four crates of bread, baguettes and focaccia still warm enough that Eve could smell the rosemary. She set them down by the door rather than on the table, like someone delivering evidence rather than a gift. Her apron said SANTOS on it in faded thread.

"Mrs. Santos," Doris said, "you came."

"I came to look. I'm not leaving anything until I understand what happens to me if somebody gets sick." Mrs. Santos folded her arms. "My lawyer friend says one lawsuit and I lose the restaurant. I have three people on payroll. I bake too much on Fridays because people don't show up to pick up their orders, and it's hedonistic, honestly, the waste. But I can't hand out food that ruins me."

Eve expected Doris to argue back, to say something about neighbors or shame. Instead Doris turned to the volunteer sign-in sheet and flipped it over, where someone had photocopied a page from something official and taped it crookedly. Eve was close enough to read it before Doris found the line with her finger. The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996. She read further, over Doris's shoulder, feeling a little like a sneak: the act gives food donors limited protection from liability, which is what encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.

"It's a federal law," Doris said, tapping the page. "Named after a congressman. Limited protection, not unlimited, but it's there so people like you can donate without being afraid."

Mrs. Santos read it herself, twice, mouthing the words. "Limited," she said. "What's the limit?"

"I'm not a lawyer," Doris said, "but it's been enough for Katz's Deli and the pancake place on ninth, and they've been donating for years."

The basement got quiet in the way it does when someone is deciding something expensive. Eve realized she wanted the woman to leave the bread with an intensity that surprised her, wanted it more than she had wanted anything since arriving. She thought about mentioning the rosemary smell, the focaccia, how the volunteers at noon would take it in their lunch break and say her name. She didn't say any of that. It wasn't her bread to be generous with.

"Was it a good lawyer, your friend?" Eve asked.

Mrs. Santos looked at her. "He does divorces."

"Maybe he doesn't do food."

Mrs. Santos laughed, one syllable, and then she stopped laughing and looked at the crates for a long moment. "My mother ran that kitchen before me," she said. "She sent the day-old bread home with her workers in paper bags. Nobody ever sued her, but nobody ever told her it was safe, either. She just did it because it was wrong to throw it out." She bent and picked up a crate and set it on the table, then the second, then the third, then the fourth. She wrote her name on the donation sheet in careful cursive and underlined it.

Doris put Eve on bread duty, bagging rolls in groups of six, and Mrs. Santos stayed to help, telling Eve that focaccia was a Sunday thing, that baguettes sold worse in summer, that Eve's hairnet made her look like a surgeon. Amadou, working faster now that the conveyor held fresh bread, asked Mrs. Santos if she'd bring the same next Friday, and Mrs. Santos said she'd bring more, and then corrected herself: she'd bring the same, because she couldn't promise more, and Doris said the same was plenty.

Eve walked home at one with a bag of rolls she'd been offered and had nearly refused, thinking about the photocopied page taped crookedly to the back of a sign-in sheet, and about the fact that Mrs. Santos's generosity and her caution had both been real, and that the law hadn't made her generous, only made it possible for her to be. Whether that was the same thing Eve couldn't decide, and she carried the question along with the warm bag all the way to her building, up the stairs, and through the door, where her mother looked up from the table and said, "You smell like a bakery."

Oliver pulled the roasting pan from the oven at four minutes past five, holding it in folded towels the way his mother used to hold his sister when she was small, close and careful, and set it on the stovetop. The thermometer in his phone app said the beef had hit 125 degrees, exactly the number the recipe called for, and he felt something in his chest loosen for the first time since Tuesday.

His sister Nadia sat at the counter with her chemistry homework, watching him with the dour expression she had worn since the custody schedule was finalized. "You're doing Dad's recipe," she said.

"I'm doing a recipe." He slid the probe out and covered the roast with foil. "Sit down. It'll be ten minutes."

"Since when do you cook?"

Since their father's Sunday dinners stopped existing, he didn't say. Since their mother's new shift schedule left the kitchen empty at the hour it used to smell like rosemary. Instead he washed his hands and began the potatoes, and the two of them worked in the silence of people who used to talk more.

The ten minutes passed. When Oliver carved into the roast, the center had gone from the pink he'd aimed at to a flat, uniform gray-brown, and the juices ran thin instead of gathering dark on the board. Nadia leaned over his shoulder. "That's overcooked."

"I took it out at exactly the right temperature." He said it flatly, defensive, and then hated the sound of it. He sat down on the kitchen stool and looked at the app again, at the graph of the temperature over time, as if the numbers owed him an apology.

Then he remembered his father, one Sunday last spring, pulling a rib roast out early while their mother protested it was still cold inside. Dad, it's raw. No, it's resting. Oliver had thought it was superstition then, the kind of kitchen folklore adults passed around like weather predictions. Now he typed into his phone with his thumb: why did roast overcook after leaving oven.

The result came up fast. He read it twice, then a third time, because it contradicted something he'd believed about cooking all evening. "It's called carryover cooking," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "The food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat. A big roast like this can go up several degrees while it rests."

"So the recipe was wrong?"

"The recipe was right and I was wrong." He turned the phone so she could see the page. "It gave me the target temperature. It didn't tell me to stop before the target. I hit 125 in the oven, and then the resting did the rest of it." He laughed once, short and not quite amused. "I interpolated. I took the number I was given and filled in everything around it with my own assumptions."

Nadia pulled the phone closer and read for a while. "So next time you take it out low and let it climb."

"Next time." He looked at the gray meat on the board, at the foil still holding a little trapped heat, and thought about how he had watched the app climb toward 125 with such certainty, such trust in the single number, and how the whole time the roast had been carrying its own arithmetic forward without him.

Their mother came in at six, coat still on, and stopped at the smell of it. "You cooked."

"Dad's roast," Nadia said, before Oliver could stop her, and their mother's face did something complicated that settled into a careful neutral.

"It came out overcooked," Oliver said, standing. "First attempt. I'll get it right."

They ate anyway, the three of them, at the table with the good cloth that hadn't come out since spring. The meat was dry and Nadia drowned hers in horseradish, and their mother said it was good twice, the second time more sincerely, and Oliver found that being angry at a fact was useless in a way being angry at a person wasn't. A roast wasn't trying to deceive him. It just kept going after he thought he was finished with it.

"So you'd take it out at like 118," Nadia said, fork in the air, working it through. "And trust the rest."

"Trust the rest," Oliver said. "Which is, I know, basically an oxymoron coming from me." He'd spent four months refusing to trust anything that happened after things ended, after the boxes were packed, after his father's apartment stopped feeling like a place they were visiting and started feeling like the other half of their lives.

Later, alone in the kitchen, he wrapped the leftovers and set the app to build a graph for next Sunday: pull temperature 118, projected climb of several degrees, resting time twenty minutes. The projection line rose gently after the oven went dark, the way nothing in his life had been allowed to lately. He looked at it for a long moment, then typed a title at the top of the screen. Attempt two.

The debate tournament shared its building with the theater program, which was how Andrew ended up holding a script in the black box room while sixty debaters argued about jurisprudence two hallways away. He had come to compete, but his partner had the flu, and Ms. Okafor from drama had cornered him near the sign-in table: their student director for the one-act was suspended, the performance was in two weeks, and Andrew, who had done lights for the fall play, was apparently the only person in the building who knew where the board was. He said yes before he had decided to.

The cast was three people: Priya, who talked fast when she was nervous; Marcus, who was calm the way a lake is calm before something drops into it; and a sophomore named Dani who had never performed anywhere. They stood in a loose clump on the stage, scripts rolled in their fists, waiting for him to know what to do. He did not know what to do. He had watched directors work for years and had absorbed nothing except that they said things like "hold that beat" and drank a lot of coffee.

"Okay," he said. "Scene one. Priya, you enter from, uh, the left, and Marcus, you're at the table." Priya walked toward the table from stage right, crossing the whole playing area to get there, and stood behind Marcus's chair looking faintly betrayed. Andrew blinked. He had said left. She had gone right. "No, your left," he started, and then stopped, because she had gone to her own left and that was somehow the wrong direction anyway, and he could feel Marcus watching him work this out in real time.

Marcus set his script down. "Stage left," he said. "That's what it's called." He pointed across the stage. "Stage left and stage right, they're from the actor's point of view, facing the audience.
