His older sister, Nadia, knocked twice and came in without waiting, the way she always did. She was home from her first semester for the weekend, and she wanted something; he could tell from the way she leaned against the doorframe instead of sitting. "You doing it?" she asked. He said he was reading first. She picked up the privacy sleeve and turned it over in her hands. "Good. You're actually reading it. Dad voted for a school board guy once because the name sounded familiar."

"Did you know the ballot has a name?" Luca said. "It's called the Australian ballot. Tasmania and Victoria, 1856." Nadia raised her eyebrows. "You're going to be insufferable in college," she said, but she smiled when she said it, and then her face went serious again, which was the real reason she had come in. "Mom's downstairs telling Aunt Reza you're voting the right way. Like it's settled." She put the sleeve down. "I just thought you should know she's saying that."

Luca looked at the screen, at the wooden booth, at the date. He thought about the secrecy he had been reading about, the long argument it must have taken to make it law, the whole apparatus of sleeves and envelopes and unmarked folds, all of it built so that no one could ever do what his mother was doing downstairs: assuming his vote, spending it in advance on a phone call. At the same time he thought about her taped-up articles, some of which he had actually read, some of which had been fair. The challenger had taken money from a developer whose project the town had voted down; that part was true even if her acerbic posts about him made everything sound worse than the records showed. Both things were true at once. He did not have a word for that, and he did not need one.

His mother came up while Nadia was still there. She stood in the doorway with her tea and looked at the ballot pages lying flat on the desk. "You want help with the judges?" she asked. "Those races are impossible." He said he had the sample ballot open in another tab. She came closer, close enough to see the screen, and he watched her eyes move from the history site to the blank card pages to his hands. "You know," she said, "I'd feel better if I knew you weren't wasting this. People fought for this."

"People fought for the part where you don't get to know," Luca said.

She stared at him. "I'm not the enemy, Luca. Don't act like I'm the enemy just because that candidate has spent a year trying to vilify everyone who questions him." Her voice had gone quiet, which was worse than loud. Nadia slipped past her into the hall. His mother stayed a moment longer, and then she said something he had not expected, so quietly he almost missed it: "You know I've never actually missed one. Since I was twenty. My mother couldn't. It wasn't that kind of country." She picked a thread off her sleeve, an encumbrance she'd worn all day and only now noticed. "I just want to see it filled in. Not how. Just filled in."

After she went down, Luca sat for a while with his hand flat over the ballot pages. Then he picked up the pen, marked the races one by one, some the way his mother would have, some not, and slid the card into the sleeve. He carried it to the top of the stairs and held it up so it caught the light from the kitchen, and called, "It's filled in."

The museum's French Revolution wing smelled like dust and radiator heat, and Jordan had been standing in front of a diorama of the storming of the Bastille for ten minutes without writing anything. His essay was due Monday. Not a report on the Revolution, his teacher had said, but a historiographical essay: an essay about the historians, about how views of 1789 had shifted since 1800, and why. He had three pages of quotations from Carlyle and Aulard and Simon Schama, and no idea what any of it added up to.

He moved to a glass case holding a small printing press, the label explaining that pamphlets had spread revolutionary ideas faster than the authorities could suppress them. That was the kind of detail his paper was full of, and the kind his teacher kept crossing out. This is about events, not historians, she had written in the margin of his draft, in green ink. He needed perspectives, arguments, revisions. He needed, apparently, to care about who had told the story and what they wanted.

His grandfather had offered to pick him up at four, which gave Jordan two hours. He sat on a bench beneath a portrait of some deputy in a grandiose collar and opened his notebook. The early writers after 1800 had mostly mourned or celebrated, depending on which side their families had been on. Later, Marxists read the Revolution as a bourgeois seizure of power. Later still, revisionists questioned whether anything so tidy had happened at all. He wrote the sentences and they felt like inventory, a warehouse of opinions with no one inside them.

At four his grandfather was early, waiting in the lobby with his coat still buttoned. On the drive home he asked what Jordan had found, and Jordan admitted the problem: every historian seemed certain, and they all disagreed. His grandfather laughed and said that was the point, that he'd written a paper like that himself once, in 1960, his second year of college.

"You wrote about historians?" Jordan asked.

"About the Cold War. There was a book the year before, 1959, William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy. Started the whole revisionist school." His grandfather changed lanes, unhurried. "Williams argued that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War."

Jordan stared at him. "An American blamed the United States?"

"That's what the book said."

"Was he right?"

His grandfather didn't answer for a long moment. "People argued about it for twenty years. Some of them still do."

When they got to the house, Jordan followed him inside, essay forgotten. The book itself was gone, sold in a move decades ago, but his grandfather remembered the fight it started in his seminar, how half the room thought Williams had committed treason against history and the other half thought he'd finally told the truth. Jordan sat at the kitchen table taking notes on a napkin. What struck him was not who was right. It was that Williams had looked at the same documents everyone else had, the same speeches and cables, and seen something different, and that the difference had lasted, had forced every historian after him to say where they stood.

That night he spread his sources across his desk. The Marxists had a framework, the revisionists had a corrective, the early memoirists had their wounds. He began a new draft arguing that each generation's account of the Revolution told him as much about the generation as about the Revolution, and that the honest move was not to pick a winner but to say plainly what each view revealed and concealed. He could see, dimly, where this left him: with an essay that ended in uncertainty. His teacher might call that a failure to conclude. He kept typing anyway.

At one in the morning his cursor sat blinking after the last sentence, which was about how the historiography had no ending, only revisions. He read it twice. Then he opened his phone and texted his grandfather: was there ever a book that settled it? He waited, watching the screen. The reply came as a photo, the napkin from the kitchen table, on which his grandfather had written a single word, underlined twice. Jordan leaned closer to make it out.

Liam had cleared the coffee table of his mother's catalogs and set out six folding chairs like a tiny theater, which meant the living room now smelled of popcorn because Dex had brought a bag and refused to eat it anywhere but the "audience." The assignment was a ten-minute play about a moment from their own lives, due Friday, and Liam had chosen the night his father missed his regional swim final because of a work call. He had written three drafts, and each one had a letter in the first scene, a letter his father left on the kitchen counter saying he'd be home late, a real letter, laminated in Liam's memory.

"Okay," he said, standing on the hearth like it was a stage. "Read-through. Priya, you're Dad. Dex, you're the letter."

"I'm a prop," Dex said, delighted. "I've always wanted to be a prop."

Priya held the pages at arm's length the way she held everything, as though the world were slightly suspicious of her. She read the first scene with surprising tenderness, and Dex performed the letter by waving it over his head, and by scene three the swim final had happened and the father had apologized and the lights, per Liam's stage directions, went "dim, like a pool at night."

Then Priya lowered her script. "The letter."

"What about the letter?"

"It shows up in scene one, big dramatic close-up, Dad practically setting it on fire with his eyes, and then it never comes back. Why is it there?"

Liam opened his mouth and closed it. He picked up Dex's popcorn and ate some, thinking. "It's realistic. Dads leave letters."

"It's a play," Priya said. "Nothing on a stage is just realistic. A table read isn't life, it's life with the boring parts cut out." She flipped back a page. "There's a principle for this, I think. Chekhov's gun. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play."

"Chekhov had guns," Dex said, waving the letter again. "You have stationery. That's the parochial version."

"That's not what parochial means," Priya said.

"It could mean small-town stationery."

"It couldn't."

Liam sat down on the hearth, letting the argument wash over him like lane water. The letter was real; that was the problem. His father really had left it, and in real life it really had mattered to nobody but him, a rectangle of paper that meant a broken promise to exactly one sixteen-year-old. In a play, though, Priya was right, it sat on the stage glowing like a flare, promising the audience a payoff that never arrived. Real life could afford unexploded bombs. Ten-minute plays could not. He held both ideas at once, the true thing and the useful thing, and they did not fit together neatly, and he suspected they weren't supposed to.

"So I cut it," he said slowly, "or I pay it off."

"Or," said Priya, "your character keeps it. Carries it into the final scene. Doesn't say anything about it. The audience does the math."

Dex pointed at her with the letter. "That's ominous. I love it."

From the kitchen doorway, unnoticed until now, Liam's father stood with his coat still on, keys in hand, home early for once. He had heard the last few minutes, apparently, because his face had that careful blankness he wore at school concerts. He watched Priya, standing there with her script, feeling the room's awkwardness arrive like weather.

"You gave me a letter?" he said to Liam. Not angry. Almost curious, the way a debilitated swim coach had once asked Liam why he'd flipped on the turn.

"It's a play, Dad. You're a character. He's not exactly you."

"I'm the guy who misses the meet."

"He's the guy who misses the meet," Liam said. "You're the guy who came home early on a Tuesday to watch a table read in his own living room. There's a difference, and I'm still figuring out how much of one."

His father took a folding chair, sixth row of a one-row house. "Then I'm audience. Do I have to eat the popcorn?"

"It's mandatory," Dex said, passing the bag.

Liam stood back on the hearth, script in hand, and looked at his father, at Priya with the answer already circling her like a shark, at the letter Dex was now folding into a paper airplane. Cut it, pay it off, or let it sit in his character's pocket through the final scene, weightless and enormous at once. He honestly did not know which was truer, and the not knowing felt less like failure than like the first honest line he'd written all week.

"From the top," he said. "Priya, you're Dad. Dex, you're the letter. Try to be a serious letter this time."

Dex sailed the paper airplane across the living room, and it landed, perfectly, in his father's lap.

The argument had been going since Tuesday, and Connor was losing it in his notebook. His aunt's dining room table was buried in photocopies of the Haggadah, a folded calendar from the synagogue, and two slices of pizza going cold, because his cousin Noa insisted that ancient rules earned their authority by surviving, and Connor, who had agreed to debate her at the youth program on Friday, insisted nothing survived on survival alone. The topic was whether the commandments about festival observance still bound people who lived by train schedules and term papers, and the rules of the debate required them to argue from the text itself, no modern commentary allowed, which meant Connor had spent three evenings reading Exodus like a lawyer reading a contract.

The complication arrived when he finally called the synagogue office to confirm the social hall for Friday night. "You booked it for the twenty-third," the secretary said, "but the Seder is the night of the twenty-second." Connor stared at his own handwriting on the reservation form, where he had circled the twenty-third because the calendar on his phone called the twenty-third the first day of the holiday. He thanked her, hung up, and sat very still while the pizza congealed.

"It's my fault," he said to Noa. "I read the date off the phone. It said the holiday starts on the twenty-third, so I booked that evening."

Noa tilted her head at him the way she did when she thought he was being slow on purpose. "The day begins at sundown," she said, and went back to her photocopies. Connor sat there doing the arithmetic in reverse. If a day began at sundown, then the evening that started the festival was the one before the day the phone named, and every plan he had made was off by a night. He thought about apologizing to the secretary, about the folding chairs, about how a person could be careful and still be wrong by exactly the length of one dusk.

He spent the afternoon on the phone. The hall was free on the correct evening, the folding chairs could be moved, the custodian would stay late if Connor brought him coffee, and the rabbi, who had signed off on the debate, said only, "I'm glad you called before printing the flyers," which was somehow worse than a lecture. When Connor finally sat down at the table again, Noa pushed a passage across to him without comment. It was the verse about the festival being kept on a specific evening, and beside it she had written, in her terrible handwriting, one question: starts or ends?

He understood what she was doing. If the text itself anchored the festival to an evening, then the calendar question was not a bureaucratic accident but the very hinge of their debate. A rule that could organize time this way, that could take a day apart and reassemble it starting from darkness, was either a fossil or evidence that the text thought about time more carefully than his phone did. He had planned to argue that such rules were beautiful and finished, museum pieces; now he found himself annotating his own notes with questions he could not answer. He worked until Aunt Ruth turned on the porch light for no reason he could determine, since it was barely five and the sky was the color of weak tea.

Ruth stood in the doorway drying her hands and watched the two of them bent over the table, her nephew's earlobe red the way it got when he was thinking hard, her daughter's pen moving in circles while she read. She had watched Connor all week treat the Haggadah like a chess problem, all cerebral, no skin in it, and she had wondered whether to say something. She had decided not to. Whatever the boy was looking for, being handed it would spoil it. But now he had moved the folding-chair order and the Exodus commentary into one pile, as though they belonged together, and he was muttering about whether the custodian took his coffee with sugar.

"Uncle Marco takes it with sugar," she said. "The custodian plays chess with him. Bring two cups."

"Two cups," Connor repeated, writing it down.

Noa looked up. "You're going to argue my side now, aren't you. I can see it on you."

"I'm going to argue that the text knows what it's doing with time," Connor said, "and that I still don't know if that obligates anybody. Both of those can be true. That's allowed."

"It's sloppy."

"It's honest. There's a difference, and it's not small." He said it with more force than he intended, and Noa, who won most arguments by waiting, actually set her pen down.

Ruth went back to the kitchen and took the brisket out to thaw, because whichever evening it was, they would need it, and she had lived long enough to prognosticate about appetites rather than arguments. Her own view of the old rules had shifted twice in her life, once toward them and once at an angle, and she had stopped believing that probity required picking a side permanently. Through the doorway she heard Noa say, "Fine. New topic for Friday. We debate whether a rule has to bind you to mean anything," and Connor say, "Deal, but I book the hall this time," and the scratch of two pens starting over.

The two articles had been open on Vanessa's laptop since Tuesday, and by Thursday night they had stopped being articles and started being two people arguing across her kitchen table while she sat between them, unable to side with either. The first, from a ecology journal with a matte cover she'd found through the school database, claimed that montane bird species were shifting their ranges uphill as temperatures warmed, following the cool air they'd evolved to need. The second, published three years later by a team that had visited fewer sites but over more years, found no consistent shift at all, and suggested the first paper's pattern was an artifact of where its researchers had happened to place their survey points.

Her mother set a mug of tea down beside the keyboard, not asking, just setting it down, the way she did when she could tell a night was going long. The kitchen clock said nine-forty. Vanessa's draft, due Monday, was supposed to be a critical review, which her assignment sheet described as "a considered position on a scholarly debate," and so far her considered position was that she had typed the word "however" eleven times and deleted it eleven times.

"Still the birds?" her mother said, sitting across from her with her own mug.

"Still the birds."

She read the methods section of the first paper again, slowly, the way her junior-year English teacher had cajoled the class into reading poetry, one line at a time, resisting the urge to skim toward the conclusion. The first team had sampled forty-two ridgelines across two summers. The second team, eleven watersheds across nine years. Forty-two sites, two years. Eleven sites, nine years. She wrote both on a napkin and stared at them like they were scores from two different sports.

The problem, she realized, was that both papers could be describing the same mountains. A bird population could drift uphill in a hot year and drift back down in a wet one, and two studies watching different slices of time would each see only their own slice and swear it was the whole weather. She pushed the napkin away, then pulled it back. Somewhere, she thought, someone must have noticed this problem before her, someone with more than a napkin.

She searched the second paper's reference list for anything with the word "review" in the title, then tried "synthesis," then, on a guess, typed both authors' names together. The database returned a third paper, one neither article had cited much, published just last year. Its abstract began with a sentence she read three times: the authors had combined the results of dozens of studies on exactly this question, the upslope shift of montane species, in order to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study could.

"Wait," she said out loud.

"What?"

"Hang on." She was already skimming the methods, where the phrase appeared again in bold-faced certainty: a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question. It pooled the forty-two ridgelines and the eleven watersheds and forty other datasets besides, and what it found sat between the two papers like a referee: a small uphill shift overall, real but modest, smaller than the first paper claimed and larger than the second allowed.

She called her friend Priya, who was also writing a review, on hormones and adolescent sleep, and who answered on the second ring with her mouth clearly full of something.

"Did you find the thing where they pool all the studies?" Vanessa said.

"The what?"

"A meta-analysis. It combines the results of a bunch of studies on the same question, so it can estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can. Both of my articles are inside it. Like, statistically inside it."

Priya stopped chewing. "That exists?"

"Both of my authors are in the author list of the thing that proves them both partly wrong. It's brutal. It's beautiful."

After she hung up, she sat for a while with her hands flat on the table, the way her grandmother used to do before deciding whether bread dough had risen enough, a patience Vanessa had always read as discernment rather than delay, though she couldn't have said how she knew the difference. Her grandmother had been dead two years, and Vanessa thought, not for the first time, that the woman would have understood the napkin with the two numbers on it, the weighing of small evidence.

Because here was what the night had actually taught her, and it wasn't the answer. The meta-analysis gave an answer, a pooled slope, a confidence interval, but its own final paragraph flagged exactly the thing she'd guessed at on the napkin: study design varied, some datasets were short, some surveys were placed in ways that might bias the result. The referee was better informed than either fighter and still not omniscient. Her review, she saw now, would not be a verdict. It would be a description of how the two papers disagreed, why, and what a pooling of all the evidence so far suggested, with its edges left visible.

She opened a new document and typed the first real sentence she'd written all week: "These two studies reach opposite conclusions not because one is wrong, but because each saw part of a pattern." Then she deleted "not because one is wrong," because she wasn't sure that was true, and because she was starting to distrust sentences that settled things. She retyped it: "Each study saw part of a pattern, and only part."

Her mother came back for the empty mugs. Vanessa turned the laptop so she could see the forest of little squares on the meta-analysis's summary figure, each square a study, each horizontal line the uncertainty around it, the diamond at the bottom the pooled estimate that no single square could have drawn alone.

"That's tomorrow's you talking," her mother said, tapping the diamond.

"That's Monday's me, actually," Vanessa said, and saved the file.

Isabella found her name on the fridge before she found anyone she knew, both of them attached to the same magnet, her name in gold marker on a white poster that said CONGRATULATES OUR GRADUATES, 2022. The party was in Dev's backyard, string lights sagging between the fence and the garage, a folding table of soda cans sweating in the June heat. She had been at this school since ninth grade and she recognized nearly every face, which was the problem, because she kept noticing the faces that were not there.

"Where's Marcus?" she asked Priya, who was stacking cups with the efficiency of someone avoiding conversation.

"Marcus who? Oh. Yeah." Priya flattened a cup into the stack. "He left sophomore year. Moved, I think."

"He was in my algebra class." Isabella could still see him hunched at the back desk, chewing his pen cap into plastic shreds. She had lent him notes once, or he had lent her some; she couldn't remember which direction the debt ran, only that they had never settled it.

Her brother Marco appeared behind her with his phone out, belligerent the way he got when he'd had two beers and wanted to argue about something, anything, preferably with family. "You know half the kids who started ninth grade with you aren't here tonight," he said. "Statistically."

"That's not statistics, that's a backyard."

"I looked it up for a paper. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in 2021-22." He said it in his quoting voice, the one he used to litigate dinner-table disputes into surrender. "Your cohort. The whole country's. Thirteen out of every hundred just aren't in this picture."

"Then go find someone else's picture to ruin." She walked toward the lawn chairs, but the number came with her, the way a song does. Eighty-seven percent. She tried it against her own memories like a key against a lock: Tanisha, gone by October of freshman year, no goodbye. Devon, who'd been there in June and gone by September. The two girls who used to laugh in the stairwell until the laughing stopped. She had assumed, at the time, that they had simply dissolved, that some people were the substrate of a class, the layer underneath that everything else got built on and no one thought to mention. It had never occurred to her to count them.

She found her phone and scrolled to a message from December of junior year, from Tanisha, the only one she'd ever traded numbers with. She read it again where the string lights didn't quite reach.

Hey. Saw your photo from the choir thing. You looked happy. I'm at Heights now, it's fine, smaller. I keep meaning to write more but every time I start it sounds like an apology and I don't know what I'd be apologizing for. Anyway. You were one of the good ones. That's all.

Isabella had answered with a heart emoji and then nothing, because she hadn't known what to say either, and then a year had gone by like water through a fence. Tonight she sat with the phone in her lap and drafted three replies and deleted them, because each one tried to litigate the past into a verdict: I should have noticed. You should have told me. Nobody was wrong. The last one felt truest and also flattest, a verdict that closed the case without anyone testifying.

Priya came and dropped into the chair beside her, holding out a can of root beer as a truce. "You're doing the math face."

"It's not a face."

"You're doing it about Marcus, and Tanisha, and probably that whole missing thirteen percent." Priya popped her own can. "I do it too. I keep thinking graduation is a photo, and I keep noticing who got cropped out. But my mom says some of them graduated somewhere else, some moved, some are doing a fifth year. Thirteen percent just means they didn't finish with us. It doesn't say what happened to them."

"Your mom says a lot of things." But Isabella felt the number loosen its grip, or shift it. Eighty-seven percent was a fact, and the fact was quiet about the rest. It didn't say who had struggled and who had simply gone somewhere with better weather. It didn't say which of them, standing under these particular lights, was the lucky one and which was only the one still standing where the photograph was being taken. She wanted to hold both things at once, the luck and the loss, without letting either one erase the other, and she could feel the seam between them flexing every time she tried.

She typed a fourth reply to Tanisha, slowly, and this time she didn't delete it. It said: We graduated tonight and someone said a number and I thought of you immediately, not as a number. You were in my algebra class and you explained the coin problems better than the teacher did. I don't know where you are now. If you want, tell me. If you don't, that's okay too. She read it twice, thumb hovering over send.

Across the yard someone had turned the music up and a boy she'd known since seventh grade was dancing badly on purpose, and Marco was arguing with Dev's father about baseball, and the lights swung a little in a wind that had just come up.

She pressed send, watched the message lift off the ground, and put the phone face-down on her knee, still warm, and looked up at the yard full of everyone who had made it to a folding table in June.

Kaitlyn had been student-directing the one-act for eleven days, and the sofa had been in a different place for all of them. On Monday it sat stage left of the window frame. By Wednesday it had migrated four feet toward center, dragged there by Marcus during his big monologue, presumably because moving furniture felt like acting. She had said "hold your position" so many times the phrase had desensitized everyone, including her; it entered the room and dissolved, like a note played too often.

The play was hers in name only so far. Mrs. Okonkwo had signed the form, taken the club's disbursement paperwork to the main office, and otherwise stayed in the back row of the auditorium with her coffee, watching. "It's your room," she'd said on the first day, which Kaitlyn had initially heard as generosity and was beginning to hear as a verdict pending.

Her instinct was to leave the blocking loose. Her drama teacher last year, Mr. Farelli, had talked about letting actors discover movement from the inside out, and Kaitlyn had believed him, mostly. But Priya had a different education: two summers of community theater, where the director taped the floor and heaven help you if you wandered. "Some people need a map," Priya said now, stretching on the sofa in question. "Some people need a fence." Kaitlyn suspected the truth was less symmetrical than that, but she didn't say so, because Priya was also the one playing the sister who sat on the sofa for eleven of the play's fourteen minutes.

"Places," Kaitlyn called. "Top of scene two. Marcus, this time stay where I put you."

Marcus did not stay where she put him. He crossed to the sofa on his entrance, which was correct, but by the end of his monologue the sofa had traveled again, and Priya, who had been sitting on it, was suddenly four feet upstage of where her scene partner needed her to be. Devon, playing the brother, gamely pivoted to compensate, and the whole blocking collapsed like something tangential had been substituted for the actual scene. Kaitlyn stopped them. She stopped them again. The third time she didn't call anything at all; she just sat in the third row with her binder and listened to the pause where a line should have been.

From the stage, Devon could see her better than she thought. He watched her chew the end of her pen, cross something out, uncross it. She was eighteen days from festival and she looked like a person doing arithmetic with too few numbers. He had been in three shows at this school and directed by four kinds of director, and his private theory was that the good ones knew one big thing and the great ones knew two things that disagreed. He wasn't sure yet which kind was in the third row. Marcus, beside him, whispered, "She's going to make us run it again." Devon whispered back, "She's building up to something," and, unusually, he hoped he was right.

At the next rehearsal Kaitlyn came in with a roll of colored tape she had bought with her own money from the hardware store after the theater supply site wanted two weeks for shipping. She knelt on the stage during warmups and put a short strip where the sofa's front legs belonged, another at stage left where Priya entered, a third at Marcus's mark. Priya recognized it immediately and crouched beside her, delighted. "Spike tape," Priya said, running her thumb along the fluorescent orange. "It marks where furniture and actors go. Real directors use it for everything." Kaitlyn said, "Then we're real now," and Priya laughed in a way that suggested she had changed her mind about something and was not going to announce what.

But Kaitlyn did not tape everything. She left Marcus's cross open, one strip at the start and nothing after; and when he asked, she told him the sofa had a home now, and he could find his own way to it. She was not fully sure this hybrid worked. The fence people got fences and the map people got a map with blank sections, and there was a possibility she was just splitting the difference rather than choosing. She noted it in her binder under a question mark, next to a note that read "Marcus: does he want direction or permission," which she suspected was the same question about herself.

The run that Friday held together. The sofa stayed spiked; Priya hit her mark in the dark without looking; Marcus made his cross slowly, differently each time, and Devon stopped bracing for furniture and started listening. Mrs. Okonkwo, in the back row, said nothing at all, which Kaitlyn decided to take as the office stamp on the disbursement of her opinion. After notes, Priya gathered her bag and paused at the edge of the stage, looking down at the small orange geometry of the last three weeks.

"Leave the tape down over the weekend?" Priya asked. "In case the janitor doesn't get it."

Kaitlyn looked at the marks, at the one blank corridor where Marcus walked, and said, "No. Pull it up. We'll spike it fresh on Monday."

The community center gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn, and by the second week of January Elijah had learned to arrive twenty minutes early so he could have the far basket to himself. He was the newest player on the Rockets, a rec-league team that practiced on Tuesdays and played Saturdays, and for the first month everything had gone easily. Everyone was polite. Nobody criticized anyone's shot selection. They lost by four, then won by two, and Elijah thought the team was good.

Then Marcus started talking. Marcus, who was nineteen and worked at the hardware store, had played varsity at the high school and believed he should be the captain, though nobody had voted on a captain at all. At the third Tuesday practice he stopped a drill to tell Devon he'd taken the wrong angle on the pick, then told Elijah he passed too much, then told the coach, a wiry man named Reyes who ran the center's after-school program, that the offense had no structure. Two other players argued back. Devon and Marcus didn't speak for the rest of the hour. In the parking lot afterward, Elijah's teammate Sana said, "We were better when we all hated each other quietly."

That night Elijah was supposed to be drafting a persuasive essay for his composition class, the prompt asking him to take a position that could hold two opposing ideas at once. Instead he texted his cousin Deja, who was two years into a psychology degree at the state school. i need something true to say about a team falling apart, he wrote, not a pep talk, an actual idea. She sent back a paragraph that he read twice at his desk while his essay document sat open and blank.

It's a real theory, she wrote. A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. Forming is when everyone is polite and guards their real opinions. Storming is the conflict part, when the politeness breaks and people fight over roles and status. It sounds like your team just entered stage two, which is not the same thing as falling apart. Some groups never get through it. The ones that do start to build norms, shared expectations nobody has to say out loud anymore, and then they perform. I can't promise yours gets through it. That part's on you.

At Thursday's practice Reyes pulled the team into a huddle before drills and said only, "Work it out among yourselves, I'll be in the office," which was unlike him and which nobody liked. Marcus opened his mouth to start again on the offense, and Elijah, who had never once spoken first in a group, spoke first. "We're storming," he said. Everybody looked at him. "It's a thing my cousin told me. A psychologist, Tuckman, said groups go through four stages: forming, storming, norming, performing. Forming is the polite part, which we did. Storming is this." He gestured at the space between Marcus and Devon where the air seemed to have gone thin. "The fighting means we care who does what. It's not the end of the team."

Marcus folded his arms. "So we're supposed to just fight until it stops being a fight?" Elijah admitted he didn't know the mechanism, only the map, and there was a silence in which several people seemed to be deciding whether the map was enough. Devon, unexpectedly, said that Marcus wasn't wrong about the picks, only about the volume. Marcus said Devon wasn't wrong about the angles either, and then, to forestall the argument restarting along its old lines, Marcus said the word nobody expected: "Captain." He looked at Sana. "You actually run this team already. Take the title."

They lost their next game anyway, by eleven, but the loss felt different, more like evidence than like a verdict. Sana started calling sets with her hands, small signals that condensed what had taken Marcus whole speeches to say, and the nascent system wobbled whenever the other team pressed but did not collapse. Elijah's essay, handed in late, argued that a group and an individual could both be works in progress at the same time, and that the honest position was to hold the theory loosely. His teacher wrote in the margin that the argument lacked a strong logos, a clear spine of reasoning, and Elijah accepted the B without appeal.

The last Saturday of the season they played the Lightning, who had beaten them twice. In the fourth quarter, with the Rockets up three, Elijah caught the ball at the top of the key with an open shot, the shot he had taken at that basket alone all those January mornings, the shot that would prove everything. He passed to Devon instead, cutting without the ball, because Devon's angle was better, and Devon laid it in, and the gym got loud. After the buzzer, Reyes came out of the office where he had spent the entire game, looked at the scoreboard, and said, "Wait, you won without me? I was the one doing the storming theory."

The sign outside city hall read Youth Assembly on Local and National Government, and beneath it, in smaller letters, Bring Your Position Papers. Nathan's position paper was two paragraphs long, which was one paragraph longer than his actual position. He had written it at eleven the night before, arguing that a president fixed for four years gave a country stability, a claim he had lifted from a columnist whose reasoning he could no longer remember. He followed the crowd of teenagers through the brass doors and up the marble stairs, where a woman with a clipboard handed him a lanyard and a room number and, unprompted, a granola bar, because she had noticed him checking his pockets for the breakfast he'd forgotten.

The room had been a council chamber once and still held its curved wooden desks, though the microphones at each seat were dead, vestigial, wired to nothing. Nathan found his assigned table near the window. Across from him sat a girl he recognized from the regional debate, Priya, who was already arranging her notes with the calm of someone who had finished early. Beside her, a younger boy in a school blazer was reading his own paper with visible dread. Priya slid her spare highlighter across the table to him without a word, and he took it like a rescue line.

The morning session was a structured debate on a motion Nathan had helped draft three weeks earlier: that a parliamentary system serves voters better than a presidential one. He had proposed it on a whim, assuming it would be easy to argue either side, and had spent the weeks since discovering that he believed both sides on alternating days. The moderator, a councilwoman with a hoarse voice and a thermos of tea she kept asking people to pass back and forth, gave them twenty minutes to prepare opening statements.

Priya went first for their side, parliamentary. She started with something Nathan hadn't heard before. "My aunt lives in Manchester," she said, leaning into the dead microphone out of habit, then abandoning it. "In 2022 the UK had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, and there was no general election the whole time, because the governing party changed its leader. My aunt texted me a photo of her calendar with all three names crossed off." She let that sit for a second. "So my question for the other side is what you do with that."

Nathan had been half listening while scanning his paper, and the sentence stopped him. Three prime ministers. He turned to the kid in the blazer, whose name tag said Theo, and asked whether that was right, whether a country could really swap leaders twice in a year without anyone voting. Theo nodded. "That's why I picked the presidential side," he said. "You at least know who you're getting until the term ends."

During the break, Nathan stood by the window with the granola bar and looked down at the plaza, where a crew was setting up folding chairs for some ceremony. He had spent three weeks treating the question like a scoreboard, one system winning and one losing, and the scoreboard approach had quietly atrophied his ability to notice what was actually being traded. Priya's aunt had watched three faces cycle past without casting a ballot. But Theo, who had looked genuinely frightened behind his highlighter, had a point too: a fixed term meant that when you lost, you at least knew exactly how long you'd lost for. Two different fears, and each system was a way of managing one of them.

When they reconvened, the moderator asked Nathan for the rebuttal. He pushed his prepared opening aside, which made a small tearing sound because the pages were still stapled, and spoke from the window-view version instead. "The other side will tell you that in a parliamentary system the party can ditch a leader you never got to vote on, and they're right, that happened, three times in one year in the UK with no election," he said. "But a presidential system has its own version of being stuck. You can't remove a president for being bad at the job, only for committing crimes, so a bad four years runs all four years. I don't think either side gets to claim voters are always in control. I think the real difference is whether you'd rather be able to fire the leader quickly and unpredictably, or rarely and predictably."

He paused, and to his surprise the room was quiet rather than bored. "I'll be honest," he said. "I don't know which of those I'd choose, and I've been switching all morning. But I know they're the actual choice, and every platitude about stability or democracy I was going to open with doesn't touch it."

The debate ran another hour. Theo, who turned out to speak better than he read, gave a closing for the presidential side that borrowed Nathan's framing and argued predictability mattered more when you were eighteen and trying to plan anything at all, and Nathan found himself nodding along to the case against his own side. When the assembly voted, the motion passed by four votes, thin enough that nobody treated it as settled. Priya gathered her notes and looked over at him.

"So which system do you actually want, after all that?" she asked.

"Ask me next week," Nathan said, and began pulling the staple out of his dead pages.

The enrollment form came in a plastic sleeve with a pen chained to the clipboard, which Stella thought was an odd way to begin a lesson in trust. She was sixteen, third in line at the counter of Ridgeline Driving Academy, and behind her the Tuesday class was already filling plastic chairs. The man at the counter, Mr. Okafor, slid the sleeve toward each student like a dealer. "Read it, sign it, initial page four," he said, and the girl ahead of Stella signed without sitting down.

Stella sat down. The form was dense, and the language had a way of moving just as she reached for it: release, indemnify, assumption of risk. On page four, a paragraph in slightly larger print said that any dispute would be settled through binding arbitration rather than in court, and that by signing she waived participation in any class-action lawsuit. She read it twice. She had seen the word arbitration before, last month, in her father's kitchen, hunched over his laptop scrolling through the endless terms of his new phone app.

That night came back to her clearly. Her father had beckoned her over with two fingers, the screen's glow on his glasses. "Look at this," he had said. "I clicked agree on this app months ago. Apparently I agreed not to sue them in court. If something goes wrong, we go to some private thing instead. And we can't join together with other people who got the same raw deal." He had laughed, a small dry laugh, and said, "They buried it in the conditions where nobody reads." Stella had ascribed her father's amusement to his usual habit of finding catastrophe funny, but she had gone to bed uneasy, the way you do when you learn the floor of a familiar room has a trapdoor somewhere.

Now she looked up at Mr. Okafor. "What does this paragraph mean, exactly?"

"Arbitration clause," he said pleasantly. "Standard."

"I mean, what happens if something goes wrong."

"Then we settle it privately, not in a courtroom." He was already reaching for the next clipboard.

The girl behind her, a compact person in a wrestling hoodie, leaned over Stella's shoulder. "You're actually reading it?"

"Somebody has to."

"It's driving school, not a kidney transplant."

"Same principle," Stella said, and meant it, though she could not have said exactly what the principle was, only that it involved the difference between agreeing and consenting, which her mother insisted was not the same thing at all. Consent, her mother said, required knowing what you were saying yes to. Her mother had said this about doctors, about boyfriends, about a landlord once, standing in the doorway of their old apartment with her arms folded.

The trouble was concrete: Stella wanted the class. Her mother worked the early shift and her father's car sat in the lot all day, and without a license Stella was asking favors every week, small favors that accumulated like interest. And the class was cheap, cheaper than the other school across town, which now seemed less like luck and more like a clue. She thought of her father's screen. She thought of the girl ahead of her who had signed standing up.

She raised her hand again. "If I cross this out and initial it, can I still take the class?"

Mr. Okafor blinked. "Nobody's ever asked."

"But can I?"

He looked at the paragraph, then at her, and something in his face shifted, less irritation than recalibration. "Let me call the owner." He picked up the phone, and while he dialed, the wrestling girl slid into the chair beside Stella and started reading page two aloud in a courtroom voice, "'The student ascribes all risk of somatic injury to their own person,' which I believe is Latin for 'ouch is your problem,'" and Stella laughed despite herself, a bright involuntary sound that felt like the first crack in a frozen lake.

The owner said no to the cross-out, but offered a verbal assurance, which everyone in the room understood was worth the paper it was printed on, which was nothing. Stella sat with the pen hovering. She thought of her mother in the doorway, arms folded. She thought of the car in the lot, keys eventually in her own hand, the specific exhilaration of a first highway on-ramp, the pedal under her foot. She thought: I can sign this and know what I signed, or refuse it and stay home, and neither choice is clean.

She wrote her name, then, underneath, in small careful letters, "signed under protest," and handed the clipboard back. Mr. Okafor looked at the addition, opened his mouth, closed it, and stamped the form.

"First lesson is Saturday," he said. "Eight a.m."

Behind her, the wrestling girl was still on page six, reading slower now.

The sign taped to the double doors read MODEL GOVERNMENT DAY, ROOM 2B, and beneath it, in smaller letters, DELEGATES MUST PICK A SYSTEM BY 4:00. Victor read it twice, then pushed through into the echo of a municipal chamber that smelled of floor wax and old paper. Rows of folding chairs faced a dais where the mayor usually sat, though today the dais belonged to a graduate student with a clipboard and a megaphone she did not appear to need. Victor had signed up because his civics teacher had promised it would look good on applications, and because his father, who had grown up in a country where the parliament fell every eleven months, had said only, "Learn both, then tell me which one lets you sleep."

They drew assignments from a coffee tin. Victor pulled the card that said PRESIDENTIAL SYSTEM, DEFENSE, and a girl named Priya, from the junior college across town, pulled the card that said PARLIAMENTARY SYSTEM, DEFENSE. The graduate student explained the exercise in a voice that carried to the fire exits. Each side would design a country, write the rules for choosing and removing a head of government, and by four o'clock the whole room would vote on which constitution to adopt. Victor sat down at the long table with his team, four strangers shuffling index cards, and realized he had no argument beyond a vague loyalty to the system he had grown up under.

The parliamentary table worked fast. Priya stood, laid out their design in five minutes, and sat down. The parliament would elect the prime minister, she said, and the same parliament could withdraw its confidence and remove him, usually within days, without any trial, without any court. "The majority that makes him can unmake him," she said. "That is the whole idea." Around Victor's table someone muttered that it sounded like the prime minister worked on a leash, and someone else said the leash was the point, and Victor wrote both sentences down without deciding between them.

His own side argued for an hour about the removal rule. One boy, Khalil, wanted impeachment to require a simple majority of the legislature, so that a rogue president could be fired as easily as any other official. An older delegate, a gap-year student with a trenchant manner of speaking that flattened disagreement rather than inviting it, insisted that anything so easy would turn removal into a routine weapon and every president into a tenant. Victor, trying to referee, pulled out his phone and searched for the only removal case he half remembered from class, the one from 1868. He read the result, then read it again, and stood up without quite deciding to.

"In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote," Victor said. "Thirty-five senators voted to convict. That was one short of the two-thirds they needed." He let the room absorb it. "So the bar they set was high enough that a president everybody in that chamber apparently wanted gone survived anyway." Priya turned in her chair, and Khalil said what Victor had been thinking, which was that one vote deciding the fate of a president seemed like a terrible way to run a country. The gap-year student said it was the opposite, that a bar a single vote cannot clear was the only thing standing between them and a government that changes heads every season.

The graduate student called a recess, and Priya crossed the room to Victor's table. She did not gloat, which he had expected. Instead she asked him what he thought a president and a prime minister were actually for, and he found he could not answer quickly. They walked out into the corridor by the water fountain and argued in low voices, half as rivals and half as two people trying to get something right. She argued that her system emancipated the legislature from a leader it no longer trusted, that confidence was a living thing, withdrawn the moment it died. Victor argued back that a fixed term gave a leader room to act against the mood of the moment, that some decisions needed a horizon longer than the average quarrel. He heard himself defending a system he had never before bothered to defend, and he heard her conceding, quietly, that her prime ministers rarely had time to be anything but careful.

When the vote came at four, Victor did something neither table had proposed. He stood at the dais and offered a hybrid: a parliament elected by their new country, a prime minister who served at its confidence, and a directly chosen president with a fixed term who could be removed only by the two-thirds rule, the one that had saved Johnson and would probably save most presidents who deserved it too. "I am not sure the bar is at the right height," he said. "I only know that in 1868 it was one vote tall, and I would rather argue about that number every generation than pretend either system solves it." A delegate called out that he was an egoist, inventing a whole new constitution just to avoid losing, and Victor said maybe, but an egoist with two systems in his pocket was still better than a partisan with one.

The room voted. The hybrid lost, nineteen to fourteen, to Priya's clean parliamentary design, and she shook his hand with both of hers and told him the margin was smaller than she had predicted. Outside on the city hall steps, Victor called his father and gave the honest summary, that the parliamentary side had won, that he still could not say his side was wrong, and that the one thing he now knew for certain was a single Senate vote from a century and a half ago. His father listened all the way through, which he rarely did, and then said only, "So which one lets you sleep?" Victor looked back at the lit windows of Room 2B, where delegates were still stacking chairs, and said, "Ask me again after I've seen both break."

The office smelled of toner and the lemon polish Mr. Aduba used on the counters every morning, and by the second week of her summer job Laura had learned to tell the time by the door. Ten o'clock brought the renters, clutching printouts, asking whether the deposit on a two-bedroom was really one month's rent plus a fee, and whether they would get any of it back if the blinds were already bent when they moved in. Two o'clock brought the buyers, quieter people who sat across from Mr. Aduba's desk with bank statements folded into squares, talking about down payments as if the words were fragile. Laura filed their paperwork, marked the keys in, made coffee, and listened.

Her own problem sat in her bag all afternoon: a letter from the housing office at the college she'd start in September, listing the dorm fee next to a smaller figure for sharing an off-campus apartment with three strangers. Her mother had said, over dinner, that they'd work it out, and then changed the subject to her aunt's knees, and Laura had understood that "work it out" meant she was supposed to work it out.

On Thursday her cousin Denise came in at four, still in her hospital scrubs, carrying a folder she dropped on the counter like something hot. "Five years," she said. "Five years of paying every single month, and I looked it up today and I still owe almost exactly what I borrowed. Where did the money go, Laura? Tell me where it went."

Mr. Aduba, who was phlegmatic about nearly everything, including burst pipes and a tenant who once kept goats, looked up from his screen. "Standard repayment loan," he said. "The early payments go mostly to interest." He turned back to his screen, as if that settled it, and for him it had.

Denise hadn't heard it that way before either. "So the bank takes its share first," she said slowly, "and only later does the money actually start bringing down what I owe."

Laura pulled the amortization sheet out of Denise's folder and ran her finger down the columns, curious now in spite of herself. The monthly number never changed, but its two halves shifted as the years went by, the interest slice shrinking and the other slice growing, until near the end nearly everything went to the borrowed amount itself. It was like watching a tide change direction so slowly you had to mark the waterline to prove it. She thought of her mother's old joke that the universe was patient because it could afford to be.

"Meanwhile I've been renting," Laura said, mostly to herself, "and I understood that part. You pay, you live there, the money's gone, and the deposit is the only piece that might circle back to you if you leave the place clean." She looked up. "I thought buying was the opposite. Money in, house yours. Nobody told me it's a long argument with the bank first, and for the first stretch the bank wins every month."

Denise laughed, a short, tired sound. "You'll be a freshman and you already prognosticate better than my loan officer." She squared the folder against the counter. "At least now I know the payments weren't wasted. They were just, what's the word, front-loaded."

Mr. Aduba slid a listing across the desk to a couple by the window, and the office hummed with its usual throughput of phone calls, key tags, and people carrying their futures around in envelopes. Laura photocopied the amortization sheet and folded it next to the housing letter in her bag, then sat at the front desk and did the arithmetic she'd been avoiding. Dorm fee times eight semesters. Off-campus rent times the same months, minus her share of a deposit she might never see again, plus a bus pass. The two totals sat near each other, close enough that the difference wouldn't decide anything by itself. What she couldn't price was quieter: whether she wanted to learn a city through a landlord's rules or through a roommate's dishes in the sink.

She understood something else, too, though it was less comfortable. Denise's payments hadn't vanished; they had gone somewhere, just not where Denise had pictured, and Laura liked knowing that the system had a logic even when it wasn't her logic. What she couldn't yet say was whether the logic was fair. Maybe the bank deserved its interest for lending the money at all, and maybe that was exactly the kind of sentence people said when the money wasn't theirs. She held both possibilities open the way you hold two keys, trying each in the same lock.

At closing time she wiped the counter, switched off the printer, and pulled the folded paper out again. On the back of the amortization sheet, in the margin, she wrote the dorm number, the rent number, and then, underneath, a small question mark that she didn't try to answer. Denise knocked on the glass from the parking lot, holding up her car keys through the window, and Laura clipped the page into her notebook, waved back, and went to lock the front door.

The video arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, forwarded from Dex with three fire emojis and the caption "bro look at this NOW." It showed a shopping mall in flames, smoke rolling against a sky the color of dishwater, people running with their jackets over their mouths. A caption in the corner gave a city and yesterday's date. Loic was alone in the living room, his mother asleep down the hall, and his thumb hovered over the forward arrow for the group chat before he noticed that his own heartbeat had picked up, as though the fire were something happening to him.

He sent it. Fourteen people received it in the next ninety seconds, and the replies stacked up fast, the little word bubbles portending a night of outrage. Dajah wrote "this is terrifying." Someone Loic barely knew from his sister's graduation wrote "what is WRONG with people." Loic typed "exactly" and felt the warm certainty of agreeing with everyone at once, the feeling he would later recognize as the cheapest thing he owned.

Then Nadia replied, three minutes later, with a screenshot. "This photo is old," she wrote. "It's been online since like 2017." She had run the still frame through something called TinEye, a reverse image search engine, and she'd sorted the results with the oldest first, which showed her when the image first appeared online, years before yesterday. Loic read the message twice. The fire emojis in his own forward suddenly looked insouciant, the seal of someone who had cared only about being first.

He didn't apologize right away. First he argued, because the first feeling is always that the correction is an attack. "The video format is different," he typed. "Someone re-uploaded it, so maybe it's new footage of the same thing." Nadia sent a link. He sat in the lamplight of the living room, the TV off, his mother's magazines fanned on the coffee table, and opened his laptop on the arm of the couch.

He dragged the frame into the search bar himself. He didn't want to take her word for it; he had decided at some point that year, without announcing it, that he was going to be a person who checked things, a small-time autodidact with a laptop and a grudge against being fooled. The results loaded, and he found the oldest-first option and clicked it, and there was the same smoke, the same dishwater sky, dated years back, on sites he'd never heard of, some of them dead now, the page still standing like a burned building left standing.

He typed an apology into the group chat. It felt insufficient and he sent it anyway. "I shared something fake," he wrote. "The photo's from years ago. Sorry, everyone, check before you forward." A couple of people replied with thumbs. Dajah wrote "good looking out." Someone else wrote "lol it's not that deep," and Loic sat with that for a while, the possibility that it wasn't, that he had turned a Tuesday night into a seminar nobody had enrolled in.

He called Nadia instead of texting, because some things you want to hear in a voice. "How'd you even know to do that," he asked. She was folding laundry, he could hear the fabric. "My cousin got burned during the election," she said. "Shared a thing, got quoted at a family dinner, spent a year being the cautionary tale." She laughed a little. "TinEye's been around since 2008, so it's not like it's a secret. People just don't use it."

He told her he'd run the oldest-first sort himself, that he'd seen the earliest result with his own eyes, and she said "then you did it right." It was a small compliment and he held on to it harder than he meant to. After they hung up he scrolled back through the group chat, past his fire emojis, past the fourteen forwards, and found that two people had sent the video on after his correction, probably without reading up that far. He couldn't reach those threads. He knew that now, and it didn't portend anything good, it was just true. He closed the laptop and sat in the quiet living room, then picked up his phone and opened his sister's chat, where the video sat unsent, and typed: "Before you share anything, there's a thing you should see."

The lab smelled like wet dirt and coffee, which Kyle decided was what a real science lab should smell like, even if the posters on the wall were about something he'd never heard of before this spring: the soil microbiome, all the fungi and bacteria living in a handful of forest floor. Dr. Okafor had taken him on as a summer mentee after his chemistry teacher sent an email Kyle hadn't even known was being written. Now he sat at a stool beside the fume hood, pipetting liquid into little tubes with hands that were steadier than he expected, while his phone sat face-down in his backpack and vibrated against a spiral notebook.

He didn't check it. He had a rule about that, invented twenty minutes ago.

The vibration was almost certainly Mr. Duvall from the landscaping company, calling to confirm whether Kyle could start Monday. Fourteen dollars an hour, forty hours a week, all summer, real money by August. The research position here, by contrast, was unpaid, and its rewards were the kind adults praised in a language Kyle privately thought of as rain-word, vague and falling everywhere at once. Experience. Connections. A line on an application.

"So you're the new one," said Priya, a lanky girl in a college hoodie who had wandered over from the greenhouse bay. She watched him pipette with an expression of polite horror. "You're pushing too hard. Let the drop fall on its own."

Kyle eased his thumb. A drop detached, tidy as a bead.

"What are you doing this summer?" she asked. "Here, or the thing?"

"The thing?"

"Some people do the summer program and then leave in July for jobs." She shrugged. "Dr. Okafor pretends not to mind. My mom thinks I'm insane for staying. She keeps bringing up this study. The marshmallow one. Little kids, one treat now or two if they wait." Priya rolled her eyes toward the ceiling. "She read that a 1990 follow-up of those preschoolers found the kids who'd waited longer for the second treat tended to have higher SAT scores as teenagers. So now every time I choose homework over a shift at the pool, she's smug about it for a week."

"Wait, they followed them for years? Actual years?"

"Twelve or something. I don't know. My mom tells it like a fable." Priya drifted back toward the greenhouse, and Kyle stood there with his pipette suspended, a drop trembling at its tip.

He wanted to dismiss it. It was a fable, obviously, the kind of thing adults used to make patience sound like virtue instead of what it usually was, standing around while other people got the good seats. One afternoon with a marshmallow couldn't reach across a decade and grab a number out of some kid's future. But then, the landscaping job was also a single afternoon's decision, and everyone acted as if it would reach forward and grab his. Mr. Duvall had said the crew he joined this summer often came back every year through college, which sounded either like loyalty or like a trap, depending on the hour at which Kyle thought about it.

At the break, he used the old desktop in the lab's corner, the one with the screen the color of weak tea. The library database gave him the study without much digging: preschoolers, treats, the waiting, and then, in a 1990 follow-up, the longer waiters tending toward higher SAT scores as teenagers. He read it twice. The word that snagged him was "tended." Not guaranteed, not always, just leaned, the way a slope leans. He tried to recalibrate around it, to hold both things at once: that a choice made in one afternoon seemed to lean on a person for years, and that leaning wasn't deciding. Somewhere under all that was the fact that no one had ever offered him a second marshmallow for waiting. Waiting, in his house, had just been waiting.

Because that was the part he hadn't told Dr. Okafor, or Priya, or anyone. The word he kept behind his teeth. His mother had started picking up extra shifts in March, and the second-shift differential didn't cover what the hospital had started sending in envelopes she left on the microwave, turned address-side down. Kyle had done the arithmetic on the bus. Fourteen dollars an hour, forty hours, eleven weeks. He could carry the fall by himself, the way she'd carried everything since June of last year. That was the calculation sitting in his backpack, buzzing.

Dr. Okafor came back from the staff room with two cups of tea and offered him one, and when Kyle took it she became unexpectedly effusive about his pipetting, saying he had good hands, that good hands were rarer than good grades, that the bacteria in sample seven had done something under the microscope this morning that she wanted to show him. She leaned over the scope and adjusted the fine focus, and the screen filled with a smear of life, threads and dots moving through soil water like a slow city. "This biome," she said, tapping the screen with one finger, "has been developing in that jar since February. Every day it becomes more itself. You cannot rush it and you cannot skip ahead and see what it will be in August."

Kyle looked at the jar. Then, in a way that felt like stepping off a curb he'd been standing on all day, he took his phone out of the backpack. The screen said one missed call, one voicemail. He stood in the doorway of the lab where the dirt smell was strongest and pressed the phone to his ear, and Mr. Duvall's voice came through flat and cheerful, saying the crew slot was his if he wanted it, saying to call back by five, saying no rush, kid, it's your summer.

Behind him Dr. Okafor was still bent over the microscope, patient as soil. He looked at the clock above the sink, then at the screen, where the threads kept moving through their dark, unfinished city. He dialed.

"Mr. Duvall? It's Kyle." He watched a single bead form at the tip of his abandoned pipette, hanging there, holding on. "I need to ask you something before I answer."

The kitchen smelled of Grandpa Walt's coffee, bitter and old, and Jordan set his shoebox of alum crystals on the table between the sugar bowl and the window geranium. The largest crystal sat on a folded paper towel, blue-white and faceted, and beside it his lab notebook lay open to the page where he'd weighed everything twice.

"They're smaller than the ones in your photograph," Grandpa said, turning the box with one finger. He had the saturnine face of a man who had spent forty years underground in the gypsum mine, and he looked at the crystal the way he looked at most things, as if it had already disappointed him somewhere.

"That's the problem," Jordan said. "I started with twenty-five grams of alum. That's potassium aluminum sulfate dodecahydrate, molar mass four hundred seventy-four grams per mole. So I divide, and I get about zero point zero five three moles of the stuff, and since it comes back out of solution as the same compound, the theoretical yield is twenty-five grams. But the crystals only weigh twenty-one point four grams." He slid the notebook across. "I lost almost four grams somewhere."

Grandpa studied the figures without touching them. "And what do you call that. The number you're after."

Jordan had written the division on the back of an envelope that morning, on the bus, and he'd been carrying the answer around all day like a stone in his pocket. "Percent yield. You take the actual mass you got, divide by the theoretical yield, multiply by a hundred. Mine's eighty-five point six percent." He said it flat, because the number still embarrassed him. At the regional fair in March, a judge had asked him for it, and he'd stood there with his mouth open, having never computed it at all.

"You were supposed to win that thing," Grandpa said. It wasn't a question. Two springs ago they had driven down to the fair together in the truck with the rusted wheel well, and Jordan had taken second, and on the drive home Grandpa had said the judges wouldn't know a decent crystal if it fell on them. That was the last good stretch between them. Afterward came the silent autumn, when Jordan stopped visiting because Grandpa had told his father, at Thanksgiving, that a boy who spent his weekends washing glassware was wasting the only youth he'd get. His father, who could pontificate for a full hour on the dignity of manual labor without ever having held a shovel he wasn't photographing, had returned fire, and Jordan had spent the holiday in the car with the radio on.

"Some of it's still in solution," Jordan said. "The water holds a little alum even when it's cold. Some stuck to the filter paper. Some probably splashed when I poured." He tapped the envelope. "But I can't prove which. That's the part that got me. I know how much I lost, not where."

Grandpa got up and refilled his cup, and the chair scraped the linoleum in the way Jordan had memorized without meaning to. In the mine, Grandpa had said once, you measured what came up the shaft, and what didn't come up, you didn't guess at. You just dug differently next week. Jordan had thought that was a hard way to live. He wasn't sure now. His own method had been to calculate until the numbers matched, and when they didn't match, to decide the scale was wrong.

"Eighty-five and a half," Grandpa said, sitting back down. "In the mill that would've been a good week."

"Dr. Okafor says above ninety is excellent for a first recrystallization." Jordan heard himself and laughed a little. "But she's not the one who has to write it on the poster."

"So write it." Grandpa pushed the envelope back toward him. "Write that you know what you got and you know what it should've been. A man who hides the shortfall hides it the second time too."

Jordan looked at the crystal, at the small perfect faces of it, grown atom by atom from the water in a mason jar on his desk while he slept. He had wanted, all spring, to be the boy whose numbers came out clean. What he had instead was a number with a gap in it, and the honest sentence that the gap was real and its cause was not. He picked up the pen and began printing neatly beneath the division: actual mass divided by theoretical yield, times one hundred, equals 85.6 percent.

"Next year," he said, "I'll cool it slower. Filter it twice." He glanced up. "If I'm still welcome to use the garage for the evaporation dishes."

Grandpa turned the crystal once more in the light from the window, and the facets threw small bright coins across the tablecloth.

"Wash them when you're done," he said. "Both of you. You can tell your father that."

Grandpa's driveway sloped toward the lake road at an angle that made Dylan nervous every time he backed out, and today the cones were waiting for him. Five of them, salvaged from a road crew two summers ago, spaced to the length of Grandpa's Buick plus what Dylan had read was a car and a half. He had set them out himself at seven in the morning, before the heat, and now he stood at the curb while Grandpa lowered himself into the passenger seat with the slow ceremony of a man boarding a ship.

"You're going to memorize this driveway instead of learning to park," Grandpa said, adjusting the mirror he never adjusted while driving. "New lot today. By the post office."

Dylan drove them there with his hands at ten and two, and on the way he passed the orange signs for the bridge construction, the right lane closing in a mile. A line of cars had already gathered in the left lane, nose to tail, while the right lane sat open and empty. He signaled early and slid in behind a pickup, feeling righteous about it, and Grandpa said nothing at all, which was worse than being corrected.

At the post office lot he parallel parked eleven times. Twice he clipped a cone with his rear tire, once he ended two feet from the curb, and by the ninth attempt he had begun to feel the maneuver as something he could parametrize, distances and angles feeding into one another, wheel speed tied to the cone vanishing from the side mirror. It stopped being a sequence of memorized steps and became a single motion. He did not celebrate the good ones. He had learned, from seasons of cross country, that celebrating in practice was a form of attrition, each small satisfaction wearing down the edge he needed for the race itself.

On the drive back they hit the construction again, and this time the left-lane backup was longer, and the open right lane taunted him. His test was in nine days. He wanted, suddenly and badly, to understand what the examiner would think of a boy who sailed down the empty lane while everyone else waited in line like good citizens. It felt like cheating. It also felt like the only sane thing to do.

"Go," Grandpa said, before Dylan could ask.

So he went. He drove the full length of the empty lane, past the patient faces of drivers he could not look at, and at the cone where the lane died, a woman in a hatchback let him in with a small wave, and he took his turn, and the cars behind hers did the same, one and then another, teeth of a zipper. At the narrow bridge Grandpa turned the radio up for half a minute and then off again.

That night, in the guest room with its smell of cedar and old newspapers, Dylan looked it up on his phone with the window cracked to the lake air. Minnesota's Department of Transportation said the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, could cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. He read it twice. The state was telling him the thing that felt like cheating was the thing that worked, and he sat with the discomfort of that, because his mother had raised him on early merging as a species of courtesy, and he did not think she was wrong, exactly. Both lanes full to the end, everyone taking turns. Or everyone queueing early out of politeness, and the line stretching back past the county road. He could hold both ideas at once, but he could not make them agree, and he suspected the examiner might hold either one, depending on the examiner.

In the morning Grandpa was at the kitchen table with coffee and the crossword, and Dylan asked him which he had done yesterday, the polite thing or the right thing, and Grandpa filled in a word before answering.

"I merged late in 1988 and a man in a Grain Belt truck called me a name I won't repeat in this house." He turned the paper sideways, studying it. "He wasn't pithy about it, either. Took him a while."

"So which is it?"

"Ask the examiner," Grandpa said. "Or don't ask, and drive."

On the ninth day, in St. Cloud, the examiner climbed in smelling of pencil shavings and hand sanitizer, and three blocks from the DMV they came upon a lane closure Dylan had not known about. He held the empty lane to the merge point, took his turn at the cones when a box truck let him in, and watched the examiner make a small mark on the clipboard without expression. Dylan kept his eyes forward, ten and two, waiting to find out which kind of man was sitting beside him.

"Turn left at the light," the examiner said. "Then we'll do your parking."

Sarah spread the current map across the picnic table and weighted the corners with her father's least favorite bricks, the crumbly ones he kept meaning to throw out. The map had come rolled in a cardboard tube from her cousin Theo, who was doing a semester at sea and had sent it with a note that read, in his terrible handwriting, "You like weather. This is weather's big sister." She didn't like weather, particularly. She liked knowing why things happened, which was different, and which nobody in her family seemed to understand.

Her little brother Wren wandered out with a popsicle and planted himself on the far bench, dripping orange onto the grass. "What's that," he said, in the tone of someone prepared to be unimpressed.

"Ocean currents," Sarah said. "There's a river of warm water that goes up the Atlantic, and it's the reason England isn't frozen like Canada, even though they're at the same latitude. Look, the lines with the arrows."

Wren leaned over the map, popsicle hovering dangerously. "That's it? It's just a map."

"It's not just a map," Sarah said. "It's an argument."

She had actually said that before she was sure it was true. Her geography teacher, Ms. Okoye, had assigned them each a question to answer for the class, and Sarah's was this: explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. It sounded easy until Sarah tried it, at which point she discovered she had two maps that appeared to disagree. The laminated one from school showed the Gulf Stream ending somewhere west of Britain, while Theo's map showed warm water continuing northeast in a branch labeled North Atlantic Current, curling up toward Norway and beyond. One of them, she had concluded grimly, was a liar.

Wren tapped a spot far in the north, past Norway, where the coast made a hook. "Why is this city in a circle? Did you draw that?"

"I didn't draw anything." Sarah leaned in. The city was Murmansk. Beside it, Theo had penciled something, and she had to tilt her head against the sun to read it. WARM ALL YEAR, ICE-FREE PORT, his note said, and then, less helpfully, GOOGLE IT, I'M OUT OF MINUTES.

"That can't be right," Sarah said. "It's above the Arctic Circle. Ports up there freeze in winter. Every port freezes up there."

"Maybe the map's wrong," Wren said, cheerful. "Maybe your cousin's a dissident. Like he disagrees with the map on principle."
