She had spent the summer reading essayists who said feelings were just chemical weather, meaningless unless you interpreted them, and she had found that freeing, almost luxurious, a permission to be hedonistic about moods, to enjoy them without obeying them. But Theo seemed to be arguing the opposite, that the body's signals were worth decoding, that a racing heart might be telling you something true even if it was confused about the cause. Sitting between those two ideas, with the stadium lights buzzing above her, she could not make them sit still.

The third quarter was all defense, and the cold came on. Lily pulled the message thread back up on her phone under the blanket of the crowd's noise and reread the last thing she had sent before saying yes: "I'm bad at telling whether I actually like people or just like having someone pay attention to me. Fair warning." And his reply, which she had not let herself reread until now: "That's the most honest thing anyone's said to me all year. Same, probably. Let's find out." It was a strange thing to have written to a boy she barely knew, and she had sent it in a moment of either courage or self-sabotage, and she had regretted it and been grateful for it in roughly equal measure ever since.

Priya, meanwhile, had changed her mind about leaving. She had come up to inspect Lily and had planned to descend back to her friends within five minutes, but Marshland intercepted a pass at the goal line and she grabbed Theo's sleeve and stayed, shouting, and Lily found she didn't mind. There was something good about being seen by this family in its natural habitat, loud and easy with itself.

The interception didn't lead to anything. Marshland lost by seventeen, and Theo had been close, and the bleachers emptied slowly, everyone's breath visible under the lights. At the gate he stopped, and his heart was probably pounding from the cold and the game and the walk, and hers was too, and neither of them could have said which crossing they were on, the sturdy bridge or the frightening one.

"So," Theo said. "Same time next Friday? Or is that the bridge talking?"

Lily laughed and pulled her keys from her pocket.

"That's the study talking. I'll let you know by Wednesday."

Zachary had turned eighteen exactly eleven days before the election, which he had initially taken for a sign and then, on reflection, for a coincidence, since the universe had never before shown any interest in his schedule. He walked to the community hall with his registration card folded into his back pocket like a receipt he was afraid to lose. His grandmother had talked about voting the way other people talked about tectonic shifts, whole plates of the country grinding against each other, and he had grown up nodding along without ever quite believing that a single lever pull mattered. His roommate Dev believed something closer to the opposite, that voting was arbitrage, a small trade of your dignity for a fraction of influence, and that you made the trade anyway because fractions added up. Zachary had spent the fall sequestering the two arguments in separate rooms of his head, and this morning the rooms had begun talking to each other.

The hall smelled of floor wax and coffee gone past its natural life. A folding table held a box of donuts with one powdered donut missing, its sugar ghost printed on the cardboard. Behind the table sat a poll worker named Lorraine, seventy if she was a day, wearing a flag pin that had been pinned through a second flag pin, and beside her a younger man with a lanyard and the posture of someone who wanted very badly to be promoted to a county job with dental coverage. A line of about a dozen people shuffled between them and the voting booths, which were plastic modules the size of payphone enclosures and about as private.

"Name," Lorraine said, not unkindly.

"Zachary Reyes-Ostrander." He produced the card. "First time."

She ran a finger down the printed list, then back up, then down a second page, and Zachary felt something in his stomach perform a small, unhurried drop. "You're not here, hon." She checked the card against her list a third time, as though the list might have been embarrassed into correcting itself. "This address, the old precinct? They redrew the lines. You should be at the middle school across town."

"I can't get across town," Zachary said. "I don't have a car. My mom took the car to work." He heard how it sounded, seventeen days of being an adult and still stranded by the family sedan, and he heard the man behind him exhale through his nose.

The lanyard man leaned in. "Under the Help America Vote Act of 2002, he can cast a provisional ballot," he said, quickly, like a man laying down a card he'd been holding for hours.

Lorraine gave him a look that suggested he had said the word provisional at her. "He could," she said. "Or he could go to the right precinct."

"Does it count?" Zachary asked. "If I do it here." He was thinking of his grandmother's grinding plates, and of Dev's arithmetic, and of how both arguments seemed to assume the ballot would be, at minimum, counted.

"Once they confirm you're eligible," the lanyard man said. "The election office checks your registration. If it checks out, it counts."

"So it might not."

"It counts if you're eligible," Lorraine said, in the tone of a woman who had answered this question in four presidential cycles. "If you're registered where you say you're registered, it counts. If you're not, it doesn't." She pulled a sleeve and a pen from a drawer with the efficiency of long habit. "You fill this out, seal it in the envelope, sign the outside. They keep them separate. Then the office verifies."

Behind him, the man who had exhaled said, to no one in particular, "Some of us have jobs," which was interesting, since Zachary could see from his badge on a lanyard of his own that he was currently at a polling station not working.

Here is what Zachary understood, standing at the table with the pen warming in his hand: the provisional ballot was not a lesser vote, but it was a conditional one, a vote held in escrow while the state decided whether he was who his card said he was. It was Dev's trade with an extra step. It was also, he thought, his grandmother's whole worldview in miniature, the idea that your voice went into a machine and then had to survive the machine. He could walk forty minutes to the middle school and vote normally, arriving during fourth period at his early-college program and missing the quiz he had not studied for. Or he could fill out the envelope here, sign his name, and trust a verification process he could not see, conducted by officials he would never meet, in a room he pictured as fluorescent and far away.

He thought about his mother, who had driven him to the DMV on his birthday without being asked, and who would absolutely drive across town at lunch if he texted her, and who would also, if he did that, be late back from lunch and hear about it. He thought about the quiz, which was on supply curves, and about how little he cared, and about how caring so little felt suspiciously like a reason rather than a rationalization, and about whether those were even different things.

He took the envelope to the plastic module and filled in the ovals with a pen on a string. The booth smelled like somebody's grandmother's handbag. Through the gap between the module's curtain and its frame he could see Lorraine explaining to the impatient man that his name wasn't on the list either, and the man saying, "Unbelievable," and Lorraine saying, "It happens," with the serenity of a person who had stopped being surprised by the electorate sometime during the Ford administration. Zachary sealed his ballot in its envelope, signed the flap, and handed it over. Lorraine placed it in a separate folder, apart from the stack of regular ballots, and wrote something in a ledger.

"Am I done?" he asked.

"You're provisionally done," she said, and stamped his card.

He walked out into the cold with his hands in his pockets, and he texted his mother anyway, just to tell her he'd voted, and added a second message before he could think better of it: "I think. Probably. Ask me in a week."

The clinic smelled like the inside of a binder, all paper and antiseptic, and Victor sat on the crinkling exam table with his sleeve rolled up, trying to look like someone who belonged in a body that was being inspected. He was here for his college physical, but also, according to the packet in his backpack, for something else: in September he would start training as a peer health educator, and before the first session he was supposed to be able to explain consent, contraception, and where a person could get tested for infections. His own doctor, Dr. Okafor, had agreed to let him practice on her, which was either a kindness or a trap.

The blood pressure cuff tightened around his arm like it had opinions. Dr. Okafor watched the numbers and frowned, just slightly, the way you frown at a typo in someone else's essay.

"That's high," she said. "Were you nervous coming in?"

"A little," Victor admitted. "Also my mom has hypertension. Congenital stuff runs in my family, or maybe it doesn't, I don't actually know what counts as inherited and what's just... habits."

She wrote something down. "Do you know what your pressure reads at home?"

"We don't have a cuff."

Dr. Okafor nodded and unwound the cuff from his arm. "There's a thing called white coat hypertension," she said. "Pressure reads high here in the clinic, often from nervousness, but it's normal at home. So before I conclude anything, I'd want to check it with home readings, or a monitor you wear all day. One number, one time, in one room, doesn't tell the story."

Victor looked at his own arm, at the pink crease the cuff had left. He had walked in here certain that one reading would instantiate his fate, that the machine would look into him and hand him his heredity like a sealed envelope. The idea that the building itself could be a variable, that the same body could say different things in different rooms, was strange and a little relieving. "So how would I get the monitor?" he asked, and she wrote him a referral and told him the pharmacy kept loaners, and he folded the paper into his packet, where it sat on top of the health educator checklist.

"That's what you wanted to practice?" she said, tapping the packet. "Go ahead. Pretend I'm seventeen and clueless."

He stumbled at first. Consent, he said, was about permission that could be taken back, that had to be clear and ongoing, not assumed from silence or from what happened yesterday. He made her repeat it back to him, which felt absurd with a woman who had checked his tonsils since he was four, but she played along, and the repetition was the point: he was supposed to make the other person say it, not just nod. With contraception he did better, laying out the options like islands in an archipelago, condoms and pills and IUDs, each with its own failure rates and its own logic, no single one the whole answer. She asked questions a real seventeen-year-old might ask, whether two methods were better than one, whether you could feel an IUD, and he answered, and where he didn't know he said so.

The testing part was where his voice thinned. He explained that the campus clinic did it, that it was often free or cheap, that results were confidential even from parents, that you could ask for a full panel and not just what they offered by default. He heard himself say the words and realized he had never said any of them out loud before, only read them in the training modules at midnight with his door shut, and that some part of him had planned to keep that silence going even while standing in front of a classroom teaching other people to break it.

"Better," Dr. Okafor said. "You'll get smoother. You should also know you're going to get it wrong sometimes, say something clumsy, have a kid laugh at you. That's the job."

"Great," Victor said. "The job sounds terrible."

"The job is the reason a kid who's too embarrassed to ask me might ask you." She looked at the referral slip, then at his arm again, and said that in the meantime he should take his own pressure at the drugstore machine, twice, on days he felt calm, and bring her the numbers. Not to decide anything yet. Just to see what his body said when nobody in a white coat was in the room.

In the parking lot he called his mom to say the physical was fine, mostly, probably, pending. He sat on the curb afterward with the packet open on his knees, the referral slip beside the checklist, and texted the friend who had dared him to apply for the training in the first place: guess I have to practice on you next. He pressed send before he could reread it, and watched the three dots appear.

Aaron had signed up for the playwrighting elective because it met during the last period on Fridays, which meant he could leave through the gym doors and avoid the parking lot entirely. This plan lasted exactly one week, until Ms. Rojas announced that the final project was a ten-minute play drawn from the writer's own life, and that each playwright would have to stage it with volunteer actors from the class. Aaron's life, as he understood it, contained no ten-minute moments. It contained, mostly, waiting rooms.

He wrote about the afternoon his father taught him to drive in the empty lot behind the landfill, which was the flattest place in town and smelled like an epicurean experiment gone wrong. In the draft, the father said things like "you're overthinking the wheel" and the son said nothing, and somehow that silence took up four pages. Priya read it over his shoulder during lunch and said it was good, which from Priya meant it was good, and then she volunteered to act in it, and dragged along Marcus, who had failed driver's ed twice and considered this thematically appropriate.

The first rehearsal happened in the choir room on Tuesday, because the drama teacher had the auditorium until four. Marcus played the father with his backpack still on, holding an imaginary steering wheel at chest height like a man praying to a very small god. Priya played Aaron, which Aaron had not expected to find unsettling and did. They read the landfill scene, and then they read it again, and by the third time they were standing in the same square meter of choir room, bumping elbows, both reaching for the same invisible door handle.

"You're on top of each other," Aaron said.

"That's the playwright's fault," Marcus said. "You gave us nowhere to go."

Priya, who had done a summer at the community theatre, looked up from the script. "In scene two of my one-act there last year, we kept colliding, and the director fixed it in one night. She drew the stage on the whiteboard and moved little magnets around, like war planning. It's called blocking. It's the planned positioning and movement of actors on stage, set by the director during rehearsals."

"I'm the director," Aaron said, slowly, as if discovering a tumor.

"You are," said Priya. "Congratulations."

So on Wednesday he came in with the whiteboard markers he had stolen from the math wing and drew the landfill lot, more or less to scale, and put an X for the car and a circle for the passenger side and small arrows like migrating birds. He moved Priya's circle three feet stage left when she stood up to argue a point about momentum, and he discovered that if the father crossed behind the car while the son stayed put, the scene had a shape, a tension, two people orbiting a machine neither of them fully trusted. He had written the scene about driving. Staging it, he found he had written it about distance. He wasn't sure which one was truer, and he decided, for the moment, not to decide, just to draw the arrows.

Ms. Rojas circulated on Thursday, notebook against her chest like a shield, and watched two minutes of the run-through. "Who's blocking this?" she asked.

"I am," said Aaron.

"Hm," said Ms. Rovas, and wrote something, and left. Marcus insisted this was either a compliment or a death sentence, no third option.

The problem was the ending. In real life, the landfill afternoon had ended with his father getting out of the car, walking to the fence, and saying nothing for a while, and Aaron had never known what that silence meant, whether it was disappointment or pride or just a man who liked looking at garbage. In the play, he needed Priya to do something with her body that carried all of that, and every time he tried to place her, it felt like a lie, like he was deciding what his father had felt and pinning it to another person's shoulders. He tried her walking away. He tried her staying still. He tried, briefly, having her get back in the car and mime adjusting the mirror, which made Marcus laugh so hard he knocked over a music stand.

Friday came, and the class performed in the Little Theatre, ten minutes each, alphabetically, which put Aaron second to last. The drive scene worked. The garbage smell did not, but Priya's stillness did; the audience, thirty bored teenagers, went quiet in the way that meant something, and Aaron watched from the light booth, transfixed by his own life being held by other people. Priya stepped out of the car at the end, walked to the taped-off edge of the stage that stood for the fence, and stood there, and did not explain herself, and the lights came down on her back.

Afterward his father was in the lobby, holding the program folded into a small square, which he did when he was thinking.

"Who was the kid playing you?" his father asked.

"Priya."

"She walked away at the end." His father turned the square over once. "I remember I was going to say something, that day. Can't remember what now."

"You could tell me," Aaron said.

His father pocketed the program. "Write it into the next draft," he said. "You're the director, aren't you?"

Mrs. Okafor's office smelled of peppermint and toner, and on her desk a plastic cactus held a sign that said KEEP WATERING. Eve took the chair across from her and put the letter on the desk between them, the way you'd lay down a card you weren't sure you wanted to play.

"Read it again," Mrs. Okafor said.

"I've read it eleven times. It says congratulations. It says the class of incoming first-years. It says a lot of things about spirit and tradition."

"And it says Early Action, right there in the second paragraph." Mrs. Okafor turned the letter toward herself although she had read it too. "You applied Early Action, they answered in December, and the answer was yes. Do you know what that means, exactly?"

Eve did know, mostly. She had read the admissions website at two in the morning with her phone brightness turned low, and the sentence she kept returning to was the one about it being non-binding. "It means I got in early," she said, "but I don't have to go. I can still say no in the spring."

"Correct. So what's the problem?"

The problem was January first. The problem was that regular decision applications to the five other schools on her list were due in thirteen days, and each one wanted an essay she hadn't written, and the part of her that had spent October polishing the proof of why she belonged at Whitlock now argued, with the same rigor, that the theorem was finished and any further work was vanity. Her father called it not looking a gift horse in the mouth. Her mother called it keeping your options open, which in her mother's vocabulary was the highest form of virtue, applicable to colleges and to haircut lengths alike.

"Here's my thinking," Eve said, and unfolded a piece of paper on which she had actually written, at the top, in math class, the word lemma. A lemma, she explained, was a small result you proved on the way to a bigger one; it wasn't the theorem, but you couldn't get there without it. The acceptance was a lemma. It proved she was admissible somewhere decent, which meant the fear that she was admissible nowhere had been disproven, which meant the remaining applications had to be about something other than insurance. The question was what.

"That's either very smart or a way of making a decision sound like homework," Mrs. Okafor said. Down the hall a bell rang, and neither of them moved, because the deadline was the bell now, thirteen days of it.

"The honest version," Eve said, "is that I liked wanting Whitlock more than I've liked having it. Wanting it had this whole, I don't know, glow around it. Now the glow's kind of evanescent. It was gone by the second day, and what's left is a school with a good physics department and a dining hall I've never eaten in." She had not said that out loud before, even to Dellis, who had heard everything else, including the eleven readings of the letter.

Mrs. Okafor spun the plastic cactus a quarter turn. "You have thirteen days to write five essays you don't believe in, or you can bank the yes and be done. Some students would be done."

"Some students should be done." Eve looked at the letter. The seal was embossed, which she suspected had cost more than her winter coat. "But Early Action doesn't make me decide until spring. It just made me decide whether to decide. That's the part nobody warns you about. I thought the answer would end the process and instead it opened a door into another hallway with more doors." She had wanted, she realized, the kind of certainty that gets sequestered somewhere safe, sealed off from further argument, and the letter had refused to provide it.

"So finish the applications or don't," Mrs. Okafor said. "But decide which kind of not-knowing you can live with until May."

Eve picked up the letter, folded it along its original creases, and put it back in her backpack under the geometry homework. "Can I use your printer? I'm going to sequester myself in the library until the Bellingham essay exists, and I want to print the prompt first so I can't pretend I forgot it."

Mrs. Okafor pointed at the printer without looking up from her keyboard, and Eve stood there while it warmed, listening to it grind out a single page, the prompt emerging slowly, like something the machine was reluctant to admit.

Alexander's grandfather had led the Passover seder for forty-one years, and this year, three weeks before the holiday, he handed Alexander a worn Haggadah and said, "Your turn. All of it, from the candles to the last cup."

The kitchen where they stood smelled of his grandmother's simmering brisket, a smell that had presaged every family gathering Alexander could remember. He took the book. The spine gave way at the page with the Ten Plagues, where forty years of thumbs had pressed grape juice stains into the paper. "All of it," he said, not quite a question.

"You'll be at college next year," his grandfather said. "Somebody has to know how." He said it lightly, but Alexander understood it as a kind of countdown, a deadline with a date on it, and after that date nobody in that dormitory would need him to know anything.

The family WhatsApp group, meanwhile, had erupted into war over the seder's timing. His cousin Maya wanted it moved an hour earlier so she could take photos before sunset, and her brother Daniel, home from his first year at yeshiva, had posted a long message about how the seder couldn't begin after dark anyway, which was wrong, Alexander was fairly sure, and which Daniel defended with a confidence that made Alexander want to prove him careless rather than correct. Alexander scrolled and scrolled, and then, past midnight, he stopped scrolling and started searching instead.

He found it in a fragment of Mishnah, Shabbat 7:2. The Mishnah listed thirty-nine categories of work forbidden on the Sabbath, which the rabbis linked to the kinds of work used to build the Tabernacle. Thirty-nine. He read the list twice: sowing, ploughing, kindling, extinguishing, striking a hammer for a final blow. Somewhere online Daniel was arguing that posting a photo to the group counted, and Alexander typed out the Mishnah's line and pasted it into the chat, then deleted it, then typed something shorter: "Look up the list, then tell me which category a phone falls under." He put the phone face-down on his desk and did not entirely sleep.

At the family gathering that weekend, a pre-Passover dinner his aunt hosted so that everyone could argue in person instead of by text, Alexander was put at the head of the table to practice. His grandfather sat at his right, silent in a way that felt like an audience rather than a rest. Daniel sat across from him, arms folded, still holding his phone.

"So," Alexander said, lifting the cup of juice they were using as a stand-in, "we start with Kiddush." He got through it, voice steadier than he expected. When he reached the part where his grandfather always paused to ask the youngest child a question, he paused too, and his eight-year-old niece beat him to it: "Why is this night different?" She grinned, missing a tooth.

"Because we're practicing," Alexander said, and a ripple of laughter went down the table, which he decided to take as warmth rather than mockery. But when he reached the second cup, Daniel cleared his throat and said, "You skipped the paragraph about the sages in Bnei Brak."

"It's a rehearsal, Daniel."

"A rehearsal that leaves things out presages a performance that leaves things out." Daniel said it smugly, an epicure of other people's errors, tasting each one. Alexander's ears went hot. He almost said that at least the rabbis in Bnei Brak hadn't had a WhatsApp group, and then a better thought arrived, unbidden, and he let it stand.

"Maybe I skipped it because we're not at the seder yet," he said. "Or maybe I skipped it because I don't know everything yet. I looked up the thirty-nine categories last night, the ones the rabbis linked to the work of building the Tabernacle, because I wanted to know whether turning on my phone for the Haggadah app would be a problem." He turned to his grandfather. "Would it?"

His grandfather rubbed his jaw. "On the seder nights, which are festival nights, not the Sabbath itself, the rabbis had opinions." He smiled, withholding the opinions the way he had always withheld answers, handing over questions instead.

"Fine," Alexander said, "then before the seder I'll print everything I need, and I'll tell Maya when sunset is, and she can take her photos then. And I won't skip the sages in Bnei Brak, because you're right that skipping things becomes a habit." He said it without heat, and Daniel, who had visibly prepared a rebuttal to heat, uncrossed his arms.

They finished the rehearsal with the youngest child asking the Four Questions off-key and everyone singing anyway. Afterward, in the hallway, his grandfather pressed the Haggadah into his hands for good. "Three weeks," the old man said. "You'll want to know what you don't know by then."

Alexander carried the book out to the car under his arm, and in the driveway he stopped under the streetlight and, judicious about nothing at all, opened it to the page with the wine stains and began, quietly, to read aloud.

Gabriella had promised herself she would finish the essay before Sunday, but by Friday afternoon the document on her laptop was still two paragraphs long, and the second paragraph was mostly a sentence she had deleted three times and retyped twice. The assignment asked her to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, and to do it in plain language, as if to someone with no training. She had come to her grandmother's house for the weekend because the apartment she shared with two roommates had turned into a place where nothing got written, and because her grandmother, who had run a hardware store for thirty-one years, was the plainest speaker she knew.

She found her grandmother on the back porch shellading a chair, brush moving in long strokes, the smell of varnish warm in the September air. Gabriella set the laptop on the rail and said she needed a favor. She needed to explain something out loud, to a person, and she needed that person to interrupt whenever the explanation stopped making sense.

Her grandmother dipped the brush and said, "Go ahead, then. I'm listening."

Gabriella began the way the textbook began, which was a mistake. She talked about the money supply, then about aggregate demand, then about the transmission mechanism, and within four minutes her grandmother had set the brush down and was looking at her with the expression she reserved for a customer who couldn't decide between two kinds of paint. "You've just said a lot of words in a row," her grandmother said. "I counted. I stopped counting at forty." Gabriella scrolled back through her draft and saw that her second paragraph was prolix in exactly the way her teacher had warned against, dense and formal and hiding the fact that she didn't actually understand the chain of reasoning herself.

So she tried a different approach, the way her grandmother would have run it in the store. Suppose, she said, borrowing is very cheap. You'd take out a loan for the delivery van you've been wanting, and so would everyone else, and all that buying pushes prices up, because there's more money chasing the same shelves of goods. Now suppose the central bank raises interest rates. The loan for the van costs more every month, so you wait. So does everyone else. Less buying, cooler prices. Her grandmother picked the brush back up. "That I understand," she said. "That's just the cost of money." But then she asked the question Gabriella had been circling all week: cooled to what? What was the number the bank was aiming at?

Gabriella opened her laptop and searched, and there it was, in a Federal Reserve press release she'd skimmed past a dozen times. On January 25, 2012, the US Federal Reserve adopted an explicit inflation target of 2 percent, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index. Not the grocery-bill number people talked about at parties, but the PCE index, a broader measure. She read the line aloud twice. She had assumed the 2 percent figure was some kind of natural law, ancient and settled, and discovering that it had been made explicit on a specific January day, in her own lifetime, changed the shape of the whole essay. A target was a choice. Someone had sat in a room and decided that a little inflation was healthier than none, and had written that decision down so the public could hold them to it.

She tested the explanation again, standing at the rail while her grandmother sanded a run in the varnish. Raise rates, borrowing slows, spending slows, price pressure eases, and you ease it toward 2 percent, not toward zero, because zero leaves no cushion. Her grandmother asked whether raising rates could go too far, whether you could cauterize the wound so thoroughly you killed the patient, and Gabriella laughed and said that was exactly the critique she wanted in her third paragraph, though she'd phrase it less vividly. She liked that the analogy worked both ways: the tool was real, and it could burn.

That evening she typed until the kitchen light behind her went from gold to gray. There was an exhilaration in it that she hadn't expected, the feeling of an argument snapping into place, each link able to hold a person's weight. She wrote the plain version first, the van and the shelves, and put the machinery underneath it. She kept the questions her grandmother had asked in the margins of her mind, especially the one about how long the cooling takes, how a family waiting to buy a house experiences a year of higher rates as neither abstract nor temporary. Her essay would have to say that the mechanism was understood and the timing was not, and she found she preferred that honesty to a tidier conclusion. She saved the file, then saved it again to a second place, the way her grandmother kept a cash box under the register no matter what the bank said.

Her grandmother came out with two cups of tea and set one beside the laptop. She looked over Gabriella's shoulder at the last line on the screen, then out at the yard, where the evening had gone blue and the shellacked chair was drying in rows of pale light.

"Two percent," her grandmother said. "Written down, for everyone to see. I like that they signed their name to it."

"I'll take that as my epigraph," Gabriella said, and pulled the laptop closer.

Mr. Okafor put the problem on the board before the bell finished ringing: two countries, two goods, one question. "Explain why both of them gain from trading," he said, "even if one country is better at making both. Presentations Friday. No reading off slides."

William copied the numbers into his notebook. Alpha could make twelve shirts or six computers in a day; Beta could make four shirts or four computers. He understood the arithmetic by Tuesday, could compute the opportunity costs, could see that Beta gave up less to make a computer and should therefore specialize in computers. But when his lab partner Dana asked him at lunch why anyone would trade when Alpha was simply better at everything, he opened his mouth and nothing came out. He had the rule without the reason, which felt like owning a key to a house he'd never seen.

"You're doing the face," Dana said, spearing a fry. "The face you do before you decide something's stupid."

"It's not stupid. I just can't say it in a sentence."

"Then say it in two."

He couldn't. That was the problem, and it had a deadline.

Thursday night his mother dropped him at his grandfather's apartment so she could take the car to her shift, and William spread his notes on the kitchen table while his grandfather made tea. He'd hoped for quiet. What he got was the news playing low, and his grandfather standing at the counter saying, "They finally did it, huh. Raised the rates. About time somebody took inflation seriously." He said it the way he said most things, flat, final, a verdict already rendered.

"Is that good?" William asked, mostly to be talking.

"Good? Inflation's a thief. You save thirty years and it melts your savings. They jacked the rates up like this once before, early eighties, and it broke inflation's back. Best thing that ever happened to the dollar."

William nodded and looked back at his numbers. Then his grandfather sat down across from him, slower than he used to, and turned his mug a quarter turn without drinking.

"I was on second shift at the plant then," he said. "They let go of sixty of us in one afternoon. Unemployment went over ten percent that year. Ten percent. Whole parking lot empty by Friday."

William put his pencil down. His grandfather was not a man who told stories for effect; he told them the way a carpenter sets a nail, once, squarely. The tea steamed between them. On the news, a man in a suit was still praising the rate hikes, and William heard both voices at once, the man on the television and the man at the table, and could not make them into one true thing.

"So it worked," William said carefully, "and it also cost jobs."

"It worked," his grandfather said. "And it cost jobs. Both of those are true, and don't let anybody tell you different."

William drove the idea home in the passenger seat, his mother's headlights carving the dark. He had been trying to parametrize the whole problem as one line, one equation where you solved for the answer. But the numbers on his page were like his grandfather's decade: Alpha gains, Beta gains, and inside each country somebody's parking lot goes empty. The shirts-and-computers version let you total the gains honestly, because the gains were real, both countries could end up with more of both goods than before. What the totals hid was distribution, and hiding it was not the same as lying about it, but it wasn't nothing, either.

Friday he stood up with one index card, on which he'd written nothing. He walked the class through Alpha and Beta, let Dana object that Alpha was better at everything, and then said, "Right, that's the whole point. Better at everything isn't the question. The question is better at what compared to what else you could be doing. Beta's worse at both, but it's less worse at computers. So Beta makes computers, Alpha makes shirts, they trade, and both end up ahead." He saw it land, a small rippling of heads, and felt a flash of exhilaration he tried not to show. Then, before sitting down, he added the part he'd decided he couldn't leave out. "Ahead in total. My grandfather lost his job in the early eighties when they raised rates to kill inflation, and unemployment went above ten percent, and the inflation died anyway. Both happened. I don't know how you weigh that. I'm not sure anybody does."

Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard. "That's not on the test," he said. "But it's germane."

"Is it right, though?" Dana asked as they packed up.

William zipped his bag. "It's honest."

Charlie had until seven forty in the morning, when the bus came, and after that the quiz, and after that whatever a chemistry grade did to a transcript it quietly metabolized over the years. So she spread her notebook on the kitchen table between the fruit bowl and her mother's unopened mail, and she wrote the problem at the top of the page the way Mr. Ruiz had printed it: Given 8.0 grams of hydrogen gas burning in oxygen, how many moles of water form?

Her younger sister Nadia came in dragging her blanket and opened the fridge and stood in its light like it was morning already instead of nearly ten at night. "You're still doing that," Nadia said.

"I have a quiz. Go back to bed."

"You're doing it wrong," Nadia said, because nine-year-olds say things like that without needing evidence. She climbed onto the chair across the table anyway and pulled the notebook toward her.

Charlie pulled it back. "You can't even read this."

"I can read the little two." Nadia pointed at the equation Charlie had copied from the board, 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, and then at the drawing beside it, which Charlie had made at the science museum last spring when the demonstrator lit a soap bubble full of hydrogen and it went off with a crack like a cap gun. She had drawn circles for atoms, filling them in during the long ride home. Two circles bonded together, then a pair with a different color in the middle, then the circles again on the right, regrouped. "There's the same ones on both sides," Nadia said. "Four of those and two of those."

Charlie looked at the drawing. She had counted them once on the bus, idly, the way you count fence posts, and it had meant nothing then. It meant something now. "Two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas," she said slowly, tapping the left side, "to form two moles of water." The words fit the picture the way a lid fits a pot. She had copied the sentence off the museum placard into the margin of her notes months ago and forgotten it, and here it was, waiting.

"Obviously," Nadia said, and went to look for the cookies her mother hid behind the oats.

Charlie set up the arithmetic. The molar mass of hydrogen gas was about 2.0 grams per mole, so 8.0 grams was four moles of hydrogen. She wrote it out and checked it twice, because the calculator on her phone had died at sixty percent that afternoon for no reason she could name. Four moles. And two moles of hydrogen made two moles of water, so four moles made four. She wrote 4 mol H2O and underlined it, then sat back and listened to the refrigerator hum and the wind moving the screen door against its frame.

The part she was less sure of was the units themselves, whether a mole was a count or a weight or a trick for converting between them. Mr. Ruiz had called it a number, a very large number, and had compared the class to a virtuoso who could play every note except the one the song was built on, which Charlie had felt was about somebody else. She understood the arithmetic. What she didn't understand was why the world cared enough about atoms to keep them in such exact proportions, why two of one thing and one of another always became two of a third thing and never three, and she suspected that no amount of practice problems would tell her. Maybe later. Maybe the units would harden into sense the way Play-Doh hardens, or maybe they would stay ductile forever, bendable, a tool she could use without fully trusting.

Nadia came back with a cookie and no plate. "Is it right?"

"I think so. Four moles."

"Out of how many?"

"That's not how it works," Charlie said, and then stopped, because she wasn't sure it wasn't. Nadia bit the cookie and watched her with the patience of someone who had nowhere to be until morning.

Charlie turned the notebook sideways and did the problem again from the beginning, in different ink, the numbers coming out the same. 8.0 grams, four moles, four moles. Outside, the streetlight buzzed on, and the kitchen went the color of weak tea. She closed the notebook, put her pencil on top of it, and left both on the table for the morning, where her mother would find them first and move them to the counter beside the fruit bowl, gently, without opening them.

"Do it again," Nadia said, mouth full. "The fire part. On the stove."

"Not on the stove." Charlie carried her sister's cookie crumbs to the sink and swept them into her hand. "Maybe Saturday. With a balloon."

"With the loud one?"

"With the loud one," Charlie said, and turned off the light.

Christian's mother wanted him at the cemetery by six, before the light went, and she had given him forty dollars in tens and a list written on the back of a parking receipt. Marigolds, she had written, then crossed it out and written the real flowers, which meant she had remembered too late what his grandfather had always called them. The market closed at five. He had forty minutes, no car, and a bus that ran every half hour if it ran at all.

He had not wanted this job. His mother was at the apartment arguing with the insurance agent on the phone, using words like indemnify in a voice that got flatter the longer the call lasted, and his little cousins were useless for errands, and so it fell to him. He was the one who had spent the least time with the old man. Two summers, a handful of Christmases, a language he spoke badly and the old man had pretended not to notice. Now he was supposed to find the right flowers for a grave he had never visited, on a day whose customs he only half knew, and be back before the family walked to the gates together.

The bus came at four twenty-five, and he rode it three stops with the folded list sweating in his fist. He was thinking, in a way he didn't like, that it was all theater anyway. Petals on a slab of granite. His grandfather was either somewhere or nowhere, and no flower changed that. At the same time he could hear his mother's voice from the night before, quiet, in the kitchen: he would have done it for us. Both thoughts sat in him without resolving, and he let them.

The market stalls were folding down around him when he arrived, awnings snapping, crates stacked by men who wanted to go home. He found flowers, but the stall nearest the gate had white ones, lilies, stiff and funeral-correct. He bought nothing. At the second stall there were marigolds, but pale, almost yellow, already browning at the edges, and the woman there wanted twelve dollars for a bundle that looked half dead. He said no and kept walking, checking his phone. Four fifty-one.

Tía Rosa had told him, before he left, to go to the back corner, to the stall with the Virgin painted on the side panel, and he had nodded and then walked straight to the first stall he saw. She was not surprised when he called her, breathless, at four fifty-three. She was already pulling on her coat.

"Get out of there," she said. "The corner stall. The one I said." A pause while he ran, past the fishmonger hosing down his tables. "And not those pale ones. Cempasúchil. It has to be the orange ones."

"Why orange? Why does it matter?"

"Because tomorrow is the day, and the day has its flowers." She sounded tired, not impatient. "They go on the altars, on the graves. Everyone knows this, Christian. Except you."

That was true and it stung, and he ran with it stinging. At the corner, an old man with a broom was sweeping marigold heads off the pavement, bright orange ones, a drift of them against the curb like embers. The stall with the Virgin was closed, its shelves bare, and Christian stood there with the phone still against his ear and the minutes going.

"I'll get you the pale ones," Tía Rosa said. "I'm ten minutes away. Your mother can wait ten minutes."

"She can't. We walk in at six, all of us, that was the whole point."

"Then go with what you have. Nobody checks the color of a flower against a rulebook."

"That's not it." He was crouching now, gathering the swept-off blooms from the pavement, the ones that had fallen or been discarded, stems snapped, petals still vivid, still sharp with that smell, dense and resinous, filling his nose even over the fish and the wet concrete. He did not know yet why the smell mattered. He only knew the old man had swept them aside like garbage and that seemed wrong in a way he couldn't have defended to anyone.

Tía Rosa arrived at five past five with the pale bundle in her arms and found him sitting on the curb with a cardboard box full of rescued orange heads, not stems, just heads, hundreds of them, because he had gone back along the row of stalls asking in his bad Spanish for their bruised ones, their floor-sweepings, and the vendors had laughed and given them to him for nothing. She looked at the box, then at him.

"They're not stems," she said. "You can't arrange them."

"I'm not arranging them. I'm scattering them. A path." He stood, and he showed her the flyer he'd taken from a stallholder's nail, the one with the painted altar ringed in orange, a trail of petals leading to it from the edge of the picture. "The color and the smell. That's the whole thing. Bright and strong. It's how the dead find their way back, that's what the day is for. That's what he would have known and I didn't." He heard his own certainty and distrusted it a little, because an hour ago he had called it theater, and some part of him still thought it was, and he did not know how to hold both except to keep moving. "So I make it loud. Orange from the gate to the stone. Even if it's stems or no stems."

Tía Rosa looked at the flyer, then at the box, then down the long axis of the market where the last lights were going out. She put the pale flowers down on the curb.

"Bus comes at five fifteen," she said. "Take the box."

At the cemetery the family was already gathered by the gate, his mother checking her watch, the little cousins holding sugar skulls too big for their hands. Christian came up the path with the box against his hip, and without a word he began at the gate and scattered the orange heads along the ground, a broken bright line toward his grandfather's stone, the smell rising off his sleeves where the petals had crushed against them. His mother watched him the whole way. When he reached the grave and emptied the last of the box over it, she knelt and moved one flower, only one, setting it straight.

"He's home, then," she said.

The gym smelled of floor wax and vinegar, which meant somebody two tables over had brought a baking soda volcano, the same one that had won the year Brayden was a freshman. He set his beakers in a row and checked the balance for the third time. Fifty-eight point four four grams per mole; he had written it on his palm in ballpoint before he found the index card, and now both records disagreed with each other by a decimal place, and the bag of salt on the scale was telling him nothing either way.

"You're the equilibrium kid," said Priya Raman, who had the next table and a poster about moss that looked like it had been designed by a connoisseur of Swiss typography. Her want was obvious and she didn't bother hiding it: the regional slot went to one project, and the judge with the lanyard had already paused at her moss for four full minutes.

"I'm the salt kid," Brayden said. "Equilibrium is just what the salt does." He had dissolved sodium chloride in hot water, cooled it, watched crystals come out, then warmed it again and watched them go back in. Le Chatelier's principle, temperature shifts, a reaction running one way and then the other like a tide that couldn't make up its mind. He had twelve trials, a graph, and one number he could not make lie down.

The problem was the number. His bag held 500 grams of table salt, and table salt, sodium chloride, had a molar mass of about 58.44 grams per mole. He had done the division on the bus: 8.55 moles, give or take, 8.5556 if you didn't round like a coward. But his first trial note said he'd weighed out one mole as 5.844 grams, a factor of ten off, and every concentration on his graph was built on that. The crystals hadn't cared; the salt dissolved the same whether he called it a mole or a tenth of one. Chemistry, it turned out, did not grade your arithmetic.

He was turning the index card over, as if the back might remonstrate with him, when the judge arrived. She was young, maybe a grad student, and she picked up his beaker of saturated solution and held it to the fluorescents like a gemologist, which he chose not to point out was exactly what he had done an hour ago in the bathroom mirror.

"So when you cool this," she said, "what happens?"

"Crystals precipitate. Heat it back up, they dissolve again. The equilibrium shifts with the temperature." He moved the beaker over the hot plate, and the little igneous-looking cubes at the bottom, sharp as basalt chips, began to lose their edges, one by one, the way the gym lost students as the afternoon announcements started. She watched the last crystal go under.

"And how much salt is in there, in moles?" she asked.

Here it was. He could show her the graph, which was beautiful, all smooth curves and confident error bars, and let the mole question slide past on a generality. Or he could tell her that a kid who had built twelve trials on a decimal error had gone back that morning, weighed exactly 58.44 grams, seen with his own hands how much a single mole was, and redone the concentrations in pencil on the train, arriving forty minutes before the doors opened with his tie still in his pocket.

"I got it wrong the first time," he said. "I used 5.844 grams for a mole. It's 58.44. Sodium chloride, whole bag's 500 grams, so about eight and a half moles. The trends are the same either way, the shifts are the same, but the concentrations were off by ten. I fixed them this morning. The pencil parts are the fixed parts."

Priya, pretending to adjust her moss, had gone very still. The judge turned the graph sideways, then right side up, and tapped the penciled column.

"Which is the more honest version," she said, "the one that was wrong confidently or the one that's right in pencil?"

Brayden looked at the beaker, where the warm solution sat clear again, holding all that salt invisibly, ready to give it back the moment things cooled. "The pencil one," he said. "Ink dries before you find out what you don't know."

She wrote something on her clipboard, and Priya drifted over with her moss poster held like a shield, and the hot plate ticked as it cooled.

The vial in Violet's hand was the color of a bruise, and when Mr. Okafor set it in the ice bath, it went the pink of bubblegum, which felt like an insult to something serious. The whole class was bent over the same demonstration, hot water on one side of the lab bench, ice on the other, and everyone was supposed to write down what the color change meant about heat being a product or a reactant. Violet wrote nothing. She was watching the thermometer instead, the way the line of alcohol crept down as though retreating from something.

"Your prediction," said Priya beside her, tapping Violet's blank worksheet. "Which way does it shift?"

"I don't know yet. That's the point of a prediction, isn't it? You're supposed to stake something."

Priya rolled her eyes, but Priya had already filled in her answer with the confidence of someone who had never once been wrong in a way that cost her. Violet had. Last spring she had told her father she would not move with the family to Phoenix in June, that she would stay with her aunt and finish senior year here, and he had said fine, and the fineness of it had sat in the house ever since like furniture nobody moved. She had predicted that the household would shift, absorb it, find a new arrangement. It had mostly just gotten colder in one room.

At the front of the room there was a laminated poster about the principle itself, and she had read it the first week without interest. Today she read it again. The principle was named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. She said the name out loud, quietly, and Priya said, "Le Chatelier. He's the equilibrium guy," without looking up from her vial, and Violet thought that being remembered for one sentence spoken a hundred and forty years ago was either a triumph or a kind of erasure, depending on what else the man had wanted.

The demonstration was the concrete thing. Heat the solution and it went blue; chill it and it went pink; and the class was meant to conclude that the equilibrium shifted to oppose the change, pushing back toward the temperature you had taken away. Mr. Okafor wandered the rows asking questions without giving answers, which was his way of refusing to disenfranchise them of the discovery, though mostly it produced an ennui of blank stares. When he reached Violet's bench, she slid the vial back into the hot water and watched the purple climb through the pink like weather reversing.

"So," he said.

"So if you add heat, it consumes heat. If you take heat away, it makes heat. It leans against whatever you do to it."

"That's the principle."

"It's a bit smug," Violet said. "The system never actually wins. It just softens the loss."

He laughed, one syllable, and moved on, and Priya whispered that Violet thought everything was a metaphor for her home life, which wasn't fair because it was only sometimes true.

After school she took the long way past the science museum, because the new chemistry exhibit had a wall of panels and she had a free hour and no desire to go home to her aunt's subterranean apartment, its windows at sidewalk level showing nothing but shoes. On the historical wall, between Lavoisier and Curie, was the name again, and beneath it the sentence she already knew: the principle was named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. A kid at the panel, maybe ten, was reading it aloud to his mother, stumbling on the surname, and Violet almost corrected his pronunciation and then didn't. He would say it his own way and it would still be the same sentence.

What she kept circling, standing there, was the disagreement between the two versions of the idea she had collected. Mr. Okafor's version was hopeful: systems resist, they compensate, they find their way partway back. Her version, the one she had tested against her father's spare bedroom and the phone calls that had gone from weekly to whenever, was harder: the system only ever absorbs a portion of the blow, and everyone calls that balance. Both were true of the same sentence. She could not make them agree, and she noticed she didn't especially want to, because the wanting was the interesting part.

She took out her phone and texted her father a photograph of the panel, the name and the date and nothing else. Then she stood at the window with her hands in her pockets, watching the shoes go by, pink and blue and brown in the late light, until the phone buzzed against her hip.

Brayden had promised his host brother, Tomás, that he would read the news article aloud twice, but by the second pass he was already speeding up, flattening the Spanish into a rhythm he could control. The kitchen in Tomás's apartment in Salamanca smelled of coffee and scorched milk, and the table between them held the newspaper, folded to a page about water restrictions. In three days Brayden had to stand in front of his summer language class and debate the issue for five minutes, entirely in Spanish, and so far he had managed forty seconds.

"Slower," Tomás said, sliding his own cup across the table so Brayden could finish the milk he had been ignoring. "You are running from the verbs."

"I'm not running. I'm pacing myself."

"You are sprinting toward the end so no one notices the middle." Tomás tapped the article. "Also, you said the restrictions are in Spain."

"They are in Spain. It's a Spanish newspaper."

Tomás leaned over and put his finger on the line above the first sentence, where three words sat alone before the text began: SANTIAGO, CHILE. "This," he said. "The dateline. Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence." He said it lightly, as if pointing out a step Brayden had tripped on, not a lecture. "So this was reported in Chile. About Chile."

Brayden read the line again, feeling the small collapse of a summary he had built his whole argument on. He had spent two evenings assembling notes about Spanish farmers and Spanish reservoirs, and now half of his evidence belonged to a country he had never given a thought to. He wanted to defend himself, to say the dateline was easy to miss, small print pretending to be nothing, but that excuse sounded like exactly the kind of thing his father would say at home when he drove past an exit he didn't want to take. Instead he pulled a clean page toward him and started over, writing the word Chile at the top.

He worked through the afternoon while Tomás studied for a chemistry exam, and when Tomás's grandmother came in from the market, Brayden stood up to take the heaviest bag from her arms before she asked. She thanked him in a rapid, affectionate Spanish he caught only pieces of, and she left him the apricots she had bought too many of, which he took as a sign that his accent had not yet offended anyone past forgiveness.

By evening he had a draft, and the draft had a problem he could not sprint past. The Chilean article argued that water should be priced higher so households would waste less, and it quoted a man in the desert north who already paid more than he could afford. At home in Ohio, Brayden's uncle farmed on wells that ran low every August, and his uncle's answer to everything was the free market, which Brayden had spent years rolling his eyes at. But the Chilean argument was not stupid. Higher prices did make people careful. And the man in the article was real, standing in his yard with a dry tap. Brayden wrote one paragraph for pricing and one against, and then sat looking at them, because the assignment required a position, not a display of indecision.

He read both paragraphs to Tomás after dinner, on the narrow balcony where the putative breeze was actually just warm air shifting, and Tomás listened with his eyes closed, which Brayden had learned meant concentration, not sleep. "Which one do you believe?" Tomás asked.

"I believe pricing works and it's unfair at the same time. I think I want to say the price should rise, but the money should go back to the poorest households so the burden lands somewhere else. Someone smarter than me probably has a reason that fails."

"That's fine," Tomás said. "Say that it might fail. Five minutes is not so long. You can be honest in five minutes."

The morning of the debate, Brayden's teacher, Señora Iriarte, called him third, and he walked to the front with his notes folded in his pocket, a paper he mostly did not intend to open. He began in Spanish, slowly, the way Tomás had drilled him, and when he cited the article he named the dateline first, the way you would introduce a person properly before quoting them: a story reported from Santiago, Chile. Later, when a classmate named Priya gave her summary and said a water crisis had happened in Mexico, Brayden saw the dateline sitting at the top of her article, ignored, small print pretending to be nothing, and after class he caught her in the hallway and pointed to it without saying he had done the same thing two days before.

"Chile," he said. "That changes your second paragraph."

She looked at the line, then at him. "Does it change yours?"

"It already did," Brayden said, and handed her one of the grandmother's apricots.

The timer on the oven ticked down, and Mia spread her chemistry notes across the counter beside the cooling rack, where her grandmother's recipe for lemon bars sat propped against the flour canister. Thursday's quiz was on stoichiometry, and Mr. Reyes had promised it would be the kind of problem that separated the people who understood from the people who had merely memorized. The problem in front of her looked simple enough: given a mass of reactant, calculate the moles of product formed. She had copied the balanced equation off the board herself, 2 AlCl3 yielding 2 Al and 3 Cl2, and she felt a small pride in how tidy it looked.

She read the problem again. 53.4 grams of aluminum chloride. She looked at the equation, saw the big 2 in front of AlCl3 and the big 3 in front of Cl2, and did what seemed obvious: she set up 53.4 grams over 2 and multiplied by 3, as though the coefficients were a recipe in grams, like the two cups of sugar and three tablespoons of lemon zest in her grandmother's bars. The answer came out enormous, something like 80 grams of chlorine gas, and she wrote it down and underlined it before the smell of browning butter made her glance at the oven.

Her sister Denise came in from the porch with her epidemiology textbook under one arm, home for the weekend, and started opening cabinets without asking. "You're going to burn those," Denise said, nodding at the oven, and Mia pulled the pan out and set it on a wire rack, the crust golden at the edges and pale in the middle, exactly as the recipe promised it would be if you caught it in time.

"It's the quiz tomorrow," Mia said. "I think I got the first one." She slid her notebook across the counter. Denise looked at it for maybe four seconds, and then her face did the thing it always did, the tectonic shift from casual to serious, one eyebrow rising like a slow fault line. "Where did you get eighty grams?"

"From the equation. Two goes to three, so I took the grams times three over two." Mia heard her own confidence and, hearing it, began to doubt it, the way you can hear a wrong note only after you've played it.

Denise didn't explain. That was the deal between them, ever since Denise had helped her with algebra in eighth grade and they'd both learned that Mia remembered things better when she found them herself. "Look at the periodic table," Denise said. "What's the molar mass of aluminum chloride? Just add it up." Mia pulled the table from the back of her binder and did the arithmetic on a paper towel, 26.98 for aluminum plus three chlorines at 35.45, and got 133.33 grams per mole. She wrote it down and then sat with it, pencil hovering, because the paper towel was telling her something she hadn't wanted to hear. If one mole of the compound weighed that much, then her 53.4 grams was less than half a mole, and a half mole of reactant could not possibly produce 80 grams of product. Matter didn't work that way. Something in her setup had treated the equation as though it spoke in grams, and it didn't.

"The coefficients aren't grams," Mia said slowly, converting first, dividing 53.4 by 133.33 to get 0.400 moles. Then, only then, she applied the ratio, two to three, and the moles of chlorine came out to 0.600, a number so reasonable she almost laughed. She checked it against the back of the book where Mr. Reyes had printed one answer, and it matched, and she sat back on the stool with the paper towel still in her hand. "The coefficients give the ratio of moles, not the ratio of masses," she said, mostly to the lemon bars.

"Which you figured out yourself," Denise said, and stole a corner of the crust while it was still too hot, juggling it between her fingers. Mia copied the whole solution onto a clean sheet, step by step, and then did a second problem from scratch without looking, converting grams to moles first every time. The third problem she did while the bars cooled, and when her answer matched her estimate, she drew a small check mark in the margin, private and emphatic.

Later, when the kitchen had gone quiet and Denise had gone back to her textbooks at the table, Mia wiped the counter and thought about the check she still hadn't gotten back on her car insurance, the one her mother kept saying they'd amortize across the spring payments, spreading the cost out the way Mia now spread grams into moles before she could use them. Some conversions you had to make before the numbers would mean anything. She stacked her notes, squared the corners, and left the best lemon bar on a plate by Denise's elbow without a word.

"Hey," Denise called after her, fork already in hand. "Same time next unit?"

Alexia had signed up to volunteer at the food bank stationed behind Fairmont Seniors' Residence mostly because the form said Saturday mornings, and Saturday mornings were the ones she couldn't fill with anything better. The coordinator, a brisk woman named Doris, handed her a paper smock and told her the produce was coming in from a farm partnership, so she'd be sorting, not shelving. Behind the loading door, an old man in a cardigan sat in a folding chair as though he'd been requisitioned along with the tables. His name tag read HAROLD, and he was watching a crate of squash with an expression of professional interest.

"You're new," he said. It wasn't a question. Harold, she learned in the next ten minutes, had been an inspector for the agricultural board, forty-one years, and he now treated the food bank's intake as his personal jurisdiction. What he wanted, though he said it sideways, was to be driven to the farm. He'd heard the volunteers were going out to the fields today, and he mentioned it twice, then a third time, the way people mention things they've decided not to ask for directly.

The squash puzzled Alexia. It was good squash, unbruised, heavy in her hands, and she kept expecting the reveal, the rot, the reason it had been given away. When she asked Doris, Doris just laughed and said it hadn't been given, it had been picked up, and that the real run was leaving in fifteen minutes if anyone wanted to come. Alexia looked at Harold. Harold looked at the van.

The fields sat below a montane ridge, the farm's upper pastures still shadowed by the mountain at ten in the morning. The main harvest had already gone through, Doris explained on the drive, and what they were doing today was what remained after. Alexia bent into the dirt between the rows and found them littered with squash the machinery had missed, whole and sound, sunk in the furrows like something buried on purpose. There was a word for this, Doris said offhandedly, answering a question from one of the other first-timers: "It's called gleaning." The word sat oddly in Alexia's mouth, biblical, old, and yet here it was attached to a Saturday and a paper smock.

Harold worked two rows over, slower but exact, turning each squash before he took it, and when Alexia dragged her crate to his side he told her about the grades of produce, how a vegetable could be perfectly edible and still not be perfectly sellable, two judgments that only sometimes overlapped. She'd been thinking of waste as a single thing, one big problem, and here it was sliced into categories: what couldn't be sold, what hadn't been picked up, what nobody had come back for. The squash in her hands was the third kind. Or maybe the second. She wasn't sure the lines were as clean as Harold's grading language implied.

"Ask her if I can come back next week," Harold said to Alexia quietly, nodding toward Doris. He hadn't asked Doris anything himself, and Alexia understood suddenly that his inspections and his cardigan and his forty-one years were being held out like credentials to a woman who only needed a volunteer who could kneel in dirt. There was something both noble and slightly sad in it, and she couldn't decide which quality was the truer one, or whether they cancelled each other out, or whether that was even a question that made sense. She asked Doris anyway.

"Every Saturday," Doris said. "If he can get himself down here."

"I'll get myself down here," Harold said.

They filled the van by noon, and Alexia rode back with the windows cracked and the smell of field dust on her hands. She kept turning over the morning the way Harold had turned the squash, examining it. The food bank had seemed to her, before, like a place where charity flowed downhill from the generous to the needy, a simple slope. But the slope ran in circles: farmers who couldn't sell everything, volunteers who picked what was left, residents like Harold who sorted it and wanted, in their own way, to be needed. She had walked in assuming she was giving something away. She was less certain now what had been given, or by whom, or what exactly she'd carry back to her dorm in the fall when Saturday mornings were hers again. There would be other Saturdays, though. That much she'd decided.

At the residence, they unloaded the crates together, Harold passing each one to her with the ceremony of a man handing over evidence. He held the last squash a moment longer than necessary, a small crookneck with a pale flank where it had rested on the soil.

"This one would've rotted by Thursday," he said. "Nobody would've ever known it existed."

He set it in her hands instead of the crate. "Take it home. Consider it requisitioned."

The protocol sheet had been taped to the inside of the equipment shed since September, curled at one corner, and Brooke had walked past it a hundred times without reading it. She read it now, while the rest of the team did their warmup laps around the far field. After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play. Each step was listed in a column, and beside the column a line said an athlete moved to the next step only while free of symptoms. That was all. It looked almost too simple to matter, like instructions for assembling a shelf.

Priya jogged over from the track, hair still damp from the shower she'd taken after her morning session with the trainer. She had been symptom-free for four days, which was why today was supposed to be light drills, ball work, no contact, no heading. Brooke folded the sheet into her pocket without deciding to.

"You look perspicacious," Priya said, squinting at her. "Or constipated."

"I look like a captain who's down a center back before semifinals." Brooke tossed her the ball. "Ten touches, easy passes, nothing fancy."

The drill was simple by design. Brooke stood twelve yards off and rolled the ball to Priya's feet, and Priya turned and slotted it into an open goal, again and again, the net shivering each time with a small dry sound. The October light came in low across the park, gilding the seed heads in the unmowed strip beyond the touchline. A man flew a kite near the fountain, reeling it in slowly when it dipped.

At the ninth pass Priya stopped. She stood with her hand flat against her forehead, the way people do when a sound has been too loud, and Brooke knew before Priya said anything. "It's back," Priya said. "The headache. It's mild, but it's the same one."

Brooke's first instinct, the one she was least proud of, was to ask whether it was really the same one, or just ordinary tiredness, the kind everyone played through. The second instinct came from the folded paper in her pocket. She took it out and unfolded it against her thigh. The steps ran from rest at the bottom to full play at the top, and Priya was on one of the low ones, light drills, and the rule was that you moved up only while you stayed free of symptoms. There was nothing in the fine print about mild, or about semifinals, or about how badly Fernbrook needed a center back who could read a through ball before it was played.

"You go back a step," Brooke said.

"I know. I hate that I know, but I know."

Coach Renner appeared at the edge of the drill area with his clipboard and his particular talent for arriving at the wrong moment. "How's she looking?" he asked, and Brooke understood that he was asking a different question than the words carried. He had been trying to resuscitate this season since August, when three starters moved away and the league realigned and Fernbrook started drawing schools twice its size. He was not a cruel man. He was a tired one, and Priya's return would have meant something to him beyond the back line.

"Mild headache came back during the drills," Brooke said. "So she steps back a stage. Rest again, or whatever the stage below this is. Then she works up from there."

"We could try her Thursday, see if it clears."

"She stays free of symptoms before she moves up. That's how it works. Every step." Brooke heard her own voice, steadier than she felt. She had wanted Priya on the field so badly that she had almost been willing to translate a headache into something smaller, and the wanting was still there, honest and unresolved, sitting in her chest alongside the decision. Both things were true. She could hold them at once.

Renner looked at the goal, at the kite climbing again near the fountain, at his clipboard. "All right," he said. "Same drill, Priya, you're on distribution with me. No heading."

Priya walked off with him, slower than usual, one hand still at her temple now and then, like someone checking a bruise. Brooke stayed by the goal and re-read the sheet one more time, top to bottom, rest to full play, the small ordered stairs of it. Then she folded it and put it back in her pocket, and called for the next group to bring the balls in.

Alexandra's laptop sat open on the kitchen table between a bowl of forgotten cereal and her mother's grocery list, and on the screen the city hung there in colors she had chosen herself: pale yellow where the flood risk was low, deepening through orange into a red so saturated it looked like a warning about something else entirely. She had spent the whole evening on the first layer, the water, and now she was trying to add the second layer, the housing, and the software kept asking her questions she could not answer in a language she had only started to learn that week.

"No," she said to it, out loud, because there was no one else to say it to. Her mother was at the clinic until ten, which meant Alexandra had the apartment, the software trial that expired in nine days, and a deadline for the summer program application that wanted a project proposal by Friday. The proposal was supposed to show something. That was the whole problem. She had two maps and no argument.

She called Dev on video and propped the phone against the sugar bowl. He answered from his porch, half his face lit by the streetlight. "Did you fix the shapefile," he said, not really a question.

"Did you fix your introduction," she said back, and he groaned, which meant no. His project was cholera, something historical, and he'd been stuck on the opening paragraph for three days while she got stuck on everything after the opening. They had traded problems without noticing.

"You know what you should do," he said. "Start with the map guy. Snow. We read about him last year, in whatever class that was." He was already typing, and then he was reading off his screen. "In 1854, John Snow, a physician, mapped cholera deaths in London and showed they clustered around one water pump on Broad Street." He looked up. "One pump. All those deaths, clustered around one spot. My book says it's an early example of spatial analysis."

"Spatial analysis," Alexandra repeated, and her eyes went to her own screen, to the yellow and orange and red. He had said the phrase like a label on a jar, and she turned it over in her mouth the way you turn over a word that suddenly fits a thing you've been carrying without a name. He had mapped deaths; she was mapping water. Deaths clustered around a pump; she wanted to see whether the red parts of her city and the cheap housing parts of her city were the same parts, or nearly.

"Dev," she said, "that's literally what my map is. Except nobody's dying, probably, yet, it's just, okay, so the census tracts with the oldest housing stock are mostly east of the river, I already know that from the housing layer, and the flood model says the east side takes on water in a hundred-year storm because it's low and the drainage is bad, and I keep feeling like I'm about to see something and then the layers won't line up. The parcels are in one coordinate system and the tracts are in another and I don't know which one is wrong."

"That's not the interesting part," Dev said. "The interesting part is why you're doing it."

She hated when he did that. She let the call go quiet and pulled up the tract layer anyway, and tried the projection tool one more time, and this time she picked the coordinate system the parcels were using, not the one the tutorial had used, because the tutorial was written for a city in Texas and hers was not in Texas. The software thought about it. The two layers slid toward each other, snapped, and sat down together on the same grid.

She set the housing layer to fifty percent transparency and laid it over the flood layer, and the map transfigured in front of her, not into something new exactly, but into something she had suspected and could now see: a corridor of red where the housing layer went dark, tract after tract, the places where rent was cheapest standing inside the places where the water would go. Not every parcel, not perfectly. There was one tract in the red zone with newer buildings, brick row houses from the nineties, and another outside it that was poor anyway, and she flagged both in her notes because she didn't want the map to say more than it knew. Her mother would come home tired from the clinic, would say the body is one thing and the neighborhood is another, antigens and water systems and landlords, all of it moving through the same streets, and Alexandra wanted to hand her this map and ask her whether that was true.

"Dev," she said. "I think I've got it. It's not proof, it's just, the pattern's there." She turned the transparency down and the pattern sharpened; she turned it up and it softened, and she made herself leave it somewhere in the middle, where it was honest.

"So write that," he said. "Write that it's a beginning."

Her mother's key scraped in the lock at 9:40. Alexandra left the map glowing on the table and went to heat up the rice, and when her mother came in with her querulous, end-of-shift voice, asking whether anything had happened today, anything at all, Alexandra said, "Come look at my map. I found where the water goes."

Daniel had taped the poster of the mitochondrion to the fence between the lilac bush and the compost bin, and by noon the sun had bleached it to the color of weak tea. He sat on the patio steps with a biology textbook open on his knees, drawing arrows in chalk on the concrete. Glucose went in at the top of the driveway, broke into two smaller pieces near the grill, and the arrows converged at a lopsided oval he had chalked beside the birdbath. Inside the oval he wrote "ATP" and then crossed it out and wrote "makes ATP here," because the poster said the mitochondrion was where most of it got made and he wanted to be able to say why without looking.

The placement exam was in eleven days.
