If he scored well enough, the college would let him skip introductory biology and go straight into genetics, which was the whole reason he had chosen the school, and also the reason he could not afford to be lazy about the parts he found dull. His sister Maya was home for the weekend, and she came out barefoot with two glasses of lemonade and the particular gravitas of a person who had survived her first year of college and intended for you to know it.

"Quiz me," Daniel said, before she had sat down.

"Fine. Follow one glucose all the way through. Out loud, and if you say 'and then stuff happens,' I'm going inside."

He started at the top of the driveway and walked the chalk path as he talked, crouching to tap each arrow. Glucose split, a small payoff of ATP, some electron carriers loaded, then the oval by the birdbath where the carriers dumped their cargo and the big harvest came out. He could feel the sequence assembling itself correctly for the first time, the way a phrase finally sits right in your mouth after weeks of stumbling.

"You missed where the oxygen fits in," Maya said, but not unkindly. She was peevish about being interrupted from her book and trying not to show it, and the effort made her gentle.

"At the end. It takes the electrons so the whole thing doesn't back up." He took the lemonade anyway. "I actually know that one."

She flipped to the back of his textbook, where he had dog-eared a page with a chart he had been avoiding. "Then what's this? You've bent the corner on the codon table for three days."

"That's not going to be on it. It's genetics, not respiration."

"Read it to me."

He made a face but read it, and somewhere in the middle of the grid of letters he stopped. Every entry was three letters long. There were sixty-four of them. Then he counted the names in the right-hand column, running his finger down the rows, and found only twenty different amino acids. Leucine alone claimed six of the three-letter groups. He counted again with the lemonade glass sweating against his wrist.

"Sixty-four codons," he said slowly. "Three bases each. But only twenty amino acids. So most amino acids have more than one codon." He looked up. "Why would it be built like that? That's, like, redundancy. Like the cell braced itself."

"Beats me," Maya said. "I switched out of bio second semester. But you look like somebody just handed you a prize."

He laughed, embarrassed, and drew sixty-four short chalk ticks in a band along the edge of the patio, then grouped them into twenty clusters, some crowded and some standing alone. It was not respiration. It was not on the exam. But the two systems suddenly felt like they belonged to the same world, one burning fuel to keep the other reading instructions, and he could not make himself regret the detour. Whether the redundancy was sloppiness or protection, or something he did not yet have the words for, he could not say, and he wrote a question mark at the end of the chalk band and left it there.

Maya stood and brushed chalk dust off her shorts. "You know you're going to sit out here until dark."

"Probably," Daniel said. He walked back to the top of the driveway, stood over the chalked glucose with his hands in his pockets, and started again from the beginning.

Nicole had forty-one minutes left before the registration portal closed, and the cursor blinked in the last empty field as though it enjoyed her hesitation. The kitchen smelled of burnt toast from her brother Dev's attempt at breakfast, and from the living room her mother was arguing with the television again, which had become the house's chief occupation since September. Nicole had turned eighteen nine days ago. The birthday card from her aunt in Chennai had arrived late, as it did every year, and was still taped above her desk.

The phone buzzed. A photo from Aunt Meena: her hand raised toward the camera, middle finger stained a deep violet from knuckle to nail, her face behind it bright with something Nicole could only call ceremony. Below the photo, her aunt had written, "Democracy tastes like ink today." Nicole laughed, then stopped, because she realized she did not know why ink mattered. She typed back a question mark, and while she waited, opened a new tab beside the registration form, splitting the screen exactly in two.

The answer came quickly and it delighted her. Since its 1962 general election, India had marked voters' fingers with indelible ink, based on silver nitrate, so no one could vote twice. The stain could not be washed off; it rode the skin for days, a public tally of a private act. Dev appeared in the doorway with his toast, saw the photo, and leaned over her shoulder. "What happened to her finger?"

"It's indelible ink," Nicole said. "Silver nitrate. They've used it since their 1962 election, so nobody can vote twice."

"Like a hand stamp at a club," Dev said, and stole the last of her tea.

She scrolled further, past a column that excoriated the government for everything from farm policy to the price of cooking gas, past a think piece arguing that the country's politics had turned toward an autochthonous idea of the nation, one that drew its authority from claims of soil and origin. Nicole read that sentence twice. She was trying to hold it in her head, to turn it over, when her mother called from the living room, asking whether she had finished registering yet, and the two halves of her screen seemed to pull in opposite directions.

Because the trouble was this: her mother had opinions the way other people had furniture, substantial and hard to move, and she had made it clear over dinner last week that a person's first vote was a family matter, a inheritance passed down like the good silver. And Nicole's own leanings, formed late at night from polls and primary results and a candidate's speech she had watched three times with her headphones on, pointed somewhere else. When she had hinted at this, her mother had excoriated that candidate with such fluency that Nicole had felt her own position wobble, not because the argument was wrong but because it was her mother's voice making it.

Her friend Priya texted: "Did you register? Everyone at school is doing it today, it's basically the zeitgeist." Nicole looked at the word and thought it was exactly the kind of thing Priya would say, and also exactly true, and that both of those facts made it harder to trust. Aunt Meena's finger glowed in the corner of the screen. Her aunt lived alone, had argued with Nicole's mother about politics for thirty years and still called every Sunday, had stood in a queue in the heat and come out purple-fingered and grinning. That was a person who had not inherited her vote. That was a person who had chosen it and then shown the evidence, and kept choosing, and kept showing it.

Nicole looked at the clock. Twenty-two minutes. She could hear Dev and her mother debating whether to order lunch, a smaller argument with the same architecture as the larger one. She thought about the indelible ink, how it did not tell anyone whom you had voted for, only that you had voted; how it marked participation rather than allegiance, a stain that carried no content except presence. That was not the whole answer. She still did not know whether she was voting against her mother to become herself, or merely to prove that she could, and she suspected the two motives were braided too tightly to separate tonight, or maybe ever.

She pulled the keyboard toward her. She filled in the last field, checked the box, and pressed submit, and the confirmation number appeared on the screen like something newly minted. Then she screenshotted Aunt Meena's photo and sent it to Priya with the caption, "goals for November." Her mother called from the kitchen, "Nicole? Did you finish?"

"Finished," Nicole called back, and minimized the tab before her mother could reach the doorway.

Laura had told herself all summer that she did not care about the art elective, and by the second week of August she had almost convinced herself, which was as close as she usually got to anything. The elective met in the craft cabin at Camp Wenonah, where the smells of turpentine and bug spray mingled into something that could cure ennui or cause it, depending on the hour. Fifteen campers sat on stools around a print of Frida Kahlo's "The Two Fridas," and Mrs. Okafor had said only, "Tell me what you see. Formally. Colour, composition, symbolism. Two pages by Friday."

Laura wanted the two pages to be the best ones handed in, because she had been the best at English at school and because being the best was the only thing she had packed that still fit. This was the part she did not say out loud, and the narrator of her own summer, being Laura herself, preferred to describe her motives as curiosity.

She sat beside Danny, who painted. Danny painted the same sugar maple by the lake every single day, dawn and dusk, and on Wednesday he spread his small studies across the picnic table like cards and said, "It's the same tree. Twice a day. Maybe that's not enough variety, maybe I'm just repeating myself."

"Monet didn't think so," said Priya from the end of the table, without looking up from her sketchbook. "Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year." She said it flatly, the way she recited everything, and Danny stared at her, and Laura felt something rearrange itself behind her ribs. Thirty paintings of one stone face, and nobody called that repetition. They called it a series.

That night she took the Kahlo print to the porch of her cabin and worked with a flashlight, which Mrs. Okafor would have maligned as a way to ruin one's eyes and one's color sense, and Laura wrote about the divided canvas, the two women holding hands on a bench, the storm sky pressing down, the exposed heart on the left Frida with its artery cut and dripping, the right Frida holding a small portrait of Diego. She wrote that the white dress of the bleeding Frida and the Tehuana dress of the loved Frida made a composition split down the middle like an argument the painter was having with herself, and that the symmetry was deliberate, the kind of balance that holds because both sides are pulling.

She was proud of that sentence. She underlined it, which she never did, and she did not think about the fact that she had described Kahlo's divided self with a certain clinical enthusiasm, as if heartbreak were a design problem she could solve from a picnic table in Ontario.

Thursday afternoon, Danny asked to see her draft. She handed it over with a show of reluctance that was mostly vanity. He read it slowly, twice, and said, "You write like nothing touches you."

"That's formal analysis," Laura said. "That's the whole point."

"No," Danny said. "Priya writes formally and you can feel her breathing under it. Yours is like a coroner's report with adjectives." He said it kindly, which was worse. She took the pages back and told him that a painter of one tree, twice a day, was in no position to lecture anyone about depth, and she meant it to sting, and she saw it land, and she walked down to the lake before he could see her face do whatever it was doing.

At the water's edge sat Priya, who was, according to everyone at camp and according to Laura on most days, insufferable, doctrinaire about technique, correct about everything. Laura sat down anyway. The light was going gold the way it does at seven, and across the water Danny's sugar maple stood catching it, the same tree he would paint again tomorrow at dawn, and again at dusk, and it occurred to Laura that the tree was not the same tree at all, not to Monet, not to Danny, not to anyone who bothered to look twice.

"Priya," she said. "Is it possible to do formal analysis and still be honest? About it hurting, I mean. The painting."

Priya considered this the way she considered everything, with her whole narrow attention. "The form is how it hurts," she said. "The cut artery isn't a decoration. Describe the drip and you've described the pain. You just have to let yourself notice you noticed."

Laura went back to the porch and wrote until the flashlight dimmed. She kept the sentence about the argument the painter was having with herself, and under it she added one line: the storm sky is not background; it is pressure, and the two women hold hands anyway, which is either hope or habit, and the painting refuses to say which. She could not decide if that was a good sentence or a failure of nerve, and she decided to leave it in precisely because she could not decide.

Friday she handed in her two pages, and Mrs. Okafor read them during free swim and said nothing, only wrote at the bottom, in green ink, "See me." Laura stood at the cabin doorway with wet hair, and Mrs. Okafor looked at her over the print of the two Fridas, hand in hand under their storm, and said, "The last line. Did you mean it?"

"Yes," said Laura. "And no."

"Good," said Mrs. Okafor, and handed the pages back, and outside, down the hill, Danny was setting up his easel by the lake in the flat grey light before rain, painting the tree again.

Seth had the smaller of the two study rooms reserved until five, and his cousin Dez was already fifteen minutes late. He spread the printouts across the table anyway: an article from a parenting blog his aunt had forwarded him, with a highlighted paragraph about a study of twelve children whose parents claimed they changed after the MMR shot, and beside it the library database open on his laptop, where he had been typing search terms for an hour.

Dez came in with a soda he wasn't supposed to have in the room and dropped into the chair across from Seth. "Mom wants me to tell you she's not being irrational," Dez said. "She read things. She sent you the things."

"You're getting the shot Tuesday," Seth said. "For college. So I'm going to figure out what she read." He turned the laptop so Dez could see the screen. The article had a photo of a toddler and a caption in bold type, and the word "cover-up" appeared three times in the first two paragraphs.

"She says twelve kids is twelve real kids," Dez said. "Not a statistic."

Seth scrolled through his database results. He had learned the interface in an hour: filters for peer reviewed, for date, for study type. Most of what came up was small, mouse studies or surveys, until he landed on a Danish study from 2019. He read the abstract twice, then the numbers at the top of the methods section, because he almost didn't believe the first pass.

"This one followed more than 650,000 children," Seth said. "Published in 2019. Danish. No link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Not even in kids who had autistic siblings, which would be the highest-risk group you could pick."

Dez leaned over the table. "Six hundred fifty thousand?"

"More than that. Twelve kids versus more than 650,000." Seth wrote the comparison on the whiteboard in the corner of the room, the way his physics teacher did when two quantities belonged side by side. Twelve on the left, 650,000 on the right. He underlined nothing. The numbers looked different next to each other than they had apart.

"That's a lot of kids," Dez said. "But how do you know they didn't mess it up? The twelve-kid guy could be the honest one."

"That's the thing, I don't know that from one study either way." Seth pulled up the citations. There were other papers citing the Danish one, groups who had run their own numbers in other countries, some of them large, some small, and a letter to the editor that raised a complaint about a variable and a reply that addressed it point by point. He read part of the reply out loud, the dry back-and-forth of two research groups arguing over a definition. "Nobody's saying trust this one paper. They keep checking each other. The twelve-kid thing didn't hold up when other people tried it."

Dez drank his soda. "So it's like, whoever checks the most wins?"

"Sort of," Seth said, then stopped, because that wasn't quite honest. "More like, one result can be a fluke or a lie or bad luck, and you can't always tell which from the outside. But when it's been tried over and over by people who get nothing out of agreeing, that's the closest thing we've got." He looked at the blog article again, at the scathing tone of its last section, where the author called pediatricians whores for pharmaceutical companies and promised that the truth was being cauterized out of the public record. Seth didn't know what the author thought cauterize meant, but the word had a violence to it that made him sit back.

"Are you going to tell Mom she's wrong?" Dez asked.

"I'm going to send her both. The twelve-kid thing and this one, with the numbers. And a note that says one guy with twelve kids isn't the same as a country with 650,000, and that if she still wants to wait, that's her call, but she should see the size of what she's weighing it against." Seth closed the laptop halfway. "I can't make her read it."

Dez stood, crumpled the can, and shot it at the recycling bin by the door. It bounced off the rim and rolled under the microfiche cabinet. "Your sagacity is going to go over great," he said, fishing it out.

"Tuesday," Seth said. "You're still getting the shot."

"Tuesday," Dez said, and held the door open with his foot while Seth gathered the printouts and left the whiteboard as it was, twelve on one side and 650,000 on the other, for whoever had the room next.

The U-Haul trailed them like a disobedient dog, swaying on every curve of Route 9, and Christopher watched it in the side mirror because it was easier than watching Ohio go by. His phone sat in his lap at four percent, and he had been trying to resuscitate it with a cord that only worked if he held it at an angle no human arm could sustain for more than a minute. In the back seat with him sat a shoebox of things his mother had deemed nonessential, which was to say essential: ticket stubs, a whistle from sixth grade, seventeen folded notes he had not reread because rereading them felt like proofreading a eulogy. His father drove. His mother read aloud from her phone in the way she read everything aloud, as though silence in a car were a mechanical failure.

"There's a study," she said. "This researcher, Jeffrey Hall, in 2018. He estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about ninety hours together."

"Great," Christopher said.

"Isn't that something. Ninety hours."

"Dad. Make her stop."

His father did not make her stop, because his father believed that information was a form of affection, which was one of the many ways they were related, consanguinity being the fancy word for it, a word Christopher had learned for the SAT and resented because it sounded like a diagnosis. The plan had been that he would see Marcus and Dee yesterday, one last time, at the quarry where they'd swum since seventh grade. The plan had lasted until the movers came early and his mother decided they would leave a day ahead of schedule, and Christopher had said fine, whatever, in a voice so flat that both parents pretended not to hear it, which was its own kind of hearing.

At a diner outside Zanesville his phone got two bars and the messages arrived in a swarm. Dee: you left without saying anything. Marcus: come back for a weekend in October, my mom will drive halfway. He typed a reply to Marcus, deleted it, typed another, deleted it, and ordered pancakes he did not eat. His mother, across the table, kept glancing at him the way she glanced at the U-Haul in parking lots, checking that it was still there and still his.

Here is what she saw, sitting across from him with her coffee going cold: a boy doing arithmetic. He had a napkin and a pen, and he was writing down numbers, and she could see him mouthing them. Lunch with Marcus every school day, thirty-five minutes, times a hundred eighty days, times three years. Cross-country practice, two hours a day, most of it side by side and silent. He added in summers. He crossed things out and started over. Then he stopped, folded the napkin in quarters, and put it in his pocket, and when she asked what he was calculating he said, "Nothing," and stole her coffee, and she let him have it because the Nothing had sounded almost like himself again.

The new house had a spartan room waiting for him, bare walls, a bed frame without the mattress, and he stood in it while his father wrestled boxes up the stairs. From the window he could see the porch of the house next door, and on the porch sat a girl about his age with a laptop and a half-disassembled remote-control car, and she looked up and said, "You're the U-Haul kid." He said he was. She said her name was Priya, and that she'd lived here eleven months, and that she had signed up for the robotics club in September mainly so she'd see the same faces every week, because apparently that was how it worked, you couldn't just meet people once, you had to keep crossing their path until they stuck.

"Ninety hours," Christopher said.

"How'd you know that number?"

"My mom read it in the car. This guy Jeffrey Hall, a 2018 study. Going from casual friend to friend takes about ninety hours together."

"Yeah, that one," Priya said. "I did the math on my old friends too, when we moved. It's useless math, by the way. You can't bill people."

He went back inside and climbed the stairs and sat on the bare frame and unfolded the napkin. By his count Marcus and he had logged thousands of hours, so many that the number was almost meaningless, and yet none of those hours had been spent recently on saying the true thing, which was that he was terrified of October, of the visit being awkward, of the quarry belonging to other people now. He picked up his phone, still at eleven percent, and typed to Marcus: it's not that I didn't want to say goodbye, it's that if I'd said it out loud it would've been real. His thumb hovered. Downstairs the front door opened and his mother called that the mattress had arrived, and he pressed send, then put the phone face down on the frame and went to help carry it up.

They wedged the mattress through the doorway together, his father swearing mildly at the banister. When Christopher came back for his phone there was already a reply, and it was from Dee, not Marcus, who had apparently been forwarded the whole thing, and it said: you realize you just spent your ninety hours on us in one text, right? Come in October, idiot.

He lay down on the mattress without sheets and laughed once, out loud, alone in the spartan room, and through the window Priya was still out there with her remote-control car, waiting for someone to hold the other controller.

The community hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the folding chairs had been arranged in a horseshoe for the debate club's first real tournament practice. Alex sat at the plywood table with his notes face down, the way Mr. Ruiz had taught them, and watched the clock over the stage because he did not want to watch the girl across from him. Her name was Talia, she went to the synagogue on Delmore Avenue, and she had beaten him twice already on motions he had thought he owned.

The motion tonight was whether an ancient religious rule still binds people who live entirely modern lives. Alex had drawn the negative, which he'd wanted, because he'd assumed it would be easy. He had prepared a speech about irrelevance, about texts written before ambulances existed. He had even worked in something from chemistry class, that carbon could be graphite or diamond depending on arrangement, one substance and two lives, and maybe old rules were like that, the same words becoming something unrecognizable in a modern setting. It had sounded clever in his bedroom. In the hall, with Talia writing steadily on her legal pad, it sounded like a costume.

She stood first. She spoke about the Sabbath not as a burden but as an architecture, a day shaped so that a person could not fill it with commerce even if he wanted to. She quoted the text itself, the commandment to keep the day holy, and then she said, evenly, that the question of whether it applied in modern life was a question the tradition had already asked, in its own language, a long time before Alex's ambulance existed.

Alex stood and gave his speech anyway. He said the words he'd rehearsed and watched Talia's pen stop moving, which he took for victory until he realized she had stopped writing because she was waiting for him to finish, the way you stop arguing with someone who has not yet understood the question. He sat down with forty seconds still on the clock.

During the rebuttal round she asked him a single question. "Say a man's father has a heart attack on the Sabbath morning," she said. "The hospital is nine miles away. Is driving him a violation or a duty?"

Alex opened his mouth and found nothing in it. His whole case rested on the idea that the ancient rule had never met the modern dilemma, and she had just placed the dilemma inside the rule itself and handed it back to him. He said something about intentions mattering, and she said, "In Jewish law there's a principle for exactly this. It's called pikuach nefesh." She said it the way you say a word you've known since childhood, and she did not explain it, which somehow made it worse.

He lost the round. He went home and did not watch television. At the library computer the next afternoon he searched the term and found it, and then found it again in older sources, and the fact settled over him with the weight of something that had been sitting there the entire time: in Jewish law, the principle of pikuach nefesh holds that saving a human life overrides almost every other commandment, including the rules of the Sabbath. Not a modern amendment. Not a concession wrung from the text by sympathetic reformers. The exception was built into the structure, older than the ambulance, older than the car, waiting inside the rule like a room inside a house.

The following Thursday he asked Talia to sit with him before practice, and he slid his new notes across the table. He told her he had been wrong, and then, because conceding cleanly was its own skill, he told her where he thought he was still right. The rule contained its own exception, which meant the tradition had already done the work his side wanted to claim credit for, and that a rule which knows when to break itself is arguably more applicable to modern life, not less, because modern life is mostly dilemmas and almost no open questions. He had an embryonic version of a new case built on this, and he wanted her to attack it before he took it to the tournament.

Talia read the notes all the way through, which took longer than he expected. "You're using our law as evidence for your side," she said. "That's either clever or obnoxious."

"Can't it be both?"

She underlined one line with her pen and pushed the notes back. "Here. You say the exception proves the tradition is adaptable. My rabbi would say it proves the tradition was never rigid to begin with. You're not disagreeing with us, you're disagreeing with a version of us you invented." She looked up at him. "Fix that paragraph, and I'll take the affirmative against you at regionals. You'll lose, but you'll lose better."

Alex took the notes back and read the paragraph she had underlined. Then he folded the paper in half and put it in his jacket pocket, the inner one, where he kept things he intended to keep working on.

The library smelled of dust heated by the radiators, and Austin had spread his materials across half the table: a Portuguese newspaper, a dictionary, a notebook with a page torn out of its middle. He had told his mother he would be home by six. It was already five-forty, and he could not yet read the article in front of him, much less summarize it aloud to anyone.

The assignment came from Ms. Ferreira, who taught the evening class at the community center and had said, in her flat way, that by Thursday each student would read one short piece of Brazilian news and tell the class what it said, in Portuguese, for two minutes. Two minutes. Austin had signed up for the class in September mostly because Rafaela from his chemistry lab mentioned she went, and he had kept going even after he learned she already spoke it at home and attended for reasons of her own. Now it was Tuesday, and Thursday stood over him like a dentist appointment.

He began the way he always began, at the first word, looking up each one he did not know. The article was about a hospital. He found "fisiologia" in the dictionary and felt a small, private triumph, since physiology was one of the few units he had actually studied for. He filled three lines of the notebook. Then he checked the clock and understood, with an uneasy clarity, that at this pace he would finish the article sometime after midnight, and understand perhaps half of it, and stand in front of the class on Thursday with nothing to say.

Rafaela slid into the chair across from him at ten past six, unwrapping a granola bar. She had said she might come by, though he had half hoped she would not, so that she would not see how badly it was going.

"How far did you get?" she asked, tapping the newspaper.

"Two paragraphs. Maybe." He turned the notebook toward her so she could see the columns of vocabulary, the laborious translations. "It's about a hospital. Something about doctors. I think."

She was quiet for a moment, which he took for pity, and then she said, "Why are you reading every word?"

"Because I don't know every word."

"What do you actually need? For Thursday."

He started to answer and then did not, because the question had opened onto something. What he needed was the general idea, enough to speak about it for two minutes. He did not need the article to yield all of itself, the way a novel would; he needed its shape. His eyes went back to the page, and this time he let them travel fast across the lines, not stopping at the words he did not know, gathering only what surfaced. A hospital in the south. A shortage. Something the minister had said.

"So that's skimming," he said. "Reading quickly for the general idea. That's what I'm doing right now."

"That's it," Rafaela said.

He sat back, half delighted and half annoyed that he had spent an hour not doing it. Then a doubt arrived, the kind that made him want to check everything twice. "But if I needed to find one specific thing, like a name or a number, that would be different. That would be searching, not reading."

"Scanning," she said. "When I need the date of something, I don't read at all. I just look for numbers."

He tried it, running his eyes down the column until a figure caught: a number of beds, or of patients, he could not tell which, and beside it a name he recognized from the vocabulary he had already ground through, the health minister. He wrote both down. It felt almost like cheating, and it also felt like the first useful thing he had done all evening. Two ways of moving through a text, and for two years of school he had only ever known one, the slow word-by-word march that teachers had praised and that would have sunk him on Thursday.

He spoke his first summary aloud, quietly, into the space between them. It was clumsy. He got a verb wrong and she corrected it without ceremony, and when he tried again, the sentence came out whole, if ugly. He did it a second time, better.

"One thing I still can't tell," he said, "is whether the article is for the hospital or against it. The word they keep using is one of those equivocal ones. It could go either way."

"So say that," Rafaela said, finishing her granola bar and brushing crumbs off the table. "Say you're not sure. Two minutes of honest Portuguese is better than four of pretending."

He looked at the article again, at the sentences he could now move across like water, and began, under his breath, a third time.

Antoine had signed up because the form said the food bank needed bodies on Saturdays, and because it was housed in the basement of Fairhaven Seniors' Residence, five minutes from his bus stop. He expected cans. He did not expect the smell of industrial laundry, or the folding tables already crowded at nine in the morning, or the woman with a clipboard who looked him over and said, "You must be Antoine. Gloves are by the sink. You're on hampers with Priya."

Priya was sixteen and had clearly done this before. She laid out the empty boxes in a line and slid a printed list across the table toward him, weighted down with a jar of peanut butter. "Family of four, no baby food," she said. "Next one's a family of four with baby food and diapers. Read the sheet, pack what it says, don't editorialize." She said the last part like a motto she'd been given and had decided to keep.

He packed slowly at first, then faster. Peanut butter, rice, pasta, tinned tomatoes, and then, on nearly every second sheet, a small column of extras: formula, jars of puréed pear, finger snacks, the kind of cereal that turned to mush in milk. He kept setting them aside in a separate pile and kept being wrong about it. "No, that goes in," Priya said, not looking up. "If it's on the list, it goes in." He began counting without meaning to. Four hampers, then six, then nine, and in almost every third one his hands found the small jars, the little flat packs of crackers shaped like fish.

A resident had drifted in through the double doors, a thin man in a cardigan who introduced himself as Mr. Halloran and settled onto a folding chair beside the intake desk as though it were his assigned post. He watched the line of boxes with an expression of professional interest. "Thirty years I taught physics," he said to no one in particular. "You know what a smoke detector does? There's a little bit of americium in there, and it ionizes the air, makes it carry a tiny current. Smoke gets in, the current breaks, the alarm goes off. The whole thing works by interruption." He seemed pleased with the design of it, as if he'd had a hand in it.

Priya's own project, Antoine gradually understood, was a poster. She had a sheet of bristol board and a marker and a statistics sheet from the coordinator, and she wanted the poster finished before the doors opened at ten because a city councillor was rumored to be coming. She kept breaking off from packing to print careful block letters, then covering them with her hand when he tried to read. "It's for my civics class," she said. "But also because nobody knows. That's the part that gets me. Nobody knows."

He asked what nobody knew. She moved her hand.

CHILDREN MADE UP ABOUT ONE-THIRD OF FOOD BANK VISITS IN CANADA, the poster said, IN MARCH 2025. Underneath, smaller: Source: Food Banks Canada, HungerCount report. "It's called the HungerCount report," Priya said. "They count every visit, everywhere in the country, one month out of the year." She tapped the number with the marker. "One-third. Kids." Antoine looked from the poster back down the row of hampers he'd packed, the little jars of pear, the fish crackers, the formula tins like small brass instruments, and did the arithmetic against his own count. Nine hampers, three with baby food, and he thought, of course the number is kids, because who else is the baby food for. He had come in thinking of food banks as a matter for old men like Mr. Halloran, who lived one floor up, and for the unemployed, some vague category he'd never had to fill in. Both things could be true, he supposed, in different proportions, and the proportions were the part worth knowing.

The trouble came at half past nine, when the coordinator ran the totals and found they were four jars of formula short. Priya's mood, which had been brisk and nearly cheerful, went mercurial on him, darkening between one sentence and the next. "Someone miscounted the intake sheet," she said, "or someone took one home." Antoine felt the second suggestion land in the room like a dropped tray. Mr. Halloran cleared his throat. "In my classrooms," he said mildly, "when a beaker went missing, I found it was usually the inventory that was wrong, not the boy nearest the shelf. Probity runs both directions, you know. You have to extend it to the accused as well as demand it of them." Priya flushed, counted the intake sheet again, line by line, and found the arithmetic error in her own column. She said nothing, only crossed out a number and rewrote it, and began counting formula jars with a new and terrible care.

The councillor, when he arrived, was ten minutes late and took a coffee and stood in front of Priya's poster for a long moment with his cup halfway to his mouth. Priya stood beside it, marker still in her hand, and said, "Do you know what fraction of the visits are children? Because I didn't, before this morning, and I pack these boxes every second Saturday." Antoine watched the man's eyes move down the block letters, and he found himself listening for the answer the way he'd listened, earlier, for the dryer buzzer in the laundry room, some signal that a cycle had finished and the next thing was beginning.

Nothing got resolved in a speech. The councillor wrote something on a card and handed it to the coordinator, who read it and folded it away, and the line of clients began forming at the outer door, a young mother with a baby on her hip first in the queue, shifting her weight from foot to foot against the cold. Antoine went back to the table, took the next sheet from the pile, and reached for the small jars.

The vending machine outside the cafeteria took Elijah's dollar and gave nothing back, which felt like a small, personal insult, and he was still jiggling the coin return when Priya found him. She had her laptop under her arm the way she always did on Thursdays, the day she tallied orders for her sticker shop, and she was grinning.

"I cleared two hundred this month," she said. "After what I paid for the printer ink and the mailing envelopes and the paper. Two hundred dollars of actual profit."

Elijah gave up on the machine and followed her to the bench by the trophy case, where she opened the laptop on her knees. The spreadsheet was neat, almost fussy; every expense had a receipt number beside it. She scrolled through it slowly, savoring it, and he could see that the numbers did what she said. Money in, money out, and a tidy remainder in green.

"How many hours?" he asked.

She stopped scrolling. "What?"

"How many hours did it take? Designing, printing, cutting, packing, walking to the post office."

She looked at the screen differently then, the way you look at a staircase you've climbed without counting the steps. "I don't know. Maybe... three a night? Four on weekends. Call it eighty since September."

He did it in his head, not to be cruel but because he couldn't not. Eighty hours, even at the babysitting rate, the tutoring rate, the rate for scooping ice cream at the stand by the highway where they'd both applied last spring. She wasn't ahead. She was somewhere behind, and the green number was still glowing at the bottom of her screen like a firefly that had wandered into a jar.

"So it's not real," Priya said. It wasn't quite a question.

"It's real," Elijah said. "It's just not the whole real. What you subtracted, everything you actually paid money for, that part's called accounting profit. But if you also subtract what your own hours would've earned somewhere else, that's economic profit. That's the one that knows about you."

She shut the laptop halfway, then opened it again, as if the numbers might have rearranged themselves out of pity. Down the hall, Mr. Okafor was trying to make the drama kids pick up their backpacks before rehearsal, and everyone was ignoring him, and he kept saying "I will not be a despot about this" until the word lost its shape. Priya watched the hallway instead of her spreadsheet.

"My dad said the shop would teach me business," she said. "It did. Just not the lesson he ordered."

They sat with that. Elijah thought about his own ledger, the one nobody printed for you: the summer job he'd turned down to take a drawing class, the class he'd taken instead of driving lessons, the way every yes seemed to quietly underwrite a no he never got to read. He had been half-dozing through it for years, calling it scheduling. Priya's spreadsheet had just put columns on it.

"Okay," she said finally, and her voice had the flat calm of someone deciding something. "I could raise prices. Or I could quit and tutor, and make more, and be bored." She looked at him. "Which one's the smart one?"

He wanted to tell her that the smart one existed, that somewhere in every choice there was a version with no remainder, but the honest answer was that he didn't know, and he found he'd rather say that than hand her a doctrine. "I don't think there's a smart one," he said. "There's just the one you'd rather regret less."

"That's a terrible thing to tell someone."

"I know."

She laughed, closed the laptop all the way, and stood. Then she walked back toward the vending machine, fed it a dollar of her supposed profit, and pressed the button for the peanut bar. The coil turned. The bar tipped forward, hung at the lip of the shelf, and stopped, half in and half out, refusing both the floor and her hand.

"See," Elijah said, "even the candy knows."

Tyler's grandfather's blood pressure monitor sat in the bathroom cabinet between the antacids and a jar of cotton balls, and Tyler had carried it to the kitchen table because Saturday was the day he'd promised to learn it. His mother had asked him, quietly, three weeks ago, whether he could figure out the numbers for Grandpa Ray, who had come home from the hospital confused by two digits and a phrase, stage one hypertension, that the nurse had apparently said too fast. Nobody in the house understood what the numbers meant well enough to argue with Grandpa Ray when he insisted they were nothing.

The cuff was old. Its rubber bulb had gone friable at the seams, and when Tyler squeezed it, a fine amber dust came off on his palm, like the stuff at the bottom of a pencil case. He worked the velcro strap around his own arm, pressed the button, and watched the screen blink up 118 over 76. He wrote it on the pad beside the orange juice. Then he took it again, deliberately thinking about the history quiz he hadn't studied for, and got 124 over 81. The machine was measuring something that moved. That was the first thing he actually understood, sitting there with his arm still tingling: the numbers were not a verdict, they were a reading of a moment.

His sister Dana came down around ten, home for the weekend, and dropped a small paper pharmacy bag on the counter while she hunted for coffee. She was twenty and talked about her dormmates the way other people talked about weather. Tyler, reading the back of the monitor box, barely looked up. "Is that Grandpa's new prescription?" he asked.

"It's mine," Dana said. "Birth control. Don't be weird about it."

He wasn't going to be weird about it, and he resented the assumption, but what he said was "I wasn't," which came out more defensive than he'd planned. He turned back to his notes. In his head, vaguely, he had filed all of that medicine under the same heading, protection, the way you'd file sunscreen and bug spray together. He was about to say something like at least you're covered, when Dana, reading something on her phone, said it first.

"The pharmacist asked if I wanted information on infection risks," she said. "Because the pills don't do anything about that. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of STIs." She said it flatly, like she was quoting the pamphlet she was holding, which she was. Tyler sat with the sentence for a second. His whole filing system rearranged itself. Two different jobs, two different tools, and he had never once thought to separate them.

"That's actually useful," he said. "There's a guy on my floor who thinks the opposite." He didn't elaborate and she didn't ask.

He had broken the blender in August, taking it apart to clean it after a smoothie phase, and his mother had never asked for restitution, which was somehow worse than a bill. So he'd decided this project was part of paying it back, and he threw himself into it now with the pad in front of him. He pulled the salt out of the cupboard and looked at the label, 590 milligrams per quarter teaspoon, and wrote that down too. He found the chart the hospital had sent home with Grandpa Ray, and slowly, cross-checking two videos with his mother's nursing textbook from the shelf by the stairs, he assembled the picture: the top number was the heart pushing, the bottom was everything between beats, and consistently high readings meant the pushing was happening against too much resistance, day after day. Less sodium in the diet, and regular walking, could bring the numbers down over months. Not a cure. A shift.

"It's like the monitor," he told his mother that afternoon, while she sliced onions and Grandpa Ray dozed in front of a golf broadcast. "The reading isn't the problem, it's the report of the problem. You change what he eats and how much he moves, and the report changes." His mother stopped slicing. "So when he says the numbers are nothing," she said, "you can tell him what they're reporting." Tyler nodded, then hesitated, because the honest part was harder. "I can't promise how much they'll drop," he said. "Or how fast. The chart says it varies." His mother said that was fair, and wiped her eyes with her wrist, though it might have been the onions.

He took his grandfather's pressure that evening, before dinner, the old bulb shedding its friable dust one more time, and Grandpa Ray watched him write the numbers down. "Well?" his grandfather said. "Am I dying or not?" Tyler looked at the pad, at 142 over 94, and then at his grandfather's face, which was mostly pretending to joke. "You're sitting at a table with your family," Tyler said. "Put down the salt shaker and walk with me tomorrow."

Nathaniel had claimed the corner table at Coraggio's with a latte, a library copy of a style manual, and the growing suspicion that his history teacher had invented footnotes as a form of torture. The assignment was due in nine days: an argument, not a report, with evidence and a bibliography in proper form. He had chosen to argue that the New Deal's rural electrification programs mattered less for the electricity than for the infrastructure of expertise they left behind, which sounded impressive until he tried to write the second sentence.

Priya slid into the opposite chair, uninvited, carrying a smoothie the color of pond water. "I've been at this paper since seven a.m.," she announced, "and I have achieved a breakthrough. I found this historian who says exactly what I want to say about the Marshall Plan, and I put the whole paragraph into my own words. Every single word. So now it's mine." She said this the way other people announced lottery wins.

"Wait," Nathaniel said. "You didn't cite it?"

"Why would I? I didn't copy anything. There's not one sentence that matches." She flipped her laptop around to show him, radiating the smugness of someone who believed she had discovered a loophole in the academic legal code. Priya's actual goal, he had gradually understood, was not to write a great paper but to finish by Thursday, two days early, so she could claim the weekend for a trip to the coast her parents kept threatening to cancel. Speed was her religion.

Nathaniel, who had spent forty minutes that morning being lectured by the style manual, felt the malaise of a man who knows just enough to ruin everyone's afternoon. He dragged the manual across the table, licked his thumb, and found the page. "Listen to this part." He read aloud the sentence about how putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.

Priya stared at him. "That's absurd. I changed the words."

"You changed the words. The idea's still hers." He tapped the page. "You're borrowing her thinking without her name on it."

"You are about to pontificate," Priya said, pointing her smoothie straw at him like a weapon. "I can feel it coming. Don't."

"I'm not pontificating, I'm quoting. There's a difference. Pontificating is what Mr. Halvard does about comma splices." He was pleased with this, and she cracked a smile despite herself, which he took as a small victory in their long-running war of who got to be insufferable that day.

She slumped, chin on her fist. "So I have to go back through everything and figure out which ideas are mine and which ones I absorbed from reading at midnight. Half of them I don't even remember where they came from." This, Nathaniel thought, was the genuinely unsettling part, and he did not say so, because she had told him not to pontificate and he was trying to be a person who listened. Somewhere between her third and fourth paragraph he had realized the same trap was waiting in his own draft: he had reworded a line about the Tennessee Valley Authority so smoothly that he had half convinced himself he'd thought of it on the bus.

"You could do what the manual says," he offered instead. "Cite the ones you remember, and flag the ones you don't, and check them against your sources. I'll trade you. You read my argument and tell me if it actually says anything, and I'll help you hunt down your ghost ideas." The deal was transparently in her favor, and they both knew it, and Priya accepted anyway, because the coast was two days away and time had made her ductile on the subject of pride.

They worked until the café's afternoon light went long and gold across the table, Priya reading his thesis aloud in a terrible British accent while he winced, then both of them flipping through her sources, finding the historian's fingerprint on sentence after sentence she had sworn was original. The barista came by with a rag and asked, without any real curiosity, whether they were studying. "Torture," Priya said. "Court-sanctioned."

Nathaniel looked at his own draft, at the paragraph he now knew he owed a footnote to, and did not write the footnote yet. He underlined it instead, twice, the way you mark a door you intend to come back through.

"That one?" Priya asked, watching him.

Peyton pushed through the library doors with her poster board rolled under one arm like a club, and went straight to the periodicals room in the back, where the microfiche machine hummed under a fluorescent light nobody had ever bothered to fix. Her science fair project had won second place. Second, not first, because three classmates on the judging panel had asked her to repeat her bacteria-count in front of them and the numbers came out different the second time, and she had stood there feeling her face go hot while they exchanged looks.

She had not come to hide. She had come to prove them wrong, or to prove something, though she was not yet sure what. The librarian on duty, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor who kept a jar of peppermints for the after-school crowd, watched Peyton wrestling with the microfiche drawer and came over without being asked. "You look like someone hunting a specific fact," Mrs. Okafor said, "and the drawer is winning."

"Something about how scientists are supposed to act," Peyton said. "There has to be a rule. One experiment can't just be thrown out because somebody asks a question about it." She had spent the bus ride composing arguments in her head, transcribing the angriest of them into her notebook so she could deliver them with precision later.

Mrs. Okafor tilted her head. "Sociology shelf, maybe. The scientists have studied themselves, you know. Somebody had to." She pointed toward the stacks and went back to the desk, and Peyton followed the pointing finger past a table where a boy from her civics class was spreading out photocopies about prison reform, muttering the word recidivism to himself as he highlighted. She almost stopped to ask him whether a person could be right and doubted at the same time, but she kept walking.

The book was older than her mother, a dusty sociology reader with a cracked spine, and she found the page by accident, flipping past chapters on everything else. In 1942, a sociologist named Robert K. Merton had written about the norms of science, and one of them was called organized skepticism. She read the phrase twice. Claims had to survive critical scrutiny by the community before they were accepted. Not one claim, one judge, one afternoon. The community. She sat down on the floor between the shelves with the book open on her knees and felt something rearrange itself in her chest, and it was not entirely pleasant.

Because it cut both ways. If the classmates who questioned her result were doing what scientists were supposed to do, then her result, the one she had counted on, was not yet knowledge at all. It was a claim. It had not survived anything yet. And if she wanted it to be real, the way to get there was not a sharper argument on the bus, it was doing the count again, and again after that, and writing down every failure as carefully as every success.

She checked the book out, using the last dollar of her penurious allowance to pay off an old late fee so Mrs. Okafor could stamp the card, and carried it back to the periodicals room. The boy with the prison articles was still there, stabbing at his highlighter. "You ever cite something and have people just not believe it?" she asked him.

"All the time," he said. "That's kind of the point, though, isn't it? If it holds up anyway, it counts for more." He slid one of his peppermints, which he must have gotten from the desk, across the table to her without comment, and she took it.

On Monday she got to the biology lab before first period and set up the Petri dishes again, and when her friend Dana leaned in the doorway and said, "I thought you were done with that," Peyton said, "Apparently it's not done with me." She wrote the date at the top of a fresh data sheet, counted the first plate twice, and started the tally.

The satellite dish at the Okafor house had died two days before the final, so everyone crowded into Zoe's neighbor Mr. Delgado's living room instead, eighteen people in a room built for six, folding chairs in the aisles like a tiny stadium. Zoe ended up on the arm of the couch between her father and her cousin Marcus, who had spent the whole tournament explaining the game to her as though she hadn't watched it with Grandpa since she was nine. It was July 2018 and the whole month had felt like this, everyone declaring themselves an authority, the television commentators lionize this striker or that midfielder while the actual play went on underneath all the talk.

What Zoe wanted, and had wanted since the group stage, was for Marcus to be wrong once, publicly, in front of the family that treated him as the resident genius. He had gotten away with a month of confident nonsense. In the round of sixteen he had sworn that France's winner against Argentina was offside when it wasn't. When the goal stood, he'd said the linesman missed it, and nobody challenged him because nobody else knew. Zoe knew. Grandpa had taught her the offside law with saltshakers on a kitchen table, walking the pepper grinder slowly forward until the moment of the pass. That was the summer before he died, and she had kept watching partly to keep something of his going.

In the eighty-seventh minute, with the score tied, a forward went down in the box under a defender's trailing leg. The referee pointed to the penalty spot immediately, and half the room roared while the other half groaned. Marcus stood up with his arms out. "That's a dive," he announced. "And it doesn't matter anyway, they can't take back a penalty once he's given it. Refs can't review anything, that's the whole point, the call on the field stands."

Zoe felt her heart kick, because this was it, this was the moment she'd been waiting a month for, and she also felt something uglier underneath, the smallness of wanting it so badly. "They can review it," she said. Her voice came out quieter than she'd planned, and several heads turned. "This is the first World Cup with video assistant referees. Russia, this year. They've been checking goals and penalties all tournament." She could hear Grandpa's phrasing in her own mouth, the way he'd said penalties with a little lift at the end, pleased with the word.

"It's called VAR," said Mr. Delgado's daughter Priya, without looking up from her phone, and on the screen the referee had already stopped play and touched his finger to his ear, circling his other hand in the air. Zoe watched the box on the broadcast freeze the image, draw its lines, hold everyone in the room suspended between hope and grievance. "They can review goals, penalties, red cards," she went on, steadier now. "Even if a ref gives a card to the wrong player, the wrong guy entirely, they can fix it. That actually happened somewhere, Grandpa told me. Mistaken identity."

"Your grandpa told you a lot of things," Marcus said, but he said it toward the television, not at her, and Zoe understood it as the closest thing to a retreat he knew how to make. The wait stretched on. Her father, who had spent weeks deferring to Marcus on every contested call, kept glancing at Zoe with an expression she couldn't read, and she thought about all the times she'd stayed quiet at that same table, how easy the silence had been, what it had cost nothing to keep. She wondered whether speaking up now was brave or just late.

The referee jogged back toward the spot, raised the whistle to his lips, and awarded the penalty. The room detonated. Marcus threw his hands up in vindication, already rewriting history aloud: he'd never doubted the review system, he'd only questioned this particular decision, which was, frankly, incisive of him. Zoe's team was still losing, though. The penalty was converted in the ninetieth minute, and the comeback she'd wanted all match died with it, and she sat on the arm of the couch watching a room full of Delgados celebrate a result she had spent ninety minutes rooting against.

Afterward, while the adults argued about the referee's fitness, Priya slid her phone across the cushion toward Marcus. "You said refs can't review anything," she said. "You said that, out loud, two minutes before they reviewed the thing." Marcus read the screen, which confirmed every word Zoe had said, and something in his face closed like a door. Zoe waited for the pleasure she'd been owed. It came, a brief hot flash of it, watching him trapped in front of everyone by her grandfather's facts, delivered in her grandfather's cadence.

Then it drained away and left her with the strange arithmetic of the evening: she had been right, she had finally said so, and the only result was that her team had lost, her cousin had lost, and the reprieve of silence she'd enjoyed all tournament was gone for good. There would be no more sitting quietly in the corner with a private certainty. Her father put his hand briefly on her shoulder on the way to the kitchen and said, "Saltshakers," and nothing else. Zoe looked at the frozen replay still looping on the screen, the forward suspended mid-fall, neither diving nor fouled, forever unresolvable, and heard Marcus behind her say, "Next World Cup, I'm sitting next to you."

Rosalie had drawn the upstairs hallway four times since dinner, and four times it lay on the page like something flattened under glass. She was sixteen and the portfolio deadline for the summer art intensive was in nine days, and the hallway was supposed to be her proof that she could handle interior space. Instead it looked like a child's diagram of a hallway, doors standing straight up beside each other like cards taped to a wall. She sharpened her pencil until the sharpener drawer was full of gray dust, and then she put her forehead on the desk, which enervated rather than rested her, because from that angle she could see the actual hallway stretching away from her, getting smaller, and her drawing refusing to do the same.

Her little brother Theo was at the kitchen table with his Spanish homework, saying the same word over and over in different wrong ways. "Is it hoop-oh-eh," he asked her when she came down for water, "or hoo-eh? The workbook has this whole section on phonetics and it just makes everything more confusing." She told him it was the second one, though she was only mostly sure, and he wrote it down anyway, trusting her more than the book. Their mother was on the late shift, so the house had that evening quality of everyone solving their own problem in a separate room.

Back upstairs, Rosalie taped the fourth drawing to the wall beside her window and looked at it from across the room. The problem wasn't her line quality. The doors were well observed, the light switch was even in the right place. But nothing receded. Every part of the hallway insisted equally on its own importance, like a paragraph where every sentence was bolded. She thought about asking her mother when she got home, but her mother had gone to art school for two years before dropping out to have her and had an equivocal relationship with all of it, half proud and half sorry, and Rosalie didn't want to walk into that tonight.

So she went to the shelf instead, to her mother's old orange textbook with the cracked spine, the one she wasn't supposed to bend back because the glue was going. It fell open near the middle, as books do, to a page about the Renaissance. She read it standing up, one finger holding the page. Around 1420 in Florence, an architect named Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. She said the words to herself. Linear perspective. The technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface. She read the sentence twice more, and something in her chest shifted the way a lock shifts.

She sat down fast, before the feeling could leak away, and took a fresh sheet. First she drew a single point in the middle of the paper, low, about where the far end of the hallway would be. Then she drew lines out from it toward the corners and edges of the page. It looked like nothing, like a strange kite, like a drawing of rays. But when she hung the hallway's edges along those lines, the doors slanting inward, the ceiling sloping down toward the point, the whole thing opened. The paper suddenly had a far away in it. She actually laughed, alone, a short surprised sound, and Theo called up through the floor, "Was that you?"

She called him up anyway. He stood in her doorway with his workbook still in his hand, and she turned the paper toward him. "What do you see?"

"A hallway," he said. "It goes back." He leaned in. "What'd you change?"

"Look," she said, and drew a fifth sheet in front of him, point first, then lines, then walls, faster now because her hand knew where it was going. "It's called linear perspective. Lines that meet at a vanishing point." She tapped the dot with her pencil. "Some guy in Florence figured it out around 1420. Brunelleschi. He was an architect."

Theo frowned at the page. "So the floor and the ceiling both go to the same point?"

"They do," she said, and turned the pencil around and shaded the floor lightly, so the hallway had weight as well as distance. She wasn't sure yet whether she could do this with the staircase, or with the kitchen where the window light came from two directions. The book had gone on to other things and she hadn't read them. But the fifth drawing was on the desk getting better, and the portfolio had nine days, and downstairs her mother's car had just pulled into the driveway.

Rosalie carried the drawing down the stairs herself, holding it flat against her chest so it wouldn't bend, and set it on the kitchen table under the light.

Room 214 smelled of dry-erase marker and the radiator's scorched dust, and the math club had pushed its desks into the crooked horseshoe it always pushed them into, as though geometry could be improvised. Kyle sat with his pencil already moving, because the regional problem set was due Friday and he was three problems behind Priya, who kept score even when nobody asked her to.

Ms. Okafor had left a warm-up on the board: find the derivative of a polynomial and use it to locate the maximum. Below it she'd written two functions, f of x equals three x squared minus twelve x and g of x equals three x squared minus twelve x plus seven, and the instruction to differentiate both. She was out in the hall arguing with the copier, which meant the room belonged to whoever spoke loudest.

Priya finished in ninety seconds, flat-handed her paper, and read her answers aloud. "Both of them have derivative six x minus twelve. Maximum at x equals two."

"That's wrong," said Deshawn, without looking up. He had a sardonic way of saying things were wrong, chin dipped, like the error had personally inconvenienced him. "They can't both be the same. They're different functions. I got six x minus twelve for f, but for g I got six x minus twelve plus seven. Somebody copied the problem wrong."

Kyle had gotten the same thing as Priya, and for a moment the old reflex rose in him, the one that said two answers to one problem means one of them is garbage and it's probably his. He'd spent two years treating math as a slot where a single correct coin had to drop, and every time his coin bounced out he retreated. But last month his older sister had told him that in her lab, two people getting different results was the beginning of the interesting part, not the end, and he'd been turning that over since, unsure whether it applied to a Tuesday afternoon in a borrowed classroom.

He pulled his paper closer. He checked the g function term by term, tracing each digit with his pencil tip to keep his eyes honest. Three x squared. Minus twelve x. Plus seven. He hadn't copied it wrong, and neither had Priya, because her sheet matched his, and he could see Deshawn's sheet from here and the seven was there too, sitting at the end like a period.

"Wait," Kyle said. "Where did you get the extra seven in your derivative?"

"From the seven in the function," Deshawn said, in the tone of a man explaining doors to someone who had walked through several.

Kyle didn't answer right away. He wrote the seven by itself on the edge of his paper, then wrote zero under it, then crossed out the zero, because he wasn't sure yet and he didn't want to perform a confidence he didn't have. What he remembered from Monday's notes was a single line, almost a throwaway: the derivative of a constant is zero. If that was true, then the seven in g contributed nothing to the derivative, nothing at all, and six x minus twelve would be the answer for both, exactly what Priya had said, and exactly what he'd gotten before doubt made him want to hide his paper.

He tried it the other way first, because that was only fair. If Deshawn were right, the derivatives would differ by seven, and the maxima would land in different places, which would mean two functions that were plainly related, one just shifted upward, would peak at different x values. Kyle sketched both graphs quickly, freehand, the same curve drawn twice, the second one lifted bodily above the first. The peaks sat on the same vertical line. He drew the line and tapped it twice with his pencil.

"Deshawn," he said. "Adding seven to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged. So the derivative's the same for both. Same maximum, x equals two." He said it and then, because he was trying to be the kind of person who admitted the seams, added, "I'm sure about the graph. I'm less sure why the constant dies in the rule, only that it does."

Deshawn came around the horseshoe and bent over Kyle's sketch, close enough that Kyle could smell the gum he was forever chewing. He looked for a long time. Somewhere near the window, Marcus was telling a story about his biology teacher's obsession with speciation, how one population splits into two and both go on as if the split never happened, and Kyle thought, not for the first time, that math and biology were always eavesdropping on each other. Then Deshawn straightened up.

"The graphs," he said. His voice had lost its armor. "The graphs are the same shape." He sat down, pulled his paper back, and drew a hard line through the plus seven in his derivative. He didn't say Kyle was right. He started rechecking everything from the beginning, which was its own kind of concession, and Priya, watching him do it, permitted herself one small exhale that might have been a laugh.

Kyle looked at his own page, at the same answer written twice for two different functions, and felt something he could only call the ordinary kind of exhilarated, the small clean lift of a door coming unlocked. He still didn't understand why the constant vanished; he understood that it did, and that a shifted curve kept its shape, and that two people could square up over an answer and both walk away holding pieces of the truth. Ms. Okafor came back in with a stack of photocopies and a look of grim victory, and began dealing them down the horseshoe like cards.

Kyle took his copy and wrote his name at the top, then, underneath, in small letters, the two functions side by side with an arrow between them, up seven, same derivative, a note to a future self who would probably need it.

"Same time Thursday?" Priya asked, gathering her things before the second bell.

"Same time," Kyle said, and zipped his pencil case shut over the sound of the radiator ticking.

Jordan had been the last cut his junior year, so when Coach Priddy kept him this season, he decided he would earn the roster spot by becoming the one player who never took a bad shot. He studied his own percentages in a notebook he kept in his backpack, and by the third week of practice he had a habit that the other guys noticed: if he missed two in a row, he passed the next three times, no matter how open he was.

"You're doing it wrong," Dev said one Tuesday in the gym off Fairmount Avenue, sitting on the scorer's table with his laptop balanced on his knees. Dev was the backup point guard and the only person Jordan knew who read economics papers for fun. "You think streaks aren't real, so you punish yourself for missing. That's backwards."

The practice had thinned out to six guys shooting around. Jordan wiped sweat off his forehead with the hem of his shirt and came over. "The research says the hot hand is a myth. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody knows the old study. The famous one, from 1985. But in 2018 two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, showed that analysis had a statistical bias, and they found evidence of streak shooting in the same data." Dev turned the laptop so Jordan could see the paper, dense with symbols Jordan didn't follow, but he caught the names and the years. "The same data," Dev said again, tapping the screen. "The stuff that was supposed to prove there's no such thing actually proved there is, once you fix the math."

Jordan wanted to dismiss it, because dismissing things was easier than admitting he had organized his whole season around a mistake. But Dev was the kind of person who was never blase about being right; he printed out pages and carried them around folded into his shoes. That part Jordan had to respect.

The next game was away, a gym that smelled like popcorn and floor wax, the bleachers close enough that Jordan could hear individual conversations when the clock stopped. He started the first half two for nine, all jumpers, all taken because the shot clock was dying rather than because he wanted them. In the third quarter he hit one from the elbow, clean, and then another off a curl, and he felt something loosen in his shoulders that had been tight since November.

Here was the problem, and Jordan stood at the free throw line during a timeout and tried to look at it honestly instead of picking the version that flattered him. If he trusted the streak now, was that judgment or was it excuse? The old Jordan, the notebook Jordan, would have said you never lift your head above the numbers, that discipline calcifies into something you can stand on. But Dev's paper was numbers too. Two rigorous ways of thinking, and they pointed in opposite directions, and there was no referee standing at midcourt to say which one owned him tonight.

He got the ball on the right wing with forty seconds left and his team down two. The defender sagged off him, the whole gym apparently agreeing with the 1985 version of Jordan, the one who would swing the ball and let someone else decide. Dev was calling for it at the top, open, and for a full breath Jordan held both possibilities, the pass and the shot, the caution and the streak, neither one fully provable.

He shot.

The ball hit the back rim, climbed, and dropped through, and the net made its small dry sound while the crowd was still inhaling. Dev ran at him with both hands raised, shouting something Jordan couldn't separate from the noise. On the walk back up the floor, the other team's coach was red-faced at his clipboard, and Jordan thought, not for the first time, that the truth probably wasn't one thing or the other, and that he'd take the uncertainty if it came with nights like this.

"Same data," Dev said, grinning, as they set the defense. "Same data."

Ryan had promised his grandmother he would practice while she was in the hospital, which was how he came to be alone in her living room with the upright piano, a beginner's book, and no idea what he was doing. The book's first page showed a keyboard diagram with letters on it, and Ryan, who trusted nothing he hadn't counted himself, decided to count the keys before he played a single note. He started with the white ones, touching each lightly so the hammers wouldn't sound, and lost his place twice when the phone rang, but he got there in the end: fifty-two. The black keys came next, thirty-six of them, and when he added the two together he got eighty-eight, which felt less like arithmetic and more like discovering the piano had been keeping a secret from him. Eighty-eight doors, and he could open none of them.

His grandmother had left the book open to "Hot Cross Buns," a song he had assumed was beneath him until he tried it. His fingers landed like dropped potatoes. He played E, E, E and the note came out wrong somehow, and when he hunted for the reason he found it in his own hand: he'd been aiming for a black key, thinking it was white, because in the middle of the keyboard the pattern blurred. He laughed at himself, alone in the room, which felt ridiculous and also fine.

When his cousin Devi arrived to water the plants, she found him hunched over the middle of the keyboard like a man trying to defuse it. "You look destitute," she said, dropping her backpack. "Like a pianist who lost everything in the war."

"I lost the note E," Ryan said. "It moved."

"Keys don't move. That's the whole appeal of pianos." She came and stood beside him, and he noticed she wasn't laughing at him exactly, more near him, the way people laugh during a storm. He showed her the problem: the black keys came in twos and threes, and he kept miscounting which group he was in, so his hand drifted like a car into the wrong lane. Devi, who played flute and therefore considered herself above keyboard problems, began to pontificate about how piano was obviously the easy instrument because everything was laid out in front of you, nothing to tune, nothing to guess. Ryan listened, then pointed at the keyboard.

"Then find me E," he said.

She found it instantly, and he hated her for two full seconds, and then he saw how she'd done it. The black keys weren't decoration; they were signposts. Find a group of two, and E sat immediately to the right of it, every time, all the way up. The pattern that had been a morass of identical ivories a minute ago snapped into landmarks, like a street where suddenly all the houses have numbers.

They spent the next hour in a contest Devi invented on the spot, which was to name a letter and slap the correct key before the other person could. Ryan lost eleven times in a row, then began to win, then began to win on purpose, calling out the letters in a singsong to throw her off. She retaliated by calling out letters in alphabetical order, which was harder than it sounded, because the piano's alphabet ran out at G and started over, wrapping around like a wheel. "Who designed this," Devi demanded, missing an A. "Who said seven letters and then we start over, like it's a roller coaster."

"Some dead German, probably," Ryan said, and played his "Hot Cross Buns," all the way through, with every note where it belonged. It was a small, dumb song and he played it like it was a national anthem. Then, because it felt like cheating not to, he tried it an octave higher, and it worked, and he tried it again starting on a different note entirely, and it didn't sound like "Hot Cross Buns" anymore but it didn't sound wrong either, exactly, just like the same tune wearing someone else's coat. He didn't know what to make of that, and said so.

"That's the piano doing piano things," Devi said. "Not your problem yet."

But it sat in his head anyway, that shifting, as he practiced the song once more, clean and slow, fifty-two white keys under his hands and thirty-six black ones waiting like the second half of a language he hadn't learned. He had started the afternoon thinking the keyboard was a wall. Now it seemed more like a map, though of what, he genuinely couldn't say. He found his grandmother's phone number where she'd left it by the lamp, next to the hospital's, and dialed, drumming two black keys with his free hand while it rang.

"Grandma," he said when she picked up. "It's eighty-eight keys. I counted."

The flyer for the economics club meeting read, in Mr. Okafor's handwriting, "Trade: Who Wins?" and Tristan had circled it twice before first period, because his father had been saying for months that nobody wins, that the plant had moved somewhere with cheaper labor and taken his shift with it. Tristan wanted to walk into Room 214 and understand what had happened to his family well enough to argue about it, or maybe just well enough to stop arguing about it at dinner, where the conversations had lately gone quiet and careful, the way people talk around a hospital bed.

At the meeting, Priya had the whiteboard and the marker and the confidence of someone who had read two chapters ahead. She drew a table: Portugal making cloth and wine, England making cloth and wine, Portugal better at both. "So why would they trade at all," she asked the room, "if one country is better at everything?" Marcus, who was obstreperous by nature and proud of it, said the whole thing was a scam invented by people who already had money. Priya didn't roll her eyes, though Tristan could see her wanting to. Instead she said, "Fair. Let's actually cost it out," and Tristan, who had been silent for twenty minutes, found himself raising his hand before he had decided to.

He said it badly at first, something about how the plant in his father's town could make everything the other plant made, and maybe better, and how that hadn't saved anybody. Priya wrote his example on the board without correcting him, which he appreciated, and then asked, "But what did your dad's plant give up to make each thing? What didn't it make because it was making that?" Tristan sat with the question.
