He pressed his pencil down until the lead snapped, then sat very still while the shard rolled off the page onto the carpet.

He had told his mother the portfolio was nearly done. That was the part that sat worst with him, worse even than the drawing. She'd cleared the kitchen table for him and kept his little sister away from his pencils, and every night she asked how it was going, and every night he said good, good, almost there. He knew a word for what he was doing, from a novel he'd read in the fall: mendacity. It had sounded lofty in the novel, almost elegant. In his mouth it just tasted like lying to someone who trusted him.

A girl from his art class, Deja, came through the reading room on Wednesday carrying a stack of returned atlases. She stopped behind him, looked over his shoulder, and said, "That chair looks like it's melting."

"I know." He turned the page sideways, as though the problem might be orientation. It was not orientation.

Deja set the atlases down on the shelf cart and folded herself into the seat across from him. "My grandmother taught me a trick," she said. "You don't draw the chair. You draw what's around the chair. The empty parts. Between the legs, around the back." She tapped the air between two of the chair's legs with one finger, not touching it, like a priest blessing a very small font.

"That makes no sense."

"It's called negative space," she said. "The empty area around and between things. Artists draw that to get the outline right." She picked up his spare pencil, the one he kept behind his ear, and on the corner of his page drew the shapes between the legs: tall thin polygons, a triangle of window light, the wedge of floor shadow. Then she handed the pencil back and went to shelve the atlases, because she was, as she'd told him once, the only sophomore the library would actually pay.

Luca sat for a long moment feeling truculent about it, wanting to tell her that a chair was a chair and you drew a chair by drawing a chair. But the corner of his page sat there with its odd geometry, and the shapes were right. He could see that they were right in a way his chair had never been. The empty parts didn't wobble. They didn't lie.

He started a new page and drew nothing. That was how he thought of it, at first, and it made him laugh under his breath, quietly enough that the man at the microfilm machine didn't glare. He drew the gap between the second and third slat, then the gap between the third and fourth, then the rectangles of window framed by the space around the back, then the air beneath the seat. When he stepped back to the table to look, the chair was there. It had arrived on the page without him drawing it, outlined by its own absence, straight and solid and old. His heart palpitated once, hard, the way it did when a jazz track changed key or when Deja had sat down next to him in September. He looked at the drawing for a full minute before he let himself shade a single plank of the seat.

He was signing his name in the corner, small, when the librarian on desk duty walked over. Mrs. Okafor was heavyset and unhurried and had never once spoken to him except to point at the quiet sign. She looked at the drawing, then at the chair, then back. "You drew the light," she said.

"I drew the gaps," Luca said, which he understood, even as he said it, was the same thing, or near enough, or possibly not the same thing at all, and he decided he could live without deciding.

"Can I put it on the wall by the front?" she asked. "We rotate local student work. It stays yours, you get it back whenever."

He thought of his mother, of telling her tonight that it was done, actually done, done and hanging in a public building. He thought of the strange honesty of the method itself, that you could get at something true by drawing around it rather than at it, and he thought that his whole application essay, maybe his whole next year, might work like that, and then he thought that he might be wrong about all of it, that Friday might come and the portfolio reviewer might want chairs drawn the ordinary way.

"Okay," he said. "Yes."

Mrs. Okafor lifted the sketchbook page with both hands, careful of the corners, and carried it toward the front desk, where the afternoon light came through the tall windows and lay down across the carpet in long, exact shapes.

The library smelled of warm dust and the glue of old bindings, and Angelina had claimed the corner table by the window before anyone else could, spreading out six books on the French Revolution like a hand of cards she did not know how to play. The essay was due in nine days. How have historians' views of the Revolution changed since 1800, the prompt asked, and she had underlined the word "historiography" three times in her notebook until the paper tore. Her first draft had come back with a single comment in Mr. Okafor's green ink: this is a chronology of opinions, not an argument. She had stared at it for a whole evening, feeling like a neophyte let into a temple where everyone else already knew the rituals.

What she had assembled so far was a parade. Early writers saw the Revolution as a catastrophe or a heroic birth of liberty; Marxists later read it as a class struggle, the bourgeoisie rising against a feudal order. Then, somewhere in the late twentieth century, the ground shifted, and Angelina could not see what had shifted it or why. She kept copying out positions the way you copy phone numbers you intend to memorize later and never do.

Her friend Priya dropped into the chair across from her with a paper cup of coffee and a rolled museum flyer. "You're still doing the Revolution thing?"

"Two thousand words on why historians can't agree," Angelina said. "So far I have four hundred on the fact that they don't."

Priya unrolled the flyer and flattened it with her cup. It advertised a traveling exhibit at the history museum downtown, prints and ephemera from revolutionary France. "We're going Saturday. Come. My mother wants company and you need to not sit here all weekend turning petulant."

"I'm not petulant."

"You hissed at the printer on Thursday."

Saturday, in the museum's cool second-floor gallery, Angelina stood in front of a broadside from 1793: a woman in a Phrygian cap planting a liberty tree while citizens in simple dress looked on, all of it drawn in confident, heavy lines. She had seen the image before, in textbooks, always reduced to the size of a postage stamp and treated as decoration. A placard beside it cited its provenance and then, at the bottom, gave a reference for further reading. Lynn Hunt, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution, 1984. She read the line twice, because the placard said something else too: that scholars since Hunt's book had come to treat such images, along with political language and public festivals, as evidence for understanding the Revolution, not merely as its illustrations.

"Look at this," she said to Priya, tapping the glass. "The picture is the evidence."

"It's a nice poster."

"No, it's a source." Angelina heard her own voice go strange and quick. "In 1984 this historian, Lynn Hunt, published a book, and it turned attention to symbols, language, festivals, this whole layer of culture, and that's the shift I couldn't find. It's not that people stopped arguing about class. It's that they started asking a different question."

Back at the library on Monday, she found the book itself in the stacks, its spine softened by decades of hands, and carried it to her corner table like something perishable. She read with a pencil, sitting forward. Hunt was not arguing that class had nothing to do with the Revolution; she was arguing that you could not understand political change without its symbols, its rhetoric, its staged festivals, that culture was not a reflection of the struggle but part of the machinery of it. Angelina copied the title page into her notebook, then sat back and looked at the window, where late light was transfiguring the parking lot into something gold and provisional.

The problem was that she liked the Marxist historians too. She had spent a week inside their argument, the long grind of economic interest and class conflict, and she could not make herself believe it had all been an illusion, a story later scholars had simply outgrown. Her instinct was to pick a winner, to write that the old view was wrong and the new view was right, the way you pick a side in an argument you overhear. But the essay prompt had not asked which historian was correct. It had asked how views changed. She wrote at the top of a fresh page: not a contest, a widening. The Marxists asked who benefited. Hunt and those who followed her asked how revolutionaries imagined the world they were trying to build, in images and speeches and civic rituals. The questions were not enemies. They were successive, and each one had remade the field because it made new kinds of documents speak.

She drafted through the afternoon, pausing to reread a paragraph in Hunt where the argument turned on a festival she had never heard of, some orchestrated public ceremony whose details Angelina could not fully reconstruct from the page. She left a bracket in her draft: check this. There were other brackets too, places where she had inferred a connection between the social historians and the cultural ones that she was not yet certain the sources supported. She did not delete them. She formatted the document, set the margins, and read the last paragraph aloud under her breath, hearing where it rang true and where it only sounded sure.

Priya appeared at the table at closing time, coat over her arm. "Done?"

"Mostly." Angelina closed the laptop and slid the worn book into her bag to return on the way out. "The part I'm sure of is what changed. The part I'm not sure of is whether I've earned everything I wrote about why."

"Is that allowed?"

"It has to be. I put it in a footnote."

At the circulation desk, the librarian stamped nothing, scanned nothing, only nodded at the returning book, and Angelina set it gently on the counter, cover up, title facing the room.

The lasagna had gone cold at Charles's end of the table because he kept forgetting to eat it. Across from him his younger sister, Priya, was describing her science fair group in escalating detail: a partner who had promised the model volcano and delivered nothing until the night before, a poster finished at two in the morning by Priya alone. "So I told her," Priya said, sawing at her garlic bread, "you ruined the whole project."

Their father looked up from his plate. Their mother said, "Priya," in the tone she reserved for minor crimes.

"She did ruin it," Priya said. "Everybody says so. Cora says so, and Cora's her best friend."

Charles said nothing, but something in his chest tightened with recognition. Three weeks ago he had stood in the hallway outside the media lab after his own presentation, and he had said almost the same words, in almost the same voice, to Dex, whose slides for their joint talk had arrived at eleven p.m. the night before, half of them out of order. He had said, "You tanked it, man," and Dex had gone very still, and then quiet, and they had not really spoken since, except in the flat shorthand of people sharing a hallway.

He had gone home that night and, unable to sleep, searched through the communications workbook their seminar teacher had assigned but never discussed, a soft-covered thing with interminable chapters on conflict and listening. In one chapter he found something that stopped him. It described "I-messages," such as "I felt stuck when the slides came in late," and said they were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming. He read the page twice, then closed the book and lay in the dark, turning the sentence over. What he had said to Dex was a you-message, though nobody called it that: you tanked it, you ruined it, you, you.

At dinner now, his mother was asking Priya whether she had talked to the teacher. "No," Priya admitted, "because then it looks like I'm the problem." Their father suggested, mildly, that the girl might have had reasons. Priya rolled her eyes so comprehensively that even Charles, seventeen minutes older and theoretically above such things, felt the pull of solidarity.

"It doesn't have to be a choice," Charles said. Both of them looked at him. He felt the familiar heat of being suddenly the entertainment. "Between saying nothing and saying she ruined it. There's a way to say what happened without the blame part. Like, instead of you ruined it, you say how it was for you. I felt stuck when the model didn't show up. Something like that."

"That sounds fake," Priya said instantly. "Like a therapy contrivance."

"It kind of is a contrivance," Charles admitted, and was surprised to find he meant it as a defense. "But it's a useful one. It's called an I-message. Some psychologist pushed it back in the sixties." He pushed a piece of lasagna around his plate. "I read about it after I said something to a guy on my project team. Something like what you said. And it went bad, and I was trying to figure out what I should have done instead."

His mother set down her fork. "You and Dex? I thought you two were fine."

"We were fine until I opened my mouth." He told it plainly: the late slides, the presentation that had lurched, the sentence he had chosen in four seconds of anger and would apparently be carrying around much longer. He did not dress it up. He noticed, as he spoke, that telling it this way, with the I of it, felt different from telling it the way he had rehearsed it in his head, where Dex was always the villain and the lateness of the slides was the whole crime.

"So did you apologize?" Priya asked, which was, from her, almost tenderness.

"I sent him a text that said, my bad about how I handled that." He winced at himself. "Which is a different contrivance. The kind that doesn't enfranchise anybody, it just closes the account." Dex had replied with a thumbs-up, which had settled exactly nothing.

Priya was quiet for a moment, tearing her bread into smaller and smaller pieces. "So if I say to Hazel, I felt panicked when the volcano wasn't there," she said slowly, "she can't really argue with that. Because it's just what happened to me." Then, suspicious again: "But it still feels like a trick. Like I'm getting her to feel bad on purpose."

"It's both, maybe," Charles said. "A trick that happens to be true." He honestly did not know. It was possible the whole method was just politeness with a manual, a way of dressing the same complaint in softer clothes; it was also possible that naming what had happened to you, instead of what was wrong with the other person, changed the thing you yourself carried afterward. He had no evidence yet. He had one failed you-message and a workbook chapter.

Their father started clearing plates. Priya pulled her phone toward her, typed something, deleted it, typed again, and held the screen out across the table for Charles to see. The message to Hazel read, I felt really stuck when the model wasn't done the night before, and I want to talk about it without us both being mad. She raised her eyebrows at him. Charles gave a small nod, the kind that tries not to seem like a verdict, and she pressed send, then put the phone face-down beside her water glass and did not look at it, though she looked at it twice before helping stack the dishes.

Later, drying the pan his mother had washed, Charles pulled out his own phone and found Dex's name. He sat with the blank message field for a while. Then he typed, I felt lost up there when the slides were out of order, and I took it out on you, and I'd like to actually talk about it. He read it four times. He could hear Priya's word, contrivance, and he could hear his own doubt, and neither of them had the last word. He pressed send, set the phone on the counter, and went back to the pan.

The biology test was on Friday, and by Wednesday Sadie still could not keep transcription and translation straight in her head. She had copied the diagrams from the textbook twice, once in blue pen and once in black, and both times the arrows had multiplied until the page looked like a turgid city map, swollen with lines that went nowhere she could follow. Mr. Okafor had told them the essay question would ask them to explain how DNA is copied and then turned into protein, and he had said it in that flat voice that meant he would not be repeating it.

The field trip to the science museum was scheduled for Thursday morning, which everyone treated as a reprieve from studying and Sadie privately treated as one more thing standing between her and Friday. She rode the bus with her flashcards face down on her knee. Across the aisle, Marcus and Priya were arguing before the bus had even stopped.

"Look," Marcus said at the big rotating model in the genetics hall, a double helix the size of a flagpole, its two strands untwisting and zipping back together in a slow mechanical loop, "when a cell copies its DNA, the old molecule opens up and two new ones get built. So the copy is all new."

"That's not how I read it," Priya said. "My notes say something about old strands. Half of it's old, I'm almost sure."

"New," Marcus said. "It's a copy. Copies are new."

Sadie stood a little way off, arms crossed, pretending to read a wall panel about ribosomes. She wanted to say something and did not trust herself to say it correctly, which was the whole problem with the test too. If she opened her mouth and got it wrong, Marcus would remember it forever.

"You're both doing that thing," said Dana, drifting over with her museum map folded into a triangle. "Where you equivocate until the other person gives up. 'Sort of new.' 'Kind of half old.' That's not an answer, that's a fog."

"I'm not equivocating," Marcus said. "I'm right."

Priya pulled out her phone and scrolled through a photo of her notebook. Sadie leaned in without deciding to. Under Priya's heading, DNA REPLICATION, there were two hand-drawn helices with the strands colored differently, and a note in the margin: each new double helix keeps one strand from the original and pairs it with one newly built strand.

"There," Priya said. "One old, one new. Both of the new molecules."

Marcus frowned at the model, which had chosen that moment to unzip itself again, its two halves wheeling apart like doors. "So when it copies, the original doesn't just stand there being a template and then leave? The original strands actually end up inside the new ones?"

"That's what my note says."

"My dad would hate this," Marcus said. "He thinks everything in biology is designed toward a purpose, like the cell knows what it's building. He's got a whole teleology thing."

"That's not it either," Dana said. "Nobody's designing it. It just keeps a strand and builds on it."

Sadie had been quiet through all of this, and the quiet had been doing something to her. She had spent the week trying to memorize the process as a list, arrows on a swollen page, and Priya's margin note had landed differently: the copy was half inheritance, half construction. The old strand stayed. It was less like photocopying and more like a sentence passed down where half the words were kept and half were new. She found she could suddenly hold transcription and translation in the same grip, because the point of keeping a strand was that the information survived the copying, and the point of copying was that the information could be read out, transcribed, and then translated into protein. The two ideas she had been holding apart were one continuous thing.

"Semiconservative," she said. Everyone looked at her. "That's what it's called. Half conserved. One strand from the original, one strand new." Her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Transcription makes the message off it, and translation turns the message into protein. If the strand weren't conserved, the message wouldn't survive being read."

Marcus opened his mouth, then looked back at the model, which was zipping shut again, half its length gleaming with fresh color. "Fine," he said. "Half old. I'll say that on the test."

"Say it right," Priya said.

On the bus back, Sadie turned her flashcards over one at a time and found she knew them, not because she had drilled harder but because she had stopped treating the process as a list and started treating it as a thing that keeps hold of something while it changes. She was honest enough with herself to admit the part that still wavered: she could not yet say why the cell kept a strand, only that it did, and Mr. Okafor's essay question might ask for the why. She wrote one question in her margin for the morning.

Dana leaned over the seat. "So tomorrow, when you get the why wrong, are you going to equivocate?"

"I'm going to write what I know," Sadie said, "and star the rest."

She put the flashcards away and looked out the window at the museum shrinking behind them, its helix still turning somewhere inside, half of it old, half of it new.

Jacob stacked the last bag of dark red potatoes, each one smooth and heavy as a lump of igneous rock from the geology unit he'd half forgotten, and looked at the slip of paper in his hand. On it his orientation advisor had written two questions for the small seminar he'd been placed into at State: be ready to explain comparative advantage, and be ready to say why two countries both gain from trading. Three weeks until move-in. He had read the textbook chapter twice on his phone behind the customer service desk, and each time the words dissolved the moment he tried to hold them.

"You're muttering again," said Priya, sliding cartons of eggs onto the belt. She was a sophomore at the community college and had taken the same course, and she enjoyed reminding him of it.

"I'm rehearsing," Jacob said. "Say you're a country."

"I refuse."

"Say you make two things. Say eggs and bread. And say you're actually better than me at both."

Priya scanned a bag of lemons. "Flattering so far."

The register beeped through her answer while he worked it out under his breath. He was better than her at both, yet they still both gained if he specialized in whichever he was comparatively better at. The word wasn't "better." The word was about what you gave up, the loaf you didn't bake. Every time he approached the idea it rearranged itself, and he could feel his advisor's seminar, forty strangers around a table, waiting for him to say something coherent.

An older man came through the lane with a handbasket, banks statements folded inside a newspaper. He asked Priya whether the store had a bulletin board, because he was trying to compare two mortgage offers and kept losing track. He read a line from one sheet, then a line from the other, and shook his head. "The numbers are nothing like when we bought in 2020."

"My mom says the same thing," Jacob said, carrying the man's basket to the end of the lane. "She was at the bank Tuesday. She said the loan officer told her the Federal Reserve started raising its policy rate from near zero in March of 2022 and got it up to between 5.25 and 5.50 percent by July of 2023. She has it written on her hand."

The man frowned at his sheets. "From near nothing to that, in under a year and a half. Different world."

Priya leaned on the register. "Okay, your mom's world, the bank world, the mortgage world, whatever. Get back to your country speech."

Jacob picked up a lemon and a lime and set them side by side on the bagging counter. "Fine. Here. You're the lime country. I'm the lemon country. Say we both grow both." He turned the lemon in his fingers, the oil sharp on his thumbnail. "Say I can grow way more of both. Double the lemons, double the limes. Everyone in my country is better at everything."

"You win."

"Except." He stopped, because the shape of it had finally assembled itself, whole, for the first time. "For every lemon I grow, I could have grown four limes. That's my cost. And for every lime you grow, you only give up half a lemon. So even though I'm better at everything, I'm only really better at lemons, the way that counts. If I grow only lemons and you grow only limes and we trade, there are more of both than if we each did both. Both of us gain. That's it. That's the whole thing."

"Both gain," Priya said slowly. "Even the one that's worse at everything."

"The worse-at-everything country isn't worse at the thing it costs it least to make. That's the point. That's what the chapter kept trying to say."

The man with the mortgage papers had paused at the end of the lane, listening. "So what you're saying is everybody's got something," he said, half to himself, and rolled his newspaper tighter. He said it like a question he intended to carry out to his truck.

Jacob didn't answer right away, because the honest part was still unresolved. His chapter's last page had included critics who maligned the whole framework, who called global trade a machine for plutocracy, a system where the gains from trade pooled at the top while the egg-packing country stayed egg-packing for a generation. He believed both things somehow, that the math held and that the math left people out, and he could not yet say in one sentence where one truth ended and the other began. He would have to say something in three weeks. He could start with the lemons.

Priya picked up the lime and tossed it to him, underhand. "Okay, lemon country. Trade me."

He caught it, cold from the cooler, and held out the lemon in his other hand, and they stood there in the fluorescent hum of lane four, each of them holding the thing the other one wanted.

Justine had written her grandfather's name on the first cup of juice and her own on the second, and now she stood in Aunt Carol's kitchen holding the two cups like evidence in a case she hadn't meant to open. For eleven years Grandpa had led the Seder from the head of the table, and nobody had said out loud that this year would be different, but this year would be different, because he was in the sunroom with a blanket over his legs, dozing before the soup even came out, and her mother had said, quietly, last Tuesday, "You know it. You've watched him your whole life. Just do what he does."

The Haggadahs were stacked by the door, the same battered stack as always, and Justine counted them twice because counting things was what she did when she was about to be responsible for things. At a Passover Seder, the youngest child able to do so traditionally asks the Four Questions, which begin "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Her brother Theo was seven now and had been practicing for three weeks, whispering the first question to himself in the bathtub, in the car, once to a cashier at the grocery store who had given him a sticker for it. But Theo got nervous. Theo froze. And when Theo froze, he cried, and when Theo cried, the whole table tilted toward him, and Justine knew, with the certainty of someone who had been an older sibling for seven years, that her first Seder as leader could collapse in the first ten minutes if she didn't plan for it.

"You could just ask them yourself," said her cousin Maya, leaning against the counter, stealing an olive. "You're leading. Nobody would stop you."

"That's not how it works," Justine said. "It's his job. He's the youngest who can."

"So coach him. You're the coach now, apparently. Coach." Maya said the word like it was slightly ridiculous, and it was, and Justine took the olive jar away from her anyway.

The problem was that coaching and leading were two different shapes of attention, and she couldn't be in both at once. If she sat next to Theo and prompted him through the questions, she wasn't at the head of the table holding the order of things together. If she sat at the head, she could see Theo's face going pale from across the room and could do nothing about it. She thought about it while setting the table, while hiding the afikoman under the good napkins, while her mother said, "You're being very quiet," in a tone Justine declined to answer. She was not going to solve it by agonizing. Her grandfather had never agonized; he had improvised. Once, when the candles wouldn't light, he'd declared, "We remember them lit," and everyone had laughed and moved on. Arbitration, that was what he did all night, small rulings on who poured and who read and when the food came, and nobody had ever called it that, but Justine understood suddenly that leadership at this table was mostly just deciding things before anyone had to argue.

So she made a ruling of her own. She put Theo's chair not beside hers but at an angle, close to the head, close enough that she could reach his shoulder without standing up. Then she found him in the hallway, hiding in his dress shirt.

"Here's the plan," she said. "You ask. If you get stuck, I ask the first word of the next line, and you take it from there. Nobody will even notice."

"What if I cry?"

"Then you cry and keep asking. Grandpa mixed up the plagues two years running and nobody fired him."

Theo considered this. "Nobody can fire you if you're grandpa."

"Exactly," Justine said, though this was not exactly what she meant.

Dinner began badly, which is to say it began the way family dinners begin, with her uncle declaring the gefilte fish an abomination and Aunt Carol calling him a philistine and both of them enjoying it thoroughly. When Justine raised her cup for kiddush her voice came out smaller than she'd rehearsed, and she had to start the blessing again, and her ears burned, but the second time was steady, and her grandfather opened one eye from the sunroom doorway and said, "Louder, they're all deaf," which was untrue and helpful.

Then it was time. Theo stood up. His hands found the hem of his shirt. "Why is this night," he said, and stopped, and the table went still in the way tables do when everyone is pretending not to watch. Justine leaned toward him and said only, "different." "Why is this night different from all other nights?" Theo finished, and then the rest came out of him in a rush, all four questions, dipping and reclining and bitter herbs, barely stopping to breathe, and when he sat down he was grinning so hard he looked like he might tip over sideways. Maya raised her glass to Justine from across the table. Justine noticed, at that exact moment, that she had skipped a paragraph in the order of the service, and decided, in the spirit of her grandfather, to fold it in later without announcing the error. She had gained the table and lost the certainty of doing it right, and both of those things were true at once.

Later, after the meal, after her uncle's third monologue about a neighbor whose spending habits he described as profligate, after Theo found the afikoman and held it for ransom with terrifying confidence, Justine went out to the sunroom with a plate of macaroons. Her grandfather was awake, watching through the doorway as she broke the matzah and distributed it.

"You missed the part with the rabbis in Bnei Brak," he said.

"I put it after the meal. Nobody noticed."

"Everybody noticed," he said. "Nobody minded." He took a macaroon and ate it slowly. "Next year, do the rabbis earlier."

"Next year?"

"Next year," he said, and closed his eyes again, and Justine sat beside him and let the evening go on without her for a while.

Kyle had told himself, more than once on the walk from the hardware store, that the chair was entirely for his own satisfaction, and by the third telling it had become almost true. It was a folding lawn chair salvaged from behind the garage, its frame sound but its canvas gone to mold, and he intended to replace the canvas himself and paint it before his sister left for the airport on Sunday. He had four days. He had never painted anything that mattered.

He set up in the backyard because his mother's kitchen was still being repainted by professionals, a fact his father had lambasted at dinner for two nights running, calling it money spent on walls that nobody looked at. Kyle had agreed out loud and disagreed quietly, which had lately become his standard arrangement with his father, and which he did not intend to examine too closely.

The new canvas stretched and laced onto the frame well enough, but the painting went wrong almost immediately. He had bought five tubes of paint on impulse at the store, reasoning that more colors meant more choices, and now he sat cross-legged in the grass with them lined up like evidence against him. The blue and the red he had laid down in wide bands curdled against each other, vibrating in a way that made his jaw tighten. It looked petulant, the whole thing, like a tantrum in pigment. He had wanted something steadier for Nadia, something that said he had thought of her, and instead he had produced stripes that fought.

He scraped the worst of it off with a palette knife and went inside to his phone, telling himself he would look for ten minutes. His search for why red and blue hurt each other led him somewhere he did not expect. A physics man, of all people, had something to do with it. Kyle read the page twice, then a third time, because the date seemed too precise to be real.

"Newton," he said aloud to the empty kitchen. "In 1704. In a book called Opticks." He carried the phone back out to the grass and set it face up on the patio stone beside his brushes. Isaac Newton, who had thought about gravity and light, had arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle, and that circle was an early version of the color wheel artists used today. Kyle sat with that for a while, turning his brushes over. He had assumed the wheel belonged to painters, that some seventeenth-century craftsman had mixed his way to it by feel. Instead a physicist had bent the rainbow into a ring, and painters had inherited the geometry of it.

The wheel told him about opposites. He found a version online, turned it until the red he had used faced its opposite across the circle, and understood that the pair was useful to him for exactly the reason it had wrecked him: the two pushed against each other. So he stopped trying to make the red and blue sit side by side and gave each of them a thin border of the other's opposite, a margin of green around the red, a whisper of orange under the blue, and the bands stopped fighting. They held their ground like neighbors who had finally agreed on a fence.

He worked until the light went long and the sprinklers two yards over came on with their tin hiss. His father came out with a beer and stood at the edge of the patio, saying nothing for the length of a full minute, which Kyle had learned was how the man approached anything handmade.

"Your mother says you learned that circle thing from a scientist," his father said.

"From Newton," Kyle said. "1704. It's in Opticks." He did not add that he had chosen the whole scheme to be calm, or that the calm was for Nadia, or that some part of him had angled the chair on the lawn so it would be visible from the patio. His father drained a third of the beer and looked at the canvas, and the silence stretched, and Kyle noticed that he was holding his breath in a way that had nothing to do with paint.

It was not, he had to admit, a matter of doing it only for himself. He wanted it liked, and he wanted to seem indifferent to whether it was liked, and he could not fully have both. What he could have was the chair, which by dusk was dry enough to touch, its bands lying flat and settled against each other, a consonance he could not have named before this week and which he now saw everywhere he looked: in the fence slats against the grass, in the orange porch light against the coming dark. He folded the chair and carried it toward the garage, and behind him his father said, "Huh," which was not praise and was not nothing, and Kyle kept walking and let it be whichever it was.

The launch station had a dial for speed, a dial for angle, and a row of tin buckets bolted to the floor at measured distances, and Hailey had already missed the two-hundred-centimeter bucket four times. Marcus leaned on the rail eating fries from the museum café, which they weren't supposed to have in the exhibit hall, and offered commentary she did not request.

"You're going to lambaste me for this," he said, "but you're doing the same thing every time. Same angle, more speed, like the ball's going to politely go further because you asked harder."

"That's not what I'm doing." But it was close to what she was doing. She had gotten a 61 on the projectile quiz on Friday, and Ms. Ruiz had written in red at the top, See me about components, and Hailey had decided that seeing her before Tuesday would be an admission she couldn't afford. So she was at the museum on a Saturday, standing at a machine that shot foam balls, trying to figure it out before anyone could explain it to her. She had a notebook. She had a protractor. She had the incipient headache of someone who has been squinting at the same problem for an hour.

"Try less speed," Marcus said.

"Then it won't reach."

"Reach isn't the question. Where it lands is the question." He pointed his fry at the bucket. "You keep thinking about how hard you throw. Think about how long it's in the air."

She almost threw the protractor at him, except that the sentence snagged on something. How long it's in the air. She wrote it down. Then she wrote what she'd been assuming, which was that the ball slows down as it flies, that its forward motion bleeds away the way a skateboard bleeds to a stop when you stop pushing. That was the whole reason her predictions fell short. She was aiming like the ball would get tired.

She reset the station, dialed the angle to thirty degrees, and fired. The ball rose, arced, dropped, hit the floor short of the bucket. She watched it again, and this time she watched sideways, from a crouch, tracking the ball's shadow across the tile. The shadow crossed the floor in equal spans the whole flight. She counted the tiles under its path. Four tiles out, the shadow took the same time as the first four tiles, and the last four, and all of them.

"It doesn't slow down," she said. "Horizontally. The whole way."

Marcus came off the rail. "Say that again?"

"The forward part. It's the same the whole flight." She was already writing, pencil fast. If you ignored air resistance, and in here there was basically nothing but air and foam, then nothing was pushing the ball forward and nothing was dragging it back. So the horizontal part never changed. Only the vertical part pulled at it, only that fought the launch, which meant the whole shape of the arc came from the up-and-down fight while the forward motion just carried on, indifferent, constant, all the way to the floor.

"So the distance," Marcus said, slowly, like he was handling it with gloves, "is just how fast it's going sideways times how long it's up."

"Speed times time." She looked at her quiz, folded in her back pocket, the problem she'd missed: a ball launched at twelve meters per second at forty degrees, how far does it travel. She'd need the trig to split the launch into its two parts, sideways and vertical, and she couldn't do trig at a museum railing. But the syllogism was there, simple and ugly: if the sideways part never changes, and the height determines the time, then the distance is fixed by both together, and her answer Friday had failed because she'd treated one number as if it were shrinking.

She stood, dialed the speed to the mark she'd used before, and raised the angle from thirty to forty-five. Higher launch, longer time in the air, same constant carry forward. She fired. The ball sailed over the two-hundred-centimeter bucket entirely and knocked the rim off the bucket behind it.

"Too far," Marcus said.

"Too far is information." She lowered the angle ten degrees and fired again. The ball dropped into the two-hundred bucket with a sound like a coin in a well.

Marcus raised his fries in salute. "Write that down before you forget which angle."

"I'm not forgetting." She copied the dial settings into her notebook anyway, twice, and underlined the word constant. Then she slid the quiz out of her pocket, smoothed it on the railing, and started drawing the arc over her wrong answer, splitting it with two arrows, one sideways and flat, one rising and falling, both of them hers.

"Sixty-one," Marcus read over her shoulder. "You're going to fix all of it?"

"Every problem. Right here." She tapped the page. "Hand me the protractor."

Laurence had the ballot spread on the desk beside the keyboard, the paper as long as her forearm, and she was going down the list of judges with three tabs open, because she refused to vote for someone just because their name sounded competent. She was eighteen as of the ninth of this month, which still startled her when she wrote it on forms. Her mother kept passing the doorway with laundry, slowing down each time as if Laurence were performing surgery.

"Grandpa's coming by at four," her mother said on the fourth pass. "He'll want to see that you voted. Try to look excited, or at least awake."

"I'm not excited. I'm reading about a drainage district commissioner." Laurence turned the laptop so her mother could see the candidate's page, a wall of text in a font from another decade. "This guy has been in office since before I was born and his whole statement is two sentences about fiscal responsibility. That's it. That's all he's telling the voters."

Her mother set down the towel she'd been folding. "Then vote for the other one, or don't vote for that one at all. Nobody will arrest you."

"That's not the point." Laurence pulled the laptop back. "If I skip it, I'm letting everyone else decide, and if I vote on nothing, I'm just making noise. I want it to mean something, and I can't tell if it does." She said the last part more quietly than she meant to.

When her grandfather arrived he came in carrying a paper bag of oranges from the tree he babied through every frost, and he put two of them on the desk next to the ballot without comment, which was his way of noticing that she hadn't eaten lunch. He read over her shoulder for a while, hands behind his back, while she clicked between a county measure and an editorial about it.

"Does it matter?" she asked him finally, spinning her chair. "One vote. Everyone says it doesn't."

He picked up an orange and started peeling it in one long spiral, the way he did everything, slowly and without waste. "You know why you get to do this at eighteen?"

"Because of the Constitution. Amendment something."

"Twenty-sixth," he said. "But the push for it had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Eighteen-year-olds could be drafted for Vietnam, and people said that if you can be drafted, you should get the ballot." He handed her half the orange and sat on the edge of the bed, leaving the rest of it there, not elaborating, which for him was a kind of discipline.

Laurence ate the orange and thought about her grandfather at eighteen, about which of those two things he would rather have been given. She opened a new tab and typed the slogan in, and the results were all there, the marches, the buttons with the words printed in a circle, senators quoted saying exactly that. She read for ten minutes with the peel smell still on her fingers. "So people my age were handed a rifle first," she said, "and the vote was the consolation prize. Or the apology."

"Something like that," her grandfather said. "Depends who you ask."

She looked at the ballot again. The framing helped and it also didn't; the vote wasn't a promise that anything would go her way, and she understood that the slogan was a kind of synecdoche, the draft standing in for every way the country could use you before it let you speak. That didn't make her one ballot weigh more. If anything it made the whole thing feel smaller, a modest, parsimonious little power doled out exactly as far as it had to go and no further, circumscribed on every side by districts and electoral math and commissioners running unopposed since the nineties. And still people had marched for exactly this, this thin slice, because it was what was on offer.

"Okay," she said. She pulled the ballot closer and filled in the drainage race for the challenger, who had at least written a paragraph, and left one judicial race blank where both candidates had given her nothing at all. "I'm not voting in that one. I couldn't tell you why either of them wants the job."

"That's allowed," her grandfather said. "Blank is a answer too."

Her mother appeared in the doorway again, empty-handed this time, and Laurence signed the envelope, licked it, and held the sealed ballot up between two fingers like evidence.

"One vote," she said. "Old enough to fight."

The municipal pool had the smell of every pool Savannah had ever swum in, chlorine and hot rubber, and a record board so old its letters had the authority of antiquity, times posted by girls who now had children of their own. She read it while waiting for dryland to start, because reading it was easier than looking at Rosa, who had been named putative captain by a vote so close the coach refused to announce the number.

Dryland that Thursday was not dry. Coach Okafor had dragged a battle rope and a thick tow line onto the deck, and after the usual squats he split the team in two and pointed at the deep end gutter, where he had looped the rope through a stainless rail. "Tug of war," he said. "Winners choose the lane order for the relay on Saturday." A cheer went up, thin, because everyone was sore from Tuesday, and Marisol asked whether falling in counted as a forfeit, and he said only for her, which made even Rosa laugh.

Savannah's team lost the first pull in about eleven seconds. She had braced her heels, gripped until her palms burned, and felt, through the rope, a strange softness, as though the other four were holding back a little, saving something, or simply trusting that someone else would take the load. When they regrouped, dripping, Coach Okafor was squinting at them all with the expression of a man doing arithmetic in his head.

"Okay," he said. "New experiment. One at a time. Grip here, pull as hard as you can against the spring scale I clipped to the rail." He held up a rusted spring scale, the kind from a physics classroom, and it turned out the high school would lend anything to anyone who signed a form. Savannah went last. Alone, straining backward against the dial, she watched the needle swing further than it had for anyone else, and she heard Rosa, behind her, say "huh" in a small voice.

The numbers went up on the whiteboard in dripping marker, and then Coach Okafor added a second column, the totals from the group pull divided by five, and the whole deck went quiet in the way a classroom does when something embarrassing becomes visible. Every girl's group number was smaller than her solo number. Every one. "Look at that," Marisol said. "We're a scam." And Savannah, thinking of her psychology textbook, which she read at night the way other people read mysteries, remembered a page she had almost skimmed: a French engineer, Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had people pull a rope and found that each person in a group pulled less hard than the same person pulled alone. She had assumed it was about lazy factory workers in mustaches. It was about her. She said it out loud, carefully, giving the engineer his due.

From where Rosa stood, toweling her hair, the interesting thing was not the scale. It was Savannah's face while she recited the fact, the way she recited everything, like handing over evidence at a trial. Rosa had voted for herself for captain, obviously, and had won or lost by some number nobody would say, and for two weeks she had been waiting to find out what kind of person Savannah actually was. A person who pulled hardest alone, that much was certain now. What Rosa wanted to know was whether such a person could want anything that required other people.

"Okay," Coach Okafor said, "so science says you're all slightly useless together. Excellent. Same teams, pull again, and this time I want you calling your own name when you feel yourself easing off." This was the part he could not abrogate, the ancient rule of Thursday dryland that any drill ending in failure must be repeated until it ended in laughter, and he enforced it with the patience of a man who had run this team for nineteen years.

The second pull lasted a full minute. Savannah called her own name twice, hoarse and ridiculous, and heard Rosa call hers three times, and Marisol once, followed immediately by the slap of Marisol's feet skidding out from under her and the enormous ceremonial splash of a ninety-pound girl entering the deep end fully clothed in a team shirt. Everyone laughed, including Coach, including Marisol from the water, arms spread on the gutter like a woman reclining in a very cold bath. The rope went slack on both sides. Nobody had won. On the whiteboard, in the space for the second pull's totals, someone had drawn a wave.

Saturday, the relay went third. Savannah swam anchor, and when she dove in, trailing by half a body, she thought about the whiteboard and the number that had been smaller than her number, and about Rosa on the second leg lifting her head to call her own name into a silent natatorium, and she could not decide, even mid-stroke, whether the team had taught her to pull harder alone or whether pulling alone had taught her nothing the relay could use. She touched the wall. Somebody's hand was already there. When she pulled off her goggles, Rosa was hanging on the lane line beside her, breathing hard, saying, "Tell me the scale again. I want to write it on my mirror."

The march came through the floorboards before Peyton was fully awake, which meant her brother had gotten to the stereo first, which meant today was the day her mother had decided to make ceremonial. She lay in bed and listened to the trumpets loop around the same eight bars, the way they had looped every June of her life, and thought about how strange it was that a person could know a piece of music this well without knowing the first thing about it.

"Band practice at ten," her mother called up the stairs. "And your grandmother's coming to the ceremony, so wear the dress with the buttons."

Peyton had been avoiding the ceremony for weeks, quietly, the way you avoid a thing you can't actually escape. She had tried subterfuge. She had mentioned, at dinner, that plenty of people skipped graduation, that it was long and hot and the speeches were written for parents. She had left a college orientation brochure on the counter with the dates circled, though the orientation wasn't until August. Her mother had absorbed all of it without comment, the way a sea wall absorbs weather, and had gone on ironing.

At ten she was in the band room with her clarinet, running the march for the twelfth time that week, and it was there, counting rests, that the question finally calcified into something she couldn't ignore. "Why this song?" she said, during a water break. "Every school in the country. Every movie. Why do we all play this one?"

"Because it's tradition," said Marcus, who played baritone and considered tradition a sufficient answer to most questions.

"Traditions start somewhere." She was already typing with her thumb, one-handed, the way people did when a question had been sitting in them too long.

What she found was this: the march had become graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music. She read it twice, then held the phone out so Marcus could see. "Yale. 1905. They gave the composer a doctorate and played his march, and somehow that turned into every cap and gown on earth."

"Creepy," Marcus said, meaning interesting.

"It's not creepy, it's..." She looked for the word and didn't find it. "One school did it once, and now my grandmother is wearing a corsage because of it."

Her grandmother arrived that afternoon, early, while Peyton was still in her robe, and installed herself at the kitchen table with the tea her mother made without being asked. Peyton sat down across from her, mostly because leaving would have required an excuse she didn't have. Her grandmother had grown more ascetic over the years, having given up television, then sugar, then most of her opinions, or at least the sharing of them, so that a visit now felt like sitting with a very calm question.

"I hear you'd rather not walk," her grandmother said.

Peyton examined her tea. "It's a show we put on for other people. I don't need two hours of my name not being called to know I finished."

"You don't," her grandmother agreed, which disarmed her completely. "I skipped mine. 1968. I stood outside in the parking lot in my gown because it was June in Ohio and the gym had no air, and I listened to that same march through the doors." She turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "I remember the music more than I remember deciding anything about it."

Peyton had assumed the argument would be about pride, or photographs, or things her mother could frame. This was something else, and she sat with it while her grandmother drank her tea. There was a version of herself, the one who had tried the brochures and the dinner remarks, that wanted to treat the whole ceremony as an inherited reflex, a thing people did because Yale had done it in 1905 and nobody had thought to stop. But her grandmother standing in an Ohio parking lot in a rented gown, listening through gym doors, was not a reflex. That was a person choosing to be near a thing, even at the edge of it, and Peyton could not make the two ideas sit still together. Maybe the ritual was arbitrary and it meant something anyway. Maybe it meant something because it was arbitrary, because everyone had agreed to it, the way people agreed to a language.

"I'll walk," she said. Her grandmother nodded once, as though Peyton had reported the weather, and asked for more hot water.

At the ceremony the next evening, the band filed in first, and Peyton took her seat in the clarinet section with a good view of the whole procession. When the trumpets came in, she watched her grandmother in the fourth row, leaning slightly forward, doing the same thing she had done in a parking lot in 1968, and Peyton understood that she herself was now part of the reason, the small link that kept the thing running from 1905 to a folding chair in a gym in June. She would not have said that out loud. She wasn't even sure it was true, exactly, and she held onto the uncertainty on purpose, the way she held the clarinet, lightly, at the ready.

She lifted the reed to her lips and came in on the downbeat, half a beat late, and played.

The printmaking shed at Camp Wren smelled of ink and pine sap, and Alexia had claimed the corner table by the window for eleven days straight. Her counselor, Dana, had proposed the portfolio project on the first evening: ten artworks, one theme, an artist's statement to bind them. Everyone else had chosen by the second morning. Priya was doing doorways. Marcus was doing his grandmother's hands. Alexia had forty sketches and no theme, and the camp art show, where portfolio students would exhibit and sell to parents and visiting locals, was nine days away.

She had been drawing the lake. That was the trouble, she thought, smudging graphite dust off her wrist. Not the lake in general, but the same drowned log at the north shore, the one that surfaced at low water each August, silvered and split, half in and half out. She had drawn it at dawn, at noon, in rain, once by flashlight. On Sunday she'd taped the drawings in a row along the shed wall and stood back, and Dana had walked past and said only, "Huh," which Alexia could not interpret at all.

"Nobody's going to buy ten pictures of a log," Priya said on Wednesday, licking a stamp for the invitations. The shed had emptied after dinner except for the two of them and the moths orbiting the porch light. "My mom buys one thing a year. One. Who wants a set?"

"I don't know if they're a set." Alexia turned her compass case over in her hands. "They might just be ten mistakes with a common subject." The worry had begun to coagulate into something worse than worry, an actual reason to quit, and she had almost torn the drawings down that afternoon.

Then Marcus came in late, shaking rain off his jacket, carrying the art history book he kept under his bunk for the pictures. "I was looking for something for my statement," he said. "You know Monet did haystacks?" He dropped the book on the table, open to a page of pale grain stacks against winter light. "He showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month. Fifteen haystacks. Same field, basically."

Priya leaned over the book. "People bought those? On purpose?"

"Most of them. In a month." Marcus shrugged, as though he had merely reported a score.

Alexia sat very still. She was thinking less about money than about what the fact meant for her wall of drawings, the dawn one and the flashlight one, the version where her brother's canoe had blurred past the log. She had been treating the repeated subject as a weakness, an absence of imagination, when it might be the opposite, a discipline. But she also distrusted the comfort. Monet was Monet. A dead log in a Massachusetts lake was not haystacks in Giverny, and the parents at this show were not Parisian collectors. She said so, and Priya said, "Then it's a gamble either way, so pick the version you'd rather lose with."

The next morning Alexia went to the north shore at five and drew the log again, deliberately, the eleventh version, because she wanted to know whether the repetition had a genealogy, whether each drawing descended honestly from the one before, changing as the light changed, or whether she was simply copying herself. When she laid it against the earlier drawings, she saw it: the first pictures had been about the log's shape, and the later ones had quietly become about the water holding it, the way the current moved around an obstruction. The theme had been there the whole time, underneath her, patient.

Her statement took her two evenings. She wrote and cut and rewrote, and the paragraph that survived was four sentences long, about persistence and what a fixed object can teach you about everything around it. Marcus read it and said it was "almost trenchant," and she made him look up whether that was a compliment before she thanked him.

On the day of the show, the portfolios hung along the boathouse wall, and people drifted through with paper cups of lemonade. Alexia's ten drawings went up in a row, unframed, pinned with binder clips, priced at fifteen dollars each or a hundred for all ten. She stood behind the lemonade table pretending to pour, and watched a woman in a sun hat stop in front of the flashlight drawing for a long time, then move down the row slowly, hands clasped behind her back, the way you move through a gallery.

The woman found Dana and asked who the artist was. Alexia wiped her hands on her shorts and came around the table. "I'll take the whole set," the woman said. "My husband drowned in that lake when I was seventeen. I've never once seen it painted." Alexia looked at her hands, then at the wall, and understood that she had made something she could not fully account for, and that the sale and the grief were tangled together in a way she would think about for a long time. She took the drawings down one by one, careful with the pins, and rolled them together with both hands.

The letter from the tenant arrived on a Tuesday, and Sebastian's grandfather read it twice at the kitchen table before setting it under the sugar bowl as though to weigh it down. "Mr. Okafor wants his deposit back," he said. "All six hundred of it."

Sebastian had come to the house for the last week of summer, planning mostly to eat his grandmother's cooking and avoid thinking about the fall. Instead he found himself in the passenger seat of the Buick the next morning, riding across town to the little yellow duplex his grandparents had bought decades ago, back when the mortgage on it had seemed to his grandfather like a rope around the neck. "Thirty years we paid," he said at a red light. "Every month. And the bank held the deed until the end, like a hostage." Sebastian had known, in a vague way, that houses were paid for over time, but he had never pictured his grandfather at twenty-five, signing papers at a bank, putting down what he called "the down payment, the part you have to have up front or they won't talk to you at all."

The tenant, Mr. Okafor, met them on the porch. He was maybe thirty, with a moving truck half loaded behind him in the drive, and he wanted, plainly, his money. "I left that place better than I found it," he said. "I painted the kitchen myself. Paid for the paint out of my own pocket."

Inside, the apartment smelled of cardboard and lemon cleaner. Sebastian's grandfather walked the hallway with his hands behind his back, the way he walked his own garden, and stopped at the living room wall where a row of small nail holes marched along the picture rail like a constellation. "There," he said. "Holes in the wall. That's damage. That comes out of the deposit, that's what a deposit is for."

"No," Sebastian said, and both men turned to look at him, and he felt his face go hot, because he had not planned to say anything. But he had spent the previous night at the kitchen table with his grandmother's ancient laptop, wading through an interminable stretch of tenant-rights pages, some written in a lawyerly dialect that assumed an erudition he did not have, until he found one written in plain sentences and read it three times. "The deposit covers unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear," he said. "Small nail holes are ordinary aging. Where we live, a landlord can't deduct for that."

His grandfather's mouth worked for a moment without sound. "It's my wall," he said finally.

"It's ordinary aging," Sebastian said. "It's on the state website. I took screenshots." He had also done something else, and this was harder to bring up. "Grandpa, I photographed every wall yesterday when we came to measure for the new blinds. Every room, every ceiling corner. Because if Mr. Okafor wants to argue later, you'll want proof of the condition, and so will he."

Mr. Okafor had gone quiet at the mention of the website, and now he cleared his throat. "There's something else," he said. "The back bedroom. There was a leak from the bathroom above it, back in March. I told you about it on the phone." Sebastian's grandfather said that he remembered, and that he had called a plumber. "The plumber patched the pipe," Mr. Okafor said. "The ceiling stain stayed. I didn't cause it, but I didn't fix it either, because it's your building. I figured it would come out of the deposit fight, so I want to say now, before you decide: that stain is mine to live with and yours to fix, and neither of us should pay the other for it."

Here was the twist, and Sebastian watched it happen slowly, like weather changing. His grandfather walked to the back bedroom and stood under the brownish ring on the ceiling for a long time. "That's water damage," he said. "Not from you." He turned around. "I was going to take the six hundred dollars and repaint the whole unit. I had it figured that way. New tenant in September, new paint, and the deposit pays for it."

"Paint wears out," Sebastian said quietly. "Like nail holes."

His grandfather looked at the ceiling, then at the boy, then at the man who had rented his rooms for four years and had never once been late with the rent, and something in his shoulders came down an inch. "The kitchen paint you bought yourself," he said. "What did that cost you?" Mr. Okafor said about eighty dollars. His grandfather took out his checkbook, the old leather kind with a pen loop, and leaned on the windowsill to write. "Six hundred for the deposit," he said, "and eighty for the paint. And you'll indemnify me for nothing, because there's nothing to indemnify. It's just a wall."

Driving home, the windows down, his grandfather was silent for most of the highway. Near the exit he said, "Your grandmother told me you stayed up past one reading that website." Sebastian said that he had. "Good," his grandfather said. "When you get your own place someday, save for the down payment first, then the deposit, and photograph everything, both times, moving in and moving out." He pulled into the driveway and shut off the engine. "Now come inside. She made the plum cake, and she will not cut it without us."

Hannah found the article on Tuesday, third from the top in the database, and printed it before she had finished reading it because the abstract said the finding was significant. That word had been sitting in her thesis outline for a week: Students who use school libraries score significantly higher on standardized tests. It was going to be her central claim, and here was a study that seemed to prove it, with tables, with p-values, with a bibliography she could mine for eight more sources.

Mr. Reyes had given them the format that morning: one argument, sustained; footnotes in Chicago style; a bibliography that did not pad. "A research paper is not a pile of quotations," he had said, walking between the desks. "It is you, taking a position you can defend." Hannah had written that in her notebook. She liked the sound of it, the idea of a position she could hold like ground.

The article was forty-one pages. She read it at the back table of the library during her free period, highlighter uncapped, and it was near the end, in a paragraph she almost skimmed, that she stopped. The sample was enormous, tens of thousands of students across an entire district. And the difference in scores, the actual difference, the one the significance test had been run on, was less than half a point on a two-hundred-point scale.

She read the paragraph again. Then she flipped back to the tables and read the numbers a third time, pressing the highlighter so hard against the margin that it tore the paper a little. Half a point. Her little brother's score had swung thirty points between October and March just because he had slept badly in March.

Last fall, before any of this, there had been an evening she kept returning to without wanting to. Her father had come home with a brochure from a tutoring center, florid with testimonials, a woman's face lit like a saint's, and he had set it beside her college applications at the kitchen table. Two thousand dollars, he said, and their guarantee was statistically proven. She had pushed the brochure back toward him and he had pushed it toward her again, and neither of them had said anything for the rest of dinner, and in the morning the brochure was still there, between the salt and the applications, like a border neither would cross. They had reached a truce by not mentioning it. She had not thought about the word proven since.

Now she thought about it constantly. She found Priya at the periodicals shelf and held out the article, folded open to the page. "Tell me what this says."

Priya read for a minute, chewing the end of her pen. "Significant. It says significant like five times."

"Look at the actual numbers. The difference. Half a point." Hannah tapped the table so hard the pen jumped. "How is that significant?"

"Because that's what the test says. It's a word they use." Priya shrugged. "So it's a big deal."

"It's not a big deal. It's the tiniest possible deal." Hannah lowered her voice; the librarian had looked over. "But the sample is huge. Like, whole-district huge. So the test says significant anyway. It can be significant and basically nothing at the same time."

Priya frowned at the page, then at her. "Then why do they write it that way?"

"That's what I want to know."

She spent her study hall deciding. The easy path was to use the article the way it wanted to be used, quote the abstract, and let the word significant do her arguing for her. The harder thing, the thing Mr. Reyes had half-adumbrated with his talk of defensible positions, was to build her argument on what the numbers actually said: that the libraries study showed something real about how the word significant works, and that her thesis, the way she had written it, was built on sand. She could still argue for libraries. She believed in libraries. But she would have to argue them honestly, on grounds this study did not give her.

She opened a new document and typed a footnote after the citation, Chicago style, checking the handbook twice for the punctuation. In the footnote she wrote that the study reported a significant result and that the measured difference was smaller than half a point on a two-hundred-point scale, with a sample of tens of thousands. She read it back. It was not an attack on the authors. It was just what the paper said, placed where a reader would find it.

At the kitchen table that night, her father asked how the paper was going, and she told him about the word significant, and the half a point, and he was quiet for a moment and then pulled the tutoring brochure out from under a stack of mail. "So this," he said.

"Maybe," she said. She took it from him and turned it over, the saint-lit face and the guarantee, and set it facedown beside her laptop, next to the salt.

Michael had chosen the cello at the start of term because it looked dignified, but the only instrument left in the storeroom that Friday was a violin with a fine layer of chalk dust along its ribs, so he took it. The music room smelled of rosin and the custodian's lemon floor polish, and the radiators clanked like a stubborn percussion section. Ms. Oyelaran, who ran the after-school ensemble and never wasted words, handed him the bow and said, "Four strings. Everything starts there."

He plucked them that first afternoon, one after another, and they gave back G, D, A, E, lowest to highest, though at the time he only heard four different voices arguing. In the practice rooms along the corridor, other people's scales leaked through the walls, and he wondered whether the intervals between those strings were chosen for a reason, or whether somebody, centuries ago, had simply liked the way they climbed. He had a habit of asking questions like that, and his older sister had once told him he could pontificate about a doorknob. He had looked up the word afterwards, then used it back at her, which she found less amusing than he had hoped.

The ensemble met Tuesdays after last bell, and beside him sat Priya Raman, a tiny pugnacious first-year who had been playing violin since she was six and had opinions about everyone else's posture. Across the stands was Colm, who read music the way other people read street signs, without apparent effort, and who had cornered Michael once at the water fountain to declare that a pianist named Ólafur something-or-other was "the whole zeitgeist now, honestly, the spirit of the age, if you even know what that means." Michael had said he didn't, and Colm had nodded, satisfied, as though this proved something.

The concrete problem arrived in November, three days before the winter showcase, when the second violinist in their quartet broke her wrist on the ice behind the gym. Ms. Oyelaran put a photocopy of the second violin part on Michael's stand and said only, "You know the fingerings. Learn the thinking." Priya leaned over during the break, tapping the four strings with her pencil, one, two, three, four, and recited, like a spell she'd been given long ago by her first teacher: "Good Dogs Always Eat." She pointed from the thickest string upward as she said it. Then she went back to arguing with Colm about tempo, leaving Michael to work out for himself that the letters in her sentence were the names of the strings, that G sat lowest, that E sang highest, and that they were spaced, she mentioned later while packing her case, in perfect fifths, each string to the next.

That night he wrote to his sister at college, because she was the only person he could admit things to. "I got promoted out of desperation, not talent," the letter said. "The second violin part is all inner voices, the plumbing of the piece. Nobody hears you unless you vanish, and then they notice the silence. Also I learned the strings are G, D, A and E, lowest to highest, each a fifth apart, and there's a sentence for it, Good Dogs Always Eat, and I keep saying it in my head like a prayer before every entrance. Is it cheating to use a sentence instead of just knowing? Is that how knowing starts?" He sealed it before he could edit himself into sounding less lost.

The showcase was in the gym, under banners from a fundraiser nobody remembered, and the folding chairs filled with parents holding phones like candles. Colm's opening phrase was clean and a little cold. Priya played with her chin up, daring the audience. Michael came in late on his first entrance, half a beat, and nobody died. On his second entrance he was early, and the chord that resulted was sweeter than the one written, which confused him so much he lost his place for two bars and found it again by feel, by the hum of the G string under his knuckle.

Afterwards, Priya's father took a photograph of the quartet, and Ms. Oyelaran shook each of their hands as though conferring knighthoods. In the coat queue, Priya said, "You dragged on that third phrase. Deliberately?" Michael said maybe, that it had sounded like it wanted to linger, though he couldn't say whether the wanting was his or the music's. Priya considered this the way she considered Colm's tempo arguments, then shrugged and said it had worked. He watched Colm's mother mouth something at Colm across the hall, and Colm, grinning, raised his violin case in answer.

He walked home with the case knocking his hip, saying Good Dogs Always Eat to the frosty street, wondering whether every hard thing began as somebody else's sentence that you slowly earned the right to mean. At his corner he stopped, lifted the case, and unlatched it under the streetlight, just to look at the four strings lying in their perfect ladder. He plucked the E, thin and bright against the cold.

The coding club met in the back corner of the library, where the radiators clanked and the whiteboard still held last week's ghost of a half-erased binary tree. Maika arrived early because she wanted the seat by the window, and because she had a problem she hadn't told anyone about: her Song class refused to initialize. She had a plan for the club's showcase, a small app that matched students with local volunteer shifts, and everything depended on this one class behaving itself.

Priya dropped into the chair across from her, already talking. "I redid the pitch deck. Three slides on revenue this time. Mr. Okafor says if we can't monetize it, it's just a hobby with extra steps." Priya wanted the app to win the regional showcase, wanted it badly enough that she'd started saying things like "user acquisition funnel" without irony, and Maika had learned to nod at the deck and then go back to her code.

"Look at this," Maika said, turning her laptop so Priya could see. The test was still red. She had a class called Song with private fields for title and lengthInSeconds, getter methods that compiled cleanly, a test that constructed a Song and asserted on its title. The constructor was right there, name and everything: public void Song(String title). The test failed anyway, insisting the title was null.

Priya leaned in, chewing the end of a pen. "It compiled, though. That's the evil part. If it were broken it would yell at you."

"Java doesn't yell about things it thinks are fine." Maika highlighted the constructor and stared at it the way she stared at a page of French, waiting for a word to resolve into sense. Her mother debugged sewing machines the same way, running her thumb along a seam until the snag showed itself. Maika had always thought of that as the less useful kind of cleverness, patient and physical, nothing like the brisk logic she associated with code. She was less sure of that division now.

Across the table, Theo was showing his own project to a freshman, and Maika caught the word "sycophant" in the middle of his pitch. "The app's too nice," he was saying. "It agrees with everything you type. Like a little sycophant. I want it to argue back." He wanted his chatbot to disagree with people, which struck Maika as a strange thing to want, and also as the kind of wanting that had nothing to do with slides about revenue.

She went back to the constructor and read it aloud, quietly, one token at a time. Public. Void. Song. Then she deleted the word void and ran the test. It went green so fast she thought she'd clicked the wrong button. "It's the void," she said, louder than she meant to. "A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void. With void in front of it, it's not a constructor at all, it's just a method that happens to share a name and never gets called." Priya frowned at the screen. "So it compiled because Java thought you wanted a regular method?" "Exactly. It did what I said instead of what I meant." Maika sat with that for a second, honestly unsure whether she found it infuriating or beautiful, that the language had obeyed her so literally.

Then came the twist she hadn't planned. Priya slid her own laptop across, and there on the screen was the same shape, the same quiet betrayal: public void User(String name). "I copied your style," Priya admitted, ears going pink. "From the file you shared last week." Maika laughed before she could stop herself, and Priya laughed too, and for a moment the showcase and the revenue slides and the funnel didn't matter to either of them. Maika reached over and deleted the void, then sat back. "Your turn. Run it."

Priya hit run, and the test went green, and she said, very quietly, "Okay. Okay, we might actually have something."

The waiting room had nine chairs and Tyler had counted them twice before Dr. Okafor's office door opened and Mrs. Haddad, the health teacher, waved him and Priya inside. It was a field trip with a purpose: the clinic had agreed to let students training as peer health educators practice on real staff, explaining confidentiality, consent, contraception and testing while a nurse listened and scored them on a clipboard. Tyler had signed up because the college applications wanted evidence of leadership, which felt like a cynical reason, and because his older brother had once stood in a pharmacy aisle for twenty minutes trying to decide which condom brand would least embarrass him at the register, which felt like a real one.

Priya went first while Tyler sat in the hallway on a folding chair, running the script through his head. His problem was straightforward and stubborn: he could memorize facts, he had done it his whole academic life, but the moment someone asked a question the script didn't cover, his mind emptied itself like a sink. Mrs. Haddad had warned him. You're going to get a curveball, she'd said, and Tyler had lain awake composing answers to curveballs he invented, each one more catastrophic than the last.

Priya came out looking flushed but intact. "She asked me how the oral swab works," she said. "I described it in way too much detail. She was laughing." Then it was his turn.
