Seth had been staring at Dana's laptop for twenty minutes, and the empty result grid was starting to feel personal. The kitchen table was littered with her mother's mail, a bowl of pistachio shells, and two glasses of lemonade gone warm, and on the screen, patient and blank, sat the query.

"Run it again," Dana said.

"It's going to be empty again."

"Run it anyway."

He clicked the button. The grid stayed empty, zero rows returned, and Dana leaned back in her chair with the pugnacious satisfaction of somebody who had been right about a mystery before it was even a mystery. She worked the summer shift at her uncle's landscaping office, entering orders into a database she had mostly taught herself, and she had promised Seth she would teach him too, because he had said, once, at the edge of a conversation about their futures, that he wanted to understand how information was stored. He hadn't expected the learning to involve so much failure first.

The assignment she had invented for him was simple to say. Two tables, one of customers, one of orders. Find the customers who had never ordered anything. Seth had assumed this would take five minutes. Instead he had typed a query that said, in effect, give me every customer whose ID is not in the list of IDs found in the orders table, and the database had answered him with silence.

"Maybe the query's wrong," he said.

"Or maybe it's right and something's hiding." Dana spun her finger in the air, the universal sign for try it a different way, and Seth retyped the whole thing by hand, slowly, the way his father had taught him to change a tire: no shortcuts, name every step out loud. Still nothing. He felt the particular itch of being close to an answer, that sensation he loved and hated in equal measure, the one that had kept him up past two in the morning last spring converting his grandmother's recipe cards into a spreadsheet, just to see whether it could be done.

She reached over and pulled the laptop toward herself. "Watch this," she said, and she ran a small query against the orders table alone, counting rows. Then she filtered for something, and Seth watched the count drop by one.

"One order has a blank customer," Dana said. "My uncle's shop guy, he types the plant list first and forgets to pick a name. The system saves it anyway. So that row is sitting in there with nothing in the customer column."

Seth looked at the single offending row, a Saturday order for forty boxwood shrubs attached to no one at all. A suspicion arrived, not fully formed, more like weather moving in. He scrolled back up to his query, the one with NOT IN, and read it again as if meeting a stranger who had been standing in the room the whole time.

"Wait," he said. "So the list my subquery builds, the list of customer IDs from the orders table. That list has a blank in it now."

"Say more."

"Last week, when you showed me this on Tuesday, it worked. It listed three customers. Then Saturday happened, the boxwoods, the blank." He heard himself say it and stopped, because the rest of it assembled itself without narration: the query that had returned three rows on Tuesday returned nothing at all today, and the only thing that had changed was that one empty value. The list his NOT IN was checking against contained a single blank, and the whole result had gone dark because of it.

He tested it the only way he could think of, which was to sequester the blank row, setting it aside in its own temporary table where it couldn't touch anything, and then run his original query against everything else. Three customers appeared, instantly, the same three from Tuesday: a dentist, a school, and a woman named R. Okafor who had signed up at a garden fair and never bought a thing.

"So it's not that the query was wrong," Seth said slowly. "It's that one blank poisons the whole list. A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the subquery's list contains even one NULL."

"That's what it looks like," Dana said. "I didn't know it had a name for why. I just knew to dodge it."

They sat with that for a second. Outside, Dana's little brother was failing to land a skateboard trick in the driveway, the clatter and the scrape of it arriving through the screen door at irregular intervals, a counterpoint to the hum of the laptop. Seth thought of his father again, changing that tire, saying that a car can refuse to start for one bad wire and a mechanic who only checks the battery will call it haunted. He wondered how many other things worked this way, whole systems falling silent over one empty value nobody meant to create.

"Is there a way to write it so it can't happen?" he asked.

"There's a different join that handles it," Dana said. "I'll show you. But first."

She pushed the laptop back toward him and pointed at the screen, at the Saturday row with its missing name. "Fix it."

Seth cracked his knuckles, typed UPDATE, and paused, cursor blinking beside the word SET.

The week before Noah left for college, his father handed him a shovel and pointed at the fence line where the last strip of switchgrass separated their bean field from the Halversons' plowed ground. "Pull it out if you want," his father said, "or leave it. It's yours next summer either way." Four acres of grass, four acres that could have been beans at fourteen dollars a bushel, standing there like a spare tire nobody needed. Noah had spent all of July building the case against it, rehearsing numbers in his head the way his debate coach had taught him, but he hadn't said any of it aloud yet.

Then the orientation schedule arrived, and his first Friday of classes included a field trip to the Okafor farm, forty minutes south of campus, for everyone in the agricultural systems survey course. Noah almost skipped it. He had grown up on a farm; he knew more about dirt than the professor did, probably. But attendance was ten percent of the grade, so he boarded the bus with his earbuds in and his arms crossed, watching the tile lines scroll past the windows.

Mrs. Okafor met them at the gate in a canvas jacket, the wind pulling at her collar. She was younger than Noah expected, and she didn't lecture. She just started walking the boundary of her west field, and the class trailed after her through stubble and loose chaff, and when the wind gusted she stopped and let them all feel it, grit ticking against their jacket zippers like sleet. "Notice where it stings and where it doesn't," she said, and kept walking.

The field was striped. Bands of corn ran between bands of tall grass, maybe twenty rows of each, all the way to the creek. A girl from Chicago asked why the farm looked like that, like a barber pole, and Mrs. Okafor squatted down and pulled up a fistful of grass, roots dangling a foot and more below it, pale and matted and heavy with soil. "In the Dust Bowl, the Plains' native grasses got plowed up, and with them the deep roots that held the soil. Then the drought came and the wind carried the topsoil away." She let the root mass dangle a moment longer, then set it back in the ground and tamped it with her boot, as if returning a borrowed thing.

Noah stood at the back of the group and felt his argument rearranging itself under him. He had been thinking about the grass strips as sentiment, his grandfather's habit dressed up as virtue, something you paid for out of nostalgia. He hadn't thought of them as machinery. The wind was still coming off the Halversons' side of the fence line even here, forty minutes from home, and it stung on the bare patches and went quiet in the grass, exactly as she'd said it would.

On the bus back he called his father. "I'm not pulling the switchgrass out," he said. His father said nothing for a while, long enough that Noah could hear the radio in the kitchen, the grain report, noxious weed notices for two counties over. "You had that whole speech ready," his father said finally. "I could hear you practicing it through the screen door. Fourteen dollars a bushel. I know the number." Noah looked out the window at a tractor turning on a far field, its dust plume rising and leaning east. "The grass is holding the field down," Noah said. "That's income too. It's just income you can't see until the year you'd lose everything else."

There was a silence on the line that Noah couldn't read, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it. Maybe his father was proud. Maybe he was recalculating the farm's whole ledger. Maybe he was just tired and had stopped listening. Noah's roommate, a business major who heard only the word income, leaned over from the next seat and said, "So did you convince him, or did he convince you?" and Noah said, "Neither, I think. I changed my own mind with somebody else's information," which sounded clumsy out loud, and which his roommate repeated in a mock-elocution voice, hand to his chest, until the girl from Chicago told them both to shut up.

That Sunday, the wind came up hard out of the northwest, thirty miles an hour and rising, and Noah drove home to walk the fence line before he left for good. The Halversons' field, disked bare for winter wheat, had already begun to travel; a brown haze hung over the low ground, and the ditch on their side of the fence had a new shoulder of fine soil drifted against the wire, soft as ash. On his family's side, the bean stubble was brown and ugly but fixed, and the switchgrass ran down the slope in a gold line, hissing, its seed heads bent all one direction, and along its upper edge the drifted soil had piled six inches deep, held there, bought and paid for in a currency no market quoted.

His father came down the fence line to meet him, hands in his pockets, and stood looking at the drift. "Halverson called this morning," he said. "He wants to know if we've still got seed for that grass." Then he laughed once, short, almost regretful. "Forty years I've been telling your grandfather those strips were wasted ground. Now the man who out-yielded me every season of my life wants my weeds." He bent and picked up a handful of the drifted topsoil, let the wind burnish it off his palm grain by grain, and said, "Go get the seed catalog out of the truck."

The laundromat on Fenwick Street had two broken dryers and a vending machine that ate quarters, and Audrey had claimed the folding table by the window because from there she could watch the parking spaces along the curb. Her father called them practice bays. She called them torture devices with bumpers. Every Saturday they did three loads of wash and one load of parallel parking, because the car had to be somewhere while the clothes tumbled, and her test was in eleven days.

"Again," her father said, standing on the sidewalk with his coffee, steam fermenting in the cold air like the whole morning was quietly going sour. Audrey pulled forward past the orange hatchback, reversed until her rear wheel was level with its bumper, and turned the wheel. She ended up a foot and a half from the curb, angled like something that had given up halfway through a decision.

"Twenty-five centimeters or less," her father said, tapping the roof. "You're generous with your distance."

"I'm generous with everything. It's my whole personality." She straightened the car, tried again, and this time heard the tire kiss the curb with a sound like a knuckle cracking. She let the brake off an inch. The car settled. When she got out and looked, she was close, actually close, and she stood there in the cold feeling something she didn't have a word for yet, a small triumph that she immediately distrusted because she'd done nothing but the same thing six times until it worked once.

The highway came later, after the laundromat, because the dryer took forty minutes and the on-ramp to Route 9 was four blocks away. Audrey's father believed in the round trip: wash, drive, merge, come back, fold. "Use the time," he said, which was his answer to most things, including grief, including her mother having left in September, including money, which they didn't discuss in numbers anymore. The laundromat itself was a kind of confession. Everyone there was washing somewhere else because they couldn't wash at home, and Audrey had started to recognize the regulars: the man with the work jackets, the woman who read court documents, the teenager who slept against the wall with headphones on.

On the ramp, Audrey accelerated and looked over her shoulder. A delivery truck sat in the right lane, close, its grille filling her side mirror like a wall. She waited for it to slide left, to open a door for her, the way she'd seen cars do for her mother a hundred times. It didn't move. She ran out of ramp, braked hard at the gore point, and sat there with her hazard lights ticking while her father set down his coffee.

"Who has to yield here?" he asked. Not angry. That was worse, in a way, because it meant he'd known this was coming.

"The truck," she said. "It should move over."

"Traffic already on the highway has the right of way," he said, and that was all he said. Audrey looked at the mirror again, at the stream of cars behind the truck, and understood that nobody was going to make room, that the road was not a meritocracy where good intentions earned you a gap, that she had to find the space herself. She watched the pattern of vehicles come at her, a school of them, and picked out a hole two cars back, adjusted her speed to shrink toward it rather than demanding it shrink toward her, and merged. The car settled into the lane like a word finding its place in a sentence.

They drove in silence for a while. Audrey was thinking that her mother had always been the one who moved over, who made room, and that maybe that was a way of being good or maybe it was a way of disappearing, and she couldn't decide, and the not-deciding was itself a kind of answer she didn't like. At the laundromat they folded towels side by side, her father pairing socks with a penurious exactness, refusing to lose even one. The teenager by the wall had woken up and was watching the dryers spin as if they held something of his. Audrey laid her palms flat on a stack of warm towels, still carrying the shape of the steering wheel, and thought of the test, eleven days out, no promises attached.

"Next week the highway first," her father said, handing her the keys to lock up.

"Fine," she said. "But I pick the music."

Edouard set the lasagna down between his mother's geraniums and his brother's phone, and immediately his father began. "So the hero of the hardware store returns. Tell them what you did."

The facts were simple enough to say out loud, though they had been undulating in Edouard's head all afternoon like something alive in a jar. On Tuesday he had suggested to Mr. Kastner, the owner, that the store stay open an hour later on weekdays. More contractors would come after their jobs ended; the numbers Edouard had pulled from the register tapes supported it. Mr. Kastner had clapped him on the shoulder and said he'd think like an owner someday. Then, on Thursday, the new schedule went up, and the closing shift started at six, which was exactly when the last bus to Cedar Heights left the depot. Rosa, who had worked closings for nine years, lived in Cedar Heights. So did Marcus and the two college kids hired in May.

"Edouard," his mother said. "Your father is being facetious. Eat."

"I'm being serious. This is a serious dinner." His father forked a piece of garlic bread and pointed it like a citation. "My son improves the store's revenue and strands three employees at the curb. That's a trade-off, that's what that is. You learn about those in your ethics class? They have a name for everything now."

"They have a name for this one, actually." Edouard had spent his lunch period in the library with his phone face down on the table, searching until he found it. "There's a professor, Freeman, wrote a book in 1984, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. He argued that a business should consider everyone affected by its decisions, not only the owners. Anyone affected counts as a stakeholder. Customers, workers, the neighborhood." Saying it aloud at the table felt strange, like reciting something in a language he was not yet fluent in.

His brother, Timmy, looked up from his phone long enough to say, "So the bus people are stakeholders and Dad's a stakeholder and the store's a stakeholder. Everybody's a stakeholder. Great system, very rigorous."

"Everyone affected," Edouard said. "That's the point. That's the whole point, actually." He was surprised by how steady his voice came out, because inside he was not steady at all. He had made a recommendation with a spreadsheet and a guess about traffic, and the spreadsheet had been right, and the guess had been right, and Rosa had still ended up standing on Delaware Avenue at six-fifteen yesterday, waiting for a ride that came forty minutes late. He'd seen her from the bus window on his way home. He had almost gotten off. He had stayed in his seat, which was its own decision, and he could not stop weighing it.

"Did you say anything to Kastner?" his mother asked. She had stopped eating, which in her case was the equivalent of standing up and shouting.

"I went back this morning before school. I told him about the bus." Edouard pushed the lasagna around his plate, red sauce pooling in the trench his fork made. "He said he'd look at carpooling options. He said, and this is a quote, 'Good catch, that's why I pay you to think.' Except he doesn't pay me to think about that part. He pays me to think about the register. I thought about the register and something else happened, something I wasn't looking at."

"Unintended consequences," his father said, with the grim satisfaction of a man who had predicted rain all day and was now watching it pour. "You didn't intend to strand Rosa. Intentions don't carry people home, though."

"Right, but here's what I keep going back and forth on." Edouard put his fork down, which his family all noticed, because he never put his fork down. "If I'd thought about everyone affected, if I'd actually applied the thing instead of just finding it Thursday night like a lawyer hunting for a precedent to excuse himself with, would I have made a different recommendation? Maybe. Maybe I'd have said close at five-thirty and open earlier. Or maybe I'd have said the same thing, because the store is struggling, because Mr. Kastner has three kids in college, because he's a stakeholder too, and the whole thing is a trade-off between people who all have real claims. The book gives you the question. It doesn't do the arithmetic for you."

Timmy lowered the phone entirely, which had not happened at a dinner table since March. "So what are you going to do?"

"Monday I'm going to ask Mr. Kastner for the schedule through August, before it's posted, not after. Not to reverse anything. Just to look at all of it at once, bus times and register tapes together, and see what's actually possible." He picked the fork back up. "Maybe nothing changes. Maybe the honest answer is that the extra hour pays for a shuttle van. I don't know yet. I'm telling you I don't know yet, and I'd rather say that than pretend I solved it in the library at lunch."

His mother spooned more lasagna onto his plate without asking, which was how she said she was listening. His father opened his mouth, closed it, and ate the garlic bread instead. Through the window the geraniums moved in the evening wind, and Timmy said, "Stakeholder theory at the dinner table. Verisimilitude achieved. This family finally resembles an actual household."

"Shut up and pass the bread," Edouard said, and passed it to Rosa in his head, forty minutes late, still waiting under the streetlight.

I didn't care that Deacon had a new helmet. That's what I told Priya at lunch, twice, which should have been my first clue that I cared. What I actually wanted was to win the ethics unit, because Mr. Okafor had promised the best essay would be read at assembly, and my mother had already missed two of my assemblies this year. A win felt like a way to suture the gap without ever having to say anything out loud.

The helmet was white with a black stripe, and Deacon wore it to fourth period like a crown. "Full face, MIPS, the works," he said, tipping it back on his head. "I can bomb the Lark Street hill now and nothing happens."

"Nothing happens anyway," Priya said. "You crawl down it."

"Not anymore."

That afternoon I watched from the chain-link fence as he took the hill standing on the pedals, faster than I'd ever seen him go, the helmet bright against the asphalt. He made it, obviously. He waved both hands, which was its own kind of argument. In fifth grade, before any of us wore helmets, he used to ride down that same hill with his arms crossed like a magician, and once he skidded into the hedge and came up laughing with a leaf in his teeth. I remembered that while I stood at the fence, and I remembered, too, that he'd gone slower back then.

I was in the school library that night because of the essay, not because of him. Mr. Okafor had listed concepts on the board: responsibility, trade-offs, unintended consequences, and told us to find one real example and argue it honestly. I'd been planning to write about my mother, some specious thing about sacrifice, and I'd been planning to make it neater than it was. But I opened a behavioral economics book at the next table and found a chapter on safety measures that didn't deliver what engineers predicted. There was a term for it. Risk compensation, the book said: people behave less carefully when a safety measure makes them feel protected, so the measure delivers less benefit than predicted. I copied it into my notebook and then sat without writing anything else for a while.

"Risk compensation," I said to Priya the next morning, showing her the page. "That's Deacon. The helmet didn't make the hill safer. It made him faster."

"So tell him to slow down."

"It's not that simple. He's not wrong to wear it. If he falls, it still helps. It's just that the benefit is smaller than the box promised, because he changed his behavior." I heard myself lecturing and stopped. This was the problem with the concept: it cut both ways, and I hated things that cut both ways. My mother took the night shift for the money that let us stay in this school district, and the money came with her absence, and whenever I called that a trade-off she said I was too young to use that word about her choices, and whenever I said her choice had an unintended consequence, which was me eating dinner alone, she stopped answering texts for a day. Responsibility, I had started to think, was mostly a word adults used to close conversations.

I caught Deacon at his locker. "You went twice as fast down the hill yesterday."

"Yeah. It's safe now. That's the point of a helmet."

"The point of a helmet is if you crash. It doesn't cancel the crash." I turned my notebook around so he could see the photocopied page. "Risk compensation. It's a real thing. People act less carefully when they feel protected, so the safety thing doesn't help as much as it's supposed to."

He read it, jaw working. "So what am I supposed to do, wear the helmet and ride like I don't have it?"

"Basically, yeah."

"That's the most boring advice anyone's ever given me." But he said it looking at the page, not at me, and on Friday I saw him take the hill seated, braking in pulses, the white helmet moving at a speed I almost didn't recognize. He waved at the fence with one hand only.

I wrote the essay that weekend. I wrote about Deacon and the hill and the term from the library, and then, near the end, without planning to, about the night shift, though I kept my mother's name out of it. I didn't resolve it. I wrote that some protections are still worth taking even when they change us, and that you can't always tell which part of a person is the trade-off and which is just who they became, and Mr. Okafor wrote "honest" in the margin in green ink. The assembly was Thursday. My mother texted that she'd try to make it, and then, an hour later, that the shift swap hadn't gone through.

I sat in the third row next to Priya. On stage, Mr. Okafor adjusted the microphone, unfolded a paper, and said my name.

Nicole pushed the coffee table to the wall and set nine coins across the rug: a quarter for Priya, a nickel for Marcus, pennies for the others. Her mother had asked, twice, why the living room smelled like dust and basement, and Nicole had answered both times that the drama room was booked until six and the performance was Friday.

The one-act was thirty pages long and hers to direct, which still felt like a mistake the drama teacher would eventually correct. She knelt over the coins and moved the quarter two inches left, then back. "You stand here when he says the thing about the river," she said to Priya, tapping the carpet, "and you cross on 'impecunious,' because it's the ugliest word in the play and the crossing makes it funny." Priya walked the path once, stiff-armed, waiting.

Marcus refused to move at all. He stood by the bookshelf with his script rolled in his fist and said that his character wouldn't cross, that his character would stay planted, and that actors found those things by trying them, not by being told. "That's what blocking is for," Nicole said. "It's the plan for where everyone stands and moves." Marcus said plans were for people who didn't trust their actors, and Priya laughed in a way that suggested she had picked a side.

That night, after everyone had gone, Nicole sat on the couch with her laptop and looked up where the word came from. Nineteenth-century directors, she read, including W. S. Gilbert, planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor. She read it twice, then got a wooden block from her little brother's shelf and set it on the coffee table where Marcus refused to stand. It was a plain square of maple, and it did exactly what she told it to do.

She was not sure which of them was right, and she tried to introspect on it honestly, which mostly meant sitting still and watching herself not decide. Last year she had assistant-directed under a boy who choreographed every gesture, and the play had been precise and dead. The year before that she had acted in a production where nobody planned anything, and by opening night the cast had been blocking each other in the literal sense, colliding around a doorway in the second scene like strangers in a stairwell. Two failures, two opposite reasons. Somewhere between them was the thing she actually wanted, and she could describe it only as control that left room.

Her friend Dee came over Thursday with her chemistry flashcards, because Dee studied everywhere, even on Nicole's floor during a break. "Monomer," Dee said, flipping a card. "It's one unit on its own. Then a bunch of them link up and you get a polymer." Nicole looked at the coins still scattered across the rug, each one a separate small decision, and thought that a blocking plan might work the same way, except that actors were units that argued back.

At the final run-through, she tried it. "Marcus," she said, "I'm giving you the spot by the shelf as yours. Planted, like you wanted. But when Priya crosses on 'impecunious,' you turn your head and follow her, and that's not negotiable, because the audience needs to know you noticed." Marcus turned his head, once, experimentally, as if checking whether his neck agreed. "And everyone else," Nicole said, kneeling to slide the pennies along the carpet, "you follow this, but if something true happens in the moment, take it, and tell me after so I can change the map."

The run-through was not clean. Priya went up on a line and covered it with a cough, and one of the pennies, standing in for a boy named Elliot, ended up on the sofa while Elliot himself was still by the window. But the crossing landed, and Marcus's head turn landed harder than any of her choreography had, because it cost him something to do it. Afterward, while the others gathered scripts and shoes, Marcus stopped at the door. "Gilbert guy used blocks," he said. "I looked it up too. Whole model stage, one block per actor." Nicole held up the maple square she had left on the coffee table. "Then this is you," she said, and set it down on the shelf spot, and left it there.

The garage smelled of WD-40 and the ghost of every lawn mower Nolan's father had ever abandoned there, and at its center, balanced on two sawhorses and an upturned milk crate, stood the ramp. It was a length of vinyl gutter with one end propped on a stack of physics textbooks, which Nolan considered a nice touch, like a snake eating its own tail. At the bottom of the ramp the gutter curved into a short horizontal lip, so that a marble rolling down it would leave the edge moving purely sideways, purely horizontally, and then fall, and then, if Nolan had anything to say about it, land exactly where he predicted.

He had predicted the desk. The marble had just landed in a coffee can he had put there on a whim, which was worse, somehow, than missing entirely, because now the can was acting smug.

"You're grinning at a can," said Priya from the workbench, where she sat with her knees pulled up on a stool, a printout in her lap. She had come over under the pretense of helping, which so far had meant watching him chase marbles and eating the crackers he'd set out for himself. She was phlegmatic about most things, Nolan had decided long ago, the kind of person who could receive a failing grade or a free car with the same mild blink. "That's not a good sign for either of us."

"It landed where I said. Approximately. Within the can's radius plus the desk's width." He crouched and picked up his notebook, where he had split the marble's launch into two halves that had nothing to do with each other, which was the part that still felt like a magic trick. Sideways, the marble kept its speed forever, unbothered, seven meters a second from now until the end of time. Downward, it started from nothing and got faster, dragged into acceleration like everyone else. Two lives, lived simultaneously, only meeting again when he combined them to find where the thing came down. "The whole point is you don't mix them up. Horizontal doesn't know about gravity. Gravity doesn't care about horizontal. They're strangers on the same train."

"That's almost poetic."

"It's the only poetry I'm getting this semester." He rolled the marble back up to the top of the ramp and let it go. It clicked down the gutter, whispered across the lip, dropped, and this time missed the can by a full hand-width. Nolan stared at the wet mark it left on the concrete, transfixed, as though the marble might apologize and shuffle over. It did not. He measured the distance anyway and wrote it in the column marked should have been.

Priya slid off the stool and came to crouch beside him, holding out the printout. "Okay, since you're the local genius. My lab from the college thing. Two plates, twelve millimeters apart, hooked to the supply, and we were supposed to move the probe around and check the field against the formula. E equals V over d. Mine matched in the middle, more or less. Then I moved the probe near the edge of the plates and my number went weird. Too small. Like way too small. And my write-up is due Monday and the TA wrote, in actual red pen, 'explain this discrepancy.'" She said the last two words with the flat dread of someone reading a prophecy.

Nolan took the paper. The numbers marched down the page, well-behaved in the middle rows and then, near the end, sagging like the end of a week. "What did you write?"

"That I think I held the probe wrong." She shrugged. "Which is possible. I hold most things wrong."

He was quiet for a moment, not because he knew, but because the shape of her bad numbers reminded him of something, the same way the marble's miss had a shape to it. His mind drifted briefly into a reverie of all the perfect drawings in his textbook: neat parallel arrows, field lines marching in formation between two plates, straight as soldiers, straight as the marble's imaginary sideways life. And then his actual marble, curving off its appointed path the instant it left the ramp, because the ramp's guidance stopped at the edge and the world's sloppiness began. He got up, stepped over the crate, and dug through the milk crate of books until he found the chapter on capacitors, its edges already soft from his grandmother's habit of reading while cooking.

He flipped pages. There it was, a diagram of two plates, and at the plates' edges the once-orderly lines bowed outward, escaping into open air like prisoners gone over a wall. He read the caption aloud, slowly, following it with his finger. "Near the edges of real plates the field lines bulge outward and the field weakens, so E equals V over d holds best near the centre." He looked up. "There's a name for it. Fringing."

"Fringing," Priya repeated, testing the word like a marble on her tongue. "So the edges of my plates are fringing, and my probe wasn't wrong, it was just standing in the wrong part of the field."

"That's the good part. Your measurement isn't the mistake. The formula is the thing with the boundary." Nolan set the book down on the workbench, open to the diagram, and Priya leaned over it, her ponytail hanging into the space between the drawn plates, which he chose not to point out because he was, at this moment, generous. She copied the caption into her notebook, then added three exclamation points and a small drawing of her TA's red pen being snapped in half.

"So the middle of the field is tidy," she said, "and the edges are where everything bends out and leaks away."

"Which is why my marble's late, probably. It's fringing." Nolan pointed at the wet mark on the concrete, three centimeters from where physics said it should be, and Priya laughed the way she always did, quietly and mostly through her nose. He picked up the marble again, weighed it in his palm, and walked it back to the top of the ramp.

The kitchen smelled like burnt toast and solder, which meant Marcus had commandeer the entire first floor for his interview prep. Jason set his backpack down by the door and found his friend at the table with his grandfather, both of them adjusting their grips on each other's hands like they were tuning an instrument.

"Again," the old man said. "You're giving me a dead fish."

"It's a handshake, Grandpa. Not a hostage exchange."

"It's the first thing they'll judge you on. Jason, tell him."

Jason hesitated, because the thing he actually knew was more specific than that. "There was a study," he said. "Two thousand, led by a psychologist named William Chaplin. He found that people with firm handshakes tended to make more favorable first impressions. That's it. That's the whole finding."

"There," the grandfather said. "Firm handshakes, favorable impressions. Science agrees with me."

"Correlation," Marcus muttered. "Not destiny."

Upstairs, the real work was waiting. Their robotics team had regionals in eleven days, and Marcus was the presenter, the one who had to explain their water-quality sensor to the judges in four minutes. He ran the demo for Jason and his grandfather, who had followed them up to reclaim his reading glasses, and Jason watched him lose the room in the first thirty seconds. He fiddled with the sample vial. He said "um" the way other people breathe. He ended with "so, yeah," which was the verbal equivalent of the dead fish.

"Well?" Marcus said, after. He was still holding the vial, and his knuckles had gone pale around it.

Jason knew what he was supposed to say, because Coach Ramirez kept saying it: be honest with your teammates. He also knew that last month, when he'd told Marcus the old arm design was "kind of a mess," Marcus hadn't spoken to him for two days. Those two approaches sat in him like two incompatible things, honesty on one side, the friendship on the other, and he could not find the hinge between them.

"It was fine," he said.

"Fine means bad," Marcus said. "You do this face."

"I don't do a face."

"You're doing it right now."

Marcus's grandfather, from the doorway, did not help by being facetious about it. "Perhaps the machine could shake hands with the judges," he offered. "Since it appears to be the only one here with a firm grip." Marcus threw a pillow at him and he retreated, laughing, down the stairs.

Jason pulled out his biology flashcards, mostly as something to do with his hands. Antigen, read the top one, and he stared at the word while he tried to think. An antigen was a thing the body recognized as foreign and responded to. That was the problem, he realized. His feedback kept arriving looking like an attack, so Marcus's whole system treated it as something to fight off. "Kind of a mess" wasn't information. It was a shapeless insult with no handle on it.

"Run it again," Jason said. "I want to time the opening."

"Seriously?"

"Thirty seconds to the demo, then you're talking. Go."

Marcus ran it again. Jason counted the filler words on his fingers, marked where the vial-fiddling started, watched where the explanation of the sensor's calibration actually landed, because it was good, sharper than anything the other teams would bring. When Marcus finished, Jason made himself start there.

"The calibration part, the ninety seconds in the middle, is the best thing you've done all season. It's clear, it's confident, and it's the part the judges will remember." Marcus's shoulders came down an inch. "The problem is everything before it. You said 'um' nine times in the first thirty seconds, and you picked up the vial before you told us what it was for, so we watched your hands instead of listening. If you just stand still for the first ten seconds, the 'um's stop."

Marcus looked at the vial in his hand, then set it deliberately on the desk. "Nine?"

"I counted."

"Creepy, but okay." He rubbed his palms on his jeans. "Again?"

They ran it four more times. By the third, the opening was clean, and by the fourth Marcus had stopped reaching for the vial entirely. His grandfather reappeared at the door with two glasses of lemonade and made them both shake his hand before he would surrender the drinks, and Marcus gripped hard enough to make the old man's eyebrows go up in approval.

"See," the grandfather said. "Favorable first impression."

"Correlation," Marcus said, but he was grinning. He turned back to the desk and squared his shoulders toward the imaginary judges. "Thirty seconds. Time me."

Jason raised his phone, thumb on the stopwatch. "Go."

The assignment was on the board in Ms. Okafor's handwriting: a ten-minute play, one moment from your own life, staged by Friday. Matthew sat in the third row of the classroom and wrote nothing for most of the period. He had a moment. He simply did not want it performed by a boy from his fourth period in front of thirty acquaintances.

The moment was this: two Januaries ago, his father had missed his regional swim final, and afterward, in the parking lot, Matthew had said the sentence he could not stop hearing. "You were at work when it mattered." His father had not answered. He had unlocked the car, and they had driven home with the radio on, and that was all. Matthew wrote four other ideas that week, about a lost wallet, about a fistfight he had never actually been in, about a made-up summer job. Ms. Okafor read them in conference and slid them back across the desk. "These are costumes," she said. "Write the parking lot." She was not doctrinaire about much, but she held this line against every draft he brought her, and by Wednesday he gave in.

He cast Dev Raghunathan as himself, which was a mistake he would understand later. Dev was tall and confident and had never once, as far as Matthew knew, been ashamed of anything. Priya Nair, who had stage-managed the winter one-acts, agreed to run the rehearsal because she owed Ms. Okafor a favor and because, as she put it, she liked watching people rehearse badly and then stop. They got the black box theater on Thursday after school, one folding table for the car, two chairs.

The first run-through collapsed in ninety seconds. Dev delivered the line facing the empty chair where his scene partner, a girl named Carmen playing the silent father, sat. From the house, Matthew watched the back of Dev's head. Priya stood up from her booth stool. "You're losing your face," she said. "Cheat out. It means you turn your body partly toward the audience even while you're talking to another character, so your face and voice carry." Dev tried it, angled maybe thirty degrees toward the empty seats, and suddenly Matthew could see his mouth moving, could hear the words land instead of dying against the back wall.

Matthew had his AP Bio textbook with him, because the midterm was Monday, and during a break he sat on the stage edge reading about antigens, the molecules your immune system learns to recognize and then attacks on sight. He looked up at Dev and Carmen running the scene again, and he thought that the line he had written was like that, something in him that had been recognized once and could not now be passed over without a reaction. He did not say this out loud. Priya would have called it trying to reify a feeling into a fact, which was something she said about bad plays, plays that took something moving and made it into a statue.

The second problem was worse than staging. Dev played the argument with style, with a kind of swagger, and Matthew sat in the house getting angrier with each run. "That's not how it went," he finally said, walking up onto the stage. "I wasn't winning. I was seventeen seconds too late to take it back." Dev folded his arms. "So what do you want, man? Sad kid yells at dad, dad's silent, drive home. That's the whole play?" Matthew stood there between the folding table and the chairs. "Yes," he said. "That's the whole play. I've been trying to make it something else all week and it isn't." Dev looked at him for a moment, and then something in his posture loosened, and he said, "Okay. Run it."

On Friday afternoon the class filed in. Carmen had been given one direction only: she never cheated out. She faced Dev fully, the whole time, so the audience saw her profile and Dev's face, which meant that the silence belonged to Matthew's father while the sentence belonged to Matthew. Whether that was fair, Matthew did not know. He suspected it was not. He had put it that way anyway, and he sat in the back row with his arms crossed, honest at least about the uncertainty, because the play asserted a judgment about that parking lot that he had never actually settled in two years of thinking about it.

The scene ran ten minutes and four seconds. Nobody laughed where he had feared laughter. At the line, Dev cheated out toward the audience, the words carrying into the dark, his face open and slightly turned, and in the silence afterward Carmen stared straight ahead at him and said nothing, and the folding table held the imaginary car keys, and the lights came up.

Ms. Okafor asked afterward whether he wanted to talk about it, and Matthew said no, and she nodded and moved on to the next play. After class, in the hallway, Dev caught up with him at the water fountain. "Hey," Dev said. "That thing where I turn toward the audience. Your dad. That's you doing that to everyone, right? Facing them partly so they can hear you?" Matthew drank, wiped his mouth on his sleeve, and walked the other way down the hall, keeping his back to him.

Mr. Okafor had said the words twice, and both times they had slid off Robert like rain off waxed paper: DNA to RNA to protein, transcription, translation. Then he had said the thing that mattered. "If you can teach it to someone who doesn't know it, Robert, then you know it. Otherwise you've memorized it." The test was Friday. Robert had until then to find somebody to teach.

The garden on Delancey Street had forty plots and a shed with a rusted roof, and on Saturday mornings Robert worked his mother's plot because she worked doubles at the hospital and because last summer he'd let the tomatoes die. This Saturday he brought his notebook anyway, propped open between the stakes of the bean trellis, and read his cramped notes while he pulled crabgrass. Nucleotide. Base pairing. RNA polymerase. The words sat on the page like strangers at a bus stop.

"That's the weirdest weeding I've ever seen," said Priya, from the plot beside theirs. She was a sophomore at the community college, garrulous in the early way of someone still delighted to have opinions, and she was forever talking across the fence about her biology class. "You're going to plant a textbook."

"I have to learn this stuff by Friday," Robert said. "And apparently the only way to learn it is to teach it. You want to be my victim?"

Priya dusted soil off her hands and leaned on the fence. "I literally just had a test on it. I failed it. So I'm a great victim, I won't accidentally know things."

He started badly. He said DNA was a template, and she asked what a template was, and he discovered he didn't know, not in a way he could say out loud. He turned back to the beans, and the turning helped. The vines climbed the strings by twining, each cell along the way reading something and becoming something. "Okay," he said slowly. "The DNA is like the master copy. It stays in the nucleus, it never leaves. But the cell needs instructions out at the ribosomes, where protein gets built. So it makes a copy of the part it needs. That's transcription. RNA polymerase unzips the DNA and builds a matching strand of RNA, one monomer at a time, matching base to base."

"Like writing down a recipe instead of carrying the whole cookbook to the kitchen."

"That's it. Exactly that." He felt something click into place that hadn't clicked in class, where the diagrams had all been arrows and nobody had said cookbook.

"And then translation is the cooking part?"

"Then translation is the cooking part." He crouched and drew in the dirt with a stick, three letters at a time. "The RNA gets read in threes, and each three is a codon, and each codon calls for one amino acid. The ribosome strings them together. Amino acid after amino acid, and the chain folds up and it's a protein. It's how the instructions become a thing that actually does work in the cell."

Priya was quiet for a second, which for Priya was remarkable. Then she pointed her trowel at the water barrel by the shed, the one that collected rain off the roof through a pipe. "You know what I got wrong on the test? Not this part. The energy part. There was this guy, Mitchell, he proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane. It's called chemiosmosis." She said the word carefully, the way she said new words, tasting it. "He won the Nobel Prize for it in 1978. That part I remember, because it was on the study sheet like four times. What I couldn't get was the gradient itself."

Robert looked at the barrel. The water behind it, pressing to get out through the pipe. Then he looked past the fence to the far end of the lot, where the Alvarez family had a little dirt dam across the drainage ditch to slow the rainwater for their peppers. "Like that," he said. "Like water behind a dam. The protons pile up on one side of the membrane and they want to get across, and that wanting is the energy. The cell lets them through a gate and uses the push."

Priya stared at the little dam across the ditch, water backed up and shimmering behind it, trickling through the one gap Mr. Alvarez had left. "A farm dam," she said. "He proposed it in 1961 and everybody laughed at him? And then seventeen years later they hand him the Nobel?"

"Seventeen years," Robert said. He thought about that. He thought about Mr. Okafor saying you know it when you can teach it, and about Priya failing her test anyway, and about how neither of those things had turned out to be the whole truth. Priya had known the fact cold, the name and the dates, and still hadn't been able to picture it until a pile of dirt across a drainage ditch did the work. Maybe knowing was layers, and you never got to the bottom one. He could explain transcription now, he was almost sure, but the why of it, why threes, why this monomer and not that one, was still dark water.

On Friday Robert got an A minus. He missed one question, about the energy, and he thought of Priya and almost laughed into his scantron. After school he walked to the garden. The Alvarez dam had been leveled by the storm Wednesday night, the peppers standing in mud, and Priya was already there with a shovel, and she handed him a second one without being asked.

"They said it couldn't hold," she said. "It held for three weeks."

He set his feet in the mud and drove the blade in.

The cake had his name on it in blue icing, which Brayden took as a small omen, since blue was the color of the college logo on the banner his mother had taped above the buffet. He had not yet told anyone that he was thinking of deferring a year, and the banner seemed to presage the conversation he would have to have before the ice cream melted. He stood near the deviled eggs and practiced openings in his head.

His grandfather arrived late, as always, holding a folded newspaper under one arm like a man reporting for duty. He shook Brayden's hand formally, then ruined it by pulling him into a hug that smelled like spearmint and engine grease. "Eighteen," he said. "Legal adult. You can now be sued."

"I'll try to avoid insolvency," Brayden said, mostly to make his cousins laugh, and they did, except for the youngest, who asked what insolvency meant and was told to eat his potato salad.

Dinner was long and loud. An uncle who had once declared bankruptcy, a fact the family handled the way it handled weather, held forth on the stock market with a jaundiced eye, and Brayden's mother kept refilling glasses as though hydration were the family's only remaining defense. When the toasts began, his grandfather stood, tapped his glass, and did not say what everyone expected.

"I never graduated," he said. "High school, I mean. I left in eleventh grade."

The room recalibrated. His mother set down a pitcher. Someone's fork stopped halfway.

"I went in the Army instead," his grandfather continued, apparently addressing the potato salad. "And afterward, I got the GED. That test they made in 1942, so service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school could show they had the skills anyway. That was me. I took it after I got out."

"The same year," Brayden's aunt said, "as the Chopin concert?"

"The same lifetime," his grandfather said, and sat down, having concluded his remarks.

Later, Brayden found him on the porch with a slice of cake he wasn't eating, the fork laid across the plate at a precise angle. The yard was turning the color of late evening, and somewhere a sprinkler ticked against a fence.

"You never told me that," Brayden said.

"Never came up."

"I've known you eighteen years."

"Seventeen and some months. You weren't conversational at first."

Brayden sat on the step below him. In the window behind them, his mother was cutting more cake for cousins who hadn't finished their first pieces, an act of optimism the family had long since learned not to question. He had been rehearsing a speech all week about the gap year, the job at the machine shop, the idea that a diploma was a door and not a floor, and now every version of it sounded different in his head.

"I've been thinking about not going," he said. "In the fall. Right away, I mean. Working first."

His grandfather didn't answer right away. He picked up the fork, then set it down again, and Brayden understood that this was the older man thinking, not dismissing.

"You know what I used to think the GED was?" his grandfather said. "Secondhand. A substitute thing. Took me years to notice nobody who mattered ever asked which one I had. Then I trained fellows who had the regular diploma and couldn't read a schematic, and I stopped sorting people that way, including myself." He looked at the yard. "On the other hand, the Army didn't give me a choice about waiting. You have one. That's not nothing either."

"So which is it?"

"If I knew that, I'd have written a book instead of engines." He handed the plate down. "Take this in, would you. Your mother's giving me the look."

Brayden carried the cake through the sliding door, past the banner, past the uncle now explaining interest rates to a teenager who was texting under the table. His mother met his eyes across the room with a question in them, and he realized he still didn't have the answer, only something closer to it, and that his grandfather had left both pieces of it on the porch, next to a fork nobody had used.

He set the plate on the buffet, and before he could turn around, his mother said, "Brayden. Come here a second."

The community centre smelled of floor wax and instant coffee, and the folding chairs had been arranged into something the coach called a courtroom, though it looked more like a wake. Tyson sat at the respondents' table with a binder full of tabs he had labelled himself: Facts, Precedent, Rebuttal, Panic. He was eighteen and had never argued anything in public except with his mother about curfew, and now he was supposed to stand up in twenty minutes and defend a newspaper that had printed something wrong about a mayor.

He had drawn the harder side first. Tomorrow he would argue for the mayor; tonight he had to explain why an inaccurate story should not cost the paper anything. The error was small and human: the paper had reported that the mayor missed a council vote, when in fact he had left early and cast his ballot by proxy. Nobody disputed the mistake. What Tyson had to dispute was the punishment, and until three days ago he had assumed the paper would simply lose.

His discovery had happened by accident, scrolling in the centre's computer room while the seniors played euchre behind him. He found the case, New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964, and read the holding twice, then a third time with his finger under the words. A public official suing for libel had to prove actual malice: that the statement was known to be false, or made with reckless disregard for truth. He wrote it on his palm in ballpoint, then thought better of that and wrote it on an index card, which he now turned over and over between his fingers like a small dry piece of bread.

"They're ready for you," said Priya, who had drawn the judges' bench and was wearing her mother's black blazer for authority. She sat above him on a stacked table, flanked by two other students who had promised to ask hard questions.

Tyson stood. "Your honours, the paper made a mistake. But the plaintiff is a public official, and under New York Times v. Sullivan, 1964, he must prove actual malice. He has to show the statement was known to be false, or made with reckless disregard for truth. There's no evidence of either. The reporter called the clerk's office twice. She wrote what she was told."

One of the judges, a boy named Marcus who took debate far too seriously, leaned forward. "So the mayor just has to absorb it? He did nothing wrong and his name is wrong in the paper?"

"No," Tyson said, and heard his own voice steady, which surprised him. "He can absorb a correction. That's what the paper ran, page two, and it exonerates him for anyone who reads it. What he can't do is collect damages without showing the paper didn't care whether it was true. That's the line. It's there so a paper that honestly gets it wrong isn't bankrupted, and honestly getting it wrong is what happened here."

Priya tapped her pen. "Suppose the paper hated the mayor. Suppose it wanted him gone."

"Then it's still not enough to hate him. Hating isn't knowing. They'd have to show the paper knew, or didn't care at all, and that's a hard thing to prove on purpose. It's supposed to be hard." Tyson paused, aware he was arguing something he half doubted. "I think it should be hard. If it were easy to sue, papers would only print what was safe, and a mayor could act like a little despot with a lawyer on retainer. Silence is cheaper than defence."

"But the wall can't be impermeable," Marcus said. "Somebody who lies on purpose has to pay."

"Somebody who lies on purpose fails the test," Tyson said. "Knowing falsehood is exactly what the rule catches. The rule is not a wall against everything. It's a wall against punishing error." He heard the metaphor and winced internally; Marcus had said impermeable, not him, but the borrowed word sat in the room anyway.

Priya looked at her colleagues, then down at her notes, then made a show of deliberation. "We'll rule for the paper," she said. "Insufficient showing of actual malice."

Tyson exhaled and sat down, and Marcus slid a folded paper across the aisle. Inside was the schedule for tomorrow's round. Tyson saw his name first, at the top, arguing for the mayor, and beneath it, in Priya's handwriting, the judges' roster for that session. Marcus had been reassigned to the bench. Tyson's best questioner was now his judge, and the first note on Marcus's pad, already written, read simply: "Ask him if he still believes the wall."

Tyson folded the schedule back along its crease and started crossing out tonight's closing argument.

Maxime's phone buzzed at 9:40 on a Tuesday night with a message from Yusra: the robotics club's roster program was due to Mr. Halvorsen by eight the next morning, and it was broken. He read it twice, then carried his laptop down to the kitchen, where his mother was sealing leftovers into containers with the methodical attention she gave everything after ten.

The program was supposed to look up whether a name was on the club roster, which had grown to four hundred members after the fall recruitment drive. Yusra had written the lookup herself, and she was proud of it; she'd called it a binary search in the meeting last week and sketched it on the whiteboard while Theo nodded along. But since Monday, three members had been told they weren't registered when they plainly were, and one had been locked out of the parts cabinet over it. Yusra had sent Maxime the code, the roster file, and a single line: "Fix it or I lose my mind."

He ran it with the name "Priya Raman." Not found. He ran it with "Priya Raman" again and got the same answer, which at least meant the program was consistent. He opened the roster file next and scrolled. Alvarez, Bhatt, Chen, then out of nowhere Ozdemir, then back to Dubois. The list was alphabetical only in patches, like a shelf where someone had shoved books in wherever they fit. He scrolled to the bottom and found a block of names added after recruitment, unsorted, pasted in by whoever had handled the sign-up sheet.

In his own code, Maxime tended to compartmentalize: rendering went in one file, input in another, and never did the two acknowledge each other. He had learned this from his father, who kept the pharmacy's taxes and the pharmacy's gossip in entirely separate drawers of his head. But this problem refused to stay separated. The program and the data were wrong together, and fixing one meant understanding the other.

He remembered, then, the afternoon in September when Yusra had first shown him what she was building. They were in the club room with the window open and the fan turning the smell of solder around, and she had explained it with a deck of cards. "You look at the middle card," she'd said, laying out a row face up, ordered lowest to highest. "If what you want is smaller, you throw away the whole right half, because it can't be there. Then you do it again on what's left." She'd snapped half the cards off the table each time, and the target turned up in three steps. It had seemed, that afternoon, like a trick with no catch.

Now he saw the catch. He typed a small test: he sorted a copy of the roster, ran the lookup on it, and Priya Raman appeared instantly, with a checkmark Yusra had added. He ran it on the original file and she vanished. So the program wasn't broken. It was doing exactly what it had been designed to do, and the middle item it kept landing on was Ozdemir, and everything it threw away after that was a half of the list that might have held Priya Raman but, as far as the program could tell, could not.

Yusra, at her desk across town, had reached the stage of debugging where she read her own code aloud as if interrogating a hostage. Her mother had gone to bed and left the hall light on, which meant she was allowed to keep working but was expected to whisper. She had tested the loop bounds. She had tested the comparison operator. She had drawn the indices on graph paper with her good pen. Nothing was wrong anywhere she looked, which was itself a kind of clue she didn't yet know how to read. Her somnolence kept arriving in waves; she fought it with mint tea and the conviction that Maxime would message soon, because Maxime, whatever his other faults, was perspicacious about things being wrong in places nobody checked.

Her phone lit up. "your list isn't sorted," Maxime had written. "the code is fine." She stared at the sentence and felt something between relief and insult. She opened the roster file, scrolled, and saw the September names, all eighty-two of them, sitting at the bottom in the order they'd been signed, which was the order of whoever had elbowed to the front of the line.

She called him. "So it just looks at the middle name?"

"And throws out the half that can't have your name in it," Maxime said. "But only if it's sorted. That's the whole rule. It wasn't fair of the list to lie about being alphabetical."

She laughed once, a short exhale. "The list didn't lie. I assumed."

"Same thing, at two in the morning."

It was eleven. They sorted a copy of the roster together while still on the call, Yusra reading names and Maxime running a script that merged the September block into place, and then she pasted it back into the club directory and ran every name that had failed. All found. She mailed the file to Mr. Halvorsen at 11:52 with a note about sorting the data on import, and he would read it at seven with his coffee and add it, without comment, to the list of things the club had learned this semester.

What neither of them wrote in the note, because neither could say it cleanly, was what they still weren't sure of. Maxime believed now that the fast way and the reliable way weren't opposites, that the fast way was simply a promise with conditions attached, and that you had to check the conditions the way you checked anything, by running the ugly test and watching it fail. But he couldn't decide whether the person who pasted in eighty-two unsorted names had been careless or whether carelessness was too small a word for a thing nobody had thought to ask about. He closed his laptop and sat in the kitchen light a while, and his mother put a container of rice in front of him without a word.

Yusra stayed at her desk. Before shutting everything down she opened a new file and typed, at the top, in a comment meant for whoever came after her: "The list must be sorted before this runs. Ask me how I know." Then she capped the good pen and turned off the lamp.

The printer in the library annex took four minutes to produce Chloe's graph, and it jammed twice on the way there, so by the time she carried the warm page back to the table, Devon had already eaten half the pretzels and rearranged her note cards into a fan.

"Your part's the graph," he said. "Mine's the stuff about gases trapping heat. I figured you'd want the hard half."

She spread the page out. It showed carbon dioxide climbing across a century, and across the climb, a fine sawtooth, up and down, up and down, thousands of tiny teeth. She had chosen it because it looked scientific, and now, printed, it looked like the machine had hiccuped the whole time. "I think there's something wrong with the data," she said. "Look at the wiggles. Maybe the sensor was broken. I'll say that in the presentation."

"You're going to stand up in front of Mr. Ruiz and tell him the most famous graph in climate science is broken."

"I'm going to say it cautiously. I'll preempt the question before anyone asks." She wrote on a card: possible instrument error. Devon took the card, read it, and slid it back with the flat expression of someone deciding not to be bellicose about it.

Mr. Ruiz's rule was that presentations could not be read off cards, which Chloe considered a form of clemency he extended to the audience and no one else. Third period, she stood at the front with the graph projected behind her, ten feet wide, her supposed error rendered in glorious detail. She got through the greenhouse part. Molecules absorb heat radiating from the surface and re-emit it, some of it back downward, so the atmosphere holds warmth it would otherwise lose. That part she could say in her sleep. Then the sawtooth filled the screen, and she heard herself say, "The small oscillations here may reflect measurement noise," and Ruth Okonkwo, who sat by the window and never spoke except when she was right, raised her hand.

"Chloe," Ruth said, not unkindly, "what happens to trees in spring?"

The room was quiet in the way rooms are quiet when someone has just moved a piece on a board nobody knew was set up. Chloe looked at the graph. "They grow."

"And in fall?"

"They lose their leaves." She said it slowly, because something was assembling itself. "There's, what, most of the land in the Northern Hemisphere. All those plants. So in spring and summer they're taking carbon dioxide in, and in fall and winter the leaves die and decay and it goes back out." She traced one tooth with her finger, the drop, the rise. "That's the wiggle. The whole planet breathing."

"So the zigzags are real," Devon said from the second row, with the satisfaction of a person whose suspicion about her note card had been vindicated in public.

"Yes. They're the Northern Hemisphere's seasons. It's not noise." She stood there a second longer than she needed to. The climb was still there too, the long slope under all the teeth, the part that didn't breathe, and she pointed at that, and said the oceans and the burning of fossil fuels had put it there, and then she sat down, and Mr. Ruiz wrote something in his book that she chose to believe was positive.

Afterward Ruth caught her at the lockers. "You got there yourself," Ruth said. "I only asked about trees."

"You asked the exact right question. That's not nothing." Chloe shut her locker. "I'm still not sure I could explain why the line keeps going up even while everything breathes. The breathing doesn't cancel it. I don't fully get why not, and I'm not going to pretend I do."

"Ruiz likes that," Ruth said. "The pretending, he hates."

The presentations ran through Friday, and on Friday afternoon the grades went up, and Chloe got an A minus, the minus apparently for the word "oscillations," which Mr. Ruiz had circled and annotated with "when you mean zigzags, say zigzags." She photographed the page and sent it to Devon, who replied with a single thumbs up, and then, a minute later, a photograph of his own grade, which was also an A minus, his minus earned for telling the class that greenhouse gases work like a blanket, an analogy Mr. Ruiz had circled twice and marked "partially true, ask Chloe."

She was still looking at that when her mother texted to ask whether she'd finished her college essay, the one about a time she changed her mind. Chloe typed out a paragraph about the graph, about standing in front of a room and being wrong in the exact direction of assuming the world was noisier than it was. She read it over, decided it made her sound reflective, which she was not, and deleted it. Then she wrote the truth instead, which was that Ruth Okonkwo had asked her one question about trees and she had spent the rest of the period feeling like the floor had tilted an inch. At the bottom she added a line she liked, about how the planet had been keeping careful records all along, and the only error was hers.

She pressed send, then opened the fridge and stood in its light, thinking about leaves.

"Close the door," her mother called from the other room. "You're letting the heat out."

Anthony got to statistics early because the only seat near the window was in the back, and he liked watching the parking lot fill. Mr. Ruiz had written a number on the board before anyone arrived, 48 to 46, and beneath it the words "City Council Poll, Channel 5." When the bell finished, Dana Vasquez stood up before Mr. Ruiz could say anything.

"Can I present?" she asked. She had been trying for two weeks to get the school to fund a student survey project, and Mr. Ruiz had told her she could have five minutes of class if she brought data. She walked to the board with her laptop and clicked to a slide with a bar chart. "I put a poll on the school's app asking whether we should keep open lunch or go to closed blocks. I got 1,400 responses. Nine percent more said open. So the student body wants open lunch, and I want the administration to actually look at it at the next board meeting." Her voice was steady, but her thumbnail was pressed white against the clicker.

Anthony liked Dana, and he wanted open lunch too, but something about the slide bothered him, the way the bars were drawn tall and certain. He raised his hand. "Who answered?"

"People who use the app."

"Who uses the app?"

"Mostly freshmen," she admitted. "Because the freshmen got the orientation push."

Marcus, two rows over, leaned back in his chair. "It's 1,400 people, man. Out of like 2,000 in the school. That's basically everybody. If that many people say it, it's right." A few people nodded. Marcus wanted the argument settled quickly; he had a calculus test next period and no patience for a debate that would eat the review time.

Anthony didn't have an answer ready, so he said the only true thing he had. "Big doesn't automatically mean right." It sounded weak even to him, a slogan without a body. Mr. Ruiz, who was leaning against the radiator with his arms folded, said nothing, which Anthony had learned meant the teacher thought the question was live.

At lunch Anthony went to the library and typed "famous wrong polls" into a search, half expecting nothing, and the screen filled with the same story three times. In 1936 a magazine called the Literary Digest mailed out a survey about the presidential election and collected about 2.4 million responses, and on the strength of those numbers predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt then won in a landslide. Anthony read it twice. He wrote nothing down and then wrote it down anyway, the number and both names, because 2.4 million felt impossible to hold in his head. Whatever it was that made a poll wrong, it wasn't a shortage of people. Something else decided.

He found Dana in the hallway before seventh period, by the water fountain where the noise covered conversation. "That thing you said about 1,400 being basically everybody. There was this poll in 1936, the Literary Digest. They got 2.4 million responses and said Landon would beat Roosevelt, and Roosevelt won in a landslide."

Dana looked at the number on his notebook. "2.4 million."

"Yeah."

"So what was wrong with it?"

"I don't know yet. I'm working on that part." He could have guessed, something about who ended up in the sample and who didn't, freshmen and app users and magazine readers in 1936, but he didn't want to dress a guess up as knowledge. What he did know was the shape of it: the size of a sample and the truth of a claim were different axes, and the first did not guarantee the second. He told her that much, and she chewed her lip, and he could see her weighing her board meeting against it.

That night they sat in his kitchen with the textbook open to the chapter they hadn't reached yet, the one on sampling distributions. There was a formula for how far off a percentage could plausibly be, called the margin of error, and it shrank as the sample grew, but slowly, like a door closing by degrees. They ran Dana's numbers. With 1,400 responses her 9 percent lead survived, comfortable even. Then she pulled up the breakdown by grade and the floor dropped out of the argument: seniors were nearly absent from her data, and seniors were the ones who remembered the closed-block year. Whether the whole school preferred open lunch depended on people who hadn't answered, and no amount of arithmetic could allay that doubt. It wasn't happenstance that her sample skewed young, either; the orientation push had built the skew in, quietly, a subterranean bias under an impressive-looking total.

"So I can't take it to the board like this," Dana said. She said it flatly, and then, after a minute, "Unless I take it like this. Nine percent overall, but the sample is mostly underclassmen, and I need two hundred more seniors before the number means anything."

"That's more honest than the slide was."

"It's less persuasive."

"It might be more," Anthony said. "They're the ones who always say student government fakes its data."

They stayed at the table past ten, drafting the email she would send out, deciding to go classroom to classroom in the senior wing on Thursday instead of relying on the app. Dana typed the subject line, erased it, and typed it again. "Seniors," she read aloud, "we want your answer, even the ones of you who never check anything."

"Especially those," Anthony said, and reached over her shoulder to hit send.

Austin had promised Ms. Ferrante he would come to the summer book club with something to say about chapters twelve through sixteen, and he had read them twice, but he still had nothing except the feeling that Huck and Jim drifting down the river on a raft was the freest thing he had ever read. He found the group already assembled in the corner by the microfilm machines: Priya, Desmond, and Lorna, who was a retired nurse and the only one who ever brought her own coffee mug.

"Okay," Priya said, opening her paperback. "Mr. Alvarez wants us to try a lens this time. I picked Marxist. Property, labor, who owns the raft."

Desmond groaned. "Can't we just talk about the book?"

"That is talking about the book," Lorna said. "Go on, Austin. You had your hand up before you even sat down."

He hadn't, exactly, but he let it stand. "The part where Huck describes the fog," he said. "He wakes up and Jim is crying because he thought he'd lost him, and Huck pretends it was all a dream, and Jim figures out he's been played." He turned to the page. "And then Jim says, when he finds out, that trash is what people is that puts dirt on the head of dey fren's."

There was a quiet moment while everyone found the passage. Priya was frowning at it the way she frowned at a math problem, which Austin had learned meant she was interested.

"Huck doesn't get it," he said slowly, hearing himself arrive at the thought as he said it. "Not really. He says he was so sorry he could almost kiss Jim's foot, but a minute later he's complimenting himself for humbling himself to a black man. The joke is on Huck, and Huck is the one telling the story."

"A naive narrator," Lorna said, tapping her mug against the table.

"Yeah. That's it exactly. He reports everything honestly, he doesn't lie to us, but he misunderstands what he's seeing. So we see more than he does." Austin looked around the table, checking whether they were with him. "Every scene I laughed at, that's why. The duke and the king, the feuding families, all of it. The comedy is Huck not getting the joke he's telling."

Desmond, who had been slouched with his arms crossed, sat forward a little. "So it's like an unreliable narrator, but the opposite. He's reliable and clueless."

"Reliable and clueless," Priya repeated, writing it in the margin. "Okay, but here's my problem with the whole Marxist angle. If we're reading through the lens of class and labor, Twain owns the joke, Huck doesn't. Huck's down in the lowest white stratum of that whole river society, barefoot and beaten, and he still thinks he's above Jim. The hierarchy doesn't just exist out there, people carry it around inside them and it gets reified, made into this thing that seems solid and natural, like it's furniture."

"But Jim works," Desmond said. "He's the only one on that raft who actually does labor. He cooks, he watches the raft at night while Huck sleeps. And the reward money, that's the sickest part. Miss Watson is going to sell him for eight hundred dollars and everyone on shore treats him like walking cash. The whole economy of the town treats a person as property."

"That's the noxious part," Lorna said. "Not just slavery itself, which is obviously monstrous, but how casual it is. The ordinary people, the churchgoers, they've all made peace with it. It's in the wallpaper."

Austin had come in with an argument prepared against the lens assignment, something about how forcing a theory onto a book was like wearing someone else's glasses, and now he couldn't find the argument anywhere. He had expected the lens to flatten the book and instead the book kept opening. "Here's what I keep wondering," he said. "Does Huck change? He apologizes to Jim in the fog scene, and it costs him something, he says so. But then later he tears up the letter and says he'll go to hell, and that's not him understanding slavery is wrong. He still thinks he's doing a bad thing. He never figures out the thing we've figured out."

"Maybe that's the point," Priya said. "Twain trusts us to do what Huck can't. The reader has to finish the moral work."

"Or maybe," Desmond said, "Twain couldn't finish it either. He brings Tom Sawyer back at the end and turns Jim into a game, a plaything, for two hundred pages of the worst chapters in the book."

"That's true," Lorna said, and no one argued with her.

Austin looked at his notes, at the margin where he'd written it's just a story about a raft, and he understood that he'd been wrong about that an hour ago, sitting in his room, so certain. He wasn't certain now, and it felt less like losing something than like the difference between a photograph of the river and the river. He raised his pen.

"One more question before we break," he said. "If Huck never sees what we see, then somewhere out there, right now, there's a book where we're the naive narrator."

Priya looked up sharply. Lorna set down her mug. "Write that one down," she said.

Henry arrived at the Beanery eleven minutes early, which he told himself was a matter of the bus schedule and nothing else, and which was, in fact, a matter of wanting to choose the table near the window before Marisol got there so that he would appear to have been there for ages, casual, at home. He set down his backpack, took out his history notes on the Mongol expansion across the steppe for Tuesday's quiz, and then put them away again because studying on a date, even before the date technically began, seemed like something a person would do to seem interesting rather than something an interesting person would do.

Marisol came in at 4:02, shaking rain off her jacket, and Henry stood up so fast he knocked his spoon to the floor. He had liked her since the group project in October, when she had eviscerated his draft thesis in one sentence and then spent forty minutes helping him rebuild it, and he had decided, over three months of deliberation, that this was a good sign and not a warning. He got in line with her, bought her drink even though she protested, and carried both cups back to the window table with the concentration of a bomb technician.
