"Why that face?" his grandfather said, setting down two cups of coffee, one of them predictably for himself.

"I found something and I don't think it's right." Chase turned the book around. "It says Kohl became chancellor in 1982, but there was no election that year. That can't be how it works."

Opa pulled his glasses up from his collar and looked at the page for a long moment, then pushed the book back. "You have the internet in your pocket. Look."

Chase looked. His phone showed him the same thing the book did, from six different sources, and he sat back in the chair with his arms crossed. Helmut Kohl had replaced Helmut Schmidt as chancellor in 1982 through a constructive vote of no confidence. It was the only time the procedure had ever succeeded at the federal level. He read the sentence three times, because it seemed to be telling him that a country had swapped its head of government without anyone voting in a general election, and that bothered him somewhere he couldn't locate.

"So they just took him out," Chase said. "The voters picked Schmidt, and the parliament picked Kohl, and nobody asked the voters."

"That is one way to say it," Opa said, and drank his coffee.

"It's the accurate way to say it." Chase was already typing, already composing the argument in his head: presidential systems made you wait, a fixed term, a removal so difficult it almost never happened, but at least the removal meant something enormous. Parliamentary systems could turn a leader over in an afternoon. He got two paragraphs down fast, the way he got things down when he was angry, and they were good paragraphs, sharp ones, and he knew it.

Then he stopped, because he had made a list on the back of his hand, the way he did when a paper had two sides and he could only see one. On the left he had written voters lose voice. On the right, nothing yet. He looked out at the garden, where his grandmother's tomatoes were coming in late and the neighbor's radio was on. He thought about impeachment, about the presidential system he'd grown up admiring in the abstract, the one his civics teacher had practically dared anyone to criticize, and he thought about how long a doomed leader could cling to a fixed term, months of a country running without a functioning head. He thought about Schmidt, voted in, and then voted out by the people's own representatives, the same parliament the people had elected. He wrote on the right side of his hand: voters' reps can act fast. Then, underneath it, in smaller letters, he wrote both have a point, and hated writing it, and kept it anyway.

"I changed my mind about the paper," he said. "Halfway through."

"Which half?"

"The half where I was right." Chase deleted one of his good paragraphs, the sharp one, and it hurt a little, like tearing a page out of a notebook that was still usable. He started rebuilding the argument around the 1982 fact instead of against it. The paper could hold both systems up to the light and let the reader see what each one traded away, and it could end without a verdict, because he no longer believed a verdict was available to him. He was eighteen and had learned the word zeitgeist that semester, and he suspected that anyone who claimed to prognosticate which system was better was really just describing the mood they'd been handed. His own judgment felt nascent, half-formed, and he decided that honesty about that was worth more than the sharp paragraph had been.

"You will not finish tonight," Opa said, gathering the cups. "You will finish it tomorrow, and then you will tell me what you decided."

"I decided I'm not deciding."

"Then tomorrow you will tell me what you didn't decide, and why." Opa rinsed the cups and set them upside down on the towel, and the two spots where they had sat on the table were still warm when Chase put his hand flat on them and went back to typing.

Thomas had three interviews scheduled before the semester ended, and the first one was on Thursday at the movie theater on Delancey, where a manager named Rhonda would decide whether he got to wear the red vest and tear tickets. The problem was his eyes. Whenever Mr. Pavano, the career-center teacher, had watched Thomas answer a practice question, he wrote the same thing on the evaluation sheet: "Eye contact: intermittent." Thomas could look at a person or he could think about what he was saying, but doing both at once felt like patting his head and rubbing his stomach.

On Tuesday he found his friend Deshawn in the library, copying a psychology article onto his palm because the printer cost ten cents a page and Deshawn had principles about that. Deshawn wanted to write the best paper in the class, not just a good one, the kind Mr. Pavano read out loud, and he was mining the database for anything that would make his argument sound like it had been written by someone with a laboratory.

"You're doing interviews," Deshawn said, squinting at his palm. "This is germane, then. There was this study, 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh. They found people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements."

"Like copying them."

"Subtly. If they cross their legs, you cross yours a minute later. If they lean forward, you lean forward. Don't make it a mirror show." Deshawn wrote the names on his wrist with the pen still in his other hand. "My whole paper hinges on whether charisma is a real trait or just a bag of tricks. I'm arguing tricks."

"Arguing you're a bag of tricks."

"Everyone's a bag of tricks, Thomas. Some bags are better organized."

Thursday, Rhonda turned out to be a large woman in a cardigan who leaned back in her chair like the chair was doing her a favor. Thomas sat across from her, and after the second question, a question about handling an angry customer, he noticed she had crossed her ankles under the desk. He waited, keeping his eyes on her face because that was the other thing he was practicing, and then crossed his own. He could not manage both at once and verbalize the answer he'd prepared, so what came out was a story about his aunt returning a humidifier to a store where the clerk had shrugged at her until she left. Rhonda laughed. She uncrossed her ankles and leaned forward, elbows on the desk. Thomas counted to four in his head and leaned forward too.

"So why do you want to work here," she said, "instead of the grocery store, which is closer to you?"

He had an answer rehearsed, something about loving film. He had practiced saying it with steady eye contact in the bathroom mirror, and in the mirror it had sounded sincere. Out loud, in this room, it would have been bathos, a drop from the humidifier story to something hollow, and he could see that now, watching her wait. He decided to split the difference in his own head: the honest part, that he needed money and could work Friday nights and Sundays, and the copy, that he did actually like the theater, had seen nine movies there this year including a bad one he'd stayed through anyway.

"I need the hours," he said. "And I know which aisle sticks in the third theater, because I've sat in it. I'd tell people not to sit there." He kept looking at her while he said it, and it cost him something, like holding a plank.

Rhonda wrote something on her sheet. "You'd warn them off the sticky aisle. That's loyalty to the customer over the building." She leaned back again, and Thomas, a few seconds behind, leaned back too, and she looked at him for a moment longer than was comfortable, and he could not tell whether the mimicry had landed or whether she had caught him doing it, and there was no way to ask, and Deshawn's article said nothing about that part.

She stood and shook his hand at the door. "We'll call by Monday."

In the parking lot he called Deshawn. "She leaned forward, I leaned forward. She laughed at the humidifier story."

"The humidifier story. That's better than charisma. That's content." There was the sound of typing on the other end. "Did she lean back at the end?"

"She did."

"And?"

"I did. Then she looked at me kind of long."

"Kind of long like suspicion, or kind of long like, this kid is a bag of tricks and I respect it?"

"I don't know," Thomas said. "That part's not in the study." He stood by his bike with the phone against his ear, watching a man inside the lobby refill the popcorn warmer, scoop after scoop, until the glass case was full.

"Monday," Deshawn said. "Call me Monday."

Joseph considered himself the most patient person at the Harvest Table volunteer office, which was easy to believe on a Tuesday afternoon when the filing was done and the only sound was the hum of the old refrigerator. He sat at the front desk with the sign-in binder open in front of him, and the numbers there told a story he did not like. Every Thursday for six weeks, Renata had clocked out at 5:40 instead of 6:30. Somebody had to re-shelve the pantry boxes alone, and lately that somebody was him.

He was not angry, he told himself. He was concerned, in a professional way, the way the coordinator Ms. Okafor was concerned when grant reports came in late. He wanted to write that down, actually write it, because the office had a rule that shift concerns went through the message board tacked beside the refrigerator, and Ms. Okafor had said twice that she liked structured notes better than hallway complaints. So Joseph sharpened the good pencil and began a draft.

"Renata, you keep leaving early and you never tell anyone," he wrote, and then, because it sounded harsh, "You are being inconsiderate to the whole team." He read it back and felt a small clean satisfaction, which should have warned him. Instead he drifted into a brief reverie, imagining Ms. Okafor reading the note aloud at the monthly meeting, nodding, maybe promoting him to shift lead.

"Too doctrinaire," said Priya from the donations table, leaning over his shoulder without apology. She was seventeen and read everything, including other people's drafts. "You sound like a rulebook with a grudge. She'll read two lines and stop."

"It's structured," Joseph said. "It's professional."

"It's an accusation sandwich." Priya flipped the binder to the staff resources shelf, pulled down a thin book by a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, and dropped it on the desk. "Look at the middle part."

The middle part had a heading about I-messages. Joseph read it twice, slowly. An I-message, the page said, stated the speaker's own concern, something like "I'm worried we'll miss the deadline," instead of accusing the listener with "you" language. He looked at his draft, where the word "you" appeared four times, each one like a pointed finger.

"That's the whole trick?" he said. "Say I instead of you?"

"That's the whole trick," Priya said, and went back to sorting cans of chickpeas.

Joseph tore up the first draft, which he would later describe as a calm revision rather than what it was, and wrote a second. He kept it short and structured, a subject line, the dates, the concern, a question. Then he copied it onto the message board, where the whole office could see it, which felt brave and slightly sickening.

The board note read:

To Renata, re: Thursday shifts. I've noticed the last six Thursdays have ended at 5:40 instead of 6:30. I'm worried the pantry boxes won't get shelved before the Friday distribution, since I can't always stay late. If something is going on with your schedule, could we talk about covering it differently? I'd rather sort it out than let it build. Joseph.

He went home feeling like a diplomat. He told his brother he had handled a workplace conflict with emotional maturity, and he half believed it, except for the part of him that had wanted, faintly and dishonestly, for Renata to feel stung.

Thursday came. Renata arrived at four with wet hair and a hospital parking sticker on her jacket. She read the board note standing up, one hand on the refrigerator door, and then she turned around.

"My mom has dialysis Thursdays at six," she said. "The clinic is twenty minutes away. I've been telling Ms. Okafor I had to leave, but I never put it on the board because it felt like asking for special treatment. I thought I was being discreet." She paused. "Your note is the first time anyone said it in writing where I could answer it in writing."

She took the good pencil, which was hers anyway, and wrote below his note: "Joseph, thanks for saying it as a concern instead of a complaint. I'll ask Priya to shelve Thursdays, and I'll take her Saturday morning slot. Also, I can stay this Thursday, my mom's appointment moved to Friday."

Joseph read it standing where she had stood, one hand on the refrigerator. The patient diplomat, the office peacemaker, had spent six weeks shelving boxes alone and never once asked her why, because asking would have meant discovering that the problem was not inconsideration but information, and that the person who never communicated anything in writing had been, all along, him. He picked up the pencil to write one more line, and beneath her words he printed, slowly: "I should have asked sooner. My fault, not just the schedule's."

Faith arrived eleven minutes early, which she decided to treat as a character flaw rather than a virtue, and took the stool at the window counter of the creamery with the best view of the door. The shop smelled of waffle cones and scorched sugar. Behind the glass, a teenager on summer furlough from some college scooped pistachio with the reluctance of someone who had already enervated himself with the heat, dragging the scoop in slow, defeated circles. Faith ordered a small maple walnut because it seemed like an epicurean choice, the kind of thing a person with developed taste would pick, and then regretted it because she did not actually like maple walnut that much.

Caleb was due at four. They had met at the used bookstore where she worked Saturdays, where he had spent forty minutes in the philosophy section and finally bought a paperback about the history of experiments, apologizing twice for taking so long. She had liked the apologizing. She had liked even more that he read the acknowledgments standing at the register before he paid, as though the book were a letter addressed to him.

He came in at 4:03, hair flattened on one side from a helmet, because he had biked. He had told her he would bike, and he had. That was already more reliability than certain people she could name. He sat down across from her and put the paperback on the counter between them like a passport.

"Did you finish it?" she asked.

"Almost. There's this one study I keep thinking about." He turned the cone the girl brought him, vanilla with sprinkles, as if rotating it might help him decide where to start. "In 1974 these two researchers, Dutton and Aron, had a woman interview men on a bridge. Some of the men had just crossed this frightening suspension bridge, the wobbly kind over a gorge. The others crossed a sturdy bridge, a normal one. The men who'd just crossed the frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call her afterward."

"Call the interviewer?"

"That's the whole thing. More of them called."

Faith licked her maple walnut and thought about it. "So a scary bridge makes you think you like somebody."

"Or makes something happen that they mistook for liking. That's the part I can't stop chewing on." He looked genuinely bothered, which she found more interesting than the study. "The book doesn't say why. It just says they called."

Outside, a man was parallel parking a sedan with great patience and no success, pulling forward, adjusting, easing back. The window put a hot stripe of light across the counter between their cones. Faith watched the car and tried to locate her own pulse, which was doing something steady and unremarkable, and she was not sure whether to be relieved or insulted.

"Okay," she said, "so here's my problem. I was nervous all morning. Like, stomach-flip nervous. And I couldn't tell if that meant I liked you, or if I was just scared of the date itself. Two separate things, same feeling."

Caleb set down his cone. "That's exactly the bridge thing."

"It's the opposite of the bridge thing. Those men didn't know they were on anything. I knew. I'm standing on the sturdy bridge, and I'm scared anyway." She had not planned to say that much. The maple walnut was not improving with exposure, and she kept eating it out of stubbornness.

"Maybe you're on both bridges," he said. "Maybe you like me and you're scared of the date, and you'd still be calling the interviewer either way."

"But the study doesn't cover that."

"No. The study just covers who called." He smiled, briefly, at his own cone. "I like that you're arguing with a study from 1974."

The scooper, wiping the counter with a rag, drifted past and turned the thermostat down a notch, and the compressor's hum changed key. Faith thought about her mother, who believed you should never trust a feeling you couldn't explain, and her sister, who believed you should never explain a feeling you could simply have. She had spent most of her life trying to decide between them, and here, with melting ice cream and a boy who read acknowledgments, she arrived somewhere in the middle: the pounding heart was ambiguous, this was true, but you could still choose what to do next, and the choosing was its own kind of evidence. What she could not yet say was what the choice would be. That part stayed open, like a door she could see light through.

She pushed the maple walnut aside, unfinished, an honest surrender.

"I'm not going to know today," she said. "I just want to say that out loud so I stop pretending."

"Understood." Caleb tore a napkin into two halves and offered her one, though she hadn't spilled anything. "For whenever you need it."

They sat with that for a minute. Outside, the man finally parked, climbed out, and stood looking at his car and then at the gap it had left from the curb, weighing some private question of good enough.

"Do you want to walk somewhere?" Caleb asked. "There's a footbridge over the canal. It's the sturdy kind."

Faith took the napkin anyway and put it in her pocket. "Show me."

The bell over the door had not rung in forty minutes, and Andrew spread his calculus notebook across the counter between the lottery machine and the rack of scratch-offs. His uncle had left him alone with the register until nine, which meant three more hours of interrupted paragraphs. He was trying to understand why anyone would want the area under a curve, and the book kept answering him with notation instead of reasons.

He had drawn the curve on graph paper, a smooth hill sinking toward a valley and rising again. Under it he had sketched rectangles, first four of them, then eight, then sixteen, each set filling the space between the curve and the x-axis a little more exactly than the last. He added up their areas and wrote the totals in a column. The column was creeping toward some number it never quite reached. He could see that much. What he could not see was what the number was for.

The bell rang. Mrs. Okafor came in for her evening newspaper and a bag of the hard ginger candies she claimed helped her knees, and while he counted her change he held the column of sums in his head. When the door shut he sat back down and wrote, "more rectangles, closer to the true area," then crossed out "true" because he did not know yet whether the area was a thing the curve had or a thing the rectangles invented.

His friend Priya pushed through the door at eight with her backpack still on one shoulder. She set a worksheet on the counter, smoothing it flat beside the coin tray. "Yours too?" he said. "Mine," she said. "Question four. I found where the derivative is zero, but I can't tell if it's the top of a hill or the bottom of a valley. The graph on my calculator keeps zooming out into nothing."

Andrew pulled the sheet toward him. The function was cubic, ugly with fractions, and she had already worked out the first derivative and found the point where it came to zero. "So that's your critical point," he said. "At x equals a." She nodded and chewed the end of her pen. He remembered a page from two chapters back and turned to it, then closed the book again, because the page had not made sense the first time and he wanted to try without it.

"You differentiate again," he said. "The derivative of the derivative." He worked it out on the graph paper, lining up his arithmetic so she could follow, and when he substituted her value of a the second derivative came out negative, a clean little minus sign in front of a fraction. "If the first derivative is zero there and the second derivative is negative," he said, "the function has a local maximum at that point. It's a peak, not a valley." Priya looked at the paper, then at her calculator, and zoomed in instead of out. The curve arched over exactly where he had said it would. "Second derivative test," she said, writing the name at the top of her solution, and he copied the name into his notebook because he suspected the two problems were the same problem wearing different clothes.

"The peak tells you where the curve turns," he said slowly, "and the turning is where the rectangles stop being wrong in one direction and start being wrong in the other." She raised an eyebrow. He drew a fresh curve, marked its maximum, and shaded beneath it. "If I want all of this, the whole area, I have to know where the shading ends, and the shading ends where the curve does something. Turns. Peaks or bottoms out." He was not sure this was the whole truth of it, and he said so, and she said that was fine, she only needed question four.

They worked until a man came in for cigarettes and had to be carded, and then until a kid bought a blue slushie that dripped a dye line across the floor, which Andrew mopped while Priya guarded the worksheet from the wet. While he wrung the mop he thought about his father's line about hard work, that bromide about how effort always pays, and decided the rectangles were a better argument: effort pays in the limit, in a place you approach but never stand. His father would hate that sentence. Andrew found the thought more enthralling than the worksheet, and he did not trust it for that reason.

When Priya left, she took the graph paper with the shaded region, folded into quarters, and told him he had a ductile mind, bendable without breaking, which she claimed was a compliment from her metallurgy-obsessed grandfather. He said it was the nicest thing anyone had said to him at that register. At nine his uncle returned, counted the drawer, and asked what Andrew had been scribbling all night. Andrew turned the notebook around to show him the rectangles crowding under the curve, closer and closer, never quite arriving. His uncle put on his glasses and leaned over the counter. "So where does it end?" he said. Andrew tapped the peak Priya had found, the point where the second derivative had gone negative and the curve had chosen, at last, to turn. "Right there."

The park rink had been flooded the night before, and the ice still undulated faintly where the hose had wandered, long shallow swells that caught the morning light. Emilie stood at the boards with a clipboard she had bought on Monday, the ink on her practice plan already smudged from being carried in the same pocket as a half-eaten orange. Saturday, it said. Warm-up, fifteen minutes, then passing drills, then scrimmage, then nothing at all on Sunday. She had written "nothing at all" in capitals, because she did not trust herself otherwise.

"You made a schedule," Dani said, not quite a question. Dani was the best player on their rec team and knew it, which made everything she said land at an angle. "Coach let you run practice?"

"Coach is at his daughter's tournament." Emilie held the clipboard against her chest. "He said I could fill in. One week. If it goes badly, it goes badly once."

Dani took a pass from Sabine at center, swept in, shot high, and skated back without looking at the clipboard. "We lose because our passes die on sticks. All season. Some schedule fixes that?"

Emilie had thought about this for three nights, which was part of the problem; the plan had been inchoate until Wednesday, when she watched a clip on her phone over and over, rewinding a single moment. Now she set down the clipboard, took a puck, and skated to the faceoff dot. "Watch the pass, not me."

She drew the puck back, rolled her wrists, and sent it up. It lifted, a hand off the ice, hung flat through the air above Sabine's outstretched stick, and came down soft, landing on the blade of Petal at the far circle. Petal settled it and fired it into the empty net before anyone had moved.

"What was that?" Sabine said.

"Saucer pass," Emilie said. "Watch again."

She did it again, slower, and this time it wobbled and clipped Petal's stick, but it got there. The third one flew clean, flat, and landed true. "It only works if it comes down flat," she said, mostly to herself, and skated a wider loop to try from a worse angle.

"That's the drill, then," Dani said, and there was no mockery in it now, or none Emilie could hear. "Everyone. Puck over the stick. Petal, you're the defender, put your blade where it hurts."

They ran it for forty minutes. At first the pucks went everywhere, sailing over the glass, plopping dead at Petal's feet, and Emilie stopped the line twice to shorten the distance rather than say anything about hands or follow-through, because she did not actually know if follow-through was the right word. She only knew the puck had to fly flat and come down on the blade, and she let the distance teach the rest. By the end, Sabine could clear two sticks at once, and even Dani, who had opened with an easy saucer of her own as if she'd been hiding it all season, went quiet when Petal banked one past her stick and onto Sabine's tape at full speed.

Scrimmage after, then the cool-down Emilie had scheduled, jogging the perimeter, which Dani skipped and Petal did twice. When they were gathering cones, Coach's text arrived: How'd it go. Emilie typed and deleted three answers. "Good" was true and useless. "Their passes still got blocked in scrimmage, just less" was more honest, and it was the part she could not explain, whether the drill had fixed anything or only shown them how far they were. She settled on "Did saucer passes. Need work," and put the phone face down on the bench.

"Same plan next week?" Petal asked, helmet still on, her breath fogging up inside the cage.

"Monday rest, Tuesday edges, Wednesday passing again." Emilie folded the clipboard into her bag without ceremony, like something she would need on Tuesday. "Sunday's off. I mean it."

"Even for me?"

"Especially for you."

Petal laughed, and behind her the two of them stood a moment longer at the boards while the Zam driver waited with his arm hanging out the window, and Emilie watched the last swells of the ice disappear under the first pass of the blade.

The folder sat open on the kitchen table when Brandon came downstairs, and inside it was a contract with his mother's signature on the last page, dated yesterday. The first page said VACATION CLUB MEMBERSHIP AGREEMENT in gold letters, and under that, in a font so small he had to squint, the words terms and conditions appeared four times before the second paragraph. His mother was at the sink, not washing anything, just holding a sponge.

"Some man at the hotel," she said. "There was a booth in the lobby. He said it was a one-day rate." She had gone to her high school reunion, and on the way out, between the banquet room and the parking garage, a man in a navy blazer had folded her into a chair and slid papers across a folding table. Nineteen hundred dollars. She had signed where the arrows pointed, initialed where the little tabs said Buyer Initials, and driven home exhilarated, she admitted, by the idea that she had done something spontaneous for once in her life.

Brandon took the folder to his room and set it beside his keyboard. He was eighteen and had signed exactly one thing in his life, a student loan entrance counseling form, and he had read every line of it twice because the words liability and default had a weight to them, like stones in a river. His mother had not read anything. He opened the contract and found the section headed CANCELLATION, which said the buyer waived all rights to cancel after accepting the introductory bonus, whatever that was. A gift bag, she'd told him. A beach towel and a cooler.

He typed can you cancel a contract signed at a hotel booth into the search bar, and the results came back so fast it felt like the machine had been waiting for the question. The Federal Trade Commission, a page with the plain look of official antiquity, pale blue headings and no advertisements, described something called the Cooling-Off Rule. Buyers could cancel certain sales made at home or at temporary locations, the page said, until midnight of the third business day after the sale. He read the sentence three times. A hotel lobby booth, he was fairly sure, counted as a temporary location. It had been a folding table. The man had carried his brochures in a rolling suitcase.

"Mom," he called down the stairs, "when did you sign it?" Saturday. Today was Monday. He counted on his fingers, then counted again, because business days, he suspected, did not include Sunday, and he did not want to be wrong about the arithmetic of getting her money back. Tuesday, Wednesday, midnight Wednesday. He looked at the clock: 4:40 in the afternoon, and the days ahead of him suddenly felt glacial, each hour between now and that deadline moving slower than any hour of summer ever had.

The contract itself turned out to have a Notice of Cancellation form stapled inside the back cover, two copies, with lines for a date and a signature. The salesman was required to have told her about it, his mother said; he had mentioned something about paperwork while pointing at the signature line, and she had nodded, which she now understood was not the same as consent to anything except being nodded at. Brandon filled out one copy in his own careful handwriting, printing her name where it said the buyer, and then stopped, because the form asked for a signature and the signature was hers.

He brought it downstairs. She dried her hands and read it, all of it, which took a while, and Brandon watched her face do something complicated, embarrassment folding into stubbornness folding into relief. "I was so sure I'd missed my window," she said. "He made it sound like the moment I picked up the pen, it was done."

"That's kind of the whole trick," Brandon said. "The signature makes you feel like it's finished. But the rule gives you the third business day. Midnight." He slid the pen across the table to her. She signed the notice, and then he addressed an envelope to the vacation club's office, which was listed in the terms, in a strip mall two towns over, and wrote the words Cooling-Off Rule on a sticky note and pressed it to the front, in case anyone at the other end needed reminding what the paper was.

They drove to the post office together before it closed and asked the clerk at the counter for a stamped receipt, which the FTC page had suggested, and Brandon held the little slip of paper up to the window light as they walked back to the car, wondering whether the man in the navy blazer kept a tally of the envelopes that came back, and whether he ever wondered, on his slow nights, how many of his buyers had gone home and found a son at a computer.

The study room smelled like whiteboard marker and vending machine coffee, and Thomas had drawn the whole pathway twice already: glucose, the slow split of glycolysis, the shuttle into the mitochondria, the electron transport chain bleeding down its gradient until ATP spun out of the machinery. He wanted one thing this week, which was to hold the sequence in his head well enough to write it out cold on Friday's quiz, because the quiz was the first grade of the semester and the semester was the first thing he had ever chosen for himself. He was, by his own admission, something of an autodidact; he had taught himself guitar from videos, taught himself to code from forums, and now he was discovering that a body of knowledge organized by someone else, with checkpoints and deadlines, demanded a different posture than the sprawl of teaching yourself.

Across the table, Priya had her laptop open, scrubbing through footage on the timeline. She was the sardonic one, the one who had told him on the first day that pre-med students peak in tears, and she edited her lab report videos with the same merciless efficiency. He watched her lift a stretch of clip, her own voice stumbling over the word "substrate" three takes in a row, and drag it out of the sequence so the remaining clips snapped together.

"You cut the bad takes," he said.

"I cut everything that isn't the sentence," she said. She clicked play and the video ran clean, one unbroken explanation.

He looked down at his diagram and something shifted in him, not a lightbulb, nothing so clean, more like a door in a house he had lived in for years without noticing. He flipped to the back of his notebook, where his reading notes on the cell chapter sat half-finished, and found the paragraph he had underlined and then ignored because it had seemed beside the point. The cell did the same thing, he saw now. It copied a gene into RNA, and the copy was full of stretches that went nowhere, and those stretches, the introns, were cut out of the newly made RNA, and the remaining exons were spliced together before the messenger RNA ever left the nucleus. Priya's video and the cell were doing the same kind of work: keeping the parts that said something, joining them into one usable message.

"You know this is what your cells are doing right now," he said, and told her, pointing at the underlined lines, the introns cut out, the exons spliced, the finished messenger RNA leaving the nucleus. "You're editing like a ribosome's assistant."

"I'm going to take that as flattery," Priya said, though she leaned over to read the paragraph anyway.

They fell into a rhythm after that. When he lost his place in the respiration pathway, stalled between the Krebs cycle and the inner membrane, she would ask him questions drawn from her own editing: which step was a bad take, which was the kept footage, where did the mitochondria get its final cut. It worked better than his flashcards had. The pathway began to feel less like a list to memorize and more like a story with cuts and splices, a long take of glucose trimmed down by stages into the thirty-some ATP the quiz would demand, and he could finally walk the whole route without stumbling. What he could not figure out was why the cell bothered making the useless stretches in the first place, and Priya, when he asked, only shrugged and said maybe the raw footage mattered for reasons nobody had told them yet. He wrote the question in the margin and left it there, honest about not knowing, and that open margin bothered him less than he expected.

On Friday he wrote the pathway from glucose to ATP in one unbroken column, arrow after arrow, the gradient, the membrane, the machinery, and when the quizzes came back Monday his grade was the highest in the class. He carried the paper to the study room to show Priya, planning to thank her, planning to say something about how two ways of seeing a thing could be spliced into one.

She wasn't there yet, but her laptop was, open on the table, and on the screen was her own quiz, returned face up. Beside the diagram of the cell she had written, in her cramped hand, "introns cut out, exons spliced before mRNA leaves nucleus," and next to it in red pen, the teacher's note: correct, but this was the wrong chapter.

"It was on the quiz," Priya said from the doorway, dropping her bag. "The one I got wrong was the mitochondria."

Faith had claimed the corner table by the periodicals at three o'clock, and by four she had spread her life across it: two articles, a style guide, three highlighters, and a cherry cola going flat beside her elbow. The assignment said compare and evaluate, not summarize, and that single word, evaluate, had already cost her an evening. Her teacher had said a critical review was an argument about which piece of scholarship deserved trust, and Faith had underlined deserve twice, because trust was the thing she was least sure how to measure.

The two articles disagreed about later school start times. The first, published in a journal called Sleep Research Monthly, followed two thousand students across a district that moved its start from 7:30 to 8:15 and found modest gains in attendance and none in grades. The second, by a researcher named Okafor, was wilder: a single school, one semester, and claims of a full point of improvement in GPA, effects so large they made Faith suspicious in a way she couldn't yet name. She had chosen the pairing precisely because they clashed. Now she had to decide what the clash meant.

Her friend Dara found her there at four-thirty, dropping a backpack onto the chair opposite and stealing a sip of the flat cola without asking. "Still the start-time thing?" Dara said. Faith turned her laptop around. "The big-effects one. I can't find its journal. It's not in the database anywhere. There's just this page where he posted it himself, last month." Dara leaned in, chewing the straw. "My brother did that with his physics thing. He called it a preprint." Faith wrote the word down. "What's that mean?" "He said it's a paper posted publicly before peer review. So nobody's checked it yet. No independent experts chosen by a journal, nothing."

Faith sat with that. She had been treating the two articles as equals, giving each a paragraph, the way she'd been taught to be fair to both sides of every question since middle school debates about zoos and uniforms. Fairness, it turned out, was not the same as equal weight. The Okafor paper was faster, bolder, newer, and it had skipped the queue entirely. The journal article had been slow, hedged, and examined by strangers whose job was to find its flaws before she ever saw it. Which one should she trust more, and by how much, and how was she supposed to say that in a review without sounding like she was just dismissing the exciting one?

She opened a new document and typed a sentence she immediately hated: "Both articles offer valuable perspectives." It was the kind of pithy nothing that sounded wise and meant nothing, the sort of line teachers circled in red. She deleted it. Then she tried again: "The two studies differ not only in findings but in the degree of scrutiny their findings have undergone." Better, though it tasted like a sentence from a person pretending to be older than she was. She kept it.

Dara, who had wandered off to the shelves, interposed herself back into the conversation by sliding a book across the table, a guide to evaluating sources, and tapping a chapter titled "Publication Status." "Librarian put this out on display," Dara said. "Or a display fairy." Faith read the chapter standing up, one hand on the table. It made the distinction again, cleanly: publication in a journal meant review by independent experts chosen by that journal; a paper posted publicly beforehand had not yet been checked that way. It also said something Faith hadn't considered, that peer review was imperfect and slow, that journals rejected good work and passed bad, that being unpublished was not the same as being wrong. Okafor might have posted his paper because he wanted feedback, or because a journal had already turned him down, or because he thought the findings mattered too much to wait. Faith couldn't know which, and the review had to be honest about not knowing.

The memory arrived without invitation: sophomore year, her father explaining his work over dinner, something about a client whose money he was responsible for, how being trusted with what belongs to someone else changes what you're allowed to do with it. He'd used the word fiduciary, and Faith had looked it up afterward, a person bound to act in another's interest. She thought of it now because a reviewer, she decided, was something like that. Her readers would trust her judgment, and she owed them care with it, not just balance. Her father had also once told her he'd trusted a contractor who turned out to have faked his license, and that trust, he said, was a thing you spent and couldn't get back. She had watched him weigh that choice for months afterward, still weighing it, probably. Maybe that was just what deciding looked like from the inside: never quite finished.

She drafted for another hour. She wrote that the Okafor paper's large effects demanded more scrutiny, not less attention; that its unreviewed status was not a verdict but a condition, a fact about the paper rather than a finding about the world; that the journal study's smaller, duller numbers carried more weight for now, while the stronger claims deserved the examination they hadn't yet received. She left a sentence unfinished because she couldn't find its end: "Whether the difference in publication status explains the difference in findings is a question that." She stared at the period she hadn't typed.

Dara stood to leave, hoisting her backpack. "You done being a scholar?" Faith looked at the screen, at the half-sentence, at the two articles lying open and unequal beside it. "I don't know," she said. "Ask me after peer review." Dara laughed and pushed in her chair, and Faith reached for the flat cola and drank the last of it anyway.

The fluorescent lights of the empty classroom made everyone look slightly ill, and Priya was standing in the corner with her fists on her hips, chin lifted, like a stock photo of a superhero. Makayla set down her flow pad and watched from the desk by the window, where she had been trying to write comments for the scrimmage they had just finished. She had until Thursday to tell Priya something true about her speaking, and so far all she had written was "good energy," which was a lie of the most cowardly kind, because Priya's energy was the problem.

"Power pose," Priya said, catching her looking. "You stand like this for two minutes and your body chemistry changes. Testosterone up, cortisol down. It's science." She held her chin higher, as if the pose itself might carry her through the regional tournament on Saturday.

Makayla didn't answer right away. She had actually looked this up, three weeks ago, after her own disaster of a speech at the invitational, when she had locked herself in the restroom and tried the pose herself, arms spread wide under the hand dryer, feeling ridiculous and then, somehow, slightly less terrified. That night she had gone home and searched for it, expecting to find the study Priya was describing, and she had found it. A study from 2010 had claimed exactly what Priya said: testosterone up, cortisol down. But then she had kept reading, because the numbers had seemed too tidy, and she had found something else. A larger study, from 2015, had tried to replicate it and found no such hormonal effect at all. The hormones didn't budge. What people did report, in both cases, was feeling more powerful.

The distinction had sat with her for weeks, not because it mattered to her own nerves but because it seemed to matter to everything. If the pose only made you feel powerful, then it was a story you told your own body, and stories could be true in one way and false in another. She had not decided what she thought about that. Her mother, who was sanguine about nearly everything, would say it didn't matter as long as it worked. Her older brother, who trusted nothing he couldn't measure, would say it was a placebo dressed up in a lab coat. Makayla suspected the answer was somewhere in the middle, in the territory where a feeling could be real without being measurable, but she hadn't found the words for it yet, and now Priya was walking toward her with her cape of invisible confidence still on.

"Can I read you my case again?" Priya asked. She had read it three times already that afternoon, faster each time, as though speed could hide the places where her evidence didn't connect.

"Actually," Makayla said, and her stomach did the thing it did before she had to say something honest. She had spent two years on this team being pleasant and useless, the person who said "nice job" and meant nothing by it, and Mr. Okafor had finally made her feedback partner specifically so that would stop. "Can I tell you about the last round instead? Like, specifically?"

Priya sat on the edge of the desk, wary, and Makayla pushed the flow pad toward her, where she had drawn a little chart of the round. "Here, in your second speech, you dropped your evidence on wage data, which was your best card, and you spent forty seconds on the part that didn't matter. And here, you talked so fast during the counterplan that I couldn't write any of it down. If I can't flow it, a judge can't either, and the judge doesn't love you the way I do."

"You said good energy," Priya said, in the voice of someone cataloguing an injury.

"I know. That was me being a coward." Saying it out loud was its own kind of power pose, Makayla thought, and then wondered whether that was even a fair comparison, whether telling the truth and standing like a superhero could belong in the same category. She didn't say that part. "Your structure is good. Your research is the best on the team. The speed is what's going to incapacitate you on Saturday, not your nerves. The nerves you've already figured out."

Priya looked at the flow pad for a long moment. "The pose thing," she said finally. "You looked it up, didn't you. You have that face."

"I did. The 2010 study claimed it raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, like you said. But a bigger one in 2015 tried to replicate it and found no hormonal effect. The testosterone didn't go up. The cortisol didn't go down." Makayla watched a small foreboding cross Priya's face, the look of someone whose ritual was being disassembled in front of her, and she hurried toward the part that mattered. "But people still reported feeling more powerful. Both times. So it's not a lie to your body. It's just not a chemical one."

Priya was quiet, fists still half-curled on her hips, as if she hadn't decided yet whether to put them down. Then she picked up the flow pad and squinted at the little chart. "Forty seconds on the framing section," she said. "Which part should I cut?"

"The middle eight seconds, where you apologize for the format," Makayla said, and Priya laughed, an abrupt surprised sound, and pulled out her timer. "Okay. Read it with me at half speed. And if I go fast, kick my chair."

"That's not kind feedback," Priya said, already standing, already squaring her shoulders.

"It's specific," Makayla said, and kicked the chair leg once, lightly, to show she meant it.

Ashley had spent the first week of camp avoiding the art shack, because the art shack was where everyone went to make lanyards and glazed turtles, and she wanted to make something real. But on Tuesday the printmaking table was empty, the inks were actually dry, and the paper was heavy and toothy, so she sat down and started a landscape of the lake from memory. She had been drawing the same lake all summer in her notebook: water, hills, the strip of land that joined the camp's island to the shore like an isthmus in miniature, though she had never called it that until a boy in her cabin pointed at it and used the word, and it stuck.

Priya from the neighboring cabin leaned over her shoulder and said, "Move the waterline. Put the horizon a third of the way down."

"Why a third?"

"Because that's where horizons go. Rule of thirds."

"Who made that a rule?" Ashley asked. Priya had no answer, only a shrug, and the shrug bothered Ashley more than the advice did. She had come to camp with two ideas in her head that she could not get to sit together: that making art meant following what worked, and that following what worked was a small kind of dying. She did not say this out loud. She said, "It looks fine the way it is," and kept the horizon dead center, and Priya wandered off to the glazing kiln.

The print came out wrong. Not bad exactly, but inert, the lake sitting in the picture like a specimen pinned under glass, everything symmetrical and nothing alive. Ashley held it up to the light and hated it with the specific hatred reserved for your own careful work. Her counselor had told her on the first night that camp was for trying things, which Ashley had found obdurate and useless as advice, the kind of thing adults said instead of anything. But she thought of it now anyway.

The art shack had one shelf of books, warped by humidity, and she went through them on Wednesday afternoon while a group of eleven-year-olds slapped paint onto birdhouses. In a faded volume on composition she found the sentence, and she read it twice, and then a third time with her finger under the words. The phrase rule of thirds had been written down first by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book, Remarks on Rural Scenery. She carried the book to Priya at the picnic table outside and set it down between their sandwiches.

"Some guy named John Thomas Smith," Ashley said. "1797. Remarks on Rural Scenery. He's the first one who wrote the phrase down."

"See," Priya said. "It's a real rule."

"That's not what it says." Ashley was surprised by her own certainty. "It says one guy wrote it down in 1797. It doesn't say he was right, or that it was always true, or that it has to be true for me." But even as she said it, she was looking at the lake, at the actual lake, where the far shore sat low against the water and the sky took everything above it, and she could see that the world itself did not halve neatly. The horizon out there was already sitting somewhere below the middle. Smith had noticed something, she thought; he had not invented it, he had caught it.

So on Thursday she cut a new block, and this time she set the waterline a third of the way down, but she kept the isthmus off-center to the left, running against the grain of every suggestion Priya had made, and she pushed the hills until they crowded the top of the frame, unresolved, unfinished. The print that came off the press was better. Not good. Better. It had a nervous energy to it, the land pressing down on the water, and when Priya saw it she stood quiet for a second and said, "I like it better off-center. The isthmus, especially. I was wrong about that part."

"You were right about the other part," Ashley said. "That's the annoying thing."

She pinned both prints to the corkboard by the shack door, the symmetric one and the new one, side by side, so that anyone walking past would have to decide which they liked without being told. Priya wrote under the first one, in pencil, SMITH, 1797, and under the second one she wrote nothing, and Ashley understood that too, because some things you cannot instantiate in a caption. She stood in front of them until the mosquitoes drove her inside, and through the screen door she could still see the lake past both horizons, the real one, doing whatever it wanted.

The graph had been taunting Elliot since Monday: a thin black line rising like a ramp past every squiggle and dip before it, with the years 1958 to now printed along the bottom in cramped type. By Thursday he was supposed to stand in front of the senior seminar and explain it, and explain too how carbon dioxide lets sunlight through and holds back the heat trying to escape, which he mostly understood and mostly could not say out loud. Mr. Okafor had paired him with Dana, who had already written her half of the talk, and whose half was better than his half, and who kept glancing at his notebook with an expression he couldn't read.

He stayed after the bell in the library's back corner, where the old science shelves smelled like dust and glue. He was hunting for a clearer way to say greenhouse effect when a thin book on the history of charts fell open in his hands. There it was: a map printed in London in 1769, drawn by Benjamin Franklin, of the Gulf Stream. Franklin's cousin Timothy Folger was a Nantucket whaling captain, and it was Folger's knowledge of the water that went into the chart.

"Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769," Elliot said aloud, before he could stop himself.

A girl two tables over looked up. Dana, it turned out, who had been pretending not to watch him the whole time. "Using what, guesses?"

"No. His cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain. The captains knew the water. They were saving days by avoiding the current." He turned the book toward her. On the map the stream curled across the Atlantic like a vein, drawn from talk and memory rather than instruments.

Dana came and sat down, which surprised him, because they had spoken maybe forty words to each other all semester. "So the satellite people think they discovered all this," she said, "and really some whaler's cousin drew it first."

"It's not the same thing," Elliot said. "Folger knew where it was. He didn't know why." That distinction had just arrived in his head fully formed, and it pleased him more than he let show. He thought of his grandfather, who trusted weather in his knees over any forecast, and who called climate science a fashion. Two ways of knowing. One had a two-hundred-fifty-year-old map. The other had the ramp-shaped line in his notebook.

"Show me your part," Dana said, and he slid the graph across, and she frowned, and he saw the frown, and his stomach dropped. "Your axis is wrong," she said. "You flipped time and concentration. Your line goes down." She said it without any insouciant shrug, without softening it at all, and he sat there feeling stupid and grateful in equal measure. He had been so entralled by the shape of the rise, that long accelerating climb, that he hadn't checked what the axes actually said.

They redrew it together on graph paper, the library lights buzzing overhead, and while his pencil moved he tried the sentences out loud. Sunlight comes in. The earth warms and radiates heat back out. Carbon dioxide absorbs some of that outgoing heat and re-radiates it, so more of it stays near the surface. More gas, more held heat. Dana made him say it three times, then asked, "But how do we know it's us and not a volcano or the ocean?" and he didn't have an answer ready, and instead of panicking he wrote the question down. "I'll say exactly that tomorrow," he told her. "That's the part I'm still uncertain about, and I'd rather admit it than fake a mechanism."

She looked at him for a second longer than necessary. "You know the whole zeitgeist is confidence, right? Fake it till you make it." She said it lightly, but something underneath it wasn't light, something about a world that rewarded people who never said I don't know. He thought of Folger, who must have said it constantly, to every captain who would listen, and Franklin, who printed the not-knowing right onto the map.

The next afternoon Elliot stood at the front of the room with the corrected graph projected huge behind him. He explained the axes first, then the mechanism, then held up a printout of the 1769 chart. "This is a Gulf Stream map Benjamin Franklin had printed in London in 1769," he said, "drawn from the knowledge of his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain. Ship captains were saving days by avoiding the current long before satellites." A boy in the second row raised his hand and asked about the volcano question, the exact one, and Elliot smiled and said, "That's the part I haven't worked out yet. Give me till Friday." Dana, from her seat by the window, turned theFolger map face-down on her desk so only she could see it, and traced the current once with her finger, slowly, all the way across the page.

Isaac had planned to finish his demographics project at home, but his mother's conference had swallowed the apartment for the weekend, so he'd exiled himself to the food court with his laptop, a cold slice of pizza, and a printed stack of population pyramids that he now had to exhume from the bottom of his backpack, where they had fossilized under gym clothes. The assignment was due Monday: choose a country, read its pyramid, and predict whether it would need more schools or more nursing homes over the next thirty years. Isaac had picked Qatar almost at random, because it was small and he liked the shape of its name.

The chart did not look like a pyramid. It looked like a wasp: a narrow head of children, a swollen striped middle, and almost nothing at the top. He stared at it, then turned the paper sideways, then held it up to the skylight as though the truth might come through from behind. The middle bulge was enormous, and it was lopsided in a way no pyramid had a right to be.

"That's a printing error," he said to nobody.

"There's no printer in the world that makes only men," said Priya, sliding into the seat across from him with her own tray. She was in his geography class and had the suspicious good cheer of someone whose project was already done. "What is that, a bee?"

"It's Qatar. It's supposed to be a population pyramid." He pointed at the long bars on the left side of the bulge, the side his textbook's legend said was male. The female bars beside them were less than half as long. "Unless Qatari women have been secretly leaving the country in huge numbers, this chart is broken. I'm going to fail. Mr. Okafor will frame my failure in the staff room."

Priya leaned in, chewing thoughtfully. "Maybe it's not broken. Maybe it's real and it's just weird."

"Charts aren't weird. Charts are honest. That's the whole point of charts." Isaac said this with the conviction of a boy who had, until this moment, never deeply trusted anything else. He turned the paper over. Blank. He turned it back. Still a wasp.

He did what any seventeen-year-old researcher does: he pulled out his phone and typed Qatar population pyramid male bulge, half expecting to find a forum full of people complaining about a bad dataset. What he found instead stopped his thumb mid-scroll. The bulge was real. Some Gulf states, Qatar among them, showed a large bulge of working-age men because many foreign male workers lived there. He read the sentence twice, then a third time, and felt the ground of the assignment shift slightly under him, like a ferry leaving the dock while you're still looking at your ticket.

"Okay," he said slowly. "So the chart isn't lying. The men are there. They're just, a lot of them, not from there." He spread his hands over the wasp's midsection as though warming them at a fire. "So if I'm predicting schools or nursing homes, what do I even do with them? They're in the pyramid but they're not really in the, the population. Or they are in the population. Argh."

"That sounds like a you problem," said Priya, stealing a pepperoni. "Also a Qatar problem, honestly."

"It's both problems. That's the problem." Isaac began scribbling in the margin. The children at the top of the chart, the narrow head, were the school question; the near-empty peak was the nursing home question, or the lack of one. But the bulge, that striped middle full of working-age men, didn't fit either prediction cleanly, and he couldn't decide whether to count it, average it out, or flag it and move on. His notes said all three, in that order, and then a small drawing of a wasp wearing a hard hat.

Priya peered at the notes. "Wow. Demographic acumen. You should put that on a business card."

"You don't know what acumen means."

"Neither do you, obviously, or you'd have an answer."

Mr. Okafor, when Monday came, walked the rows with his hands behind his back and paused at Isaac's desk longer than at anyone else's. He looked at the pyramid, at the margin notes, at the wasp in the hard hat, and at the final paragraph, which ended with a question mark Isaac had written in pen and then, unable to help himself, circled.

"So," said Mr. Okafor. "Schools or nursing homes?"

"That depends who you count," said Isaac. "Which depends on who you think the pyramid is for. I have an answer for the citizens and a different answer for everybody in the chart, and I don't know which one you want, and I'm not sure I think there's a right one. Also I think my brain is igneous, it cooled under pressure and now it's stuck like this."

"That's geology," said Mr. Okafor.

"It's also my weekend."

Mr. Okafor smiled and moved on without marking anything, and Isaac looked down at his circled question mark, and then at the wasp, and then out the window, where the flagpole rope was tapping in the wind.

"Mr. Okafor," he called after him. "Seriously. Which one would you build?"

"I'd build a canteen," said Mr. Okafor, without turning around, "for all those working-age men."

Alyssa taped the whiteboard to the rink boards where the U14 girls could see it, then untaped it because the diagram looked like a ransom note. Behind her, twelve twelve-year-olds were already firing pucks at the empty net, the way they did every practice, and by the end of every practice they would still be terrible at passing. She knew this because she had watched them for three weeks. They could skate. They could shoot. The moment a pass had to travel more than six feet, it ended up in someone's skates or against the glass, and they laughed, and the game went on.

"They only want to scrimmage," her cousin Dev had told her when she took the volunteer job. Dev ran the association like a small technocracy, ice time allocated by spreadsheet, and he had been peevish about giving her the Tuesday hour until she promised to submit practice plans in advance. "You get fifty minutes. Don't waste it on drills they'll malign behind your back."

She had written the first plan at her kitchen table with a psych textbook open beside her, left over from the community college course she'd started in the spring. She'd skimmed it for coaching and found a study instead: violinists at a music academy, 1993, K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues. The best players hadn't logged the most hours overall; what separated them was what the researchers called deliberate practice, effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, instead of just accumulating time. Alyssa had read the paragraph twice, then gone to the window. Her own hockey career had ended at sixteen with nothing to show for eleven years of ice except smooth crossovers and a wrist shot she could still land in her sleep. Hours. She had logged so many hours.

Flashback first, though, before the plan could exist: Alyssa at fourteen, sitting on the bench during a tournament in Pembroke while her coach drew up a power play on his clipboard. He had never once told her what she was bad at. He'd told her she was doing great, that she was a gamer, that she brought energy, and she had believed him right up until the rep team cuts came out and her name wasn't on the list. Her mother had said maybe it was politics. Alyssa had known better even then, and had never asked anyone to tell her the truth, which was its own kind of politics.

So on Tuesday she blew the whistle inside the first two minutes. Pucks went in the bucket. The girls groaned, one of them, Priya, loudly and with feeling.

"We're not scrimmaging today."

"Why not."

"Because we scrimmage every day and you still can't pass."

"We can pass."

"Show me. Ten feet, tape to tape, ten in a row." They got to four before Shauna put one into the corner, and everyone looked at the ceiling of the arena as though it might intervene.

Alyssa set up the drill she'd designed at the kitchen table: two lines, one passer, one receiver skating across the slot, pass had to lead the skater, and every miss meant the passer had to call out what she'd done wrong before she could rotate. Shauna's first five attempts went wide or behind. "I don't know," she said, the sixth time. "Tell me where it went," Alyssa said. "My feet?" "So fix it." On the eighth, Shauna pulled up mid-release, set her hips, and the puck arrived on Priya's tape as she crossed the far post. Priya didn't even break stride. Nobody said anything, but the next girl in line skated harder to her spot, and Alyssa wrote something on the whiteboard in block letters: WEAK PASSING UNDER MOVEMENT. 8 MISSES BEFORE 1 CLEAN. It wasn't a lesson, it was a number, and the girls kept glancing at it.

The number moved. Eleven attempts, then seven, then, near the end of the hour, a string of six clean in a row before the Zamboni light came on and Dev appeared at the gate with his clipboard.

"Fifty minutes, no scrimmage. The parents are going to malign me in the parking lot."

"It's called deliberate practice," Alyssa said. "It works on the thing you're worst at. That's the whole point."

Dev watched Priya take a pass in full stride and bury it, top corner, no celebration, just a hard loop back to the line. He wrote something on his clipboard.

"Same plan Thursday?"

"Same drill. Harder."

He nodded and let the gate clang shut behind him. The girls were already whacking pucks toward the bucket themselves, without being asked, and Alyssa stood at the whiteboard and drew a small box beside the number six, left it empty, and capped the marker.

Alexandre spread three books across the library table: one on Westminster, one on the French Fifth Republic, and a photocopy of a civics reader someone had left in the returns bin. His debate partner had dropped the class two days ago, which left Alexandre alone with a question he now had to argue both sides of by Thursday: whether a parliamentary or a presidential system does a better job of choosing and removing a head of government.

He built the comparison in two columns on graph paper. In a parliamentary system, the legislature picked the prime minister, usually the leader of the majority party, and could remove that person with a vote of no confidence, sometimes within days. In a presidential system, voters elected the president directly or through an electoral college, and removal required impeachment, a long, formal process with a high bar. He wrote it out twice, once favoring speed and accountability, once favoring stability and separation of powers. Both versions looked convincing on paper, which was the problem.

The girl at the next table leaned over. "Is that for Mr. Okafor's class? The systems debate?" She introduced herself as Priya, a first-year at the community college, and said she was preparing for a mock court on Thursday too, a different case, involving free speech. "My problem is the other side has this quote everyone uses. 'You can't shout fire in a crowded theatre.' It sounds unbeatable."

"Sounds like it," Alexandre said.

"Do you know where it's from?" she asked. "Because I found out last night and it changed my whole strategy."

He didn't know. She slid a printout across the table, a case citation, Schenck v. United States, 1919. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, she said, wrote the opinion. "Holmes said free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic. That's the actual line. Falsely. In a theatre. Causing a panic. My coach says if I can get the other side to quote the shorthand version, I stand up and ask them who wrote it, and when."

Alexandre read the paragraph twice. Holmes had written it in 1919, in Schenck v. United States, and the sentence had conditions the famous version dropped. He thought about his own two columns, how easily "parliamentary systems remove leaders faster" could become a slogan that shed its qualifications, the way the fire line had shed its adverb. He wrote "1919" in the margin of his graph paper and drew a line to both columns.

Priya practiced on him. "The government may not restrain speech except in narrow circumstances," she recited, then went belligerent for the cross-examination, jabbing a finger at an imaginary witness. "Counsel, who wrote the words you just quoted? When did he write them?" She lost the thread halfway and started over. "I need this," she said. "There's a scholarship tied to the competition. Second place gets nothing."

They worked in parallel for an hour. When she left to recuperate her voice, which had gone hoarse from repeating the cross-examination, she asked him to listen one more time and rate her delivery. He said the finger-jabbing was too much, and she wrote "no finger" on her notecard.

Alexandre went back to the columns and made himself argue each side out loud, quietly, at the table. For the parliamentary side: a prime minister who loses the confidence of the legislature can be out in a week, which means the head of government never strays far from the majority that sustains them. For the presidential side: a fixed term insulates the executive from legislative mood swings, and impeachment's difficulty is a feature, not a defect, because it prevents removal from becoming a routine weapon. He caught himself drifting toward the parliamentary side because it felt tidier, then reminded himself that tidiness was exactly what the fire quote offered, and that the shorthand had outlived the facts.

He did not resolve it. Instead he wrote a third column for what stayed uncertain: whether quick removal made leaders more accountable or merely more cautious, and whether a hard impeachment process protected stability or protected a president who had lost the legislature's trust entirely. Both questions, he admitted in the margin, depended on which failure a country feared more, and countries feared different things for reasons history, not logic, supplied. He underlined nothing.

At closing time he stacked the books and left the graph paper folded in his bag. Outside, in the parking lot, Priya was on the phone by the bus stop, still arguing her case to whoever had answered. "He wrote it in 1919," she was saying. "Holmes. In Schenck. You have to make them say it first." Alexandre walked past with a small wave, and she held up her notecard, which read, in large letters, NO FINGER.

The October light through the gym's high windows turned the floor a dull gold, and beyond the chain-link fence outside, the arboreal edge of the park had already gone rust and yellow. Lucas stood at the baseline with the rest of the junior varsity squad, waiting for Coach Reyes to finish writing on his clipboard, and tried not to look at Danny, who was two spots down the line and pretending to stretch a hamstring he had never once pulled.

The problem was simple and Lucas had been turning it over for two weeks: the team loafed. Not in games, exactly, but in practice, in the conditioning drills, in every moment when the sprint was collective and the shame could be spread thin across twelve bodies. When they ran lines as a group, the whole pack drifted to the pace of its slowest concealer. Lucas wanted playing time, and playing time went to the coach's eye, and the coach's eye, he suspected, could not tell who was actually working inside a crowd of identical jerseys.

"Sprint times today," Coach Reyes said, slapping the clipboard against his palm. "Individually. One at a time, everyone watching, everyone timed."

Danny groaned, loud enough to destabilize the loose attention of the line, and a couple of guys laughed, and the laugh was the old sound, the sound of the group absorbing a complaint so that no single person owned it. Lucas felt the laughter move past him like weather.

First up was Marcus, a center who usually drifted through conditioning like a man wading through shallow surf. Marcus ran the length of the floor four times, touched each baseline, and crossed the finish at a time Lucas would not have believed on Sunday. The clock said otherwise. Then Avery, then Razaan, then a sophomore whose name Lucas kept forgetting, all of them faster than they had been on Monday, some of them faster than they had been all season.

"Cooper," the coach called, and Danny jogged to the line.

Danny ran hard. Lucas watched him do it, watched the lazy joke of a boy push through four lengths at a time only two tenths slower than Lucas's own best, and understood something that had been sitting in the back of his mind since a unit in psych class he had half slept through. In groups, people put out less. He could not have said why, and he did not try. But when each runner's time went up on the whiteboard with a name beside it, the effort was different, and the difference was not small.

After practice, in the parking lot under the bare sycamores, Lucas caught Danny pulling his hoodie over his head. "You know what that was," Lucas said. "Back there."

"A timed sprint?"

"Social loafing," Lucas said. "People slack off in groups. Less when everyone can see who did what."

Danny zipped his bag with a slow, deliberate tug. "So you're saying I'm a loafer."

"I'm saying we all were. Me too. Monday I hid in the pack same as anybody." Lucas heard how it sounded, the confession arriving too neatly, and let it sit there ungilded. "I wanted the times posted before I even knew what it was called. I told Coach the scoreboard wasn't enough for conditioning."

"You asked him?"

"Tuesday."

Danny looked at him for a long moment, and under the look was the whole season: the two of them competing for the same starting spot, the months of Danny's jokes marking the border between them, and now this, the fact that Lucas had quietly rearranged the rules of the world they both lived in. "So now everybody has to sprint their ass off every practice," Danny said. "Because you wanted an edge."

"Because I wanted it to mean something when I beat you out," Lucas said. "If you loaf and I don't, I never know if I was better. Now we both go all the time, and whoever wins the spot wins it for real."

The honesty landed wrong at first, or right in a way that stung; Danny shouldered his bag and walked three steps toward the lot before stopping. The wind moved through the trees above them, scattering a few leaves across the asphalt. "It's like the group kind of falls apart on its own," Danny said, not turning around. "Like entropy or something. Unless somebody's keeping score."

"Something like that," Lucas said. He was not sure it was true, was not sure the analogy held, was not sure whether wanting a fair fight made him honorable or just made him someone who had found a more elaborate way to win. The uncertainty did not feel like weakness. It felt like standing at the free-throw line knowing the shot could go either way.

"Fine," Danny said, turning back. "Tuesday, then. You and me, first two names on the board. Loser carries the balls all week."

"Losers carry the balls," Lucas said. "That's what managers are for."

"That's what you're for if you lose." Danny grinned, and it was almost the old grin, altered by something Lucas could not yet name.

Tuesday morning the gym was cold and the whiteboard was blank and clean, and Lucas stepped to the baseline first, sneakers squeaking against the gold-lit floor.

The debate topic was printed on the whiteboard in Señora Vega's tidy, vestigial cursive, a style nobody under forty used anymore: "Should the school day begin at ten instead of eight?" Under it, the rule that had Sara's stomach folding in on itself like a paper crane: five minutes, entirely in Spanish, no English, or the team lost a full letter grade.

"Entirely," her partner, Danny, whispered as they huddled over a single shared desk in the back corner of room 214. The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the oranges Señora Vega kept in a bowl like some ascetic offering, never eaten, just displayed. "Even the part where I panic? What do I do, panic in Spanish?"

"You say 'no sé' with conviction," Sara said. "People respect conviction."

Danny was fluent by accident; his grandmother lived with his family and Spanish came out of him the way breathing did. Sara had gotten to this class by working, flashcard by flashcard, Saturday mornings sacrificed to verb conjugations the way other people sacrificed them to sleep. She wanted the five minutes because the university admissions packet had a line about demonstrated proficiency, but also, though she would not have said this out loud, because she wanted to hold the language in her hands without feeling it slip.

At lunch they practiced in the cafeteria, which smelled of industrial pizza and floor wax. Sara got through ninety seconds on adolescent sleep research before disaster: "Los estudiantes need, uh, los estudiantes necesitan more sleep, because their brains are still, uh, developing, which is why the schedule should change." She heard the English words land like dropped trays. Danny winced. Sara put her forehead on the table next to her milk carton.

"I did it again," she said into the laminate.

"You do it every time you get nervous," Danny said. He peeled his orange, though it was Señora Vega's kind of orange, small and sour. "You know it's not a failure thing, right? There's a word for it. Code-switching. Moving between two languages in one conversation. My abuela does it constantly and nobody would call her weak in either language. It's common among people who are actually fluent."

Sara lifted her head. "I'm not fluent."

"You're close enough that your brain treats English like a door it can walk through," Danny said. "That's the thing. It's common among fluent bilinguals. It doesn't mean what you think it means."

She turned this over through sixth period chemistry, writing LA CLAVE at the top of her notes and then, feeling dramatic, crossing it out. What Danny was describing was not the opposite of skill. It was almost a symptom of it. Which meant the rule, entirely in Spanish, was asking her not to erase a weakness but to close a door on purpose, for five minutes, that fluent people left swinging. She could not decide whether that made the rule stupid or whether it was exactly the discipline she needed, and she liked even less that both could be true at once. She decided to hold the question instead of answering it, the way you hold a hot cup, testing.

Fourth period the next day, the desks were pushed into two facing rows. Señora Vega sat by the window with a stopwatch and a clipboard, sunlight moving across her bracelets. Danny went first, sailed, floated, occasionally seemed to forget he was being graded. Then it was Sara's turn, and Marcus from the opposing side folded his arms like a lawyer in a show about lawyers.

She started. The Spanish came, a little slow, then faster. "Los estudiantes adolescentes necesitan dormir más porque sus cerebros siguen desarrollándose. Si la escuela comenzara a las diez..." Marcus interrupted with a question about parents' work schedules and her mind went white, and the English came up her throat like water.

"Because, because the parents would, los padres tendrían que..." She stopped. Somewhere a pencil tapped. Marcus smirked, the specific smirk of someone winning on a technicality rather than an argument. Sara put her hand flat on the desk, felt the cool press of laminate, and thought: this is a door, and I am allowed to close it.

"Repito," she said, slowly, and each word after that was chosen like a coin from the bottom of a purse. "Los padres tendrían dificultades, sí, pero las dificultades existen en ambos casos. La pregunta no es si hay dificultades. La pregunta es cuáles podemos soportar." She heard the room go quiet in a different way, not bored-quiet but listening-quiet. When the stopwatch beeped she had thirty seconds left and a full argument on the board of her mind, unspent.
