"My theme is, I don't know, keeping going while something watches." He said it and immediately heard how it sounded, like a slogan on a mug. Priya was kind enough not to laugh and honest enough not to nod.

They spent the afternoon in the room. Priya, who wanted to study biology and had once described herself, bitterly, as "a failed polymath, decent at everything, spectacular at nothing," argued that the animals had to mean something biological too, that the monkey was her fertility and the hummingbird, suspended on thorns, was freedom caught. Luca argued back that you couldn't diagram a painting like a frog. "It's not germane what the monkey meant to her biographically if what it does in the painting is hold her," he said, and Priya said that was the most useful thing he'd said all day, which he suspected was an insult, and accepted it anyway.

By five o'clock he had filled six pages: himself at his desk with the cat on the bookshelf, himself on the bus with the cat in the window reflection, himself at his grandmother's kitchen table with the cat under the chair where the dog should have been. Some of it was terrible. The bus one looked like an ad for public transit. But two of them, the desk and the kitchen, had something in them that made him keep turning back to the pages, and he knew enough now to trust that turning back.

Ms. Adeyemi's email required the artist's statement by Friday along with sketches of all ten, and Luca sat on the bench after the gallery announced closing, drafting it in the back of the sketchbook. He wrote that the series was about what it was like to make anything while a part of you watched and predicted failure. He wrote that he did not know yet whether the watching thing was fear or grief or just attention, and that he thought the not knowing was part of the subject. He read it over and didn't cross any of it out.

Priya gathered the sandwich wrappers while the guard unlocked the front doors. "Statement done?"

"Done enough. Nine more drawings by Friday."

"That's impossible."

"It's extremely possible," Luca said, zipping his pencil case, and then, more quietly, because the room was almost empty and the cat in the painting was still peering over Kahlo's shoulder the way it had been all afternoon, "It's just going to be a long week." He stood, tucked the sketchbook under his arm, and walked out backwards, looking at the painting until the door swung shut between them.

I am, by my own account, the most honest person on the robotics team, which is why it stung so much when Dev told me I had let everyone down. I've been turning that over all summer, through the last weeks of senior year and into this party at Marisol's house, where her cousin's playlist is too loud and somebody's little brother keeps opening the screen door to let mosquitoes in. The party is for Marisol's eighteenth, and half the team is here, and of course Sami is here too, which is the whole problem, or the whole solution, depending on which version of me you believe.

Here is what I tell people happened: at regionals in March, Sami's wiring harness failed twice during inspection, and I said something, because I always say something. Here is what actually happened: I said nothing either time. I stood by the pit table with my arms crossed and watched her re-solder the same bad joint, and when she looked up at me for confirmation I gave her a thumbs up, because she'd been having a hard month and I didn't want to be the one who made it harder. We missed the alliance picks by one match. Dev, our driver, didn't speak to me on the bus home.

At the party I find him by the cooler, fishing out a cream soda that is definitely not for him since it's Marisol's dad's. "You're still mad," I say, which is a generous framing, as though his anger were an overreaction I've patiently tolerated.

"I'm not mad," Dev says. "I'm done being surprised by you." He cracks the can. "Priya told me you told her the intake arm design was 'fine.' She spent two weeks on it. It wasn't fine, and she told me she would have fixed it in a day if you'd said one specific thing."

One specific thing. That phrase has been following me around like a stray. My sister, who reads management books for fun, an amalgam of ambition and self-help she consumes the way I consume chips, threw one at me in June. She said, "In her 2017 book Radical Candor, Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly." I'd rolled my eyes at the time, some atavistic male reflex against anything with the word "radical" on the cover, but the sentence stayed. It stayed because I recognized myself in its failure, in the gap between its two halves. I had cared personally, fine. I had cared so much it made me useless.

Across the room Sami is teaching Marisol's little brother to juggle with limes, dropping them, laughing, picking them up again. She's not fragile. She never was. I'd decided she was, and then dressed my cowardice up as gentleness, told myself I was being kind when I was really being absent. There's a way of pathologizing other people's hard months, treating sadness like a diagnosis that means they can't hear the truth, and I'd done that to her without ever asking what she actually wanted.

"You should tell her," Dev says, following my eyes. "Not for me. Not for the team, we're all graduating. For you, man, because you're going to be somebody's roommate in August, somebody's lab partner, and they're going to need you to say real things."

I take my drink and cross the room, and it takes approximately forever, maybe eight seconds. Sami catches me mid-approach and grins. "Cole! Marisol said you're going to that engineering program, the big one. You deserve it."

"Thanks. Sami, hey." I put my cup down on the counter so my hands have nothing to hide behind. "At regionals, the wiring harness. I saw the cold joint before inspection, both times, and I didn't tell you because I thought you couldn't handle it that week. That was wrong of me, and it cost us a match, and I'm sorry." My voice comes out steadier than I feel. "If it happens again, tell me to shut up and check the joint."

She's quiet long enough for the playlist to change songs. Then she says, "You watched me solder that thing twice and said nothing?"

"I gave you a thumbs up."

"I know. I thought it looked good because you gave me a thumbs up." She laughs, but it isn't entirely a laugh. "I failed my driving test that month and my grandmother was in the hospital and I still would have rather you just said, Sami, redo the joint, it looks like a cold one. I'm not made of sugar."

I start to apologize again and she waves it off, juggling her three limes, tossing me the fourth. "So how was the party for you," she says, "before you came over here to confess?"

"Honestly? Terrible until about a minute ago."

"Good," she says, and drops all the limes on purpose, and Marisol's little brother cheers like something has been won.

John had claimed the camp stove the way other people claimed armchairs, with a whole-body authority that discouraged negotiation. His mother had raised an eyebrow; his sister Delia had raised her phone, apparently to photograph whatever disaster followed. The roast sat in the cast iron Dutch oven, a two-kilo lump of pork shoulder his father had triumphantly produced from the cooler that morning, and John's ambition was larger than the lump itself. He wanted to cook it perfectly, exactly to temperature, because for once he wanted to be the person in the family who was right about something precise.

He crouched by the oven with the instant-read thermometer like a man defusing something. Sixty-three degrees was the number. He'd looked it up twice on the walk in, and a third time while the coals were settling, which Delia had noticed and commented on with a small, savage joy. The coals ticked and shifted under the pot. Somewhere behind the tents a squirrel conducted its own negotiations with a bag of trail mix nobody had sealed properly.

"Sixty-three," he announced, when the needle finally crawled there. "That's done. That is textbook done."

"You've said textbook four times since breakfast," said his father, from the folding chair where he was pretending to read and actually watching a beetle cross the picnic table with what looked like professional interest.

John hauled the pot off the heat, lid and all, set it on a flat rock, and stood over it in the manner of a person expecting applause. Delia took the photograph. The family milled toward the table, plates in hand, someone poured water, someone else argued that the someone before them had taken the good cup. Ten minutes of this passed before John carved, because he'd also read somewhere that you were supposed to let a roast rest, and resting seemed like the kind of rule a careful person followed.

The first slice told a story he didn't like. Gray, all the way through, the pale overcooked gray of a cafeteria. He carved a second slice hoping the first had been a local problem. It was not. His father chewed thoughtfully. His mother said, kindly, that it was fine, which was worse than any insult because everyone at the table could hear the word fine being carried out on a stretcher.

Here is what Delia saw, because she was watching her brother and not her plate: John staring at the roast with the expression of a boy who had followed the map exactly and arrived in the wrong country. He poked the meat with the thermometer again, out of some grief-driven instinct, and the needle sat higher than sixty-three, several degrees higher, as if the roast had continued without him. He looked at the coals, which were nowhere near the pot. He looked at the pot, which was nowhere near anything hot. He said, quietly, "It kept going."

"It's called carryover cooking," Delia said, holding up her phone. She had searched it the moment the gray slice hit the light, faster than a chess clock. "A big roast keeps cooking after it leaves the heat. The temperature can come up several degrees while it rests."

"That's a real thing?"

"That's a thing with a name and everything. People pull roasts early on purpose."

John sat down on the cooler as though the cooler had asked him to. All evening he had been thinking of cooking as a matter of obedience, temperature as a door you walked through once. Now the roast seemed more like an argument that continued after you'd left the room. He was circumspect by nature about changing his mind, having once defended a wrong answer in geography class for a full week, but the evidence sat steaming on the platter, gray and complete.

"Okay," he said. "Okay. So next time I take it out at, what, sixty? Fifty-nine?" He was already recalculating, and Delia watched the transformation catalyze his whole posture, failure converting directly into scheming, his grief reallocated to the next roast, which did not yet exist. Their father offered that they had no more meat, and John said that was a temporary condition of the universe, not a permanent one.

"Tomorrow, then," his mother said. "You'll undercook it on purpose and feel very clever."

"I'll undercook it with discipline," John said. "There's a difference."

Delia took another slice of the gray pork, doused it in the applesauce nobody else wanted, and ate it with genuine appetite, because she was sixteen and appetite was still a form of mutualism between her and the world: the world fed her, and she forgave it. "Honestly," she said, mouth full, "the outside slices are fine. It's just the middle that's a mistake."

"The middle is where the lesson lives," said her father, finally, softly, and John, who had been about to argue, found he had nothing to say, so he reached over and ate the mistake himself.

Alex got the job by answering a flyer stapled to a corkboard outside the pool office, the kind of corkboard where lost sunglasses went to die. Camp Kettle Run needed a junior counselor for eight weeks, and the director, a sunburnt man named Duane, had shaken his hand and said seven twenty-five an hour like it was the password to a club. Alex had said great, because he was eighteen and had never earned anything before, and the number had meant nothing to him either way.

The first week he learned the actual work. He counted heads at the creek, six times in an hour, because kids slipped behind rocks the way water did. He pried a Fishing game out of a tree. He ate lunch beside Marisol, the arts counselor, who was twenty and saving for a nursing prerequisite, and who described the camp's pay with the affection people usually reserve for a bad ex.

On Thursday of the second week his cousin Theo texted him a photograph of a paycheck. Theo worked at a day camp one town over, except that one town was across the state line, and his stub read nine dollars and change an hour. Same job, roughly. Same bug spray, same collapsing canoes. Alex stood in the supply shed holding his phone and his own stub side by side and felt the specific indignation of the newly employed.

"I don't get it," he said to Marisol at the picnic table, sliding both phones toward her. "He's fifteen minutes away. He's not better at this. He got stung by a wasp on Monday."

Marisol looked at the numbers while unwrapping a granola bar with her teeth. "Different state," she said. "Different rules, probably."

That evening Alex looked it up on the family computer, half expecting a scavenger hunt, and found it faster than he'd expected. The federal minimum wage was seven twenty-five an hour, and it had been that since July 24, 2009, before he'd started kindergarten. He read the date twice. Somewhere out there his entire working life, all three days of it, had been priced by a number older than his learner's permit. But the same pages said a lot of states and cities set their own minimums, higher ones, and Theo's state was apparently one of them, and Alex's was not. Nobody had broken a rule. There were just two rules, and a line in the woods between them.

He sat with that for a while, and then, being eighteen, he began arguing with himself in the shower. One voice said quit, find the other camp, cross the line, that's what a rational actor does. The other voice said the kids here knew his name now. A boy named Dev, who was six and spoke mostly in tornado facts, had assigned Alex a seat at lunch. It would be possible to chase ninety more cents an hour and transfigure a decent summer into a spreadsheet, and Alex wasn't sure he wanted to be the kind of person who did the arithmetic on Dev.

He tried the argument out on Theo on Saturday, mostly to hear it outside his own head. "I could apply out there," he said. They were sitting on Theo's tailgate, splitting a bag of gas station popcorn.

"You should," Theo said. "It's the same job for more money."

"It's not the same job. My wasps are better wasps."

"That's the most parochial thing you've ever said."

"It's not parochial. It's fifteen minutes. It's just, the kids are at mine, so mine is different." Alex heard how it sounded. He kept going anyway. "The federal minimum wage has been seven twenty-five since July 24, 2009, and some places just decided not to leave it there. That's it. That's the whole mystery. One place stayed, one place didn't."

Theo chewed for a while. "So you're staying because of a date from 2009?"

"I'm staying because of a kid who thinks I'm the authority on sharks." He paused. "And maybe because quitting over ninety cents seemed like a lot of paperwork."

"Your mom's going to call that pedantry."

"My mom calls everything pedantry. She called a parking ticket pedantry."

On Monday Alex found Duane by the flagpole and asked, as casually as he could manage, whether the camp could ever match the rate across the line. Duane said they'd look at it next season, which Alex understood, in the way you understand weather, to mean no. He clocked in anyway. At the creek he counted heads, and counted again, and Dev tugged his sleeve to report that a crayfish had claws because of evolution.

"Show me," Alex said, and got down on his knees in the mud beside him.

Benjamin had agreed to lead the Seder in February, when it still felt like a distant, abstract favor, and now it was April and the kitchen smelled of brisket and his grandmother's florid handwriting was spread across the table in front of him, three pages of instructions that contradicted each other by page two. His grandfather, who had led the meal for forty years, was in the study with the door half open, not helping, which Benjamin understood was its own kind of statement.

"You're putting the Seder plate on the wrong end," his cousin Dara said, leaning over his shoulder. She was fourteen and enjoyed being right more than she enjoyed anything else at family gatherings.

"It goes where Zayde puts it."

"Zayde puts it near the head. You're at the head now. So it goes near you." She slid the plate down the tablecloth, the shank bone catching the light, and Benjamin let her. It was easier than arguing, and anyway he had a different problem: the sequence. Kadesh, then what. Urchatz. Then what came after Urchatz. He had studied the haggadah on the train down, folding over page corners, and on the train the order had seemed obvious, a river flowing in one direction. At the table, with fourteen relatives arriving in forty minutes, the river kept forking.

Their rabbi had said something in his office a week earlier that Benjamin had written in his phone and read eleven times since. He had gone to ask which blessing went with the second cup of wine, and instead of answering directly the rabbi had said, "You know the meal is called a Seder because the word means order. The whole night follows a fixed sequence, start to finish." Then he'd smiled in a way that suggested this was either a comfort or a warning, and told Benjamin the second cup came before the meal, and let him go. Benjamin had walked home thinking that "order" was a strange name for a night built around a story of chaos and wandering, forty years of desert between two orderly cups of wine.

His mother found him in the hallway, still holding the haggadah like a shield. "Relax," she said. "You've been coming to this table since you were born. Your body knows more than your notes do." That was her whole philosophy, more or less. She'd married into the family and still, after nineteen years, poured the second cup at the wrong time every other year, laughing, saying the wine didn't mind. Benjamin loved that about her and also it terrified him, because Zayde did mind, quietly, and this year Zayde was watching from the study with the door half open, and if Benjamin poured the wrong cup at the wrong time he would see it as proof of something.

The guests came in a flood of coats and casserole dishes. His aunt Rivka kissed him on both cheeks and said, "So you're the leader now," and the word leader sat strangely on him, like a jacket cut for a bigger man. He took his seat. Fourteen faces, some patient, some hungry, all waiting, and Dara gave him a small nod that meant she had decided to be on his side, at least publicly.

"Kadesh," he began, and lifted the first cup.

The early steps went well enough, the way the first mile of a race always does. Then his uncle started a story about a Seder in Buenos Aires in 1987, a genuinely good story, and while everyone laughed Benjamin felt the next step slide out of his grip, and he sat there with his hand flat on the page, transfix, everyone's eyes on him, waiting. Two voices in him at once: his mother's voice saying the story is the point, and his grandfather's voice saying the order is the point, and no voice at all saying which was right.

Then he found the page corner he'd folded, and the folded corner was enough. "Urchatz," he said, and they washed, and later he found the next corner, and the next, and somewhere around the matzah he stopped needing the corners because the sequence began to carry him instead of the other way around. He understood, mid-sentence during the Four Questions, which Dara's little brother stumbled through with the flat, doomed courage of a boy who has practiced, that his mother and his grandfather had been describing the same night from two sides. The order was not a cage; it was the shape the story poured itself into so that it could hold everyone at once, the quick and the slow, the believers and the ones there for the brisket. Or maybe that was too generous. He honestly could not tell yet whether he had reconciled anything or only survived it.

When they reached the meal itself, the talking and passing and reaching, Zayde came out of the study at last and sat down across from him. He looked at the Seder plate, correctly placed, and at the four cups lined up, two empty, two full, in their proper futures. He picked up his fork, paused, and said, "After the meal, it's Tzafun. The hidden piece. You remember where it's hidden?" and Benjamin nodded, though he did not, and started eating fast so his grandfather wouldn't ask twice.

Rosalie had the bowl in pieces on the kitchen table before her grandmother had been gone a full month, and she had no idea how to put it back together. It had broken in the move, wrapped in a dish towel at the bottom of a box marked KITCHEN, MISC, as though the word could soften it. She had been carrying the box herself. She had heard the sound before she understood it, a small knock inside the cardboard, and she had set the box down in the new kitchen and stood with her hands on the counter for a long time before she opened it.

Now it was October, and the pieces lay on a bed of newspaper between a jar of brushes and her laptop, where she had been scrolling through tutorials all afternoon. Five pieces, one of them no bigger than a thumbnail. The bowl was indigo on the outside, black glaze inside, and around the rim a rough crescent of unglazed clay where her grandmother's thumb had worn the glaze away over forty years of stirring.

"It's going to be visible no matter what I do," Rosalie said to her mother, who was unloading groceries at the counter behind her.

"Then don't do it at all," her mother said. "Keep the pieces in the cabinet with her other things. Nobody's asking you to fix it."

"You're literally standing next to the cabinet saying that."

Her mother stopped, a bag of rice in each hand, and Rosalie watched her decide not to argue. That was the mercurial weather of their house now, calm one minute, storming the next, and both of them had learned to read the sky before speaking.

The tutorials were no help. They all wanted invisibility: two-part epoxy, clamp it, sand it, paint it to match. One man on video spent eleven minutes demonstrating a filler compound and then held the bowl to the light like a jeweler, proud that the break had vanished. Rosalie closed the laptop. She kept thinking about the crescent of worn clay, the way her grandmother had never once tried to hide it, had stirred with her thumb hooked over the rim anyway. A repair that erased the break felt like a small travesty, a lie told in miniature, and she didn't fully know why she felt that strongly about a bowl.

Her friend Priya came over that evening, took one look at the table, and said, "Oh, you should do kintsugi."

"Which is what?"

"My mom has a mug someone fixed that way. You repair it with lacquer mixed with gold. Like powdered gold, actual dust, and you put it right in the seams." Priya picked up the largest piece and turned it to the lamp. "It's Japanese. The whole point is you don't hide the crack. The break becomes part of the bowl. Like it's supposed to be there, because it's part of what happened to it."

Rosalie had captivated herself, within an hour, with the idea so completely that she ordered the lacquer and the gold before Priya left, even though the real urushi was backordered and expensive and her mother raised both eyebrows at the receipt. A cheaper kit arrived first, epoxy-based, gold powder in a tiny screw-top jar. The instructions said to work slowly. The instructions said the seams should be thin. The instructions did not say that a sixteen-year-old's hands would shake, or that she would leave the pieces taped overnight in the wrong alignment and have to soak the whole thing apart in warm water and start over on a Saturday while her mother pretended not to watch from the doorway.

The second attempt took all weekend. On Sunday night she set the finished bowl under the lamp, turned it, turned it again. The seams were not thin. They ran across the indigo like rivers drawn by someone impatient, gold-bright and crooked, and one had a fingerprint pressed into it, hers, unmistakable. It was not beautiful the way the videos were beautiful. It was not even beautiful the way her grandmother's bowl had been beautiful, that smooth worn thing.

She carried it to her mother anyway and set it on the counter. Her mother held it up and was quiet for longer than Rosalie could stand.

"It's crooked," Rosalie said. "And there's a fingerprint. I know."

"I made her a sweater once, the year before you were born," her mother said. "Cropped one sleeve short and never told her. She wore it for a decade with one cold arm." She set the bowl down and ran her thumb along the largest seam, the one that crossed the crescent of worn clay, and Rosalie saw that the gold caught the crescent and carried it through, made it part of the same line. "Fill it with something," her mother said. "She'd want it used."

Rosalie wasn't sure that was true. She wasn't sure whether she had honored the bowl or only made her own grief visible in it, whether the honest thing would have been to leave the pieces separate in the cabinet. She filled it with clementines anyway and set it in the middle of the table, and in the morning, coming down for school, she found her mother eating cereal out of it at the window, the gold seams lit up in the early light.

Gavin locked the bathroom door at his grandfather's house, set his phone on the edge of the sink, and faced the mirror. He had eleven minutes before lunch, and on Monday he had to stand in front of his health class and explain three things: what consent actually means, how contraception works, and where a person goes to get tested for infections. Mr. Ruiz had called it a "wellness briefing," which made it sound like a report on stretching, but Gavin knew the room would go quiet the second he said the word condom.

He started with consent, because it was the part everyone assumed they already understood. "Consent isn't the absence of a no," he said to the mirror, watching his own mouth shape the words. "It's the presence of a yes. Freely given, reversible, informed." He had read those words so many times they'd begun to feel like someone else's, and he wondered whether that was how it worked with anything you learned, whether saying a thing over and over gradually handed it from you to the room and back again. His elocution was stiff. He tried again, slower, and this time he heard a version of himself that sounded like he might actually believe what he was saying.

There was a knock. "Gavin? Lunch in ten. Soup and sandwiches." His grandfather's voice came through the door like it was traveling a long way. Gavin opened the medicine cabinet for a drink of water and found, inexplicably, three cans of soup stacked beside the toothpaste. His grandfather stored things wherever there was room, the house having filled up over decades the way a river silts.

Gavin picked up a can. Cream of mushroom, serving size one cup, sodium 890 milligrams. He turned it over, then checked the second can, chicken and rice, 940 milligrams. Somewhere in his health folder, half-memorized for the same presentation, was a fact from the World Health Organization, and now it surfaced with the odd clarity of something finally useful. "Grandpa," he called through the door, "did you know the World Health Organization says adults should eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day? That's less than 5 grams of salt. Two cans of this stuff and you're already most of the way there." There was a pause, then a grunt, then footsteps retreating toward the kitchen, and Gavin stood there holding the can, feeling the strange satisfaction of having caught the world in a small, countable act.

He got back to it. Contraception next: he laid out the options in plain language, condoms, the pill, IUDs, and the one point he wanted to land, that no method was a personality or a promise, just a tool with a failure rate, and that doubling up methods was how careful people actually lived. Then testing: the county clinic on Delmore Street, walk-in hours on Tuesdays, no insurance required, results by phone. He'd called them himself last week, just to be sure the number was real, and the woman who answered had said "Thanks for asking," in a tone that made him feel briefly enfranchised, like a citizen of something he hadn't known he belonged to.

The hard part, he thought, rinsing his hands, wasn't the facts. The facts sat still. The hard part was that his class contained Dana Okafor, who asked sharp questions, and Ty, who joked about everything, and probably someone who had already needed the clinic and never told anyone. How did you say "get tested" in a way that didn't make that person feel seen in a way they hadn't consented to? He tried a sentence aloud, abandoned it, tried another. The mirror gave him nothing back except his own uncertain face, which was at least honest.

There was a second knock. "Soup's on. And Gavin, I checked the label like you said. You want the low-sodium one, it's in the pantry, but your grandmother bought that mushroom kind in 1997 and it's fine, so choose."

Gavin looked at the cans in the cabinet, at his phone with its eleven bullet points, at the door between him and lunch. He could keep rehearsing through the interminable afternoon his grandfather would otherwise fill with stories about the hardware store, or he could go out and eat soup with too much sodium in it and let the presentation arrive on Monday the way most true things arrived, slightly unrehearsed. He pocketed the phone, opened the door, and followed the smell of mushrooms down the hall. At the table he picked up his spoon, looked at the bowl, and said, "So, low sodium. Who came up with that, anyway?"

The door of the studio had a brass knocker shaped like a treble clef, which Henry thought was trying too hard. He had been taking cello lessons for six weeks, and every Thursday he arrived early and sat on the bench in the hallway, listening through the wall to the lesson before his, a girl working through some Brahms he couldn't name yet. His teacher, Ms. Ansel, believed in starting from sound rather than symbols, so for the first month he had only listened and hummed before she let him touch the instrument at all.

The trouble started with Dev, his best friend since seventh grade, who had come over on Tuesday with a bag of chips and an opinion. "You know it's pointless, right," Dev had said, feet on Henry's desk chair. "Gladwell's book, Outliers, 2008. The ten-thousand-hour rule. You're sixteen. You'd be like thirty before you were any good." Dev was reading economics blogs lately, having decided that stagflation was the most interesting thing that had ever happened to a country, and he delivered facts the way other people delivered insults, with relish and no malice.

"That's not what it says," Henry had said, though honestly he had only heard about the book secondhand, the way everyone had, the number floating around school like a rumor with a footnote. Ten thousand hours. He'd done the arithmetic in his head that night, lying awake, estimating: two hours a day, five years, or one hour a day for ten. Either way the number was a wall, and he was standing at the bottom of it holding a practice mute.

He had meant to ask Ms. Ansel directly, but Thursday came and she was in one of her moods where the metronome did all the talking. He was working on a shift from first to fourth position, and his hand kept arriving late and heavy, like a guest who hadn't recuperated from the trip before knocking. "Again," she said, and tapped, and he did it again, and again it was late. On the fifth try something happened that he couldn't have described: his elbow moved first, and the hand simply arrived where it needed to be, and the note bloomed instead of landing.

"There," she said, and stopped the metronome. "Do you know what you just did?"

"I got lucky."

"You let the wrong thing lead. You've been sending your fingers first, like they're the ones with the map." She wrote something in her notebook, which he'd never been allowed to see. "That took you forty minutes. Some people take a month, practicing an hour a day. Some take a week."

That night he did what he should have done weeks ago and looked it up himself, Dev's chips still half-finished on the desk. It took four searches before he found the actual claim and then the part after it: Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers had popularized the ten-thousand-hour rule, but Ericsson, whose research it came from, had later said that the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Henry read it twice, then a third time, feeling something between vindication and vertigo. The number wasn't a lie exactly, but it wasn't the whole thing either, the way a recipe that only listed cooking time and no ingredients wasn't quite a recipe.

He texted Dev a screenshot, then deleted the caption he'd drafted, which said told you, because it wasn't quite that simple either. Dev texted back a single word, "fair," and then, "still gonna be old though." Henry laughed at that alone in his room, which he recognized was the lowest form of laughter, but he took it.

The thing he couldn't resolve, walking to the bus stop with his cello case cutting into his shoulder, was what to do with both halves of it. Ten thousand hours was real enough as an idea, a way of saying that mastery was far away and not negotiable, and pretending otherwise was how people quit in month three. But quality was real too; his forty minutes that afternoon had moved him further than a week of noodling. Neither cancelled the other. He was left holding a number too big to think about comfortably and a principle too vague to hold onto, and the honest position, as far as he could find one, was that he'd practice like the quality mattered and accept that the hours would count themselves or not.

The putative ceiling, Dev would call it later, arguing over the school cafeteria's rectangular pizza, and Henry would let him have the word because it was a good one. "A putative ceiling," Dev said, pointing a fork at him, "can still be a real ceiling."

"Sure," Henry said. "But you're still thinking about economics and I'm thinking about my elbow."

On Thursday he got to the studio early again and sat on the bench, and through the wall the girl before him had moved on to something slower, a single held note that wavered and then steadied. He put his hands together on his knee, elbow out, fingers loose, and waited for the treble clef knocker to sound.

The walk-in door swung shut behind Oliver and the cold pressed against his neck like a hand. Saturday mornings he arrived at Rocco's before the delivery trucks, and Chef Deshi had decided that this month Oliver would learn what she called the whole arc: plan a week of meals, write one list, shop it once, cook in batches on Sunday. Oliver wanted this for reasons he hadn't said out loud. His mother had started working nights at the hospital, his father was gone until spring, and the refrigerator at home held mustard, half a lemon, and a science of takeout containers. Last week she had fallen asleep with her shoes on at the kitchen table, and Oliver had stood in the doorway holding a bowl of cereal he'd made her, unable to decide whether to wake her.

"Six dinners, two lunches," Chef said, slapping a clipboard down beside a crate of onions. "Braise one thing that improves overnight. Cook a grain that holds. Roast a tray that becomes three different plates." She demonstrated rather than lectured, and Oliver wrote in the margins of his list: chili, then chili over baked potatoes, then chili with cornbread. She watched him portion chicken thighs into labeled bags, and when his knife wandered crooked she adjusted his grip without comment, then quietly cut the last two breasts herself so he could catch up.

The week's plan needed a dessert, because Wednesday was his mother's birthday and she would be awake for it only between four and six in the afternoon. On his break he drove his own car, the old hatchback, to the restaurant's supplier and bought chocolate: two dark bars for the frosting he'd planned. He set the bars on the passenger seat, went back inside to carry in a produce order, and by the time he returned the car had been sitting in the sun for an hour. The wrappers were slack and warm, and when he peeled one back, the chocolate wore a dull grey film, streaky, white in places, like frost that had grown from the inside. He turned the bar under the fluorescent light of the kitchen doorway, transfixed by the pattern, and felt his whole birthday plan tilt.

Chef Deshi was in the office reconciling invoices when Oliver carried the bars in and laid them on the steel counter. She had seen a hundred teenagers panic over ruined ingredients, and she watched now as he hunched over the chocolate, running a thumbnail along a grey streak. He took out his phone, typed with his thumbs, frowned, typed again. "Fat bloom," he said at last, half to himself. "That dull grey or white streaky film. It's what happens to chocolate that wasn't tempered right, or that melted and reset." He looked up. "My car melted them. So they reset like this." She kept her face still, though she wanted to grin; the supplier stocked a lesser couverture and she'd suspected as much. "So what's your plan," she said, "now that your frosting is grey?"

He stood there a long moment. His first theory, that the bars were spoiled and had to be thrown out, no longer seemed tenable; the websites disagreed about that, and the chocolate smelled like chocolate. He wanted the etiology right before he decided anything, the way Chef talked about diagnosing a broken hollandaise before fixing it. Melted and reset. That was the key phrase. Whatever had gone wrong had happened in his car, in heat, and if heat had done it, then more heat might undo the shape of it, if not the streaks. "I can't frost a cake with it," he said slowly. "But if I melt it all the way into brownies, the streaks don't matter. Nobody sees the surface. It just becomes chocolate."

Chef Deshi nodded once and pulled a sheet pan from the rack. "Bake them here today, take them home Wednesday morning," she said. "And write this down in your plan, because this is the real lesson. A weekly plan isn't a promise the week can't break. It's a net." She measured sugar into a bowl for him, then set the eggs in warm water to take the chill off, small courtesies she performed for every cook and no one ever mentioned.

At home that Sunday, Oliver braised the chili, cooked a pot of barley, roasted squash and onions, and labeled everything with masking tape and a marker. His mother woke at three in the afternoon, padded into the kitchen, and stood in front of the open refrigerator without speaking. Shelf after shelf of containers, dated, stacked, deliberate. "You did all this," she said. He shrugged and told her about the chocolate, about the car and the grey streaks, and she laughed until she had to sit down on a stool.

On Wednesday he baked the brownies at four, while she showered for her night shift, and by the time she was dressed the kitchen smelled like the restaurant's. She took one bite with her coffee and closed her eyes. "Happy birthday to me," she said, and reached for a second piece before her coat was even on.

The community room at First Meridian sat behind the teller windows, past a corridor of gray carpet that smelled like the copier had ionized the air, sharp and faintly metallic. Carson had walked past it every Saturday for two years while depositing his paycheck from the garden center, and he had never once seen anyone use it. Plastic chairs stacked against the wall. A banner reading Financial Literacy For Every Age. Today the banner seemed like an omen, or at least a joke at his expense, because what he wanted from the room was a punk show.

The plan had come together at speed, the way his band's plans always did. Devin knew a guy with a PA system. Priya had promised to make flyers with a photocopier at the library, twenty-five cents a page, so the show could cost three dollars at the door and still break even. All they needed was a venue, and every church basement and VFW hall in town had said no to amplified music, which was how Carson found himself standing at the desk of Ms. Alvarez, who slid a pink folder across the counter and said, "Community room rental agreement. Two pages. Read it before you sign anything."

He read it standing up because the waiting chairs were bolted in a row facing the tellers like a jury. The first page was dense with language he half recognized from the terms and conditions he scrolled through on his phone, the ones he agreed to without looking. Lessee. Premises. Terms subject to change without notice. Then, halfway down the second page, a clause in bold: The lessee agrees to indemnify and hold harmless First Meridian Bank against any and all claims arising from the event.

Priya had come with him, ostensibly for the ride, actually because she didn't trust him to notice things. She read over his shoulder, her finger landing on the word. "Indemnify," she said. "What's indemnify mean? Because it sounds like they're about to indemnify us."

Ms. Alvarez, who had been watching with the patience of someone who had processed a thousand auto loans, leaned toward them. "To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts," she said. "Yours, or your guests'. It's written next to hold harmless, which means they can't be blamed for it either."

"So if somebody wipes out on the carpet," Priya said slowly, "we pay."

"Or your insurance does. Do you have insurance?"

"We have a drum kit," Carson said.

Ms. Alvarez did not laugh, but something moved behind her eyes that might have been laughter filed for later. She pointed at the signature block instead, and that was where the trouble actually started, because beneath the line marked Lessee was a second line marked Parent or Guardian, and beside it the word Consent in small capitals. Carson was sixteen. His signature, on its own, was decoration. The contract wanted his mother's.

He called her from the lobby, under a framed photograph of the bank's original 1911 building, an imposing pile of autochthonous limestone quarried, according to the brass plaque, three miles from where it now stood. He liked that, stone that had never left home, though he doubted it got much say in the matter. His mother picked up on the fourth ring.

"A show. At the bank." She said it flat, the way she said things when she was already three questions ahead of him. "How many people."

"Forty. Maybe fifty."

"In a room with a bank's property in it."

"We're moving the chairs out. There's a closet."

"Who pays if something breaks?"

He looked at the pink pages in his hand. There it was, the answer, in bold. "We do," he said. "That's the indemnify part. If anybody gets hurt, or anything gets damaged, it's on us, not them. I'd be signing that it's on us." He heard her breathing change on the other end, that shift from interrogation to deliberation, and he pushed, because the date was eleven days away and Devin had already told people. "It's three dollars a ticket. It's forty people in a carpeted room with a fire exit and a bank manager down the hall. It's the safest show anyone's ever thrown."

"There's no such thing as a safe show," his mother said. "There's a show you can afford to be wrong about."

He stood there holding the phone, the clause running through his head. He wanted to say that fifty kids in a supervised room with a signed agreement was nothing like the shows in parking lots that the town actually worried about, that a contract nobody read was more dangerous than one he had read twice. But he also couldn't shake the arithmetic underneath it: if it went wrong, wrong landed on his family, and he was asking her to carry that weight so he could play forty minutes of music. Both things were true. He didn't know which one counted more.

"Cap it at thirty," his mother said finally. "You count heads yourself, at the door. And the PA guy signs the form too, or there's no show. I'll come after my shift and sign the last line, and I'm going to read the whole thing first."

Priya was watching him from the row of chairs, and when he hung up she raised an eyebrow. Carson walked back to Ms. Alvarez, set the folder on the counter, and slid it toward her unopened.

"Can we get a second copy?" he said. "Two people have to read it before Friday."

The kitchen smelled of cinnamon and cheap red wine, and Jake stood over the cutting board with a knife he did not entirely trust. His grandmother had always made the charoset, spooning it out of a chipped bowl with the certainty of someone who had done it fifty times, and this year, with her hips new and her kitchen off limits, the spoon was his. His mother had handed him the recipe card at noon and said only, "You're leading tonight, so own all of it," and then she had gone to set the table, leaving him alone with two apples, a pile of walnuts, and the weight of the whole evening.

Leading the Seder was an idea he had volunteered for in August, when it had seemed abstract, something he could list on a college application in the fall, a thing adults said showed maturity. Now it was a table of eleven people arriving in two hours, his little cousins who would ask the Four Questions whether or not he remembered to invite them to, his uncle who corrected everyone's Hebrew, and his grandfather, who had led the meal for forty years and had handed it over with a shrug that Jake still could not read.

He chopped the apples into pieces as small as his patience allowed, then the walnuts, then dragged the knife through the mixture until it began to look like something, thick and lumpy and rust colored. His younger cousin Dani slid into the kitchen on socks and stood at his elbow, the way she always did, waiting to be given a job. "You can stir," he said, and pushed the bowl toward her, and she stirred with the seriousness of a surgeon.

"What is it?" she asked, dipping a finger toward the paste.

"Charoset," he said, and then found he had nothing after the name. He knew it went on the Seder plate, knew everyone took a scoop during the meal, knew his grandmother had made it every year of his life. He turned the fact of it over and found nothing inside. "It's sweet," he offered, which sounded like a review of a dessert rather than an answer.

Dani considered this. "Sweet stuff is usually, like, the good part of the story. The baby in the river. The parting of the sea."

He looked at the bowl. The mortar, his grandfather said from the doorway, where he had been standing long enough to have heard the whole exchange. "Charoset is the mortar. The enslaved Israelites used it to lay bricks, in Egypt." He said it the way he said the blessing over the first cup of wine, flat and certain, and then he came in and stole a walnut and left again, cane ticking against the tile.

Jake stood there with the spoon in his hand. Sweetness standing in for mortar. A dessert that was also a burden, meant to be tasted and remembered as work. It was the kind of doubling he was starting to notice everywhere, in the classes he had picked for the fall, in the arguments he had with his father about whether leaving home was a betrayal or an obligation. His instinct was to pick one reading and defend it, the way he defended anything, loudly, and he could feel the essay forming already, the clever take. But the charoset did not choose. It sat in the bowl being both things, and his grandfather had stated the fact and walked away without telling him which one to feel.

At the table, hours later, he got through the Four Questions, through the washing, through the breaking of the middle matzah, his voice steadier than he had expected in the warm noise of eleven people. When they reached the Seder plate he lifted the dish of charoset and hesitated, because he had planned something to say and suddenly it felt gratuitous, a performance of meaning rather than the meaning itself. Dani was watching him from across the table with her chin on her fists. He set the bowl down instead and said, "Everyone take some. Taste it." They did, the spoons clicking, his uncle nodding, his cousins grimacing at the wine. He held his own spoon in his mouth and let the sweetness sit there alongside everything else it stood for, and he did not explain it, and nobody asked him to.

After the meal, in the kitchen, his grandfather stopped on his way to the door. "Next year," the old man said, "double the walnuts."

The article was twelve lines long, in Portuguese, and Sydney had read it four times before her grandmother set a kitchen timer on the table between them. "Five minutes," Vovó said, tapping the timer's red face. "Then you tell me what it says. Out loud, in Portuguese, your own words. No reading to me like a robot."

Sydney had wanted this summer at her grandmother's house in Fall River for reasons she hadn't fully admitted even to herself: the good bread, the hydrangeas, the radio playing fado while Vovó cooked. What she had not wanted was the deal they'd struck before her parents' car pulled away, that she would spend forty minutes a day on Portuguese, her grandmother's language, the one Sydney had only ever absorbed in fragments at holidays. She wanted to know it properly before college, before it was too late to claim something that had always hovered at the edges of her family. But wanting and being able, she was learning, lived in different rooms of the same house.

Reading had gone well all month. She could work through a paragraph with a dictionary, silently, at her own pace. Yesterday she had even read a whole article about rising ferry fares and felt a small, private triumph. So this morning, when Vovó had slid the newspaper across the table, an item about a library losing its funding, Sydney had thought the task would be the same thing with a clock on it.

The timer ticked. She began, "O artigo fala sobre..." and then stopped. The library, she had. The funding, she had, sort of. What she did not have was the verb for what the town council had done, the word for "cuts," the way to say the library would close by autumn. She knew the facts of the article cold. What she couldn't do was say them. It was like reaching for a light switch in a familiar room and finding the wall smooth. "Eu não sei como dizer," she said finally, feeling her face go hot, and pushed the paper away.

"There," Vovó said, not unkindly. She poured more coffee, because she had noticed Sydney's cup was empty, and set it closer to the girl's hand. "Now you know exactly what to look up."

That night Sydney lay on the foldout couch cogitating on the strange satisfaction underneath her embarrassment. In her duffel bag was a book her aunt had given her, a linguistics text bought secondhand for a college course, and she got up and found it, angling the lamp so as not to wake the house. Flipping through, past diagrams and dense paragraphs, she stopped at a page with a heading that named what had happened to her at the kitchen table. Merrill Swain, the book said, had proposed the output hypothesis: that trying to speak or write a language makes learners notice gaps in what they know, which helps them learn. Sydney read the sentence twice. Reading, she had believed all month, was where learning happened. But the gaps had stayed invisible until she opened her mouth.

She tested it, because she distrusted anything that convenient. The next morning she asked Vovó for another article, and this time she didn't just read it first; she tried, out loud, alone in the bathroom mirror, to say what it was about before she looked anything up. The holes announced themselves immediately: "flood," gone; "volunteers," gone; "evacuate," gone, though she could have recognized all three on a page. Her nemesis, she decided, was not vocabulary but the difference between recognizing and producing, and it had been hiding behind her own competence the way a deleterious habit hides behind an otherwise good one, quiet until the moment it costs her something in front of someone.

By the fourth morning they had a routine. Sydney would read the article, attempt a summary aloud, fail in specific places, and then dig for exactly those words while Vovó washed dishes and pretended not to listen. On Friday the article was about a farmer's market expanding, and when the timer went off Sydney said, haltingly but completely, what it was about: the market, the new stalls, the Saturdays through October. Her grammar was crooked in at least two places and she could hear it, and let it stand, and finished anyway.

Vovó dried her hands and sat down across from her. She didn't correct anything. She looked at the newspaper, then at Sydney, and something in her face had gone soft and proud at once.

"Say it again," she said. "I want to hear it twice."

Eve had the application folded into the pocket of her swim shorts all morning, and by lunch she had unfolded it four times, smoothing the crease each time so the paper would not look handled. The interview at the coffee shop in town was Thursday at four. She had exactly one thing to put in the experience section, a junior-year group project on watersheds that had gone badly in a way that was partly her fault and partly everybody's, and she did not know how to tell it so it sounded like something learned rather than something survived.

At the day camp she was a junior counselor, unpaid, which was the whole problem. Her job was to stand at the shallow end of the pool and count heads, nine heads, over and over, while the real counselors ran games on the grass. She counted by sevens because it kept her attention from going soft. When a boy named Devon, the other junior counselor, tipped his whistle up to speak, she assumed he was going to ask her to trade stations.

"Four o'clock," he said. "That's a bad slot. Nobody's hiring at four." He was seventeen and had worked at a hardware store since March, which made him, in the economy of the pool deck, a man of the world. He sat down on the wet concrete with his clipboard as though settling in. "You know what they'll ask. Tell me about a time you had a conflict on a team."

"That's the question I'm afraid of," Eve said.

"You have to use STAR," Devon said. "Situation, Task, Action, Result. Every answer's got those four pieces." He tapped the clipboard in four places as he said it, like a drummer counting in. "Interviewers don't want how you felt. They want what you did."

She wanted to argue with that, because how she felt about the watershed project seemed like the only true part of it, but she also wanted the job, which paid real money for standing indoors near espresso instead of outdoors near chlorine. So that afternoon, during rest hour, she sat under the awning by the craft tables with a legal pad and tried to lay the project out in the four shapes Devon had tapped. Situation: five students, one semester, a model of the local watershed. Task: her task, which was the stream-flow data, and also, unofficially, keeping Marco from doing everything alone the night before it was due. She wrote those quickly. Action stalled her. She had not confronted anyone; she had stayed late and rechecked numbers nobody would read, an ascetic little penance that produced nothing. Result: a B-minus and Marco not speaking to her for a week.

From the picnic table across the yard, the crafts counselor, Ruth, watched the girl under the awning write, cross out, and write again. Ruth had seen the application go around the staff room; she knew about Thursday. She did not go over. In her experience advice given unasked hardened into resentment, and the girl seemed to be doing the harder thing anyway, which was testing her own story against a shape someone else had handed her. The legal pad filled. At one point the girl looked up at the lake, flat and silver at that hour, and then back down, and crossed out half a page.

Eve was working on the problem of honesty. The STAR shape wanted an ending where she had taken a clean action and gotten a clean result, and her real ending was murkier: she had said, finally, one true sentence to Marco in the parking lot, that she'd been afraid of making it worse so she'd made it worse by saying nothing, and he had shrugged, and they had not become friends again but had stopped being enemies, which was a result, she decided, even if it was a small and ductile one, bending under weight without quite breaking. What she could not decide was whether to include the fear. Devon would say no. But the interviewer was a person who had presumably once been eighteen and afraid, and Eve thought that a person who had been afraid might want to know whether a candidate could contextualize her own mistakes, could say where they came from, without drowning in them. She wrote both versions of the answer, the polished one and the true one, side by side.

On Thursday she wore her one blouse that was not a camp shirt and took the bus into town. The coffee shop smelled like scorched milk and lemon cleaner. The manager, a woman with a pen behind her ear, asked the question second, exactly as predicted, and Eve heard herself begin with the situation, the task, and then pause at the fork between her two versions, the legal pad pages standing invisibly side by side in the air. "The action I took was late," she said. "I said nothing for three weeks because I was afraid of the argument, and then I told him the truth in a parking lot. The result was we could work together again. It wasn't a fix. It was just better."

The manager wrote something. Outside the window, a man was hosing down the sidewalk, and the water ran along the curb toward a storm drain, which was, Eve realized, exactly what their model had been about. The manager looked up.

"Do you take your coffee with anything?"

The departures board kept flickering DELAYED beside the 6:40 to Porto, so Alexandre found a seat near the window wall, unfolded his mother's old laptop on his knees, and opened the project he was supposed to finish before Monday. Around him the terminal settled into its nighttime register: a janitor pushing a wide mop between the rows of bolted chairs, a sullen teenager two seats down with his hood up and his earbuds in, a family sleeping under airplane blankets as though the airport were a campsite they had chosen.

The project belonged to the summer course his geography teacher had pressed on him, a practicum in something called a geographic information system, which his teacher described as maps stacked like transparent sheets on a light table. Layer one was flood risk for the city of Coimbra, shaded in bands of blue. Layer two was housing stock, each block a small polygon. The assignment was to overlay them and name the neighbourhoods where the two layers agreed, where people lived on ground the water claimed.

Alexandre had grown up in one of those neighbourhoods, if the maps were right about it. The spring he was eleven, the Mondego had come up through the storm drains and taken the ground-floor flat where he and his mother lived, and afterward she had moved them uphill to a fourth-floor walkup above a hardware store, and she had said, at the time and often after, that they would never live on low ground again. He had chosen Coimbra on purpose. He wanted to see the flood map disagree with her, or agree with her, and he was honest enough with himself not to know which result he was hoping for.

He loaded the two layers and set them both visible. The housing polygons appeared where he expected, a dense grid on the flat eastern bank. Then the river arrived, and it arrived wrong. The blue channel of the Mondego cut straight through the middle of the city hall, a building Alexandre had stood in front of, a building that was on dry pavement a full kilometre from any water. He zoomed out, sure he had panned something sideways, but the river only lay there, patient and impossible, crossing the market square, forking around the university library.

"You look like a man watching a crime," said a voice. The woman in the next seat had a boarding pass for Lisbon tucked under her coffee cup and the particular posture of someone who flew twice a week and had stopped finding it interesting. She nodded at his screen. "That's a river in a strange place."

"It's in the middle of the city hall," Alexandre said. "I've been inside that building. There's no river in it."

She leaned over, and the screen's light caught her glasses. "I build these systems," she said. "For a utility company. And I will give you one hint and nothing else, because my son is your age and he learns nothing when I lecture." She tapped the corner of the screen, where the layers' properties sat in small grey text. "Look at what each layer says about its coordinate reference system. Compare them. That's the whole hint."

He opened the properties. The housing layer named one coordinate reference system; the flood layer named another, its coordinates recorded in a different way altogether. He sat with that for a moment, watching the maintenance trucks out on the tarmac, their beacon lights sweeping the wet asphalt. The layers were both describing the same city, the same ground, but each was describing it in its own terms, and the software had simply believed both of them at once and drawn the consequences. He found a tool in the menu, the word reproject sitting beside it, and applied it to the flood layer, telling it to match the housing layer's system.

The river moved. It slid half a kilometre north and settled into its true channel, and the whole map reorganised itself around that correction, the way a sentence changes when you finally hear which word was misplaced. And now the overlay told him something. The flood band reached across the eastern bank and covered, almost exactly, the grid of streets where he had lived until he was eleven. His mother's old flat sat inside the deepest blue. But the band also covered two blocks uphill from it, solid nineteenth-century buildings his mother had always called safe, and it left dry a low riverside stretch near the market that she refused even to walk through. Her instincts were a map drawn from one flood, one spring, one year, and the flood risk layer was drawn from many, and the two did not agree, and he could not yet say which one to trust about the years to come.

The woman had gone back to her book, but she looked over when he sat forward. "It lines up now," he said.

"Then you're the one in a hundred who reads the metadata," she said. "My colleagues, and I say this with love, are pragmatists. They want the map finished by Friday." She stood, gathered her coat, and paused with her boarding pass in hand. "The honest ones footnote what they're not sure of. Remember that when you publish something."

Alexandre dragged the two layers on and off, one over the other, watching the blue band and the housing grid coincide and separate. Somewhere behind him his flight number was called, a voice too calm for the word final, and he closed the laptop without saving and stood, and put it in his backpack, and got in line.

Alexis signed in at the folding table by the loading dock and wrote his hours on the sheet like a debt being paid. Forty service hours before November, his counselor had said, if he wanted the application to look like something. The warehouse smelled of cardboard and onions, and a woman in a hairnet handed him an apron too big for him.

"You're on the line," she said. "Gloves first."

He followed her past pallets of canned corn to a steel counter where a girl his age, Priya, was already ladling soup into trays. She showed him the portion line in one sentence, demonstrated once, and left him to it. Across the counter came a queue of people, mostly older men, some with shopping bags folded flat in their pockets the way you keep a receipt you might need.

A man with a windbreaker and a missing front tooth stopped at Alexis's station and did not move along.

"You're new," the man said. "I can tell. The new ones look at everybody's face. After a month you look at the bowl."

"I'm not looking at anything," Alexis said, and realized he had been looking at everything.

"Sure." The man took his tray, then tilted his chin at the far wall. "You read that poster yet? Back there, by the fire door."

Alexis hadn't. He ladled soup for three more people, scanning between them. The poster was faded, the color of weak tea, with a photograph of a warehouse not so different from this one and a paragraph of small print he could only half make out from the line.

"St. Mary's Food Bank," the man said, as if answering the question Alexis hadn't asked out loud. "Phoenix, Arizona. That was the first one anywhere. A man named John van Hengel started it." He paused to let a woman pass with her tray. "Nineteen sixty-seven."

"How do you know all that?" Alexis said.

"I read it every day for two years." The man tapped his temple. "When you stand in this line as much as I do, you memorize the wall."

Priya leaned over during a lull. "Ignore Mr. Dell. He's the most loquacious person in this county. He once explained the history of the paper bag to me while I was trying to work."

"The paper bag has a history," Mr. Dell said with dignity, and carried his tray to the tables.

The line thinned after seven, and the woman in the hairnet, whose name was Rosa, put Alexis on tray duty, clearing the long tables as men finished and drifted out. This was the part he had dreaded, the part he'd imagined would feel like charity, which in his mind rhymed with pity. He picked up Mr. Dell's empty tray and found the man still sitting, turning a paper cup in circles on the table.

"You want to argue," Mr. Dell said. "I can see it. You've got an argument in you like a stone in a shoe."

"I don't have an argument."

"You do. It's this: a food bank is a bandage, not a cure. Somebody should be fixing the reason there's a line at all, and handing out soup lets everybody feel good instead." He said it without heat, the way you recite something you've said many times, and Alexis felt caught, because that was close to the essay he'd been drafting in his head on the drive over, the one about systemic causes that he thought would impress an admissions reader.

"Something like that," Alexis admitted.

"Van Hengel, in Phoenix." Mr. Dell set the cup down. "You know what he did before any of this? He worked in a soup kitchen, and a woman told him she was dumpster diving behind grocery stores for food her kids could still eat. Perfectly good food, thrown out. So he went and asked the stores to give it to him instead, and he stored it, and other places sent people to him, and that became St. Mary's." He shrugged. "A bandage, maybe. But the first bandage is also the first person who looked."

Alexis stacked the cups. "That doesn't fix anything permanent."

"Neither does standing in line. But here's what I know that you don't. Some nights I don't eat, and I'm grateful there's a bowl anyway, and both of those things are true at the same time." He stood, buttoning the windbreaker with careful ceremony, as though it were a better coat. "You can hold both, if your hands are big enough. Took me forty years. You've got a head start."

Alexis carried the trays to the wash station, where Priya was already spraying them down, water running loud.

"You argued with him," she said. "Nobody argues with Mr. Dell. He wins."

"He didn't win." Alexis stacked the wet trays on the rack. "He just made it so I can't write my essay anymore."

"Your what?"

"It doesn't matter." But he was already rethinking it, the essay about systemic causes, which he now understood he had wanted to write more for how it sounded than for what it was. There was a worse thought underneath: that he had driven here to collect hours from people's hunger, and that fact would stay true no matter what he wrote, and that showing up anyway might still be better than not showing up, and that he couldn't yet say where the line fell between those two things. Both true at the same time. He tested the idea and it held, barely, like a shelf nailed at one end.

At nine, Rosa called last call, and the stragglers came through for bread and fruit. Mr. Dell was among them, and he took an apple and, for once, said nothing at all.

Near closing, Rosa found Alexis wiping the steel counter a second time, though it was already clean.

"You don't have to do that."

"I know," Alexis said. He wrung out the cloth and hung it on the rail. "Is he here every night?"

"Rain or shine. Why?"

Alexis looked down the empty line of tables, then at the poster by the fire door, small print and all. "Next week, when I come back, I want to read the whole thing."

The party was for Dana's seventeenth, and Dana's mother had put out a bowl of punch so large it suggested she expected the whole street. Camille stood near it with her phone in her pocket, not checking it, which took effort, because in her notes app was a video she had watched four times that week. A man in a blazer had stood in front of a whiteboard and said that seven percent of communication was words, thirty-eight percent was tone, and fifty-five percent was your face. Which meant, as far as Camille could tell, that what you actually said barely counted at all. She had an interview on Tuesday for the frame shop on Delancey, her first real interview, and she intended to walk in smiling.

"You look like you're planning something," Dana said, arriving with two cups of punch and giving her one.

"I'm rehearsing a face."

"That's the saddest sentence anyone has said to me all year."

Camille explained the video, gesturing at her own features as though they were a presentation. Words, seven percent. Tone, thirty-eight. Face, fifty-five. "So I'm just going to make eye contact and smile a lot and let the percentages do the work."

Dana's cousin Theo, who was nineteen and home from his first year at college, had drifted over during the explanation, eating chips with the patience of someone waiting for a bus. "Who did the study?" he asked.

"Some guy. Mehrabian, I think."

"Albert Mehrabian," Theo said. "We covered him in psych. Those numbers came from experiments about conveying feelings, and he said himself it doesn't apply to all communication."

Camille felt something in her plan lose structural integrity. "He said that? Where?"

"In basically every clarification anyone's ever asked him for. People quote the numbers like they're a law of physics. They were about feelings, not everything."

She took a long drink of punch to avoid answering immediately. She had spent three days not writing out answers to interview questions, on the theory that words were a rounding error, and now she was standing at a birthday party doing arithmetic in reverse. If the numbers only covered feelings, then the actual content of "why do you want this job" was back on her plate, unrefrigerated, going stale. She tried to ruminate on this quietly, but Dana's other friend Priya had arrived, and Priya worked at the coffee place and had opinions.

"Honestly the words are half of it," Priya said. "My manager rejected a girl because she said 'whatever' about the schedule."

"That's tone," Camille said.

"She said the word 'whatever,' in words."

Across the room, Dana's mother, Mrs. Okonjo, was lighting candles on a secondary cake, for the vegetarians, and calling out that anyone who wanted a job at her new location should talk to her before she got busy. This was directed at nobody and everybody. Camille's mother had mentioned, twice, that Mrs. Okonjo was hiring, in the tone mothers use for things they consider destiny.

Camille set down her cup. "Mrs. Okonjo, could I ask about the job?"

They sat at the far end of the table, between the vegans and the presents. Mrs. Okonjo asked the standard questions, and Camille answered them watching the woman's face, which was impossible to read, a smooth professional mask that gave back nothing, and Camille thought, not for the first time, that any statistic about faces fell apart against a face like this. She caught herself starting to smile her rehearsed smile and let it go. "I'm careful with detail," she said instead, and gave the example of the two weeks she'd spent reorganizing the art room supply closet by medium and then by color, which nobody had asked her to do.

"You did that voluntarily?"

"Our art teacher cried. She's not a detractor of mine, is what I'm saying."

Mrs. Okonjo laughed, a real one, briefly. "Tuesday, four o'clock. Bring the closet story."

On the walk home, Camille thought about what remained uncertain, which was most of it. She didn't know what the smile had contributed, or whether the closet story had carried the day, or whether Tuesday would need a different Camille entirely. She only knew that the words had mattered, that the face had probably mattered some, and that nobody had ever run an experiment on a frame shop on Delancey. She took out her phone, opened her notes, and typed "why do you want this job," then, after a pause, "in actual words."

She was still typing when the streetlight came on.

The cemetery gate was open, which surprised William, because in his mind it had always been chained. He carried the folded newspaper clipping about the debate tournament in his jacket pocket, three hundred miles away, two days before Eid, and he had said nothing to his grandmother yet. She walked ahead of him between the rows with a watering can she refused to let him carry, and when she reached the flat gray stone with his grandfather's name on it, she knelt and began pulling weeds with her bare hands, the way she did every Friday of Ramadan.

"Sit," she said, not looking up. "You came all this way to stand?"

He sat on the dry grass beside her and took out the clipping. He told her the format, that each debater had to argue both sides of a resolution, that his was whether an ancient religious rule still bound modern life, and that he'd chosen the Ramadan fast. He told her the trip fell squarely inside the month. Then he told her the part he'd been circling for a week: the assignment required him to argue from the text itself, and he didn't have the text. "You do, though," he said. "Dad says you used to read it to Grandpa."

She sat back on her heels. Her expression turned acerbic, the look she saved for cousins who praised store-bought roti. "So now you want the Quran for a trophy."

"For an argument," he said. "Which might be worse, I don't know."

She was quiet long enough that a grackle crossed the whole cemetery and landed on the stone beside them, unbothered. Then she recited, slowly, in the Arabic she'd memorized at fifty, and then gave him the English, because his Arabic had never gone past the alphabet. The verse from the second surah, Al-Baqarah. Fast the numbered days. But whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then the same number of other days.

He wrote it on the back of the clipping, hand shaking slightly, because he could already see the whole case built on it. "So the rule carries its own exception," he said. "The text anticipates travel. It's not a modern loophole someone carved into it."

"The word you're looking for," his grandmother said, "is rukhsa. But don't get clever with me. You are not ill."

He started to answer and stopped, because the honest answer was that he didn't know yet whether he was travelling in the sense the verse meant. A bus seat and a hotel and a podium three hundred miles from home. He thought of the debaters he'd watched online who valorized pure principle, the ones who treated any concession as corruption, and he understood suddenly that he did not want to be one of them, and that not wanting it was also a kind of position he'd have to defend.

Rahila watched her grandson scribbling on that flimsy paper, and she felt something she was too proud to call grief, so she called it weather. She wanted him to fast, that was the truth of it, and beneath that she wanted him to want to, and beneath that, in the place she kept her husband, she wanted the boy to sit at this stone in thirty years with someone who would ask him the same question. All afternoon she had been composing a lecture about duty and about how his grandfather had fasted through chemotherapy, days the verse would have excused, and she had decided against it, which cost her something. Instead she said the one thing she trusted to hold: "He made up his days in the winters. Short days. He liked that. He said God was generous with the arithmetic."

William laughed, and it felt wrong at a graveside and right anyway. He asked her whether an airplane and a hotel counted as a journey, and she said the verse didn't say airplane, it said journey, and that the debate, as far as she could see, was what a journey was. He saw the shape of it then, both sides of the resolution living inside one sentence, the exemption generous and the debt still real, days to be repaid, nothing simply erased.

"You'll decide when you're on the bus," she said, standing, brushing grass from her knees, taking back the watering can even though his hands were free. "Decide then, not now. Now you're just arguing."

They walked out through the gate together, and at the car she stopped him with a hand on his sleeve. "When you make up the days, if you make up the days, come here first. One of them, at least. Bring nothing. Just come."

He said he would. She held his eyes for a moment as if checking the promise for cracks, then got in and pulled the door shut, and the grackle, having heard everything, lifted off the stone and went wherever it goes.

Raphael spread his homework across his grandfather's kitchen table, which smelled faintly of cedar and decades of coffee. The problem was a polynomial, some expression in x with a coefficient he kept dropping, and beneath it the instruction: find the derivative, then locate the maximum. His grandfather, Louis, set down two mugs and looked at the page the way he looked at a faulty fence, with a patience that implied the fault was temporary.

"Exam in August," Raphael said. "Placement. If I do well I skip first-semester calculus." He did not add that Nadia had texted him at midnight, her message still glowing in his phone: "i know you said the summer was for your grandfather. i'm not asking you to come home early. i'm asking you to admit you're hiding." He had typed three replies and deleted each one, because each one was true in a way that made him flinch, and he had chosen instead to photograph the lake and send nothing.

Louis did not proselytize about work the way some grandparents did, but he held convictions about attention. He believed a boy could learn anything if he sat still long enough in the right room. He believed this room, facing the boreal treeline with its wall of black spruce, was the right one. He pulled a chair beside Raphael and read the problem over his shoulder without touching the paper.

"What is a derivative, to you?" Louis asked. "Before the rule."
