Daniel thought of the pyramids again, the way a wide base of young people meant a country would need schools, and a top-heavy shape meant nursing homes, and how neither reading told you when, only that the need was coming, a probability you could plan for but not schedule. He had been treating the whole subject as abstract, something for exams. It felt different sitting next to a man about to spend his savings. "Maybe," he said. "Or maybe you buy it and carry flood insurance and it never takes water in your lifetime. Both things are true. I can't tell you which one happens."

"You sound like your mother." Ray laughed, but he took out his phone and photographed the listing, zoomed in on the disclosure line. "I'm calling the insurance office Monday. Before I sign anything."

They climbed the last mile in easier conversation, about Daniel's roommate assignment and the hawk, which had come back and was riding the updraft above the ridge. At the trailhead Ray stopped by his truck and put a hand on Daniel's shoulder, brief, the way he did things.

"You still want to test out of that class?"

"I think I might actually take it," Daniel said. He slung his pack into the bed of the truck and got in, and Ray turned the key.

Charlotte found her father in the garage on the morning of graduation, hunched over the lawn mower with a socket wrench, though the lawn had already been cut twice that week. She stood in the doorway holding her cap, still flat in its packaging, and watched him loosen a bolt that did not need loosening.

"You're hiding," she said.

"I'm maintaining equipment." He set the wrench down and looked at her gown, which she had put on early because her mother wanted pictures before the heat arrived. "You could help me with this bolt."

She crouched beside him and held the nut steady while he turned. This was how they had always talked, side by side, hands busy, neither of them required to look at the other. He asked whether she had decided about the deferral yet, and she said no, and he said nothing, and she was grateful for the nothing.

The trouble was this: the university had offered her a place in the fall, and the wildlife center two towns over had offered her a paid internship for the same months, with housing above the raptor barn and a supervisor who had once let her transcribe a whole season of migration logs just because she asked. Her mother thought the internship was a detour dressed up as a calling. Her father thought whatever she thought, mostly, which was its own kind of pressure. Charlotte had spent two weeks making lists, and the lists had become two small saturnine piles on her desk, each one refusing to collapse into the other.

Her friend Priya arrived at noon with a garment steamer and a bag of bobby pins, having declared over text that Charlotte's household clearly could not be trusted with wrinkles. In the kitchen Priya steamed the gown while Charlotte's mother fanned the fabric with a cutting board, and for a while the room was just steam and laughter and the smell of the lemon cake cooling on the sill.

Charlotte said, mostly to the steam, "I keep feeling like it's a funeral for something."

"For what?"

"For being this. For this house, this kitchen. Everything I know how to be." She heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "Four years and then it's over, and they hand you a hat."

Priya lifted the gown off the hanger and held it up to the window light, checking her work. "You know what the ceremony's actually called," she said. "Commencement. It means beginning. That's why they used the word, because you begin a new status. Like being a bachelor or a master." She shook out a crease at the hem. "So it's not a funeral. It's a launch, technically."

"Technically," Charlotte said, but something in her chest rearranged itself slightly, the way furniture moves when you finally stop dragging it sideways.

At the school, under a sun that made the bleachers shimmer, Charlotte sat between Priya and a boy named Marcus who had cried at the winter concert and was now crying again, discreetly, into his sleeve. She passed him a tissue from the sleeve of her gown without looking, and he took it without looking, and that small machination of kindness passed between them the way such things do, unannounced. When the principal read her name, her mother's camera flash went off three times, too early, and her father stood up in the fifth row before anyone else in the row did, hands in his pockets, then out of them, then in again.

Afterward, in the parking lot, the deferral still undecided in her pocket like a stone, Charlotte found Priya by the chain-link fence. "Beginning a new status," Charlotte said. "Bachelor or master."

"Or intern," Priya said.

"Or intern." Charlotte turned her cap over in her hands, the tangle of the tassel catching the light. "I still don't know which one, though. That part they don't put in the word."

"They don't," Priya agreed. She took the bobby pins out of Charlotte's hair, one at a time, and dropped them into the cup of her palm. "You've got until Monday to call them. Come on, your mom's holding cake hostage until you get in the picture."

Charlotte followed her across the hot asphalt, cap in hand, and behind them the empty stadium doors swung slowly shut on their own.

Sophie spread the current map across the flat top of the cooler and weighted its corners with four shells, because the wind at Crane Beach had already flipped it twice. She had sprained her ankle two weeks earlier playing football, and the doctor had said three more days of resting it, so she sat with the leg stretched out and told herself the beach counted as recuperating as long as she did not walk on the sand. This was not entirely true. She had walked from the parking lot on it, and it ached now in a low, persistent way she preferred not to examine.

The map showed the North Atlantic in blues and oranges, arrows thickening along the eastern edge of the United States and swinging northeast toward Europe. Her brother Theo had brought it home from the planetarium where he worked weekends at the front desk, and he had told her one thing before handing it over: the test on Tuesday would ask her to explain how warm water carried north by the Gulf Stream keeps northern Europe milder than other places at the same latitude. That was the whole assignment. Sophie had said she understood. She had not understood, but she had wanted Theo to leave the room.

Marcus arrived at eleven, carrying a sandwich and his own copy of the map, which he had photocopied at the library without asking. He sat down beside her without commenting on the ankle, which Sophie appreciated, though she later told her mother he had been sympathetic about it. He had not said a word about it.

"Start at the beginning," Marcus said. "Pretend I'm the class."

"The current moves north along the coast," Sophie said, tracing the orange band with one finger. "Then it turns east. Warm water goes across to Europe, and Europe is warmer than it should be. Norway has ports that don't freeze." She stopped. "That last part I still need to check."

"You're reading it like a road," Marcus said. He tapped the legend in the corner, where speeds were printed beside the color scale. "How fast is it actually going? Theo told me yesterday."

Sophie looked at the numbers. "At its fastest, the surface speed reaches about 2.5 metres per second. It's one of the fastest ocean currents there is." She did the conversion in her head, slowly, because she was not quick at it and because she wanted Marcus to think she was. "That's roughly a brisk walking pace. The water is walking to Europe."

"That's slower than I imagined," Marcus said. "It always looked violent in pictures, all that turbid water churning at the shore, brown with sand. You'd think something that warms a whole continent would be racing."

They sat with that for a while. The tide came in over the flat where they had set up, and Sophie had to pull the map back and reweight it with the shells, and one shell rolled away into the foam and was gone. She thought about speed, about how something could be slow and still decisive. In ethics class they had spent two weeks on utilitarianism, the idea that you judge an act by what it produces for the greatest number, and she had written an essay defending it and then, the night before it was due, rewritten the conclusion to say she wasn't sure. Mr. Okafor had given her a B and written "good hesitation" in the margin. She had not decided whether that was praise.

"Here's my problem," she said. "I can say the warm water goes north and east. I can say the speed. But when I stand up Tuesday, someone will ask why the warm water goes where it goes, and I don't have that yet, and I don't think I'm supposed to have it yet."

"So say what you have," Marcus said. He opened his sandwich and did not offer her half, though Sophie would tell Theo afterward that he had. "Walk them through the map. Use the walking thing. People remember walking."

She practiced it twice, out loud, pointing at the orange band, saying the speed, saying one of the fastest ocean currents, saying that Norway lay at the same latitude as places far colder than Norway. The second time was better. The wind picked up and lifted one corner of the map, and she caught it against her chest, and the ink smudged a little against her wet sleeve.

Marcus packed up at one. Sophie stayed, because the tide was turning and she wanted to watch the water reverse itself across the flat, slow and gray and apparently indifferent to the fact that she could now, more or less, explain it. She folded the map along its worn creases and put it inside her jacket, against the side that was not sore.

"Tuesday," Marcus called from the top of the dune path. "Don't walk them into the deep end."

Sophie raised one hand without turning around. The water slid up over her footprints and erased them, and then it drew back, and then it came again.

The moving truck had left, and Noemie stood in the empty living room where the rectangles of unpainted wall marked where her mother's paintings had hung for eleven years. In four days she would start at Kingsbridge High, junior year, in a town whose name she had not known how to pronounce until the realtor corrected her twice. Her boxes were stacked in the new house already, but she had insisted on coming back once more, alone, on the bus, to walk the old rooms. What she wanted was simple and impossible: to be in two places at once, the way she had been all summer, half here and half already gone.

On Monday the school was louder than her old one, or maybe the same volume arranged differently, so that everything sounded like a language she could almost speak. In third period the teacher gave them a warm-up question, something about where they were from, and Noemie watched a boy named Deshawn answer for the whole class as if it were a game he had won before. When her turn came she said the name of her old town and felt it land in the room like a coin dropped on carpet, noticed by no one. She wrote it in her notebook instead, and under it she wrote the names of Priya and Kas, her two best friends, who had promised to call every Sunday and who had called twice.

Wednesday she ate lunch in the library because the cafeteria had a geography she could not read yet, every table a country with closed borders. The librarian, Ms. Okafor, did not try to talk to her, which Noemie appreciated, and instead slid the day's newspapers across the counter for anyone who wanted them. Noemie read them the way she read everything lately, hungrily and without direction, looking for a reason to feel the way she felt. On the second page she found it, not a reason exactly but a word.

The article said that in May 2023 the US Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, had issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States. She read the sentence three times. An advisory, she gathered, was not a law or a warning exactly, more like a formal way of saying pay attention. She had thought of epidemics as things that happened to bodies, fevers and coughs, and here was one that happened in the spaces between people. It destabilized something she had been telling herself, that what she was going through was private and therefore hers alone to endure. If it was an epidemic, then it was common, which should have been depressing and was, oddly, the opposite.

She copied the sentence into her notebook, and a boy at the next table leaned over. "Homework?" he asked. He had a laminated schedule sticking out of his back pocket and a way of sitting that suggested he had decided she was interesting before she had decided anything about him. His name, when he offered it, was Theo.

"No," she said. "It's real. The Surgeon General called it an epidemic. Loneliness. This May."

"Huh," Theo said. "So it's, like, official." He looked at the paper, then at her, and she could see him doing the same math she had done. "That's kind of terrible and kind of nice at the same time."

It was a better sentence than she could have made, and she wrote that down too, which made him laugh. They talked through the rest of lunch, not about loneliness but about the library's broken printer and the fact that the school's one good window faced the parking lot. Still, the fact sat under the conversation the way a table sits under a meal. She found she was doing something she recognized from her old friendships, testing him with small true statements to see which ones he would catch.

That night she lay on her mattress on the floor of the new room and thought about calling Priya. The problem was not the call itself but what it would mean, because Priya communicated in two registers, the affective one, all hearts and voice memos, and the analytical one, which Noemie's mother called arguing for sport and Priya called rigor. Noemie's own position had always floated between them, and lately she had been trying to pin it down. Was she lonely in the way the article meant, or was she just new, and were those different things? She honestly did not know, and she was tired of pretending the not-knowing was a failure.

She called Priya on Sunday, not the scheduled hour but eleven at night, when the wanting outweighed the pride. Priya answered on the second ring, voice thick with sleep, and did not say where have you been. "I read something," Noemie said. "The Surgeon General, in May, he put out an advisory saying loneliness and isolation are an epidemic in the US." There was a silence long enough that she checked the screen to see if the call had dropped.

"That's either devastating or the best news I've ever heard," Priya said, and laughed, and Noemie laughed, and then neither of them said anything for a while, but it was the good kind of nothing, the kind that used to fill the back of Priya's car on long drives. Eventually Priya said, "Kas says hi, by the way, she's asleep on my floor, she'll be furious she missed this." Noemie asked how furious, on a scale, and Priya said a nine, and Noemie said only a nine, and Priya said fine, a nine point five.

They talked until Noemie's phone was hot against her ear, about nothing that mattered and everything that did, and when Priya finally yawned herself off the line, Noemie did not hang up right away. She sat on the floor with the dead phone in her lap, looking at the window, where the streetlight made a small bright country of the sidewalk. Tomorrow she would find Theo at lunch, she thought, and sit where he could see her. She picked up her notebook and, under the sentence she had copied, drew a second rectangle beside the first, the way the unpainted walls had looked, and wrote in it: Day one was May something, or maybe it was today. Then she turned off the light and lay listening to the unfamiliar house settle, tick by tick, into its own slow rhythm, and somewhere down the hall, faint through the wall, she heard her mother turn over in her sleep.

Ms. Roque handed the quizzes back at the start of fourth period, moving down the rows with the unhurried air of someone who already knew how the afternoon would go. Peyton turned her paper over and saw the red circle first, then the score beside it: seventy-four. Beside question three, in red, Ms. Roque had written two words that Peyton read three times before they stopped looking like a mistake. "Endpoint?"

The problem had given a polynomial restricted to the closed interval from zero to four, and Peyton had done what she thought was the whole job. She had taken the derivative, set it equal to zero, solved for the critical point, and reported the maximum value there. It had felt complete, even elegant. Two marks were gone, and she did not understand why, and the not understanding sat in her chest like a swallowed stone through the rest of the explanation about tomorrow's homework.

At lunch she spread the quiz on the table in the corner of the cafeteria, the table where the overhead vents made a sound like distant surf. Dev sat down across from her with his tray and looked at the red circle without asking. He was choleric on the best of days, prone to slamming lockers when the vending machine ate his dollar, but with math he went quiet and patient, as if the subject demanded a version of himself he kept folded away.

"I got the critical point right," Peyton said. "It's in the interval. It's a maximum. I even did the second derivative to check."

"Then why'd she take off two?"

"Endpoint," Peyton said, reading the word aloud again. "That's all she wrote."

Dev leaned over the page. His finger traced the interval along the top of the graph she'd sketched, from zero to four, then tapped the right side of it. "What's the function doing all the way over here?"

Peyton looked. At the critical point, x equals one, the curve crested and turned over; she had drawn that part carefully, the little hill she was proudest of. But the interval kept going after that, and on the right side the graph climbed again, slowly at first, then steeper, and at x equals four it was higher than the hill. The y-value at the endpoint beat the y-value at the critical point. She had found the top of the hill and never looked at the edge of the world.

"It's bigger at the end," she said slowly. "The function's largest value is at four, and the derivative there isn't zero. It's not even defined as zero, it's just the edge."

"So you have to check the endpoints too," Dev said. "Both ends."

Peyton pulled out her notebook and wrote it out plainly, the way she would want it explained to her if she knew nothing: on a closed interval, the largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative is not zero, so the endpoints must be checked as well. She underlined the last clause twice. It was not a hard idea now that she had it; that was the part that stung. It was the kind of idea that hid in the gap between doing the procedure and asking what the question actually wanted.

She thought about that gap on her walk to the library after last period, past the athletic fields where the practice nets hung loose and the wind made them undulate like something breathing. There was a way of doing school where you followed the steps and trusted them, and there was a way where you kept asking what else the situation could be. She had spent most of seventeen years in the first way, and it had mostly worked, and now she could see that the second way was not a betrayal of the first but a continuation of it. The derivative was still right. The critical point was still real. She had just stopped too soon, and stopping too soon looked exactly like finishing until something made you look again.

In the library she redid the entire quiz from memory, both problem threes and both problem fours, checking every endpoint both times. On the second one the critical point did win, and she wrote that down too, because the point was not that endpoints always won. The point was that you had to look. She copied the corrected work onto a fresh sheet, folded it once, and left it in Ms. Roque's mailbox in the math office with a sticky note on top.

When she got home there was an email waiting, four sentences long. Ms. Roque said the correction was accurate and the note was well put, and that if Peyton wanted, she could stop by Thursday to talk about the bonus problem on the next test, the one nobody ever attempts. Peyton read it twice, then opened her textbook to the section on optimization and put a thin pencil line under the first sentence of the first example.

"Closed interval," she said out loud, to the empty room, and turned the page.

The laptop lab at Camp Whitmore smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Ashley had claimed the corner terminal on the first day precisely because its screen had a dead pixel she could pretend was a period at the end of every sentence. She liked the idea of a machine that punctuated itself. For six days she had been building a Book class in Java, private fields buried inside it like seeds in a packet, getter methods the only doors in. Mr. Okafor, the taciturn instructor who answered most questions by pointing at the Java documentation and walking away, had finally given them the last assignment of the session: write a JUnit test, make it pass, and demo it Friday morning. Ashley wanted the demo. She had not yet wanted anything at this camp with her whole chest, and the wanting itself felt new, like a muscle she had only now found a use for.

Her Book class was finished, or nearly. She had made the title and author fields private, written getTitle and getAuthor, and stared for a long time at the constructor, wondering whether it was strange to feel protective of data nobody else wanted. Her mother, a connoisseur of closed doors and locked cabinets, would have approved of privacy as a design principle. Ashley had inherited the instinct but not the temperament for it; she wanted to hide things and then immediately show them to someone, which was, she supposed, what a getter was for.

The test she wrote was simple. She made a Book with the title "Salt" and asserted that getTitle returned "Salt". She ran it. Red. Failure. She read the message twice, and it was wrong in a way she could not immediately name: it said the test expected something she had never typed. "That's not what I expected," she said to the empty terminal beside her. "I expected the other thing. Or did I?" She had a brief, vertiginous feeling that the machine knew something about her intentions that she didn't.

Across the lab, Marcus was having a louder version of her morning. He had been at the camp two weeks, sent by parents who seemed to believe that immersion would inure him to computers the way swimming lessons inure a child to water, an assumption Marcus had quietly resented until this week, when resentment turned, without ceremony, into interest. He had built his Book class following Ashley's example, because she was the only one who explained things without sighing. Now his test was failing and the message was lying to him, or so he believed. "It says it expected forty-eight," he told the room. "I never said forty-eight. My book has three hundred pages. Why is it telling me it expected forty-eight?" He said it again, quieter, as if the number might behave differently at a lower volume.

Ashley came and stood behind his chair, and this is where their two mornings met. She looked at his assertion, then at the red bar, then at his assertion again. "Flip them," she said. "Try putting the expected value first and the actual second. assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second." Marcus looked at her as though she had told him the vending machine accepted leaves as currency. "It matters which side?" "I think the message reads like the first argument is what you wanted," she said, "and the second is what you got. Mine was backwards too. It told me it expected the wrong thing and I believed it, because I assumed the machine was reporting my intent instead of my argument order."

He swapped them and ran the test again, and the failure message transformed into something legible, an accusation he could actually check against his code. He found the bug in his constructor in under a minute, a misspelled field assignment, and the bar went green so suddenly that both of them flinched. "So the test wasn't wrong," Marcus said. "I was reading the message like it was about me. Like it knew what I meant." "It doesn't know what you meant," Ashley said. "It only knows what you typed." She liked the sentence and distrusted it at the same time, because there was a version of it that applied to people too, and she wasn't sure that version was true. People sometimes received what you meant instead of what you said. Sometimes the order of things mattered and sometimes the order was a disguise. She filed the question away unanswered.

At the Friday demo, Mr. Okafor called names alphabetically, and Ashley was first, which she had not planned for. She stood at the front terminal, opened her test file, and then did something she had decided on only the night before. She ran the version with the arguments reversed, let the confusing failure fill the screen, and asked the room, "What does this message actually say, and who is it saying it about?" A girl in the second row said it was the computer's mistake. A boy said the class was broken. Ashley flipped the arguments and ran it green. "Same class," she said. "Same test. Different order." She did not say more than that, and she caught Mr. Okafor, near the door, almost nodding.

Marcus went third, and here was the twist he had prepared without telling her: his demo used her example, the flipped arguments, the red bar, the green bar, and then he kept going. He had written a second test, one where the expected and actual values were equal no matter the order, and he ran it flipped on purpose. Green. "If the values match, the order doesn't show," he said. "So you can pass a test and still have it written wrong." He looked at Ashley when he said it. She felt something turn over in her, half pride and half vertigo, the feeling of watching her own discovery be handed forward and come back larger than she'd left it, wearing someone else's jacket.

After the demos, they walked down to the lake with the dying afternoon light making the water look like a screen someone had dimmed. Ashley skipped a stone, and it went twice. "Do you think Okafor knew?" Marcus asked. "Knew what?" "That we'd figure out the argument order ourselves. Or that one of us would figure it and the other would make it into something bigger." Ashley skipped a second stone and it went four times, and she watched the rings cross each other before she answered. "I don't know," she said. "But here's what I keep wondering. When the message said expected forty-eight, it wasn't lying. It was telling the truth about the wrong question." She turned the next stone over in her hand. Marcus said, "Then what's the right question?" She drew her arm back.

The band room smelled like cork grease and old carpet, and Nevaeh had been alone in it for forty minutes, failing at the same sixteen bars. The solo in the Holst suite was supposed to flutter, all sixteenth notes in the upper register of her oboe, and every time she pushed the tempo her tongue tangled and her fingers arrived late, as if they were getting their instructions from somewhere far away.

Marcus came in for his trumpet, saw her red-faced over the reed, and dropped into the chair beside her. "You're rushing the hard part," he said. "Everybody does. My teacher says don't pathologize it, it's just hands being slower than ambition." He pulled her metronome across the stand and dialed it down until the numbers stopped somewhere near the bottom.

"Sixty," he said, tapping the casing. "That means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second."

She had assumed practice meant playing it correctly at performance speed, over and over, until correctness took. That was her mother's philosophy, applied to piano at age eight and chemistry now: repetition at full difficulty builds character. Marcus believed the opposite, that you earned speed the way you earned trust, in small, boring increments, starting from wherever you actually were. She had always thought his way sounded like an excuse for going slow. Now she set her lips to the reed and played the passage with one note per tick, and it was so slow it embarrassed her, every sixteenth note landing on a second like a dropped coin.

But nothing tangled. The fingering that had been impossible was merely easy, and that difference felt like a trick being played on her. She raised the tempo by eights, and at seventy-two her tongue slipped on the turn, so she went back down, and the little weight on top of the metronome swung left and right through the silence like a tiny metronome of its own. Through the high windows the late light came down in a diaphanous column, catching the dust the percussive chaos of fourth period had left in the air.

"You know what my grandma says," Marcus said, feet up on a chair. "Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. Her whole generation is built on some aphorism like that." Nevaeh rolled her eyes at him, but quietly, because the saying had just proved itself on her own reed, and it was annoying when wisdom arrived in a form you could get embroidered on a pillow.

By the time the custodian's cart squeaked past in the hallway, she could play the passage cleanly at ninety-two, still short of the printed one hundred twelve, and she understood something she could not yet say in a sentence. Her mother's way was not wrong; the piece did demand eventual speed, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of cowardice. But speed was a result, not a method, and treating a method like a result was why she had spent three nights in a row quitting early and calling herself talentless. She could hold both ideas now without either one cancelling the other, though she still wasn't sure what to do on the days when slow practice stopped feeling like patience and started feeling like defeat. That part she would have to find out the same way she had found this out, one second at a time.

She packed the oboe, swabbing the bore, easing the reed into its little plastic coffin. At the door she paused, then went back, set the metronome to sixty, and played the sixteen bars once more, slow and perfect, the tick and the notes locking together like a latch.

"One beat per second," she said to Marcus, and turned out the lights.

The rain had been going since noon, and Jade had claimed the window table at her grandfather's house with her laptop, a mug of tea she wasn't drinking, and an assignment that refused to pass. The task looked simple on paper: given a sorted list of ten thousand student ID numbers, write a program that finds a target quickly. Her program worked. It was just slow, and the autograder, in its flat digital voice, kept telling her so. She had written a loop that walked the list from the front, checking each number against the target, and somewhere around the nine hundredth failed test she pushed the laptop away hard enough that the tea shivered.

Her grandfather came in carrying a phone directory, an actual paper one, thick as a paving stone and a decade out of date. "You look disaffected," he said, setting it beside her. "Worse than the time the dishwasher broke."

"It's my code. It checks every single number until it finds the right one." She pulled the laptop back. "Ten thousand numbers, one at a time."

"Find Kowalski," he said, tapping the directory. "Go on. Show me how your program would do it."

She felt the trap but walked into it anyway, flipping pages one by one from the K's, and he watched with an expression of theatrical grief, the way he watched people butter bread wrong. Four pages in she stopped, because her hands already knew a better way, the way everyone's hands did, and she flipped instead to the middle of the K section. Kessler. Kowalski had to be after that, so she split what remained, then split it again, and her finger landed on the name in four moves. She sat back. "That's it. That's the whole thing. You go to the middle, and the sort tells you which half to throw away."

"Throw away half the book every time," her grandfather said, counting on his fingers. "Ten thousand down to five thousand, five thousand down to twenty five hundred." He got to eleven fingers' worth before giving up. "That's very tidy. Write it before you lose it."

She externalized it the only way she trusted, narrating aloud while she typed: the list had to be sorted, or the middle told you nothing; each comparison cut the search space in half, so ten thousand numbers took about thirteen steps instead of ten thousand; a linear search never knew more than it had already seen, but this one learned from every guess. Her grandfather kept handing her objections like a lawyer, what if the target wasn't there at all, what if the list had duplicates, and each one sent her back to the keyboard, which was, she had to admit, more useful than the autograder's silence.

It was while she was fixing the edge case for an empty list that she thought of Marcus, at coding club, the week before. He'd been rebuilding the roster project and had changed the way a student's name was stored inside his class, some internal detail, and Jade had braced for everything to break, because in her experience everything always broke. Nothing broke. The roster still compiled, the buttons still worked, and when she'd demanded to know why, Marcus had shrugged and said one word, "Encapsulation," and then, because she'd kept staring at him, he'd pointed at the class and said the data was hidden behind methods, so the rest of the code used the object without depending on how it stored anything. She'd felt stupid for not knowing the word, and had been quietly disaffected about it ever since, skipping the last two club meetings.

Now, with her grandfather humming over the directory, she saw that the two ideas were cousins, though she couldn't have said exactly how. The sorted list kept a promise about itself, and the class kept a promise about itself, and both promises let you stop caring about the parts you couldn't see. Grandpa didn't need to know the directory's printing history to find Kowalski, and the club's buttons didn't need to know Marcus's internal arrangements to display a name. She wasn't sure the analogy held all the way down, whether hiding information was really the same as ordering it, and she wrote a question to herself in the margin of her notebook rather than pretending she'd settled it. Her whole ontology of the assignment had shifted anyway: the problem wasn't ten thousand numbers, it was that she'd been treating a sorted list like a stranger's messy drawer.

She ran the tests. All twelve passed, and the autograder printed a runtime she had to read twice, small enough to look like a typo. Her grandfather was still at the window table, flipping through the directory for no reason she could determine, apparently reading the plumber ads for pleasure.

"Grandpa. Ten thousand numbers. Thirteen guesses."

"Four for Kowalski," he said, not looking up. "My method's better."

The note was still on the refrigerator when Samuel came downstairs, his mother's slanted handwriting reminding him that the workshop at the community center started at nine the next morning. He had agreed to run it three weeks ago, mostly because Dara, who was supposed to co-teach, had looked at him across the gymnasium with an expression that made refusal feel like a small betrayal. Then Dara's family moved to Ohio, and the whole thing, consent, contraception, where to get tested at the clinic on Marsh Street, was his alone.

He spread the pamphlets across the kitchen table. The clinic had sent a box of them, along with a list of talking points somebody had clearly written in an office far from any actual teenager. Samuel read the first one aloud to the empty room and heard how it sounded, like a lawyer reading a warranty. He thought of Mr. Okonkwo's health class last spring, the day the unit on relationships had been reduced to a photocopied list of refusals, and how Samuel, penurious in his willingness to volunteer, had raised his hand for anything that got him out of sitting still. That was how the community center had gotten his name in the first place, he realized; he had burnished a small favor into a reputation he now had to live up to.

The screen door banged and his mother came in with a paper bag from the pharmacy, the kind they gave out with a flu shot. She set it on the counter and rubbed her arm. "They did my blood pressure while I waited," she said. "One twenty-five over seventy-eight. The pharmacist circled something on the sheet and told me to bring it to Dr. Patel."

Samuel pulled the sheet toward him. Above the reading there was a small chart, categories printed in gray columns. He found the row that matched: systolic 120 to 129, diastolic below 80. "It says that's called elevated," he said. "One twenty-five over seventy-eight is systolic in that range, and the seventy-eight is below eighty, so it fits." His mother stood very still, holding a jar of coffee, and he watched her work through it the way he watched people work through most unwelcome information, first the numbers, then the word.

"So not high," she said. "Elevated."

"Not high. Elevated," he said, and pushed the sheet back toward her, because it was hers.

She carried her coffee into the living room, and Samuel sat back down at the table with the pamphlets and felt something shift, small but definite, like a door eased open on a stiff hinge. He had been planning, all evening, to lead with the list. Definitions, clinic hours, the address of Marsh Street. Now he understood that a list assumed the listener already wanted the information, and his mother standing at the counter had taught him otherwise in under a minute. People received news about their own bodies the way she had, carefully, with one hand still on the coffee jar. Whatever he said tomorrow had to make room for that.

He tried it out on his brother, who was twelve and willing to be bribed with the last of the ice cream. "If someone says yes to something on Monday," Samuel asked, "does that mean they've said yes to it on Friday?" His brother considered the spoon. "No, because Monday-you and Friday-you aren't the same person." Samuel wrote that down. It was better than anything in the pamphlet. They moved on to contraception, and his brother asked questions in the flat, unembarrassed voice of someone doing math homework, and Samuel answered them the way he wished someone had answered his, without the hermeneutics of a classroom, the parsing of what the teacher really meant, the fear that asking would be its own confession.

He thought again about the spring, about the day Mr. Okonkwo had said, in front of everyone, that the clinic unit would be skipped for time. Samuel had accepted that, had even been relieved. He changed his mind about it now, sitting at the table with the ice cream carton between him and his brother. It was not relief he had felt; it was the quiet pleasure of not having to know things that were already true about him and about half the room.

At ten his mother came back for water and stood behind him, reading over his shoulder. "You're going to tell them about the clinic on Marsh Street?" He said he was, that it was walk-in, that the visit cost nothing. "And about consent," she said. "The real version, not the version they gave us in 1994."

"The real version," Samuel said. "Which is that it changes, and it has to be asked again, and asking doesn't ruin anything."

She put her hand on his notes, not taking them, just resting it there over the words. His brother, reading a comic at the end of the table, said without looking up, "One twenty-five over seventy-eight. Elevated."

His mother laughed, short and surprised, and Samuel capped his pen.

The ice cream shop had a hand-lettered sign that said two scoops for the price of one on Thursdays, which was how Alyssa ended up on a first date that doubled, technically, as a discount. She had suggested Thursday herself, in a text she rewrote three times before sending, and now she sat at a wobbly table by the window watching the door and pretending to study the flavor board as though she might still change her order.

Marcus arrived four minutes late, holding the door for a stroller and then for a woman who wasn't going anywhere near the door, which made her like him and also made her nervous, because a person that courteous could not possibly be comfortable with the silence she was already planning to fill badly. He ordered cardamom pistachio. She ordered vanilla, then worried that vanilla made her sound like an ascetic, a person who had renounced pleasure entirely, and added rainbow sprinkles with the defiant air of someone making a point.

"You went simple," he said, sliding into the chair across from her. "Respect."

"I contain multitudes," she said, and he laughed, an actual laugh, not the polite exhale she'd been braced for.

The trouble was that she had prepared for this date the way she prepared for exams, which was to say she had researched it. Her sister had left a psychology textbook behind when she moved out, and Alyssa, unable to sleep the night before, had read a chapter on conversation while eating toast at one in the morning. One study had snagged in her mind. It was from 2018, by Erica Boothby and colleagues, and it had found something the researchers called a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. She'd read the sentence twice and felt briefly, unreasonably consoled, as if a fact could be carried into battle.

It could not, it turned out, be carried into battle, because halfway through her second scoop she knocked over the napkin dispenser, and while gathering napkins off the floor she said "flaccid" when she meant "flat," describing a book she'd read, and Marcus said "flaccid?" in a tone she spent the next several minutes trying to decode. He was cerebral, that much was clear; he'd brought up a documentary about Antarctic drilling and used the word "solvent" correctly. She kept up. She thought she kept up. She had no evidence either way, which was the entire problem.

"So this was fun," Marcus said when they were scraping the bottoms of their cups, and she heard the word "fun" as a formality, the verbal equivalent of a handshake. He paid for both of them despite her reaching for her wallet, and then he stood there outside the shop with his hands in his pockets, rocking slightly on his heels, and said, "Okay. Well. See you, maybe?"

"Maybe," she said, and watched him walk toward the bus stop without looking back, which she took as a verdict.

Walking home, she began the autopsy. There was the napkin disaster. There was the moment he'd mentioned a band and she'd said she'd "heard of them" in a voice that implied she had heard of them the way one hears of Luxembourg. There was the long pause after she'd asked about his brothers and he'd said it was complicated. She replayed each one, trying to suture the evening back together into something she could evaluate, and every seam she closed made the whole thing look worse. He hated it. Obviously. He said "maybe." People who liked things said things more definite than "maybe."

Then the fact from the textbook surfaced again, unhelpfully, like a lifeguard arriving after the drowning. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them. Usually. She stood on the curb outside the dollar store and had it out with herself. One voice said: you have direct evidence, Alyssa, you were there, you experienced every limp laugh in real time. The other voice said: you experienced yourself, not him. His experience happened inside his head, where you have never once been, and a study that went and looked inside people's heads found that the person doing the judging tends to guess low.

Both voices were hers, which was the annoying part. She could not dismiss either one. The evidence of her own memory said the date went badly; the evidence of the research said her memory was probably a biased witness. Somewhere between the two, a position assembled itself: she did not know how it went. She could not know, tonight, from here. What she could do was act as if the gap were real and see what happened, which felt less like confidence than like running an experiment on herself.

She took out her phone and typed, deleted, and typed again. "I had a good time. The flaccid thing will haunt me forever but the ice cream was solid." She sent it before the first voice could file an objection, then put the phone face-down in her jacket pocket and walked the last three blocks at a pace that pretended not to care.

On her street, half a block from home, the phone buzzed. She stood under the streetlight to read it. "I actually laughed so hard at flaccid that I almost dropped my cup. Also I got the wrong bus because I wasn't paying attention. Do you want to get ice cream again, or like, actual food?"

Alyssa read it twice. She looked up the dark street, then back down at the screen, and started typing, "actual food," with one thumb, while a moth circled the light above her head in patient, idiotic loops.

The cuff hissed and went slack, and Sienna read the little column of mercury the way the manual had taught her, following the needle with her eyes while she let the air out slow. One twenty-four over eighty-two. She wrote it on the back of a receipt and looked at her father, who was sitting at the kitchen table with his sleeve rolled up and his arm still resting on the paperback he'd used as a heart-level prop.

"That's better than Tuesday," she said.

"Tuesday I'd eaten the salami," he said, as though that settled it. He was an unrepentant, almost epicurean believer in cured meat, in olive oil that cost more than books, in salt the way some people believed in weather. Her mother, whose milieu was the farmers' market and the walking group that met Saturdays at the reservoir, kept trying to reform him from the other direction, and Sienna had begun to notice that dinner at their house was less a meal than a negotiation between two philosophies of the body.

The assignment was due Friday: take a real reading, interpret it, and explain in a page how diet and exercise change the numbers. She understood the mechanics well enough now, how the top number caught the heart pushing and the bottom number caught the pause between beats, how the readings only meant anything stacked against each other, one day against the next. What she didn't understand yet, and what she kept circling, was whether the numbers were the health or only its shadow. Her father could be one twenty-four over eighty-two and feel immortal, or, she supposed, be something enviable on paper and feel like ash.

She'd been thinking about that since Dr. Okafor's office in March, the checkup her mother had scheduled before track season. The nurse had gone down her list, height, weight, shots, and then said, almost in passing, "And we'll do an HIV test today, if that's all right with you." Sienna had blinked at her. She hadn't asked for one. She hadn't done anything, she'd wanted to say, and then felt stupid even thinking it, because that wasn't how anything worked and she knew it. "It's routine," the nurse said. "The CDC recommends everyone ages thirteen to sixty-four get tested at least once as part of routine health care. You're seventeen, so here we are." It had taken four days for the negative result to appear in the patient portal, and Sienna had checked it the way she checked her grades, refreshed and refreshed, though she'd already known she was fine. She just hadn't known knowing would matter to her until she had to wait.

What had struck her, sitting in the paper gown with her socks still on, was that word, routine. The test wasn't a punishment or an accusation. It was like checking your blood pressure, a thing the body got asked to account for whether or not it felt sick. She'd assumed her whole life that tests came after suspicion, and here was a whole system that ran on looking before anything was wrong. She still didn't know which way of thinking she trusted more. The looking-before philosophy felt cold, in a way, as if it wanted to desiccate her into data points, numbers with no flavor left in them. But the other way, waiting until you felt bad, had let too many people she'd read about walk around for years carrying something quiet.

Now, in the kitchen, she took her father's reading again the way the manual suggested, two readings a minute apart, and averaged them. One twenty-two over eighty. "The walking is doing something," she said. "You walked with Mom's group Sunday and Tuesday."

"Forty minutes, downhill both ways, somehow," he said. "Does your page get to mention that your subject is a specimen of one?"

That was the other thing she'd been turning over. Everything in her textbook spoke in populations, risk falling by tidy fractions across thousands of people, and it was all true and none of it was about her father specifically, whose salami consumption was, statistically speaking, its own event. She could write that exercise lowers it and salt raises it and both statements would be true and neither would promise him anything. She was honest enough with herself to put that in the paper, a paragraph saying that the numbers gave you a direction, not a guarantee, and that she found the direction worth following anyway, which was a belief more than a finding.

She rolled the cuff back onto its plastic holder and set it on the table between the salt cellar and the bowl of blood oranges. Her father reached for an orange instead of the salami, which she chose to notice and chose not to mention. "Same time Thursday?" he said, peeling it in one long spiral that held together all the way down. "Your subject requests to be measured before dinner, not after."

The cuff hissed and tightened around Mr. Okafor's arm until the needle on the gauge trembled and settled, and Aiden watched it the way he was learning to watch it, not for a number but for the moment the sound returned. He let the pressure fall slowly through the stethoscope, listening for the first soft knock of the pulse and then the last one. "One twenty-eight over eighty-two," he said, and Mr. Okafor, who ran the waterfront and taught the first-aid elective, raised an eyebrow as if to ask whether that meant anything. Aiden swallowed. "The first number's when your heart contracts. The second's when it rests. High over time, and your arteries take a beating. Salt pushes it up. Regular exercise pulls it down, and so does losing a little weight, but that takes months, not a weekend." It was the longest sentence Aiden had said aloud all summer, and Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard and told him he'd pass the practical if he stopped gripping the bulb like it owed him money.

Aiden had come to Camp Wren as a counselor-in-training mostly because his mother thought it would burnish his college applications, a word she used so often it had begun to sound like furniture. He privately considered the whole CIT wardrobe an affectation, the whistle and the lanyard and the laminated name tag, and he wore them with the reluctant precision of someone playing a part he hadn't auditioned for. Still, the first-aid training was real. Numbers either added up or they didn't, and the body was a machine with readable gauges, and that steadied him in a way that canoe instruction and camp songs did not.

On Thursday evening Priya found him at the picnic tables behind the infirmary, where he was practicing with the cuff on his own arm. She sat down across from him and folded her hands and did not look insouciant the way she usually did, chin up, ready to make a joke of anything. She looked like someone doing arithmetic she didn't want to finish. "Something happened with Josh on the lake trip," she said quietly. "The condom broke. Two nights ago. I've been trying to figure out what to do since then and everyone here would know by breakfast."

"Two nights," Aiden repeated. The number sat in his chest like a stone, because the first-aid manual had taught him that with almost everything, minutes mattered, and he had assumed this would be the same or worse. "Is there a pharmacy in Millbrook?" Millbrook was the town seven miles down the county road, and the camp van went only on Saturdays.

"There's one, I looked it up. But I don't even know if it's too late, or what I'd ask for, or whether they'd call anyone." Priya was seventeen like him, and both of them knew exactly what their parents had said, in different ways, about situations like this. His father's position had always been that knowledge of certain things was itself a kind of permission. Priya's mother, he gathered, had a different but equally firm position. Neither position was standing at a picnic table at nine at night needing an answer.

Aiden had spent the summer learning that a reading meant nothing without knowing what changed it, and the habit of that thinking moved in him now, arranging what he knew from what he didn't. "The van's out," he said. "But there are bikes behind the maintenance shed, and lights on the road the whole way. I'll go with you if you want. If we leave now we're back before eleven." He was already standing, and the cuff slid off his arm and coiled on the bench like something shed.

They rode in the dark with headlamps, Priya's front wheel sometimes brushing his, the frogs in the ditches going quiet and then starting again behind them. At the pharmacy a night clerk with reading glasses unlocked the case, and when Priya asked her question in a voice smaller than any Aiden had heard her use, the clerk answered briefly, glancing at the box. "You want the emergency contraceptive. It works mainly by delaying ovulation, so the sooner you take it after unprotected sex, the more effective it is. Two days is still within the window, but every day counts." Priya bought it, and outside under the buzzing sign she read the leaflet by the light of their headlamps, and Aiden turned away to give her the minute she seemed to need, and drank from his water bottle, and watched a moth throw itself at the light.

On the ride back she was quiet, then said, "So it doesn't end a pregnancy, it just holds the door shut early," and Aiden said that was his understanding of what the clerk meant, and neither of them pretended to be surer than they were. He thought of the gauge and the two numbers, and how the body gave you readings but not guarantees, and how you acted anyway, on the best information, in the time you had. At the camp gate Priya stopped her bike and looked at him. "Thank you for not making it weird." "I probably made it a little weird," Aiden said, and she laughed for real, the first time in three days, and they walked the bikes into the shadows past the sleeping infirmary.

The debate about the third period had started, as most things in Mr. Okafor's classroom started, with Marcus leaning back in his chair and saying something he had not fully thought through. "If a president is doing a good job, why can't he just keep running? Wouldn't the people decide?" Mr. Okafor, who disliked answering questions he thought students could dismantle on their own, wrote parliamentary on one side of the board and presidential on the other, and said nothing. Jordan, three rows back, recognized the silence as an assignment.

Jordan wanted the scholarship to the summer program in political science, and the application asked for an essay comparing how a parliamentary system and a presidential system each choose and remove a head of government. He had written two pages already, both of them, he suspected, wrong in ways he could not yet name. Now Marcus had handed him the exact question his essay kept circling. He pulled his legal pad out from under his chemistry folder and began a list: PM chosen by the party, president chosen by the voters. PM removed by a vote of no confidence, president removed by impeachment. He stared at the list, waiting for it to become an argument, and it refused.

"Jordan," Mr. Okafor said, without turning from the board. "You've been writing for four minutes. Say something."

He had not expected to be called on, and the page in front of him was still just two columns. "In a parliamentary system," he said slowly, "the head of government isn't elected by the whole country. The party picks the prime minister, and the parliament can remove him whenever he loses their support. A vote of no confidence. So it's faster. But it means the voters never chose him directly."

"And presidents?" Marcus asked, still tipped back in his chair.

"Directly elected. Fixed terms. But here's what I keep getting stuck on." Jordan tapped his pen against the pad. "Removal is supposed to be hard. Impeachment takes a whole machinery, a whole process. It's not designed to be quick."

"Which is better?" Priya asked from the window row, and Jordan said, honestly, "I don't know yet," and a few people laughed, but Mr. Okafor didn't.

At lunch, Jordan found Marcus by the vending machines, holding a bag of chips he wasn't eating. "Your question this morning," Jordan said. "The popular president running forever. I looked it up during study hall. The 22nd Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice."

Marcus frowned at his chips. "So even if everybody wanted him?"

"Even then. Twice, and that's it." Jordan watched Marcus turn this over, watched him arrive somewhere. "So it's a third thing," Marcus said. "Not choosing, not removing. A limit that happens before either one. Like the system doesn't totally trust popularity."

Jordan wrote that down on his hand because his legal pad was in his locker. That afternoon, sitting on the bleachers behind the gym with the essay open on his laptop, he remembered his grandfather, who had told a story every Thanksgiving about a council in the village where he grew up, how the elders could stand up at any meeting and withdraw their confidence in the man who spoke for them, and how the speaker would simply walk home before dinner. Jordan had been eleven and had thought it sounded brutal. His grandfather had said, "It wasn't brutal. It was ordinary. He'd be back the next week, arguing again, just not standing in front." He had liked watching his grandfather introspect in that slow way of his, turning a memory over before releasing it. It occurred to Jordan now, with the laptop warm on his knees, that he had been raised on two vocabularies without noticing: the fixed and the flexible, the term and the confidence.

He tried to put both on the page. The presidential system, he wrote, makes the head of government rigid in office, protected by fixed terms and a difficult removal, and the parliamentary system leaves the same figure ductile, shaped continuously by the parliament that made him. Then he deleted "shaped continuously" because it sounded like a thesaurus. He kept "ductile" because it was the true word, and because the essay was supposed to sound like him.

His younger sister, Devi, found him there after her soccer practice, backpack still on, and read over his shoulder with the shamelessness of a ninth grader. "So the prime minister can just be fired? By his own people?"

"Not fired exactly. Removed. If parliament votes no confidence, he has to go."

"That seems worse for him."

"It might be better for everyone else," Jordan said. "That's the part I haven't figured out. Whether stability is the same thing as safety." He looked at the screen, at the sentence he had just typed, and left it there, unresolved, with a colon after it and nothing following, a small hole he had decided not to fill with something easy.

Mr. Okafor, passing the bleachers on his way to the parking lot, paused with his keys in his hand. "The essay for the scholarship?" he asked, and Jordan nodded. "If a pedagogue tells you the answer, it isn't yours," Okafor said. "I'm told I have a reputation. Try to keep my fingerprints off it." He walked on toward his gray sedan.

Devi sat down beside him, unzipping the backpack, producing two granola bars and handing him one. Jordan took it, typed a question mark into the hole in his paragraph, and then deleted the question mark too, leaving the sentence bare. Somewhere across the field the sprinklers came on, ticking across the grass in slow arcs, and he hit save.

The practical exam was on Thursday, and Jessica had claimed the corner station by the window because the light there made the chalk dust visible and somehow that helped her think. Her task, printed on a card in her lab partner's neat handwriting, was to diagram a cell and annotate it so that anyone reading could follow how DNA becomes protein. Marcus had drawn the cell itself, a generous oval with a dark circle inside it, and he was now hunched over the label sheet, cutting out the words with scissors as though they were evidence for a trial. Jessica stood at the board with a marker, waiting to place the first arrow, and she noticed that her hand had stopped.

The problem was the mitochondrion. Marcus had drawn it large, hummingbird-hearted, and Jessica's instinct was to start there, because that was where energy lived and energy was where everything began. She had written the word "glucose" at the top of the board and was about to draw the arrow straight into the dark circle when she paused. Something in Monday's notes pushed back at her. She flipped back three pages in her notebook, past the transcription diagrams and the wobbly sketch of a ribosome she had drawn during a fire drill, and found it in her own handwriting, slightly smeared.

"Give me the scissors," she said, and Marcus handed them over without looking up. She cut the arrow she had been about to tape down and moved it outward, so that it floated in the pale region between the cell membrane and the mitochondrion. "Glycolysis happens out here," she said, tapping the space with two fingers. "In the cytoplasm. Outside the mitochondria." Marcus looked up then, because her voice had the particular flatness she used when she was talking herself into believing something. She drew a line splitting the word glucose into two smaller words. "One glucose splits into two pyruvate. Net gain of two ATP." She wrote "2 ATP" in the margin and circled it, then crossed out the arrow she had first imagined going inward. "After that it can go to the mitochondrion. But the first step, the first step is out here."

Marcus came around the table and studied the board, arms folded, scissors still in one hand. "You had it going inside a minute ago," he said. "I saw the chalk."

"I know. I was wrong, and then I wasn't." She said it too quickly, and he laughed at her, the way he laughed at most things, without malice. He was the kind of person who treated being wrong as a clerical matter, something you corrected and moved past, while she treated it as a debt, something that had to be paid down before she could sleep. Once, in an argument about whether their bio teacher would accept late lab reports, Marcus had told her she wanted the syllabus to indemnify her against every possible outcome, and though he had meant it as a joke, she had thought about the word for days. She wanted guarantees. The cell on the board offered none; it offered only a sequence, and sequences had a way of continuing whether you understood them or not.

They worked through the rest of it together, and it was here that the two halves of Jessica's thinking finally met. She had always split her brain between the version of herself that memorized and the version that asked why, and the two had spent most of high school in separate rooms. But building the diagram forced them into the same sentence. Transcription, Marcus cut out in blue, because the mRNA copy moved out of the nucleus toward the ribosome, and Jessica followed it with her marker, writing letters in threes, showing how each codon was matched, tRNA by tRNA, into a chain of amino acids. When she reached the end she wrote "PROTEIN" in capitals and then, feeling facetious, drew a small crown above it. "It's the logos of the whole cell," she said. "Everything else exists to make this one thing and get it where it needs to go." Marcus looked blank, so she pointed at the folded chain of amino acids. "The reason. The whole account of why any of it happens." He nodded slowly, and she could not tell whether he had understood or was only being kind, and she decided she could live with not knowing which.

What stayed uncertain was bigger than the diagram. Somewhere between the glucose arrow and the crowned protein, Jessica had understood that a cell runs on hundreds of these sequences at once, and that her poster, with its four arrows and one obedient mitochondrion, was a lie of clarity, the way all good diagrams were lies of clarity. She kept the uncertainty in her chest instead of writing it on the board, because the board was for Thursday, and Thursday had its own rules.

By the time the bell rang, the diagram was finished and defensible. Jessica read it through twice, top to bottom, glucose splitting in the cytoplasm, pyruvate arrowing toward the mitochondrion, the nucleus opening its blue transcript to the ribosome, the protein folded and crowned at the bottom. Marcus taped the label sheet beside it and stepped back with her to admire the whole apparatus, which looked, she thought, almost publishable.

Then he picked up the assignment card from the table, turned it over, and read the last line aloud. "Draw a prokaryotic cell." He tapped the dark oval in the middle of their diagram, the mitochondrion they had spent forty minutes respecting. "Jess. Bacteria don't have these."

The one-act was scheduled between Mya's debate rounds, which meant she had forty minutes to block a scene she had only read twice, in a practice room that smelled like floor wax and somebody's microwaved soup. She had volunteered to direct because Mr. Alvarez needed someone and because she assumed directing meant arguing, which she was good at. It turned out to be something else entirely, something closer to arranging furniture with feelings, and she was discovering that the skills did not transfer. She could compartmentalize the two halves of her day, debate and drama, only in theory; in practice she kept wanting to cross-examine her actors.

"Stop standing in a line," she said. "Families don't stand in a line."

"We're waiting for our cue," said Devon, who played the younger brother. He was obdurate about the line, arms crossed near the window.

Priya, who played the mother, held the prop envelope and turned it over in her hands. "This is my problem," she said. "The letter doesn't come out until the end, so for the whole scene I have nothing to do. I'm just sitting at a table being suspicious of soup."

The scene was simple: a mother and her two children at dinner, one envelope on the table, and a disclosure held until the final beat. Mya had assumed the suspense came from withholding. Withholding was what she did in debate cross-examination; you saved your best card for the rebuttal. But the room was small, the audience would be four feet away, and a scene that relied on the audience not knowing anything meant the audience spent three minutes knowing nothing at all.

"Show it to the audience," Priya said. "Early. Before the scene even starts, have me take it out, look at it, hide it under a napkin. Then Devon sits down across from me and eats his dinner like the night is normal."

"That ruins the surprise."

"It's not a surprise if nobody's tense," Priya said. "It's dramatic irony. The audience knows something I won't tell them, and the whole scene gets to be about how long I can sit on it."

Mya wrote in her blocking notebook, paused, crossed it out, and wrote it again. In the margin she drew the table from above and the sightlines from the first row of chairs, which was a debate habit, mapping what the judge could see. From that angle, if Priya angled her body slightly toward the window, the audience would catch the letter and Devon would not.

They ran it. Priya entered, set the envelope on the table, broke the seal with one finger, read whatever was written there, and slid it beneath the folded napkin. Mya watched from the folding chairs that stood in for the audience. Devon came in complaining about a bus. Priya ladled out imaginary soup and asked about his homework, and the whole ordinary exchange had gone strange, because Mya knew what was under the napkin and he didn't. When Devon reached for the bread near it, Priya's hand moved half an inch and stopped, and Mya, sitting four feet away, forgot to take notes.

They rehearsed it twice more, adjusting. Devon wanted a business with the salt shaker. Priya wanted to fold and refold the napkin between lines, and Mya let her, though she wasn't sure it worked, and said so, and Priya kept it anyway. Some of it Mya could defend and some she couldn't; she wrote "uncertain, keep" in the margin, which was not a thing she was allowed to write on a debate flow sheet.

Her phone buzzed between runs. A text from her debate partner, Ravi: "Pairings up. We're affirmative round three, and the judge is the one who docked us for speed last time. Also I can't find our inherency evidence. Did you take the accordion file? Also why are you directing a play."

She typed back: "Because Mr. Alvarez asked. Because I thought it was arguing. It's not, it's worse. Check the side pocket of my bag for the file." Then, before she could delete it, she added: "The thing where you let the audience see the hidden letter early so the family scene after feels tense actually works. Don't tell anyone I said a three-minute scene was hard."

Ravi replied with a single question mark, and she put the phone face down on the folding chair.

The round was called over the loudspeaker before she could run the scene a fourth time. She gathered the notebook, the envelope, the napkin. Priya was still at the table, holding the letter, reading it again as though it might have changed.

"What does it even say?" Devon asked, jerking his chin at the envelope.

"Doesn't matter," Priya said, sliding it back under the napkin. "They only need to know I know."

Mya stood in the doorway with her tub of evidence under one arm, looked back at the two of them posed in the half-light of the practice room, the mother and the son and the breadbasket, and then hurried down the hallway toward the gym, where the affirmative was already waiting.

The basement smelled like damp carpet and microwave popcorn, and Theo's laptop had been wheezing since October, so moribund was really the only word for it. Jaxon sat cross-legged on the floor with his own machine balanced on a chemistry textbook, a blank file open in the editor. In nine days they had to submit their project for the regional coding competition, a program that looked up students in a roster of two thousand names, and Jaxon had never written anything this large. He had, until tonight, never written a class at all.

"You're hiding the data," Theo said, leaning over from the beanbag. "Watch. Private fields. Then the only way in is through the getter."

"That seems paranoid," Jaxon said.

"It's polite. The class keeps its own house, and you knock."

So Jaxon typed, slowly, checking every brace. He made a Student class with private fields for name and ID, then a getName method that handed the name back, then a setter for the ID because Mr. Okafor's spec said IDs could change after enrollment. He wrote a test, three lines in a main method, and ran it, and for once nothing turned red. The little green run bar appeared and he sat very still, feeling something in his chest unknot.

Priya arrived at nine with her board games she had no intention of playing and a bag of sour candy. She pulled up the roster spec on her phone and frowned. "It says here we search for one name. One lookup, then the program prints the record and quits."

"Then we sort it," Theo said immediately. "Sorted list, binary search, that's the smart way. You cut the list in half over and over."

"Sorting two thousand names is a lot of work for one lookup," Priya said. "I think we just walk the list start to finish. One linear search."

"A linear search sounds like giving up," Theo said. "Anybody can walk a list."

They argued around the ping-pong table for ten minutes, the kind of argument where both people are mostly defending their pride. Jaxon said nothing. He kept thinking about the green bar, about how the class kept its own house, and about what his grandmother always said, a maxim she repeated so often he could hear her voice: do the work once if the work only happens once.

At 9:40 Priya's phone buzzed, and she read the text out loud because it was from their fourth teammate, DeShawn, who was home with the flu.

"Tell them my decision," she read. "Sorting takes more work than one linear search. Way more. So sorting just so we can run a binary search only pays off if we're going to search the same data many times. We search once. One and done. I vote we walk the list. Also I am dying, send soup."

"That's not a real vote if you can't be here," Theo said, but without heat.

"It's a real vote," Jaxon said. "It's also right." He turned his laptop so they could both see. "Look at my test. I wrote the class so the fields are private, so nobody touches the data directly. The class decides how things get done and the outside world just asks. That's what we should do with the search. The smart way isn't the fancy way. It's the way that matches how many times you'll actually use it."

Theo slumped back into the beanbag and blew out a long breath. "Fine. But if the judges see linear search and think we're amateurs?"

"Then we comment the code," Priya said. "We write, this list is searched once, so one linear search costs less than sorting it. DeShawn can draft that from his deathbed."

Jaxon smiled at that, but he kept typing. Because there was one thing he had not said out loud, and it sat in his stomach like a swallowed stone: he had checked the fine print on the spec, a later page, and there was a line about an optional feature, a "future extension" allowing repeated lookups if a user typed more than one name. If they implemented that, the searching would happen many times, and then the whole calculus flipped, and sorting would be worth it after all. He could not tell yet whether the judges would ever run that extension, or whether it was a trap for teams that overbuilt.

"Hey," he said. "Before we lock this in."

Both of them looked at him. The laptop fan hummed, the furnace ticked somewhere above, and on screen his little Student class waited, private and patient, guarding its two fields.

"There's a line on page six," Jaxon said, and turned the screen toward them.

The screen door banged behind Ava before she had even set down her bag, and her grandmother was already saying, "You'll take the back bedroom, the desk there doesn't wobble," as if the visit had been arranged for weeks instead of texted at midnight, the night before, in a message that read only: can I come tomorrow? thesis due monday. driving up after class. Now the house smelled of coffee and lemon polish, and Ava spread her sources across the desk like a hand of losing cards: four library books, two printed articles, a PDF on her laptop with highlights in three colors that had stopped meaning anything by the second page.

Her argument, to the extent she had one, was that campaign finance rules had quietly turned American politics into something closer to an oligarchy than the civics textbooks admitted. Her professor had written "Interesting. Now prove it" on her proposal, which Ava had taken first as encouragement and then, over the following week, as a threat. The problem was that every source seemed to argue a different version of the claim, and each version was plausible, and plausibility, she was beginning to suspect, was not the same as truth. One article in particular annoyed her, a smooth op-ed whose reasoning felt like a sidewalk with one raised brick, something to trip over if you weren't watching. She couldn't articulate why it was wrong. Maybe it wasn't. That was the part that kept her up.

"You've been staring at that machine for an hour," her grandmother said from the doorway, holding two mugs. She had been a high school librarian for thirty-one years and had opinions about research that she mostly kept to herself, which Ava found both restful and slightly menacing, like a cat watching you type.

"It's the notes," Ava said. "I have to do footnotes and a bibliography and I don't fully understand the difference between any of it, and the software keeps doing things I didn't ask it to do."

Her grandmother set down the mugs, looked at the screen for a long moment, and said only, "Hm," in the tone of a woman watching someone else do a puzzle she had already solved. Then she went to water the tomatoes, which was her way of leaving the room without leaving it.

Ava inserted her first citation, a quotation from the op-ed about money functioning as speech, and watched the software do exactly what she had feared: a small superscript bloomed in the text, and the note itself slid down to the bottom of the document, gathering on the final page with the others like gulls on the last pylon of a pier. She pressed undo. It happened again. She wanted to cry, briefly, and then she wanted to think, because somewhere under the panic a memory surfaced: her professor's assignment sheet, which she now dug out of her bag and smoothed flat on the desk. The sheet said notes must appear at the bottom of the page where each reference occurs. She read it three times. The software had moved everything to the end of the paper, which meant the software was wrong, or the assignment was, and one of those could be fixed and the other could not.

She went to find her grandmother, who was arguing with a tomato stake in the garden. "The program put all my notes on the last page," Ava said. "Is that cheating?"

"Is it what the assignment asked for?"

"No. It wants them on the page where I quote the thing."

"Then it's not cheating," her grandmother said, snipping a dead leaf with small scissors she kept in her apron pocket. "A note at the bottom of the page where you use it is a footnote. What your machine made instead is called an endnote. It collects at the end of the paper." She turned a tomato toward the sun and added, "There's a setting. You'll find it faster than I could tell you." Which was, Ava understood, both true and a compliment, and she went back inside smiling for the first time all day.

The setting took forty minutes to find, and in the process she deleted a paragraph and had to rewrite it, and the rewrite was better, and that annoyed her too, because it meant the good version had required the disaster. The notes climbed back onto their proper pages, one per page, small as insects at the bottom margin, and something about seeing them there, huddled beside the sentences that needed them, changed how she read her own draft. Footnotes that lived on the last page had felt like debts deferred; these felt like conversations happening in the room.
