She could also see, now, which of her claims were load-bearing and which were decoration, and the op-ed's argument, sitting in her browser tab, looked suddenly less like a raised brick and more like a brick painted on the sidewalk. Its reasoning was specious, she decided, writing the word in the margin and then, after a moment, underlining it: convincing on the surface, hollow underneath, money as speech, speech as equality, equality as democracy, each step sliding smoothly past the gap where the evidence should be.

By evening she had eleven footnotes, a bibliography alphabetized twice because she got it wrong the first time, and an argument she half believed. Half was the honest number. The data supported concentration of influence; it did not quite support the word oligarchy, and she wrote a paragraph saying so, conceding the uncertainty, and it cost her the ending she'd wanted, the clean damning one. Her grandmother came in at dusk with a plate of sandwiches and read the concession paragraph over her shoulder.

"You talk yourself out of your own point," she said.

"No," Ava said. "I'm leaving the door open for the point to walk back in with better evidence."

Her grandmother laughed, a short surprised sound, and set the plate down beside the laptop. "Then you'd better feed it." She tapped the sandwich. Outside, the sprinkler kicked on, and somewhere down the block a dog began its complaint to the evening.

The mock election was Mr. Okafor's idea, a dress rehearsal two days before the real one, and the classroom had been arranged into rows of folding tables with cardboard voting booths at the front, the kind borrowed from the county whenever the school ran out of ways to make civics feel urgent. Morgan had turned eighteen on the fourth of October, which meant that Tuesday would be her first actual vote, and she kept thinking about that with an odd, hollow excitement, like holding a ticket to somewhere she had never been.

The trouble began when Deshawn leaned across the aisle before the bell. "Half of us don't even show up," he said. "You know that, right? Young people. Everybody talks like our generation decides elections, and then half of us stay home."

"That's not true," Priya said, spinning in her chair. "It was way higher last time. Everyone voted."

"It was fifty percent," Deshawn said. "I read it somewhere. Half. Exactly half."

"You're making that up."

They looked at each other, and then, because there was no one else to ask, they looked at Morgan, who was known for checking things. She didn't know. She had a phone in her pocket and a number in her head that she couldn't verify, and the bell was ringing, and Mr. Okafor was already saying that the booths would close at the end of the period, forty-two minutes, and that every student who intended to vote in the mock election had to decide before then.

The debate section came first. Priya argued that low turnout among young voters was a myth spread by people who wanted youth to feel powerless, a way of keeping them quiet; Deshawn argued that if you couldn't be bothered to show up, your complaints were theater. Mr. Okafor moved between them like a referee, offering nothing. "Morgan," he said once, "you've been quiet." She said she was thinking, which was true but also a way of not saying she was calculating, because there was a second problem she hadn't told anyone about: her registration had been returned for a wrong apartment number, and the corrected form had to be postmarked by Saturday, and her father, whose car she needed, worked until six.

She asked to use the classroom computer for five minutes. What she found was a research center at Tufts University called CIRCLE, which had estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election. She read it twice. Half had come out, half had not, and the number sat strangely between Deshawn's cynicism and Priya's faith, refusing to belong to either. She wrote the figure on the whiteboard in dry-erase marker and stood back.

"Fifty percent," she said. "CIRCLE, at Tufts, for 2020. So you're both a little right, and you're both using it wrong." Priya protested that fifty percent was nothing to celebrate; Deshawn said it proved his point about apathy; and Morgan, feeling something assemble itself inside her, said no, it proved neither, because a number like that wasn't a verdict, it was an opening. If half showed up, the other half was not a fixed quantity. It was a margin. And margins could move.

"But which argument does the number support?" Priya demanded. The booths were open now. Students were filing forward, marking pretend ballots, and the countdown on the board said eleven minutes, and beyond the classroom window the October light was already going amber, and somewhere across town a post office would close at five tomorrow.

"Neither," Morgan said. "That's what I keep trying to say. You want the number to be a weapon, and it's not, it's a description. It tells you where we are. It doesn't tell you where we have to stay." She heard her own voice waver and pushed through it. "Deshawn, if turnout is only half, then the ones who do come are worth more, not less. Priya, if it's only half, then we can't pretend the work is finished. The same fact. Two directions. I think you hold both at once, and I think that's the honest position, and I'll admit I don't know how to make the other half move. I don't. But I know which half I'm going to be in."

She walked to the booth, pulled the cardboard flap shut, and marked the ballot in the blue pen that hung from a string. Then she came out, folded her paper into the collection box, and took out her phone. Three texts sat unsent to her father, drafted and deleted. She typed a fourth, asking him to leave work early, and added the address of the post office on Fenwick, and pressed send.

Deshawn was watching her from the doorway. "You actually registered," he said. It wasn't a question.

"Ballot's in the mail by five tomorrow," she said, "or it isn't." She shouldered her bag and walked past him into the hall, phone flat against her palm, waiting for the screen to light up.

Andrew arrived at the community art studio on the first Saturday of October carrying a cardboard tube of drawings he already suspected were not good enough. The studio occupied the back half of a converted laundry on Delancey Street, its tall windows fogged with heat from the kiln room, its shelves crowded with other people's half-finished bowls. Ms. Reyes, who ran the portfolio class, had one rule for the fall: ten artworks, one theme, and an artist's statement to hold them together. Applications to art high schools and summer programs all asked for the same thing, and she had been blunt about the stakes. Without a coherent portfolio, she said, talented kids got passed over, effectively disenfranchised by a process that rewarded clarity over raw skill.

Andrew's problem was that he had no theme. He had nine drawings of his neighborhood, three of his brother's hands, and a painting of a dead moth he'd found on the windowsill, all technically fine, all saying nothing in particular. While the others taped thumbnail sketches to the wall, he sat at the long table pretending to brainstorm, writing words he crossed out: memory, family, windows, decay. Each one felt like a costume he'd put on for the application.

The studio's other Saturday regular was a woman named Ofelia, sixty-something, who came to paint watercolors while her grandson Theo took the teen class. Ofelia kept a postcard taped above her station, a Kahlo self-portrait, and that morning Andrew finally looked at it instead of past it. A woman in a thorn necklace, a monkey on her shoulder, a small dead bird hanging at her throat like a pendant.

"That's dark," Andrew said, nodding at the bird. "Is it just decoration, or what?"

Theo leaned over from the next table. "It's a hummingbird. She's just showing off, probably."

Ofelia set down her brush. "Not decoration, mijo. The dead hummingbird hanging at her throat, that's a Mexican folk charm, for luck in love." She said it the way she might have said the bird was a sparrow, plain fact, and went back to her watercolor. "My mother kept one in a drawer for years."

Andrew looked at the postcard for a long moment. A dead thing worn as an ornament meant to attract love. Suffering arranged into decoration. He thought of the moth painting, which he had made after his grandmother's funeral and then told everyone was just a study of wing patterns. Something in the back of his mind turned over and did not settle.

He spent the rest of the session sketching badly and thinking uselessly, and on the bus home he wrote in his notebook: things people wear to invite love, or luck, or safety. Thorn necklaces. Saint medallions. His brother's hospital bracelet, which he had kept in a drawer for eight months without admitting why. At the next class, he brought that bracelet in a plastic bag and set it on the table, and Theo said, "Dude," softly, and Ms. Reyes, who could be scathing about laziness, said nothing at all, which from her was a kind of applause.

The theme held, mostly. Andrew photographed the bracelet on white paper, drew it oversized in graphite until the embossed letters blurred into texture, painted a self-portrait with the bracelet at his throat the way Kahlo wore the hummingbird. Ofelia watched him work and one Saturday offered him a small paper packet. "For reference," she said. Inside was a dried flower, brittle and brown, from a bouquet her mother had once kept for luck. He pressed it under glass for piece number seven. Not everyone understood. One classmate, Marcus, who had appointed himself the studio's resident critic and whose compliments always arrived bent toward whoever could help him, told Andrew the bracelet piece was sentimental, that grief art was a cliché. Andrew considered the source; Marcus had spent three weeks buttering up Ms. Reyes like a sycophant, and his praise and his scorn both pointed in the same direction, at himself. Still, the word stung, because it was half true.

The honest difficulty, Andrew found, was the artist's statement. His first draft claimed his theme was transformation, which sounded impressive and meant nothing. His second draft was confessional in a way that made his neck hot when he reread it. The truth was more complicated and less resolved: he wanted to say that people carry charms against loss even knowing the charms don't work, and that he had made ten images of this without deciding whether it was brave or foolish, and that the bracelet in the drawer had been both a way of holding on and a way of not moving. He wrote a third draft that admitted the uncertainty and read it to Theo on the studio's back steps, the kiln exhaling warm air behind them.

"So you don't know what it means," Theo said.

"No. I know what the objects mean. I don't know what keeping them means. There's a difference."

Theo considered this, turning his pencil over in his fingers. "My grandmother says you don't keep the charm because it works."

Andrew waited. Down the street someone was washing a storefront window, the squeegee moving in long patient strokes.

Theo shrugged. "She says you keep it because your mother kept it. That's all. She'd know about the hummingbird ones."

On the last Saturday of the session, Andrew hung the ten pieces in a row along the studio's longest wall, bracelet drawing to pressed flower, and stood back with his statement folded in his back pocket. Ofelia came over with her postcard and taped it at the end of the row, unasked, so the dead hummingbird hung there too, at the throat of the whole arrangement. "Eleven," she said, and went back to her watercolors, and Andrew left it exactly where she'd put it.

Ashton slid the pay stub across the kitchen table before his mother had even sat down. "Four hundred and twelve dollars," he said. "That's what I made. Look what I actually got."

She set her mug down and pulled the stub closer, tilting it toward the window light. Their restaurant receipt from Saturday night lay beside it, and Ashton tapped the single line near the bottom where the taxes were. He had been staring at both papers all morning, the stub and the receipt, as if together they might confess something.

"It says HST," he said. "One line. Thirteen percent, all at once. I thought there'd be two. Federal and provincial."

"There used to be," his mother said. "Ontario folded them together. Harmonized Sales Tax. One line on the bill now."

He turned the receipt over, half expecting a second charge hidden on the back like fine print on a contract. There was nothing but a smudge of teriyaki sauce. "So when Mr. Kwan charged me thirteen percent on the pad thai, part of that was going to Ottawa and part to Queen's Park, and I'd never know the split from looking at it."

"You'd know it if you did the returns," she said. "Which brings us to this." From her bag she took a folded sheaf of papers, the ones from the accountant's office, the ones she had been carrying around for a week like a stone in her pocket. "I need your help. And I need you to be honest about whether you can give it."

Ashton's mother wanted to fire the accountant. He had gathered this not from anything she said but from the way she said nothing, from the prolix three-page letter the man had sent, full of clauses that circled and circled and never landed on a plain number. She had read it aloud on Tuesday, and by the second page even the cat had left the room. What she wanted, Ashton suspected, was permission. Not from him exactly, but from someone.

The pay stub was his own small war. He had started at the noodle place on Baldwin Street three weeks ago, minimum wage, four shifts a week, and the first cheque had genuinely mesmerized him: not the amount, which was modest, but the architecture of it. Gross pay. Then the deductions, itemized like a bill of particulars. Federal tax, provincial tax, CPP, EI. Each one a small subtraction with a reason attached, apparently. Net pay sat at the bottom, smaller and somehow more real than the number above it.

"They took money for a pension," he said. "I'm sixteen. I don't have anything to retire from."

"CPP isn't only for you," his mother said. "It flows through everyone. Like an aquifer. You pay into the ground now, and later you draw from what everyone poured in together."

"That's the second water metaphor you've used this week."

"It's a dry subject. It needs watering." She spread the tax return across the table and weighted the corners with the salt shaker and her keys. "Here's what I can't work out. He says I owe eleven hundred dollars. I don't believe him, but I can't disbelieve him either, because I don't understand the form. Can you?"

Ashton looked at the return the way he'd looked at the receipt, hoping for a hidden side. Lines and boxes, schedules lettered like annexes to a treaty. Somewhere in there, he knew, were his own tuition receipts from last year, his mother's employment income, the deductions she'd claimed and the ones she'd missed. He thought of his pay stub, how the subtractions had names and the names had logic. Maybe the return was the same thing read backward. Money the government had already taken, and places to say why some of it should come home.

"Start at the income," he said slowly. "Your T4. That's like my gross pay. Then the deductions are boxes where you argue for giving some back. Tuition, the transit pass, the work-from-home thing."

"You're guessing."

"I'm pattern-matching. There's a difference, but it's thin."

They worked through it for two hours. Ashton filled a legal pad with arithmetic, cross-checking line 15000 against the T4 box 14, hunting for the tuition amount like a man looking for his keys in the same pocket four times. Twice he got the math wrong and his mother caught it. Once she got it wrong and he caught hers, and she laughed, a real laugh, the first since the letter arrived.

Near the end, they found the tuition credit sitting unused on a carryforward line, exactly where the accountant's letter had failed to mention it. Applied, it brought what she owed down to under two hundred dollars.

"He missed it," she said quietly. "Or he didn't look."

"Or he looked and decided it was too small to bother with. But it's not small to us."

She took off her glasses and rubbed the bridge of her nose. "I was going to fire him this morning. Before you came down. I had the email drafted."

"And now?"

"Now I think maybe the problem isn't him. It's that I handed it over and walked away and never looked once. You looked for two hours." She refolded the return, but not before Ashton saw her rest her palm flat on the page, the way you'd steady something living. "Next year we do this together. Both of us, the whole way through."

He stacked the receipt and the pay stub together, the two documents that had started his morning, and pinned them to the corkboard by the fridge. The HST line faced outward, thirteen percent, one line, plain as anything. He didn't fully understand it yet, the splitting and the flowing and the pension ground water. But he understood his own net pay now, to the dollar, and where every deduction went and why.

"I'm keeping these," he said.

"Keep them somewhere safer than a corkboard."

He threaded the pin through the pay stub twice, then a third time, and stepped back to check that it would hold.

The news broadcast came from a laptop balanced on Grandad's kitchen table, where the smell of burnt toast still hung in the air. Felix had come to the house for two quiet days of revision before his politics entrance interview, and instead the lower house of some parliament he couldn't yet locate on a map was voting, live, on whether its government still had its confidence. He watched the division numbers crawl up the screen. The government lost.

"So what happens now?" he asked, because Grandad was the only other person in the house and the question had to go somewhere.

"Dunno. New prime minister by Friday, I'd have said." Grandad buttered a second slice of toast without looking at the screen.

"That's the thing," Felix said. "I don't think that's right." He pulled his notebook toward him, the one with the comparison charts he'd been building for three days, and felt the floor of his preparation tilt. His interview was in forty hours. He was supposed to argue which system was better at choosing and removing a head of government, presidential or parliamentary, and he had written two pages on the presidential side because it was the side he actually knew. He had watched that side his whole life. Fixed terms, a single name on a ballot, a removal process so long and so rare it had only ever been a paragraph in his textbook. He had written almost nothing about parliaments because they confused him, and now one was falling apart on the table in front of him.

He called his mother first, but she was in a meeting. Then he sat on the back step with the laptop and read, properly read, the coverage. The losing prime minister would not simply be replaced by Friday. A government that lost this kind of vote in the lower house, the reporters kept repeating, had to resign or call a general election. He said it aloud once, to the wet garden and the pigeon on the fence. "Has to resign, or call a general election." Not maybe. Not usually. Has to. The whole cabinet, the entire government, because one chamber had stopped believing in it, on an ordinary Tuesday.

He took it back inside to test it against Grandad, who was filling in a crossword in biro. "Say the president we've got," Felix said. "Say congress just decided, tomorrow, that they'd stopped trusting him. Nothing happens, right? He serves out the term."

"Good," said Grandad. "I voted for the man, not for four hundred other men. Your lot over there, they can chuck a government out on a whim."

"Except it's not a whim, it's a vote, and the government's gone the same day." Felix heard the argument assembling itself, faster than he could write. "And it works the other way too. They chose that prime minister through parliament, not through us. You get the head of government the legislature will tolerate, and you lose them the moment it won't."

Grandad tapped his biro twice. "And I'd rather have a lemon for four years than a revolving door."

"That's actually the trade," Felix said, and it came out before he'd checked it, and then he sat with it. He'd spent three days trying to pick a winner and here, between the toast crumbs and the crossword, was the actual shape of the thing: one system underwrites stability with a fixed term you can't shorten, the other underwrites accountability with a removal you can't refuse. He couldn't have both. Nobody could. He wrote that in the notebook, then crossed out "nobody could" because it sounded too much like wisdom and he hadn't earned it yet.

Later they watched the evening bulletin together, the follow-up, the same chamber half empty now. Grandad was quiet through it, which Felix had learned meant thinking rather than agreement. On the screen a junior minister was being interviewed on a street corner, saying the words "no confidence" as if everyone watching had been born knowing them, and Felix realized his nascent command of all this, forty hours old and borrowed from a Tuesday broadcast, would have to be enough.

"They'll call the election," Grandad said at last, not asking. "They always do, eventually."

"Or resign," Felix said. "It's one or the other. That's the rule." He closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again, because he wanted to keep the picture of that chamber in his head: the doors, the counting, a government ending on a voice vote. His interview would ask him to defend a side. He still didn't know which side he'd defend, only that he finally understood both, and that somewhere between the fixed term and the fallen government there was a position he could hold honestly, even if he couldn't yet say it out loud.

He went back to the notebook and wrote, at the top of a clean page, "Which do I actually believe?" Grandad put the kettle on and said, from the kitchen, "You'll want tea for this part."

Naomi set her phone face-down beside her plate before her mother could say anything about it, which meant she spent the first ten minutes of dinner not hearing a word. Her uncle Ravi was holding forth about his neighbor's fence, garrulous as always, and her little cousin was dropping peas one by one onto the floor with the patience of a scientist, but Naomi kept seeing Dev's slide deck. Slide fourteen. The math was wrong in a way she'd caught at eleven the night before, and she had said nothing, and neither had anyone else on the team of five, and the presentation was Thursday.

"Earth to Naomi," her mother said. "You've cut your chicken into a grid."

"Sorry. Group project."

"Ah," her uncle said, delighted, as if she'd offered him a topic. "Group projects. The great character-building scam. I did all the work in every group I was ever in, and I turned out fine."

"You turned out garrulous," her mother said, and everyone laughed, including the pea scientist.

Naomi laughed too, and then stopped, because something about the joke snagged on the actual problem. It wasn't that she'd have to do all the work. It was that all five of them had looked at slide fourteen, she was nearly sure, and all five had decided that pointing it out was more dangerous than letting it sit there. She knew Marcus had rewritten his section twice without saying why. She knew Priya had asked, in the chat, whether everyone was "feeling good about the numbers," which was not a question, and no one had answered it, including her.

She turned her phone over and searched the phrase that had been circling her all day, the one her econ teacher had mentioned offhand last spring and then never returned to: teams afraid to admit mistakes. The first result was a study. She read a line of it twice, then a third time.

"Naomi."

"One second. This is actually important."

"No phones at the table is an injunction, not a suggestion," her mother said, but she said it mildly, and she leaned sideways to look, because her mother could never not look.

"There was a researcher," Naomi said, mostly to the table now, because she'd realized halfway through the second read that she wanted witnesses. "Amy Edmondson. In 1999 she described this thing where a team shares a belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks. Like admitting a mistake. She gave it a name."

"What name?" her cousin asked, from underneath the table, where the peas lived.

"It's called psychological safety," Naomi said.

"Sounds like a wellness app," her uncle said.

"No, it's the opposite of a wellness app, it's whether people on a team can say 'I messed up' without the floor opening." She was talking fast now, which she did when two ideas were snapping together. "That's us. That's our group. Marcus redid his whole section in silence. Priya asked if we were 'feeling good' about the numbers. Nobody said the numbers were wrong, because we're all protecting ourselves from looking like the dumb one, and meanwhile the dumb thing is still in the deck."

Her mother refilled her water glass without being asked, a small kindness Naomi registered even mid-sentence.

"So what do you do," her uncle said. "March in and announce the team lacks psychological safety?"

"That's the part I keep getting wrong in my head." She pulled her fork through the rice, making a channel. "If I open with the theory, it's a lecture, and it makes it worse, like I'm diagnosing them. My dad always says feedback should be specific and kind, and I used to think that was a dodge, like the 'compliment sandwich.' But I think the specific part is the honest part and the kind part is the delivery, and they're not opposites. I could say, 'I found an error on slide fourteen, I almost missed it myself, can we fix it together.' That's true and it gives Dev a way to hear it."

"And if Dev's defensive anyway?"

"Then I don't know," Naomi said, and found she meant it without despair. "That's the part no study fixes. Maybe it's a risk you just take, which is sort of the point of the whole thing."

She ate three bites in a row, actually tasting them for the first time, then picked the phone back up and typed a message to Dev: found something on slide 14, not a big fix, want to look together tomorrow at lunch? She put the phone face-down again and watched it, face-down, as if she could see through it.

Under the table, her cousin released one final pea.

The branch on Chapel Street smelled of carpet cleaner and photocopier ink, and Landon took the last seat in the waiting row clutching two folded leases he had printed at the school library the night before. He was seventeen, with a conditional offer for Manchester and a September deadline, and his mother had put the decision in his hands with a flatness that he understood to be trust, or a test, or both. Above the tellers a screen rotated through mortgage rates. Number forty-three glowed on the ticket in his fist.

He had come to the bank because his debit card had been declined twice that week, a peccadillo of expired documentation rather than empty funds, and while he waited he spread the leases across his knees. Flat one sat above a chip shop on Oldham Road: 725 pounds a month, bills excluded, deposit quoted at 1,050 pounds. Flat two was a room in a shared house in Fallowfield: 640 a month, water included, deposit quoted at 800. The agent's handwriting on the second one slanted as though it had been done in a doorway.

"Forty-three," called a woman at the far desk, and Landon gathered the pages and went.

Her badge said Priya and her desk had a stapler, a bowl of wrapped mints, and a rack of leaflets fanned like cards. She fixed the card in four minutes, checked his passport against the screen, and then glanced at the papers he had not stopped reading. "Student housing?" she said. "You're the third one this week." She pushed the mint bowl toward him and, while he took one, slid a leaflet from the rack without ceremony, the way a person hands over a napkin.

He thanked her and pocketed it and went to the chair by the window to do the arithmetic he had promised his mother he would do. The chip shop flat wanted gas and electric on top, which the current tenant had told him averaged 95 a month in winter, and water at 24, and broadband at 20 split two ways. He wrote the figures in the margin of the lease in his small, upright handwriting. The Fallowfield room already included water, and the tenant there had texted him a photo of a bill: 61 a month for electric, split four ways. He added it all, crossed out, added again. The flats landed within eleven pounds of each other, which felt less like an answer than a rearrangement of the question.

He was folding the pages when the leaflet shifted in his pocket and he pulled it out. It was a thin printed sheet about tenant fees, and near the bottom, in ordinary type, was a line he read three times. In England, a tenancy deposit was capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent was under 50,000 pounds, and at six weeks' rent when the annual rent was 50,000 pounds or more. He sat with that for a moment, working the shapes of it. Five weeks. Not five months' worth, not a number a landlord could simply choose.

He did the sums on the back of the leaflet. The chip shop flat was 725 a month, which made a week 167 and change, and five weeks came to about 840. The landlord was asking 1,050. He checked the division twice, once longhand, because the margin of the lease had become a palimpsest of crossed-out numbers. The Fallowfield room worked out differently: 640 a month was roughly 148 a week, five weeks near enough 740, and the quoted deposit of 800 sat above that by sixty pounds. He leaned back. One flat over the cap by more than two hundred, the other over by sixty, and he had walked into the branch that morning thinking the deposits were simply prices, the way a loaf of bread was a price.

He went back to Priya's desk while she was filing. "This cap," he said. "Does it apply to rooms in shared houses too, or just whole flats?" She said she wasn't a letting agent, but the leaflet was the government's own wording and she'd not known it to make exceptions, and that disputes went to a scheme she'd never had to use. "Five weeks," she said, tapping the leaflet, "unless the rent's fifty thousand a year or more, and then it's six." He nodded and thanked her, and on the walk back to the window he noticed he was already composing the phone calls in his head, testing phrasings.

He called the Fallowfield agent first, from the doorway of the branch where the signal was better. The woman who answered listened, put him on hold, came back and said the 800 was a typo, that the deposit would be 740, and that she'd email a corrected page within the hour. Her voice carried no embarrassment, as though typos in deposits were a recognized genre. Landon said that would be fine, and meant it, and felt something in the transaction transmute from suspicion into procedure, a problem becoming paperwork.

The chip shop landlord answered on the fourth ring, from somewhere windy. "Thousand and fifty," he confirmed. Landon read him the line about the cap, slowly, the way Priya had tapped it. There was a pause long enough for a lorry to pass. "That's the going rate around here," the landlord said. "Take it or leave it, lad, I've got viewings Thursday." Landon said he'd think about it, and hung up, and stood in the doorway with the phone warm in his hand.

The total monthly costs sat in his margins, nearly level, eleven pounds apart. Fallowfield was now legal and corrected and slightly cheaper all-in, and he found he wanted it, and also that the wanting felt less clean than it had an hour ago, because the arithmetic hadn't actually chosen for him, it had only removed one way of being cheated. He folded both leases together with the leaflet between them, like a slice of ham in a sandwich, and texted his mother: one flat works, the other one's asking too much, I'll explain tonight. Then he went back inside to return Priya's pen, which he found he was still holding, and she waved it off and told him the mints were free.

The volunteer office at the community center smelled of burnt coffee and old construction paper, and by August Justine had habituated to both so completely that she only noticed them on Mondays, after the weekend scrubbed her senses clean. She had taken the summer job because the application for the state scholarship wanted three hundred hours of service, and because her mother had said, gently, that sitting at home revising her personal essay for the fourth time was not the same as living. She filed forms, restocked the snack table for the after-school program, and answered the phone when Mrs. Alvarez, the coordinator, was mid-crisis with a printer.

The crisis that Wednesday was bigger than a printer. Mrs. Alvarez stood at her desk with a legal pad covered in crossed-out lines, pressing the phone between her ear and shoulder while she typed. "No, the picnic is still on," she said. "Yes, we moved it to the twentieth. I'm emailing all the families right now, this afternoon, before anyone else calls." She hung up, rubbed her eyes, and pulled a spreadsheet toward her. Fifty names. Justine knew the number because she had alphabetized that spreadsheet herself two weeks earlier, sorting the parents of every child in the summer program by last name while Mrs. Alvarez taught a CPR refresher in the gym.

Justine carried a stack of permission slips across the room, and as she set them down she saw the email taking shape on the screen. The cursor blinked in the To field, and Mrs. Alvarez was pasting the whole column of addresses in a single block, one name after another, fifty addresses marching across the line like a train with no end. Something in Justine's chest tightened, though she could not immediately have said why. She thought of her own mother, who guarded her email address the way some people guarded their house keys, and who had once spent an afternoon unsubscribing from everything after a school newsletter went out with every parent listed in plain view.

"Mrs. Alvarez," she said. Then, when the coordinator looked up, "Sorry. Quick question about that email."

"It has to go out in ten minutes, Justine."

"I know. It's fast, I promise." Justine leaned toward the screen, careful not to touch anything. "If you put all fifty addresses in the To field, every parent who gets it can see every other parent's address. People who don't know each other." She had learned this the hard way in the spring, when a group organizing her college visit weekend had sent a message with forty addresses exposed, and a man named Gerald had replied to all, twice, about parking. "If you use Bcc instead, the recipients are hidden from everyone else. Nobody sees anybody's address but their own."

Mrs. Alvarez's hand stopped on the mouse. "Blind copy," she said slowly, reading the field label as if seeing it for the first time in twenty years of emails.

"That's the one. You put one address, yours or the office's, up in To, and everyone else down there." Justine pointed at the row of small letters stacked along the edge of the compose window. "Fifty parents who've never met can't end up with each other's information."

For a moment Mrs. Alvarez did not move, and Justine braced herself. She had heard the coordinator argue with the fire marshal about occupancy limits; she had watched her go belligerent with a vendor over spoiled fruit, chin out, refusing to yield an inch. But now the woman only exhaled, long and tired, and said, "I've been sending these lists for three summers." She said it without defensiveness, more to herself than to Justine, the way a connoisseur of her own mistakes might catalogue a flaw in a favorite painting. "Three summers, and nobody ever said anything."

"Maybe nobody wanted to correct you," Justine said. "You're kind of the boss of the building."

Mrs. Alvarez laughed, a short sound that cracked into something warmer. She highlighted the long chain of addresses in the To field, cut it, and pasted it into the Bcc row instead. Then she typed her own address at the top, checked the subject line, and paused. "The picnic's still the twentieth. You think I should say that first, before anything else, so nobody skims past it?"

"Yes. Short paragraphs. And maybe put the rain plan in its own line so people can find it without reading everything." Justine pulled a chair around beside the desk, not waiting to be invited, and read over the draft as Mrs. Alvarez reshaped it: the date up front, the potluck request on its own line, a courteous closing that thanked parents for their patience with the scheduling change. Where the draft had said "as previously indicated," Justine suggested "as we mentioned last week," and Mrs. Alvarez nodded and made the change without fuss.

The send button sat there, gray and patient. Mrs. Alvarez rested her fingers above the keyboard and glanced at Justine. "Anything else I'm about to get wrong?"

Justine smiled and shook her head, though privately she held a small uncertainty in reserve, a wondering about whether some parents might have wanted to see each other's names, might have wanted the picnic to be a place where lists of strangers became a community. She did not say it. Some things could stay unresolved until the replies came in.

Mrs. Alvarez clicked send, and the fifty addresses folded themselves invisibly into the dark.

The grocery store car park was half empty at nine on a Saturday morning, and Samuel's mother had agreed, after some negotiation over the shopping list, to let him practise between the trolley bay and the low wall by the entrance. She sat in the passenger seat with her own agenda: she wanted the week's shop done before the bakery counter sold out of the seeded loaf, and she had told him twice that he had twenty minutes, not a minute more.

"Again," she said, unwrapping a mint she didn't offer to share. "You stopped too far out. A bus would take your wing mirror off."

He reversed between a silver hatchback and a battered van, easing the wheel, watching the van's bumper fill the rear window. His instructor, a patient man named Ellis, had given him a little phrase to hold onto: slow car, fast hands. It wasn't quite an epigram, but Samuel had begun to internalize it, the way a swimmer stops thinking about breathing, and the car slid into the space with only a soft kiss of the curb that he felt through the pedals before he heard it.

"Is that it?" his mother asked. "Is that a fail?"

"I don't know." He set the handbrake and looked at the curb, grey and dented by years of other learners. "Ellis says something about faults. Minor ones. You're allowed some."

She snorted, gathered her bag. "Allowed some. This country." She got out and went towards the trolleys, and Samuel sat a moment longer, engine ticking, wondering whether the touch of the curb was the kind of mistake that mattered or the kind that didn't.

He found out on Tuesday, in the waiting room of the test centre, because a boy a few years older was pacing by the noticeboard with his provisional licence flapping in his hand. "Fifteen," the boy was saying to nobody, to the room, to Samuel. "You can get fifteen driving faults and still pass. That's what it says. Fifteen. Just no serious ones, no dangerous ones." He laughed once, a short unsteady sound. "I clipped the curb on my park and I've been sick about it for an hour."

Samuel had his own test at ten past nine, and he listened while pretending to read the fire instructions. Fifteen faults. So a fault wasn't failure by itself; failure was a matter of kind, not count, unless the count grew large. The distinction felt important in a way he couldn't yet put into words, something about how a day could hold many small errors and still be a good day, provided nothing in it was serious.

When his own examiner, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, slid into the passenger seat, she was brisk but not unkind, and the drive itself was quieter than he had expected. The roads were capricious that morning, a delivery lorry double-parked outside the chemist, a jogger crossing against nothing in particular, but he kept his hands moving and his speed honest. On the parallel park, asked to do it between two cones in a side street, he came within a tyre's width of the curb and left it there, not perfect, not touching.

Then the motorway. The route sheet took them up the slip road, and the traffic in the near lane was moving faster than he liked, and he watched his mirror, signalled early, and waited for a gap with the patience Ellis had drilled into him, fast hands, slow decisions. A gap opened behind a grey estate; he took it, matched his speed, and merged the way water joins a current, almost without event. The examiner wrote something on her clipboard and said nothing, which he chose not to interpret.

Back in the test centre car park, she filled out the sheet and passed it to him, and he saw the faults marked in the first column, more than he would have guessed, less than the other kind, which was empty. "I'm recording that you passed," she said, peeling off her glasses. "Sign at the bottom."

In the corridor afterwards the older boy was still there, sitting now, staring at his own sheet. Samuel, clutching his, almost said something about the curb and what it turned out to mean, and then didn't, because he wasn't sure the boy's sheet said the same thing his did. He pushed through the doors into the grey morning, unlocked the car with his mother's spare key, and sat in the driver's seat for a moment before texting her: I passed. Can I drive us to the shop?

The library smelled of warm dust and the glue of old bindings, and Grayson had claimed the table by the window where the afternoon light fell in a long, patient stripe. He spread out his notebook, the calculus textbook, and a printout of the practice problems Ms. Okoro had posted, though he had already worked the first three and erased them twice. The unit was integrals, finding the area under a curve, and everyone kept saying it was just the reverse of derivatives, as if reversing something were simple, like walking a hallway backward.

"You're holding your pen like it insulted you," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from him. She opened her own notebook to a page of neat, small figures, rectangles drawn beneath a curve, skinny ones and fat ones, marching from left to right.

"It's the notation," Grayson said. He tapped the page. "The book writes the derivative as dy over dx, like a fraction. Then it turns around and says it's not a fraction. Which is it? I can't do the integral if I don't know what the symbols even are."

Priya leaned over and looked. "My brother went on about this once. He said that notation, the dy and the dx, comes from Leibniz. Gottfried Leibniz. And it's still what everybody uses, mathematicians today, everything." She shrugged. "He seemed to think that was a big deal."

Grayson wrote the name in his margin, then looked at it. So the symbols were older than the country they sat in, older than the library, and nobody had replaced them in all that time. That meant they were either perfect or so entrenched that no one could afford to change them. He wasn't sure which possibility he liked less, but he noticed, with something like relief, that the dy and dx now had a person attached to them, a man who had looked at a curve and reached for the language of fractions because fractions were what he had.

"Okay," he said slowly. "But look here." He drew a curve, then sketched a rectangle under it, then a second thinner one beside it. "You can parametrize the region, sort of. Slide along the x-axis and stack up slices, thin ones. Each slice has a height, which is the function's value, and a width, which is a little piece of x." He wrote dx beside the thin rectangle. "And then the sum of all of them, the areas, height times width, that's the sum of the y's times the dx's."

"You just wrote the same notation the book did," Priya said.

"I know. That's the strange part." He sat back. "It's not a fraction, but it behaves like one when you stack the slices, because you're multiplying a height by a width and getting an area, the way you would with any rectangle. It's a fraction that only makes sense in the limit, when the slices get infinitely thin. Or it's a picture of a fraction." He heard himself and stopped, worried he had talked past the truth rather than into it. "I think," he amended.

They worked in quiet for a while after that. Priya computed an area under a parabola and got a negative number, and they discovered together that part of her curve dipped below the x-axis, and that "area" apparently meant signed area, some regions subtracting from others, a rule neither of them had been warned about. Grayson found the curve in the harder problem had a vertical asymptote, a line the function crept toward and fled, so the region under it opened like a mouth, and he left that one alone for now.

At four o'clock the light had moved off his table and onto the shelves, and the librarian wheeled a cart of returns past them without slowing. Grayson had filled six pages. His integrals were not always right, but they were right more often, and he had stopped treating dy/dx as a riddle and started treating it as a tool that had survived three centuries of use, which was its own kind of credential, though not, he admitted to himself, proof of anything.

"Last one," Priya said, and turned her notebook toward him. She had solved the asymptote problem, the one he had skipped, and her answer was a finite number, a small clean area for a region that stretched upward forever. "How can that be?" she asked. "It goes up forever and the area stops?"

Grayson looked at the number for a long moment, then at the curve climbing its invisible wall, and pulled his chair around to her side of the table.

Rosalie had ruined four pounds of chocolate by Sunday afternoon, and the kitchen smelled like a bakery that had lost an argument with itself. She was preparing for the farmers' market in two weeks, where she planned to sell chocolate-dipped orange peel and plain dark bars wrapped in waxed paper, and she had discovered that melting chocolate and letting it harden again produced something gray and streaked, a thing that bent instead of snapping. Her mother had offered the double boiler and then retreated to the porch with her coffee, which Rosalie understood as a form of tact.

The problem, as far as she could piece together from her phone propped against the flour canister, was crystals. Cocoa butter could set into several different crystal forms, a small taxonomy of shapes, and only one of them behaved the way she wanted. Her physics teacher would have called it a phase diagram; her grandmother would have called it patience. Rosalie sat on the counter with her ankles crossed and read the same paragraph four times, and what she pulled out of it was this: Form V was the good one, and Form V cocoa butter crystals melted at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature.

She said the number out loud to the empty kitchen, and it struck her as almost theatrical, the way the universe had arranged a substance to hold its shape in a warm room and then surrender the instant it touched a tongue. Her friend Priya, who was given to grandiose pronouncements about nearly everything, would have expatiated on that for a quarter hour if given the chance. Rosalie texted her anyway: come over, bring the thermometer from your dad's toolbox.

Priya arrived with the thermometer and a bag of pretzels and read over Rosalie's notes while chocolate melted in the double boiler, careful and slow, no water allowed to spit into the bowl. "So you heat it, cool it, heat it a little again," Priya said. "Like you're teaching it something."

"Like I'm convincing it," Rosalie said. She stirred with a spatula in slow figure eights, watching the thermometer drop degree by degree. At thirty-two Celsius she seeded the bowl with a handful of chopped bar chocolate, already tempered, already organized at the molecular level in whatever way she couldn't see, and she felt the molten mass thicken against the spatula as if it were deciding something. She spread a test smear on parchment and waited ten minutes that felt longer than the whole afternoon.

The test patch set glossy, without bloom, and when she broke off a corner it snapped, a clean bright sound like a small branch. Priya, who had been narrating the wait with unnecessary commentary, went quiet. Rosalie pressed a square of the new chocolate into her palm and held it. It sat there, solid, acquiring only a faint softness at its edges while the seconds passed. Then she put a piece on her tongue and closed her mouth, and it melted immediately, entirely, into sweetness and something almost fruity underneath.

"Okay, that's strange," Priya said, watching her. "It didn't melt in your hand."

"It's the Form V crystals," Rosalie said. "They melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature. So it holds on the table and goes the second it hits your mouth." Priya looked at her own palm, then at the bowl, then took a piece and performed the same experiment herself, holding it, then tasting it, like a judge at a science fair. "Mouth, not hand," she reported, as if confirming a rumor.

The two weeks before the market were not entirely triumphant. One batch seized when a drop of condensation slid off the bowl's edge; another bloamed overnight in the garage where Rosalie had left it too near a window, and she had to start over, remelting and recooling, coaxing the crystals back into line. She kept a notebook with temperatures and times and failures, and she was honest in it, honest in a way she had never been with school assignments, where being wrong felt like being caught. Here being wrong was just data. On the morning of the market she carried two trays in a cardboard box, and Priya carried the folding table, and they set up between a honey seller and a man with radishes.

The day was warm for October, and by eleven the sun had moved onto their corner of the market. A woman bought an orange peel, held it while she dug for change, and frowned at it. "This isn't going to melt all over my hand?" Rosalie shook her head and told her about the temperature, the thirty-three point eight, the margin below her own body heat, and the woman looked from the chocolate to Rosalie to the sun and back, not entirely convinced, and ate it standing there. She bought three more before she left, and Priya leaned across the table and said, quietly, "Mouth, not hand."

Arianna had told everyone it would be fine, and she kept telling them, which was the first sign it wasn't. "It's the same weekend as the Calc exam," her friend Jess had said three weeks ago, and Arianna had waved her off, "No, Eid's in summer this year, like last year. We'll have the whole break." She said it with the confidence of someone who had never actually checked, only remembered, and memory is a loyal employee; it tells you what you've already decided. Now the festival filled four blocked-off streets with the smell of fried dough and cardamom, and her phone sat torpid in her pocket, holding a message she hadn't answered.

The plaza delimiting the north end of the fairgrounds was hung with white lights, and her little brother ran ahead toward the henna tents while her mother steered her toward the prayer area with a hand on her shoulder blade, the way you move furniture. "After prayer we eat, then your uncle's," her mother said. "You'll be home by nine." Arianna did not say that the Calc review session ran until ten. She nodded, because nodding was easier, and because she had already decided she would skip the review session and tell Jess she hadn't.

At the prayer line, her cousin Yusuf was folding his jacket over his arm, and when she grumbled about the timing he laughed at her. "You really thought it stays in summer?" he said. "The Islamic calendar is lunar, about ten to eleven days shorter than the solar year. So Ramadan and Eid come roughly ten to eleven days earlier every year." He said it the way you'd say water is wet, and she stood there recalculating every assumption she'd built her June around. "Earlier every year," she repeated. "Every single year." "Every year," he said, and went to find a spot on the mats.

She excused herself to the port-a-potties and instead walked to the fence at the fairground's edge, where the noise thinned. She typed fast, thumb stumbling: "You were right. Eid is now. My cousin says the calendar is lunar, 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so it moves earlier by that much every year. I thought it stayed put like a holiday. I thought I knew my own life's schedule. Not at the review session tonight. I'm sorry. A." She read it over, deleted "I thought I knew my own life's schedule" because it sounded like an apology for more than a calendar, and sent the rest.

The message arrived on Jess's phone during second period study hall, and Jess read it twice. Arianna made it sound like a tragedy, which was very Arianna; last month she'd claimed the chemistry teacher had it in for her, and the exam had come back with a 94. Still, Jess typed back carefully, because the friendship was worth more than being right: "The review is recorded, prof posts it same night. Go be with your family. But you owe me mango thing whatever it's called from the festival." She hesitated over the send button, then pressed it, then set the phone face down and went back to limits she actually understood.

Arianna read the reply near the biryani stall, where her mother was arguing amiably with an aunt about whether the rice here was as good as anyone's grandmother's. She turned the phone over and over in her hand. She had told Jess she was missing the session, full stop, a small martyrdom, and the recording had existed the whole time. She was, she had to admit, a person who curates; she'd once described herself to a college essay as "an aesthete of her own difficulties," and had cut the line before submitting, worried the admissions reader would find it precious. She found it precious. She also found it true.

Her brother came back with green henna climbing his wrist like ivy, badly done, and thrust his hand at her to admire. "It's a rocket ship," he said. "It's a snake with ambitions," she said, and he laughed and grabbed her sleeve and pulled her toward the stage where a man in a lavender kurta was testing a microphone, one, two, one, two.

Her mother found her there, standing in the crowd with the exam still folded somewhere inside the evening, not solved, only seen from a new angle. She knew the session would be watched at midnight, that she would be tired tomorrow, that Eid would slide backward through the seasons her whole life, April to March to February, and that she would have to learn to count instead of remember. What she didn't know yet was whether she'd tell Jess about the recording or let her keep believing in the sacrifice. Her brother tugged her hand again, insistent, and she let herself be pulled forward as the drums started.

The scale read 24.6 grams, and Katherine read it aloud twice, as if the number might change if she gave it a second chance. On the counter sat the sealed plastic bag from her brother Danny's science fair project, the one he had abandoned three days ago when the seventh grade judge asked him a question he could not answer. The bag contained baking soda, vinegar, and a balloon of gas trapped against the sides, the reaction long finished. Katherine had weighed it before she opened her chemistry notebook, and now, after everything inside had rearranged itself, she weighed it again. 24.6 grams. Exactly.

"Write it down," Danny said from the doorway, in his dour way, chin resting on the doorframe. He had been sulking since the fair, convinced the universe had cheated him. "You weigh it, then you weigh it again, then you stare at it. That's not going to fix my grade."

"I'm not trying to fix your grade." She turned the notebook toward him so he could see the two numbers, side by side and identical. "Before the reaction, all that stuff was reactants. After, it's products. Same bag, same everything, still 24.6 grams."

"So?"

"So nothing leaked out and nothing appeared. In a closed system like this, the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants." She tapped the bag. "It's called the law of conservation of mass. Your judge asked you where the fizzing went, and this was the answer, and you had it sitting right there in your hands."

Danny came closer, picked up the bag, and turned it over. He was quiet for a moment, which for Danny was practically an apology. "Then why did I lose?"

Katherine didn't answer right away, because the honest answer was that he had lost for a hundred small reasons, and she was not sure the bag could rescue any of them. What she was sure about was her own exam, tomorrow morning, on equilibrium. She pulled the notebook back and reread the problem set. A reaction at equilibrium, held at some temperature, and then the temperature raised. Which way does it shift? The textbook language was Le Chatelier's principle, the idea that a system pushed out of balance pushes back, but the diagrams kept sliding apart in her mind.

Here was what bothered her, and she said so to Danny, who had flopped into the chair across from her with the resigned air of someone with nowhere better to be. The mass never changed. That was settled, beautiful, fixed. But equilibrium itself was not fixed at all; it moved when you changed the temperature, spitting out more products or swallowing them back. Two truths that seemed to face in opposite directions. "It's like a dialectic," she said, drawing the word up from somewhere in an English class she'd half slept through. "One idea, then the opposing idea, and you have to hold them together instead of picking a side. Mass holds still. Equilibrium moves. Both are true."

"So which answer do you write down?"

"That's the part I keep getting wrong." She flipped to the marked-up quiz from last week, the one with the red slash through question four. She had guessed that raising the temperature always pushed toward products, because hot things expand, or something equally unexamined, and Mrs. Okoye had written "Why?" in the margin, which was worse than an X. Katherine sat with it now. The heat wasn't a substance you could weigh; it didn't add mass, didn't subtract it. It was more like a shove, and the system leaned away from the shove. If the forward reaction behaved as if it soaked up the heat, then adding heat pushed the system backward, toward the reactants, until a new balance formed. And if the forward reaction gave heat off, the shift went the other way. The mass of the whole closed setup stayed put through every one of those shifts, patient and unbothered, while the balance point itself wandered.

She worked the practice problem again, and this time she wrote the direction and, beside it, the reason in her own words: the system shifts to oppose the change in temperature. She could not claim total certainty; she still could not say why nature behaved this way rather than some other way, and she suspected the textbook could not either, not really. But she could predict, and prediction was the thing being graded. She underlined the answer, then reached across and slid the sealed bag toward Danny.

"Take it," she said. "Tomorrow, ask your teacher if you can redo the demo. Weigh it in front of everyone. 24.6 before, 24.6 after."

Danny looked at the bag, then at her, and pulled it across the table into his lap.

The flyer had been taped to the gym door since September, curling at one corner like a leaf that refused to fall: Spring Trip, Washington D.C., $640, deposits due by February. Ava stopped in front of it every day on her way to fifth period, and every day the number sat there, patient and indifferent, the way numbers are. She had $212 in a savings account her grandmother had opened when she was nine, and four months.

At lunch she spread the problem in front of her friend Denise like a hand of cards. "If I put in eighty a month from my paycheck, that's what, three-twenty plus the two-twelve. I'm still short." She tore the crust off her sandwich and lined the pieces along the table's edge, sedimentary layers of bread, each one settling on the last. "Unless it grows somehow. Does money in savings grow?"

"Mine has interest," Denise said, thumbing through her phone. "Like point-something percent. My mom calls it sad money. It grows, but slowly."

"Slowly how?" Ava leaned over. On the screen, a calculator app, and Denise typed in numbers with the flat authority of someone who had done this before, which she had, because Denise's mother made her balance the family checkbook as punishment for various crimes. "Two hundred at two percent," Denise said. "Four dollars a year. It doesn't just add four forever, though. After the first year it's two-oh-four, and the two percent works on that. So the next year it's a little more than four."

Ava sat back. The interest fed on whatever was there, and what was there kept getting bigger, so the interest kept getting bigger too. "So waiting is worth something," she said slowly. "Even boring waiting."

That afternoon her brother Marcus picked her up in the Camry he'd bought in August, used, from a lot off Route 9 with flags snapping in the wind. He was twenty-one and treated the car like a wound he was proud of. At a red light he pulled his phone from the cup holder and frowned at it, and Ava, who noticed everything when she was curious and nothing when she wasn't, noticed the frown.

"What."

"They sent the loan statement." He held it out. Four payments made, it said, and beside it the remaining balance, and Ava did the subtraction in her head and then did it again because the answer didn't move. He'd paid almost seven hundred dollars and the balance had dropped by barely more than three.

"That can't be right." She took the phone and scrolled, as if the missing money might be hiding further down. "You paid seven hundred and it only went down three-something?"

"That's what the guy said it would do," Marcus said, gripping the wheel as the light turned. "Each payment's interest gets charged on what's left, so the early payments mostly go to interest. Later they go more toward the actual loan." He said it flat, like reciting a scar. "Front-loaded. I didn't really get it until I saw it."

Ava looked at the statement, then out the window at the strip mall sliding past, the nail salon, the payday loan place with its neon OPEN sign, the bank with its quiet stone front. Two directions, and money traveling both. In the savings account, interest landed on a balance that grew, so the growth fed itself. In the loan, interest was taken first, off the remaining balance, so the balance she and Marcus actually wanted to shrink shrank slowly at the start, faster later, like something paying its dues before it was allowed to leave. She didn't know yet whether the two were opposites exactly, or only mirror-ish, and she held the question the way you hold a stone you intend to look at again later.

"Could you pay extra?" she asked. "Toward the balance part?"

"The principal. Maybe. I'd have to ask."

"Ask." She handed the phone back. "Because if extra knocks the balance down early, then there's less for the interest to feed on the whole way. That's how it works, right? Less there, less charged."

Marcus glanced at her. "When did you become a bank."

"I need six hundred forty dollars by February and I'm trying to think like money does."

He laughed, short and surprised. In the driveway she sat in the car a minute longer after he took the phone inside, doing arithmetic on the fog of the window with her fingertip. Eighty a month, plus what she had, plus whatever the interest added, and it wouldn't be enough, probably, unless she picked up Shira's Saturday shifts at the bakery, and she was still deciding whether she wanted the trip more than she wanted the Saturdays. Inside, Marcus called out, "Hey, I'm calling the loan place," and she wiped the numbers away with her sleeve and went to hear what they said.

Ella sat at the kitchen table with her physics problem set open to the last question, the one worth the most marks. Between two charged plates separated by 0.04 metres, a potential difference of 200 volts, compute the field strength at the midpoint. She had written E equals V over d twice and crossed it out twice, because the word "midpoint" kept snagging on something she couldn't name.

Her grandfather was at the sink filling a kettle, telling her younger brother Tomás about the summer he worked on a dredge on the alluvial flats of the river, sorting silt from gravel by hand. He was a raconteur of the kitchen-sink variety; every chore became an occasion. Tomás, who was twelve and had no homework, was flicking water at the window with his fingers.

"Stop that," their grandfather said, without turning.

Tomás adjusted his aim and flicked a stream sideways from the tap instead, a thin arc of water that rose, bent, and landed in the draining rack. Ella looked up from her paper to tell him to quit it, and then kept looking. The arc curved. She grabbed her phone and photographed it before the tap got shut off.

"Send me that," she said.

"Why?"

"Just send it."

She pulled the photo up beside her notebook and sketched the arc freehand, then laid her ruler along the top of the jet's rise and dropped verticals from it to the curve at even intervals. The distances grew in a pattern she recognized, the same one her graphs made in math when she plotted x squared. A parabola. She had seen that exact shape before, on a school trip to the science museum in the city, where a water jet arced between two spouts and a placard beside it said that Galileo had shown that the path of a projectile, ignoring air resistance, is a parabola. The placard had the date too. She checked her memory against her notes app, where she'd typed things up on the bus home, and found her own line from that day: Two New Sciences, published in 1638. She'd written the title down because it sounded like a book she might want, and then never found it anywhere.

"Tomás," she said, "what's the name of the book Galileo wrote?"

"How would I know?"

"Two New Sciences," their grandfather said from the stove. "There were only the two, and my father said that was two more than most men manage." He stirred the pot and did not elaborate.

Ella turned back to her problem. The thing that had snagged her, she realized now, was a wrong picture: she had been imagining the field strength tapering toward the middle, weaker halfway between the plates, as though the charges pulled at the edges and faded in between. But the parabola was teaching her something about idealizations. Galileo's curve held only if you ignored air resistance, the placard had said; the water jet curved anyway, close enough, because the ideal case described the real one within a tolerance you could see. Between parallel plates, the field wasn't a fading thing. It was uniform, the same at the midpoint as anywhere else, because that was what the ideal case meant between plates: E equals V over d, one value everywhere between them. Her crossed-out attempts had been right. What had been wrong was her suspicion of them.

She did the arithmetic in the margin. 200 divided by 0.04. She moved the decimal twice and got 5000 volts per metre, and checked it by dividing again. Then she sat with the number and made herself be honest about it. The plates in her textbook were perfect and infinite in every direction that mattered; the ones in a lab would have edges where the field frayed. Her answer was true of the ideal case, and the midpoint of the ideal case sat inside the real case like the parabola sat inside the water. She wrote the answer and underlined it once, and then, on a separate line, wrote "assuming uniform field," because that part she was not certain of and did not intend to pretend to be.

Later she caught herself trying to introspect on why the wrong picture had held her for two days, but there was nothing there, only the fact that a picture had felt right and been wrong, which she supposed she would meet again in college.

She texted a photo of the finished page to Priya, who replied with a single thumbs-up and then, a minute later, "wait how did you get the midpoint part." Ella typed: "it's the same everywhere between the plates," and set the phone face-down as Tomás flicked another arc of water across the sink.

The parking lot behind the shuttered Kmart still had its lines, faded to the color of old milk, and Justine's father had chosen it for exactly that emptiness, arriving at seven on a Saturday so no one would see her stall the car. His own want was barely concealed: he had waited sixteen years for a child old enough to want the keys, and he had spent the drive over narrating his father's driving habits as though handing down scripture. Justine knew he wanted this hour to be a thing they shared, an inheritance, and she half wanted that too, which made it harder when she didn't.

Her friend Priya had ridden with her to the lot, sprawled in the back seat with a slushie, and had already issued her doctrine. "Two seconds," Priya said, leaning between the front seats. "You count one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, and if you pass the same spot before two, you back off. Two is plenty. My brother taught me and he's never had a ticket."

"Three," her father said, not turning around. "At least three seconds."

"That's what old people do," Priya said, and sucked loudly at the straw.

He eased the car to the far end of the lot and they swapped seats, and Justine put her hands where the instructor poster said ten and two, though her father immediately said nine and three was better now, and she changed, feeling the day begin to accumulate small corrections. She let off the brake too fast and the car lurched, and she laughed the way you laugh to keep something else from happening in your face. Her father only said, "Again," in the voice he used when he was trying very hard not to be the kind of man who yelled.

For a while it was only starts and stops, the wheel surprisingly light in her palms, the lot a slow geometry of turns. Then her father pointed at the service road beyond the lot's broken gate, two lanes of Saturday traffic, and said, "You're ready for that." Priya said, "She's not," and he said, "The lot doesn't teach you anything but the lot." Justine pulled out anyway, because she wanted the road more than she wanted to be careful, and it was on the road, behind a hatchback with a mattress strapped to its roof, that the two doctrines collided.

"Count it," her father said. "Pick a line on the pavement, a sign, anything fixed. When the mattress car passes it, start counting. See how long until you reach it."

"One-one-thousand, two-one-thousand," Justine said under her breath, and reached the painted arrow before she finished the second. She eased off the gas until the count ran to three and felt the road widen around her, the hatchback shrinking into something she could think about instead of react to. Priya made a scornful noise from the back, and Justine said nothing, but she noticed that when a drizzle started, beading on the windshield faster than the wipers could sweep it, three seconds felt suddenly small.

"It's raining," she said. "Does that change it?"

Her father was quiet a moment, in the way of a man checking whether he actually knew. "You add a second for each difficulty," he said. "Bad weather, heavy traffic. So rain makes it four."

"Who decided that?" Priya demanded.

"The National Safety Council recommends it," he said, which was the most authoritative thing he'd said all morning, and also the least like him, a borrowed certainty. Justine counted to four behind the mattress car and watched the gap open, and thought that Priya's two seconds were not exactly wrong so much as made for a world with no rain in it, and her father's three were not exactly right so much as made for a world where everything might go wrong at once. The truth she could hold was somewhere between: the count wasn't a number you learned once, it was a number you earned again with every new thing the road did.

She would have liked to say this out loud, some announcement of her own perspicacity, but the moment for announcements passed; the light ahead turned yellow and she braked harder than she meant to, and the car behind them honked, and Priya said, "See, that guy was at two," and her father laughed before he could stop himself. Justine realized he was not laughing at her. It was the honk, the rain, the mattress, the whole rattling pageant of the road, and he looked younger than he had at breakfast.

Later, back in the Kmart lot, the rain stopped and they sat with the engine ticking. "Again next Saturday?" he said, and she heard how carefully casual it was, how much it mattered to him that she say yes, as if the lessons were a way of inculcating something larger than driving, some habit of counting and looking ahead that he wanted planted in her before September took her three hundred miles away. She said yes. But when she dropped Priya at home that afternoon, Priya leaned in the window and said, "Two seconds, Juste. Don't let him turn you into a paranoid." Justine put the car in drive, found a seam in the pavement, and counted, under her breath, all the way to three.

The kitchen at Ferro's smelled like burnt sugar and lemon, and by eleven on Saturday morning it belonged to Morgan, more or less, since her uncle only trusted her with the station farthest from the heat. She stood over a bain-marie of dark chocolate, stirring with a metal spatula, watching the thermometer crawl down through 100 degrees. Her uncle had shown her once, in April, how tempered chocolate should behave: shiny when it set, and it snapped when you broke it, a clean sound like a knuckle cracking. Untempered chocolate bent. It went dull and streaked and refused to commit to any shape at all.

She had ruined two batches already this morning. The first had seized when a drop of water found its way in, turning gritty and stiff in seconds, and the second she had rushed, pulling it off the heat too soon, so that when she spread a test smear on parchment it dried matte as an old chalkboard. On her third attempt she moved slowly, added the reserved chunks of unmelted chocolate one at a time, and wondered whether this was what people meant by patience. It did not feel like patience. It felt like a negotiation, her thermometer, her stirring, and the chocolate's own private opinion about temperature, all three of them arguing toward an agreement she couldn't hear.

Her phone sat propped against a container of cocoa powder, open to her other project. Sunday night she meant to cook a week of lunches for her mother, who worked doubles at the hospital and otherwise ate vending machine crackers dressed up as lunch. Morgan had found a schedule, seven containers, Sunday afternoons, everything at once. But she'd paused on a government food safety page, and now she read it twice, then a third time, because something about it didn't fit her plan.

"Three to four days," she said out loud, to nobody, to the chocolate. "Refrigerated cooked leftovers, three to four days." She did the arithmetic on the back of a delivery slip with a pencil stub. Cooked Sunday, day one was Monday. Four days got her through Thursday. Friday's container, Saturday's, Sunday's: those were days five, six, seven. The page said the limit was three to four days refrigerated, which meant the last three lunches had to go in the freezer or the whole plan fell apart. She'd been so pleased with her seven neat containers lined up like evidence of her own competence, and now the arithmetic told her the fridge could only carry her partway.

"You're talking to it now," said Dani, the pastry cook, sliding past with a tray of tart shells. "That's stage two."

"What's stage one?"

"Talking to yourself. Stage three is it answering."

Morgan laughed and went back to stirring. The chocolate was coming down through the low nineties now, and she kept it moving in slow figure eights, coaxing rather than forcing. That was the word her uncle used, coaxing, and she'd thought it was florid when she first heard it, the kind of overworked language chefs loved, but watching the melted chocolate catch and smooth around the spatula she admitted it was simply accurate. You could not command chocolate into temper. You offered it the right temperature and waited for it to decide.

There was an older customer, Mr. Aldous, who came in every Friday and ordered the same torte and stayed two hours, and once Morgan had heard her uncle eulogize him to the waitstaff as the last true epicure in the county, a man who tasted everything slowly and forgave nothing. The kitchen took those customers seriously. It also took seriously the woman who ordered dessert for a six-year-old's birthday and cared mostly that it looked cheerful. Morgan had assumed, when she started, that only the first kind of customer mattered, that caring about food meant caring about perfection. But her mother's frozen Friday lunch was going to be reheated in a hospital microwave and eaten standing up in a supply room, and it still mattered, maybe differently but not less. She hadn't worked out yet whether those two ways of caring about food were the same thing wearing different clothes or genuinely different things. She suspected she wouldn't know for years.

She took the bowl off the heat at 88 degrees and held her breath. Then she dipped the tip of a knife and set the smear of chocolate on the marble slab to wait. Waiting was the part that undid her. Every instinct wanted to touch it, test it, hurry it along, the same instinct that had wrecked batch two. But the chocolate kept its own schedule the way the leftovers kept theirs, and both schedules were indifferent to her preferences. That was the strange comfort of it, actually: the rules didn't bend for anybody, not for the Friday epicure, not for a sixteen-year-old with a thermometer.

While she waited she opened the freezer in the corner of the kitchen, the big stainless one that hummed like a held breath, and counted the shelf space. Three containers would fit on the middle shelf if she laid them flat. She'd transfer them from fridge to freezer on Wednesday night, she decided, before day five arrived, and she'd tell her mother to move one down each evening so it thawed by lunchtime. It wasn't the plan she'd started with. It was a better one, or at least an honest one, built on what the food actually could and couldn't do rather than on how tidy the containers looked in a row.

"Morgan," Dani called, "your test's ready."

She peeled the smear off the marble. It was glossy, really glossy, the surface like a dark lake at dusk, and when she snapped it in half the sound came, clean and bright, echoing slightly off the tile walls. Dani looked over and nodded once, which from Dani was a speech.

Morgan held the two halves up to the window light and turned them, watching the shine move. "Again," she said, reaching for the spatula.

The gown was too hot before the ceremony even started.
