She practiced on Priya for an hour, and Priya, whose actual want surfaced only gradually, interrupted near the end. "If I asked Mom to go with me," she said, "would they let her in the room?" Sarah said she didn't know, that it probably depended, that Priya could call and ask without giving her name. Priya nodded and didn't look up, and Sarah understood that the question had not been hypothetical, and that she was not going to ask which part of it wasn't. This was the price of being the sister who knew things: you got the questions, and you rarely got the story behind them.

Their mother came home at nine with takeout and the interminable retelling of a staff meeting, and somewhere in it she began to excoriate a colleague, a man named Rick who had apparently taken credit for the quarterly numbers, and Sarah listened with half an ear while highlighting her contraception cards. Her mother's frustration had a familiar shape, the shape of someone whose competence was treated as ambient, and Sarah thought about disincentives the health teacher had mentioned, the ways fear of judgment kept people from clinics, and how both her mother and a scared sixteen-year-old at Ames Street were governed by the same arithmetic: if speaking up costs more than staying quiet pays, people stay quiet. She filed the thought for her closing slide and then deleted it from the closing slide, because it was too true for a Friday afternoon audience.

The night before the presentation, Sarah rehearsed alone in her room. She said the word consent eleven times until it stopped sounding strange. She rehearsed the clinic part with the most care, the part about walk-in hours and what the nurse would ask and how long results took, because that was the part that was actually a set of stairs someone could climb. When she got to the end she stood in front of her mirror and realized she still had the clinic printout folded in her jacket pocket, 118 over 76, the word normal in blue ink. Below 120, below 80. She had walked in healthy and had not known it, and half the people she'd be talking to tomorrow would walk in scared and not know that either.

The next afternoon she stood at the front of the room with her cards, and the first slide came up, and Tommy Wilcox in the second row said something about the tea video that she couldn't quite hear, and a laugh moved through the room like weather. Sarah looked down at her cards, then back up.

"This part takes four minutes," she said. "Then you can go back to whatever you were doing." She turned to the next card, and began.

Eric had promised himself he would finish the hallway drawing before fifth period ended, and he had forty minutes left, a pencil sharpened to a needle, and a hallway that refused to be a hallway. It lay on the paper like something flattened by a steamroller, a row of lockers marching across the page with the depth of a filing cabinet. He had drawn the drinking fountain three times. Each time it sat on top of the lockers instead of beside them, like a very clean frog.

"You've redrawn that fountain so many times it's going to ask for a contract," said Priya from the next stool, not looking up from her print of crows. She and Eric had a running arrangement: she critiqued his drawing, he critiqued her titles, and both of them ignored the teacher's suggestion that they critique their own work for once.

"The hallway's broken," Eric said. "It's a hallway for people with no depth perception. Flatland High School."

Priya leaned over, held her pencil at arm's length against his paper, and squinted like a pirate. "Everything's parallel. Your lockers are all the same size, and the door at the end is the same size too. That's why it looks like a poster for a very boring school."

He knew she was right, and he hated how right she was, because he had spent two nights on the tile pattern alone. The tiles. He had drawn a hundred tiles, each one exactly, obediently square, and somewhere in the back of his mind a suspicion had been forming that the tiles were the traitors. When he stood in the actual hallway, the far tiles looked smaller. He had never once drawn them smaller. He had, apparently, been running a hallway according to his own private laws of geometry, laws the hallway had never agreed to follow.

He flipped to a clean page and started over, this time being sneaky about it. He drew one point in the middle of the paper and then, feeling like a con artist, made the locker edges run toward that point like they were late for a bus. The tiles shrank as they went. The door at the end came out small, and strange, and then, all at once, deep. The hallway opened like a drawer sliding out of the page. He sat back so fast his stool squeaked.

"Whoa," Priya said. "What did you just do?"

"I don't know. I made the lines go toward one spot." He tapped the point with his eraser. "It's like everything's running away from the viewer to hide back there."

"That's a thing," Priya said, already pulling out her phone with the guilty speed of someone who knew the teacher would confiscate it in a heartbeat. "My brother did a report on it. Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective. Drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point, to show depth on a flat surface."

"So I accidentally invented it in an art room in Ohio."

"You're about six hundred years late and an ocean short, but sure, Columbus it however you like." She grinned. "Brunelleschi would be furious that you tried to expropriate his idea with a number two pencil."

"It's not expropriation if I didn't know it existed. It's independent rediscovery. It's very dignified."

The teacher drifted past, looked at the new drawing for a long moment, and said only, "Better," which from her was a standing ovation, and moved on. Eric looked at the vanishing point and felt both pleased and slightly cheated. He had wanted to invent something, and instead he had reinvented something, which meant either that he was six centuries late or that the idea was so true that a seventeen-year-old with a mechanical pencil could stumble into it on a Tuesday. He could not decide which of those he preferred, and the point itself, that small dot where the whole hallway went to disappear, gave him no help at all.

"Draw the drinking fountain now," Priya said. "It can finally live beside the lockers instead of on them, like a civilized amphibian."

Eric positioned his pencil, then paused. "One problem. If everything runs to the point, the fountain's edges have to aim there too, and it's off to the side. Do I give it its own point?"

"That's not a problem, that's Thursday."

He laughed, sharpened the pencil again, and began the fountain for the fourth time, angling its lines carefully toward that one small dot at the end of the hall.

The chocolate had failed twice before Zoey understood that failure was the whole curriculum. Her first batch, poured onto waxed paper in her grandmother's kitchen, had set overnight into something gray and dusty, bending like an eraser when she tried to break it, and the second had bloomed with pale streaks while she slept, as though winter had gotten into the pantry. She was eighteen and had two weeks at her grandmother's house before orientation, and she had promised herself she would leave with one skill that had nothing to do with anything she would study.

She found the answer in a battered paperback, "Chocolate Science for the Serious Amateur," shelved between a canning manual and a book of florid inscriptions her grandmother had collected from old greeting cards. Cocoa butter, the book said, could crystallize in six different forms. Zoey read the sentence three times, then read it aloud to the empty kitchen. Six. And only one of them, form V, gave chocolate its shine and its clean snap. Every other form was dull, or soft, or streaked, or all three. Tempering was the art of coaxing most of the cocoa butter into that single form and keeping it there.

"Six forms," she told her grandmother at lunch, spreading butter on toast. "And only form V gives you shine and snap." Her grandmother nodded and asked whether Zoey had eaten, though the toast was in Zoey's hand. It had been like this since spring. The doctors used words like progression, and Zoey had stopped flinching at them; the summer had desensitized her to small wrongness, the repeated asking, the keys in the refrigerator. What she had not gotten used to was the kitchen itself, which still worked perfectly, still smelled of her grandmother's old precision, the copper bowl hanging on its hook like a retired instrument.

The method she pieced together from the book was simple to state and merciless in practice. She chopped a bar of dark chocolate into pieces the size of thumbnails, set two thirds of it in a steel bowl over simmering water, and stirred until it melted entirely, erasing every crystal the chocolate had ever known. Then she pulled the bowl off the heat and beat in the remaining third, cold from the pantry, chopped fine. The seed chocolate, the book called it, and she liked that; it sounded like something you could believe in. She stirred and stirred with the thermometer lying in the bowl like a lazy fish, watching the numbers fall through the range where form V could survive and the other forms could not.

Her grandmother drifted in while the chocolate was at ninety-one degrees, sat down at the table in her pink cardigan, and watched. "You used to read recipes like scripture," Zoey said, stirring. "I remember you saying that." Her grandmother frowned, working at the memory the way she worked at names now, patiently, with her fingers laced. "A recipe is a text," she said finally, with the careful dignity of someone reciting something she trusted, "and a text wants interpreting." Zoey laughed, surprised. In her grandmother's good years she had taught a seminar on interpretation, on hermeneutics, and had treated a béchamel the way she treated a poem: as something with a history that had to be honored and then changed.

"It wants interpreting and it wants obedience," Zoey said. "Both at once. That's the terrible part." The thermometer read eighty-nine. She dipped a knife tip and waited, and this time, when the smear set, it set in under two minutes, glossy as wet stone. She almost shouted. She poured the tempered chocolate into the bar molds she had bought with her last paycheck, tapped out the bubbles, and slid them into the cool pantry, and her grandmother said, "You always did have cold hands. Like your mother."

The bars set for an hour. When Zoey turned one out of its mold, it came free with a click, and the surface was so dark and even it looked like a pane of night. She broke a corner off and the break was audible, a hard, dry, decisive sound, and the broken face showed a clean grain. She carried a piece to her grandmother, who held it and studied it as though it were a small mirror. "Beautiful," her grandmother said, and put it in her mouth, and chewed, and for a moment her whole face was young. Then she said, "What is this?" and swallowed, and the moment closed like water over a dropped stone.

Zoey wrapped the rest of the bars in foil. There were six of them, and she labeled each with a strip of masking tape: FOR MOM, FOR DAD, FOR THE ROOMMATE I HAVEN'T MET. She would take them to campus in a cooler pack, three hundred miles, and hand them out during that first week when everyone was performing themselves. It had cost her something to make them, the whole afternoon, and the last of her certainty that her grandmother was only tired. She knew now, and knowing sat in her like the seed chocolate had sat in the bowl, hard and necessary, melting slowly.

On the last morning, she tempered one more batch, smaller, and poured it into the mold shaped like a maple leaf, her grandmother's favorite. She worked without the thermometer this time, testing by the cooling on her lip, because she had learned the numbers and then learned to leave them behind, which felt like the only kind of mastery worth having. The leaf set perfectly. She set it on a saucer in front of her grandmother with a cup of coffee, and her grandmother picked it up and turned it over and smiled.

"I made these," her grandmother said. "Years ago. I never could get them shiny like this." She broke the leaf in half with a snap that rang in the quiet kitchen, and ate her own chocolate, and did not offer any back.

The kitchen table had been Sophia's desk for three days, and by now it held the shape of her thinking: two pencils, one snapped near the eraser, a printed score of Mozart's Piano Sonata in A major, K. 331, and a phone face down beside the sugar bowl. The assignment was due Friday. Mark the first movement's form, her professor had said, as though form were a thing you could outline in pencil, when really it moved under her hands like water.

She had begun, as everyone began, with the obvious. The theme stated itself in the first six measures, plainly, almost childishly. Then came the variations, and her certainty dissolved. Her textbook insisted that sonata form meant an exposition, a development, a recapitulation, and that these sections could be found, bracketed, labeled. The textbook made it sound like sorting mail. But measure by measure, the melody kept transmuting itself, ornament folding into ornament, until Sophia could not say where the theme ended and its disguise began. She drew a bracket, erased it, drew it shorter, erased it again.

Her phone buzzed at half past seven. A message from Danny, who played piano in the jazz ensemble and had never once, in four years of friendship, asked her for anything academic.

"Big favor," the message read. "Playing a thing Saturday for my cousin's engagement party. Somebody gave me the melody only, no accompaniment, and I can't build anything from a bare tune. You know theory. Could you write the chords in for me? Just put them over the notes, the way you'd want them. I'll pay you in samosas."

Sophia typed back, "Over the notes how?" because she genuinely did not know what he meant. She had spent two years reading scores from the bottom up, bass to soprano, harmony as something latent in the counterpoint.

"Like a lead sheet," he answered. "Chord symbols above the staff. C, Am, G7, whatever fits, written over the spot in the melody where the chord goes with it. That's how it works. Then I can see what to play under the tune at a glance." Then, a few seconds later: "Please. My cousin already paid the deposit on the hall."

She looked at the message for a long moment. It was such a backwards way of thinking. In Mozart, the harmony was the melody's shadow, inseparable from it, implied in every leap and resolution. In Danny's world, the melody stood alone on the staff and the chords floated above it like weather markers, C over this bar, G7 over that, the accompaniment reducible to a handful of letters. She wrote back that she would try, and pulled the simple tune he had photographed toward her, a folk-ish thing in C major with no accidentals to trouble anyone.

The work was easier than she wanted it to admit to being. She hummed the melody, felt where it rested on G and wanted to go home, and wrote G7 above that measure. Where it sank toward the third of the chord, she wrote C. An Am appeared over the phrase that darkened, briefly, like a cloud crossing a lawn. The letters accumulated above the staff in her small, judicious handwriting, and the strange thing was that the tune became clearer to her, not less mysterious but more legible, its phrases suddenly visible as harmonic decisions rather than as a ribbon of sound.

She photographed the page and sent it, then sat back down at Mozart with the two ways of thinking still running in her at once. On the lead sheet, structure was written above the music, explicit, a row of signs. In the sonata, structure had to be inferred from below, from the grain of the thing. She picked up her pencil again and, instead of asking where the exposition ended, asked what the music itself was doing when it left home. The moment the harmony pulled away from the tonic, the moment a small restlessness entered, she marked a double bar. Her hand was nearly steady.

The phone rang. Not a message this time, an actual call, and Danny's voice came through tinny and too fast. "It's perfect, thank you, but listen, the real reason I asked you." A pause long enough for her to hear a television somewhere behind him. "My cousin's fiancé is a conservatory guy. He's going to be watching me play. I didn't want to tell you that before because you'd have said no, you always say no when it matters to someone's reputation."

"You're my reputation now?"

"Saturday night. Eight o'clock. The samosas are already ordered." He hung up before she could answer, which was his way of preventing refusal.

Sophia set the phone back beside the sugar bowl, face down again. The room had gone quiet enough that she could hear the refrigerator's hum, and she recognized, with some irritation, the particular ennui of a Friday evening spent indoors, the feeling that everyone else was already somewhere else. She looked at her score. Her brackets stood now where the harmony said they should: an exposition that ended when the music reached its second key, a development she had traced through the wandering, a recapitulation that began, quietly, exactly where the theme returned home. Whether her professor would agree, whether the labels were truth or merely her best guess, she could not yet say, and she let that uncertainty sit on the table beside her without sweeping it away.

She copied the page in ink, folded it, and wrote on the outer sheet, in letters as small as chord symbols: Sophia, third floor, if the fiancé hates it. Then she carried it out to the mailbox at the curb, and the lid of the blue box clanged shut behind it.

Rose found the notice taped to the circulation desk of the public library, between a flyer for toddler story hour and a laminated map of the county bus routes. First-time volunteers welcome, it said, Saturday, seven a.m., dress for mud. She had been meaning to do something that wasn't school, something that would look less like a line on an application and more like a fact about her, and she had been circumspect about which something, because she distrusted her own motives and didn't want to be the girl who photographed her own kindness. She copied the address onto the back of a receipt and checked out a novel she would not read.

Saturday came cold and clear. The food bank's van waited in the library parking lot, which served as the meeting point, and beside it stood a man in a canvas jacket counting heads on a clipboard. Eleven volunteers, most of them older than Rose, all of them strangers. The man, whose name was Teodoro, drove them out past the edge of town to a farm where the squash field had already been picked over once by the crew that mattered, the paid crew, the main harvest.

"You'll see squash out there still," Teodoro said as they stepped down into the rows. "Anything you gather goes to the food bank. It's called gleaning." He said it the way he might have said the word for a bird or a tool, and then he handed out crates and gloves and walked off toward the far end of the field.

The rows were messy in a way Rose hadn't expected. The plants lay half flattened, and under them the squash had gone pale where the ground had touched them, scarred where a machine had brushed past. She picked one up, turned it over, and hesitated over a soft brown patch the size of her thumb. Whole or not whole. She looked up to ask someone and saw that the other volunteers had already scattered, bent and working, their crates filling without ceremony. Nobody was going to tell her. She set the blemished one aside and kept the rest.

Dana, the volunteer nearest her, was maybe sixty and moved with the ease of a person who had done this many seasons. "Soft spots mean it won't store," Dana said, not looking up. "Hard ones are just ugly. People think food bank means perfect produce, and then it rots in the field because nobody paid for it." Rose asked whether the farmer couldn't sell it, and Dana shrugged one shoulder. "After the main harvest, what's left isn't worth the labor to him. But it's still food. So we come." Rose worked that around while she worked the row. It seemed to her a strange economy, that a thing could be worthless and good at the same time, and she tested the idea against each squash she lifted.

By mid-morning the problem found them. The crates were full, more than half the field still unpicked, and the van had room for only what was crated. The second shift, Teodoro announced from the end of the row, had fallen through, so whatever they didn't get today would be disked into the soil on Monday. Rose watched the volunteers glance at each other, at the sun, at their phones. One by one they began to say they had things, errands, a granddaughter's recital. Teodoro didn't argue. He began stacking crates with the flat efficiency of a man preparing to lose.

Rose had been quiet all morning, and quiet people can sometimes say a thing plainly. "We don't all have to stay," she said. "Some of us could keep picking while the van runs the first load over. Then it comes back for the rest." Dana looked at her, then at the field, then at Teodoro. Teodoro turned his clipboard over as if the answer might be written on the back.

From where Dana stood, it looked like this: a girl of eighteen, mud to the knees of a jacket too thin for the weather, holding a scarred squash in both hands like evidence in a case she was still arguing with herself. Dana had spent enough years in this work to know that schemes hatched at eleven in the morning often died by noon, and she was not going to flatter the girl by pretending otherwise. But she had also spent enough years to know that a full crate driven to the pantry at noon fed someone at six. "I'll stay for the second round," Dana said. "I've got nothing until four." Two of the recital people, cajoled less by Teodoro than by their own shame, muttered that they could stay an hour, and the numbers on the clipboard stopped being a countdown.

The van went loaded and came back empty in time for lunch. Rose's arms ached in a way that felt specific, one muscle for lifting and another for bending, and she had learned that a soft spot was a judgment and an ugly skin was nothing at all. She still wasn't sure, when she thought about the morning, whether she had done a good thing or a merely sensible one, or whether there was a difference, and she decided she would have to come back another Saturday to find out. She stood at the tailgate stacking the last crates, and Dana handed her a squash with a long green scar down its side. "Perfect," Dana said.

Henry kept telling himself he understood interest rates, which was easier than actually understanding them. He had the index cards spread across the kitchen table like a hand of solitaire, each one holding a sentence he'd copied from a website whose authority he had never checked, and he had been staring at them long enough that the words had begun to dissolve into shapes. It was the last week of August, the particular summer ennui that settles in after the graduation parties end and before college begins, and he was trying to sublimate all his restlessness into preparation, because tomorrow his grandfather was coming to dinner and would ask.

He had told his mother he knew the material cold. "Grandpa's irascible, but I can handle him," Henry had said, and she had given him a look he chose not to interpret. All he knew for certain was that the old man had opinions about the central bank, loud ones, and that at some point during dinner he would say something like "raising rates just strangles people," and Henry, who had appointed himself the family's defender of economic literacy, intended to explain how raising rates actually slows inflation. He just needed, first, to understand how raising rates actually slowed inflation.

The cards were no help. They used words like "demand" and "cooling" that themselves needed cards.

Through the window he saw the neighbors' lemonade stand, folded card table and crooked sign, run by Priya, who was twelve, and her brother Sam, who was nine and mostly decorative. What he heard next stopped him. They were arguing. Priya wanted to raise the price from fifty cents to a dollar, and Sam, gripping the pitcher with both hands, was objecting on the grounds of fairness. Henry drifted out onto the porch, ostensibly to check the mail, and let their argument reach him.

"Everything's going to cost more next month," Priya said. "Mom says the cups alone went up. So we have to charge more now, before it happens."

"So charge like sixty cents," Sam said.

"If everything's going up, sixty won't cover it later. You have to get ahead of it." She said it with the flat certainty of someone quoting an adult, probably their mother, and Henry felt the strange vertigo of watching his index cards come to life in a nine-year-old's hands.

He came down off the porch. "Can I ask you something? Why do you think everything's going to cost more?"

"Because it always does," Priya said, as if he were the child.

"But what if you didn't think that? What if you were sure the cups would cost the same next month as they do now?"

Priya considered this with the seriousness the question deserved. "Then I wouldn't charge a dollar. I'd maybe go to sixty, like Sam said. Or keep it fifty." Behind her, Sam was already revising the sign with a stub of pencil, hedging his bets at seventy-five.

Henry stood very still on the hot sidewalk. He was not, he realized, the person he had been describing to his mother all week, the one who knew this cold. He had been reciting. But here it was, happening in front of him with a pitcher and a pencil: what people expect changes what they ask for. If Priya expected higher prices, she demanded a bigger increase now, a whole extra fifty cents, and her raising the price made the price higher, actually higher, for every kid on this street. If she trusted that prices would stay low, she'd ask for less, a dime, nothing, and the smaller increase would keep things low, which was, he understood suddenly, the same thing the central bank was after. Not magic, not strangling. Trust, manufactured on purpose. The whole country was a lemonade stand, and people's expectations were doing half the work. He felt the thought click into place and also felt its edges, the parts that didn't click, the distance between a card table and an economy, and he let that stay open rather than paper over it.

At dinner his grandfather set down his fork and said, "So. Your mother tells me you've got opinions about the rate hikes."

"I think I can explain it now," Henry said. "Want to hear about a lemonade stand?"

His grandfather's expression changed into something Henry had never seen on him before, and he reached into his jacket, which still hung on the back of his chair, and produced a worn business card, sliding it across the tablecloth. Henry picked it up. The name was his grandfather's. Below it, in small type he had to squint at, were the words he had somehow never been told in eighteen years of family dinners: Central Bank, Research Division.

"Priya," his grandfather said, "the one running the stand. What did she decide?"

"Seventy-five cents," Henry said. "Sam talked her down."

Jacob checked the mailbox at 4:15, the way he had every afternoon for nine days, though the mail never came before five. The box was empty except for a coupon circular and a water bill, and he stood there holding the little door open as if another letter might materialize behind the first one. His father had installed the mailbox at the edge of the gravel drive fifteen years ago, sinking the post in concrete, and over time the ground around it had turned friable, so that the whole thing listed toward the road like a man listening for something. Jacob straightened it every so often without thinking. Today he held it upright while he counted the days left before the state university's reply deadline, which was not really a deadline at all, just the last day he could say yes.

The letter, when it came, would be the fourth. Two colleges had already said no, and one had said yes but wanted thirty-eight thousand dollars a year, a figure he had read aloud to his mother and then never mentioned again. The state university was the one he could actually pay for, more or less, which was why his older sister, Dani, had taken over the kitchen table for the past three nights.

He could see her through the window when he came back up the drive, hunched at the laptop with their mother beside her, both of them lit by the screen in the dark kitchen. They were filling out the FAFSA, the form for federal financial aid, and Dani kept explaining it to him in fragments whenever he passed through. "It's how you get the Pell Grant," she said once, not looking up. "Federal money you don't pay back. And federal loans, the ones with the better rates." Another night she added, quieter, "It's not just the federal government. The state uses it too, and the colleges themselves. Almost everybody bases their aid on this one form." Their mother typed the tax numbers with one finger, then two, then asked Dani to read the line back. The state's aid deadline was tomorrow at midnight, and Dani wanted her own answer, a transfer out of the community college and into the nursing program, and that want was tangled up in the same form, the same numbers, the same parents' income.

Jacob had spent the whole application season telling anyone who asked that it was simple math. You ranked the schools, you weighed the costs, you picked the highest expected value. He called it rationalism, half as a joke, when his uncle asked at Christmas how he was choosing. But the math kept refusing to stay simple. The yes for thirty-eight thousand sat in his desk drawer, and every time he opened the drawer for a pencil he felt the weight of it, and he could not make it into a number that behaved. He wanted the big school the way you want a person, which was to say irrationally, and he wanted to be the kind of person who didn't want things that way.

On the ninth night, near eleven, Dani called him into the kitchen. "Read this," she said, and turned the laptop toward him. The form wanted to know whether their parents had filed a joint return, and then it wanted a figure from line something of that return, and their mother had gone to bed with a headache, leaving the question half answered and the deadline two hours off. Jacob found the return in the filing cabinet himself, his hands steady in a way his stomach was not, and read the number while Dani typed it. "So the aid just follows from this?" he asked. "One form, all of it?" "Federal, state, the schools' own money," Dani said. "It all starts here." She hit submit at 11:41 and then sat back and put her hands over her face, and Jacob stood there awkwardly until she said, through her fingers, "Go check the mail. Just in case."

There was nothing, of course. But he stood at the box in the cold anyway, and it was there, with the post leaning against his palm, that he understood something he could not have put in an essay. The form Dani had just filed was a machine for turning one family's circumstances into money, and the machine did not care what he deserved or what he dreamed. That should have made him feel reduced. Instead it felt almost like being absolved. The choice had never been only his; it had been made partly by tax returns and deadlines and whatever Pell Grants added up to, and he could stop treating the wanting as a personal failing.

He came back in and found Dani at the sink, drinking water, the kitchen dark again except the light over the stove. "I decided something," he said. "If the state school takes me, I'm going. The thirty-eight thousand one, I'm letting it go." Dani set down the glass. "Last week you said it was worth the debt if you got in." "Last week I was doing math with feelings and pretending they were numbers," he said. She laughed, a short surprised sound, and then grew serious. "Then maybe I can stop feeling guilty about wanting the nursing program," she said. "Mom keeps saying we can't both." Jacob shrugged. "The form says what it says. We'll see what it says."

The next afternoon he walked down the drive at 4:15 again, knowing better, and stopped anyway when he saw the white edge wedged among the coupons. The envelope was thin, which the internet said could mean anything. He carried it back to the porch steps and sat down with it unopened on his knee, and from inside the house he could hear Dani at the kitchen table, already back on the laptop, looking up the nursing program's aid page. He slid his thumb under the flap and lifted the edge, and the porch boards creaked under him as he leaned forward to read the first line.

Jessica's father tossed her the keys the way he might have tossed her a softball, underhand and unremarkable, and she caught them against her chest in the driveway while the June heat pressed down on the both of them. She had turned seventeen two weeks earlier, which meant she could finally predicate her independence on a piece of plastic from the DMV, but first she had to survive her father's teaching, and she knew from her cousin that this was no small thing. He had already reorganized the passenger seat three times, moving a water bottle, then a phone charger, then the water bottle back, as though the car's interior were a paragraph whose syntax had to be exactly right before anything could proceed.

"Seat, mirror, seatbelt," he said. "In that order, every time."

She adjusted the rearview mirror until the whole rear window sat inside its frame, then leaned sideways to fix the left mirror, and he watched without correcting her, which felt like a kind of applause. The engine started louder than she expected. She eased the car down the driveway with her foot hovering over the brake the way a pianist hovers over a wrong note, and they rolled out onto Farrow Street, where the speed limit was twenty-five and the maple branches made a shifting ceiling of light.

"The steering wheel isn't a suggestion," her father said after a hundred yards of small, anxious corrections. "You can commit."

So she committed, and the car straightened, and for three blocks she understood what everyone had been talking about. The whole street opened up in front of her. She could see the crosswalk ahead, the stop sign, the woman walking a dog, and she signaled for a right turn and took it wide, then tighter, and her father said "better," and she believed him.

They turned onto Miller Road, which had two lanes in each direction, and her father told her to get into the right lane for the turn at the pharmacy. She checked the right mirror. Empty road, silver and still in the afternoon glare. She put on the signal and began to drift over, and her father's hand came off his knee and pressed the wheel back toward its lane, and at the same moment a blue hatchback slid past on her right, close enough that she could see the driver's face, a college-aged guy mouthing something at her through his window.

"Whoa," she said, or something like it, her pulse in her ears. "I looked. I looked in the mirror."

"There's a spot the mirror can't cover," her father said. "Called a blind spot. You have to turn your head."

She pulled over at the pharmacy lot, her hands still shaped around the wheel, and turned her head to look at the space beside the car where the hatchback had been. Nothing there now, just hot asphalt and a shopping cart. "So even with the mirror," she said slowly, "there's an area I can't see at all. From the seat. No matter how I adjust it."

"That's why you turn your head before changing lanes," he said. "Mirror, then shoulder, then move."

She sat with that for a moment. It bothered her in a way she couldn't immediately name, and then she could: she had believed that seeing was mostly a matter of arranging the instruments correctly, the way she arranged her desk before studying, the way she built an essay's structure before writing a word of it. Arrange everything and the whole field would be visible. But the blind spot didn't care about arrangement. It was a permanent gap in the machine's perception, and the only remedy was for her to physically turn and look with her own eyes, to accept that no setup was complete.

"That guy was so close," she said, and heard her own voice come out petulant, which embarrassed her, so she straightened it out. "I'm sorry. I really thought the mirror was enough."

"He'll forget it by dinner," her father said. "You won't. That's the trade."

They did the pharmacy turn, then drove out to the old airport road where the traffic thinned to nothing, and she practiced the sequence until it became something other than thought: signal, mirror, shoulder, wheel. The first few times she overdid it, turning her whole torso and drifting in the lane, and her father laughed and said, "Your head, not your whole biography," and she laughed too, the sound startled out of her. By the fifth attempt she could glance over her shoulder and keep the car straight at the same time, and the glance had stopped feeling like an admission of failure and started feeling like what it actually was, a habit of humility built into the motion of driving.

Driving home, she caught herself wondering whether the mirrors could be positioned to shrink the blind spot, angled further outward, maybe, and whether her father's method was simply the old way of doing things. She asked him, and he shrugged and said some people did angle them differently, and that she could experiment when the car was hers. She liked that answer better than a lecture. She liked that there was a question left over, something she would have to work out with her own shoulders and her own mirrors, on her own roads, after he stopped riding beside her.

Back in the driveway, she parked crooked and had to try twice, and neither of them mentioned it. She cut the engine and sat with her hands on the wheel.

"Same time Thursday?" her father said.

"Same time Thursday," she said, and turned her head, out of pure habit now, to check the empty street behind her before she opened the door.

The party had thinned to the kitchen by eleven: Leah, her robotics teammate Priya, three boys arguing about a card game, and a bowl of punch going warm. Priya sat on the counter with her phone, and every so often Leah caught her scrolling back through the team chat, to the message Leah had sent two days before. Five lines of compliments about the arm mechanism Priya had designed, then one sentence about the wiring, which was, honestly, a hazard. Priya had not spoken to her since.

Leah's mother had a phrase for parties like this, the late hour when everything went soft with somnolence and people said what they meant. Nothing good is decided after ten, she liked to say, but Leah was seventeen and had decided plenty after ten, and tonight she intended to decide something else.

She took two plastic cups of punch and crossed the kitchen.

"You're hiding," she said.

"I'm recharging." Priya took the cup anyway. "Also I'm rereading your message. The wiring thing."

"I said your arm design was the best thing on the robot."

"You said five nice things." Priya set the cup down without drinking. "I counted. And then you said the wiring could burn out the board, and that's all I've heard in my head for two days. Five against one, and the one wins."

Leah had read something about this, late one night in the spring, chasing a citation for a psych paper she'd half written and never finished. A review from 2001, led by a researcher named Roy Baumeister, called "Bad Is Stronger Than Good." It had found that negative events and remarks usually affected people more strongly than positive ones of similar size. She'd underlined it at the time because it seemed obvious and also unbearable, the way gravity was obvious and unbearable, and then she had gone and lived it without noticing.

"There's this thing," she said. "A review. 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good,' 2001, Roy Baumeister ran it. Bad stuff hits harder than good stuff the same size."

"So I'm statistically normal."

"So I did it wrong." The boys at the far end of the table erupted over the card game, someone adjudicating a dispute about whether a jack could be played on a nine, and Leah waited for the noise to settle. She had spent two days drafting apologies and burning them, because an apology would have taken back the true part, and the wiring was genuinely dangerous. What she wanted, she realized, standing there with punch sweating in her hand, was to be believed twice: once when she praised, and once when she criticized, and the two beliefs kept trying to cancel each other out.

"Here's what I should have said," Leah told her. "Your arm mechanism is the best thing on the robot. That's not a warm-up, that's the whole review. And the wiring is a fire risk, and I should have asked to fix it with you instead of handing you a sentence and leaving."

Priya's face was mercurial, quick to storm and quick to clear, and now it did neither; it just held still, which was worse to wait through than either.

"You think I can't hear criticism."

"I think I gave you a bundle and let you sort it alone. And the bad part was heavier. Not because you're weak. Because that's just how it weighs."

Priya slid off the counter. For a moment Leah thought she was leaving, and she began rehearsing the walk home, the cold block to the bus stop, the whole conversation replaying with the bad parts outweighing the good, because of course they would. Instead Priya opened the team chat and held the phone out.

"Rewrite it, then. Right now. The wiring part. Specific, and like you're talking to me and not to a document."

Leah typed slowly, deleting twice. She wrote that the gauge was too thin for the current draw, that it had heated up in the last test run, and that she wanted to reroute it together on Saturday before the qualifier. She read it aloud. Priya listened all the way to the end, then took the phone back, and looked at the message, and then at her.

"Saturday," Priya said. "Bring snacks. The good kind, not the kind you bring."

The appointment was for eleven, and Maxime arrived at the bank at ten forty with two printed emails in his jacket pocket, both from landlords in the city where he would start school in September. The first offered a studio at the edge of campus: six hundred and eighty a month, heat included, electricity and internet extra. The second was a shared flat closer to the river: five hundred and fifty, but everything separate, water, hydro, wifi, and a laundry machine that took coins. He had come to open his first account, alone, and to ask someone in a gray vest whether the numbers he had scribbled on the backs of the pages were actually arithmetic or just anxiety dressed up as arithmetic.

While he waited on the padded bench by the tellers, he took out his phone and reread the message his mother had sent that morning. "Your father says use the two-second rule no matter what, and longer if it's raining or snowing or dark. He says city drivers don't leave room, so you have to leave it for them. Call me after the bank." It was a short message, the kind she sent instead of the long ones, and he understood that she was practicing for the autumn, when short messages would be all they had.

The two-second rule had a history for him. Last winter, in the months before his test, his father had driven him out past the water tower on the old highway and made him count. When the truck ahead passed a mile marker, Maxime was to say one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand under his breath, and if he reached the sign before the two was finished, he was too close. In the snow that day his father had made him hang back even farther, watching the marker come and go with the wipers keeping their slow time, and Maxime had felt something close to exhilaration, the car seeming to belong to him at last, the road unspooling under his own decisions. He had passed the test in February. His father had said only, well, all right, and shaken his hand as though at the acquittal of a defendant neither of them had been sure of.

"Maxime?" The account manager's name tag said Sylvie. She had a small office with a plant that was dying politely in the corner, and she spread his two leases across the desk without asking why an eighteen-year-old wanted a financial opinion. "So let's be honest about the studio first. Heat included is real money here, that's maybe eighty a month you don't pay in January. Electricity, call it forty. Internet, fifty, but you'd split nothing." He watched her underline his own scribbles and add figures he hadn't thought of, a bus pass for the far one, laundry for the near one, renter's insurance for both.

"Wait," he said. "The shared one. Hydro isn't the same as heat?" She smiled the way people smile when they remember not knowing. "Hydro can be the heat, depending on the building. Here it says baseboard, so the electric bill climbs in winter. Your friend in the other bedroom uses the shower, uses the kitchen, and you pay half of all of it." He wrote winter in the margin of the river flat, then drew a box around it, and the box began to look like a cell.

The totals came out closer than he had expected. The studio at eight hundred and change, the share at seven sixty, and Sylvie pointed out that the difference was one Friday night a month, which made him laugh and then feel caught, because he knew which of his future selves she meant, the one already planning a hedonistic first term with people whose names he'd learned in a group chat. "That self also needs the bus," she said. "That self also wants the room with the door that locks."

He opened the account with the money from two summers at the garden centre, and Sylvie printed a debit agreement and slid a pen across the desk. While he signed, he thought about the drive home, forty minutes on the highway, and how he would pick a sign, any sign, and count one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand behind whatever car was ahead of him, and how in the dusk it would be longer than that, because his father had been right about the dark, and his mother's message had said so, and he was still checking.

He hadn't decided between the leases when he left. In the parking lot he sat in his car with the engine off, the two pages on the passenger seat, the studio with its included heat and its isolation, the flat with its split bills and its stranger who might become a friend or might leave his dishes. His mother's text sat unanswered on the phone in his hand. He typed, "Studio is 40 more but closer to everything, flat is cheaper if the guy is normal," and then, before he could second-guess it, he started the car, signalled, and pulled out toward the road.

The line outside the fire station wound past the hydrant and halfway to the hardware store, and Ella stood in it with her registration card going soft in her hand from the rain. She had forty minutes before her uncle's truck left for the airport, and the line moved in short, stubborn shuffles. Behind her, two volunteers from the Kessler campaign were arguing, not quietly, their clipboards tucked under their arms like shields.

"It's a tie," the taller one said. "Fifty-one to forty-eight, but the margin of error is four points, so it's a tie, and anyone who says otherwise is reading tea leaves."

"It's not a tie," the shorter one said. "Three points is three points."

Eella turned around. "It's within the margin of error," she said, because she had read that phrase in the newspaper on Tuesday and it had lodged in her head like a seed. The taller volunteer looked at her with something between gratitude and suspicion.

The shorter one, whose badge said DARA, shook her head. "It just means the poll can't say who's ahead," Dara said. "Not with confidence. But it doesn't mean they're exactly even." The taller volunteer, MARKUS according to his badge, opened his mouth, closed it, and then said, quietly, "That's not what the guy at the office said."

Eella had spent the drive to the fire station arguing with her own brother about exactly this, and she had lost the argument by being loud rather than right. He had said the poll was a tie; she had said Kessler was winning because the number was bigger; both of them, she understood now, had been claiming more than the number could carry. A poll was not a photograph of the whole town. It was a photograph of a few hundred people, and the margin of error was the smudge on the lens.

"Here's what I can't figure out," Markus said, and now he was talking to her directly, which she regretted and did not regret. "If we can't say Kessler's ahead, then what do we tell people at the doors? The office wants a script by noon. They want us to say the race is tied so nobody stays home."

"Say the poll can't say who's ahead," Ella said. "Say that. It's true and it's shorter than arguing about it."

Dara laughed once, a short bark, and pulled her phone out to check the time. The line moved forward three people. A man in a wet canvas coat near the door was telling anyone who would listen that all polls were lies invented by television stations, and his voice had the bombastic, carrying quality of someone who had decided volume was a form of proof. An older woman in front of Ella turned and said, "Some of us are still voting, Harold," and he subsided.

Eella checked her own phone. Thirty-one minutes. The truck was not going to wait, and her uncle was the kind of man who treated a departure time as a moral test, so missing him would debilitate her whole plan of getting to the airport and, eventually, to the college orientation she was supposed to be flying toward this afternoon. She had built her day like a row of dominoes: vote, truck, plane, new city. The line was the first domino and it refused to fall.

But she was still turning the argument over, because it was the first real thing she had gotten to think about all morning. If the lead was smaller than the margin of error, the poll was silent on the question of who was ahead. It did not say tied. It said nothing, or almost nothing, and there was a difference between nothing and an answer that people kept forgetting. Her brother would say she was splitting hairs. Maybe she was. But the polling place itself was the argument made flesh: five hundred people in a slow line, each one a number no poll had fully counted, each with the ordinary sentience of a person deciding something alone in a booth, which no sample could weigh in advance.

She turned back to the volunteers. "The script could say either candidate could be ahead," she said. "That's what the number actually supports. Then tell people to vote anyway."

Markus wrote it on the back of his flyer, the pen denting the wet paper. "Either candidate could be ahead," he repeated, as if testing whether the words would hold weight. Dara was already dialing the office. The line moved again and Ella was suddenly at the table, showing her card, printing her name in a square, receiving a sticker she pressed onto her jacket without stopping to center it.

In the booth she filled the bubble for Kessler, then stood for a moment with the pen hovering, not over doubt exactly, but over the strangeness of choosing when the numbers had refused to choose for her. She fed the ballot into the machine, heard it click, and walked out into the rain, where the truck was idling at the curb and her uncle was checking his watch.
"Doors close at noon," Markus called after her, waving the flyer. "We'll make it."

She raised a hand without turning around and ran for the passenger door.

Jacob had the graph half drawn when the power flickered, and for a second he thought the outage had come early, that the storm the radio had promised all afternoon had finally arrived to ruin his night. The lights steadied. He sharpened his pencil with his thumb against the blade of a pair of scissors, because the sharpener had been dead since March, and went back to the two axes labeled wheat and cloth.

The assignment was due first period, eight hours away, and the textbook's example sat in front of him like a locked door. Country A could make forty bushels of wheat or twenty bolts of cloth if it pushed all its labor one way or the other, and the homework asked him to show what happened when A traded with Country B, which was worse at both. He had drawn the frontier for A, a straight line sloping down, and then the answer key in the back of the book had marked a point outside it. He checked it twice. The point was beyond the curve, in the blank space where the graph said nothing could exist.

His sister Ruth came through the kitchen with her soccer bag over one shoulder and her cleats dripping rain onto the linoleum. She wanted the table, because she had a project of her own, a poster about volcanoes that was due Friday and that she had left until now, and the table was the only surface in the house big enough for it.

"I'm using this," Jacob said, without looking up.

"You're using half of it." She spread her poster board along the far edge and started cutting red paper into lava. Their mother was working the late shift, and the note on the fridge said leftovers, oven, three fifty, which meant Jacob was also responsible for dinner.

He tried to resuscitate his understanding from the class notes, but his notes were mostly a drawing of Mr. Okafor's tie and the phrase "comparative advantage" boxed twice, which was the name of the concept and, at the moment, the whole of his knowledge of it. He remembered Okafor saying the word, and he remembered not writing down anything after it because the bell had rung. Now the outside-the-curve point sat there like an accusation.

Ruth leaned over his paper, chin propped on her fist, rain still in her hair. "Why is that dot in the middle of nowhere?"

"That's the problem." He tapped the frontier. "Everything on this line is what Country A can make itself. The dot's past it. The book says that's where they end up after trading, but that's impossible. You can't be outside your own line."

"Then erase the dot."

"It's the answer."

"So the book's wrong." She went back to her lava with the serene confidence of a fourteen-year-old who had never once been punished by an answer key.

Jacob sat with the presentiment that the book was not wrong, that the error was in him somewhere, and the feeling was close to the one he'd had sophomore year when he'd argued with a geometry proof for an hour before realizing he'd assumed what he was supposed to show. He set the oven, put the leftovers in, and stood at the counter eating crackers while he stared at the two frontiers side by side, A's and B's, B's line squat and low, worse at wheat and worse at cloth both.

He tried it with actual numbers, because numbers could not be argued with. If A made only wheat and B made only cloth, and then they swapped some of each, Jacob could pick the swap himself, any swap, and see where each country landed. He chose an exchange that sounded fair to nobody, ten bushels for six bolts, wrote it out, and plotted the result. A's new point sat outside its line. He plotted B's. Also outside. He did it again with different amounts, and again, and the points kept landing in the impossible region, in the blank space, as if the graph's own arithmetic had turned bellicose and decided to overrun its borders.

"Ruth. Come here."

"I'm doing lava."

"Two minutes. Look." He held the pencil at the point. "This line is everything A can make alone. Right? Alone, no trade, all the combinations are on this line or under it. But if A makes just wheat and trades some of it for cloth from B, A ends up right here." He tapped the outside point. "Same for B, over on its graph. By specializing and trading, both of them end up with combinations they could never have produced on their own. They're past the line. That's the whole point of the dot."

Ruth frowned at it, chewing the cap of a marker. "So the line is only the line if you're by yourself."

"That's it. That's exactly it." He wrote the sentence in his notebook, near enough to the boxed phrase that the two ideas now touched. Whether it would survive being said out loud in class tomorrow, whether he really understood it or had only followed the numbers to a place he couldn't defend, he couldn't tell yet. He had a feeling the teacher would ask why it worked, and Jacob did not yet have a why, only a that.

The oven timer went off. He pulled the tray out with a dish towel, burned his thumb, ran it under the tap, and divided the food onto two plates while Ruth rolled her poster to one side to make room. They ate at the half-cleared table, and she told him the volcano poster was now going to have a graph on it, a graph of something, she hadn't decided what, because graphs looked scientific and she needed the extra credit.

"Put it outside the lines," Jacob said.

"Eruptions don't have lines."

"Everything has lines. That's what today taught me."

Sarah had been at the community center every Tuesday and Thursday since September, first for open gym and then, when the rec league needed a fifth, for the volleyball team that practiced in the echoing gym with the cracked scoreboard. Her father had wanted her to find something structured before college, some discipline to inculcate a routine into her last summer at home, and she had agreed mostly to stop the conversation. Now it was October, and the season was down to three games, and Priya had a doctor's note folded into her sock.

Priya had taken a ball to the temple two weeks earlier, off Sarah's own serve, a shank that nobody could have called. Since then she had come back in stages, and Sarah had learned the shape of it almost without meaning to. First Priya only watched, sitting on the folded mats with the lights dimmed for her. Then she did light jogging along the sideline. Then, last Thursday, she was cleared for the non-contact drills, and tonight she was supposed to try actual play, scrimmaging, the last step before full games.

"Read my note if you want," Priya said, pulling it out of her sock in the hallway by the water fountain. "It says every step, rest to full play, and I only move up if I stay free of symptoms the whole way. One headache and I drop back down." Sarah read it twice. The paper was soft from being carried.

They were eleven minutes into the scrimmage when Sarah noticed Priya standing still at the net, one hand pressed to her eyebrow. Not hurt the way a rolled ankle hurts, but paused, the way you pause in a library. Sarah called the ball early, took the set herself, and put it down flat so the rally ended. Then she walked over.

"Head?"

"Kind of," Priya said. "Started when I tracked Dara's serve. It's not bad."

Coach Reyes blew the whistle and came over, arms crossed, and Sarah watched him weigh it. They needed tonight. Thursday was the semifinal, and Priya was their only real blocker, and everyone on the court knew it. "If it's not bad," he said slowly, "you could sit five and see."

Sarah heard the offer for what it was, and it wasn't dishonest, exactly, but it was specious, a reasonable-sounding cover for wanting her on the floor. She thought of her father, who had argued last week that a promise to yourself was the only contract nobody else could break, and of Priya's note, which said the opposite in a way: that you advanced only when nothing in you objected. For a second the two ideas sat side by side in her head, neither one winning.

"It says while," Sarah said. "You move up only while you're symptom free. Not five minutes of being symptom free." She hadn't planned to say it out loud, and she felt Reyes's eyes on her, but Priya was already nodding, already reaching for her knee pads' strap.

"I know," Priya said. "I go back a stage. Light drills, no scrimmage." She looked at Reyes, and something in her face made the decision hers, which Sarah understood was the only way it could stand. Reyes exhaled through his nose, then shrugged, and told Dara to switch to the net.

After practice Sarah helped Priya carry the ball cart to the equipment closet, because Priya wasn't supposed to lift much yet and because it was a small thing that cost Sarah nothing. They stood in the hallway under the humming fluorescent panel while Priya re-read her own note.

"I'll be honest," Sarah said. "I don't know if the doctor's way is right about everything. Maybe you'd have been fine. Maybe five minutes' rest fixes it and nobody knows." Priya tilted her head, considering, not arguing. "But you're the one who has to live in your head all year," Sarah went on, "and I only have to live with losing Thursday. That math seems pretty easy."

Priya laughed, folded the note, and slid it back into her sock. In the gym, Reyes was killing the lights one bank at a time, and the last square of brightness shrank toward the door where the two of them stood.

"Walk me out," Priya said.

Gabrielle arrived at the farmers' market with her grandmother's canvas bag, forty dollars of her own babysitting money, and a plan she had defended at the kitchen table the night before. Her father wanted spaghetti and meatballs, the same dinner they had eaten every Sunday since she could remember, a tradition she privately considered parochial, as though the family palate had stopped exploring somewhere around 1998. She wanted to cook the pork loin from the Hsu farm stand, with the plums and the rosemary, the recipe she had torn from a magazine and taped inside her notebook like a confession. In the end she bought both, because in her family refusing anyone anything was a kind of arson.

She moved through the stalls with purpose, joking with Mr. Alvarez about whether his tomatoes were as good as he claimed, and letting him eviscerate a competitor's melons with one raised eyebrow. She counted her change. She argued herself down from the flowers and then, at the last stall, argued herself back up. By eleven she was carrying pork, plums, rosemary, a bag of tomatoes "for the meatballs, in case," and a terrible confidence that dinner would prove something, though she could not have said what.

Her brother Theo had left for college in August, and he texted while she was waiting in line for bread. "Cooking the family meal? Who are you and what have you done with my sister." Then, a second message: "Seriously though. Dad will say it's too fancy. Mom will say it's delicious to spite him. Report back." She read it twice, smiling, and did not answer yet, because answers felt like promises.

She cooked in the late afternoon with the kitchen windows open, the plums collapsing into the pan, the pork seared and then resting under foil. Her mother drifted through and stole a plum. Her father drifted through and said, "Smells like a restaurant," which in his dialect could mean anything. He changed his mind before dinner, though, out loud, at the table, which for him was practically opera. "This," he said, pointing his fork at the plums, "is better than the meatballs. Don't tell the meatballs." Everyone laughed, even Gabrielle, even the dog, who was hoping to be consulted.

Afterward they sat on the back porch in the blue evening, and it was hot, the kind of hot where the porch swing complained and the lemonade went watery. The platters came out with them, because no one wanted to go back inside, and the pork sat in its juices on the table while they argued about whether Aunt Rosa's new boyfriend was truly terrible or just boring, a debate with a long and distinguished history. Gabrielle looked at the meat and felt a small cold thought arrive.

She went inside and found the thermometer magnet on the fridge, the one from a food safety pamphlet her mother had never read. Her phone was faster. She searched, and there it was, plain as arithmetic: perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or for more than one hour when it's above 90. She read it twice. She stepped back onto the porch, where the air itself felt like a held breath, thick and ninety-something, and looked at the clock inside her own head. They had been out here longer than one hour. Longer than two.

"Everything's done," she said, gathering the platters, and her father said, "Done?" and she said, "Done for. The meat. It's been sitting out in this heat, and the rule is two hours in the danger zone, one hour if it's over ninety, and we are way past one." Her mother said, "The danger zone," slowly, as though tasting the phrase. "That sounds like a movie your brother would like." Gabrielle scraped the pork and the plums into the trash while her father mourned quietly and dramatically, one hand on his chest, and the dog watched the garbage can with frank theological despair.

Later, alone in the kitchen, she washed the pan and thought about her grandmother, who had raised five kids on leftovers and prayer and would have laughed at the waste, and about Theo's food science textbooks, which he quoted at dinner like scripture. Two inheritances, and she could hold both, she decided, roughly; she would trust the thermometer and the rule, and she would cook less next time, and she would still not tell her grandmother. The plums had been perfect, though, and the pork was gone, and there was no version of tonight without that.

She texted Theo a photo of the empty trash can and the thermometer magnet. "You were right about the danger zone. Dad loved dinner and then I eviscerated it, per USDA. Consanguinity entitles you to half the blame for my cooking genes." She dried her hands and set the pan back on the stove, and outside, faintly, she could hear her father and the dog, negotiating over the last piece of bread.

The cuff hissed, tightened around her mother's arm, and then the numbers appeared on the little screen: 152 over 96. Annabelle wrote them in the notebook she had started that morning, the one with BLOOD PRESSURE written on the cover in letters that looked more official than she felt.

Her mother was in the garden pulling bindweed, which was her way of not thinking about the appointment she had on Thursday. Annabelle carried the monitor out to the porch and held it up. "It did it again," she said. "Over 150."

Her mother sat back on her heels. "The nurse said one high reading isn't the end of the world."

"I know. But it's the third one this week." Annabelle turned the notebook toward her. She had made a chart, because charts were something she could do. "The top number is when your heart beats. The bottom is between beats. High means the blood's pushing too hard on the vessel walls, and the nurse at the pharmacy said that has to do with the salt we eat, because salt makes you hold water, and more fluid means more pressure. And exercise makes the heart stronger so it doesn't have to push as hard at rest." She said it all in one breath, the way she had rehearsed it, and her mother laughed.

"Listen to you."

"I'm going to explain it to Grandma on Saturday so she stops telling you it's just nerves." Annabelle had decided this in the night, lying awake. If she could understand the numbers, she could stand between her mother and Grandma's bellicose certainty that doctors were inventing problems to bill for. Grandma had taken their grandfather off his pills years ago and considered it a victory. Annabelle wanted ammunition that wasn't a fight.

Inside, her phone buzzed. A message from her sister Dee, who was nineteen and had an appointment at the campus clinic that afternoon, an appointment she had not told their mother about. Annabelle leaned against the kitchen counter to read it.

"Okay so. Update from the clinic," Dee wrote. "You were right that I should ask instead of panicking. The nurse went through everything with me. She said the pill is fine if you take it every single day, but nobody's perfect, and real life happens. Then she said the IUD and the implant fail in fewer than 1 in 100 users a year, because once a clinician places them, they don't depend on daily use. Fewer than 1 in 100, Annie. A YEAR. I practically demanded the implant on the spot." Then, a minute later: "Don't tell Mom. I mean it. I'm paying for it myself with my job money, it's my business. But I wanted you to know first."

Annabelle read it twice. She had been the one who suggested the clinic, mostly because Dee had spent two weeks wild-eyed and snapping at everyone, externalizing a fear she wouldn't name. Now the fear had a shape and a number, and the number was small, and Dee was calling it her business. Annabelle understood that. She also understood that their mother would be hurt to find out later, the way she had been hurt about the tattoo, and that keeping this secret would mean sitting at dinner holding it under her tongue like a coin.

She typed, "Your business. My mouth is a vault," and then, because she was sixteen and couldn't help it, "does it hurt."

"A sting, then nothing. I'll be at dinner Sunday. Tell Mom I'm buying the good bread."

Annabelle set the phone face down and looked at her notebook. Two things she was keeping track of now: her mother's pressure, and her sister's privacy. In biology they had just started genetics, and the teacher had shown them a family pedigree the way you'd show a map of landmines. Heart disease on one side, diabetes on the other. Your genotype wasn't a verdict, the teacher said, it was more like a hand of cards, and how you played it mattered. Annabelle thought of the salt shaker on the table, of her mother skipping her walks when she was tired, of Dee riding a bus across town to handle her own body without asking anyone's permission. The cards were dealt, but the playing went on and on, in choices the size of a dinner.

That evening Annabelle cooked, which she almost never did. She found a recipe with no added salt, used lemon and garlic instead, and set out the monitor beside her mother's plate. "After we eat, and after you sit for five minutes with your feet on the floor," she said. "That's how you're supposed to do it. Not right after gardening."

"Since when do you know how I'm supposed to do anything?"

"Since Thursday's coming and Grandma's coming Saturday and somebody in this house has to be calm about it." She slid the lemon chicken across the table. "Also, we're walking tomorrow morning. Slow is fine. The nurse at the pharmacy said even walking makes the heart stronger over time, and then it doesn't have to work so hard, and the numbers come down."

Her mother cut a piece of chicken, tasted it, raised an eyebrow. "There's no salt in this."

"There's lemon in this."

After dinner her mother sat with her feet flat on the floor, arm resting on the table, and let the cuff do its work. Annabelle watched the screen the way she'd watch a pot about to boil. 148 over 92. She wrote it down without saying anything, and her mother watched her write it, and neither of them called it good or bad. It was a number in a column, the second-lowest of the week.

On Sunday, Dee arrived with the good bread and a small bruise on the inside of her arm that she kept her sleeve over, and their mother said, "Sit, sit, before it gets cold," and Dee caught Annabelle's eye across the table and tipped her chin, half a nod, half a question. Annabelle cut the bread and passed it, and outside the window the garden went dark, and the notebook lay closed on the counter with its chart waiting for Monday.

Jackson had been volunteering at the Harbor Street Community Office for six weeks, and until Tuesday morning nobody had asked him to write anything.

Mrs. Adeyemi, the coordinator, called him over to the desk by the window. "I need a favor," she said. "Dara's out sick, and this email to the parks department has to go out by noon. The grant meeting is Thursday, and if we don't confirm the picnic shelter by then, we lose it." She slid a printout across the desk. "Read this and tell me what you think."

Jackson read it. Dara, the part-time staffer, had written a page and a half about the history of the summer program, the weather last July, a complaint about a broken water fountain, and then, in the final paragraph, a request to reserve the Riverside shelter on August 12. It meandered like a river deciding where to go. He could tell Dara was trying to sound professional, stacking formal phrases to burnish the message, but the polish hid the point instead of brightening it.

"It's polite," he said carefully. "It's just that the ask is buried."

"Can you fix it by eleven?" Mrs. Adeyemi was already halfway back to the phone, where a parent was asking about bus passes. "Keep it respectful. Mr. Okafor over there can be touchy about tone, so don't be blunt."

Jackson sat down at the volunteer computer. He typed a draft, deleted it, typed another. The question he kept circling was simple and stubborn: what did a professional voice actually sound like? He'd written school essays meant to impress a teacher, but this was different. Somebody on the other end had forty other emails and a shelter calendar, and the kindest thing might be to stop performing and just say the thing.

He was still rearranging paragraphs when Ren, the college intern, leaned over his shoulder with a granola bar. "What's the mess?"

"Trying to figure out where the request goes," Jackson said. "Dara put it last, like a reveal."

Ren chewed for a second. "My cousin's in the Navy. She drills this into everybody. 'Bottom Line Up Front', BLUF. It's a US military writing standard. You put the main point or request in the first lines of a message, before the supporting details."

"So the ask goes first, and the reasons come after."

"Exactly. She says nobody overseas has time to hunt for the point."

Jackson turned back to the screen. It felt almost rude, like walking into someone's office and talking before saying hello. But maybe, he thought, leading with the request was a form of respect, an admission that the reader's time mattered. He wrote a new draft.

Dear Mr. Okafor,

I'm writing to confirm our reservation of the Riverside picnic shelter for August 12, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., for the Harbor Street summer program's family day, roughly 80 attendees.

If the shelter is available, could you reply by Wednesday so we can finalize the grant paperwork? Below is the background, in case it's useful.

He kept the history Dara had gathered but cut it to four sentences. He left out the water fountain complaint entirely, then second-guessed himself and added one line, since Dara had clearly wanted it mentioned: "Separately, we'd appreciate knowing when the drinking fountain near the east entrance might be repaired." Maybe that was wrong, mixing requests. Maybe it was honest. He couldn't decide, and he let it stand.

Mrs. Adeyemi read it at 11:20, her face dour with deadline worry until the second line, when it eased. "This is good. Short and clear." Then she paused. "The fountain thing. He'll read that as a criticism of his department."

"Is that bad? Dara wanted it on record."

"It's a question of whether we need the shelter more than we need the complaint." She handed it back. "Your call. You're the one writing it."

Jackson sat with it for a moment. Two instincts pulled at him: Dara's instinct to document everything, soften everything, wrap the point in velvet; and the BLUF instinct to state the point and get out of the way. Neither felt complete on its own. The email could be direct and still be generous. He moved the fountain line to the end, after the background, and reworded it: "One small unrelated note, no urgency: the drinking fountain near the east entrance has been out of service, and families would be glad when it's working again."

He hit send at 11:52.

At 2:40 the reply came. Mr. Okafor confirmed the shelter, said he'd have the permit signed by Wednesday morning, and added a single line about the fountain: a work order had been filed in June, and he would check on its status. Then, at the bottom: "Thank you for making your request easy to find."

Mrs. Adeyemi printed it and pinned it to the corkboard above the office printer. "Dara should see this when she's back," she said, and Jackson noticed she'd circled the last sentence in red pen.

He stood there a minute longer than he needed to, reading it again. He still didn't know whether he'd been right to keep the fountain line at all, or whether softening it had been wisdom or cowardice. That part stayed unresolved, the way real things did. But he copied the email into a file he labeled "forms and templates," and saved it under a new folder name: BLUF, and other things I don't know yet.

Ren passed by with the last of the granola bar. "So what's the verdict? Military style?"

"Half," Jackson said. "Blunt up front, polite at the back."

"Sounds like stoicism with manners," Ren said, and laughed.

Jackson didn't answer, but he wrote that down too.

Alexander taped the floor of the black box theater on a Tuesday afternoon, three long strips of spike mark forming a doorway that didn't exist yet, and understood for the first time how much of directing was pretending a room into being. Ms. Ruiz had handed him the one-act without ceremony, a script called "The Alluvial Fan" about two brothers fighting over a river that kept changing course, and said only, "It's yours to ruin or not." The stage manager, Priya, watched him measure the diagonals twice because she'd seen freshman carpenters trust a single measurement and recuperate from the mistake for a week. The actors arrived at four, and the older brother, Marcus, clapped Alexander on the shoulder as if they were equals, which they were not yet.

He had planned the opening blocking in his notebook all weekend, little arrows and x's marching across a diagram that made sense from above. "Start downstage center," he said, "then cross to your left when she enters." Marcus took two steps toward the wings on the audience's left, the wrong side, and Priya called a halt before Alexander could find words. Everyone waited. He was seventeen and had never told anyone older than a dog what to do.

"Sorry," Marcus said, not sorry, just efficient. "Which left?"

Alexander looked at his diagram, then at the stage, and felt the two orientations slide apart like overlaid transparencies. "Stage left," he said. "Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view, facing the audience." He heard his own voice go flat with the effort of not sounding like a textbook, and Priya wrote it on the running sheet anyway: director means stage directions, always. The correction cost him something he couldn't name yet, a small tax on every future instruction.

The second rehearsal went worse in a different way. He had blocked the brothers' final argument as two long parallel crosses, mirrored and geometric, because the diagram was beautiful, and Priya had to point out, gently, that the actors were now spending the climax as far from each other as the stage allowed. Marcus and Danny, playing the younger brother, stood at their marks like alluvial deposits the river had abandoned, and the scene's heat drained out through the distance. Alexander had drawn pictures instead of asking what the people needed. That was the harder lesson, and it didn't fit in a notebook margin.

He tried again on Thursday with the diagram closed on the floor. "Stand wherever the fight starts," he said, "and move when you have a reason."
