"I'll try to remember that." Nicolas pulled a pencil from his backpack and wrote the formula at the top of the page. He remembered the atomic masses from the table he'd copied in class: carbon was 12.01, oxygen was 16.00. He added them and wrote the answer in the margin.

His grandmother came through with a dish towel over her shoulder and set a glass of iced tea beside his elbow without asking whether he wanted it. "How is the studying?" she said, and then, to her husband, "Did you take your pills?"

"I took them," his grandfather said, in a tone Nicolas recognized as not entirely reliable. He was eighty-one now, and last month he had told the same story about the 1970s twice in one dinner, first as a story about stagflation and then, forty minutes later, as a story about a man he used to work with, as though the two versions had nothing to do with each other. Nicolas's mother had pulled him aside afterward and said, gently, that it was going to be like this more and more.

Nicolas worked through the calculation. The problem asked how many moles of carbon dioxide were in 88 grams of it, and he divided by what he'd written in the margin and got a little over three, which then fed into the equilibrium question about whether heating the system would push it toward the products or back toward the reactants. He wrote that heating shifted it toward the side that absorbed energy, crossed out the reactants, circled the products, and moved on to the second problem feeling almost steady.

At the second problem, the numbers stopped working. The grams wouldn't divide evenly, the moles came out ugly, and when he tried to fix it by adjusting the equilibrium shift too, the whole answer fell apart. He sat back and stared at the margin where he'd done the simple part, the part that couldn't be wrong. Carbon, 12.01. Oxygen, 16.00. He added them again on a fresh corner of the page and got the same thing he'd gotten before.

Then he looked at his own formula, the CO2 with its small subscript two, and he saw it. Two oxygens. The molar mass of a compound was the sum of the masses of the atoms in its formula, all of them, which meant for carbon dioxide it was 12.01 plus 16.00 plus 16.00 again. 44.01, not 28.01. He had cut the oxygen in half, and everything downstream had been quietly wrong while feeling completely right. He erased the margin, rewrote it, and did the division again with the correct number; the moles came out clean, and the equilibrium answer that had wobbled now sat still.

"I forgot to double the oxygen," he said out loud, half to the table.

His grandfather folded the paper the rest of the way down. His face had that phlegmatic calm it got these days, unhurried, hard to read. "Twice sixteen is thirty-two," he said. "Plus twelve. Forty-four." He tapped the margin with one finger. "My teacher would have loved you today."

"It's not that funny."

"It's a little funny." But he was looking at the page with something more serious underneath, and Nicolas understood, without either of them saying it, that his grandfather had followed the arithmetic perfectly and would maybe not remember, by Sunday, that the conversation had happened at all. Nicolas thought about how the wrong answer had felt just as solid as the right one, and how he would have written it on the quiz with total confidence, and how nothing in the feeling of it would have told him. You just had to go back and count the atoms again, both of them, every time, and even then you couldn't be sure you'd caught everything.

He copied the corrected number onto a clean sheet so it would be the first thing he saw Friday morning. His grandmother took his empty glass and put her hand briefly on his grandfather's shoulder as she passed, and his grandfather covered it with his own hand without looking up from the newspaper.

James had won his first two rounds of the tournament, which was, he told himself, exactly according to plan, and so the free hour before round three belonged entirely to the one-act. He had the script in the side pocket of his blazer, three copies, because the cast numbered three, and he had reserved the empty classroom at the end of the humanities hall at eleven, which was a thing he had definitely done rather than a thing he had walked past and found conveniently unlocked.

Priya was already there, sitting on a desk with her heels hooked on the chair rung, and Devon came in late, still carrying his flowpad from the previous round. James arranged the copies on the desk. "We're going to sit and read it first," he said. "No standing, no moving. Just the words."

"A table read," Priya said. "My cousin does community theater. You sit around and read the script through before anybody stages anything, so you can hear how the dialogue actually sounds."

"I was going to say that," James said, and opened his copy, and to be fair to himself he had been going to say something adjacent to it. The classroom smelled of whiteboard marker and the hallway beyond it roared with tab room chaos, forensics kids arguing about speaker points, and here in this pocket of quiet the play began. Priya read the mother. Devon read the son. James read the stage directions in a level voice, unbothered, a director in full command of an incipient production that did not yet exist.

The trouble, in James's private accounting, was small. There was a line on page four where the son tells the mother he never wanted the lake house sold, and when Devon said it aloud it landed with a thud, formal and stagey, nothing like the way any eighteen-year-old on earth would say it to his mother. James had read that line perhaps forty times on his own and it had sounded fine, which was itself informative, since apparently a script sounds one way alone in a bedroom at one in the morning and an entirely different way in a room with other bodies in it. He had believed, before this, that writing was enough, that the page contained the thing. The page did not contain the thing. The thing happened between people, or it did not happen.

"That line's wrong," Devon said, before James could gently arrive at the same conclusion through a series of Socratic questions he had been composing since breakfast. "Nobody talks like that. 'I never consented to the divestment of the property.' Who says that."

"I say that," James said. "In rounds. That's debate. That's the whole problem, actually." And he heard himself say it and understood that it was true, that he had spent four years learning to interpolate evidence into arguments the way a mason slots bricks, and somewhere along the way the mortar had gotten into his ear. He could not tell yet whether the play was an escape from that or just debate wearing civilian clothes. His coach would have said there was a teleology to it, that everything in forensics bends toward the ballot, and James wanted the play to bend toward nothing, but he did not know how to make something bend toward nothing, or even whether that was coherent, whether a story needs a target the way a case needs one.

"We could change it," Priya said.

"I wrote it for the sound of it, not the truth of it," James said. "Or I thought I wrote it for the sound. Let's do the line again." He had them read the scene twice more, seated, scripts flat on the desks, and on the third pass Devon dropped the formal version and said, quietly, "Mom, you sold the lake without asking me," and Priya let the silence run four full seconds before her answer, and the silence did more than either of their lines. James wrote nothing down. He just listened. That was a new instrument and he was not yet sure how to hold it.

Then, because he was who he was, he tried to hold it anyway. He cleared the desks to the wall and stood Devon at the door and Priya at the window, eleven feet apart, which he measured by eye and later described as twelve, and ran the scene again with bodies in it. Blocking, he explained, was the term for where actors move and when, and he had read two chapters about it in a book he would, in later retellings, have studied exhaustively. In fact Devon refused to stand at the door. Devon wanted to sit on the floor with his back against the wall, and James's first instinct was to overrule him, and his second instinct, arriving late but arriving, was to let the actor's body vote. The seated version was worse for the geometry he had imagined and better for everything else.

A girl from another school put her head in the door and said pairing for round three was posting, and Devon left at a run, and Priya folded her copy of the script and put it in her bag and paused at the desk where James was still standing.

"So is the line changing or not?"

"I'll know when I hear it again," James said. "Saturday. My house. Kitchen table, obviously."

"Obviously," Priya said, and knocked twice on the doorframe on her way out, which he chose to take as applause.

The training room behind the planetarium dome smelled of dust and projector oil, and Brayden sat at the end of a table of folding chairs, copying a graph onto his notepad. The graph showed carbon dioxide rising across a century in a sawtooth line, small dips and recoveries riding a long, steep climb. He was there because the planetarium had accepted him as a weekend explainer, and because his grandfather, convalescing after the surgery in March, had said it would look good on an application and keep him out of the house where every conversation turned to illness. His real want was smaller and stranger: he wanted to be the kind of person who could stand under the dome and answer anything.

Mrs. Okafor, the volunteer coordinator, gave them worksheets and left the room, which was her way of testing them. The worksheet asked how greenhouse gases trap heat, and Brayden wrote that they absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it, some of it back toward the surface, so the atmosphere holds energy the way the glass of a greenhouse does. He knew that much from physics. The graph was harder. The sawtooth bothered him. He traced the little dips with his pen and could not say what they were.

The girl across the table, Priya, watched him. "You've been staring at that for ten minutes."

"The teeth. They go down every year and then back up."

"Plants," she said. "Northern summer. The hemisphere breathes in." She turned her sheet over. "That's not the one I'm stuck on."

Hers was a different sheet, the one on ocean heat. A boy of about eleven, there for a birthday party that had drifted away from the supervised group, had stopped at their table and pointed at her diagram of the North Atlantic. He asked why the wind direction mattered for a warm current, whether the warmth just sat where it was. Priya started to say something and stopped, and the boy looked at Brayden instead, because Brayden was the one wearing the volunteer lanyard.

Brayden's first answer was wrong. "The wind cools the water," he said, "so the heat sinks." The boy frowned, and Priya mouthed no. Brayden felt his face go warm, the projector fan suddenly loud in the quiet room. He took the diagram and turned it so the boy could see, and he made himself slow down, the way he had learned to do when a proof collapsed in calculus. He put his finger on the ocean.

"Okay, forget the wind for a second. In summer, the ocean takes in heat and stores it. All that warmth is sitting in the water. Then in winter, the ocean releases that stored heat into the air above it." He moved his finger east. "And the prevailing winds over that part of the ocean are westerlies, which means they blow from west to east. They pick up that warmed air and carry it onto northwestern Europe." He tapped the coastline. "So the wind direction matters because it decides where the released heat goes. If the winds blew the other way, the warmth wouldn't land there."

The boy read the diagram again, lips moving. "So the ocean is like a battery."

"Charging in summer, discharging in winter," Brayden said, and the boy nodded slowly and wandered back toward the party, already looking at the ceiling as if the stars might also be a battery.

Priya slid her sheet across. "You just explained my worksheet."

"I got it wrong first."

"I know. That's why I let you." She tapped the sawtooth graph on his pad. "The breathing, and the storage. They're the same idea at different scales. The ocean holds heat seasonally, the atmosphere holds it continuously. That's your greenhouse, actually. The gases raise the enthalpy of the whole system, the total heat content, and the graph is the receipt." She said it flatly, not showing off, and Brayden wrote enthalpy in his margin because he wanted to look it up properly later, not because he would admit not knowing it now.

They were called into the dome after that for a rehearsal, and Brayden stood at the console while the projector woke, the room going torpid and dark around the slow wheel of stars. Mrs. Okafor asked him to present the carbon dioxide graph to the group as if they were visitors. He held the laser pointer on the sawtooth, said the hemisphere breathes in every summer, and followed the long climb upward with the red dot, and found that his hand was steady. Afterward Priya caught his eye across the dome and tilted her head at the boy from the birthday party, who was standing at the exit, waiting, holding a folded page of his own diagram.

"You dropped this," the boy said, holding it out to Brayden, though Brayden had not dropped anything. At the top of the page, in pencil, the boy had written a battery, discharging.

The library's second floor smelled of carpet glue and old bindings, and Laura had claimed the corner table by the window since four o'clock, three legal pads fanned in front of her like cards she was refusing to show anyone. In two weeks she would stand before a panel of local judges at the regional mock court tournament and argue a free speech case, and the tournament's particular cruelty was that each advocate had to argue both sides: petitioners in the morning round, respondents in the afternoon. She had written until the two positions began to bleed into each other, until she could no longer tell which argument she actually believed.

Priya arrived at six with a milkshake and the truculent expression she wore whenever she'd been thinking about something all day and had decided everyone else was behind. "You're doing it wrong," she said, dropping into the chair across from Laura.

"I haven't said anything yet."

"Your face said it. You're trying to pick a side. That's not the assignment. The assignment is to be good enough that the side picks itself for you, both times."

Before Laura could answer, a boy from the study carrels drifted over, backpack straps bunched in one fist. Derek, from her government class, the one who never spoke unless something was actually bothering him. "Can I ask you guys something? You do the mock court thing, right? This morning in first period, Ms. Harrowwell told Marisol she had to stand for the pledge. Not say it, just stand. Marisol said no. She got a referral. So can they make you stand, or not?"

Priya set down her milkshake. "No. West Virginia versus Barnette, 1943. The Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance. Marisol should take the referral to the principal and cite it."

Derek repeated the case name back slowly, writing it on his hand. "Nineteen forty-three. Six to three. Okay." He went back toward the carrels, and Laura watched him write it again on a sheet of paper, more carefully, as though his skin might smudge the law.

"That," Priya said, "is your problem in one referral slip."

"What do you mean?"

"You just watched a rule protect somebody. Feels good. Feels like the case is settled, speech wins, done. Then this afternoon you argue the other side, and you'll hate yourself unless you understand why the three dissenters weren't monsters." She tapped Laura's legal pads. "So tell me why a school might want everyone standing. Steelman it. I'll be the judges."

Laura looked at the window, at the parking lot lights coming on. She had been raised in a house where certain words did double duty, where her mother said "community" and meant "obedience," and she'd spent two years at debate learning to call that coercion out loud. Now Priya was asking her to build the case for it. "A school is a small public," she began, halting. "If a public can't ask anything of its members, not even standing, then it isn't a public. It's just a room full of individuals. The three in the majority had utilitarianism on their side and still lost, I mean the dissent, the dissent said the country needed unity more than it needed to protect one conscience."

"Careful," Priya said. "Which three?"

"The three dissenters. In Barnette." Laura heard the words leave her mouth and felt the floor tilt, because she'd had it backward for a week. She'd been telling herself the dissent was about safety in wartime, about order, and that the majority's logic was the utilitarian one, the counting of harms. She grabbed the casebook and turned pages until Justice Jackson's opinion lay open under the desk lamp. She read the line about no official orthodoxy being prescribed by the Supreme Court, then read it again, and something in the argument she'd built for the respondent side, the side defending compelled speech, quietly collapsed and rebuilt itself in a different shape.

"Say what you figured out," Priya said. "Out loud. That's the whole tournament, saying it out loud before a stranger makes you."

Laura closed the book on her thumb. "I had the values reversed. I thought standing together was the practical argument and freedom was the principle. It's not. Compelled unity is the principle, a real one, a whole way of thinking about what a country is, and freedom is the practical one, the thing that actually works, that lets a nation hold people who don't agree. I can argue both now. I understand both now. What I can't do is tell you which one I'd vote for, because I keep switching, and I think switching might be the honest condition."

"That's the answer nobody wants," Priya said, "and the only one worth hearing." She gathered her keys. "Ten tomorrow. Bring the Harwell thing, we can work Marisol into a hypothetical."

Laura stayed after the lights dimmed to the yellow of the night section, copying the case citation onto a fresh card, and she was still there at nine when Derek came back through on his way out. He stopped at her table, and instead of the question she expected, he said, "Marisol stood today. Fourth period, before she even went to the principal. She said the fight was exhausting her more than the pledge did, so she just stood up." He shrugged into his backpack. "Funny, right? You spend all that time learning she doesn't have to, and she goes and does it anyway."

Laura looked down at the card in her hand, Barnette, 1943, six to three, and realized she could not decide whether Marisol had lost something or found it. She slid the card into her pocket next to her speech, where both sides of her argument sat folded together, and started stacking the legal pads to go home.

The suite smelled like buffalo sauce and wet coats, and Carson had exactly twenty-two minutes until the halftime trivia board lit up on the jumbotron, twenty-two minutes to decide whether his grandfather was a liar or just old. The contest had been announced at the end of the first quarter: one question per suite, answers texted in before the second half kicked off, and the prize was a locker room tour, which Carson wanted more than he had admitted to anyone, including himself.

"It was the Packers," Grandpa Ray was saying, wedged into the corner seat with a plate balanced on his knee like a man who had done this a hundred times. "Packers and the Chiefs. I remember it like yesterday." He was a gourmand of halftime spreads even now, working through the chicken wings with a methodical devotion, pausing only to gesture at the field below with a dripping bone.

Carson's mother rolled her eyes from across the room. "Dad, you were four in 1967." She said it lightly, the way she said most things about Grandpa Ray, but Carson had learned that lightness could carry weight, the way a paper airplane carries a stone if you fold it wrong.

"Five," Grandpa Ray said. "And I remember the score. Thirty-five to ten." He pointed the bone at Carson. "You think I make things up."

Carson didn't answer that, because the honest answer was sometimes, and the second honest answer was that he wanted Grandpa Ray not to have made this up. The trivia question had blinked onto the screen at the end of the first quarter: WHEN AND WHERE WAS THE FIRST SUPER BOWL PLAYED, AND WHAT WAS THE FINAL SCORE? His cousin Priya had already started typing "Green Bay" into the family's shared answer, because everyone knew the Packers were a Green Bay team, and something about that had snagged in Carson's mind like a sleeve on a nail. His grandfather had said Los Angeles. On the screen, the Chargers' kicker lined up for a field goal, and the whole suite went quiescent, even the twins, even the dog, waiting while the ball sailed wide left and the room broke into groans.

"Wait," Carson said, and Priya's thumbs stopped. "Grandpa, you said it was in Los Angeles. Not Green Bay."

"Of course it was in Los Angeles." Grandpa Ray looked faintly wounded, the way he did whenever anyone demanded evidence for his memories. "Big stadium out there. January. Cold everywhere else in the country but not there." He licked sauce off his thumb. "Fifteenth, I think. January fifteenth."

Priya was frowning at her phone. "That can't be right. Why would they play a Packers game in LA?" But she said it as a question, not a verdict, and Carson recognized the tone because it was his own, the little hitch before you commit to believing something. Fourteen minutes to kickoff of the second half. He thought about how they had all spent years humming to Grandpa Ray's stories, letting him have them the way you let a kid win at cards, and how it would be a strange kind of cruelty for this to be the one story that was true. It would also, he admitted to himself, be a strange kind of gift.

He got up and found his uncle Devin by the window, the one family member with actual data on his phone, the one who had made a small fortune in fantasy football and treated every dispute like a courtroom. "Uncle D. First Super Bowl. Don't tell me who told you what. Just look it up."

Devin looked at him for a long second, and Carson understood that his uncle had already heard the argument from across the room, and had already, probably, looked it up, because that was who Devin was. "You asking for Ray or for the trivia?"

"Both. Separately."

Devin turned the screen toward him. Carson stood transfixed by it for a moment, not because the information was dramatic but because it was ordinary, plain black text: January 15, 1967, Green Bay Packers 35, Kansas City Chiefs 10, Los Angeles. Every number where his grandfather had said it would be. Down on the field, the halftime crew was hauling the stage pieces into position, and somewhere a clock was running that Carson couldn't see.

He walked back and sat down next to Grandpa Ray without saying anything, then took Priya's phone and typed: January 15, 1967, Los Angeles. Packers 35, Chiefs 10. He hit send with nine minutes still on the clock, before he could think better of it, before he could weigh whether he was doing it for the locker room or for the old man. The answer could only be submitted once. Priya made a small sound of protest that trailed off into nothing.

The jumbotron flickered. Then, in letters ten feet tall: SUITE 114. CORRECT.

Grandpa Ray set down his plate. For a second he didn't say anything at all, just looked at the screen, and Carson watched his throat move.

"Told you," he finally said. "Like yesterday."

The biology classroom stayed open until five on Thursdays, and by four o'clock the smell of whiteboard marker had soaked into everything. Eva had claimed the far table because it had the good model kit, the one with plastic nucleotides that actually clicked together, and she spread her notes across it like a hand of cards she was losing. Her presentation was in two days: explain how DNA is copied and then turned into protein. She could say the words, transcription and translation, but when she tried to say them in order, out loud, the whole thing came apart like wet paper.

Devon arrived first, dropping his bag on the chair beside her. Then Priya, who had brought two granola bars and ate both. Marcus came last, still holding his phone, and the four of them were supposed to be Eva's audience for a practice run. She stood at the whiteboard, drew a rectangle, labeled it DNA, and said, "Then RNA polymerase makes a copy, called mRNA, and that's transcription." So far, so good. Then Marcus said, "You forgot the part where the code gets read in the cytoplasm," and Priya said he was wrong, and the practice run ended before it started.

"Translation happens at the ribosome," Devon said. "That's where amino acids get strung together." He said it slowly, the way he said everything, as though the sentence might break if rushed. Marcus waved his phone at them. "That's not even the fight. The fight is carbon dioxide. Where does the first CO2 come from? I said glycolysis. Priya said the Krebs cycle."

Eva wrote CO2 on the board and underlined it twice, which was more attention than it deserved from her. Glycolysis, she thought, breaks glucose into pyruvate, and she could not remember a gas being released there. But she had not read that chapter carefully, and she knew it. She said so. "I actually don't know. Don't let me guess out loud, I'll just make something up." Marcus looked personally wounded. "You're the one presenting." "I'm presenting DNA to protein," she said. "Cellular respiration is a different day of my life."

Priya took the marker and drew a box. "The mitochondrion. There's an inner part, the matrix." "Like the movie," Marcus said. "Like the movie," Priya agreed, and for a second everyone was quiet, respecting the movie. She drew pyruvate moving into the matrix and then, beside it, a small arrow and the label CO2. Devon leaned in and read aloud from his own notes, which were better than everyone else's because Devon wrote things down. "In the mitochondrial matrix, each pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide." He read it a second time, slower.

"So not glycolysis," Eva said. Marcus put his phone face down on the table, which for him was a kind of surrender. "Not the Krebs cycle either, then," Priya said, though nobody had fully claimed the Krebs cycle, and Eva decided not to point this out, because being right in the tone she would have used was a travesty of being right. She let it go and picked up the model kit instead.

She clicked nucleotides together while they argued about whether she should say "the first CO2 of respiration comes before the Krebs cycle even begins," which was accurate but sounded like a dodge. What she was actually doing was thinking about her own presentation, because the pyruvate argument had loosened something. DNA to RNA was a copying step, one alphabet to a near-identical one. Then translation changed alphabets entirely, nucleotides into amino acids, the way pyruvate became something else in the matrix and gave off a gas on the way. She did not say this comparison out loud, because it was nascent and half-wrong and she was not going to decorate her presentation with a metaphor she could not defend. But it ordered her thinking.

She stood up and gave the practice run, start to finish, and it went better than it augured, since she dropped the marker twice and called the ribosome a "ribosomething" on the first try. Marcus clapped with his granola-wrapped hands. "You still didn't say where the first carbon dioxide comes from," he said. "It's not my topic," Eva said, and then, because he had waited all afternoon: "It's the pyruvate, in the matrix. One CO2 per pyruvate." She packed the model kit, snapping the last nucleotide into its slot, and left the whiteboard covered in arrows for the janitor to judge.

The sled drill came at the end of every Tuesday practice, after the passing patterns had been run into the grass and the cones stood crooked where cleats had knocked them. Coach Reyes had three of them load the weighted sled and push it twenty yards as a unit, shoulders against the bar, and he stood at the far sideline with a stopwatch he never seemed to read. Dominic took his spot at the left end and waited for the whistle.

They were slow. Not just Tuesday but every Tuesday that September, slow in a way that didn't match how any of them moved alone. Dominic had watched Femi sprint the length of the field in the last minute of a match and arrive at the far post still furious with energy. He had watched himself, in the mirror of his own body, chase down a breakaway in the season opener and feel his lungs open like a door. Yet when the three of them leaned into the sled together, the thing crawled.

"Again," Coach Reyes said that Tuesday, and then, quieter, almost to himself, "You each push harder when I time you one at a time. I've been watching it for a month."

That night Dominic sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open, collating what he could find: a name, Ringelmann, which he typed into a search bar and then into another. He read slowly, twice. A French engineer, Maximilien Ringelmann, publishing in 1913, had found that people pulling a rope in a group each pulled less hard than they did alone. Dominic read the sentence out loud to the empty kitchen, then copied it into the notebook he kept for calculus.

He brought it to Femi before Thursday practice, holding the notebook open between them on the bench. Femi read it with his shin guards still in his hands.

"Ringelmann," Femi said. "Never heard of him."

"He measured it. Rope, groups, 1913. Everybody pulls less when they're in the group." Dominic closed the notebook. "It's not just us being lazy. It's what happens."

"So what do we do about it?"

Dominic had thought about this on the walk over, past the tennis courts where the nets sagged and a single player served balls to no one. Part of him wanted to say that knowing was enough, that a named thing was a handled thing. Another part, older and more skeptical, suspected that a fact like this was less an answer than a description of the problem. "I don't know yet," he said. "Maybe we count our own steps. Maybe we agree that each of us is responsible for his own push, and nobody assumes the other guy is carrying it."

"Meaning we all secretly think the other two have it," Femi said. "That's kind of comforting, actually. I thought I was just getting soft."

The infield grass was still wet when Coach called the sled drill on Thursday. Dominic lined up at the left end again, with Femi at center and Elias, a junior who rarely spoke, at the right. Before the whistle, Dominic said, without turning his head, "Your own push. Don't worry about ours." He heard Femi laugh once through his nose.

The sled moved. Not beautifully, not like a machine, but it moved the way it moved when Coach timed them individually, and Dominic felt his own thighs burn in a way he recognized from the opener. Afterward, doubled over with his hands on his knees, he tried to be honest with himself about what had changed. Perhaps the words had. Perhaps only Tuesday's rest had, or the cool in the air. He wanted to credit the sentence in his notebook and could not entirely.

At the water table, Elias drank and then said, "Was that real, or did we just want it to be?"

"That's the problem," Dominic said. "I can't tell the difference yet."

Over the next three weeks, the question stopped being a project and became a small persistent habit of mind, the way a player keeps checking his shoulder. He noticed it in the matches too. When the team defended as a block, each of them seemed to run a half step less than he did when the play broke and only one man was back. It felt endemic to them, not a flaw anyone had chosen but something grown into the structure, the way the goalposts leaned very slightly toward the south end. Whether it could be cured, or only watched, he didn't know. Coach Reyes, who had a reactionary streak about anything that smelled of sports science, dismissed the stretch bands a trainer once suggested and kept his stopwatch in his pocket, so Dominic assumed the sled drill would continue exactly as it was, unmeasured, which in its own way suited him.

On the last Tuesday of the season, the air had the smell of cut grass going cold, and the light failed early enough that the far goal stood half in shadow. Coach called the drill a final time. Femi, Elias, and Dominic took the bar, and before the whistle, Elias said quietly, "Own push," as if reminding himself of a word in a language he was still learning.

They pushed. The sled hissed over the wet turf, and Dominic felt the bar hard against his shoulder, felt the specific and separate weight of his own effort, which was all he had ever been able to feel of anyone's. When it crossed the twenty-yard mark, Coach said nothing, and Femi straightened up and looked back along the track of flattened grass.

"Again?" he said.

The parking spot in front of the Foodway sloped downhill, and Nevaeh took it anyway, easing the car in beside a cart corral while her sister Dee held her coffee and said nothing, which was its own kind of commentary. It was only Nevaeh's third time driving without their mother, and the slope made the parallel park crooked, so she pulled forward and tried again, straighter, and then sat with her hands still on the wheel.

"Which way do the wheels go?" Dee asked, because Dee had been in the car for the lesson last month and remembered everything, even the things Nevaeh would rather she forgot.

"Into the curb." Nevaeh turned the steering wheel until the front tires pointed toward it. "Downhill, facing downhill next to a curb, toward the curb. That way if the brakes ever fail, the car rolls into the curb instead of out into traffic." She had gotten that question wrong on the first try, in a strip mall parking lot with the instructor tapping the window, and she'd repeated it to herself so many times since that it had lost all meaning except as rhythm, pure phonetics, four syllables and then four more.

Inside, the Foodway was cold and bright, and Dee steered them past the produce toward the little seating area by the deli, where two laminated folders came out of her tote bag like something contraband. Two apartment leases. Dee had toured both buildings on Saturday while Nevaeh was at work, and now she slid the pages across the table and said, "Tell me which one."

"I don't know how."

"You know math. That's the whole skill."

The first lease was for a one bedroom on Calder Street, six hundred and eighty a month, but the listing said tenant pays all utilities. The second was a studio above the dry cleaner on Pine, seven hundred and forty, with water and trash included, only electric and internet on the tenant. Nevaeh got out her phone and opened the calculator app, and then the notes app, because the calculator didn't hold enough numbers at once. The woman at the deli counter called number forty-seven and nobody answered it.

"How much is electric usually?"

"I called the power company," Dee said. "They said sixty to eighty for a one bedroom this time of year. The internet's forty-five either way." She said it all quickly, like she'd been waiting for someone to ask. That was when Nevaeh understood that Dee had already done this math herself, maybe more than once, and what she wanted wasn't the arithmetic. She wanted somebody else to say the answer out loud so it would be real.

Nevaeh added it up anyway, carefully, twice. Calder Street came to six eighty plus eighty plus forty-five, eight hundred and five, and that was without water or trash, which Dee estimated at another forty from what the office had told her. Pine came to seven forty plus maybe sixty electric plus forty-five internet, eight forty-five, but no surprises, no separate bills arriving in February like small seismic events. The difference between them was almost nothing. The difference between them was everything.

"They're about the same," Nevaeh said. "Calder's cheaper if the bills stay low, but they might not, and I can't know that. Pine costs more every month but you know the number going in." She looked at her sister. "If it were me I'd take Pine. But I don't actually know which one you should take, because I don't know how much you need the number to be predictable versus just small."

Dee was quiet, rotating her coffee cup a quarter turn and then another quarter, and Nevaeh watched her metabolize it, the small shift in her face when a thing she already knew got confirmed by someone else. Dee was nineteen. Dee had a job at the clinic and a duffel bag already half packed in the trunk of this same car, parked uphill on the slope outside with its wheels turned toward the curb. This apartment was not a hypothetical. This apartment was Dee leaving, and Nevaeh had just done the math that helped her go.

"We should get the stuff on Mom's list," Dee said finally, and gathered the folders back into the tote, Pine's folder on top. "She wants lemons and that coffee she likes. And you're carrying the basket, because I carried the folders."

Outside, in the cold, Nevaeh looked down the slope at the car and at the tires turned toward the curb, holding the whole fact of it in her head again, and then unlocked the doors.

"Eight forty-five," Dee said, getting in. "Say it back to me."

The laundromat on Felton Street had one working table, and Naomi claimed it at nine forty on a Tuesday night, spreading both leases beside the dryer vents like a general deploying maps. Her mother's clothes tumbled behind her, towels and scrubs and the gray cardigan she wore to every shift, while Naomi smoothed the creased pages and set her phone calculator between them. A boy about her age sat two machines down, watching a sock go around and around as though it owed him money.

"You look like you're planning a war," he said.

"Two apartments. One of them is trying to trick me." She held up the first lease. "This one's twelve hundred a month, but they're giving a month free. The other one's down the street, eleven fifty, no tricks. Or fewer tricks."

He drifted over, dragging his laundry basket with him, and dropped into the chair across from her. His name was Theo, which he offered along with the observation that her spreadsheets were on actual paper, which he called "brave." She called it "my printer is broken," and they agreed to call it brave anyway.

The problem was the free month, which sat in her head like a word she could almost spell. She wrote twelve hundred times twelve on the margin of a flyer for a lost cat named President, then subtracted twelve hundred for the free month, and stared at the number: thirteen-two hundred for the year. She divided by twelve and got eleven hundred even, and sat back so fast the chair squeaked. Eleven hundred. The expensive apartment, with its move-in special, actually came out fifty dollars cheaper every month than the cheap one down the street. She said it out loud to make it real. "One month free on a twelve-month lease at twelve hundred, and it's like paying eleven hundred a month. Not eleven fifty. Eleven hundred."

"Wait, say that again," Theo said, and she did, and he pulled out his own phone to check her arithmetic, which she pretended to resent and secretly appreciated. He was circumspect about it, double-checking her carry on the long division like a man defusing something, but the number held. She wrote EFFECTIVE RENT in block letters, underlined it twice, and felt the particular satisfaction of a trap turned inside out.

Then came the part the flyers had not settled. Utilities. The twelve-hundred building made tenants pay electric and water; the eleven-fifty place covered water but not heat, and heat, in a city whose January she had only visited, was an unknown. She called the electric company's after-hours line and got a recording, called the water department and got a man named Gerald who said, "Can't tell you what your bill'll be, hon, only what mine was," and told her anyway, at length, until she had a number she could predicate nothing on except that Gerald existed and was cold. She laughed, actually laughed, alone in a laundromat at ten twenty, over a stranger's heating bill. Theo laughed too, though he had no idea at whom.

Her mother had texted twice: You decide. Whatever you think. Her mother worked nights and had handed over the leases like a baton, saying only that she'd never been good with this kind of thing, the way people say it about swimming or forgiveness. Naomi understood that whatever she chose, she was choosing for both of them, and that the cheap-looking apartment and the clever-looking apartment and the utilities she could not price until the first true cold snap would all land on the same kitchen table in the spring. The free month was real money, that much she had proven. The rest was weather she hadn't lived through yet.

She folded the leases, one into each back pocket of her jeans, uneven weights, like coins of different countries. The dryer buzzed. She pulled out the gray cardigan and held it a moment, still warm, then folded it over her arm the way her mother liked, sleeves crossed, and texted: The twelve hundred one. I'll tell you why when you're home. Theo raised a hand in salute as she pushed through the door, and outside the night had already gone cold, the wind coming off the parking lot flat and wide as a steppe, and she stood in it a second longer than she needed to, feeling for the first time exactly how much heat costs.

Ava had promised herself she would study during her shifts at the clinic, and so far she had studied the ceiling, the coffee machine, and a dog named Biscuit who was recovering from eating a sock. Her biology exam was in four days, and the study guide sat open on her lap in the break room, flattened by a cold mug. Cellular respiration, chapter nine. Glucose went in, ATP came out, and between those two facts lay a machinery of steps she could recite but not see. Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain: the words were like a language she could transliterate but not speak, each one converted from the page into sound without meaning attached.

Dr. Okafor found her there at eleven, when the waiting room had gone quiet. "You look like someone watching a debt collect interest," she said, and Ava laughed despite herself, because that was almost exactly it. She explained the exam, the impossibility of memorizing a process that happened in cells smaller than dust. Dr. Okafor considered the study guide, then the wall clock, then said, "Come on. Cage six."

In cage six was a greyhound called Meteor, thin as a coat rack, who had arrived that morning limp with exhaustion after running himself nearly to nothing at the park. He was on fluids, and his chart noted that his muscles had burned through their glucose stores so fast that the chemistry of his blood had tilted. Ava knelt by the cage while Dr. Okafor listened to his heart, and it occurred to Ava, kneeling there, that everything she was failing to learn was happening inside him at that moment, in millions of mitochondria, at a speed no one could watch.

"He's out of fuel," Dr. Okafor said, "and we're refilling him the slow way." She left, and Ava stayed, because Meteor's breathing had settled into something even and calm, and because it was easier to think near a living thing than near a textbook.

Two summers ago, her father had taken her to the science museum in the city, the last trip before her parents' separation made such trips impossible. She had been sixteen and sullen, and she remembered drifting away from him toward a mechanical model mounted in a glass case. It was a cutaway of a cell, and in the corner, a small assembly of plastic parts spun like a turbine, over and over, driven by a hidden motor. A placard explained that it showed an enzyme called ATP synthase, and that in a real cell protons flowing through it made part of the enzyme spin, and that the spinning motion was what built ATP. She had stood there longer than she meant to, watching it turn, while her father photographed a dinosaur two rooms away. She had not thought about it once since. Now, on the floor of the clinic, she thought about it so hard her head hurt.

She dug out her phone and found a diagram of a mitochondrion. There was the enzyme, drawn as a lollipop shape stuck through a membrane, and there were the protons shown as arrows crowding through it from one side. The model at the museum had not been decoration. It had been the answer, spinning patiently in a glass case while she failed to pay attention. The transport chain was not the point; it was the setup, pumping protons across the membrane so that they would want to flow back through, and when they flowed back through ATP synthase, part of it spun, and the spin built the ATP. It was a motor. Every cell in Meteor's exhausted body was full of little motors, winding down for lack of glucose, and the fluids dripping into his leg were, in the most roundabout and cosmopolitan way, delivery trucks for fuel to engines she could finally picture.

"Nothing," Ava said, when Dr. Okafor passed through again and asked what she was grinning at. "It's a motor. The enzyme. It spins."

"It does," said Dr. Okafor, and moved on to cage four.

Ava stayed until her shift ended, copying the pathway onto an index card: glucose broken, electrons carried, protons pumped, protons flowing back through the synthase, the spinning, the ATP. She was aware that she still did not understand everything, that somewhere in the middle of the process were numbers and gradients and something her textbook called enthalpy, which she had skipped and might keep skipping, and she was honest with herself about that gap. But she had two pictures now, the spinning model and the sleeping dog, and where they overlapped the pathway ran on its own. When she stood to leave, Meteor lifted his head and watched her, ears up, as if he too were waiting to see what she would do next. She held out the back of her hand to the cage bars, and he leaned forward and touched it with his nose.

The sedan on the showroom floor was silver, or close to it, a shade the brochure called Lunar Mist, and Maria had circled it twice already without touching it, because touching things felt like a first step toward owning them. She had two thousand one hundred dollars in a savings account that her grandmother had started when Maria was nine, an account that had recently begun earning interest, small deposits of money the bank added just for letting it sit there. Forty-one cents last month. Fifty-three the month before. The growth was slow, but it ran in one direction, and she liked that about it.

Her mother was at the sales desk with a man named Duane, who kept sliding papers across the table like a card dealer who already knew the hand. Maria could hear the word "monthly" arriving again and again, a word that sounded small and manageable until you multiplied it by sixty. Sixty months. Five years. The loan on the used sedan, Duane said, could be theirs at seven percent, and he said it the way people say the weather is humid, a condition of the universe rather than a choice anyone had made.

Maria sat down in one of the waiting chairs, which was the exact chair from every dentist's office she had ever visited, and took out her phone. She had gotten her first credit card three weeks ago, a slim blue thing with a limit of five hundred dollars, because the online form had said she was pre-approved and she had wanted, for once, to be approved at something first. She had charged twenty-six dollars at the bookstore. The statement had arrived yesterday with two numbers on it: a minimum payment of twenty-five dollars and a full balance of twenty-six.

She opened the card's app and read the fine print, which was set in gray type on a gray field, evidently designed by someone who hoped she wouldn't. Somewhere in the third paragraph she found the phrase "grace period." It said that a grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, then held the phone away from her face as if distance would make it simpler.

"So if I pay all twenty-six dollars," she said to the empty chair beside her, "they charge me nothing extra."

The empty chair did not adjudicate the matter, but the sentence on the screen seemed to. Pay twenty-six, owe twenty-six. Pay twenty-five, the minimum, and the twenty-six would begin to grow, the way her savings grew but in reverse, in the wrong direction, compounding toward whoever held the debt. It occurred to her that the two systems were mirror images: interest could work for you or against you, and the only difference was which side of the ledger you were standing on. She had always assumed the sides were assigned. Now she suspected they were chosen, or at least drifted into, the way her mother was drifting toward the finance office.

Her mother had been an iconoclast about debt for as long as Maria could remember, the woman who paid cash for a lawnmower, who cut up a store card in the parking lot of the mall while Maria watched through the car window, mortified. And here was that same woman nodding at a payment schedule, because the old car had died on the interstate in February and the new job started Monday and the bus did not run to the office park. Principles, Maria was learning, were not abandoned so much as negotiated with, item by item, in rooms that smelled like new vinyl.

Duane came over with a clipboard and a smile calibrated to the wattage of a man about to save a family. "You're the daughter," he said. "Great. You want to take a look at the payment breakdown? It's a real education."

"I'm already getting one," Maria said, and held up the phone, screen toward him, the grace period sentence still open. She wanted to see whether he would flinch. He did not flinch. He squinted at it with the polite interest of a man being shown a photograph of someone else's children.

"That's a good card," he said. "You pay it off every month, it costs you nothing. More people should start that young." Then, without a seam: "Now, on the sedan, here's what the interest looks like over the life of the loan." He turned the clipboard toward her, and the number at the bottom of the column was larger than the price of the car itself. Not by a little. The car cost eleven thousand dollars, and the loan, over sixty months at seven percent, would cost more than thirteen, and Duane pointed at the monthly figure as though the other number were not also sitting right there, in plain view, waiting to be noticed.

Maria looked from the clipboard to her phone, from the turbid gray paragraph that had quietly told her the truth to the clean white column that was telling her a version of it, and back to her mother, who was signing something at the desk with the pen chained to it. There was a case for the loan; she could make it herself, in her own head, the way a lawyer argues for a client she half doubts. The car meant the job, the job meant the rent, the rent meant they did not move in with Aunt Carol. That was real. But the number at the bottom of the column was also real, and she could not make the two of them agree.

She paid the twenty-six dollars on her phone, the full balance, due date still nine days away, and watched the confirmation appear. Then she walked over to the desk and stood beside her mother, not saying anything yet, just reading the paper upside down, which she had taught herself to do in seventh grade out of boredom and which now, unexpectedly, felt like a kind of power.

"Mom," she said. "Before you sign that last page, can we read the bottom line together?"

On the third day of model parliament, Layla discovered that her bill was nonsense. She had written it in one evening, eight clauses about banning vending machines that sold energy drinks in schools, and she had been proud of its moral clarity. Now Mr. Osei had posted every submitted bill on the classroom wall, and hers was next to a bill by Priya Raman, and Priya's looked like a legal document while Layla's looked like a persuasive essay with numbered paragraphs.

"Who's going to enforce it?" Priya asked when Layla sat down beside her at the long table by the window. "Clause four says schools shall not permit the sale of noxious beverages. What counts as noxious? What counts as a school? Does a sixth-form college count?" Layla said she'd fix the definitions, but fixing definitions turned out to be its own kind of quicksand. If she named specific drinks, the bill went stale the moment a new brand launched. If she named caffeine thresholds, she needed numbers she didn't have. She spent a full study period drafting and redrafting clause two and ended up with something longer and less clear than what she'd started with.

The next morning she found Priya in the library with her laptop open to the UK Parliament website. "Look at this," Priya said. "In the United Kingdom, government bills are drafted by lawyers in the Office of the Parliamentary Counsel before being introduced to Parliament." She turned the screen so Layla could read it herself. "That's why theirs look like that. There's a whole office of lawyers whose job is the writing. We're doing their part and the MPs' part." Layla felt something between relief and irritation: relief that the difficulty wasn't her personal failing, irritation that the simulation had quietly handed them a task that actual professionals spent careers learning.

What she couldn't stop thinking about, though, was what the lawyers' involvement meant for the arguing. In her draft, every clause had been an argument wearing a costume; clause four had existed to say energy drink companies were behaving badly. A drafter's clause, she realized, reading Priya's version, was supposed to be neutral enough that even an opponent could apply it honestly. That was a different kind of writing, almost a different kind of honesty. She wasn't sure which she trusted more.

The committee session on Thursday put the question to a test she hadn't expected. Marcus, playing the industry backbencher, moved to amend her bill so that "the Secretary of State may issue guidance on permitted beverages" instead of the outright ban. It was, Layla had to admit, beautifully drafted; it sounded like action while doing almost nothing, and she suspected the subterfuge was deliberate. "So you want to replace a rule with a suggestion," she said. Marcus smiled. "I want to replace a rule the House will vote down with a suggestion it might pass. Your bill loses everything. Mine saves half."

Layla looked down at her clauses, at the margin notes Priya had penciled in, and tried to hold both thoughts at once. The ban was the right policy; she still believed that. But a law that failed in division was only a gesture, and Marcus's hollow amendment was at least a law. Her mother, who had grown up somewhere that government felt like a thing done to you rather than by you, had taught her that a perfect law nobody passed was worth less than a small one that restrained somebody's worst impulse. Priya, whose parents marched and wrote letters and believed compromise was how you got subjugated slowly, thought the opposite. Layla had spent two years assuming one of them was simply correct.

She stood to speak. "I'll accept the amendment," she said, and the room reacted before she'd finished, Marcus triumphant, Priya stiffening beside her. "But I want clause six changed. If the Secretary of State issues guidance, schools have to publish whether they're following it. If it's only guidance, then let everyone see who ignores it." The chair called for objections; Marcus studied her for a long moment, tapping his pen against the desk, trying to find the trap in it, and she waited, not sure herself whether there was one.

The amended bill went to debate on Friday, then to its vote, and passed on a division of nineteen to eleven, with four abstentions. It would go to the model House of Lords, then, if it survived, to their teacher-as-monarch for royal assent, a stamp and a bell. Priya walked out with her without speaking until they reached the lockers.

"Half a law," Priya said. "You're satisfied with that?"

"I'm not satisfied," Layla said. "I'm not sure what I am." She closed her locker and held the folder with the printed bill against her chest. "Ask me after the Lords."

The exam was on Monday, and Alexis had chosen the back room of the Harbor Veterinary Clinic on purpose, because at home her textbook lay open next to her bed like an accusation. Here, at least, there were cages to hose out and a refrigerator of vaccines that hummed when the air conditioning quit, and she could spread her flashcards on the counter between the scale and the jar of dog treats. She had volunteered every Saturday since October, mostly to pad her college applications, and Dr. Reyes had started letting her stay past noon, which meant she was trusted, which meant she could not leave.

The problem was the mitochondria. Or rather the map of them that her biology teacher had drawn on the board, all arrows and little stars where ATP was supposed to appear, as if a cell were a subway system and glucose a commuter with somewhere to be. Glycolysis she could manage; glucose split in the cytoplasm, a small profit of ATP, pyruvate shipped inward like freight. After that the arrows multiplied. The citric acid cycle turned pyruvate into carbon dioxide and loaded electron carriers, the electron transport chain let those electrons fall down a staircase of proteins, and somewhere in the falling the cell made its living. On paper it was tidy. In her head it collapsed into a heap of arrows with no direction.

A terrier named Biscuit arrived at one o'clock, lethargic and off his food, and Alexis held him on the table while Dr. Reyes palpated his abdomen and asked questions of the owner, a large man in a rain jacket who watched with the particular stillness of someone trying not to cry in public. Blood work, the doctor said. Alexis carried the sample to the bench, and while the centrifuge spun she looked at the little tube and thought, without deciding to, that Biscuit's glucose was in there, and that every cell in his body was quietly burning it, that his lethargy was a shortage of ATP somewhere, a power failure at the level of the mitochondria, too small to see and absolutely real.

"Why is it called the citric acid cycle?" she asked when Dr. Reyes came back to the bench. She had meant to ask her teacher on Friday and had not, because in that classroom questions felt like confessions.

Dr. Reyes was mixing something and did not look up. "Look it up yourself. You'll remember it better."

That sounded like a rebuke, but Alexis had worked here long enough to know it was the opposite. There was a tablet mounted by the pharmacy shelf, and while the centrifuge finished she typed the question with one finger. The answer came quickly, which surprised her. Hans Krebs and William Johnson had described the citric acid cycle in 1937, working out the sequence of reactions that everyone now learned in tenth grade. Krebs had shared the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it. She read the sentence twice. Johnson's name was attached to the discovery and not to the prize, and she could not tell from the screen whether that was an injustice, an accident of committees, or something Johnson had never wanted in the first place.

"Krebs," she said aloud. "The cycle has a person's name on it because of him."

"Mm," said Dr. Reyes, in the phlegmatic way she answered everything, and carried Biscuit's spun sample to the analyzer.

Alexis sat with it while the machine ticked. Two men had mapped a process that had been running in every living thing for a couple of billion years, and within twenty years of drawing the map one of them stood in Stockholm. It was like naming a river after the first person to chart it, except that the river had been flowing through her, and through Biscuit, and through the yawning man in the rain jacket, the entire time. Her textbook vilified memorization and demanded it anyway; it wanted the cycle reproduced arrow for arrow on the exam. She had been resentful of that all week, and now the resentment felt smaller, or at least more complicated. The arrows were not invented rules like the dress code. They were found things, like a coastline.

Biscuit's results came back and Dr. Reyes read them in silence, then said something quiet to the man in the rain jacket, and the man nodded and held the terrier's face in both hands. Alexis turned back to her flashcards, not wanting to watch. She laid them out along the counter in order, glucose at the left, ATP at the right, and this time she tried to read them less as a subway map and more as a chronicle, the way Krebs must have seen it: pyruvate entering the mitochondrion, joining a four-carbon molecule to become citrate, citrate oxidized step by step, carbon dioxide released, electrons gathered onto carriers like cargo onto pallets, and then the transport chain, the long downhill delivery, the ATP produced at the bottom of the fall. She moved a finger along the cards as she went, and for a moment the sequence held together, not memorized but imagined, a supply line running inside a dog on the table behind her.

"You're studying," Dr. Reyes said, coming over to wash her hands.

"Biology exam Monday. Cellular respiration. I was hating it, but then I found out it was discovered, not just made up. Hans Krebs and William Johnson, 1937. Krebs got the Nobel Prize for it. He shared it in 1953."

"With Fritz Lipmann, probably," Dr. Reyes said, drying her hands, "but I'd have to look that up too." She glanced at the cards. "When I was studying for my boards I made my roommate quiz me over dinner. She thought the whole thing was deranged. All that erudition spent on pigeon breast mitochondria." She picked up the ATP card, looked at it as if it were a specimen, and set it back down. "Krebs used pigeon breast, actually. Flight muscle. Very dense mitochondria."

Alexis wrote pigeon breast in the margin of her notebook, underlining it twice, though she did not yet know where it would fit in what she knew.

The man in the rain jacket carried Biscuit out in a blanket, and the clinic went quiet except for the refrigerator. Alexis gathered her cards, and one slipped from the counter and landed face down, the electron transport chain, and she picked it up and read it again standing, not sitting, as if the standing made it more of a decision. Krebs had gotten the cycle wrong before he got it right; the screen had said something about earlier wrong turns, though it hadn't said whose. She would look that up too, later, on the bus, or she wouldn't. What she had now was a map with a name on it and a prize divided in a way she didn't fully understand, and a dog whose cells, whatever else was wrong with him, had been burning glucose all afternoon without needing anyone to understand how.

She zipped the cards into her backpack and hosed out the empty cage.

Sebastian arrived at the clinic twenty minutes early because the woman from the health department had said, twice, that the peer educator certification had to be finished by four o'clock, when the building locked its front doors. He sat in the waiting room between a man with a wrapped wrist and a toddler repeatedly dropping a plastic dinosaur, and he read the laminated card in his hand until the words went turbid, the way a page does when you stare too long and stop seeing anything at all. Consent, contraception, testing. He was supposed to be able to explain all three to another teenager without flinching, and in eleven hours he was scheduled to stand in the school library during study hall and actually do it.

The training had been three Tuesday evenings and a Saturday, and he had signed up for reasons he hadn't fully examined. Partly it was the college application, which he was honest enough to admit. Partly it was Priya, though he had told no one that, and the memory of their last night together in June still sat in him like a swallowed stone. They had been careful, mostly. Mostly. She had been on the pill since spring, and somewhere along the way the condoms had quietly stopped, a decision neither of them had made out loud so much as drifted into, the way you drift into deeper water without marking the moment your feet leave the bottom.

"Sebastian?" A nurse named Rosa with a lanyard heavy with buttons led him back through a corridor that smelled of disinfectant and old coffee. The exam room she put him in had a paper-covered table he was told to ignore, a chair, and a girl of about sixteen slouched in the corner chair with her backpack hugged to her chest. "This is Marisol, she's volunteering as your practice patient. This is your roleplay. If you pass, you're certified for tomorrow. If not, we reschedule for January."

January. Applications were due in November. He pulled his chair around so he was not behind the desk, because that had been one of the first things they taught: don't sit behind anything.

"So," Marisol said, reading off her card, "my boyfriend and I are thinking about having sex. I went to my doctor and she gave me a prescription for birth control pills. Does that mean we're safe?"

Sebastian opened his mouth and said the thing he had believed for most of a year, the thing that had made June feel simple. "The pill's really effective," he said. "If she takes it right, you're protected."

Rosa didn't say anything, but she turned a page on her clipboard, and the smallness of the sound reached him before its meaning did. Protected. He heard himself the way Priya must have heard him in the parking lot outside the pharmacy, when he'd said something similar and she'd laughed and said, "You're sure?" and he'd said yes, and neither of them had checked, because checking would have meant admitting they didn't know, and not knowing felt like something to stigmatize, a failure you kept quiet rather than a fact you looked up.

"Wait," Sebastian said. He turned the laminated card over, though the answer wasn't on it. "No. I said that wrong. The pill protects against pregnancy. That's what it does." He looked at Marisol. "Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections. The pill doesn't do that. So if you want both kinds of protection, the pill alone isn't it." Saying it out loud rearranged something in him, a chronology he had never bothered to order: the appointment Priya made in April, the conversation they never had in May, the clinic he had not driven her to in July, before she left for her grandmother's in Tampa with the phone calls getting shorter.

"Okay," Marisol said, in character again. "So where would I even get tested? Isn't that, like, embarrassing?"

"It's this kind of place," Sebastian said. "You walk in, you don't need a parent if you're over sixteen, you can ask for a urine test or a swab depending on what they're checking. Most infections are treatable, and a lot of them don't have symptoms, so you can't go by how you feel." He was steady now, though underneath the steadiness a question kept ticking: whether he would call Priya tonight, and what exactly he would say, and whether saying it would be for her or for the version of himself he was currently performing. He still didn't know. He put it in the same pocket as the other thing he didn't know, whether the mostly-careful of June had been enough, and whether the appointment he had finally made for himself, next Thursday at three, would tell him something he could bear.

"Consent," Rosa said. "Last piece."

"Every time, out loud, and you can take it back," Sebastian said. "If someone's quiet, that's not a yes. If they said yes last week, that's not a yes for today." He remembered asking, and he remembered not asking, and he let both memories stand there without choosing between them.

Rosa made a final mark on the clipboard. "Certified. Be at the library by eight tomorrow." Marisol zipped her backpack, and in the parking lot, before he had even found his keys, he had the phone out and Priya's name on the screen, thumb hovering over the call button while the November light went gray over the cars.

Alyssa would tell you she took the job at FixHub only for the money, and she would almost believe it, though the truth was that she liked the smell of the place, the warm plastic and isopropyl alcohol, the drawer of cracked screens glowing faintly like a box of dead light. Marcus, the owner, had hired her to mind the counter and log repairs, and for three weeks that was all she did. Then one slow Tuesday he slid his laptop across the counter, opened a spreadsheet so large it had stopped being a spreadsheet and become a database, and said, "Customers in one table, orders in the other. Tell me who never bought anything."

She had promised herself she wouldn't care about this. Caring about school things during summer felt like letting the college admissions season follow her into the back room, and she had wanted, with an earnestness she later found embarrassing, to be a person who was desensitized to achievement, who could let a puzzle go unsolved. She was not that person. By Thursday she had written her first query, a LEFT JOIN that kept every customer and matched orders where it could, then filtered for the rows where the order column came back empty. The screen returned seven names. She sat very still, the way she did when a text message said something she had to read twice.

Marcus looked over her shoulder, coffee in hand, and said, "There's another way." He typed a second query beneath hers. This one kept each customer for whom a subquery found no matching order row, and it had a name, and he said it aloud as he typed: "NOT EXISTS." Same seven names, same answer, written in a different way. He drained his coffee and went to the bench to heat a battery connector loose, leaving her with two queries that agreed with each other completely and told her nothing about which one to trust.

She ran them a dozen times each, on the real data and then on a small pretend set she built herself, four customers and six orders, then four customers and no orders at all. Both queries returned the same answer every time. This unsettled her more than a disagreement would have. In her experience, two different arguments reaching the same conclusion meant either that the conclusion was solid or that she had made the same mistake twice, and she could not tell which from inside her own head. Her erudition, such as it was, mostly from a semester of AP Computer Science and a habit of reading forum threads past the point of comprehension, gave her no precedent for this. She was honest enough with herself to admit that the admission itself was inchoate, a feeling without a shape, the sense that she was standing at the beginning of something that had rules she hadn't learned yet.

The bell over the door rang. A woman came in with a phone held together with a rubber band and asked, hopefully, whether her photos were still on it. Alyssa took the device, filled out the ticket, and said the careful thing Marcus had taught her to say, that they would try. The woman's face did the thing faces did, and Alyssa noticed herself noticing it less sharply than she had in June. Repair work, it turned out, could desensitize you too. She logged the ticket in the orders table, and it was a walk-in with no customer record, and she thought suddenly: this person is in neither table. No query would ever find her.

When the shop emptied she went back to the laptop. She wrote out both queries by hand on the back of a receipt, tracing the logic line by line the way her grandmother used to trace knitting patterns, and something clicked, quietly, the way things clicked for her, arriving whole rather than built. The LEFT JOIN kept everyone and asked which matches were missing; the other one kept each customer for whom the subquery found nothing, and though she could not have said why the two must agree, she saw that they were asking the same question in different accents. She chose the second for the report she'd show Marcus, because it read more plainly to her, and she chose it without proof that plainer was better. That part stayed uncertain and she let it stay.

At closing, Marcus read her printout, the seven names of customers who had come in once, given their information, and never ordered a thing. "Mrs. Okafor," he said. "She was in when the power went out. I told her I'd call her back." He tapped the paper. "Never did." He folded the list into his shirt pocket and started stacking the drawer of cracked screens, and Alyssa wiped the counter and thought about the woman with the rubber band, in no table anywhere, and the seven names, found twice over by two roads that led to the same place.

"Same answer," she said to Marcus, mostly to hear it out loud.

"Same answer," he said, and turned off the lights.

The garden behind the food bank had been a parking lot two years ago, and it still looked like one trying to be forgiven. Xavier had signed up for the Saturday shift because his scholarship application wanted evidence of community engagement, forty hours minimum, and he had calculated that nine Saturdays at four hours each, plus travel, would preempt any awkward November scramble. He was good at that kind of arithmetic. His mother called it planning; his guidance counselor had used the word "extrinsic," in a tone that suggested she thought it was a diagnosis.

A woman named Ruth handed him gloves and a bucket and pointed at the raspberry canes along the fence. "Pick what's ripe. What's not ripe stays." Then she went inside to weigh people in at the desk, which was, Xavier gathered, where the real work happened. The garden was a sideline. Its produce went into the hampers as the fresh item, the single tomato taped to the top of the bag like a bow on a gift nobody had wanted to need.

He was not alone. A girl about his age was already halfway down the row, moving faster than him, her bucket ringing with fruit. "Dee," she said, without looking up. "You're the new one. Try to keep the canes from whipping back, they'll get you in the eye and then you'll be a liability, and Ruth makes you sign a form." She picked three berries to his one. She had, he learned by the third row, been coming since she was twelve, and she wanted, with a specificity that startled him, to run the whole operation someday. She'd drawn up a rotation schedule on graph paper. Ruth had said it was too complicated. Dee had not forgiven this.

Around ten, Ruth called them inside to pack hampers, because the Saturday line had backed up past the coat racks. The warehouse room smelled of cardboard and floor wax. Dee assigned him to the baby-food shelf without being asked to assign anyone anything, and he began assembling the small bright jars into groups of six, the way a laminated sheet instructed, then adding the juice boxes and the snack packs that went into any hamper flagged for kids.

He hadn't expected the flags. He'd imagined, he realized, a room of single men in windbreakers, the food-bank patron of the news segment, and instead the floor was loud with children doing the specific boredom of waiting, one boy conducting an invisible orchestra with a breadstick. He counted flags out of something to do with his hands while his mind idled. Nine hampers on the table. Six had the kid additions. He did it again on the next table. Eleven, seven.

"There's a thing," Dee said, not pausing, taping a tomato. "It was on the flyer from HungerCount, that's Food Banks Canada's report. In March 2025, in Canada, about a third of food bank visits were children. One in three." She said it flat, the way you'd say the mall closes at nine. She had clearly said it many times, to many new ones, and it had stopped being information to her and become something more like weather.

He kept packing. A woman at the desk argued gently with Ruth about the size of her family, and Ruth argued gently back, and the probity of the whole exchange sat strangely with him afterward, both of them so careful, as though honesty were a thing that had to be protected on both sides. He thought about his forty hours, the form in his backpack with its signature lines, and about Dee's graph paper, and he understood that he had walked in holding two completely different ideas of the same room. In one, the hours were the point and the garden was the setting. In the other, the tomato was the point and the hours were nothing. He was not sure the second idea, now that he had it, made the first one false. The scholarship was real. His mother's rent math was real. The forms existed whether or not he despised them.

But the flyer number was also real, and it was not going to be less real in November. He decided, sorting juice boxes, that he would come back after the forty hours were done, and that he was honest enough with himself to admit he did not yet know whether that was a promise or a prediction. Some things you couldn't know until Saturday came and you either showed up or didn't. He suspected that was the actual test, and that it was badly designed, and that it was still the test.

At noon the line thinned. Ruth gave them each a cheese sandwich and a peach, the excess of some donation, and Dee sat on the loading dock eating hers with her legs swinging, the rotation schedule sticking out of her back pocket where she'd shoved it. "You did okay," she said. "For a liability who hasn't signed the form." Xavier peeled his peach in one long strip, careful, the skin coming away whole, and set the bucket of raspberries down between them.

On the third morning of the portfolio intensive at Camp Wenlock, Morgan spread her nine finished pieces across the floor of the craft lodge and understood, finally, what her advisor had meant when she said a theme had to be a question, not a label. Nine works, and no thread between them except that Morgan had made them: a watercolor of the lake at dawn, a charcoal self-portrait with the eyes left blank, a series of small studies of the dining hall's bent spoons. The tenth was due in two days, along with an artist's statement, and the statement was the part that kept her awake.

"Ten pieces, one idea," said Priya, folding herself down onto the pine boards beside the drawings. Priya was here from a magnet school in the city and kept a sketchbook of hands, only hands, three hundred of them by her own count. "You have nine pieces and zero ideas."

"I have ideas. I just have too many." Morgan straightened the self-portrait so its edge ran parallel with the floorboard. "That's different."

"That's the same thing with better lighting."

The critique session that afternoon made it worse, though not in the way Morgan expected. A boy named Deshawn, presenting his own portfolio, had pinned up a painting of a melted clock over a highway median, and in his statement he'd written that he was working in the tradition of Surrealism.
