He sat under a framed poster of a sailboat with the word PERSPECTIVE beneath it, holding a shoebox of receipts his mother had handed him that morning like it was a live grenade. He was sixteen, it was March, and he had earned four thousand dollars last summer sweeping floors at Ferraro's Deli, which meant, according to a letter from the tax office, that he owed them paperwork.

His mother had said it would be simple. His mother said a lot of things.

Mr. Kwan himself appeared in the doorway, a small man with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair, holding a mug that read WORLD'S OKAYEST ACCOUNTANT. He looked at Riley, looked at the shoebox, and said, "Ah. A first return."

"I have receipts," Riley said, and opened the box to prove it. Inside: bus passes, a receipt for work boots, three receipts for sandwiches from the deli itself, and one for a video game that he had put in on the theory that it had been a stressful summer.

Mr. Kwan sat down at the desk across from him and pulled the box closer with two fingers, the way an epicure lifts a lid off a dish he suspects will disappoint him. He separated the game receipt from the others without comment and set it aside, face down, as if sparing everyone embarrassment.

"First, the paycheques," he said. "You kept some?"

Riley produced four stubs, soft from being folded into his back pocket. At the top of each was his gross pay, and beneath it a line that said income tax, then another line, smaller, for something called CPP. The numbers at the bottom were always less than the numbers at the top. He had noticed this over the summer without letting himself think about it too hard, the same way you notice a dent in a car you are still paying for.

"This line," Riley said, tapping the income tax row, "I get that back? Since I'm sixteen?"

Mr. Kwan smiled at the ceiling. "We'll see. Now. You spent money to earn money. Boots, bus passes. Those can be deducted."

"Deducted from what?"

"From your income. The tax is calculated on what's left."

Riley nodded slowly, and then stopped, because he had something else in the box. He pulled out a folded sheet printed off the government website, a page about a credit for students, and flattened it on the desk between them. "And this? It says credit. Is that the same thing?"

"It is not." Mr. Kwan turned the page toward himself. "A deduction lowers the income the tax is calculated on. A credit subtracts directly from the tax you owe."

Riley stared at the page. He was quiet for long enough that the cardamom smell became noticeable again, and somewhere down the hall a printer finished a job and sighed itself to sleep. He had assumed the two words were just that, words, two doors into the same room. But they were different rooms. The deduction shaved the top of the mountain; the credit came off at the bottom, where the actual bill lived. If someone offered him a deduction worth a hundred dollars or a credit worth a hundred dollars, he understood now, in the way you understand a stove is hot, which one to take.

"So the credit's better," he said. "For the same amount."

"Usually," said Mr. Kwan, and went back to sorting receipts.

Riley's first instinct had been truculent, a summer of arguing with his mother about whether he should even file, whether the whole thing was a trap for people who couldn't afford accountants. He felt that flare up again now, faintly, and then subside, because the man across the desk had just handed him something sharper than a grievance. He tried to internalize the difference, repeating it in his head: deduction shrinks the income, credit shrinks the bill. He was aware he might be getting only part of it, that there was probably a reason "usually" had been added, some fine print living somewhere he hadn't read. He let that sit. He didn't ask. He would find out later, or he wouldn't.

"What about this?" he asked instead, producing a receipt from a bookstore where he'd bought a graphing calculator, which had cost more than the boots, the bus passes, and one of the sandwiches combined. On the bottom of the receipt, beneath the total, was a line that said HST, a number he had never examined. Eight percent, plus the provincial part. He had paid tax on the calculator while earning money that would be taxed again, and something about the loop of it made him want to laugh without much energy behind it.

"That one's sales tax," Mr. Kwan said. "Different animal. It doesn't go on this form."

"Where does it go?"

"Everywhere." He said it without looking up, and there was something almost fond in it, the way a farmer might say rain.

They worked through the rest of the shoebox in silence, mostly. The bus passes qualified. The boots qualified. The sandwiches did not, on the grounds that Riley would have eaten anyway, an argument Riley lost before he finished making it. At the end Mr. Kwan typed for a while, and a number appeared on his monitor, small and green, and Riley leaned forward to see whether it was money going out or money coming back, and could not immediately tell which direction he was rooting for.

"So do I get a refund," Riley asked, "or do I owe?"

Mr. Kwan turned the monitor around and let him read it himself.

The physics lab stayed open until five on Tuesdays, and by the second Tuesday of October Maika had claimed the corner bench by the window as her own. On the whiteboard she had copied the problem set from memory: a ball launched at eighteen meters per second, at thirty degrees above the horizontal, from a cliff of unspecified height. Below it, her first attempt sprawled in three colors of ink, each color a different wrong idea about what to do with the velocity. Mr. Okafor had written "see me" beside her quiz, and she had, and he had said only, "You're treating velocity as one thing. It isn't one thing."

She had not understood what he meant, which was why she was here, erasing the board for the fourth time.

"You're still here too," said Denis, from two benches over, where he was calibrating a spark timer for his own make-up work. He was the only other person in the room, and he seemed as unhappy about that as she was. "The cliff problem? Everyone got that one except us."

"Everyone got it except everyone who thinks velocity is a single number you plug in somewhere," Maika said, and even as she said it, she heard how hollow it sounded, because she did not know what else it was.

"Come look at this before you erase more of the board," Denis said. He slid a photograph across the bench, a picture from the science museum his little sister had dragged him to on Saturday. It showed a glass-and-brass apparatus in a display case, two flat metal rings stacked one above the other with a gap of air between them, and beside it a placard. "I took this because it looked like our lab equipment, kind of. Then I read the placard twice and took a picture of that too."

She leaned in. The placard said that Robert Millikan had measured the charge of the electron with this apparatus: the electric field between two horizontal charged plates held tiny charged oil drops still against gravity.

"Two plates," Denis said. "Horizontal ones. That's why it looked familiar. Like a sandwich."

"Still against gravity," Maika read aloud, and something in her chest shifted, the way a stuck drawer shifts when you finally pull at the right angle. She looked at the photo, then at her ruined diagram, then at the photo again. Millikan's drops hung motionless because two forces acted on them at once, and the apparatus cared about each one separately, one pulling down, one pushing up, the drop not choosing between them but being subject to both. "The ball off the cliff," she said slowly, "is doing two things at the same time and they don't talk to each other. One is falling, straight down, like it was dropped. The other is moving sideways, at whatever speed it left with, and nothing slows it down."

"So which number do you plug in?"

"Neither. Both. Separately." She was already at the whiteboard, drawing the cliff, the ball, and then two arrows breaking away from the diagonal launch velocity like a fork in a road. "The diagonal is just these two arrows added together. Cosine of thirty gives me the horizontal piece, sine gives me the vertical. The vertical piece is what gravity gets to ruin. The horizontal piece just... continues." She wrote the horizontal velocity beside the arrow and was startled by how small the arithmetic was, once the numbers had been pried apart. Fourteen or so meters per second, sideways, forever until the ground interrupted.

"Millikan didn't average his forces either," Denis said, looking at the photograph again. "He stacked them against each other and waited for still."

"It's not the same thing," Maika said, because it wasn't; oil drops hovering between plates and a ball arcing off a cliff were different problems, and she was wary of analogies that collapsed under their own weight. "But it's the same move. Split it."

She solved the problem in eight minutes. The fall took barely more than a second, the ball traveled a distance she could have jumped, roughly, if she were tireless and made of rubber, and when she checked against the answer key Mr. Okafor had left with the lab monitor, the numbers agreed. She sat back. Somewhere in her notebook, from a chemistry unit on air quality, there was a diagram of acid deposition, and she thought, irrelevantly and pleasantly, that her old approach had been a kind of pollution, everything mixed together and raining down at once.

What she could not yet do, and was honest enough with herself to admit, was say why the split worked. She could perform it, could fork any diagonal into its two quiet components, but if someone asked her why the universe allowed horizontal and vertical to ignore each other so completely, she would have to say she didn't know, not yet, maybe not for years. That felt tenable, though. More tenable than the fog she had been living in since September. The uncertainty had a shape now, and it was the shape of a question, and questions could be worked.

Denis packed his bag and paused at her bench. "Same time next Tuesday?"

"Same bench," Maika said, and resuscitated the failed quiz from the bottom of her backpack, smoothing it flat on the table beside the photograph of the two plates, side by side, like two versions of the same argument. She picked up the pen and began drawing arrows in the margin, one pointing down, one pointing across.

The taxi let Alexis out at the gate of the cemetery, where her aunt Hiroko was already waiting with a bucket and a small ladle. Behind Hiroko stood rows of stone monuments leaning up the hillside, each one a dark shoulder against the summer sky. Alexis had arrived in Japan four days earlier, three days after her grandfather's funeral, which she had missed because of the flight, and she was only now understanding that she had never once spoken to him on the phone for longer than the time it took to say hello, yes, this is Alexis, how are you, obāchan.

"You brought water from the tap there," Hiroko said, pointing to a stone basin under a cedar. "We rinse the stones. He liked things clean." It was the second thing Alexis had learned about her grandfather since landing; the first was that he kept a notebook of every typhoon that had passed through the town since 1961, which Hiroko had shown her the night before, turning the pages while Alexis looked at the small precise handwriting and tried to find herself somewhere in it.

The first day of Obon, Hiroko had explained at breakfast, was for welcoming the spirits home; the family had lit a small fire outside the door, mukaebi, and Alexis had stood in the doorway while the smoke drifted up the alley, feeling something atavistic stir in her, an inherited reflex to a ritual she had never practiced. Now they washed the stone, and Hiroko set out a tiny cup of sake and a satsuma with the peel opened in a spiral, an idiosyncrasy of his, she said, that he had insisted on every year for his own parents. Alexis copied the ladle motion as exactly as she could, letting the water run down the granite, and when her arm trembled from the weight of the bucket, Hiroko simply took the other handle without a word.

"He would have liked that you came late and stayed long," Hiroko said. "Even in August, the heat delimits the day here. You do things early, or you wait for evening. He waited for evening."

"Was he kind?" Alexis asked. It came out more bluntly than she intended, and she watched a line of ants cross the path rather than her aunt's face.

"He was difficult and he was kind," Hiroko said. "Both are true. You don't have to choose."

That evening the whole family walked down to the river, Alexis carrying a paper lantern with her grandfather's name brushed on the side in ink she had watched her cousin's hand form, stroke by stroke, that afternoon. The bank was crowded with families, children wading, old men in yukata steadying lanterns against the current. At the edge of the water a woman in a municipal vest took each lantern and set it gently out, one after another, until the river's surface was a slow constellation moving downstream. Alexis understood without being told that this was the sending back, okuribi, the return, the way the festival ended; the fire at the door had brought the spirits home, and these lights would guide them away again.

She crouched at the waterline and held the lantern while the woman steadied it, and the flame trembled in the draft off the river. "You can let go," the woman said, and Alexis's hands did not open. Behind her, her little cousin tugged at her sleeve and offered her a pebble, solemnly, as though it were something important, and Alexis took it with her free hand and put it in her pocket.

"He didn't know me," she said to Hiroko, still crouching, the lantern pulling slightly against her fingers as the current took an interest in it. "I'm sending back someone who was mostly a stranger."

"You're sending back what you have," Hiroko said. "That's what everyone is doing."

Alexis opened her hands. The lantern joined the others, tipping once, righting itself, catching the last light, and she stood and watched it until she could not tell which small fire was his among all the others going down the dark river toward the sea.

Leah had been coming to Mr. Okafor's office every Tuesday in February, and every Tuesday he asked the same question. "Still nothing from Harmon's?" Harmon's was the garden centre where she had spent the summer hauling flats of impatiens and running the register, and where she was owed a form she had been told to wait for. "They said it's coming," she said, setting her binder on his desk. Inside the binder were her pay stubs, every one kept in order, each showing her gross wages, the federal income tax withheld, the amounts for Social Security and Medicare, and the smaller number at the bottom that had actually landed in her account. She had wanted to file in January. She had wanted the refund by now.

The refund mattered. The community college in Midvale required a two-hundred-dollar deposit by the first week of March, and Leah's savings had been eaten by car repairs in November, when the Corolla's alternator died on the isthmus of highway between her town and the next one, that narrow stretch with water on both sides and no shoulder to speak of. Her mother had said she could help, but her mother's hours at the hospital had been cut, and Leah had watched her say it while refilling her coffee with the same grounds from that morning. So the deposit was Leah's to cover, and the refund was the only money she could see coming.

She understood her own pay stubs well enough. She could look at a stub from July, the one where she had worked fifty-one hours in two weeks, and see how income tax had been taken out of her wages before she ever touched the money. What she could not quite metabolize was the other half of the picture, the tax return itself, the form that would add up a whole year and compare what she had already paid against what she actually owed. That was the part Mr. Okafor did for people, and the part that required the paper from Harmon's.

"Every employer is supposed to give each employee a W-2 by the end of January," Leah said, reciting it the way she recited chemistry. "Showing last year's wages and the taxes they withheld." She had learned it from a government webpage at the library, printed it, and highlighted it in two colors.

"That's the rule," Mr. Okafor said. He was signing letters and did not look up. "Without it, we're guessing at numbers we shouldn't guess at."

She had tried being polite about it. Then she had tried being early, appearing at Harmon's at opening time, when Mr. Harmon's brother was unlocking the gate and the plants in the greenhouse aisle were still torpid from the cold night, leaves folded in on themselves like sleeping hands. He had told her the person who did the forms was "working on it." Today she decided to stop asking and start sitting. She brought a folding chair from the car, set it up beside the register where she used to work, opened her binder across her knees, and waited.

Sales tax came up while she waited, because a woman bought four bags of potting soil and complained at the total. "It's the sales tax," Leah said, pointing at the register screen, where the price of the soil appeared first and then the tax, added on top, a separate line before the sum. "Different thing from income tax. This one's on what you buy, not what you earn." The woman paid, still complaining, and Leah wrote nothing down, but she noticed that she had explained it without hesitation, and that noticing steadied her.

An hour in, Mr. Harmon himself came out from the back, saw her, and went into his office without speaking. Twenty minutes after that he came back holding an envelope. "This got sent to your old address," he said. "The one on your hiring paperwork. It came back to us." He held it out as though it were slightly her fault, and she took it before he could change his mind. The envelope had a green sticker and her handwriting from June on the back, her emergency contact, her mother's old apartment number. She did not open it there. She thanked him, folded the chair, and drove to Mr. Okafor's with the envelope unopened on the passenger seat because her hands were doing something strange and she didn't trust them at highway speed.

He opened it with a letter opener, angled so she could see. The form inside listed her wages for the year and, below that, the total federal income tax withheld, numbers she recognized from her own stubs, now gathered into one place. There were boxes for other things too, and Mr. Okafor said, "Now, do you have anything that might count as a deduction? Anything you kept receipts for?" and Leah said, slowly, that she had kept every receipt for the steel-toed boots and gloves she had been required to buy, somewhere in the same binder, and she started turning pages while he watched. Outside the window a man was salting the sidewalk, and the grains scattered white against the grey. She found the receipts, flattened them on the desk one by one, and slid them across to him.

The lab smelled of sulfur and floor wax, and Tyson had been staring at the same diagram for eleven minutes. Glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, the electron transport chain: arrows flowed across the page like a subway map, glucose dissolving into pyruvate at the top and ATP materializing at the end, inside a mitochondrion drawn as a fat bean. His exam was Monday. His grade in Biology 12 was balanced on the exam the way a coin balances on its edge, and his father had made the stakes plain enough that Tyson had felt the duress of it all week, studying under a lamp while his friends were out at the lake.

Across the bench, Priya was building a model of a mitochondrion out of clay, because she wanted the extra credit and, he suspected, because she wanted to be the kind of person who made things with her hands. She kept smoothing the inner membrane into folds, creasing them with the edge of a ruler. "Cristae," she said, when she caught him looking. "More folds, more surface area. Don't ask me why that matters yet, I haven't gotten there."

He hadn't gotten there either. He could recite the steps, glucose to pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, but the arrows went one direction on the page and nowhere at all in his head. He understood things better when he had to give them away, which was why, when his phone buzzed against the counter, he answered it even though he wasn't supposed to.

It was his cousin Drew, calling from the farm, where Drew spent the summers hauling feed and, apparently, wondering. "Tyson, that thing you said last month, about cells having instructions in them. Grandma's cows have the same kind of instructions as us?" Drew was fourteen and asked questions the way other kids threw rocks, casually and with force.

"Same kind, sure. It's called DNA." Tyson got up and walked to the window, away from Priya's careful folding.

"So when the cell needs to make something, it just sends the DNA out? Like mailing the recipe book to the kitchen?"

And here Tyson stopped, because the honest answer was that he didn't know, or rather that he had known in September and lost it somewhere. He had a vague image of a copy, a working copy, and he stood at the window trying to rebuild it. He remembered his teacher saying something about an enzyme, a machine that read the DNA without tearing it up, and he remembered the word polymerase surfacing in his mind the way a fish surfaces, briefly and then gone. Then it came back whole.

"No, actually. It's the opposite of mailing the book. The DNA stays where it is. There's an enzyme, it's called RNA polymerase, and it reads one strand of the DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA. That's the copy. The messenger RNA carries the gene's instructions out to where the protein gets made."

"Why not just send the DNA?"

"Because you don't mail the original, I think. You keep the master safe and send a copy that can get wrecked in the mail." He said it and then heard it, and something turned over in him, some small gear catching. The cell kept its archive locked away and made a disposable working copy, and the whole thing ran on that division of labor.

When he hung up, Priya was remonstrating with her clay, poking at a fold that had collapsed, calling it obdurate as though the clay were a stubborn animal. He sat back down and looked at his diagram, and for the first time he saw the logic under the arrows, not a subway map but a supply chain, glucose broken apart because breaking things apart releases what they're holding, the released energy captured in small, spendable coins of ATP. The cell didn't get something for nothing. It traded, step by step, and every arrow was a price paid.

"I think I finally get it," he said. "Not memorize it. Get it."

"Get what?" Priya held up the bean, folded and lopsided, sunlight coming through the window and making the wet clay shine.

"Why the steps have to be steps. Why it doesn't just burn the sugar all at once. It's like the copy thing, it's all about control."

"You should explain it to me, then," she said, and pushed the diagram across the bench toward him. "Tuesday, after your exam. I'll bring the clay."

Vincent had claimed the corner table at Marrow & Bean because it had the only outlet that worked, and he defended it the way you defend anything you can't legally own: with a bag on one chair, a jacket on the other, and a posture of permanent occupation. He was supposed to be drafting his deferral essay, the one explaining to the admissions office that a semester off was not the same thing as giving up, though so far he had produced a title and a bolded sentence he already hated.

Two tables over, a girl was talking to herself, or to her laptop, which amounted to the same thing. "The data's right there," she said, jabbing a finger at her screen. "I have eleven sources. Eleven." She caught Vincent looking and, instead of embarrassed, seemed relieved to have an audience. "Sorry. Persuasive essay. Due tomorrow. My professor is going to fail me."

"Eleven sources sounds like a lot," Vincent said.

"That's what I thought." She turned the laptop toward him like evidence at trial. Her claim, underlined twice, read: The city should not pathologize homelessness by treating it as a mental health crisis rather than a housing failure. Below it, a wall of statistics, studies, a citation from a philosopher named Toulmin. "But my professor wrote on the draft that I have a claim and I have grounds, whatever that means, and then just a question mark. A question mark. Like I'm supposed to know what's missing."

Vincent pulled his chair over, which felt like a decision, though it was really only two feet. The citation at the bottom of her bibliography caught his eye: The Uses of Argument, 1958, Stephen Toulmin. He'd scrolled past the same book the night before, hunting for structure words to steal for his deferral essay. "Can I see that page?" he asked, and she handed over the library copy she had wedged under her binder, its spine cracked at a chapter about an argument's backbone.

He read faster than he had all week. Claim, grounds, warrant. The claim was what you wanted to prove. The grounds were the data, her eleven sources. And the warrant was the thing explaining why those grounds actually supported the claim, the bridge between them. She had built two towers and assumed the river would cross itself.

"Okay," he said. "Say I told you my uncle got furloughed from the plant and his mental health went bad. You'd say that proves your claim, right?"

"Obviously. Housing and income instability, psychological decline."

"But my roommate would say the opposite. He'd say the mental health problem came first, that's why he lost the plant job, so it proves we need therapists, not apartments. Same story. Both of us have grounds. Neither of us has the thing that says which way the arrow points."

She stared at him. "The warrant."

"If I'm pronouncing it right."

She opened a new document and typed the word at the top of the page like a dare. Then she said, "So my warrant has to be something like: when cities treat a condition as medical, they fund clinics instead of housing, and the studies show the housing approach works better where it's been tried. Which means I have to actually say that. Out loud. In sentences."

"In sentences is the traditional method."

He watched her rebuild the essay in real time, and the strange part was that it was helping him too, though not about housing. His own essay had a claim, taking a semester off is responsible, and grounds, his father's recovery, the money, the hours at his uncle's shop. But he had never written the line that connected them, the line that said why the grounds proved anything. Maybe there wasn't one. Maybe the admissions office would read his eleven sources and draw the arrow however it liked. He could control the claim. He could control the grounds. The warrant was where he had to argue, in the open, where somebody could disagree.

"What's yours about?" the girl asked, nodding at his mostly blank screen.

"Me being scared and calling it a plan."

She laughed, a short, unguarded bark that made the barista look up. "Write that down," she said. "No, seriously. That's a claim about yourself. Grounds are easy. Warrant's the hard part, apparently." She copied the book's page number onto a napkin and slid it across to him. "Stephen Toulmin, 1958, The Uses of Argument. He's the reason you're about to fail your coffee."

"You're the reason," Vincent said. "Toulmin's just the alibi."

He opened a new document and typed the sentence he'd been avoiding: If a deferral is granted to students with clear obligations at home, then my situation qualifies because, and stopped. Because. He could hear the argument fork right there, the nascent disagreement waiting in the word, and for the first time all week he didn't mind it.

The girl had already written half a page, muttering, "Warrant, warrant," like a spell. Vincent leaned back, read his sentence again, and started typing.

The phone store smelled like floor cleaner and warm plastic, and Dylan had been standing at the display case for eleven minutes, measuring the distance between himself and the phone he wanted. It cost seven hundred and forty dollars. He had two hundred and ten in his sock drawer at home, saved from a summer of mowing lawns, and the saleswoman had just said the word "financing" in a voice that made it sound like a door swinging open.

"You could take it home today," she said. "Zero down. You'd pay monthly, and there's interest, of course, but it's manageable." She was young, maybe twenty-two, and she kept glancing at his mother, who was pretending to read a wall of screen protectors with great scholarly attention.

"What does interest mean, exactly?" Dylan asked. He was sixteen and he suspected the question made him sound like a child, but he asked it anyway, because not asking felt like walking into a room with the lights off.

"It's what the lender charges you for borrowing. The money grows while you owe it." She said it quickly, not unkindly, the way someone recites a thing they've said a thousand times.

His mother came over then. "There's a pamphlet in the car," she said. "From my card. It shows things like that. We can look before we decide anything." She touched the saleswoman's sleeve, a small apology for taking her time and giving none back, and steered Dylan toward the exit with the light grip that meant she had thoughts she hadn't arranged into words yet.

In the car, she dug through the door pocket and handed him a folded statement, the paper gone soft at the creases. "I'm not hiding anything," she said. "I just want you to see it before some brochure in there makes it sound free."

He unfolded it on his knees. The numbers were small, the kind of print that seemed designed to incapacitate a reader's will halfway down the page, rows of charges and payments and a word he didn't know yet. Then he found a box near the bottom, a shaded rectangle with two timelines inside it. If he paid only the minimum, the statement said, it would take years to clear the balance. Not months. Years. He read the number twice, then a third time, because the first two readings felt like misprints.

"Mom. This says if you pay the minimum, it takes years to pay off." He held the page toward her at a red light. "Years. On this."

"I know," she said. "It's the law, actually. Under the Credit CARD Act of 2009, the statements have to show it. How long it would take by making only the minimum payment." She said it flatly, the way you say a thing you learned the hard way and now carry around like a scar.

"So it's not a secret. It's right there on the paper, and people still do it."

"People still do it," she agreed. The light changed. Behind them somebody honked, briefly, and gave up.

Dylan sat with the statement in his lap and tried to hold two ideas at once, which was harder than it looked. The first idea was that financing put the phone within reach today, and that reach had a pull on him he could feel physically, a warmth in his chest like standing near a stove. The second idea was that borrowed money grew while you owed it, and the same force that made debt swell, the saleswoman had said, also made savings grow, so that his two hundred and ten dollars, left alone, would quietly become more. The two facts faced each other in his head like passengers who had been assigned the same seat. He thought of his friend Marcus, who believed money was pure determinism, that your finances were fixed at birth and every choice was just theater. Dylan had always half-believed it too, because it was easier than the alternative, which was that every month you chose which direction the growing went.

"Part of me still wants it," he said. "The financing. I'm not going to pretend I don't."

"I'd worry if you didn't," his mother said. "Wanting things isn't the problem."

They sat at the next light without speaking. He noticed her hands on the wheel, the way she'd worked the register at the pharmacy for eleven years, the way she'd put five dollars in the church jar last Sunday when the jar was for a family whose apartment had flooded. He folded the statement along its old creases and put it in his back pocket, not the door pocket, where it would sit under other papers and be forgotten.

"How much more would I need," he said, "if I saved till, like, November?"

She did the arithmetic in her head, or pretended to. "About five months of lawns. Depends how many people still need mowing."

"Mrs. Okafor does. She asked me last week, actually." He looked out the window at the phone store shrinking behind them, its bright sign, its putative door to having things now. "I'll text her when we get home."

His mother smiled at the road. "Tell her Thursday's open."

The email had come at noon: her uncle needed the list by six, before the garden store's supplier meeting, and Eve had said yes before she understood what she was agreeing to. Two files, he'd said. Customers and orders. Find the customers who never ordered anything. It sounded like nothing, like sorting buttons, and now it was almost four and she was in the back corner of the public library with a laptop whose battery icon had turned the color of a warning.

She had taught herself the basics that morning, the select and the where, and those had felt like doors opening. But the two files sat apart from each other like strangers in a waiting room. The customers table had a column called customer_id, then name, then email. The orders table had order_id, then customer_id again, then amounts and dates. She knew the answer lived somewhere between them, in that repeated column, but every query she wrote returned either everything or nothing, and the library clock moved with the indifference of something that had never once been on her side.

"You're typing harder," said Marcus, dropping into the chair across from her with a stack of manga he had no intention of reading. He was in her chemistry class and had followed her here out of boredom, which she had stopped pretending to mind.

"I'm typing with conviction. It's different." She turned the screen toward him. "I need the people who ordered nothing. But the nothing isn't in any table. The orders table only has the people who did order. It's like the guest book at a party. The people who stayed home aren't in it."

Marcus leaned in, chewing the end of a pen cap. He pointed at the repeated column. "So that's the link? The same number in both files?"

"That's what I keep assuming. But I don't know which one points to which. If I get it backwards, I'll match orders to customers that don't exist, and I won't even know it's wrong. It'll just be a lie that looks tidy."

He squinted. "In my brother's textbook there was a thing about that. A column in one table that points to the other table's ID. It's called a foreign key." He went back to his manga, having delivered this the way he delivered everything, sideways and without ceremony.

Eve sat very still. In the customers table, each customer_id appeared once and only once; she checked, scrolling, her breath shallow, because if even one repeated the whole structure collapsed. It didn't. Every row had its own number. So the customers file held the true identifiers, one per person, and the orders file merely borrowed them, each order carrying a number that pointed back to a single customer. The direction was fixed. An order's customer_id pointed to the customer's own ID and never the reverse. She wrote it in the margin of her notebook like a law she had discovered rather than learned, and for a moment she felt the strange satisfaction of something that had been shapeless becoming solid under her hands.

The query itself, once she understood the join, took eleven minutes. She asked for every customer, matched to their orders, and kept the rows where no order came back, the ones whose order columns sat empty like unsent letters. The database ground through it. Across the room a toddler was being escorted out mid-tantrum, the shelves of new arrivals stood capricious in their ordering, and Eve had spent the afternoon in a war of attrition against her own assumptions, but the result appeared at 5:31: a single row.

One customer had never ordered anything. She checked the name twice, then three times, because the account had been created six years ago with a family email she recognized better than her own. It was her uncle. The man who owned the store, who had never once bought so much as a packet of seeds from himself, sat in his own customer list like a ghost at his own party. Every other account, even the ones that had gone quiet for years, had bought something. Only he had not.

She screenshotted it, attached it, and typed the email with her hands almost steady. She could already imagine his face, the way he would either laugh or pretend he had a reason, some theory about setting an example, though she knew, with the certainty of someone who had watched him subjugate his own free time to that store for as long as she could remember, that he had simply never thought of himself as a customer. At 5:52 she pressed send.

Her phone buzzed before she had closed the laptop. "One name?" the message read. "That can't be right." Then, thirty seconds later, a second message, just a photograph: her uncle at the register, holding up a single bag of potting soil he had apparently just rung up for himself, grinning at the camera like a man destroying the data.

"Fix it," she said out loud, already reopening the file. "The deadline's in eight minutes and the data just changed."

Nathaniel's grandmother had turned her sunroom into a theater. That was her word for it, anyway, though the stage was a floral rug and the lighting was a dimmer switch she operated from behind the fern. He had come for two weeks in August to write a ten-minute play, one scene from his own life, and perform it for whatever relatives could be lured to the house with the promise of lemon cake.

The scene he chose was the morning his father drove him to the hospital to see his mother after her surgery, and how they had sat in the parking garage for forty minutes not talking, and how his father had finally told a story about a chicken. Nathaniel did not know yet that the story would be hard. He wrote the first draft in a single afternoon at the kitchen table, feeling briefly like a virtuoso, and printed it on his grandmother's ancient printer, which groaned like it resented every page.

The table read happened on Thursday. His cousin Priya came over, plus Priya's friend Marcus, who had done one summer of community theater and therefore considered himself an authority. Grandmother sat in her wicker throne with the script and a pencil, and Priya read the stage directions aloud in a news-anchor voice that made everything sound like a hostage situation.

They got through it. Marcus cleared his throat in the way people do before delivering a verdict. "The letter," he said.

"What letter?"

"The mom's letter. In the first scene. Nathaniel's dad pulls it out of the glovebox, and then it just never comes back. We never learn what's in it."

"It's a prop," Nathaniel said. "People have things in gloveboxes."

Marcus leaned back, delighted to have caught something. "My drama teacher calls that Chekhov's gun. Anton Chekhov, the playwright. Anything you clearly show on stage early should matter later in the play."

Grandmother looked up from her pencil. "In my day we called that foreshadowing, but I suppose guns are more dramatic than letters." She said this mildly, but Nathaniel felt it land like a verdict of her own. He had been caught, too, just less obnoxiously.

He argued for a while, because arguing felt easier than fixing it. The letter was atmosphere, he said. Real life was full of objects that never explained themselves. Priya pointed out that a play was not real life, it was real life boiled down, which was a sentence Marcus immediately claimed as his own. Then Priya, who could not help being fair even when Nathaniel was being a pill, said maybe the trouble wasn't the letter itself, it was that the scene seemed to think the letter mattered. The dad handled it, turned it over, put it back. The scene had aimed the gun and then forgotten it.

That night he sat in the sunroom with the dimmer switch at half, thinking about his mother's actual glovebox, which contained registration papers and a flashlight and eleven napkins from a sandwich shop that had closed years ago. He had made the letter up. He had put it there because a prop needed filling, and now the prop was demanding a reason to exist, like a guest who would not leave the party. There were two ways out, and he tried to hold them in his head at once. One was to cut the letter, which felt like losing something he could not name. The other was to let it come back, which felt like lying, because in the parking garage no letter had ever been read aloud.

He worked at it for two days. Cutting won, mostly. But he gave the chicken story a small extra beat, a callback the dad makes when they finally get out of the car, and Priya read that part again and said, "There. That's your gun. You just had it pointed at the chicken the whole time." Marcus objected that a chicken was not a gun, and Grandmother observed that Marcus's own performance of the dad had been penurious in its emotional range, which sent Priya into a fit of laughing and sent Marcus to the kitchen to sulk with the lemon cake, where he was quickly consoled by it.

On the day of the performance, the relatives arrived in force: two aunts, an uncle who clapped at the wrong moments, and Grandmother's neighbor Ruth, who had been promised cake and brought a folding chair in case of seating shortages. The sunroom held eleven people and one nervous playwright. Nathaniel had tried to forestall a crisis by taping down the rug's curled corner, and by deciding, at the last minute, not to play his father himself but to hand the role to Marcus after all, because Marcus did a better dad than Nathaniel could, and because Nathaniel had discovered he would rather watch the scene than be inside it.

It went well, mostly. Marcus forgot one line and invented a worse one, Ruth's chair collapsed during the parking garage silence in a long tin shriek, and in that strange shattered moment, with everyone frozen, Nathaniel's uncle said, "Well, that's garage ambience," and somehow it was. Afterward his aunts hugged him too hard and too long, and Priya said, "Ten minutes exactly, you absolute showoff," and Grandmother found him by the dimmer switch and put the pencil in his hand.

"Keep it," she said. "I marked all the places you cut too soon." He looked down at the margins, crowded with her small handwriting, and realized he would be coming back next summer whether or not anyone asked him to. "One more thing," she said, steering him toward the kitchen. "Ruth ate your piece of cake, and I need you to be brave about that."

Victoria was not, she would have told anyone who asked, the kind of person who got rattled by a poster contest. She simply wanted her design for the library's reading campaign to print properly, which was a reasonable want, and if she had stayed until five o'clock in the art room two days running, that was diligence, not panic. The deadline was Friday. Mr. Okafor had said, in his unhurried way, "A3 for the wall, A4 for the handouts," and left them to it, which Victoria took as a vote of confidence in her specifically, though he had probably said it to everyone.

The trouble began with her drawing. She had lettered the slogan by hand across an A4 sheet, a girl reading under a tree made of torn paper leaves, and it was good, she knew it was good. But when she photocopied it onto A3 at the public library printer down the street, the machine stretched the image to fill the page, and the tree's branches thinned into pale threads. On her second attempt the copier fit the whole design inside the larger sheet and left an ugly border, the girl marooned in white. Priya, working at the next table, kept glancing over, and Victoria kept her shoulders loose and her voice level, because she was not competing with Priya, whatever Dana thought. She wasn't.

"It's like the machine wants a number," Priya said, chewing her pen. "A scale percentage. But what?"

"That's what I'm going to find out," Victoria said, and she said it calmly, though she had already snapped one pencil clean in half, which she blamed on the pencil being cheap and ductile, bending before it broke, nothing to do with her grip.

She took the two sheets, A4 and A3, back to the art room and laid them side by side on the cutting mat. Dana leaned over her shoulder, smelling of turmeric from lunch, and said, "Hold them up to the window. Compare the shapes." Victoria did. The corners did not line up the way rectangles usually did when you enlarged them; the proportions matched somehow, angle for angle, which shouldn't have been possible. She measured. The A4 was 210 by 297 millimetres. The A3 was 297 by 420. The long side of the small sheet had become the short side of the large one.

"Look," she said, turning the A3 so its long edge ran vertical. "The A3 is the A4 with extra paper on one side. Same shape, just bigger." Dana squinted. Victoria took a fresh A3, the good heavy kind the school could apparently still afford, laid it flat, and cut it in half with the guillotine, one clean stroke. Two pieces fell apart on the mat. She set one against her original A4. It covered it exactly, corner to corner, like a shadow.

"That's not luck," Dana said.

"No." Victoria sat back on her stool. She remembered, distantly, a page from the library printer's manual she'd skimmed while waiting, a line about ISO 216, some standard, and she'd skipped it because it looked like fine print. "It's ISO 216," she said. "The paper sizes. A4's sides are in a ratio of one to the square root of two, so when you cut a sheet in half you get two sheets of the same shape. Every size in the set works that way." Dana repeated the ratio under her breath as if tasting it, and Victoria felt something loosen in her chest, the same feeling as when a proof closes in math class, every line accounted for. All afternoon the copier's refusals had incapacitated her, and the answer had been sitting in the paper itself, patient as furniture.

The scale was easy after that. If the shapes matched, the enlargement was just the ratio of the sides, and she found the percentage on her calculator and keyed it into the library machine the next day, one number, the machine humming, the image blooming onto A3 with every leaf intact. She printed the handouts at A4, and the two versions matched, exactly, the girl under her tree reading at two sizes like an echo. She held them up together and grinned at Priya, who grinned back, and it occurred to Victoria, briefly and uncomfortably, that she had spent most of the week treating Priya as a judge rather than a friend, which was probably not Priya's fault.

Still, one thing nagged at her, and she was honest enough, at least with the cutting mat at five o'clock, to admit it. She hadn't worked out why the ratio did what it did. She knew that it did, knew it the way she knew her bank balance after her grandmother's monthly remittance arrived, ten pounds for art supplies, no note, and she hadn't once spent it on anything as practical as pens. Was knowing that a thing worked the same as understanding it? She suspected not. She also suspected that the difference might not matter by Friday, and that this was the kind of question people asked to sound deep at parties, and both suspicions sat in her at once without settling.

On Thursday she pinned the A3 to the classroom wall and taped the A4 handouts in a fan below it. Mr. Okafor stopped, looked for a long moment, and said, "The proportions hold." Victoria nodded as though she had planned everything from the start, which was not quite true, and not quite false either, since the finished thing was hers whichever route it had taken. Dana came over with the two offcuts from her halved A3, holding them up like a magician about to reveal a card. "Same shape," Dana said. "Every single time you cut one." Victoria looked at the pair of them, then at her poster, then out the window where the real trees stood in the wind, none of them the same shape at all.

The line at the middle school gymnasium was longer than Mackenzie had expected, and she spent the first ten minutes of her adult life as a voter studying the back of a man's canvas jacket, a drawstring bag in her hand holding nothing but her driver's license and a granola bar. In October she would have been too young; in November she was not; the arithmetic of it still startled her, the way a door you had watched for years could open on an ordinary Tuesday.

When she reached the table, a volunteer with reading glasses on a beaded chain asked for her name so she could find it in the binder. Mackenzie slid her license across and said she had never registered anywhere, but here was her ID, and she was registered to vote in the sense that she was a citizen and eighteen. The volunteer's smile did something patient. "Honey, in this state you have to register before you can vote." Mackenzie felt her ears go hot. She had driven forty minutes from the dorms for this.

"There's no registration in North Dakota," she said, and heard how it sounded, like a claim about dragons. "I'm from Fargo. We just show up. You show ID and they check you off." The volunteer turned to a younger woman restocking pens, who leaned in with the mild delight of someone who actually knew something. "It's true. North Dakota's the only state without voter registration. They abolished it in 1951. You show identification at the polls instead." The older volunteer peered over her glasses at Mackenzie, no longer patient, something almost envious in it. "Huh," she said. "Fifty years I've run this table."

Mackenzie stepped out of line to text her father, thumbs clumsy in the cold air outside the doors. Turns out I can't vote today. ND doesn't register people so I never did, and here you have to do it in advance. She paused, then added, The deadline was three weeks ago. I thought being 18 was the deadline. His reply came while she was still standing there: You weren't wrong, exactly. You were North Dakota wrong. Then, a second message: My father voted every single year of his life and never once registered. Nobody made him. Go get coffee and we'll fix it for next time. Something in her chest loosened at we'll, though she was fairly sure she would be the one filling out the form.

She thought about her grandfather while she walked, because the word for what he had passed down was patrimony, even if what he had passed down was a habit: the Tuesday drive to the church basement, the pencil stubs, the little flag sticker he wore on his collar the rest of the day like a scout badge. She had assumed his ease was national, that the whole country worked the way his precinct did, and now she understood that his ease had been a kind of local luck. Two systems, one country. Hers had been the easy one, and she had not known it was luck until this morning.

Back inside, because she could not simply leave, she asked the younger volunteer whether there was anything she could still do. There was not, not for this election, but the woman walked her to a folding table near the exit and showed her the registration form, and Mackenzie filled it out standing up, printing carefully, using her dorm address and her mother's maiden name for the last four digits of her social. A querulous man behind her in the original line was complaining to anyone who would listen that the machines had been wrong last time, that his vote had been eaten, that nothing counted anyway. The older volunteer said, without heat, "Then why'd you wait in line, Gary?" and Mackenzie laughed before she could stop herself, and Gary, surprisingly, laughed too.

Outside, the sky had gone the flat gray that seemed to presage snow but never quite committed, and she sat on the low concrete wall by the flagpole and called her dad instead of texting. "Did you know?" she asked. "That it's just us? That literally no other state does it that way?" He said he had half known, the way you half know things about home, and that he should have told her when she moved, put it on the list with getting her oil changed. She told him about Gary, and the form, and the flag stickers, which her dad said they still gave out, in a box by the door, if you asked.

"So next year," her dad said. "You'll be ready." She said yes, and meant it, and also understood, sitting there with the uncast vote still in her like an unstamped letter, that ready was a word with more rooms in it than she had explored. She pulled her jacket tighter and walked to the parking lot, the completed form folded into thirds in her back pocket, its edge pressing against her hip with every step.

The line outside the church hall on Delmore Street moved in short shuffles, and Brayden checked his wallet twice to be sure the voter information card was still there. His mother had worked polls for years and had habituated him to the ritual of elections, the sharpened pencils, the folded cardboard screens, but he had never been on this side of it. Today he was eighteen, registered, and carrying an argument he hadn't been able to settle in his own head all week.

Behind him, a girl about his age was talking to an older man in a quilted coat. "I thought you had to be twenty-one," she said. "My dad said he couldn't vote until he was older than us."

"Federal voting age," the man said. "Canada lowered it from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970." He said it the way people recite hockey stats, and then the line moved and he went back to his phone.

Brayden turned the number over. 1970. His grandfather would have been nineteen that year, suddenly eligible mid-decade, probably one of the first eighteen-year-olds in the family to mark a ballot. Brayden wished he could ask him, but his grandfather had been dead since Brayden was eleven, and the remaining memories were of a man who complained about taxes and grew dahlias, and who had once said, watching an election night on television, that young people vote like they're throwing rocks.

In front of him, two poll workers were laughing about someone's dog. One of them, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, noticed his card as he stepped up. "First time?" she said.

"Is it obvious?"

"You're holding it like a ticket that might not scan." She found his name on the list, folded the ballot into thirds without looking at it, and slid it across. "Straight to the box after."

The voting screen smelled of pencil shavings. Brayden stood there longer than he meant to. He had gone back and forth all week. His economics teacher, who liked to trace the etiology of every policy back to its first cause, had argued that the party promising lower costs would help his family most; his sister, home from university, had argued the opposite with equal force, and both of them had used numbers. The trouble was that he believed parts of each. He had started wondering whether a considered position was even possible, or whether everyone just picked a side first and built a bridge to it afterward.

His grandfather's line came back to him, throwing rocks. Maybe that was what 1970 had looked like to the people who already had the vote, a crowd of teenagers hurling something. Or maybe his grandfather had meant it as advice: don't vote to break things, vote to build one. Brayden noticed his own incipient bitterness, the itch to mark the ballot against whoever his father supported, purely because his father had been loud about it at dinner, and he recognized the feeling as not a reason. He put the pencil down for a second. Then he picked it up and marked the candidate he could actually defend out loud if someone asked him why, one whose platform he'd read twice and still had doubts about. The doubts were honest. He let them stand.

He fed the ballot into the box, and the poll worker with the glasses said, "There you go, citizen," in a tone that was half teasing and half not.

Outside, the girl from the line was waiting on the steps, scarf up to her chin. "Did you know it was only since 1970?" she said. "That people our age could vote. That's so recent. My dad voted at twenty-one and I voted at eighteen and nothing else changed."

"Something changed," Brayden said, though he wasn't sure what, exactly.

"Like what?"

He shrugged. "We're in the line now. We have to have an opinion even when we don't."

She laughed, a short sound that scattered into the cold. "I marked mine and I still don't know if it was right."

"That might be the whole thing," Brayden said. "Voting, I mean."

She pulled her scarf down so he could see her mouth. "You want to get coffee? There's a place on Delmore and I have forty minutes before my shift."

He looked back once at the church hall, at the box inside holding his folded answer, and then he zipped his coat. "Sure," he said. "I'm Brayden."

The docent at the Greenbrier bunker had a laminated badge and a cough drop she kept moving from one cheek to the other, and Addison liked her immediately, because instead of launching into the rehearsed speech about thirty years of secrecy she said, "You look like you're here on a mission."

"I am, kind of." Addison held up her phone, notes open. "I have a debate Tuesday about who started the Cold War. I got assigned the side that says nobody really did. Or everybody a little. And I can't find the word for it."

The docent, whose badge said RUTH, tilted her head. "There's a word for it?"

"There has to be. My opponent has one, revisionist, that's the school that says the United States started it, or at least pushed it. And then there's the old view, the orthodox one, that the Soviets did. But my position is the mushy middle, and mushy middles have names too, I just don't know mine." Addison had been in the car six hours with her mother, who was upstairs in the gift shop buying postcards of the bunker entrance for people who would not understand them, and the drive had dissolved into a kind of ennui that only let go of her when the blast door came into view, gray and enormous and absurd under the West Virginia hills.

Ruth led her down the corridor, past the exhibit cases with their dormitory beds and their jars of government-issue candy. "I'm not a scholar," she said. "I was a schoolteacher. But I'll tell you what I know, and you can weigh it." Addison noticed that Ruth slowed at the ramp, matching the pace of an older man with a cane who had joined their small group, and that she waited for him before she spoke again, so he wouldn't miss anything.

What Ruth knew, it turned out, was mostly memory. She had been a girl during the Cuban missile crisis, hiding under a desk while her father, a man she described as "bellicose about everything except that week," went quiet. Addison wrote that down, then crossed it out. Anecdotes wouldn't win a debate. But she also wrote it down again, smaller, in the margin, because it felt like evidence of something.

"You want a book," Ruth said finally, stopping by a case of yellowed evacuation plans. "I remember my husband reading it. John Lewis Gaddis, 1972. The United States and the Origins of the Cold War, 1941-1947. He said that fellow argued neither side could bear sole responsibility."

Addison stopped typing. "That's it. That's my whole position, in one book from 1972."

"Somebody's probably named the position by now," Ruth said. "They name everything."

The man with the cane caught up, breathing a little hard, and Addison stood aside so he could see the case. He looked at the evacuation plans for a long moment and then said, to no one in particular, "Post-revisionist. That's what they called it. I taught this for thirty years. Post-revisionism." He tapped the glass once with his cane, softly, like punctuation.

"Post-revisionist," Addison repeated, typing it. "That's the exact word. Thank you." She looked up from her screen. "Do you think it's right, though? The both-sides thing? Gaddis, I mean."

The old teacher demurred, smiling, one hand raised a little as if to hold the question at arm's length. "I think it's the question I liked arguing about least with my students, because the clever ones could never settle it. The ones who wanted one villain hated it, and the ones who wanted no villains hated it more." He turned back toward the corridor, and Ruth moved with him, offering her arm at the spot where the floor changed from concrete to carpet, and he took it without ceremony, the way people take things they've been offered a hundred times.

In the parking lot, Addison sat on the hood of the car with her notes and her mother's sandwich, half of it wrapped back up for her mother because she'd noticed it was the kind with the mustard she liked. She read her own arguments and found them thinner than the walk had made them feel. One villain or none; both, somewhat; the dates 1941 to 1947 sitting there in the title like a fence around the question, and everything after it outside the fence. She typed: my position is the one people hate because it makes you do the work yourself. She left it in. Tuesday she would stand up and say post-revisionist, and Gaddis, and 1972, and she would say what she still couldn't prove, which was that maybe responsibility was like the bunker itself, built by everyone who was frightened, at enormous expense, for a war that never came.

Her mother came out with the postcards and leaned on the car beside her, and Addison handed her the other half of the sandwich without saying anything, and they looked together at the green hills hiding the door.

The garage smelled of dust and old grass clippings, and Logan had claimed it for the weekend because the kitchen table was no longer negotiable. He was painting his grandfather's old tackle box, transforming the rusted green steel into something covered in koi, orange and white fish curling around the latch. He had promised it to his sister Nora before she left for her first semester, which was now four days away, and the deadline had begun to feel like a held breath.

He had learned two ways of thinking about a project like this from two different people. His grandfather, a machinist, believed in doing the thing once, correctly, with cleanup as part of the work itself. His art teacher junior year, an ebullient woman named Ms. Okafor, believed in momentum, in following an impulse before it cooled, and she had once told the class that a finished imperfect thing beat a perfect thing unfinished. Logan had spent a year treating those ideas as rivals. Now, with the tackle box half covered and Nora's departure looming, he was not sure they were rivals at all.

The trouble began on Saturday afternoon. He had thinned his acrylics with water all morning, rinsing brushes in a jar between fish, marveling at how easily the paint moved while it was wet. Then Nora called from inside the house, asking for help carrying bins to her car, and he set his three best brushes on the bench and went in. They hauled dorm bedding and a fan and four boxes labeled in her careful handwriting, and she thanked him with a hug that lasted longer than her usual ones, and by the time he got back, the sun had moved across the garage floor and two hours had gone.

The brushes were ruined. He picked one up and the bristles held their shape like a tiny frozen fan, stiff as a toothbrush found behind a radiator. He ran it under the tap and the water beaded off. The paint had been water-based all morning, thinning and rinsing like ink, and now it simply refused the water entirely, as if the brush had decided to become something else while his back was turned.

"You left them out," Nora said from the doorway. She had followed him back out with two mugs of lemonade, and she stood there looking at the stiffened brushes with an expression that was half apology and half diagnosis. "That happened to half my brushes last spring. Acrylic cleans up with water while it's wet, but once it dries, it won't. It just won't."

"I thought I had more time," Logan said.

"You thought a lot of things were more forgiving than they are." She set down the lemonade and picked up the stiffest brush, turning it over. "So what now?"

He sat on the stool and considered. His grandfather would have thrown the brushes away and said the lesson was the point. Ms. Okafor would have said the lesson was nothing next to the koi, and would have handed him a palette knife. He tried, for a moment, to historicize the problem, to imagine how his grandfather's generation of careful men would have judged a boy who abandoned his tools for a hug and a box of sheets. Then he stopped, because the judgment felt borrowed and useless. The brushes were stiff. His sister was leaving. Both of those were true at once, and the second one mattered more, and he was not going to pretend otherwise, even to look disciplined.

He worked the rest of Saturday and most of Sunday with the brushes that remained and a cheap flat brush he found in a drawer, its synthetic bristles coarse enough to leave visible streaks. The streaks, it turned out, looked like water. Where he had planned smooth gradients of white belly into orange scale, the stiff-bristled strokes made ripples, and the koi seemed to be moving. Nora came out Sunday evening in her socks, saw the finished box under the work light, and did not say anything for a long moment.

"You did that with the ruined brush?" she asked finally.

"The ruined brush and one from the junk drawer."

She ran her thumb along the latch, over a fish's eye. "It's better than the other way would have been, isn't it."

He wanted to say yes. He had a whole argument ready about mistakes becoming texture, about how a revisionist reading of the afternoon might call it luck instead of carelessness. But he genuinely did not know whether the streaks were better or whether he was only making peace with what he could not undo, and he found he did not want to hand her a tidy answer on her last night home. "I don't know," he said. "I like it. I'm still annoyed about the brushes."

Nora laughed, a short surprised sound, and tucked the tackle box under her arm like something she intended to keep forever. "Good," she said. "Bring the lemonade in when you come."

The kitchen had gone quiet except for the hum of the proofing oven and the scrape of Justin's spatula against steel. He had been at the marble slab for forty minutes, moving dark chocolate back and forth in long ribbons, watching it thicken, testing it against his lip the way Chef Amara had shown him once and only once. She was laconic by nature, and tonight she was also busy, so Justin was mostly alone with two hundred grams of couverture and a thermometer that read thirty-one degrees, which was either exactly right or exactly wrong depending on which of his two reference books he believed.

The book from the library said tempering was chemistry, a matter of precise phases and temperatures, and Justin liked that. His father was a machinist who inculcated in him, through years of shop talk at dinner, a faith in instruments and reproducible results. The pastry forums, though, kept insisting that you learned tempering in your wrist and your lower lip, that no probe could tell you the moment the chocolate was ready. He had spent a week trying to decide which camp to join, and the chocolate in front of him, streaked and beginning to dull at the edges, was refusing to settle the matter.

He poured the tempered batch into the polycarbonate mould, tapped out the bubbles, and slid it into the cool room. While it set, he unmoulded yesterday's attempt, the one Chef Amara had glanced at and said nothing about, which was worse than criticism. He turned the mould upside down over the counter and thumped it. Nothing came out. He thumped harder. One shell released, its surface blotchy and matte, and the other five stayed wedged in their cavities like teeth in a jaw.

"Why won't they come out?" he asked when Amara passed with a tray of laminated dough.

"Properly tempered chocolate shrinks a little as it sets," she said, already moving on. "That's what pulls it away from the mould."

Justin stood there with the one blotchy shell in his palm. So the sticking wasn't a flaw of the mould or the tapping. It was evidence. The batch yesterday had never been in temper at all, no matter what the thermometer had claimed, no matter how carefully he had followed the chart. He turned the shell over. It bent slightly when he pressed it instead of snapping, and he understood that the instrument had told him a number and the number had told him nothing about the chocolate itself.

He could have taken this as the forums' victory, intuition over instrumentation, but that felt too easy, a contrivance more suited to an essay than a kitchen. Instead he went back to the cool room and looked at tonight's mould. When he inverted it, the shells dropped out before he could even tap, landing on the cloth with a clean, bright clatter, their surfaces shining like wet river stones. He picked one up and broke it. The snap was sharp, audible across the quiet kitchen, and Amara looked over from her dough.

"Better," she said.

"There's a whole area of physics to it," Justin said, surprising himself. "But I checked it with my lip too. Right before I poured. It felt cool, like the back of a spoon."

"So the thermometer lies sometimes," Amara said, folding her dough over the butter block with three efficient strokes.

"Not lies. It just doesn't know everything." He lined up the new shells next to the old blotchy one. "The shrinkage is the part I trust. If they release, they were in temper. It's the chocolate telling on itself." He paused. "I think I want both. The numbers to get me close, and then the wrist part to finish, and then the mould to tell me if I fooled myself."

Amara dusted flour from her hands and came to look. She picked up the failed shell, flexed it, set it back down next to its shining siblings. Tomorrow you do two hundred grams blind," she said. "No probe. Then we compare." She went back to her tray, and Justin gathered the old chocolate onto his slab to re-melt and try again, because tempering, he was beginning to see, wasn't a thing you achieved once but a thing you returned to. The night's work stood in a neat row on the cloth, five dark shells catching the fluorescent light, and he broke one more in half just to hear it.

Eva stood at her grandmother's sink washing the good teacups, the ones with hairline cracks that her mother always said should be thrown out and never were. The funeral had been four days ago. The kitchen smelled of lemon dish soap and the cold-cream soap that her grandmother had kept by the stove for reasons no one had ever impugned, because no one had ever wanted to argue with her about soap.

The problem was the movie. On Tuesday, two days after the burial, Eva had gone with her cousin Dara to see an action film, and she had laughed at it, really laughed, the loud kind, and then had sat in the theater afterward feeling like she had committed a crime. She had told no one. Now she was washing cups because her hands needed something to do, and her aunt Ruth was at the table behind her wrapping leftover casseroles in foil.

"You're scrubbing those like they owe you money," Ruth said.

"They're recalcitrant," Eva said, holding one up to the window. Tea stain, stubborn, along the rim. "Grandma's tea did that. She'd leave the bag in for ten minutes."

"Fifteen. She liked it bitter enough to stand a spoon in."

Eva dried the cup and set it on the rack. Then she said, without planning to, "Can I ask you something weird?"

"I sell insurance. Nothing is weird anymore."

"Tuesday I went to a movie. With Dara. And I liked it. Like, a lot. I laughed. And then I felt like garbage about it for two days, because how can I be laughing when she just, you know." She put the dish towel down and folded it into thirds, because folding was also something hands could do.

Ruth tore off a strip of foil and smoothed it over a dish with one long stroke. "Did you love her?"

"You know I did."

"Then let me tell you what a pamphlet from the bereavement group told me, because I read everything now, it's my new hobby." Ruth squared the foil edge against the counter. "There's these two researchers, Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, and they have a dual process model. It says grieving people go back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, instead of moving in one direction. So you're not supposed to just feel sad forever in a straight line. You oscillate. That's their word. You swing between the two."

Eva turned that over. "So the movie was the rebuilding part."

"Or maybe you just have bad taste in movies. Both things can be true." Ruth pointed at a casserole. "Hand me the tape."

Eva brought the tape, still thinking. The model made sense of something she hadn't known needed sense made of it: the way she had cried hard on Monday over a grocery list in her grandmother's handwriting, and on Wednesday had spent an hour comparing dorm prices online without crying at all, and had assumed the Wednesday version of herself was a fraud. If the model was right, neither day was a betrayal. She was just moving between the two, the way people apparently actually did, not the way movies about grief showed it, one long gray march toward acceptance.

But she didn't want to accept the whole idea too fast either. She had read enough in school to know that a tidy theory could be a way of not thinking. She sat down across from Ruth. "Okay, but here's what I can't figure out. How do you know when you're doing it right? Like, what if I'm just using the back and forth thing as an excuse? What if I use it to never really face anything?"

Ruth considered that while she wrote on a foil label. "That's a better question than my pamphlet answered."

"So you don't know either."

"Nobody knows, honey. You do the best swing you can."

That was not satisfying, and Eva respected it anyway. Her mother came in then with two bags of her grandmother's coffee mugs, the everyday ones, and a quiet detente settled over the kitchen, the kind where everyone agreed not to mention that the mugs should probably go to the church rummage sale and nobody said so out loud. Eva took the mugs one at a time and washed them, too, even though they had already been washed, because her grandmother had drunk out of them every morning for fifty years and that seemed worth one more rinse.

Dara texted her a picture from the theater lobby: the two of them Tuesday night, mid-laugh, blurry, terrible. Eva looked at it for a long moment, then turned her phone face down on the counter and picked up the last mug, the blue one with the chip on the handle.

"Want me to dry?" Ruth said.

"No," Eva said. "I've got this one."

The bowling alley smelled of rented shoes and cherry slushie, and Kaylee stood at the counter wondering whether she should pay for her own games before Dante arrived, or whether paying first would look like a statement. She had thought about it on the bus, weighing the two positions like a girl holding identical gifts in either hand. If she paid, she was independent, unbeholden; if she waited, she might seem to expect something. In the end she bought her shoes, rented two lanes by mistake, and had to ask for one lane back, which the clerk gave her with a look she chose not to interpret.

Dante came in at six exactly, which she liked, carrying nothing, wearing a jacket she had seen him in at school maybe four times and never once thought about until now. "You found it," she said, and he said, "I looked it up twice on the way," which she also liked, because it was an admission, and admissions were the currency she trusted.

He had asked her out on Tuesday, by the trophy case outside the gym, and she had said yes quickly, then spent the rest of the week deciding whether the quickness had been a mistake. Her mother, over dishes, had said only, "You don't owe anybody a second date, and you don't owe anybody a reason." Kaylee had rolled that around all week, and by Friday she had arrived somewhere adjacent to it: she didn't owe Dante a reason, but she might owe herself a fair look before making one up.

The first game, she won by nine pins. He laughed about it in a way that felt real, not performed, and she filed that away. On the second game, somewhere in the fourth frame, she noticed that they were both leaning on the ledge the same way, elbows down, chin on knuckles, watching her ball drift toward the gutter. She straightened up. A second later, so did he.

Her brother Will, home from his first semester of college, had told her about a study over winter break, in between complaints about his roommate. In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. Will had called it the chameleon effect, and Kaylee had filed that away too, the way she filed everything, in the drawer marked possibly useful, possibly nothing.

Now she watched. She crossed her ankles; two frames later his ankles crossed. She spun her cup in her hands; he got a cup of his own and spun it, laughing about something unrelated. And the strange thing was that she could not tell, watching him, whether it meant anything at all. If people liked a partner more when that partner mimicked them, then maybe he was doing it to be liked, which would be an affectation, a strategy, and she would have to decide how she felt about being managed. Or maybe it happened below everyone, some current neither of them steered, in which case there was no one to blame and nothing to decode.

"You're staring at your shoes," Dante said. "They're really something."

"They're size nines and they've been on four hundred feet."

"Mine have been on more," he said, and lifted one to show her, and she thought, without wanting to, he's matching me again, joking the way I joke.

By the eighth frame she had tried both ways of thinking and could not land on one. She tested him once more, deliberately, draping her arm along the ball return, and when his arm followed, thirty seconds later, she felt a small flat disappointment and a small warm spark at the same time, and could not have said which was the truer response. Maybe the study didn't cover this direction, her watching for it, both of them awake to the possibility. Maybe noticing ruined whatever the noticing was about.

She got a strike in the ninth, all ten pins folding sideways at once, and Dante stood up and held out his hand, palm up, noncommittal, offering the high five or something smaller, letting her choose. She looked at the hand. Her mother's rule said she owed him nothing; her own quieter rule said she owed him the truth of this moment, which was that she liked him and did not yet know why, and might not find out tonight.

She high-fived him, then kept her hand there a beat longer than the gesture required. "Overtime," she said. "Next game's mine to lose."

I have always been good at math, which is why it annoyed me that this particular chapter was taking three nights.
