The kitchen table had my textbook open to section 4.2, a sheet of notebook paper with a parabola sketched badly at the top, and a bowl of cereal going soft because I refused to stop mid-problem. My sister Priya came through for a glass of water and looked over my shoulder the way older sisters do, like she was checking a receipt.

"It's a fence problem," I said before she could ask. "A farmer has two hundred feet of fencing, one side's against a river, and I have to maximize the area. So I write area equals length times width, and the constraint is two widths plus one length equals two hundred."

"So solve it."

"That's the part I'm learning." I tapped the page. "You take the derivative. If the area is a function of width, the derivative tells you how fast it's changing at any point. Where it's a maximum, the slope is zero, so you set the derivative equal to zero and solve. Watch." I wrote it out. Width times two hundred minus two widths, all divided by one, which simplified to two hundred w minus two w squared. Then the derivative: two hundred minus four w. Set it to zero. Width is fifty. "See? Fifty by one hundred. Maximum area."

Priya pulled out the chair across from me and sat down, which she almost never does. She's a sophomore at the state college and she had been effusive about calculus all through my senior year, always saying I'd love it, always asking whether I'd signed up yet. I'd told her it was fine. The truth was I'd nearly dropped precalc in October, and only the fear of my father's opinion had kept me in the seat.

"That's half of it," she said. "You found the top of the hill. Now look at the next section."

I turned the page. The next section was about area under curves, and my stomach dropped a little, because I'd glanced at it earlier and seen a figure with maybe a hundred rectangles drawn under a curve, each one skinny, all of them stacked to approximate the space beneath. The text wanted me to add up the areas of those rectangles. I actually started writing the numbers down, rectangle by rectangle, and got to the eleventh one before Priya put her hand flat on the page.

"You were really going to add a hundred rectangles," she said. Not a question.

"It's the area. That's how you get the area."

"There's a shortcut. Look at the back of the book."

I flipped to the reference pages, and there it was, boxed, almost casually, like it was nothing: the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. I read it twice. It said that if F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. An antiderivative, as far as I could tell, was just running the derivative backward, undoing it, the way subtraction undoes addition. I sat there with my pen stopped on the paper.

"So I don't add the rectangles at all," I said slowly. "The f is the curve. I find some F whose derivative is f, and then the whole area under the curve from a to b is just F at the end minus F at the start. Two steps. The exact answer, not an approximation."

"Now you understand why I kept talking about it."

I went back through my notes and checked the fence problem against this new idea, because I wanted to see whether they connected. They did, in a way I hadn't expected. The derivative took me from area to slope; the antiderivative took me from slope back to accumulated area. Same machine, run in opposite directions. I had spent three nights thinking calculus was one hill, and it turned out to be two faces of the same mountain, and I honestly could not tell yet which face I was standing on, or whether the picture would hold up when the functions stopped being polynomials and turned into sines and logs.

I wrote the theorem out once in my own hand, closed the book, and ate the soggy cereal anyway, because I don't waste food.

"You're going to call me tonight when you get stuck on integrals," Priya said, rinsing her glass.

"I won't get stuck."

She set the glass upside down on the drying rack and picked up her phone, already halfway to the living room, and I opened the book again.

The office smelled of toner and the lemon wipes her mother used on every desk at closing, and by two o'clock Faith had alphabetized three drawers of invoices without being asked, which she considered a form of surrender. Her mother worked at a company that sold filter parts to machine shops, and school had let out early, and the house was being fumigated, so here she was, sixteen and unpaid, in a chair too low for the counter.

"I need the ones who never bought anything," her mother said, standing at the printer with a stack of customer labels. "The boss wants to call the dead accounts before the new year. Can you get me that list from the system?"

Faith turned to the second monitor, the one reserved for the database. She had learned the basics last summer, enough to pull up a single table, but the request sat there in her mind like a puzzle missing its middle. The customers lived in one table, all nine hundred of them. The orders lived in another, thousands of rows deep, each one stamped with a customer ID. The question was how to prove a negative, how to find the people who existed in one place and left no trace in the other.

Her first instinct was to look for customers whose ID did not appear in the orders table, and she typed something with NOT IN, running it the way you test a doorbell. The database ground through it and returned a list, and she felt a small flare of triumph, until she checked two names against the orders by hand and found one of them, Kowalczyk Machine, had ordered forty times since March. The list was wrong, or partly wrong, and she could not tell which parts, which was somehow worse.

"That bad?" her mother said, watching her face.

"Worse," Faith said. "It's confidently bad."

She sat back. What she wanted, she realized, was not a clever trick but a way of seeing, a picture where absence was visible. She thought of the seating chart from her aunt's wedding, the empty chairs glowing with what they meant. If she could lay every customer beside their orders, side by side, the ones with nothing beside them would stand out by their emptiness, like place settings no one came to claim. It was less like searching and more like arranging, and the difference between those two ways of thinking felt important, though she could not yet say why.

She read the documentation the way she read recipes, skimming until a phrase snagged: a LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first table and matches what it can from the second. She said it aloud, quietly, just to hear it. "LEFT JOIN." Then she built it, customers first, orders second, and when she ran the query the result had every customer in it, with order columns filled in or blank. The blank ones were her answer, or half of it. She remembered a rule from somewhere, that empty in SQL was not zero and not nothing you could compare with an equals sign, and she added the condition her memory supplied: WHERE the orders' customer ID IS NULL. She hesitated over it, because she was trusting a memory she could not verify, and ran the query anyway.

Forty-one rows. Kowalczyk was not among them. She checked five names against the orders table, one by one, and found each one genuinely silent, no orders ever, going back to the beginning of the data. Then she found the flaw in her first attempt, or part of it: some rows in the orders table had no customer ID at all, blank where a number should be, and her NOT IN version had swept customers into the dead list because of those blanks. This new approach sidestepped that entirely, the way a surgeon might cauterize a bleeding edge rather than chase every vessel. It still bothered her that she understood the failure only incompletely. She had a working answer and a half-understood mistake, and both were hers.

"Is this it?" her mother said, coming over with her coffee. She read the screen, lips moving slightly. "Forty-one. I would have guessed hundreds." She pointed at a name. "Pereira. He came to the open house in October, ate all the shrimp, and never ordered. I remember him."

"Then the list is probably right," Faith said, "or right enough." She wondered whether probably was an honest word here, and decided it was, since she had tested five names out of forty-one, which was a sample and not a proof. She printed it anyway. The label stock was an encumbrance, jamming twice in the tray, and she stood there feeding it sheets, thinking that the whole afternoon had felt embryonic, like the start of a skill that would look different once it grew, and she would not be able to remember this exact clumsiness later no matter how hard she tried.

Her mother peeled the first label off the sheet and held it up to the light. "Pereira," she read. "You're first, shrimp man."

The community centre on Delmore Street kept its rooms as spartan as a promise: metal chairs, a foldout table, one radiator that clanked like it was arguing with itself. Avery arrived every Tuesday at four because the youth civic programme was the cheapest thing in the city that might get her noticed by the delegation committee, and because Tomas was always early, always already reading.

He had come from Ottawa two years ago, and tonight he slid a photocopied sheet across the table with the heading Types of Democratic Systems. "For Friday," he said. "Mr. Okonkwo says the quiz is worth half our placement score." Avery had wanted that placement since autumn, a paid summer with the provincial youth parliament, and she had told her mother it was already as good as hers.

"Easy," she said, smoothing the sheet flat. "Our way and the other way. In America we elect the president, they pick a prime minister in their parliament. That's basically it." Tomas raised an eyebrow, which annoyed her, because he did it slowly, as though her answer had disappointed him personally.

They drilled each other, trading questions across the table while the radiator clanged. She answered most of them fine. She knew first past the post, knew what a whip did, could list three differences between a statute and a regulation. Then Tomas leaned back and asked the one she had been dreading without knowing it. "Say Congress turns against a president halfway through. Majority hates him. Every vote, he loses. What happens?"

Avery opened her mouth. The clock above the door ticked twice. She could hear someone bouncing a basketball in the gym down the hall, and she let the sound fill the silence while she decided whether to guess or whether guessing was worse than admitting she didn't know. In her chest a small, cold idea took shape: she had been denigrating this whole topic for weeks, treating it as a box to tick, and the box had turned out to have a floor she'd never looked under.

"They can remove him," she said. "Vote him out. That's the whole point of checks, isn't it?"

"No," Tomas said, and he didn't gloat, which somehow stung more. "That's my country, not yours. Here, the president is elected separately from the legislature, for a fixed term. The legislature can't remove him just because they disagree with him." He tapped the sheet. "In a parliamentary system, the leader is chosen by the legislature and it can pull him down whenever it loses confidence. Yours can't do that. Yours waits for the term to end."

Avery stared at the paper. She had lived under this arrangement for eighteen years, had watched a president fight with Congress for months on the news while her mother muttered about mendacity and thrown shoes at the screen, and never once asked why nothing gave way. It had seemed like stubbornness, or failure, rather than design. "So when everyone's against him," she said slowly, "nothing happens."

"Nothing happens," Tomas agreed. "Until the fixed term runs out. Unless it's something else entirely, but that's not on our sheet."

She turned the fact over the way you turn a stone to see what's underneath. In Tomas's system, a leader was only ever as strong as the parliament's mood; the country could change its head of government overnight, and just as quickly regret it. In hers, a president could stand alone against the whole legislature and simply endure. Which one was safer? She liked the idea of a government that could not deadlock itself into paralysis, and she liked the idea of stability that survived a bad month, and she could not make herself choose between the two, and she suspected the honest answer was that it depended on whether you trusted the voters more than you trusted the institutions, or the other way around, and she did not yet know which she trusted.

The gym door banged open down the hall, and a boy in a Raptors jersey put his head in. "Okonkwo's here early. Quiz moved up. Tonight."

Avery gathered the sheets with hands that were steadier than she expected. Tomas held the door for her, and as they walked toward the main room, she heard Mr. Okonkwo's voice already reading the first question to the assembled chairs: "In a presidential system, how is the head of government chosen, and can the legislature remove a leader merely for disagreeing with them?"

Avery sat down, uncapped her pen, and wrote, "Separately. Fixed term. No."

Ava spread the papers across the kitchen table the way her mother laid out a pattern before cutting fabric: pay stubs on the left, receipts on the right, her first tax return, still blank, in the middle like a question nobody had asked yet. She was seventeen, three months from graduation, and she had decided she would understand money before September, when residence fees and meal plans and a city she didn't know would start making claims on her. The gas station where she worked paid her every two weeks, and every two weeks the number at the top of the stub and the number at the bottom told two different stories.

The gap between those numbers had been bothering her since January. Four hundred and eighty-two dollars became three hundred and ninety-something, and the lines in between read like a language she had never been taught: federal tax, provincial tax, CPP, EI. She had tried asking her father once, and he had waved a hand and said it was all a racket, which assuaged nothing, because knowing something was unfair was not the same as understanding it. Her father pronounced on most subjects that way, a small autocrat of the kitchen, and she had learned to stop asking him things she actually wanted answers to.

Her friend Noor worked at a bakery in Montreal. They had been comparing jobs over texts for weeks, half bragging, half complaining, and this afternoon Noor was coming over, bringing her own stubs, because she had the same resolution Ava did. When Noor arrived, shaking rain off her jacket, Ava slid the kettle on without being asked; Noor's hands were always cold and she always wanted tea, and Ava had stopped needing to ask about that a long time ago.

They lined up the stubs side by side, Ava's Ontario ones on the left, Noor's Quebec ones on the right, and leaned over them like two cartographers comparing maps of the same coastline drawn by different empires. The pay was nearly identical. Everything below it diverged. "Yours says QPP," Noor said, tapping her stub. "Mine says CPP." Ava frowned. "What's QPP?" "Quebec Pension Plan. We're not in the Canada one." She traced down further. "And I don't have EI either. I have QPIP." She read it out slowly, parental insurance, and Ava pulled her laptop toward her and typed, and for a while there was only the kettle ticking and the sound of keys.

So it was true, and stranger than she'd guessed: outside Quebec, a typical paycheque showed deductions for income tax, Canada Pension Plan contributions and Employment Insurance premiums, while Quebec ran its own pension and parental insurance plans instead. Two friends, same age, same minimum-wage grind, standing in different systems without ever having chosen either. Ava thought of all the students who would cross a provincial line in September, herself maybe among them, carrying stubs that would suddenly rearrange themselves. "So when you retire," she said, "does it all come from the Quebec one?" Noor shrugged, morose for a second over her cooling tea. "My aunt says it doesn't matter, there'll be nothing left by then anyway."

Ava wasn't willing to be that fatalistic, but she wasn't willing to be her father either, dismissing the whole apparatus as a racket because it was easier than reading it. The receipts helped. She had saved every one since New Year's, a small superstitious pile, and now she sorted them by feel, the glossy ones from the pharmacy, the soft ones from the coffee shop near school. On each, below the price, a second line: the harmonized sales tax, thirteen percent, adding itself to her chapstick and her bus pass with the patience of a tide. Her mother, passing through for a glass of water, paused at the table. "What's all this?" "My financial literacy," Ava said, and her mother put a hand briefly on her shoulder and said, "Good, someone in this house should have some," which was as close as she came to criticizing her husband in front of their daughter.

The tax return was the part Ava kept circling back to. Her employer had given her a slip with her total earnings and the tax already taken off, and the return, when she finally understood its shape, was a reconciliation: the government had guessed, through the year, what she owed, and now she got to correct the guess. Given how little she made, the guess had probably been generous to the government and stingy to her, which meant a refund, which meant the box at the bottom of the blank form was, for once, pointed in her direction. She began filling it in, box by box, her handwriting smaller than usual, as though the form might startle if she moved too fast.

Noor leaned over and read the refund estimate aloud, and they both laughed, because it was thirty-one dollars, and because thirty-one dollars was also a tank of gas, or two weeks of coffee, or a birthday present for Noor's sister. "I'm going to frame it," Ava said. "Frame thirty-one dollars?" "Frame the feeling of it." Noor stole the last of the tea and pushed the empty mug across the table, and Ava got up and filled it again.

Later, after Noor had left, Ava sat alone with the lamp on, copying her CPP line into a notebook, then writing QPP beside it with a question mark, because she still didn't know what happened to someone who worked in both provinces, and the internet had given her three answers that disagreed. She underlined the question, twice, and left it there, an honest hole in an otherwise tidy page. Then she stacked the receipts, squared the stubs, and turned off the lamp. "Thirty-one dollars," she said to the dark kitchen, and grinned.

Kyle had come to his grandmother's house for the weekend with one goal, which was to avoid thinking about Marcus, and so of course Marcus was all he could think about. Marcus had missed the Tuesday deadline for the robotics code again, the third time this season, and Kyle had told the group chat exactly what he thought of that: "you're lazy." Two words, sent at eleven at night, followed by an hour of nobody typing anything, which was somehow worse than an argument.

His grandfather found him on the porch Saturday morning, sulking over a bowl of cereal. "You look like a boy who lost a chess match to himself," his grandfather said, and disappeared inside before Kyle could protest that he didn't play chess. When Kyle followed him in, annoyed at being teased, he found the old man in the study, holding out a paperback with a cracked spine. "Take this. You have the face of someone about to write something he'll regret, and I've run out of porch to hide on."

The book was about leadership, which Kyle would normally have used as a coaster, but he was desperate enough to read anything. He sat on the kitchen floor between the radiator and the dog and read about the Situation-Behavior-Impact model, which came from a place called the Center for Creative Leadership. The idea was that you name when it happened, what the person actually did, and what effect it had. It sounded almost too simple to work, like being told the secret to juggling was to not drop anything. But there was a line in the book about how vague labels like "lazy" told a person nothing they could act on, and Kyle felt that line tap him on the shoulder like a teacher who had seen him passing notes.

"It's called the Situation-Behavior-Impact model," he told his grandmother at lunch, testing the words out, "and before you ask, no, I have not become a leadership dilettante overnight. I'm a dilettante of exactly one afternoon." His grandmother said she'd been a dilettante of marriage for fifty years and it had served her fine, and Kyle laughed so hard he had to put down his sandwich.

The problem was that when he pulled out his phone to fix things, "you're lazy" kept rewriting itself into other insults. "You're unreliable" was just the same word in a suit. He called his co-captain, Priya, hoping she'd do the hard part for him, but she refused on principle. "You lit it, you put it out," she said. "But if it helps, being specific isn't being mean. My mom does it to my dad about the dishwasher and he actually improved." Kyle said that was the least romantic thing he'd ever heard, and Priya said it was the most.

So he walked the backyard with the dog, muttering drafts. His putative apology, the one he'd been planning since Tuesday, turned out not to be an apology at all but a request that Marcus apologize to him, and Kyle had the honesty to recognize the difference and delete it. That was the strange part: the model wasn't just a format, it forced him to figure out what had actually happened instead of how he'd felt about it in the dark at eleven at night. When had it happened? Tuesday. What had Marcus done, in the world, in verifiable reality? He hadn't sent the navigation code by the deadline. What effect did it have? Kyle had stayed up until two rewriting it himself and had snapped at his little sister the next morning over nothing. He hadn't even connected those two things until he tried to write them down.

The message he finally sent was three sentences long and took him forty minutes. "On Tuesday, the code was due and I didn't get it from you until Friday. I rewrote the navigation myself that night and was a wreck the next day. Can we figure out what's going wrong before Thursday's build?" He read it eleven times, showed it to his grandmother, who said it was nicer than most things his grandfather had ever said to her, and sent it before he could turn it back into "you're lazy" with extra steps.

Marcus replied with a photo of his little brother in a hospital waiting room, then, a minute later: "sorry man. thursday for sure." Kyle sat down hard on the porch steps. He didn't know if the model had fixed anything, really; the code might still be late on Thursday, and "sorry" was doing a lot of work in that text. What he knew was that he hadn't known about the hospital, and that "you're lazy" would have made him the kind of person who'd said it anyway. His grandfather came out with two mugs of tea and sat down beside him without asking anything, which was its own kind of feedback, delivered with precision. "Well?" he said eventually. Kyle held up the phone. "Thursday," he said. "We'll see."

The footnotes ran down the page like a staircase, each one shorter than the last, until Kate reached the third that said only "Ibid." and stopped reading altogether. She sat back in the corner chair of the school library, the kind with the torn green cushion that everyone avoided, and stared at the word as though it might blink first. Around her the late-afternoon light came through the tall windows in slanted panels, and somebody two tables over was clicking a pen in a rhythm she could almost predict.

Her assignment, due Monday, was a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and she had chosen a question she barely understood: whether human intelligence is shaped more by genes or by environment. The first article, thick with equations and the word "heritability" used in ways that contradicted her casual sense of it, argued for a strong genetic component. The second, which she had expected to be its opposite, was more readable, almost lyrical, and its footnotes were where the Ibid. began.

"Is this even English?" she asked, turning the photocopy sideways, as if the word would look different from another angle. Her friend Priya slid into the chair across from her, carrying a granola bar and her own stack of sources for the same assignment, because Mr. Ferrante had given it to the whole class and Priya had left hers until the last weekend, as usual.

"Is what English?" Priya leaned over. "Oh. Ibid."

"Every second note says it. Then I turn the page and there it is again. What is it doing?"

"Ibid. means ibidem," Priya said, peeling the wrapper off her bar. "Latin, in the same place. It's citing the same source as the note just before it."

Kate looked down at the page and felt something shift, the way a magic-eye picture resolves when you stop trying. The long footnote, the first one on the page, was a citation of a monograph on twin studies. Every Ibid. beneath it was that same monograph, again and again, the article standing on one set of shoulders and pointing at them repeatedly. "So this whole page," she said slowly, "is basically one source?"

"Basically, yeah."

She spread both articles on the table, and the question she had walked in with, which article was right, began to seem like the wrong question, though she could not yet say what the right one was. The first article's footnotes were a garden of different names, journals in Dutch and German, a citation of a 1930s study she would never track down in a million years. The second article's footnotes were a monoculture. How would a reader know, she wondered, unless they squinted at the stairs? She started a list on the back of her English notes: Article A, diverse evidence, dense prose. Article B, persuasive, one root.

The comparison was supposed to be about the science, she knew that. Mr. Ferrante wanted claims weighed against claims. But she kept noticing that her own judgment was being steered by things she could not defend in an essay, like how the second author's prose had mesmerized her for an entire train ride home, so smooth it felt like agreement, whereas the first author's equations had made her feel stupid and therefore defensive. She had nearly written "the second article is more convincing" before realizing that convincing and right were not the same thing, that the smoother article had offered her a bromide about potential and nurturing while the difficult one had at least shown its arithmetic.

She tried drafting a paragraph on the substance anyway. The first article argued that the phenotypic variation in test scores, the variation you could actually observe in real people, could be decomposed into genetic and environmental components, and that the genetic portion was substantial. The second argued that environments were so unequal that any such decomposition told you about the society being measured, not about children in general. She wrote three sentences, crossed out two, and sat chewing her pen. Both could be true at once, she thought, or at least both could be true about different populations in different decades, and the honest version of her essay might have to hold them both without crowning a winner, which felt like a violation of everything a five-paragraph essay had ever taught her.

Then she flipped back to the first page of the second article to check the author's affiliation, and stopped. The name was different, a hyphenated surname instead of a single one, but the acknowledgment line thanked "my colleagues at the Minnesota lab," the same lab named in the first article's abstract, and when she checked the first article's bibliography she found the second article listed there, cited twice. The second author had been a co-author on the first paper's dataset. The two articles she had chosen as opponents were, in some sense, one long argument with itself, the same mind or the same data appearing on both sides of the ring.

"Priya," she said. "Look at this." She laid the pages side by side and traced the connection with her finger, the shared lab, the shared dataset, the chain of citations looping back. Priya leaned in, chewing, and her eyebrows went up.

"So what are you going to write? That they're basically the same person arguing with themselves?"

"I don't know yet." Kate pulled the pad toward her and wrote, at the top of a fresh page, "What does it mean to compare two perspectives that grew from the same soil?" She underlined it once, then sat looking at the question, the pen still in her hand, the light moving off the windows.

Zachary had signed up because the form was due Friday and the scholarship committee liked the word "service," a word he had until now associated mainly with tennis. The food bank occupied the basement of a church whose ceiling pipes sweated in the heat, and a woman named Ruth handed him a hairnet before he had finished saying good morning. "Canned goods on the left table," she said. "Anything opened or homemade comes to me. Not you. Me." She said this the way people say don't touch the stove, which made Zachary immediately curious about who had touched the stove.

He sorted cans for an hour, learning the taxonomy: soups with soups, beans with beans, a category Ruth called "mystery," which appeared to mean anything with a label in a language nobody at the table could read. A retired engineer named Desh worked beside him and held forth, in a pleasant drone, on the carbon footprint of tin. Zachary had expected the other volunteers to be like his mother, earnest and guilt-driven, or like his economics teacher, who believed charity was mostly signaling. Desh was neither. Desh was a polymath, or at least a man with an opinion about everything from soil depletion to the melting point of margarine, and he sorted beans while he talked, and the two activities seemed to have nothing to do with each other.

The trouble arrived at eleven, carried in a foil-covered dish by a woman in a rain jacket though it had not rained. She set it on the intake table with the confidence of someone delivering a solved problem. "Lasagna," she said. "For the families. I made it this morning, the good ricotta." Behind her, two children were attempting to climb the donation bin.

Zachary, being nearest, reached for it, because it was heavy and because reaching for heavy things was, so far, the entirety of his training. "Sir," the woman said, "you'll burn your hands," and she was right; the foil was still warm. He stood there holding a hot lasagna and no policy.

Ruth appeared from the back with the speed of someone who had done this before. "That smells incredible," she said, and she meant it; Zachary could tell because she closed her eyes for half a second. "But we can't take home-cooked food. We can't check how it was prepared or stored, so it can't go out to people." The woman's face did something complicated, a sort of settling, like a house deciding whether to shift. "It's a rule," Ruth added, softer, "and I didn't write it, and I've turned down my own sister's soup."

"That seems insane," Zachary said, later, in the loading area. He had been introspect-ing about it all through the lunch rush, if there was such a verb, and what he kept circling was this: the woman had made food for neighbors out of her own money and her own morning, and a system built to feed people had refused it. Desh wiped his hands on his jeans. "The rule protects the people eating, not the people giving," he said. "You can't verify her kitchen. You can verify a can." He tapped one, a dented thing labeled montane stew, which Zachary had earlier shelved under mystery. "Nobody cooked this in a bathtub."

"But she's right there," Zachary said. "We could just ask her about her kitchen." "And she'd say it was spotless," Desh said, "because everybody's kitchen is spotless when they're asked. The rule isn't about her. It's about the thousand people we don't know." Zachary thought about his economics teacher, who would have said the rule was institutional cowardice, trust replaced by paperwork. He thought about his mother, who would have said the rule was just common sense and the woman should take the lasagna to a shelter that took hot food, except he didn't know if such a shelter existed, which was its own problem.

He found he could hold both positions at once without either one winning. The rule was cold and the lasagna was warm and neither fact canceled the other. What he could not do was stand in the loading area holding nothing, which was what he was doing, so he went back inside.

The woman was still there, actually, sitting on a folding chair near the door while Ruth walked her through a printed list of places that accepted hot meals, underlining things in pencil with the gravity of a treaty. Zachary stopped at a respectful distance. "It smelled really good," he offered. The woman looked up. "It was," she said. "My mother's recipe. She'd have made me bring it somewhere anyway, she never let food sit." One of the children had surrendered the donation bin and was now reading a cereal box with total absorption, and Zachary thought, not for the first time that day, that children had the right relationship to everything.

Ruth finished underlining and handed over the list. "Next time," she said, "bring cans. Big ones. I'll put you on the good shelf." The woman laughed, a short surprised sound, and gathered her foil dish, which had gone from warm to merely heavy in the way of abandoned efforts. At the door she paused and looked back at Zachary specifically. "You'll be here next Saturday?" she asked. "I want someone to tell me if the cans taste any good."

The festival took up four blocks of Fremont Avenue, closed to cars and smelling of scallion oil and gunpowder from the leftover firecrackers. Maelie walked half a step behind her mother, carrying a paper bag of oranges, while her father pointed out the inefficient layout of the food stalls as though someone had asked him. Her cousin Dax, who was nine, ran ahead with a paper dragon on a stick, wheeling around so the dragon's head snapped at strangers' knees.

At the community association booth, Maelie's mother took out a stack of red envelopes and began counting bills onto the folding table. She was handing them out to the younger cousins, a dollar a year of age plus a little extra, and Dax had already stretched out his hand. Maelie had her own envelope to prepare, because she had a job now at the campus library and her mother had told her that this year she gave, she did not only receive. She had forty dollars in twenties, folded and ready.

She was sealing the envelope when her grandmother caught her wrist. Not hard, but with the particular authority of someone who assumed she would be obeyed. She said something in Cantonese that Maelie partly followed, then switched to English for the last part. "Not forty. Never forty. Four sounds like death." Dax, still breathing hard from running, said "Cool," in the tone he used for sharks and volcanoes, and Maelie's mother took one of the twenties back and replaced it with a ten and a five, making thirty-five.

Maelie stood there holding the lighter envelope. Her father, an engineer who had once argued at Thanksgiving that numerology was the desiccated husk of arithmetic, ancient people mistaking coincidence for pattern, watched the whole transaction and said nothing. That was unusual for him. When she raised an eyebrow at him, he shrugged and said the oranges needed carrying, and turned toward the citrus stall as if it had been an emergency.

She found him there a minute later, buying tangerines he did not want. "You think it's nonsense," she said.

"I think it's a superstition," he said. "I also think your grandmother survived a war, two crossings, and thirty years of night shifts, and if a number costs me five dollars to leave alone, that is the cheapest peace I have ever purchased." He put a tangerine in the paper bag. "There's an externality to being right at full volume. Other people live downstream of it."

Maelie had spent the school year in a philosophy seminar where the teacher, a grad student with a cold, had liked the word "epistemic." She had learned to call things unjustified beliefs and to feel a small clean superiority doing it. But her father was not exactly endorsing the number either. He was saying something stranger: that a belief could be false and still load-bearing, holding up something true, like a wall built on the wrong blueprint that had nevertheless stood for eighty years. She could not find a term for that in her notebook. The closest thing she had was a paragraph on Pascal, and Pascal had seemed, when she read him at two in the morning, like a man bluffing.

She carried the oranges back through the crowd. Dax was standing at the goldfish-toss game with her grandmother, who was handing him coins with visible reluctance, since the game was, in her classification, a swindle endemic to street festivals. Maelie gave Dax the envelope. He tore it open, counted, and frowned. "Thirty-five," he said. "That's not even."

"That's the point," Maelie said.

He looked at the bill and coins in his palm, then at the dragon stick tucked under his arm, then at their grandmother, who was watching him with an expression Maelie could not read, some mixture of amusement and something older. Dax put the money in his pocket without arguing, which for Dax was a first, and pointed at the fish bowls. "Five dollars says I get one."

"You don't have five dollars," Maelie said. "You have thirty-five, and you're not betting it."

"It's an expression." He was already dragging their grandmother toward the counter, the dragon's head banging against her hip, and their grandmother was saying something about the odds, and Maelie stood in the noise of the street with the empty envelope still in her hand, holding it the way you hold something you have decided, for now, not to throw away. Then her mother called her name from the bao stall, twice, and she went.

The kitchen timer belonged to Sophie's grandmother, and it had one setting that mattered: five minutes. Sophie had borrowed it on Sunday, carried it up to the spare bedroom, and set it on the dresser beside her vocabulary notebook, because on Thursday morning a teacher she had never met would press a button on a screen and expect her to argue, in French, for five unbroken minutes, on a topic announced only when the timer started.

The topic list was public, at least. Seventeen possible questions, all versions of the same argument: whether the city should raise transit fares. Sophie had spent the weekend assembling her case, and by Monday afternoon she had two of them, one from each grandmother. From Mamie, who had ridden the Metro for forty years: fares punish the poorest riders, and a city that lionizes its transit system in tourism ads ought to fund it like the essential service it claims it is. From Gran, here in this house, who had never once owned a transit pass: nothing subsidized stays honest, and someone has to pay the driver. Sophie liked that the two women disagreed. She liked less that she now had to reconcile them in a language she could think in only slowly, the way she could think in English quickly.

"Cinq minutes," she said to the empty room, and pressed the timer.

The trouble arrived on schedule, about ninety seconds in. She had her opening, her transition, her statistic about fare evasion, and then she reached for the word for tax and found nothing. Not the French word, not the English word, only a hole where the word should have been. Her mouth stopped. The timer's dial ticked behind her like something alive. She stood there in the yellow light of the spare room, staring at the crocheted runner on the dresser, and heard her own silence as a kind of failure, and started over from the beginning, and hit the same hole at the same second.

She was lying on the bed with the notebook over her face when she heard the vacuum cleaner stop downstairs, which meant Gran was done with the hall, which meant Gran would appear eventually, which meant Sophie had perhaps ten minutes of privacy left in which to solve this before anyone asked how the studying was going. She sat up. She said the sentence out loud in English, the sentence with the hole in it, and then, because the timer was still set and because it was the only clock she trusted, she pressed it again and made herself keep going through the hole. "L'argent," she said slowly, "que le gouvernement prend, um, aux gens, aux compagnies, pour payer les choses publiques." The money the government takes from people and companies to pay for public things. It was clumsy. It was also, she realized, exactly what the word meant, spread out flat like a sentence instead of folded into a noun.

She ran it twice more, and the hole stopped feeling like falling. Then the door opened without a knock.

Gran stood there with a folded newspaper under one arm. "You've been at it an hour," she said. "What is that you're doing, when you stall like that? I could hear you from the landing."

"It's called circumlocution," Sophie said, before she thought about it. "You describe the word you can't remember instead of stopping. Apparently it's a real thing. It keeps you talking." She had read it in an exam prep forum at midnight, in a thread full of other people's holes.

Gran set the newspaper down on the dresser, next to the timer, and did not pick it up again. "Fair enough," she said. "Now do the fares again. From the top." She settled into the chair by the window as if this had been the plan all along.

Sophie reset the dial, and somewhere in the second minute she made her argument about causality, how the forum debaters claimed fare hikes would fix the deficit, how you could not actually trace the money that cleanly, and Gran shifted forward in the chair and interrupted in accented but perfectly serviceable French, "Mais les chauffeurs, Sophie. Qui paie les chauffeurs?" which was germane, which was the whole counterargument, and which Sophie had not known Gran could say. She stared at her grandmother for a beat, the timer ticking on behind her, and then answered, in French, because stopping was no longer the thing her mouth knew how to do.

"You lived in Montreal," Sophie said afterward, when the timer had rung and they were both laughing at her verb tenses.

"Two years, before your father was born. He never asked. Ask me the hard one tonight, the fares one again. You wobbled."

"Deal," Sophie said, and reached for the dial.

Hunter spread the timeline across his grandfather's kitchen table, taping the last corner down while the coffee was still too hot to drink. Grandpa Frank wanted the counter cleared before lunch, and Hunter wanted the whole thing finished before Saturday, when he would have to stand in front of his class and defend a position he had not yet chosen. The assignment was simple on paper: two historians, two explanations of how the Cold War started, and the evidence weighed against each. Mr. Reyes had said, almost cheerfully, that either answer could earn an A, which struck Hunter as a way of making the choice harder, not easier.

Frank set down his mug and looked at the line of index cards. "You put the Long Telegram at the front."

"It's February 1946," Hunter said. "Kennan's cable from Moscow. That's where the containment idea starts. Historian number one, the one I read first, says that's the real beginning. Ideas before actions."

Frank tapped a card further along the strip. He had taught middle school geography for thirty-one years and had opinions about how maps, and apparently timelines, ought to be arranged. "And this one?"

"March 1947. The Truman Doctrine." Hunter read off his own card. "Truman pledged support for countries resisting communist pressure. Started with aid to Greece and Turkey."

"There's your beginning," Frank said.

"You always think it's whatever came after the war you were in."

"That's not fair," Frank said, but he didn't sound wounded; he sounded like he'd heard the argument before, in his own head, maybe. He sat down across the timeline so that it ran between them like a border. "A telegram is a man thinking. A doctrine is a country deciding. Which one changes what people do?"

Hunter hadn't expected his grandfather to take a side. He had expected him to make a sandwich and leave the table clear. Instead Frank pulled the Greek and Turkish cards toward himself and squared their edges, which was what he did with things he intended to keep talking about.

Historian number two, the revisionist, argued that the doctrine was the moment the United States stopped pretending and started building an empire of client states, that the rhetoric of freedom dressed up something colder. Historian number one called that cynical, said it valorized suspicion over fear, making a virtue of assuming the worst about your own country. Hunter had underlined that sentence twice and then felt embarrassed by the underlining, as if he'd taken a side by accident.

"Here's my problem," Hunter said. "If I say the telegram started it, then it's about ideas, and ideas are hard to prove. If I say the doctrine started it, then I have to decide whether the money for Greece and Turkey was defense or something worse. The evidence fits both."

"Then say so."

"That's a coward's answer."

Frank laughed, one short note. "I spent a spring in 1968 deciding whether to enlist. My father had a picture of Truman on the workshop wall his whole life, because of the doctrine, he said, because somebody finally drew a line. My brother called it an oligarchy with better manners, America deciding for other countries and calling it rescue. I stood between them at that table, the one we still have, and I said nothing, and they both walked away believing I'd agreed with them."

Hunter looked up from the cards. He had never heard this. The family story he knew was that Uncle Ray and Frank hadn't spoken much since the seventies, and nobody said why, and it had something to do with a girl before it had anything to do with politics.

"The telegram or the speech," Frank said. "You could do worse than to tell your class that the evidence supports both, and that the question of which came first depends on what you think a war is made of."

"It's made of money," Hunter said. "Six hundred million in aid, and nobody fired a shot over it."

"Somebody fired a shot over it," Frank said. "Just not in Greece." He stood, took his mug to the sink, and ran water over it longer than he needed to. "I'll be outside. Clear the table by noon."

Hunter worked for another hour. He moved the Long Telegram card half an inch left, then back. He wrote a sentence at the bottom of his notes, crossed out the first clause because it sounded turgid and dishonest, the kind of hedging that filled space without saying anything, and wrote instead: the doctrine is where the commitment became public and costly, and the telegram is where the fear first found its words, and the record does not settle which mattered more.

When Frank came back in at noon, smelling of cut grass, Hunter was rolling the timeline into a tube. "Well?" Frank said.

"I'll tell them the truth," Hunter said. "That I don't know where it started. Only where it stopped being somebody's opinion."

Frank took one end of the tube and held it while Hunter found the rubber band.

"Your great-grandfather would have argued with you till midnight," he said.

"Then I'd have been right where you were."

The studio smelled of resin and old radiator heat, and Mrs. Okoye's metronome sat on the piano lid like a small brass beetle that had wandered in from another century, anachronistic now that everyone kept time on their phones. Rachel unwrapped her cello on the second Tuesday of September, the same way she had every Tuesday for six years, and set the music on the stand: the Chopin polonaise she had taught herself over the summer, the piece she could play from memory with her eyes closed.

She got through the opening page before Mrs. Okoye raised one hand. Not the palm-out gesture of a conductor, just two fingers lifted off her knee, the way you would signal a waiter for the check.

"Play measures forty-one and forty-two," Mrs. Okoye said.

"They're awful," Rachel said. "That's why I skipped to the part I know."

"That's why we're playing them."

Rachel set her bow back on the string. The two bars contained a shift from third position to a harmonic she could not reliably find, followed by a string crossing her left hand wanted no part of. She missed the harmonic. She missed it again. On the fourth attempt she got it and then fumbled the crossing immediately after, which felt somehow worse, because it proved the problem was not one problem but two.

"Again," Mrs. Okoye said, and turned the metronome to sixty. "Just the shift. Nothing after it."

They spent the rest of the half hour on those two bars and a stretch in the slow movement that Rachel had been papering over since June. When the lesson ended, Mrs. Okoye wrote the measure numbers on a sticky note and pressed it to the inside of Rachel's folder like a prescription. "The polonaise can wait," she said. "It will still be there."

At home, Rachel did what she always did after a hard lesson: she played the polonaise from the top, the whole glorious run of it, fast enough that the hard passages blurred past on momentum. It felt wonderful. It felt like the summer itself, all that freedom she'd had before senior year started grinding. And then she recorded herself on her phone, because Mrs. Okoye had asked her to once, and listened back, and heard the truth. The shift was still a hole in the recording, a small swallowed silence exactly where the harmonic should have been. Playing the piece through had not fixed it. Playing the piece through had mostly let her practice not noticing.

That night she found the book. Her brother had left a stack of them in the garage when he moved out, and one was about how people get good at things. She read a chapter before bed, sitting on her floor with her back against the bed frame. The chapter had a phrase in it, deliberate practice, which it defined as working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, and it claimed this improved skill more than simply playing through pieces already known. She read the sentence twice. Then she thought about the sticky note in her folder, and the hole in the recording, and the fact that Mrs. Okoye had never once let her play a piece straight through in a lesson, and she understood that this was not cruelty or habit. It was policy. Her teacher had been running the experiment for six years and Rachel had only now read the results.

The next morning she tried it. She set her phone to record, picked a single goal, land the harmonic cleanly four times in a row, and played only the shift, nothing else, twenty times. Each time she listened back immediately. The misses sounded different once she could hear them: some were late fingers, some were a crooked thumb under the neck. She fixed one thing at a time. It was the least fun hour of cello she had ever spent, and at the end of it the harmonic was still not perfect, but it was honest. She could hear exactly how far off she was, which meant she knew exactly what to do Tuesday.

She kept at it for a week. On Thursday her friend Dana came over and asked why Rachel was playing the same three seconds of music over and over like a scratched CD, and Rachel tried to explain. Dana watched her miss the harmonic six consecutive times and said, "This looks miserable. Why not just play the fun part?"

"Because the fun part doesn't change anything," Rachel said. Dana shrugged and went to raid the kitchen, and Rachel went back to the shift, and she noticed she did not entirely disagree with Dana either. There was something in the repetition that closed the world down to a pinhole, and she missed the wide way the polonaise used to open up under her hands. She had not abrogated her right to enjoy it, she decided; she had only set it aside for a season, like a coat in summer.

There was also her mother to negotiate, because on Saturday her mother heard the same three seconds eleven times through the living room wall and came to the doorway with dish towel in hand. They reached a detente of sorts: Rachel would drill before noon, and after dinner she could play whatever she wanted, as loud as she wanted, and her mother would not say a word about the conservatory application sitting unfinished on the kitchen table.

Tuesday came. In the studio, Mrs. Okoye did not ask for the polonaise. She asked for measure forty-one, and Rachel set her bow and placed the shift, and the harmonic bloomed out clean and round, and then the crossing, which she had practiced separately all week, followed it like a sentence that had finally found its verb. She played the two bars again to be sure. The second time was clean too, though a little careful, and the third time, when Mrs. Okoye nodded once and turned the metronome up to sixty-six, was clean and not careful at all.

"Interesting week," Mrs. Okoye said, tapping the sticky note. "You found something."

"I read my brother's book," Rachel said. "It called it deliberate practice. Working on the specific weakness, with a goal, and feedback right away. Better than playing what you already know." She looked down at the strings. "The part I can't decide is whether I like it. It works. I just don't know if I want to like something that works."

Mrs. Okoye considered that for a moment, then set a new piece on the stand, a sonata Rachel had never seen, and pointed to the third line, where the notes clustered thick and low near the frog of the bow.

"We'll start there," she said. "Measure forty's all yours."

The keys were colder than Jordan expected, as though the car had been waiting in the driveway overnight with its own opinion about being driven. His father stood by the mailbox with his coffee, but it was Ms. Aroyo, the instructor, who held the clipboard, a saturnine woman of about sixty who had apparently decided that encouragement was a resource to be rationed.

"Seatbelt," she said. "Mirrors. Tell me what you see."

Jordan adjusted the mirror until the driveway's hedge filled it, then corrected until the road appeared, empty and gray at seven in the morning. He had waited two years for this, through a knee surgery that had emptied his savings and a winter of riding the bus past the hospital where his grandmother was slowly forgetting things. She had offered her old sedan for the lesson, and it sat in the driveway now with a rosary still looped around the rearview mirror, which Ms. Aroyo had looked at and, to her credit, not touched.

"Signal, check over your shoulder, and pull out when it's clear," she said. He did it, the car lurching once before he found the friction point, and then they were on the road, doing twenty-five in a quiet neighborhood, his hands at ten and two like the manual had shown. His father shrank in the mirror to a small waving figure by the mailbox and then was gone.

At the second stop sign, Ms. Aroyo asked him to pull over. "A question," she said. "You're going twenty. Now imagine you're going forty, twice as fast. How much longer does the car need to stop? Guess."

"Twice," Jordan said. She waited. He thought of his physics teacher, Mr. Okafor, who had once drawn a curve on the board and called the class's intuition lazy. "No, wait. It's the square. Braking distance is proportional to the square of your speed, so doubling the speed makes the braking distance about four times as long." He said it and then heard himself say it, the way you sometimes only understand a thing aloud.

"Right," Ms. Aroyo said, and there was, briefly, something almost warm in it. "So what does that mean for how you drive?"

"It means the road lies to you," Jordan said. "Twenty feels safe and forty feels kind of safe and they're not the same at all. You get desensitized. Like people who drive this street every day and roll the stop signs because nothing has ever happened here."

She made a mark on her clipboard. "Keep going."

He drove on, and the neighborhood opened onto a wider road, and Jordan found himself thinking about his grandmother, who had taught his mother to drive in a church parking lot and who now, when he visited, argued calmly that the thermostat and the bank and the traffic lights were all run by the same unelected technocracy, a word she had picked up from television and wielded at nurses. He had always corrected her, gently, and she had always smiled at him in a way that suggested she found his corrections decorative. Two ways of seeing the world, hers and his, and lately he had begun to suspect that neither one was complete. She distrusted everything she couldn't see working; he trusted systems so completely that he had never once wondered what a car was doing when he pressed the brake.

Ahead, a ball rolled out from between two parked cars, followed a half second later by a small dog, no child behind it, but Jordan braked hard anyway, the seatbelt biting his shoulder, the car stopping well short, and his heart going like a clock in another room.

"Good," Ms. Aroyo said. "You saw the ball and read the whole sentence, not just the first word." She let the silence sit for a moment. "Now, at twice this speed, could you have stopped in that space?"

He looked at the distance between the bumper and the ball, still rocking gently in the gutter. Four times as long, he thought. He tried to picture it stretching down the block, past the hedges, past the house with the flag, and he found he couldn't be sure his own foot would have been fast enough even in the space he'd had. That, at least, he was willing to admit he didn't know.

"No," he said. "I don't think so."

"Correct answer is 'no,'" she said. "The honest one, anyway."

They drove back with the windows cracked, the rosary swinging gently at every turn. When they pulled into the driveway, his father was still out by the mailbox, coffee gone cold in his hands, pretending he hadn't been standing there the whole time. Jordan put the car in park and looked at the rosary a moment, then reached up and turned it so the beads hung straight.

"Same time next week?" Ms. Aroyo asked.

"Same time," Jordan said, and shook her hand through the window, and behind him, the engine ticked as it cooled.

The synagogue kitchen smelled of aluminum and burnt sugar, and Sienna had requisitioned its longest table for a rehearsal that no one had asked her to run. Around it sat her younger cousins, her mother, and her grandmother Ruth, who had led the Passover seder for forty-one years and had announced, in February, that this year she would only sit and eat. Sienna had volunteered before she understood what she was volunteering for.

She had the Haggadot stacked at each place, the seder plate assembled except for the shank bone, which her mother was still hunting for at the butcher. She had practiced the blessings into her phone until her brother mocked her from the hallway. What she had not practiced was the argument, and the argument arrived with her cousin Daniel, home from his first year at a yeshiva in Baltimore, wearing the certainty of someone who had recently learned the word for it.

"You're reading it wrong," he said, when she explained the four sons as four stages of a single person's life, the way her grandmother had always done. "That's not in the text. You found the wicked son in yourself and decided the verse was about you. That's eisegesis. Reading your own ideas into the words instead of drawing the meaning out of them. The opposite is exegesis, and Rabbi Zuckerman says it's how you tell a real interpretation from a made-up one."

"I didn't make up anything," Sienna said. "Bubbe taught it to me."

"Then Bubbe made it up." Daniel did not say it unkindly, which somehow made it worse. He had been a bellicose kid, all elbows and argument, and this new calmer delivery was harder to fight. He turned his palms up, the gesture of a person who believed the text would settle the matter on its own.

The kitchen went quiet enough that they could hear the pilot light. Sienna looked at the stack of photocopied pages in front of her, at the passage she had underlined three times, and admitted to herself that she could not remember which parts were the verse and which parts were her grandmother's voice. She had been studying both at once for months, the way you study a song and its singer together.

She found her grandmother in the sanctuary, sitting in the third pew from the back where she always sat, and asked her plainly whether the four sons were four people or one. Ruth took a long time answering, long enough that Sienna began arranging and rearranging the prayer books on the shelf beside her, as if tidiness could hurry the hermeneutics along. "Your Daniel's rabbi would say I read myself in," Ruth said finally. "I was a wicked son once, in my father's house, and the Haggadah was the first place that made sense of it. Does that make it false?"

Sienna carried the question back to the kitchen, where Daniel was showing the little cousins how to fold the napkins into something like cups. She set her Haggadah on the table and marked two passages with her grandmother's old paper clips. "Here's what the words say," she told him, pointing to the first. "Four sons, four questions, plain as that. And here," she touched the second, "is where the words go quiet and somebody has to decide what they're for. I'll lead it as four sons, like you want, because that's what's on the page. But when we get to the wicked one, I'm going to ask everybody at the table which one they've been. That part's me, and I'll say so out loud, so nobody thinks the Torah said it."

Daniel looked at the paper clips for a while. "That's actually not terrible," he said, which from him was a citation of approval.

On the night itself, the dining room at her grandmother's house held nineteen people and a roast that had nearly defeated two ovens. Sienna's voice cracked once at the opening blessing and did not crack again. She poured the second cup, sent her cousin Moshe to hunt the afikoman, and read the four sons straight, in order, letting the plain words carry their own weight. Then she set down the book. "Bubbe always told us these could be one person at four different times," she said. "The Torah doesn't say that. Bubbe does. So think about it, and when you're ready, tell me which son you are this year."

Her uncle Sam, who argued about parking spots, went first. Then Moshe, sheepish, said something that made his mother laugh and reach for his hand. Daniel, three seats down, folded his napkin into a cup and then a flat square, then a cup again. "The wise one," he said. "Obviously." But he was smiling as he said it, and his eyes moved down the table toward their grandmother, who was watching Sienna pour the third cup with a steady hand.

Abigail arrived early to claim the good seat, the one by the window, because today was the debate and she intended to win it. The question on the board read: Can a single experiment prove anything? She had argued all week with Marcus in the lab that one clean result was enough, that everything else was bureaucracy, and she had said it in a voice she privately knew was louder than the argument deserved.

Mr. Ferrell, whom Marcus called the last of the pedagogues, never lectured if he could make students collide instead, so he had set the room in two facing rows. Abigail opened her notebook to a page of prepared points. She remembered writing three of them last night, in order, with a heading. When she looked down, the page held only two, and the second one trailed off mid-sentence, as if her past self had fallen asleep mid-thought. She decided she must have written the third point on a different page, in the blue notebook, at home. She was almost sure of it.

"The Higgs boson," Marcus said, opening, and she felt the floor shift, because that was her third point, or something like her third point, and he had it now. "July 4, 2012. CERN announced it only after two separate detector teams found the same new particle." He paused, savoring the room's attention. "ATLAS and CMS. They worked independently. They didn't share their data first. Two giant detectors, same tunnel, same collisions, and neither team got to peek."

Abigail's rebuttal, which she delivered with more steadiness than she felt, was that this was waste, duplication, two machines where one would do. "If ATLAS saw it," she said, "why build a second one the size of a cathedral just to check?"

"Because a check is the whole point," said Priya from the back, and Mr. Ferrell wrote the word replication on the board without turning around, and under it he wrote peer review, and under that he drew nothing, just tapped the chalk twice.

The argument went on, but Abigail was no longer entirely in it. She kept thinking of her father, two summers ago, in the hospital corridor, when a single test had shown something on a scan and the doctor had said, gently, that they would run it again, differently, before anyone believed it. Her father had made a joke about being popular. Abigail had been furious, she remembered, at the delay, at the caution, at the refusal to just say what was true. She had told Marcus about it later and had told him the second test confirmed the first. She realized now, sitting in the third row by the window, that the second test had not confirmed it. She had said that to Marcus because it made a better story, a cleaner grievance against slowness, and she had repeated it to herself until it smoothed over into memory.

So when her turn came again, she did not use the rebuttal she had rehearsed. "I want to concede something," she said, and Priya mouthed the word concede with a sardonic lift of an eyebrow, and Abigail flushed but went on. "One result tells you something happened. It doesn't tell you it happened for the reason you think, or that it happens again. I still think two detectors is expensive. I still think July 4 is a showman's date for an announcement." She heard herself and stopped, because she was drifting toward a speech, and speeches were what she had accused Mr. Ferrell of all semester. "What I mean is, both things can be true. The caution is what makes it knowledge instead of news. But the caution costs something too. It's slow. Sometimes it's too slow for the people waiting on the answer."

Marcus looked at her across the rows. "So you're switching sides?"

"I'm not switching. I'm saying my side was thinner than I wanted it to be."

The bell would ring in four minutes and Mr. Ferrell would declare, as he always did, that no one had won, which was his way of winning. Abigail copied the three words from the board into her notebook, and under them she wrote her father's hospital and the date July 4, 2012, and then crossed out the hospital because it was not evidence, it was only her, and left the date.

After the others were gathering bags, she said to Marcus, quietly, "That thing I told you about my dad's second test. It came back different. I told you wrong."

Marcus zipped his bag. "Then what did they do after that?"

"They ran it again," she said, and looked at the empty board.

The workbook had come from the library in town, four days overdue, and Joshua read it in the hayloft because that was the only place on the farm where nobody asked him for anything. In ten days he was supposed to be at the university, sitting in a lecture hall for the first time in his life, and the orientation packet had included a page of review material with the words "transcription and translation" underlined twice, as though everyone in the world already knew what they meant. He did not. He read about a strand of DNA being copied into a message, and the message being read out to build a protein, and he copied the diagrams onto the back of a feed receipt until the ladder shapes looked like the fence rows he'd walked since he was six.

The chart was what stopped him. It listed the four letters of the code, A and T and G and C, and it said the letters were read in groups of three, called codons. He did the arithmetic himself on the receipt, multiplying it out in the margin: four choices for the first position, four for the second, four for the third. Sixty-four possible codons. Then he counted the names along the side of the chart, the amino acids, the building blocks the codons stood for. He counted twice, touching each one with the pencil. Twenty.

He was sure he had it wrong, the way he'd been sure, the first time he rebuilt an irrigation pump, that the gasket went on the outside. He went down the rows of the chart letter by letter. Leucine appeared again and again, under codon after codon. Serine the same. Six of the sixty-four all pointed at the same amino acid, and he sat back against the bales with the receipt in his lap and the dust moving in the light, and he thought that the code was wasteful, or that it was generous, and he could not yet tell which. He had always tried to dichotomize things into broken or working, but the chart refused the sorting. "There are sixty-four codons," he said out loud to the empty loft, "and only twenty amino acids. Most of them have more than one codon." Saying it made it real, the way saying a prayer did, though he hadn't prayed since the funeral.

His grandfather would have understood it in a minute. Eli Ozawa had saved seed his whole life, forty years of choosing which wheat to plant and which to let go, and he had died in March without ever hearing the word codon. It was Eli who had paid the deposit on the university, out of an ascetic savings account that held almost nothing else, and Joshua had promised him at the hospital bed that he would learn the science of it, the part Eli had done by instinct and by hand. The promise had felt clean then. Now it felt like the apportionment of an estate, everybody getting a share of a man who could not be divided.

His sister Ruth found him at the kitchen table that evening with the chart propped against the salt shaker. She was fifteen and had already announced she was not leaving, that the farm needed somebody with both hands and no lectures to attend. "Read it to me," she said, not sitting, holding a pail of eggs she refused to set down, and he understood she was not asking about biology.

"You take the DNA and you copy a stretch of it into a message," he said. "That's transcription. Then the message gets read in threes, each three standing for one amino acid, and the amino acids get strung into a protein. That's translation. But here's the thing." He turned the chart toward her. "Sixty-four threes are possible. Twenty building blocks. Lots of threes mean the same thing."

Ruth set the pail down finally. She looked at the chart the way she looked at a sick heifer, steadily, looking for the lie in it. "So there's more ways to say a thing than there are things to say."

"That's one way to put it."

She was quiet while the kettle ticked. From where Ruth stood, the whole scene looked different than it had from the loft: her brother hunched over the table like their grandfather over seed trays, and on the wall behind him the map of the university town, already creased from handling. She had spent a month being angry at him for going, dividing the family neatly into the one who stayed and the one who left, and the chart had just broken the arithmetic. He could go and still be of this place. The words were many; the meaning was one. She hated that it comforted her, and it comforted her anyway.

"Grandpa never knew this," Joshua said. "Forty years and he never knew why the wheat worked." He looked at the chart again, at the rows of threes, at the twenty names, and he knew he would explain it in a lecture hall someday and get part of it wrong and be corrected in front of two hundred strangers, and he knew he would not be able to ask Eli whether the deposit had been worth it. "I can't decide if it's sloppy or if it's the whole point."

Ruth picked up the pail and carried it toward the cellar door. At the threshold she turned. "Say the codon thing again, the numbers. I want to get it right for Dad."

"Sixty-four and twenty," Joshua said. "Most have more than one." She nodded once and went down the stairs, and he sat listening to her boots on the treads until the sound gave out.

Maxime had told everyone at school that he volunteered all the time, which was true if you counted the one afternoon in grade ten when he'd sorted bottles for an hour, so when his guidance counsellor slid the form across the desk he signed it mostly to keep the story alive. The form said Riverside Seniors' Residence, Saturday, nine o'clock, warehouse side entrance. He imagined a line of grateful people, imagined himself handing over bags of pasta with an easy smile, the kind of smile he had never in his life managed on command.

The warehouse turned out to be exactly what it said: a warehouse. A woman named Delphine gave him a clipboard and pointed at pallets of canned tomatoes, and for two hours he counted and logged, entirely alone except for a radio playing something French his grandmother might have liked. Nobody came for groceries. At ten he went to find Delphine, trying to sound casual rather than lost. "So when do the people start arriving?"

She looked at him the way you look at a shoe on the wrong foot. "Nobody picks up food here. This is the food bank. A food bank is a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly." She said it flat, the way you say something you've said forty times, and turned back to her manifest.

So the seniors' residence, he learned, was one of the agencies. The pantry ran out of the common room on the ground floor, between the fish tank and the piano nobody played, and Delphine drove him over at eleven in a van that smelled of cardboard and oranges. Maxime sat with the clipboard on his knees and thought about how he'd described his morning to himself that morning, competent, experienced, practically a veteran of charity work, and how none of that had been true, and how the false version had still gotten him into the van. Both things seemed to hold at once, and he didn't try to sort them out before they arrived.

The common room had been rearranged so the shelves formed a narrow aisle, and by noon there was a queue of residents and people from the neighbourhood pushing walkers or carrying folded bags. An old man named Armand expostulated loudly about the disappearance of the good biscuits, holding up a box of generic ones as evidence, until the woman running the shelf, Madame Roy, told him that the good biscuits would return when the donations turned over, which was a way of saying maybe never. Armand took the generic ones anyway. Maxime watched him choose to accept it, and understood that accepting things was maybe also a skill, one he had not been tested on yet.

He was put on bread. A girl from another school, Noor, worked beside him, and she was faster, and she knew residents by name. When he mentioned the warehouse and how he'd expected crowds, she laughed without unkindness. "Everyone thinks that the first time," she said. "That the big building is where it happens." But it was where it happened, he thought, or half of it; the pallets he'd counted that morning were becoming, at this table, the exact number of loaves now going into bags. His counting had been real. It had just been real somewhere else.

The afternoon had a rhythm he hadn't expected, conversations that started about bread and ended up elsewhere. A resident named Gisèle told him the period after the residence's old activities coordinator quit had been what she called an interregnum, months of nothing scheduled, and how the pantry had filled the empty afternoons even for people who didn't need the food. She took two loaves though she needed both, so he didn't argue with the second half of her sentence. He was beginning to suspect that people carried more than one reason for most things they did, and that his own two reasons, the story for school and something under it he couldn't yet name, were not so different.

At four they closed the shelves. Noor left quickly, waving. Delphine appeared in the doorway with paperwork, and Gisèle, waiting for her elevator, told Maxime that afternoons like this one were evanescent and that he should not bother holding on to them, since they vanished no matter how tightly you gripped, and the vanishing was the part that made them worth having. He wanted to tell her he'd be back next Saturday, but he wasn't sure yet whether that was true or just the next version of the story he told, so he said he'd see, and she nodded as if that were the most honest answer in the building.

He rode back to the warehouse with Delphine, logging returns in the fading light. On Monday he would tell his friends he ran a pantry, or worked at a food bank, or something in between, and whichever words he chose would be partly true. For now there were thirty-one cans of tomatoes left on the pallet, and the clipboard, and his own handwriting from that morning, which looked, he noticed, exactly like the handwriting of someone who had done this before.

"Same time next week?" Delphine asked, not looking up.

He clicked the pen twice. "Yeah. Same time."

The cones were laundry baskets, two of them, weighted with bricks and set along the curb of his grandfather's street at a distance Grandpa Ed had measured with his feet. "Pull up even with this one," Ed said, tapping the hood of his ancient Buick, "then turn the wheel all the way and back in slow." Michael had done it eleven times that week. He had clipped the baskets four times, kissed the curb twice, and once, on Thursday, slid the car in so cleanly that Ed had gone quiet for a moment before saying only, "Again."

The lease had come on Wednesday, forwarded from the apartment office in the college town, and Michael had read it at the kitchen table while Ed made tomato sandwiches. He had budgeted everything in the spring, back when the numbers had seemed solid: rent split with a roommate, a bus pass, food, books, a phone. The lease was thirty-one pages, and on page nineteen, under a paragraph about liability, he found a sentence that stopped him. He read it twice, then a third time, then carried the page to the counter.

"It says I have to carry renter's insurance," he said. "It covers my own belongings, not the building. It's not covered by what I'm already paying. It adds a monthly premium." He set the page down between the tomatoes and the salt shaker, feeling the arithmetic rearrange itself in his head before he'd done any of it.

Ed looked at the sentence over his glasses. "Renter's insurance," he said. "That's the one. Your grandmother had it on the duplex for years." He went back to the sandwiches and did not explain further, which was his way of leaving the problem where it belonged.

That night Michael sat on the foldout cot in the den with his notebook open to the budget page. Eleven dollars and change a month, the quote from the insurance website said. He looked at his columns. The bus pass was fixed. Books were a guess.
