Now, in study hall, he had it pulled up again, and something about the light in the video bothered him. The shadows fell toward the camera. It was the kind of detail he would never have noticed a month ago.

A month ago, before Ms. Ferrante's unit on media literacy, he would have shared it without a second thought. He remembered that clearly, and the memory was not flattering: the doctored graduation photo of the principal he had passed along in September, laughing, imputing malice to a man who had done nothing except appear in an image someone else had bent. When the principal turned out to have been away that week, Nicolas had deleted his repost and said nothing, and the silence had felt worse than being caught.

Deepa slid into the chair beside him, her backpack still on one shoulder. "You're doing the assignment already?"

"Not the assignment." He angled the screen toward her. "This."

She pulled her own keyboard over, typed something, squinted. "Wait. I know that image."

"It's breaking."

"It's not." She turned her laptop so he could see. "We did this in class Tuesday. You were out. Watch." She saved a frame from the video, the rooftop, the bedsheet, and dropped the file into a search bar. "TinEye," she said. "It came out in 2008, my sister used it in college." A column of results loaded, thumbnails of the same rooftop in different articles, different years. She clicked a sort option at the top of the list. "Oldest first."

The oldest result was from four years ago. Same roof, same sheet, same man, above a story about a different flood in a different country. Nicolas sat back. The whirring fan filled the pause. Two thousand shares, and the water was real water and the man was a real man, but the video was four years old wearing today's date like a coat.

"So it's fake," Deepa said.

"Not exactly." He leaned in again. "It happened. Just not now." That distinction seemed to matter and he couldn't yet say why, except that calling it fake would let everyone dismiss it, and calling it breaking would make everyone panic, and neither was true. He thought of the principal again, of how quickly he had imputed a whole character to a cropped photograph. He had been obdurate about it, too, defending the joke to Dev for two full days before the dates stopped matching up.

He screenshotted the TinEye results, the oldest-first ordering with its four-year-old article sitting at the top like a foundation stone, and attached it to a reply to Dev: "real footage, old event, wrong date." Then he pasted the same message under the video itself, where the share count had reached three thousand. He watched it sit there, small and gray among the exclamation marks, and part of him thought it was useless, a pebble in a river, and part of him thought about symbiosis, how Ms. Ferrante had described fact-checkers and sharers as organisms that needed each other, the checkers useless without spreaders and the spreaders dangerous without checkers. He had been one kind. Maybe he was becoming the other. Maybe he was becoming something in between that didn't have a name yet.

Dev's reply arrived before the bell: "ok but people should still see it, floods like that happen all the time." Nicolas read it twice. It was, he had to admit, not entirely wrong, and he sat with that, cursor blinking in an empty reply box, until Deepa nudged his arm and pointed at her screen. She had found a second video, same flood, this one uploaded last week, and she was already dragging a frame into the search bar to see how old it really was.

Nevaeh adjusted the mirror before her mother could tell her to, and the car seemed to settle around her, its smallness suddenly apparent, the roof close enough to touch. The parking lot of the community college was empty on a Saturday morning except for a groundskeeper pushing a cart along the far fence. She turned the key the way the manual had said, and the engine caught on the first try, which felt like a small mercy.

"Foot on the brake before you shift," her mother said, but Nevaeh had already done it, having read the chapter twice the night before, once at the kitchen table and once in bed with the flashlight her little brother used for reading comics under his blanket. She eased the car into drive. The lot's painted lines slid past the windshield, white and patient.

Her brother Marcus had gotten his permit two months before her, on the day he turned sixteen, and had spent that evening mapping out all the places he would take people. Lake behind the middle school, the taco truck on Fourth, his friend Dario's house out past the golf course. He had gone around the kitchen reciting names like a man distributing gifts. Then their mother had told him the sequence, and Nevaeh, thirteen then, had watched his face reorganize itself.

"It's called graduated licensing," Marcus had said that night, flat with disappointment, turning the laminated permit over in his hands. "First the permit, then a provisional license with restrictions, and only after that the full license." He had read it off the state website himself, slowly, as though saying it aloud might make it negotiable. It did not. He had sat in the driveway the next day anyway, in the driver's seat of the empty car, not driving anywhere, just holding the wheel with both hands.

In the lot, her mother said, "Signal, then check your mirror, then look over your shoulder. The signal doesn't replace the look." Nevaeh signaled, checked, looked. The empty lot offered no consequence for carelessness, which was somehow its own problem; she wanted the stakes to be real so that her attention would be real too. She pulled out onto the access road, and the first oncoming car passed close enough that she gripped the wheel tighter than she meant to.

"You're fine," her mother said. "He had the whole other lane."

They drove the loop around the college, past the gymnasium and the bus turn-around, and Nevaeh began to feel the pedal under her foot as a conversation rather than a command. Press, ease, press. When a bicyclist appeared ahead on the shoulder, she slowed early, well before she needed to, wanting to forestall any possibility of the woman on the bike having to make a decision about her. Her mother noticed. "That was good. Early is better than late."

At the stop sign at the edge of campus, Nevaeh braked fully and sat for a second with her hands at ten and two. "Can I ask you something?" she said.

"You just did."

"Mom."

"Ask."

"Do you think the rules are right? The ones Marcus hates. That you can't just get your license and drive whoever you want." She watched a sparrow cross in front of the hood and land on the sign itself, unbothered by the machinery idling below it.

Her mother was quiet long enough that Nevaeh thought she was composing something sagacious, the kind of thing adults kept in a drawer for occasions like this. Instead she said, "When I was seventeen I failed my first road test. Rolled a stop sign. My father said the examiner was too strict. I knew he was right and my father was being kind." She tapped the window with one finger. "I needed someone to not be kind about that particular thing."

"That's not an answer."

"It's the material for one. Go when you're ready."

Nevaeh went, turning left onto the busier road, and the traffic made everything she did meaningful. She held her speed. She thought about Marcus in the driveway, and about the bicyclist, and about the rolled stop sign from twenty years ago, and she understood that she was being asked to hold two things at once: that the restrictions were a shape imposed on her from outside, and that the shape was drawn around a real danger that she, personally, statistically, embodied. Sixteen-year-olds were not a phenotype you could select against, but they were, as a group, the thing the rule was drawn around. She was inside the group whether she drove well or badly, and the rule did not know her, and the rule might still be right. Both of those could be true. She wasn't sure yet how to live inside a rule that didn't know her, whether that was humility or erasure, and she decided she would have to keep driving long enough to find out.

"Turn here," her mother said, "and pull over where the curb is flat."

Nevaeh signaled, checked, looked over her shoulder, and brought the car to the curb in one smooth arc that surprised her with its competence. She set the brake and let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

"So can I drive us home?" she said.

"Permit," her mother said, and unclipped her seatbelt to slide over. "You drive, I ride, and neither of us tells Marcus you did better than him on day one."

"He already knows he was worse," Nevaeh said, and then, as she pulled back onto the road, "I'll drive him to the taco truck when I'm allowed. First thing."

Her mother was already halfway out the door and laughing. "Get your seatbelt," she said, "before I change my mind about everything."

Mr. Kwan hired me on a Tuesday, and by Friday I had already decided he was stealing from me. I want to be clear about that up front, because I was wrong, and because being wrong took me three days and a woman named Delores to figure out. I am good at math. I tutor freshmen in algebra for gas money. So when my first envelope came up short, I did the only reasonable thing: I multiplied my hours by my rate, checked it twice, and stared at the difference like it was a stranger standing in my kitchen.

The job itself was fine. Holsom's Hardware, two aisles of paint and a back wall of screws sorted into little drawers nobody had alphabetized since the nineties. Mr. Kwan wanted me Saturdays and two afternoons a week, restocking, running the register when the line got long. I'd applied because the transmission in my mother's Corolla was making a sound like a spoon in a garbage disposal, and the shop in Bellview wanted five hundred dollars by the following Friday or they'd release the bay to someone else. That was my deadline, and I was watching it the way you watch a pot you're sure is about to boil over.

The envelope said I'd worked nineteen hours at nine dollars an hour. That was one hundred seventy-one dollars. The check inside was for one hundred sixty point four zero. I did it on the register's scrap paper during my break, then again at home on the good calculator. Ten dollars and sixty cents, gone. I told myself it was an accounting error, but somewhere between Holsom's and my bedroom the idea began to calcify into something harder: Mr. Kwan had quietly shaved the number, assuming a sixteen-year-old wouldn't notice. That's what people assume about us. That we can't multiply.

Saturday I tested him. I asked, casually, whether the register printed hours wrong sometimes. He said the register was fine. I asked whether pay ever got "adjusted" for new employees, and he looked at me over his glasses and said no, and I thought, well, he would say that. My mother's mechanic called that afternoon to say the price had gone up to five forty. I hung up and lay on my bed doing the arithmetic of my life: five hundred forty dollars, minus one hundred sixty point four zero, minus the eighty in my sock drawer, meant I needed three more paychecks, which meant the Corolla sat dead in the driveway for weeks. Something had to be wrong with the math. Somebody's math.

Delores worked the register on Sundays, a big slow-moving woman who had been at Holsom's for eleven years and referred to every customer under thirty as a detractor of the human race, though she said it with something close to affection. I came in on my day off, ostensibly to buy masking tape, actually to ask her whether Mr. Kwan had ever shorted her. She laughed so hard she had to grip the counter.

"Boy, sit down," she said, and pulled a stool over. "You did your hours times your rate." I said yes. "And it came up short by about six percent." I admitted it was six and a fifth percent, precisely, because I had computed it to the second decimal, and she laughed again. "That's Social Security," she said. "Employers withhold six point two percent of your wages for Social Security tax, up to a yearly wage limit." She said it flat, like reading a label. "Mine stops coming out around August. I make enough by then that I hit the limit. Yours won't stop. You won't get near it."

I sat there recalculating in my head, and the whole edifice of my suspicion came apart in about four seconds. Six point two percent of one hundred seventy-one is ten point six zero two. Mr. Kwan hadn't taken anything. The number was the number. Delores watched me do it, watched my face change, and said nothing, which I've since decided was the kindest thing anyone did for me that month.

What stays uncertain is this: I still don't know exactly what I was so ready to believe about him, or why the missing ten dollars felt like proof of something larger, some story I'd already written about adults and shortcuts. I apologized Monday, mumbled something about my math being off, and he shrugged and handed me a box of washers to sort. I didn't tell my mother any of it. I called the shop in Bellview, asked about a payment plan, and then, while I was waiting on hold, started sorting the washers by size, smallest first, my fingers moving faster than my thoughts for once.

Delores came through the back door with her coffee and looked at the row of little drawers I'd lined up across the counter. "Look at that," she said. "The profligate one, organizing."

"Mr. Kwan's nephew," I said. "He's the profligate one. He ordered three kinds of washers nobody buys."

She sat down on her stool and pointed at the smallest drawer. "Start there. Tell me which ones we actually sell."

The clinic on Marsh Street closed at four, and Maya's bus back to her mother's house left at five, which gave them one hour and a grandmother's kitchen in which to figure everything out. Layla set her phone on the table between a bowl of runner beans and a plate of metamorphic rock slices her grandfather had collected in the Ozarks, pressure and heat written into their banded faces, and she thought that was as good a description of the past month as any.

"You can't tell Mom," Maya said. She was sixteen and had her jacket on already, though the bus was an hour away, as if she might have to run.

"I'm not telling anyone. That's the whole point." Layla had promised herself she would do this right, that she would be the older cousin she'd needed at sixteen and never had. Health class had given her the words, and AP Bio had given her the framing, the idea that the body keeps itself balanced, maintains its homeostasis, and that knowing how to protect that balance was not shameful but practical. Still, saying the words aloud to Maya's face was different from writing them in a notebook. She wiped the table with a cloth, an old habit at their grandmother's, burnishing the wood to the dull shine it always kept, and made herself start.

"Okay. First, consent. It's not the absence of a no. It's the presence of a yes, out loud, from someone who knows they can change their mind and it still counts." She kept her voice level. "If you're unsure at any point, you stop. That's not ruining anything. That's the rule working."

Maya nodded, chin down, picking at the hem of her jacket.

"Second, contraception. Condoms are the only ones that protect against infections, not just pregnancy, and they have to be on before any contact, not halfway through. If you want something longer term, the clinic can talk you through it, but tonight, condoms. And don't let anyone tell you they're too big. That's not a thing."

"Devon said that once," Maya said quietly.

"Then Devon can practice opening the wrapper until he gets humble about it." Layla watched a small grin cross her cousin's face and felt something in her own chest loosen.

"Third, testing. If you've already done something, or you're about to, you can get tested and treated without Mom signing anything. I'm almost positive. But almost positive isn't good enough, so we're calling before four." She pulled up the clinic's number, then hesitated with her thumb over the screen. Her own mother still reviewed her explanations for everything, and the instinct ran deep, that anything involving your body required a permission slip, a countersignature, an adult standing behind you. She dialed before the instinct could win.

The hold music was a tinny version of something she half recognized. Their grandmother drifted through for her reading glasses, paused at the tension around the phone, and set down a glass of sweet tea at Maya's elbow without a word before disappearing into the front room, and Layla was grateful in a way she didn't stop to examine.

"Marsh Street clinic, this is Renee."

"Hi. My cousin wants to come in for STI testing and she's sixteen. Does a parent have to sign a form?" Layla held Maya's gaze while she asked, because the question was hers too, had been hers for two years.

"All fifty states and Washington, DC, let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission," Renee said, in the tired, competent tone of someone who answered this forty times a week. "Some states do set a minimum age, so tell me which state you're in and we'll check."

Layla gave the state, listened, and wrote the walk-in hours on the back of a grocery receipt. When she hung up, she slid the paper across the table to Maya, who read it twice, as though the words might revise themselves.

"So I just walk in," Maya said.

"You just walk in. Before four today, or any Saturday morning." Layla reached over and straightened the collar of Maya's jacket, which had folded under itself, a small thing, but her grandmother had done it for her a hundred times and it meant stay, you're cared for. "And whatever happens with Devon, or doesn't, you don't owe me a report. You just get to be safe."

Maya stood, crumpling the receipt into her pocket with a kind of care, smoothing it flat again through the fabric. From the front room their grandmother called out that the 5:10 was unreliable and the 4:40 was worse, so they'd best leave now if they meant to make either.

Layla grabbed the keys off the hook by the door, and Maya was already on the porch, one foot on the first step, looking back.

The scholarship application wanted two hundred volunteer hours, and Jackson had been counting his at St. Bridget's like a prisoner scratching tally marks on a wall. He had sixty-one. Today he was restocking the hydration station on the fourth floor, filling little green pitchers with ice and water, when he noticed that the family lounge outside Room 412 had gone quiet in the way rooms do when something heavy is being said.

"I want to be clear about the morphine," a doctor was saying through the half-open door. Jackson had seen her before, Dr. Reyes, the one with the gray braid who never used the elevators. "It will ease his breathing. That is what I intend. But at this dose, there is a chance it could shorten the time he has left. I want you to hear that from me and not from a nurse's note after the fact."

A woman's voice, thin and frayed: "So you're asking us to sign something that kills him faster."

"I'm asking you to let me treat his pain."

Jackson stood in the hallway with a pitcher sweating in both hands. He had assumed, without ever putting it into words, that doctors simply did good, the way furnaces simply produced heat. The idea that a good act could carry a foreseeable harm inside it, like a stone in a peach, was new, and he carried it with him down to the lounge where the patient's grandson sat hunched over an untouched coffee. Jackson only meant to be kind. He said that he'd overheard the doctors, that morphine could end things sooner, that maybe the family should fight it. The grandson's face changed, and he was through the door of 412 before Jackson had finished his sentence.

The charge nurse found him twenty minutes later and lambasted him in the supply alcice, her voice low and shaking, telling him that patient information was not his to repeat, that he had walked into the middle of a decision that had nothing to do with him. "The family's talking to a lawyer," she said. "If it goes anywhere, you could be part of a deposition. Sworn testimony, Jackson. About something you don't understand."

That night he sat on his bedroom floor with his phone and typed in what he remembered: harm you foresee but don't intend. The results led him to the doctrine of double effect, traced back to Thomas Aquinas, who had argued that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end. Jackson read it three times. Foresees, does not intend. The doctor hadn't been hiding anything from the family; she had been laying the whole trade on the table, the pain relief against the days it might cost, and asking them to weigh it. Jackson had taken the scale and thrown it at the grandson.

He asked to see the charge nurse before his next shift, and he told her he would say exactly what he had done, to the family, to a lawyer, to anyone, but that he had gotten the doctor's meaning wrong. Dr. Reyes was the one who came to find him instead, in the hallway by the ice machine. "I heard what you told them," she said. "You made it sound like we were choosing his death. What we were choosing was whether he spends his last days gasping or resting. Those are not the same conversation."

"I didn't know there was a difference," Jackson said.

"There is, and then there isn't," she said. "Aquinas gives you the frame, but the frame doesn't carry the weight for you. The family asked me yesterday whether the morphine was worth two days of his life. I said I couldn't answer that. Nobody can. We chose the morphine."

Mr. Okafor died four days later, on a Thursday morning, and the lawyer's letter never came, so there was no deposition, only a note in Jackson's file that his shifts would be supervised for the rest of the summer. His friend Diego texted him a picture from the lake, three girls on a dock, the caption calling it a hedonistic July, and Jackson typed "have one for me" and put the phone face down. On his last supervised shift, the grandson appeared at the fourth-floor desk, holding a paper bag of mangoes. "You stuck your nose where it didn't belong," he said, "but after you did, my mother finally asked the doctor the questions she'd been swallowing for a month. So." He set the bag on the counter. "He liked these cut into stars."

Jackson carried the mangoes to the break room, took out the little paring knife, and began cutting.

The basement smelled like dust and the ghost of a hundred microwave dinners, and Marcus's desktop computer, a humming anachronistic tower that his father refused to retire, took almost four minutes to boot. Dylan sat cross-legged on the carpet with his laptop open, a practice problem from the University's placement challenge glowing on the screen: implement binary search on a sorted array, then write two sentences explaining why it outperforms a linear search. The prize was a spot in the honors section, and the challenge closed at midnight.

"You're staring," Marcus said from the beanbag, where he was adjudicating a dispute between his little brother and a neighbor kid over whose Mario Kart win counted, since someone had paused mid-race. "Staring doesn't compile."

"I'm thinking about how it works," Dylan said. "That's different."

He wrote the loop first: compare the middle element to the target, and if the target is smaller, throw away the top half; if larger, throw away the bottom half. Keep a low and a high pointer and squeeze them toward each other. It was strange to him that this was allowed, that you could simply ignore half the data and still be sure the answer, if it existed, was in what remained. The array had to be sorted, though. That was the price. An unsorted array gave you nothing, because the middle element told you nothing about its neighbors.

Marcus's sister Ruth came down for her laundry, which lived in a corner of the basement like a tenant, and looked over Dylan's shoulder. She was a sophomore, an epicure of error messages, the kind of person who read a compiler's complaints the way other people read menus, with appetite. "What's the holdup?"

"The explanation part," Dylan said. "I have to say why it beats linear search. I know it does. I just don't know how to say it."

"Say it with numbers," Ruth said, folding a towel. "A million sorted items. Linear search, worst case, checks all million. What about yours?"

Dylan did the halving on paper. A million, then five hundred thousand, then a quarter million, and down and down, and he counted the cuts. Twenty. "Twenty checks. Worst case." He looked at the number skeptically, as if it had cheated somehow. "That can't be right. That's fifty thousand times fewer."

"Sorted data," Ruth said. "That's the whole trade. You pay for the sorting once, and the searching gets cheap forever. Whether that's a good deal depends on how many searches you're going to do." She carried her laundry upstairs, which Dylan understood was her way of saying the conversation was over.

He thought about that while he typed. One search on unsorted data, and linear was honest work, no preprocessing, no debt. A thousand searches, and binary was the only sane choice. It wasn't that one algorithm was better. It was that they answered different questions about how you planned to live with your data. He wrote his two sentences, then deleted them, then wrote them again, more carefully, including the word sorted, because leaving that out felt like lying by omission.

Now he needed a class to hold it all, so he refactored. He made a Searcher class, and to make it convenient he gave it a constructor that took the array as a parameter, so a searcher would be born already knowing its data. It was, he thought, an improvement. Then he ran his old test file, the one he'd written an hour ago, the one that had passed.

It didn't compile. The error sat there, blunt and unhelpful: the constructor Searcher() was undefined. His test called new Searcher() with nothing in the parentheses, the way it always had, the way that had worked before he'd written his fancy parameterized constructor. He scrolled between the two files like the answer might be hiding in the scroll bar.

"Ruth!" he yelled up the stairs, then caught himself. No. He read the error again, and then he looked at what he'd changed, and only at what he'd changed. Before, he had written no constructor at all, and new Searcher() had worked. After, he had written one constructor, the one with the array parameter, and suddenly the empty parentheses were a crime. He tried an experiment: he deleted his constructor entirely, recompiled, and the old test passed again. So the empty-parentheses version, the no-argument constructor, was something the compiler supplied when you wrote none yourself. The moment he supplied any constructor of his own, that free default one was no longer added. He hadn't broken his test. He had taken away something he'd never known he was being given.

He fixed it properly, keeping his parameterized constructor and adding a matching no-argument one by hand, and the whole suite went green. He told Ruth this at midnight, when she came down again, and she nodded as though he had reported that water was wet. "So what's your explanation?" she asked. "For the challenge. Why does binary search win?"

Dylan gave his answer, the trade, the sorting, the twenty versus the million, and Ruth shrugged and said it would pass. He submitted it with eleven minutes to spare. The confirmation page loaded slowly on Marcus's ancient router, and while it loaded Marcus leaned over and pointed at the sample input the challenge provided: a single array, unsorted, one search requested.

"You'd have to sort it first," Marcus said. "One lookup. Your whole elegant machine costs more than just walking the row."

Dylan looked at the sample, then at his beautiful halving loop, and laughed. He was already opening the file. "So for one search, linear wins."

"Depends how you live with your data," Ruth said from the stairs, and the basement light clicked off above him.

Jasmine had acclimated to the smell of the bakery by her third shift, which was faster than most new hires managed, according to Dev at the cash register. Her job was simple on paper: box the pastries, work the till on weekends, count the drawer at close. The till was the part that taught her things. Every sale rang up two extra lines, five percent federal and seven percent provincial, added on top of the sticker price, and every so often a customer would stare at their receipt like it had lied to them.

She was counting out change on a Saturday afternoon when Priya texted her a photo. Priya was in Manchester for the summer, staying with her aunt, and the photo was of a receipt from a coffee shop. "Why does nothing add up here," the message read. "Muffin says £2.40 on the shelf, receipt says £2.40. Where's the tax?"

Jasmine leaned against the counter between customers and looked at her own receipt tape, the one still curling out of the register. Her £2.40 equivalent, a three-dollar croissant, rang up as $3.36. She typed back that taxes got added at the till in Canada, on top of the price. Priya sent a shrug emoji, then a screenshot of a UK government page. Jasmine read it twice. The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, had been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.

"So the tax is hiding inside the price," Jasmine said out loud, mostly to herself.

"They call it VAT," Priya wrote. "Value added tax." That was all the message said, and somehow that made it clearer than a paragraph would have.

Dev looked over from the bread slicer. "Talking to your British girlfriend?" He said it the way he said everything, flat, and Jasmine didn't bother correcting him. She was doing arithmetic in her head, dividing £2.40 by 1.2, getting £2.00, watching forty pence of tax dissolve into a shelf price. It felt almost like arbitrage, knowing the true cost of a thing while everyone else paid the polite number on the tag, though she knew that wasn't what arbitrage meant. It was closer to being let in on a quiet arrangement.

Friday was payday. Jasmine had been waiting for the cheque all month because she needed ninety dollars for the deposit on a used amp, and her first full pay period, with two weeks of closing shifts folded in, should have cleared it easily. She opened the envelope in the back room and stood very still. The number was smaller than she'd worked out in her notebook, smaller by about forty dollars, and under the gross pay line were deductions she hadn't fully accounted for: income tax, and something called CPP, and EI. She'd known they existed the way you know weather exists, as a general condition. She hadn't thought they'd arrive so soon, in her first month, at seventeen.

She brought the stub to Dev, who squinted at it. "You filled out your TD1?" She didn't know what that was. He shrugged. "Ask payroll. Or claim it back, you make nothing, you'll get a refund when you file." She wrote the numbers on the back of the receipt from the amp seller, who'd held it for her until Monday, and she felt the small tectonic shift of a plan grinding against a fact. Ninety dollars minus the shortfall. She counted the bills in her wallet twice, as if arithmetic might renegotiate.

That night her mother found her at the kitchen table with the stub, the UK receipt photo, and her own receipt from the bakery laid side by side. "What's all this?" her mother asked, and Jasmine explained: here a tax you can see being added, there a tax folded into the price so quietly you had to do division to find it, and on her paycheque a tax taken before the money ever reached her, which was somehow the quietest of all. "Different systems," her mother said, filling the kettle. "All of them take their share. You just learn where to look."

On Monday Jasmine went to the amp seller's basement door with fifty-five dollars and the rest promised from the next pay period, and while the man considered it she checked his handwritten receipt and saw he'd charged no tax at all. "You're supposed to charge HST," she said, not sure why she said it, and he looked at her a long moment before reaching for the cord.

"Take it," he said. "Fifty-five, and we forget the paperwork."

She carried the amp up the stairs and out into the street, and only at the corner did she realize she'd left all three receipts on her mother's table, the evidence of everything she'd worked out, and she turned back toward the house instead of the bus stop.

The assignment on the board read "Customers who ordered nothing," and Tyler read it four times before it stopped looking like a contradiction. Mr. Okafor had given them two tables, Customers and Orders, and a question that seemed to assume you could search for something that wasn't there. Tyler opened his laptop next to Priya, who was already typing, and behind them Marcus was holding forth as he always did, this time about how anyone who spelled out the letters S, Q, L was basically admitting they'd never touched a real database.

"It's sequel," Marcus said, leaning his chair back onto two legs. "Nobody who actually works says it letter by letter."

"My cousin works at a bank," Priya said without looking up, "and she says S-Q-L, every day, and nobody has fired her yet."

"You're being doctrinaire about it," Tyler said, mostly to get Marcus to stop rocking, and Marcus looked wounded in the theatrical way that meant he'd keep the argument going all period. Tyler turned back to his screen. He typed the join he understood, Customers joined to Orders on customer ID, ran it, and got a tidy list of exactly the people who had bought something. The question wanted the opposite. He tried adding NOT to the condition and got a wall of duplicates so long the scroll bar shrank to a sliver.

"Your INNER JOIN subsumes them," Priya said, glancing over. "Every customer with one order gets swallowed into the match, so the no-order people never show up at all." She tapped his screen. "You need the join that keeps the left side even when the right side is empty."

"A LEFT JOIN," Tyler said, and she shrugged, unimpressed by his parroting, which was fair. He retyped it, Customers LEFT JOIN Orders, ran it, and there they were, every customer, with blank spaces where the order columns should be for a handful of names. Not nothing, exactly. Empty cells. He stared at the nulls, the little gaps that meant nobody had ever clicked buy, and it occurred to him that the trick wasn't finding nothing, it was making nothing visible so you could filter for it. He added WHERE Orders.order_id IS NULL, and the list shrank to eleven names. Mrs. Adeyemi. R. Cortez. A person called Test Account 3.

"It's pronounced sequel," Marcus announced from behind them, "because that's literally what it was called. Look." He turned his laptop around to show a scanned page from some ancient IBM document, yellow-edged, the typeface like a typewriter's. Tyler leaned over and read it aloud, quietly, so the rest of the lab wouldn't hear: SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and was first called SEQUEL.

"So we're both right," Priya said, which Marcus received like a hostage negotiation. "The old-timers say sequel because of the original name, and everyone else spells it out."

"That's not both right, that's me being more historically authentic."

"It's metonymy," Priya said. Marcus blinked. "Calling the whole language by one old name, like calling your car your wheels. It doesn't make you authentic, it makes you a poetic device." Tyler laughed into his sleeve, and Priya allowed herself half a smile before going back to her code.

Tyler looked at his eleven names again. Somewhere in the fact Marcus had dug up, in a language renamed but still doing the same work fifty years later, there was something that matched his query: the thing that persists, showing up in every result, even though its original label had gone empty. He decided not to say that out loud, because Marcus would either steal it or mock it, and because he wasn't sure the comparison actually held. It might just be a coincidence of mood. He filed it under uncertain, which was a bigger folder than it used to be.

Mr. Okafor drifted by and looked at Tyler's screen, arms folded. "Eleven customers, Mr. Reyes. Can you tell me why the nulls were necessary?" Tyler started to explain the left side surviving the empty right, and Priya cut in, deadpan, "He learned it from a poet. We call the language SEQUEL now, for authenticity." Marcus raised both hands in triumph.

"Sequel," Mr. Okafor said mildly, and walked on.

Levi had worked the front desk at Ridgeview Fitness for five weeks, long enough to learn the register, the towel count, and the laminated script for new members. The script was taped to the underside of the counter, and it used words he had never said out loud before his first shift: terms, conditions, liability waiver, monthly billing authorization. He said them forty times a week now. They had sensitized him to the paperwork everywhere else, too. He read his phone plan's renewal notice twice on the bus home, looking for the trap.

On a Tuesday evening in August, a boy came in with a duffel bag and a folded printout of the membership offer. His name was Marcus, he was seventeen, and he wanted the student rate before football conditioning started. He had a debit card in his hand and a school ID. Levi slid the contract across the counter and handed him the pen, and Marcus signed his name in careful block letters, and everything would have been fine except the form asked for his date of birth, and Marcus wrote it honestly.

"I need a parent's signature," Levi said. "It's the policy."

"Both my parents work nights," Marcus said. "I have the money. I have the card. What does it matter whose name is on the line?"

Levi did not have an answer. He looked at the script under the counter, but the script only covered pricing tiers and cancellation fees. He told Marcus he would ask his manager and hold the paperwork in the drawer, and Marcus said he would come back Thursday, and he took the pen with him by accident, a small theft neither of them noticed.

The manager, Ms. Okafor, was off until morning. Levi's coworker Danny was on the closing shift, and Danny was a dilettante who had opinions on contract law, real estate, sourdough starters, and the zoning dispute at the taco place across the street. "It's because he could cancel it," Danny said, spraying the treadmills. "A minor signs, a minor can walk away from it. That's the whole thing. It's voidable by the minor. Look it up if you don't believe me."

"I'm not looking up your theories."

"Look up whoever you want. It's common law, it's most of the country. The gym can't hold a kid to a contract. Kid can void it, gym can't. That's why they want the parent." Danny pointed the spray bottle at him. "There are exceptions. Necessities. Food, that kind of thing. A gym membership is not a necessity, no matter what Marcus's football coach thinks."

Levi did look it up, on his break, sitting on the stacked mats in the stretching corner with his phone. Danny had it right, which annoyed him. In common-law jurisdictions, including most of the US, a contract made by a minor was generally voidable by the minor, with exceptions such as contracts for necessities. Levi read the sentence three times. It was not that Marcus could not sign. It was that his signature meant one thing for the gym and another thing for Marcus, and the gym had decided it did not like the arrangement.

The next morning Levi found the policy binder behind the desk, and in the membership section there was a memo in Ms. Okafor's florid handwriting, all loops and crossed sevens, dated three years back: No memberships to under-18s without parent or guardian signature. Refund if already billed. Levi read it and understood that the policy was not a rule about who could join. It was a rule about risk. The gym wanted a signature it could enforce, and Marcus's parents, working nights, were the enforceable ones.

When Ms. Okafor came in at ten, Levi asked her about it. "What if the parent can't come in? Can they mail it, or do it over the phone?"

"They can mail it, they can fax it if they find a fax machine, they can come in on a Sunday," she said. "Why, do you have one?"

"Kid came in last night. Football season. He's coming back Thursday."

"Then Thursday we get him the form to take home." She was restocking the protein bars and did not look up. "Or he waits until his birthday."

Levi spent Wednesday thinking about it during the slow hours, between checking people in and wiping down the key rack. He had assumed the policy was a wall. Now it looked more like a door with a particular handle, and the question was whether he was supposed to tell Marcus where the handle was. He could explain the whole thing: that Marcus's own signature was legal but fragile, voidable, that the gym wanted his parents because their signatures could not be taken back. He could also just say "policy" again, the way the script did, and let Marcus believe there was nothing on the other side.

Thursday evening Marcus came back, duffel over his shoulder, and put the stolen pen on the counter without comment. "My dad's asleep by the time I get home," he said. "He sleeps at four in the afternoon. Conditioning starts Monday. If I'm not there Monday, they give my spot to a junior."

Levi took the contract out of the drawer and laid it flat. He turned it so Marcus could read it, and put his finger under the line that said the agreement was voidable by any member under eighteen, that exceptions applied only to contracts for necessities. "That's why they need your dad," he said. "Not because you can't sign. Because you can sign and then cancel it whenever you want, and they can't stop you, and they hate that. Your dad's signature they can hold onto."

Marcus read the paragraph twice. "So if I sign it and they bill me, I can void it?"

"That's what it says. I looked it up. It's most of the country, the common-law places. I'm not a lawyer."

"And a gym isn't a necessity."

"That's the exception, apparently. Food, stuff like that. Not this." Levi slid the take-home form across the counter, the one with the second signature line, and set the pen on top of it. "You can take this for your dad, or you can sign yours and void it later if they mess up your billing, but I don't know what happens then. I've only been here five weeks."

Marcus picked up the pen and looked at the two lines, one under his own block letters from Tuesday, one blank. Behind them, someone dropped a weight plate, and the sound rang off the mirrors and faded. Marcus tapped the blank line with the pen clip, twice, and said, "My dad gets up at two. He's awake for like an hour before work."

The kiln had been broken since March, so the community studio smelled of acrylic and turpentine instead of fired clay, and Sarah had claimed the table by the window because its light came in flat and honest across the afternoon. Her portfolio was due in nine days. On the table lay her third attempt at the harbor piece: gray water, gray sky, a line of pilings marching out toward a buoy that refused to matter.

"You've got the horizon dead center," said Priya, leaning over from the easel she shared with two oil painters who never came on Saturdays. "Put it a third of the way down. Rule of thirds."

Sarah sat back. "Who made that a rule?"

Priya shrugged, already turning back to her canvas. "Some dead guy, probably."

That should have been the end of it. Instead Sarah found herself that evening in the college library, because the studio kept a shelf of donated art books and the shelf had failed her, and there was something in the question that wouldn't quiet down. She wasn't the kind of person who introspect her way into libraries, or at least she hadn't been; apparently she was now. She found it in a scanned copy of an old book, its pages photographed so carefully she could see the foxing: Remarks on Rural Scenery, by John Thomas Smith, 1797. He had written the phrase down first, "rule of thirds," in a book about rural scenery, of all things, two hundred and odd years before Priya told her to move her horizon. She copied the citation onto the back of a gas receipt and rode the late bus home holding it like a ticket.

The next Saturday she arrived first and redrew the harbor. Horizon a third of the way down, the pilings entering from the left, the buoy now sitting, not floating, at a point that felt almost unfairly deliberate. The painting looked better. That was the trouble with it. It looked like every photograph on every wall of every dentist's office she had ever sat in, a composition so absorbed into the world that using it felt like quoting without speech marks.

"See?" Priya said when she came in, coat still on, shaking rain off it. "Told you."

"It's from a book," Sarah said. "John Thomas Smith, 1797. Remarks on Rural Scenery. First wrote down the phrase 'rule of thirds.'"

"Okay," said Priya, delighted and uninterested at once, the way she was about most things that weren't paint. "So it's old. Old things work."

But Sarah had spent the week thinking about how a man looking at rural scenery in 1797 had casually set a boundary she was now standing inside, and how her grandmother's quilts ignored every such law and still stopped your breath, and how the pilings in the actual harbor at Revere Beach did not arrange themselves in thirds. The rain intensified against the window, streaking the light she had chosen the table for. She picked up a rag and wiped the buoy off. Then she wiped the horizon off, the whole careful line of it, and let the gray water and the gray sky bleed into each other at a height chosen by nothing but her own wrist.

Priya watched this with genuine alarm. "You're going to submit that?"

"I don't know what I'm going to submit," Sarah said, which was true, and which cost her something to say out loud, because the portfolio wanted confidence and she had been practicing confidence all autumn like a scale.

The afternoon organized itself around her not deciding. A retired man named Walter, loquacious after his second thermos of coffee, narrated his own progress on a lighthouse to anyone in range. Two kids from the high school argued about whether orange was a real color. Priya painted in her deliberate, stabbing way and did not mention the horizon again, though Sarah caught her looking, twice, at the place where water met nothing.

Near closing, Sarah did a small thing. In the lower third of the canvas, roughly, though she refused to measure, she set the buoy back in, small and black against the formless gray. Not at an intersection, not at a power point, whatever those were called. Just low and left of center, where a buoy would actually ride. The rest she left unresolved, water and sky agreeing to be the same color, the pilings dissolving at their tops like an archipelago seen through fog, half-real.

"That's it?" Priya said, packing her brushes.

"That's what I have," Sarah said.

Priya stood in front of it for longer than she stood in front of anything, head tilted, and Sarah understood that the verdict, whatever it was, would not be spoken tonight. Walter shut off the lights from the switch by the door, and the harbor went dark all at once, water, sky, and buoy together.

Alice had braided the challah twice, and the first braid had collapsed into something that looked less like bread than a biology experiment, so she set it on the counter as a warning to the second. The kitchen smelled of yeast and burnt sugar where she had misjudged the oven rack, and her grandmother's handwritten list on the refrigerator had a rhythm she was trying to memorize: candles, wine, bread, blessing over the children, then the meal. For the first time, nobody was going to hand her the siddur at the right moment. She was going to lead all of it, tonight, for eleven relatives who had opinions about everything, including the opinions of other relatives.

Her phone buzzed on the counter, and she unlocked it with a knuckle because her hands were dusted with flour.

Text from Noa: "Reminder, I'm arriving with my opinions. Also Danny read something this week and is dying to share it. Prepare yourself. Love you, good luck, don't desiccate the chicken like last March."

Alice snorted and typed back, "The chicken in March was a tribute to jerky. Tonight will be different." But she checked the roasting pan anyway, spooned the pan juices over the breast, and slid the dish back in. Her mother drifted through for ice and said nothing, which was its own kind of vote of confidence, or possibly of terror.

The cousins arrived in a clatter of boots and supermarket bags. Danny, nineteen and newly armed with a religion course, cornered Alice by the stove before he had even taken off his scarf. "Okay, so the Sabbath commandment, right? It appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Exodus 20, the reason is that God rested after creation. That's why it matters." Noa, unpacking grape juice on the far counter, spun around with the slow delight of someone who has been waiting all evening for this. "Wrong book, wrong reason. In Deuteronomy 5, the reason is that God brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt. Remember that you were a slave. That's why it matters."

"You can't say wrong book," Danny said. "They're both in the Torah."

"Then they disagree," Noa said, "which means one of them has to be the real one."

Danny looked at Alice, apparently under the impression that whoever was running the ceremony could also referee theology. She stalled by checking the challah, which had risen into something almost handsome, and found she genuinely did not know. She had grown up lighting candles without ever asking why the commandment came with a reason attached, let alone two. "I'll rule on it after the wine," she said, and lit the candles with her hands circling three times, a gesture she had copied from her grandmother for years without thinking about what it was for.

The kitchen filled and the table filled and the noise rose, and Alice got through the blessings one at a time, her voice steadier than she expected, though she forgot the blessing over the children and had to be elbowed by her uncle. She was not sanguine about the elbowing; she was grateful for it. Between the soup and the main course, Danny and Noa resumed their argument over the bread basket, and Alice, who had spent the soup course thinking, held up her hand.

"Here's what I think," she said. "You're not actually disagreeing. Exodus says rest because God rested after making the world. Deuteronomy says remember you were freed from slavery, so give your workers the day off too." She paused, aware that her grandmother had stopped chewing. "One is about imitating God, and one is about remembering people. You can do both at the same table." She looked at the Challah, the candles guttering low in their holders. "Though I'm not sure the Torah meant them as one idea or two. That part I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend I do."

Noa pointed a butter knife at her. "That was suspiciously wise for someone who burned the soup."

"The soup is fine," Alice said, "it's rustic."

Her grandmother leaned back in her chair and said, to no one in particular, "I used to argue the same thing with my sister at this table. She took the Egypt side. Egypt people always take the Egypt side." Danny asked what she meant by that, and the old woman just reached for more bread. Alice ladled out the next bowl of soup and set it down in front of Noa, who had opened her mouth again.

"Eat," Alice said. "You can overthrow her theory after dessert."

Jake found the voter information card on the kitchen counter on Monday morning, addressed to his mother, and realized with a cold flip in his stomach that nothing had ever come for him. He was eighteen in April. He had talked about this election for months, at the table, on the bus, in the group chat where Devon insisted that first-time voters who hadn't done their research were worse than people who stayed home. Jake had argued the opposite, that showing up mattered even when you were unsure, and he had said it with the confidence of someone who assumed the showing-up part was automatic.

He checked the Elections Canada website on his phone, thumb hovering, and found the sentence he needed: an eligible voter who was not on the voters list could register at their assigned polling place on election day. He read it twice. Nothing in the mailbox, nothing mailed in advance, and still he could walk in. It felt almost too easy, the way things that matter sometimes do.

"You're not on the list?" his mother said from the doorway, car keys in hand. She was voting before work and had offered, twice, to drive him. "I thought you registered when you turned eighteen."

"I thought it happened automatically."

"Nothing happens automatically," she said, and then, softer, "bring ID. Something with your address." She kissed the top of his head the way she had since he was small, which he tolerated now rather than enjoyed, and left for the school where she taught.

He walked to the church gym two blocks over after his afternoon class, a thin folder of documents under his arm, feeling like a dilettante among the retired people staffing the tables, the ones who had done this in ten elections and knew the smell of the room. His father had voted the night before at the advance poll, in and out in eight minutes, and had said over dinner that a person who couldn't be bothered to sort out his registration in time probably shouldn't be casting a ballot anyway. His father said things like that. Jake had spent most of his life treating his father's certainty as either a wall to push against or a comfort to lean on, and only lately had he begun to notice it could be neither, just a way of talking.

The line moved slowly. Behind him a woman rocked a stroller with one foot; ahead, an old man argued gently with a poll worker about where the pencil had gone. When Jake reached the registration desk, a volunteer with reading glasses on a chain looked up his address, had him confirm it, printed a slip, and pointed him to the ballot table. No lecture. No fee. Ten minutes of standing in a church gym and the thing his father had framed as an obstacle had simply, quietly, not been one.

He took his ballot behind the cardboard screen and stood there longer than he expected. Devon's voice in his head said know everything or stay home; his father's voice said decide fast, certainty is the point. But standing there, pencil in hand, he thought the truth was smaller and stranger than either of them. He had read the platforms. He had changed his mind twice in three weeks, first over the housing policy, then over something a candidate had said about the north that he couldn't stop turning over. He did not feel like a fraud for still being unsure. He felt like a person doing a hard thing at the exact scale at which the thing was hard, and it occurred to him that his uncertainty was not a congenital defect to be hidden but the ordinary condition of anyone honest, and that honesty was itself a kind of vote, cast for the idea that citizens are allowed to think.

He marked the ballot, folded it, and slid it into the box. The poll worker tore the corner off his slip and said, "There you go, first one?"

"First one."

"You can come do it again in four years whether you're sure or not," she said, already looking past him at the line.

Outside the light had gone amber over the parking lot. He texted Devon a photo of his folded registration slip, then his father a single line: registered at the poll, took ten minutes. He put the phone away before either could answer and started the walk home, the leaves coming down around him in slow spirals, the gym doors still propped open behind him with their little line of people shuffling forward.

At eleven forty on a Tuesday night, Abigail lay across her bed with her phone two inches from her face, thumbing through the group chat, which had been named SENECA FALLS 2.0 by Priya in September and had since covered college rejections, a rumored prom theme, and the vice principal's parking habits.

The argument tonight was a Washington Post article Priya had linked, about a warehouse somewhere in the Midwest where workers said they were scanned and timed down to the second. Priya wanted everyone to sign a petition and email it to their representatives. Marcus, who wanted more than anything to be the person in any room who had already thought of everything, replied within four minutes: "you know bezos owns that paper right." Then, before anyone could answer: "he bought it. 2013. 250 million."

Abigail sat up. She read his message twice. "From who," she typed, because that seemed like the kind of thing Marcus would know, and because she genuinely wanted to know. "the graham family," he answered. "owned it forever. then sold." She stared at the words, feeling the shape of something shift. She had grown up treating the Post the way she treated the weather, a thing that simply existed and reported itself. It had never once occurred to her that it might belong to somebody.

Priya, who was impervious to this kind of gotcha, kept typing. "ok and? the article is RIGHT THERE. it says amazon treats workers like garbage. if bezos controlled it why would they print that." Marcus said owners don't censor every story, they shape the edges, they decide who gets hired and what counts as worth investigating, and Abigail thought about how her mother apportioned the grocery money at the start of each month, not by forbidding any particular purchase but by making some purchases easier than others. She didn't type that. It sounded better inside her head than it would look in a blue bubble.

Instead she opened a new tab and searched. The purchase was real, exactly as Marcus said, and it had cost less than she'd imagined a newspaper could cost, less than a third of what her school district had spent on a football stadium. Down the hall her brother's music undulated through the wall, bass rising and falling, and she thought about how the same story could rise and fall depending on who was holding it. She found a piece from the Post itself, about the deal, calm and thorough, and she found a piece from another paper that called the calm itself suspicious, and she found a thread where people who had worked at the Post for years argued with strangers about whether anything had really changed.

She went back to the chat. Priya had moved on to logistics, asking who had actually signed. Two checkmarks appeared. Then Marcus, and then nothing for a while, the typing bubble surfacing and sinking like something breathing. Abigail typed: "I think both of you are half right. The article exists, so it's not like he killed it. But it's his. We should probably read everything knowing it's somebody's." She deleted "knowing it's somebody's" because it sounded like a fortune cookie, and replaced it with "knowing who owns it," and sent that. Then she signed the petition, because the workers in the article had names and quotes and had risked something to talk, and whatever the Post's owners' interests were, the workers' complaint seemed to survive them.

Marcus replied with a single word, "exactly," which irritated her, because she had not said what he said, or at least she hadn't meant to. Priya sent a gif of a person clapping slowly, which could have meant anything. Abigail understood, lying there in the dark with her screen lighting her chin, that she hadn't resolved anything. Maybe the ownership mattered enormously. Maybe it barely mattered at all, and a good reporter with a good editor would print the truth regardless of who signed the checks, the way a river keeps moving regardless of who owns the land beside it. She could hold both of those at once. It was uncomfortable, like carrying two full bags of groceries in one trip, but she could do it.

"Abigail you alive?" Priya had sent. "you went quiet which means you're overthinking."

"never," Abigail typed. Then, because it was nearly midnight and her eyes were dry and the petition tab was still open behind the chat, she added, "I signed it. I'm just also going to look up who owns every paper I read from now on, and it's your fault." She plugged her phone in across the room, the way she did when she wanted the conversation to end on her terms, and watched the screen dim from a distance, the three gray dots already pulsing at the bottom of the thread.

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and Maxime had been adjusting the gap between his two aluminum plates for an hour before the judges started circulating. His project was a field-mapping rig: a pair of plates on a micrometer stand, a small probe, a hand-drawn graph of field strength versus position. The numbers had come out cleanly last night, which was the problem, because they had come out too cleanly, and he had not slept well thinking about it.

Noor set up beside him at eight with her terrariums and a folder of bee diagrams. She wanted, she had told him twice on the bus, an interview with the local paper, because the paper only ever photographed the robotics team and she was tired of bees being subsumed under the general heading of science-fair variety acts. She straightened her label cards and glanced at his rig. "Still cooking, Volta?"

"Verifying." He uncapped his marker and redid the arithmetic on the back of his data sheet, slowly, the way his father balanced a checkbook. He had twelve hundred volts across a gap of half a millimetre. Divide the one by the other and the field between his plates came out at over two billion volts per metre. He wrote it, looked at it, and crossed it out with a single line.

"That's a big number," Noor said, reading over his shoulder.

"It's a broken number." He tapped the power supply, a gray brick of uncertain provenance that he had bought secondhand from a man at a flea market who had assured him it worked. "If the field were really that strong, the air between the plates wouldn't just sit there."

She frowned at the gap, so narrow he could slip a playing card through it and feel the drag. "What would it do?"

"It would spark. Dry air breaks down around three million volts per metre, sea-level pressure. So there's a limit, an actual ceiling on how strong a field can be across an air gap." He said it and then heard it, and something in his chest went quiet. His whole graph was impossible. Every point on it was a field the air itself would not permit.

The first judge arrived before he could panic properly. She was a woman with reading glasses on a chain, and she bent close to his graph, then closer to the plates. "Walk me through your field calculation."

"Twelve hundred volts, half a millimetre, so I divide." He turned the sheet toward her. "Except the answer's wrong, because the air would have sparked long before I got there, and it didn't spark. I've been running it for an hour."

The judge said nothing, which was somehow worse than a question. Noor leaned in and tapped the micrometer stand itself. "Maxime. Look at your spacers."

He looked. He had built the stand from brass shim stock, and the spacers, the little strips that set the plate separation, were stamped with their thickness. He had assumed half a millimetre because the packet had said so at the flea market, from the same man, with the same assurance. The stamp on the actual strips in the actual stand read 0.5 mm. He measured them anyway with the school's calipers, borrowing them from the physics storeroom through a door Ms. Achterberg left unlocked for him. The strips measured 0.4 millimetres, and worse, they were not matched; one was thicker than the other by a tenth, so his plates had been tilted all morning, and his field had never been uniform at all.

The judge was watching him measure. "So where does that leave your data?"

"Equivocal," Maxime said. "That's the honest word for it. The field between the plates was never what I computed, because the gap was never what I assumed, and even if it had been, the air caps the whole thing at three million volts per metre anyway. If my numbers had been right, I'd have gotten a spark, not a graph." He heard himself say it and realized it was the first sentence of the entire project that he fully believed.

The judge wrote something short in her book, thanked him, and moved on to Noor's terrariums, where she stayed for ten minutes and asked about waggle dances. Noor answered steadily, eyes bright. When the woman finally left, Noor exhaled and squeezed Maxime's arm. "That was a real judge question and you gave a real answer. That's better than a pretty graph."

Maxime pulled his graph down off the board and turned the paper over to its blank side. He drew a new axis, wrote "measured, not assumed" at the top, and began remeasuring the gap with the calipers, plate by plate, recording each number as it came. Somewhere behind him a buzzer sounded for the second round of judging, and a boy two tables over yelped as his homemade Tesla coil threw a spark across six centimetres of open air.

"See," Noor said, not looking up from her bees. "Even the air has rules."

The line at the former elementary school stretched past the doors marked gymnasium, and Aiden stood near the end with his hands in his jacket pockets. He had turned eighteen in March, three weeks before the registration deadline, and his father had driven him to the county office that same afternoon, saying little on the way. Now it was November, the gym smelled of floor wax and wet umbrellas, and Aiden advanced one folding-table-length at a time toward the clipboard where a woman with reading glasses checked names.

Ahead of him a boy from his economics class, Marcus, kept turning around to talk. "My mom's voting the other way from me," Marcus said. "She found out I registered and spent an hour trying to cajole me over dinner. Lasagna, garlic bread, the whole campaign."

"Did it work?"

"I told her she'd find out on Wednesday with everybody else." Marcus grinned, then the grin faded into something more serious. "Hey, actually. Nobody's allowed to watch you mark it, right? Like, they can't see how you vote at all?"

A woman in front of them, older, holding her ID ready in her hand, half turned. "It's called the Australian ballot," she said. "That's what the secret printed ballot is called." She faced forward again, as if she had spent her whole quota of conversation on it.

"The colonies there came up with it," Aiden said, mostly to himself, and then he realized he actually knew the rest. "Tasmania and Victoria, in 1856." He had read it in a library book in eighth grade, one he had pulled off the shelf because he liked the shape of the word ballot, and the fact had stuck the way certain useless facts stuck, lodged like a seed in a crack.

Marcus squinted at him. "Australia invented voting?"

"Secret voting. The ballot itself. Before that, people could watch you, or you said it out loud." Aiden was working it out as he spoke, the reason coming to him only now, in the line. If your vote was public, anyone could stand over you, an employer, a husband, a crowd outside the window. If it was secret, the lasagna and the garlic bread ended at the curtain. His mother's persuasion, Marcus's mother's persuasion, all of it stopped at the little canvas booth, which was, he thought, either a protection or a small entropy, opinions dissipating into silence where no one could trace them.

Two summers ago, before any of this mattered to him, Aiden had gone with his grandfather to vote in the midterms. The old man had parked badly, on a hill, and insisted on walking in without his arm. Inside, at the same folding tables, the same women with reading glasses, his grandfather had stood at the booth for a long time. Aiden, waiting by the door, had watched him hover over the paper with his pencil, and had wondered, without any real curiosity, what was taking so long. When they were back in the car his grandfather said, "Your grandmother and I cancel each other out, every single election, and we've never once discussed it. Fifty-one years." He had said it the way a man states the weather, and Aiden had filed it away with the Australian ballot and the other facts that belonged to adulthood.

Now the woman with the reading glasses called, "Next," and Marcus stepped up, gave his name, and was pointed toward the machines. Aiden followed. His name was on the list. He signed it and felt the pen snag slightly on the laminated page.

The booth was smaller than he expected, a canvas sleeve on three aluminum legs, and the ballot was a long sheet printed on both sides. In eighth grade he had imagined this moment as an ending, a door he would walk through and emerge from changed. Instead it was a man in a damp jacket holding a pen in a gymnasium, deciding. He thought of his grandfather's pencil hovering. He thought of the colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, someone in 1856 deciding that a vote should be a thing no one could see, and he thought, less comfortably, that he still wasn't sure whether that was mercy or just a very organized form of loneliness. The pen waited above the first contest.

Behind him, at the entrance, a poll worker was turning someone away, gently, for lack of ID, and the man's voice rose once, scathing, before it dropped and he left through the double doors into the rain.

Aiden marked the first box, then the second, then the races he had studied and the ones he had not. He fed the sheet into the scanner, which took it with a shudder and lit a small American flag on its face. Outside, Marcus was waiting under the awning with his hood up.

"So," Marcus said. "Wednesday?"

"Wednesday," Aiden said, and pulled his own hood over his head and stepped down into the puddled lot.

The auction barn smelled of wet straw and diesel, and Ava sat on a sawhorse with her phone in both hands, reading the same paragraph for the third time while her grandfather argued with a man from the bank at the folding table by the fence line. The man kept saying words like restructuring and opportunity, and her grandfather kept saying nothing at all, which Ava had learned was worse. Outside, the rain came down on two hundred acres of soybeans that had failed twice in three years, first under drought and then under a flood that shouldn't have come in June.

She was supposed to be rehearsing. On Thursday, in her last week of high school, her government class would debate whether countries could ever actually agree on an environmental problem, and her teacher had assigned Ava the yes side, which felt like a joke. Her grandfather read the farm reports out loud at breakfast, the ones about tariffs and commodity prices and the river sediment, and none of it suggested that anyone agreed about anything, ever.

Her cousin Dario came through the barn door shaking water off his jacket. "They still going?"

"Forty minutes," Ava said. "He won't look at the papers."

Dario sat on the hay bale across from her, took off his boot, and shook a pebble out of it. "Dad says the co-op's dropping another eight growers this fall. Says the buyers want the big consolidated lots now, the irrigated ones, out west where the water rights are." He said it flat, the way people around here said bad news, and Ava thought about how the drought out west and the flood here were both weather, both money, both somebody's decision at a desk far away. It was hard to say where one thing stopped and the next began.

She went back to her phone. She'd found a thread of sources the night before, chasing her debate topic out of stubbornness, and at two in the morning she'd hit something she hadn't expected. She read it aloud now, quietly, mostly to herself. "The 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phases out ozone-destroying chemicals, was the first treaty in United Nations history to be ratified by every UN member state."

Dario looked up. "Every one?"

"Every single one. Every country that was in the UN." She turned the phone toward him so he could see she wasn't inventing it, and he squinted at the small screen with his boot still in his hand.

"Huh," he said. "The ozone thing. The hole." He pointed at an aerosol can of fly spray sitting on the windowsill, half-empty, red. "That stuff they fixed?"

"That's how it worked with the chemicals, the sprays and the refrigerants, whatever was eating the ozone," she said. "They phased them out." She didn't say more than that, because she didn't know more than that yet, and there was something in not knowing that she wanted to keep honest. She had a night left to read, and a debate to lose or win, and a phone with a cracked screen and a battery at eleven percent.

Behind them, the bank man was packing his briefcase, and her grandfather crossed the barn in the direction of the feed room without a word to either of them. Ava followed him in. He stood with his hand on the lid of the grain bin, not opening it, and the rain on the tin roof was so loud she almost had to shout.

"You want me to say it went fine?" she asked.

"No," he said. "I want you to tell me what you were reading."

She told him about the treaty, every member state, the first one in UN history ever to get all of them, and he listened with his jaw working the way it did when he was deciding whether to spit or speak. "The whole world agreed on something," she finished. "I have to argue Thursday that they can."

He was quiet for a while. "Half this county can't agree on a drainage ditch," he said. But he opened the grain bin, and the smell of oats rose up, and he looked less lugubrious than he had at the table, almost as if the fact had sutured something in him, some torn place between what he believed about people and what he needed to believe to keep planting in the spring. Ava knew her own position was thinner than that. She believed the treaty happened, and she believed the droughts were getting worse, and she could not make those two facts hold hands yet, could not say whether agreement came easier when the sky itself was the patient or when the damage was slow and dispersed, when culpability spread out so wide that no one felt it in their own hands. Her grandfather's hands were cracked from rope and cold water. The bank man's hands were clean. Somewhere between those hands the whole system lay, weather and money and treaties, and she would stand up Thursday and speak for exactly six minutes about a world that had once, in one narrow instance, said yes together.

The rain kept on. Her grandfather scooped grain into the bucket, measure by measure, and carried it past her out into the dark of the barn, where the cattle had already begun to low.

"Come on," he said over his shoulder. "You can argue with the heifers first."

Carter had written three openings for the toast his grandmother expected at dinner, and he had torn up all of them. The first was a joke about finally being done with high school, the second was a thank-you list that read like an awards ceremony, and the third had tried to be serious and collapsed into greeting-card language he couldn't say out loud. He sat in his car outside his grandparents' house with his phone open to a draft, because Grandma June had cornered him last week and said, "You're the graduate, you're saying something, seven o'clock sharp, before the cake." It was six forty.

Inside, the dining room was loud with relatives he half knew. His diploma sat propped against the centerpiece, its seal catching the light, and every few minutes someone lifted a glass toward it. Carter's grandfather, Walt, sat at the far end, quieter than usual, turning his water glass in slow circles. Carter had always thought of the two of them as parallel cases: Walt had left school at seventeen, and Carter had just finished his, and the family treated both facts as different versions of the same thing, an unfinished story that had finally come out all right.

It was Aunt Rena who destabilized that, casually, while spooning potatoes. "Your grandfather has a diploma too, you know," she said. "Same one, basically. The GED." She said it like a footnote, but Carter put down his fork. He knew the letters, knew kids who had taken that route after leaving school early, but he had never once thought of them attached to Walt, who had run a hardware store for thirty years and could rewire anything in the house.

"Since when?" Carter asked.

"Nineteen forty-two, the tests started," Walt said, still turning the glass. "For service members. Fellows like me who'd left school and gone in. When I got out, I took it. Showed I had the schooling without the school." He shrugged, as if it were a minor clerical matter, but his voice had the careful flatness Carter recognized from when he was hiding something he actually felt.

Carter wanted to ask more, but the cake was already being lit in the kitchen, and his grandmother was mouthing seven o'clock at him across the table. He had maybe ten minutes. He pushed back his chair and followed Walt out onto the porch, where the old man had retreated with his coffee.

"You never told me that," Carter said.

"Never came up." Walt looked at the yard, where the neighbor's sprinkler ticked back and forth. "People get strange about it. Some cousin of mine, real ideologue about education, used to say the GED wasn't a real diploma. Man could turn any subject into an argument, that one. You learn not to hand people the opening." He sipped his coffee. "I passed it in an army office with a pencil that kept breaking. Hardest test I ever took. But nobody wants the story, they want the label."

Carter leaned on the railing, working through it. He had spent the spring arguing with a classmate, Marcus, who insisted that a diploma meant something only if you suffered through four full years to get it, that shortcuts cheapened the thing itself. Carter had half agreed, mostly because Marcus argued with such virulent certainty that disagreeing felt like picking a fight. Now, standing next to a man who had left school for a war and come back and proven himself on a single brutal exam, he wondered whether the paper or the proving was the point. Maybe both, he thought. Maybe the diploma was just a receipt, and the receipt mattered only because of what had been purchased.

"I have to give a toast," Carter said. "Right now, basically. Can I mention it? The GED, the test, all of it?"

Walt was quiet long enough that the sprinkler completed two passes. "You'd be telling my story in your toast," he said, which was not a no.

"That's the thing," Carter said. "It's not just my story without it. Mine's boring. I showed up and did the work. Yours is the interesting one." He hesitated, honest with himself at least: he still didn't know if he was asking permission or asking for material, and the difference bothered him. "I won't make it a speech about speeches. I'll just say what happened."

Walt set the coffee down. "Say the year right, then. Nineteen forty-two."

Through the screen door, Grandma June called his name in the tone that meant the last candle was being lit. Carter went in, stood at the head of the table with his glass raised, and felt every prepared sentence desert him except the true one.
