He made them stay.

It was in section fourteen that he stopped. The clause said that the tenants would be liable, jointly and severally, for all rent and damages under the lease. He read it twice, then pasted it into a search bar. The results came back fast and flat and changed the shape of the evening: under joint and several liability, each of several people who share an obligation can be held responsible for the entire amount, not only their own share. He sat back. He and Dev and Priya were each planning to cover a third of the rent. The landlord, apparently, did not care about thirds.

He called Dev first, and Dev laughed before William had finished the sentence. "So if Priya bails, we cover her part. Obviously. That's what friends do."

"That's not what it says," William said. "It says if Priya bails, either of us can be made to cover all of it. Not her third. All of it. The whole rent, every month, until the lease ends."

There was a pause long enough that William could hear a television in the background of Dev's room. "That can't be right," Dev said. "That's ridiculous."

"It's right. I'm reading it right now."

Priya joined the call a minute later, breathless from somewhere outdoors, and William walked them through it again, slower this time. He had spent the last hour with the document, sequestered at his desk with his phone face down, and he had worked out the arithmetic more than once, hoping it would come out differently. It did not. If one of them lost a job, the other two were not exposed to a share; they were exposed to everything.

"So we don't sign," Dev said.

"We want the apartment," Priya said. "It's two blocks from the river. It's the only one we can afford, and affording it is exactly the problem, so."

William turned in his chair and looked at the printout he had made, six pages of it, clause fourteen circled in pencil. His father had signed things his whole life, he thought, shift contracts, a truck loan, papers he never read, and called that practicality. William had always privately considered it a lack of acumen, an older man's carelessness dressed up as toughness. Now he was less sure which of them was being naive, the man who signed without reading or the boy who imagined that reading was the same as control.

"We could do a side agreement," he said. "Between the three of us. If the landlord makes one of us pay more than a third, the others owe that person the difference. It doesn't change what we owe the landlord, but it changes what we owe each other."

"That sounds tautological," Priya said. "We'd be signing a contract to enforce the contract we already agreed to by being friends."

"It's not the same thing," William said, though he could hear the weakness in it. "One of them is legally enforceable and one of them is us trusting each other, and after tonight I'd rather have both."

They argued for another twenty minutes. Dev wanted to sign the lease as it stood and trust the friendship; Priya wanted to ask the landlord to strike the clause entirely, which William doubted would work and Priya suspected he only doubted because he liked knowing things. In the end they agreed to the side agreement, drafted in a shared document while they were still on the call, three signatures to be scanned by noon.

William drafted it himself, and it was almost midnight when he noticed the message waiting below the thread. It was from Priya, sent an hour earlier, before they had agreed on anything. She had written to the landlord asking about removing clause fourteen, and the landlord had already replied: the lease had been generated for three tenants, but joint and several liability was standard, and if they preferred, it could be rewritten for a single tenant with two occupants, which some renters found simpler. A single tenant. One name, one obligation, no shares at all.

William read the reply three times, then called her, and she picked up on the second ring.

"You already sent this," he said. "Before we decided anything."

"I sent it before I knew what we'd decide," Priya said. "I wanted to know what our options were." In the quiet that followed, he could hear her walking, her footsteps on pavement somewhere between the river and home. "My parents would co-sign for me alone," she said. "They offered. I didn't tell you because I wanted us to figure it out together, and now we have, and I still don't know if I'd be helping you both or just making sure I'm the one who's safe."

William looked at the side agreement open on his screen, his own name typed into the first signature line, and found he could not tell either.

"So what do we do?" Dev's voice came from the other line, where he had apparently been listening the whole time.

William reached for his pencil and turned back to clause fourteen, the circle he had drawn around it already smudged gray. "Tomorrow," he said, "we go in together, all three of us, and we don't sign anything until every line has been read out loud."

Mr. Draper's laptop cart had seventeen working machines and twenty-six students, so Lucas spent the first ten minutes of GIS class watching Devin play solitaire. When a Chromebook finally came free, it was the one with the space bar that stuck, which meant every command arrived twice. Lucas typed "flood" and the program asked him, politely, twice, whether he meant flood.

The assignment was to overlay two layers of the city map, flood risk and housing density, and write a paragraph about what the overlap meant. Mr. Draper had said the word "overlay" the way some people say "lasagna," like it was the whole meal. Lucas pulled the flood layer first, and the river appeared as a blue tongue licking through the middle of town, wide at the south end where the old warehouses were. Then he added housing, and the dense blocks, orange and red, clustered along the tongue like they were trying to get close to it.

"That's the point," said Priya, leaning over from the next desk. "People live where the water wants to be."

"The water wanted it first," Lucas said. "We just moved in anyway."

He knew the south side a little. His grandmother had lived there until the spring the creek came up through the floor vents, and after that she'd moved in with his grandfather on the north side, in the house with the filing cabinets in the basement. That was where Lucas had been on Saturday, looking for a badminton set, when he found the cabinets instead.

They were full of maps. Not printed maps, though some of those too, but sheets of tracing paper, dozens of them, each one drawn in colored pencil and labeled in his grandfather's small upright hand. Soil. Water table. Slope. Woodland. One sheet was nothing but the floodplain, hatched in blue, and under it another showed the same city with houses inked on like scattered seeds. Some sheets were stacked and pinned together at the corners, and when Lucas held a stack up to the basement's single bulb, the layers went translucent and the whole city showed through at once, water and houses arguing in the same light.

His grandfather came down for a shoebox of tax papers and found Lucas holding the stack against the bulb like a slide.

"Careful with those," he said. "Those took a summer."

"What are they?"

"Landscape architect named Ian McHarg had the idea, back around sixty-nine. His book was called Design with Nature. You stacked your maps, soil, water, all the factors, and the stack told you what the land could take." He took the pinned sheets gently out of Lucas's hand and laid them flat. "We did it by hand. It took weeks."

Lucas had looked at him, then, with the strange feeling of a door opening in a wall he'd thought was solid. "We're doing that," he said. "In class. On computers. Except it takes about four seconds."

His grandfather had smiled at the ceiling. "Everything you can do in four seconds, somebody spent a summer on first."

Now, in class, Lucas added the third layer, the one Mr. Draper hadn't asked for, a soil map he found in the public data folder, and the south side went dark where the floodplain and the housing and the soft ground all agreed. The software called what he was doing a layer stack, and the phrase felt borrowed, like something that had been sequestered in a basement for fifty years and let out.

Priya was still watching his screen. "What's the extra layer?"

"Soil. My grandfather drew this exact map by hand. Tracing paper. Colored pencil." He dragged the layers apart and together again, watching the overlap bloom and shrink. "Same idea. He got it from a book."

"He invented GIS?"

"No. The book just had the idea, the stacking. The computers came after and automated it." Lucas zoomed in on the littoral streets near the river, the blocks that touched the water like a shoreline, where the orange of the housing sat squarely on the blue of the flood risk. "That's where my grandma used to live."

The paragraph Mr. Draper wanted was supposed to say what the overlap meant, and Lucas found that the harder he looked, the less single it became. The maps said the houses shouldn't be there, but the maps also couldn't say that Ms. Arroyo had run her shop on Delancey for thirty years, or that the soft soil was the reason the rents were low enough for people to stay at all. Priya's position was clean: move people out of the floodplain, build on the high ground. His grandfather's was its counterpoint: the land decides, and you listen to it before you draw a single lot. Lucas suspected the truth needed both of them and maybe a third one he hadn't found yet, and he wrote that, honestly, at the bottom of the paragraph, in the space where a conclusion was supposed to go.

He printed the map, color being the whole point, and that evening rode his bike across town to the north side. His grandfather was in the basement again, shoebox open, receipts spread like fallen leaves. Lucas held out the printout: the blue tongue, the orange blocks, the dark argument where they met.

"Same map," his grandfather said.

"Not quite," said Lucas. "Yours is prettier."

His grandfather put down a receipt and reached for his reading glasses. "Show me where the creek comes up through the floor," he said.

The library closed at nine, and by seven Charlotte had spread her laptop, a paperback on Java, and two granola bar wrappers across the study table nearest the sockets. Her screen held a file called Player.java, forty lines her teammate Dara had written the night before the deadline for their intro programming course. The autograder had returned 0 out of 20 at four that afternoon, with no message except a wall of red compiler errors, and the professor's email had said only: teams resolve their own builds. Charlotte had until midnight.

She read the file top to bottom first, the way you read a letter you already suspect is bad news. Dara had built a Player with private fields: score, name, active. So far, so good. Charlotte's own half of the assignment, the test class, sat open in the other window, and every test she had written called methods that the compiler claimed did not exist. That was the part that made her stomach drop, a visceral certainty that she had broken something herself, because she had written the tests three days ago, tired, in one sitting.

Dara arrived at seven-fifteen with a paper cup of coffee and no apology. "I told you I'd handle the player class."

"You did." Charlotte turned the laptop so Dara could see the errors. "Every one of my tests fails to compile. It's like we wrote code for two different languages."

Dara leaned in, scanning. "Your tests are the problem. Look, I always name my methods after myself. Score give-back, I call it fetchScore. Name is giveName. Active is checkActive."

"FetchScore," Charlotte repeated. She said it the way you repeat a wrong answer in class, not cruelly, just to hear it outside her own head.

They sat with that for a moment. Around them the library went on with its ordinary evening: a man shelving returns, a kid at the catalog computer clicking the mouse much too hard. Charlotte scrolled between the two windows, Dara's methods in one pane, her tests in the other, and the mismatch resolved itself slowly into a pattern she could actually name. Her tests called getScore. Dara's said fetchScore. For the boolean, her tests called isActive; Dara's said checkActive. It wasn't two languages. It was two naming conventions, and one of them was the one everybody else used, which meant the graders' tools used it too.

"Here's what I think," Charlotte said slowly. "By the JavaBeans convention, a getter for a field named score is called getScore. And a getter for a boolean is usually named with is, like isActive. That's just how it's done. That's why my tests compile against the textbook's examples and not against yours."

Dara's jaw tightened. "So it's my fault."

"I didn't say fault." But the word culpability had already surfaced in Charlotte's mind, unhelpful and precise, and she pushed it down. Assigning blame would take thirty seconds and fix nothing; they had four and a half hours. "Here's the deal. Renaming your methods takes ten minutes. Rewriting my tests to match your names takes an hour and then the graders still fail us. Which cost do we want to pay?"

Dara was quiet, turning the coffee cup in her hands. "My way works, though. It runs."

"It runs if nobody else ever reads it." Charlotte thought of the summer internship she'd applied for, where she'd read a snippet of a real codebase in the interview prep material, hundreds of methods by dozens of hands, all readable at a glance because everyone had agreed on the same names. She hadn't understood then what that agreement was worth. She was starting to. Conventions felt like shackles until you were the third person to touch a file at midnight. "I'm not saying your names are wrong in some cosmic sense. I'm saying they're expensive. You pay for originality every time someone new opens the file."

"You could have told me that before I wrote it."

"I could have." That part was true, and Charlotte let it stand. She had assumed they were splitting the work in half when the real task was building one thing together, and she hadn't checked Dara's naming once. The cost of that assumption could not be amortized over the semester; it was due tonight, all at once.

Dara exhaled, pulled the laptop closer, and opened the find-and-replace box. "GetScore, getScore. Fine. Show me your test file so I don't miss any."

They went method by method, Dara renaming, Charlotte reading the tests aloud, the two windows inching toward agreement. At 8:40 the compiler errors thinned from thirty-one to four to one, a missing semicolon after getName. Charlotte fixed it, ran the suite, and seventeen green checkmarks stacked down the screen while the loudspeaker announced that the library would close in fifteen minutes.

"Submit it," Dara said. "Before it changes its mind."

The folding table at the Language Corner of the Riverside Heritage Festival had a hand-lettered sign that said READ ALOUD, WIN A PRIZE, and beneath it, in smaller letters, prizes subject to availability. Amy had walked past it twice before stopping, mostly because the boy behind the table had a rubber stamp shaped like a heron and was stamping it on everyone's forearms, and she wanted one.

"You pick a card," the boy said, waving the heron at her. "Read the article on the back. Then you tell us what it says, in your own words. Any language you like for the telling. The reading has to be in Spanish."

"I've had one semester of Spanish," Amy said. "One. And that semester mostly covered cafeteria vocabulary."

"Cafeteria vocabulary is a strong foundation," said a girl at the table, who was wearing a banner that identified her as Lucía, Voluntaria. "I once survived a whole week in Paris on the word croissant."

The card Amy drew was a short news item, three sentences, photocopied from something real. The first two sentences she could crawl through: something about a town, a river, a cleanup. The third sentence contained a word that stopped her cold. "Según el alcalde," she read, and then stopped, because she had no idea what según meant, and the sentence that followed it, the sentence that seemed to be the whole point of the article, hinged on it. Whoever or whatever según was, it apparently had opinions about the river.

"The trick is you can't just recite it," the boy said. "You have to say what's true in it. Fact or somebody's claim. That's the game. We're a little strict. It's the only power we have."

Amy frowned at the card. If she summarized the third sentence as plain fact, she might be saying the mayor's claim was true, when maybe the reporter was just passing it along. But if she hedged everything, she'd sound like a lawyer. She thought about how in her debate class they'd drilled a distinction between what is and what someone asserts, and how the whole point was that the difference ossifies into habit if you practice it, until you can't read a headline without asking who, exactly, is doing the saying. She had assumed English had a monopoly on this. Now aquí was a tiny word apparently doing the same job.

"Okay," she said slowly. "This word. Según. My aunt says it constantly on the phone and I've never once asked her." She turned to Lucía. "Does it mean 'according to'?"

"According to," Lucía confirmed, stamping a small heron on the corner of Amy's card as if certifying the fact itself. "So what does the sentence tell you?"

Amy looked back at the paper and felt something rearrange itself. "Then it's not the reporter saying the river is clean," she said. "It's according to the mayor. The source is marked, right there in the grammar. The whole sentence is basically wearing a name tag." She laughed, a little embarrassed by how pleased she was. "I was about to summarize a claim as a fact. I almost laundered a mayor."

"So summarize," the boy said. "Out loud. You get one shot."

Amy stood straighter, holding the card like an oath. "A town organized a river cleanup, and the crews collected a lot of trash, and according to the mayor, the water is now safe for swimming. According to him. The article doesn't promise it. It just says he said it." She paused. "Also I now believe my aunt has been citing sources at me for years and I thought she was just being dramatic."

Lucía applauded with two fingers against her palm, which Amy chose to accept as a full ovation. The boy rummaged in the prize box and produced, with visible reluctance, a keychain of a cartoon axolotl wearing a tiny graduation cap.

"That's the last one," he said. "The good ones went an hour ago. Now it's just this auxiliary keychain. It doesn't even hold keys well. It's more of a decorative axolotl."

"I want the decorative axolotl," Amy said, clipping it to her bag. "It's carrying the entire ontology of my Spanish education. One semester, one mayor, one river."

"Careful," Lucía said, leaning over the table. "That's how it starts. First según, then suddenly you're the volunteer at the folding table."

Amy was still grinning when a woman in a sun hat stopped in front of the sign, squinting at the stack of cards, and Amy heard herself say, before she could think better of it, "I can explain the rules. I basically work here."

The monument stood where the school bus let them off, a granite shaft on a hillock of metamorphic rock hauled up in 1911 to honor the founders of Aldermoor, and Kaylee had chosen it for her college essay because she thought she already knew the story. The town's plaque said the first settlers had shared grain with the starving Mi'kmaq family wintering at the river bend, a moment of charity that supposedly gave the town its name. Her grandmother had said otherwise at Thanksgiving, spitting the words like pits: nobody shared anything, she said, they took the river and the fish weir and the winter camp, and the plaque was a story the founders told their grandchildren. Kayley wanted the truth before she wrote a word of it.

Her grandfather had come along because he liked the drive and because he was the only one left who had known any of the settlers' descendants. He walked the gravel path slowly, one hand on the shaft to steady himself, and listened while she read the plaque aloud. The wind came off the river smelling of mud and thaw.

"Your essay," he said. "You want to know if it happened."

"I want to know if I should write that it happened. There's a difference." She had been arguing this out for two weeks, first with the librarian, who had produced a folder of clippings all repeating the plaque, then with her grandmother, who had produced nothing but certainty. Between the two of them Kaylee felt like a musician trying to play two scores at once, and she was no virtuoso at this yet; she could only hold both pages open and hope.

The historical society kept its archive in the basement of the library, and that was where she had found the diary. Ezekiel Harrow, 1843, a founder's son, four years of weather and wheat prices and sermons. She had photographed every page. Now she sat on the monument's bottom step with the folder open on her knees, her grandfather beside her, and turned to the winter in question, the winter of the grain.

The pages for that December were full of oxen and a frozen well and the price of nails. There was no mention of a Mi'kmaq family at the river bend. No mention of grain given away. No mention of anyone starving at all.

"There," she said, and she heard her own triumph and didn't like the sound of it. "It never happened. He would have written it down. A whole family starving right there and he writes about nails."

Her grandfather was quiet for a moment. Then he laughed, a short bark that startled a crow off the monument's capstone. "An argument from silence," he said. "You can't do much with one of those."

"What do you mean, you can't do much with it?"

"Your grandmother used to try it on me. I'd forget our anniversary, and she'd say I clearly didn't love her because I never wrote her love letters." He was still smiling at the river. "But I never wrote anybody letters. I wrote grocery lists. She knew that."

Kaylee looked down at the pages of nails and oxen. "So because he didn't write it, doesn't mean it didn't happen."

"Doesn't mean it did, either." He tapped the folder with one finger. "He wrote what mattered to him. Whatever else went on, it wasn't the kind of thing he thought worth ink. Ask yourself why."

She sat with that, and the more she sat, the more the silence in the diary seemed to hold two shapes at once. If the grain had been given, it had been too ordinary to record, a small decency, not a founding. If the camp had been taken, that had been too ordinary too, the kind of taking that went without saying. Either way, the silence told her the founders hadn't thought the Mi'kmaq family remarkable, and that, she realized, was itself a kind of answer, though not the one either the plaque or her grandmother wanted. She tried to resuscitate the essay she had planned, the tidy one about charity confirmed or debunked, and couldn't. It lay there flat on the page.

"There's another diary," her grandfather said. "Half of one. Up at the house, in the seed drawer, of all places. Rebecca Harrow's. Never catalogued. Her great-granddaughter gave it to me when she cleared out the farm, and I keep meaning to take it to the society and never do." He looked at Kaylee, and something in his face was careful, the way he looked when he was deciding whether to hand over something breakable. "She was Ezekiel's sister. She wrote different things."

"You've read it?"

"Some." He looked back at the river. "Enough."

"Enough to know about the winter?"

They sat on the step together, the monument above them saying one thing in cut granite, the diary in her lap saying nothing in faded ink, and Kaylee understood suddenly that he had known, all along the drive and all the while on the path, exactly what was in Rebecca's half diary, and had brought her here first anyway. He wanted her to find it herself. Or he wanted her to be the kind of person who would notice what a silence could and couldn't prove before she went reading anyone's sister.

"Grandpa," she said. "Is it in the truck?"

He stood up, brushing gravel from his knees, and held out his hand for the folder, and she closed it and gave it to him, and they started down toward the parking lot, the river flashing between the bare trees.

"Rebecca kept a list," he said as he opened the passenger door for her. "Every family that came through, who they were, what they carried. She thought it mattered."

The basement smelled like laundry detergent and old carpet, and Dev's laptop was propped on a milk crate because he'd broken the hinge again. Zoe pulled her chair up beside him and opened her notebook to a page with "Java, Day 1" crossed out and "Day 4" written above it. She had a problem due Sunday night, the first real one: build a class with private fields, give it getter methods, and test that it worked. On the bus over she'd been wondering whether the private thing was just a rule someone invented, or whether it actually did something, and she hadn't decided yet.

"Okay," Dev said, cracking his knuckles like he was about to lift something. "Make a Patient class. Everything goes inside it."

She typed the fields first: name, age, and an integer for antigen count, because the assignment said to model something from her other life and she'd spent the whole term in that other life memorizing what an antigen was, the molecule that triggers an immune response. She declared them private without quite knowing why, the way you lower your voice in a library.

"Try to touch one from outside," Dev said. "Go on. Write patient.age."

The compiler underlined it in red before she'd even finished the line. "Cannot access." She stared at the red squiggle with a strange satisfaction, like the language itself had drawn a curtain. So that was it: private wasn't a suggestion, it was a wall you couldn't argue with. She wrote the getter instead, getAge, small and formal, and when it returned the number she'd loaded in, she felt the wall had a door, and she was the one holding the key.

Then Dev, who could never leave anything alone, said, "Now make it interesting. Put your patients in a list and search it." He'd been pontificating all evening about how he was going to double major in computer science and economics and corner some market or other, and she'd learned to take about forty percent of what he said seriously. She wrote the loop that checked each patient in turn, printed the timing, and then she remembered the thing her cousin had mentioned at dinner, the fast one, the one that kept cutting the pile in half. Binary search. It jumped straight to the middle item and worked from there.

She added it. She ran both searches. The numbers came back, and she sat forward, because they were the same. Almost exactly the same, run after run. The clever one wasn't beating the simple one at all. She rubbed her eyes and looked at the milk crate as if it might confess.

"Wait," she said slowly. "To get to the middle, I still have to start at the front and walk through the nodes one at a time. The list isn't like an array where you just land in the middle." She scrolled through her own code, and there it was, a while loop inside the binary search, stepping forward link by link just to find the center. Every time. Every cut. "So it doesn't matter that I'm halving the search. I'm paying for the halving by walking the whole first half anyway." Dev leaned over and looked, and for once he didn't say anything for a second.

"Do you fix it?" he asked finally. "Like, is there a fix?"

"That's what I don't know yet." She tapped the pen against her notebook. Maybe the answer was to store the data some other way, some structure she hadn't learned, or maybe binary search just wasn't for this kind of list, the way you don't use a fork for soup. The assignment hadn't said anything about search speed. It had only wanted the private fields and the getters and the tests. She wrote three test methods, watched them all go green, and felt the small clean click of that, even with the bigger question still open beside it.

Outside, someone's car alarm went off and then thought better of it. The basement clock said nine-forty. Zoe saved the file twice, which was a habit, then closed the laptop halfway and looked at the red squiggle still burned somewhere in her memory. She was starting to think that understanding a thing meant knowing both where it worked and where it turned useless, that even fast ideas had places they went moribund, and she wondered, not unhappily, how many other things she'd been taught would turn out like this.

"Same time Thursday?" Dev asked, already stacking the milk crate under the desk.

Carter's grandfather had left the garage exactly as it was the day he stopped coming out to it, which was the same week the doctors used the word hospice, and so the workbench still held its ascetic arrangement of tools: one wrench per hook, one coffee can of screws, a chemistry textbook propping up the short leg of the bench. Carter had come out here in March to be alone and had stayed because the textbook was there, and because the numbers in it were a kind of company.

The problem on the page was the kind his teacher, Ms. Okafor, called stoichiometry, though Carter had learned the word before he understood what it named. Given 18 grams of carbon, how many moles of carbon dioxide could you form, assuming oxygen was unlimited. He read it four times. He wrote 18 in the margin and then crossed it out and wrote it again, as though the crossing out were a form of starting over.

"You're doing homework in Grandpa's garage," his sister Dana said from the doorway, a mug of something steaming in her hand. She said it the way she said most things lately, half accusation, half question, and Carter couldn't decide which half to answer.

"It's quiet out here," he said. "It's where I think."

"You could think anywhere. You pick here."

She was right, and the reason was one he hadn't said out loud to anyone: the last real conversation he'd had with his grandfather had happened at this bench, in August, about whether it was better to fix the old radio or let it stay broken as a kind of record. His grandfather had argued for leaving it, that a repaired thing erased its own history, and Carter had argued for fixing it, and the radio had never gotten fixed or thrown away, and now it sat on the shelf above the periodic table his grandfather had taped to the wall decades ago, its paper gone yellow at the corners.

He turned to the periodic table now because the problem required it. He needed the molar mass of carbon, and he found the element in its small square, the 6 above the C and the number below it, 12.01. He copied it onto his page. Then he paused, because something about the number snagged in his memory, a fact from a Tuesday in September, Ms. Okafor saying it fast, almost in passing: that the same number on the table worked for one atom and for a whole mole. One carbon atom averaged about 12.01 atomic mass units, and one mole of carbon weighed about 12.01 grams. He sat with that for a moment, pencil still, hearing her exact phrasing as best he could recall it.

"That's the same number," he said to Dana, who had come in and was leaning against the car, drinking whatever was in the mug. "One atom of carbon averages about 12.01 of these tiny units, and a whole mole of it is about 12.01 grams. Same number. One's for a single atom, one's for a pile of them you can't even see all of."

"Okay," Dana said. "Why is that?"

"I don't know why. It just is. Nobody explained it and I'm not going to be able to."

"So you're memorizing something you can't explain."

"No," Carter said, and then corrected himself, because honesty mattered more here than winning. "Partly, yes."

He set up the calculation anyway, because the problem didn't require him to know why, only that. Eighteen grams divided by 12.01 grams per mole. He did the division in the margin the way his grandfather had taught him to do division in margins, small and neat, and got approximately 1.5 moles of carbon, which meant, since each carbon atom would pair with two oxygens to make the carbon dioxide, about 1.5 moles of the product. He checked it against the answer in the back and it matched, and the matching felt less like triumph than like evidence, one small thing confirmed in a world where most things weren't.

He thought about the radio on the shelf, broken and kept. He had wanted, in August, to predicate his whole argument on the idea that objects existed to work, that function was the point, and his grandfather had wanted to predicate his on the idea that objects existed to mean. Carter had filed these under opposite headings, a simple taxonomy, fixed versus preserved, and had been proud of the clarity. Now he wasn't sure the categories held. The number 12.01 served the atom and the mole at once, one scale and another, without contradiction, and maybe the garage could do the same, could be a workshop and a memorial simultaneously, and maybe the radio could be both broken and complete.

Dana set her mug down on the bench, in the ring of pale stains where the coffee can of screws didn't quite reach, and Carter watched her look at the periodic table, at the yellowed squares, at the handwriting in the corner that said CORBON before someone had crossed out the B and written an R above it, in what was unmistakably their grandfather's hand, an error preserved and corrected at once.

"He spelled it wrong," she said.

"He fixed it without erasing it."

Dana picked up the radio, turned it over, found the seam where the back panel should have come off, and held it out to him across the bench.

The waiting room of the Fenwick Clinic had eleven chairs and a rack of pamphlets, and Justine had been told to choose three of them before her shift started. She was there because Ms. Adeyemi's health class had offered extra credit to students willing to train as peer educators, and Justine had signed her name before she thought about what it would involve. Now she was thinking about it. The pamphlets fanned under her hand: one about condoms, one about IUDs and implants, one about the walk-in testing hours on Thursdays.

"You look like you're grading them," said Priya, the senior volunteer, sliding into the chair beside her. "Pick the ones you'd actually hand somebody."

Justine took the contraception one, the testing one, and a third with a cover that just said Consent in gray letters. Priya nodded and clipped a laminated badge to Justine's collar that read Trainee.

The training was simple in principle. When clients checked in, peer educators sat with them first, answered basic questions, and passed along anything clinical to the nurse. Priya had explained the contraception pamphlet twice, pointing at the diagram of the implant in the arm and the chart comparing condoms, pills, and IUDs. Then she explained the testing procedure: no appointment on Thursdays, a urine sample or a swab, results by phone in a week, and treatment through the same desk if anything came back positive. Justine wrote it all in a small notebook with a bent spine.

The first client was her classmate Dana, which Justine had not augured well when she saw her walk in, hood up, sitting like the chair might charge her rent. Priya stepped out to the supply closet on purpose, and Justine was alone with her badge and her pamphlets and someone she had known since seventh grade.

"I need the testing thing," Dana said. "Thursday, whatever."

Justine opened the pamphlet and slid it across. Urine sample or swab, results by phone in a week, treatment through the desk if needed. Dana looked at the paper but not at it, the way people read when they are waiting to say something else.

"Can I ask the other thing," Dana said. "The consent one. Not for a class. For me."

Justine's stomach did something tectonic, a slow grinding shift she kept off her face. She said, "Okay."

"If somebody said yes at the start," Dana said, "can they take it back? Like partway through. Or is it, once you said it, you said it."

Justine had written this one down too, and she had underlined it once, and she had thought it was strange enough to underline a second time but hadn't. She turned the gray pamphlet around so they could both see it.

"You can take it back," she said. "Consent has to be freely given, and you can withdraw it any time, even after things already started."

"So the yes before doesn't count later."

"It counts until you change your mind. Then it stops counting."

Dana's jaw moved. "Does that count even if you don't say the word no? Like if you just go quiet."

Justine looked at her notebook, where she had not written that part, because Ms. Adeyemi had not covered it, because probably nobody had thought a room of seventeen-year-olds would need it. She thought about saying something smooth, something a platitude could carry, the kind of sentence adults handed over when they wanted to be done. She didn't have one.

"I don't know," she said. "I know the rule. I don't know all of it."

"Nobody does," Dana said, and it was the first full sentence she'd spoken like herself.

Priya came back with a box of gloves, and Justine walked Dana to the check-in window for the Thursday sheet, and the receptionist gave her a time and a card with the clinic's number on it. At the door Dana stopped, hood still up, and turned around.

"You're going to do the role-play thing in class, right," Dana said. "The one where somebody asks about the yes earlier."

"Friday."

"Say the part about the going quiet too. Make something up if you have to."

She left before Justine could answer. Justine stood in the doorway between the waiting room and the hallway, holding the gray pamphlet, and marked a line in her notebook under the question she could not answer. Then she went back to the chair and spread all three pamphlets in a row on her lap.

Mason had pushed the couch against the wall and taped an X on the carpet where the lamp was supposed to stand, and now Priya kept walking through the lamp. "You wrote the stage direction," she said, holding her script like a shield. "I'm following the stage direction." The stage direction was his, from two nights ago, when blocking had seemed like a solved problem, a diagram of arrows. Now the arrows collided.

The living room was the whole theater. His mother had conceded it until six each evening, which meant the one-act had to be built, broken, and rebuilt in ninety-minute installments, with the vacuum cleaner parked in the corner like a security guard. It was his own script, which was the problem. He had written it in April, about his brother Danny's last summer at home, and he had thought directing it would feel like rereading a letter. Instead it felt like standing in someone else's memory, and the someone was him.

They stopped and started eleven times before his phone buzzed on the arm of the couch. It was Danny, texting from his apartment upstate: "Heard you're making a play about me. Bold move. Are you the narrator? Do you get to say mean things about everyone and then leave?" Mason read it twice, and Priya read it over his shoulder, and neither of them laughed, though the joke was a fair one.

"Maybe that's what's wrong with scene two," Priya said slowly. "It's all happening, all at once, like the past is a room you walk into. But that's not how you told it to me in the car. When you told it, you'd stop. You'd say, I remember this wrong, probably. You'd back out of it."

Mason sat down on the rolled-up rug that stood in for the fireplace. He had read something once, in the drama anthology from the school library, and now he dug the book out of his backpack, past the granola bar and the blocking diagrams, and found the page with the bent corner. He read it silently first, then out loud. "Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie a memory play. First staged in Chicago, 1944. It's narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family." He looked up. "That's what this is supposed to be. Not a reenactment. A person standing outside it, telling it."

Priya took the book, flipped to the first page of the play, and scanned the opening speech. "So you'd be on stage the whole time," she said. "Watching us." She paused at the word memory, tapping it with one finger. "And things could be soft. Blurry. He says the music and the light are nonrealistic."

"That's not how I blocked it," Mason said, and heard how dumb that sounded, arrows against an idea. He had been directing like the past was a machine he could reassemble exactly, every entrance and exit accounted for, everything subsumed under the diagram. But the diagram had nothing to say about why he'd written the play at all, which was that he missed Danny and couldn't say so out loud in the present tense.

They rebuilt the second scene on the spot. Mason stood by the window, out of the action, and narrated: Danny at the kitchen table, Danny lying about where he was going that night, and Mason watching from four feet away, narrating the lie as it happened. Priya played him as disaffected, slouched, glance sliding off every question, and it was so accurate it hurt, and the hurt was the first honest thing the scene had produced. When they finished, nobody spoke for a second. "Okay," Priya said. "That's the play."

He texted Danny a photo of the taped X on the carpet, the standing lamp, Priya mid-gesture. Danny replied fast: "Who plays me?" Mason typed and deleted two answers before settling on the true one: "You do. I just stand outside it and talk." He put the phone face down, told Priya from the beginning, and stepped back to the window as she became his brother again. "Six o'clock," his mother called from the kitchen. "Two more minutes," he said, and kept watching.

The docent at the Old State House had already remonstrated with her twice about touching the display cases, so Peyton kept her hands in her jacket pockets and stood in front of the glass with only her eyes. Inside lay a traveling exhibit on revolutionary print culture: pamphlets broadsided with rage, a miniature of Marie Antoinette, and one fat, sober volume bound in calfskin. The label read, "Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790." Peyton had come here to escape her essay, and here was her essay, under glass.

Her assignment was a historiographical essay, which her teacher had described, unhelpfully, as "the history of the history." She was supposed to trace how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800. Not the Revolution itself, the arguments about it. She had a stack of photocopied excerpts in her backpack: a liberal historian from the 1830s, a Marxist from the 1900s, a revisionist from the 1970s, all of them disagreeing not only with one another but, she was beginning to see, with someone earlier, some original position they kept pushing against without naming it clearly.

Beside her, a man in a dour gray coat was reading the label with the slow attention of someone who had paid eleven dollars and intended to get his money's worth. "Burke," he said to no one. "My father swore by this book."

"It's before 1800," Peyton said, and then felt immediately that she had said something strange, because the man turned.

"Everything is before 1800 eventually," he said. "Published in 1790. He condemned the Revolution, you know, for destroying tradition. Chivalry, inherited institutions, all of it. Set the conservative view." He said "conservative" the way her grandfather said the word "carburetor," a thing that had once meant more to somebody.

Peyton took out her phone and typed the sentence into her notes, thumb hovering. Her essay was supposed to start after 1800. For three days she had been circling a structure: begin with the liberals, who thought the Revolution had been glorious and only tragically derailed, then the Marxists, who thought it was a class struggle playing out its logic, then the revisionists, who thought the whole grand narrative was sentimental. It was tidy. It had a shape like a diminuendo, each school quieter and less certain than the last, until history almost disappeared into pure argument.

But every one of those writers, she now noticed, rereading her photocopies there on the museum bench, was arguing with something. The liberal praised progress against someone who had sneered at it. The Marxist spoke of the old order's apologists. They were all answering a voice from before their starting line, and the voice under the glass was that voice. If she began at 1800, she would be describing an argument without one of its participants, like listening to half a phone call and narrating the other half from guesswork.

She remembered, with a small sting, her old history teacher from sophomore year, Mr. Adeyemi, telling her that essays were houses and you should never begin building in the neighbor's yard. She had liked that line. She had used it, since, to excuse beginnings that stayed inside the lines. The man in the gray coat had wandered toward the miniature of the queen, and Peyton sat with her notebook open, the sting of the remembered rule fading into something more like curiosity.

There was a problem, though, and she wrote it at the bottom of the page so it could not be quietly forgotten: Burke had not been a historian. He wrote in 1790, while the Revolution was still young, before the Terror, before the empire, before anyone could know what it would become. If she led with him, she was starting her historiography with a book that was not history but opinion, prophecy, a politician's grief dressed as analysis. And yet every historian after 1800 who mattered to her essay had lined up either against him or, generations later, quietly back toward him. Maybe the history of the history could not begin where the assignment said it began. Maybe it began at the moment someone first said no.

She did not know yet whether that was a defensible thesis or a loophole. She could picture her teacher's pen: "Your essay is about post-1800 historiography, Peyton." She could also picture a better essay, one that admitted its own border was drawn by convenience.

The lights in the exhibit hall dimmed for the four o'clock reset, and the case with Burke's book went gold, then soft. The man in the gray coat passed her on his way out and nodded at the glass. "Give them hell," he said, or maybe "give it hell," she couldn't tell, and Peyton turned back to the display, copying the publication date one more time onto the fresh page, 1790, and drawing an arrow from it forward into the blank.

The radiator in the computer lab clanked at intervals, and Madison had learned to type in the gaps between the clanks. On her screen was half a class: public class Part, then nothing. The assignment wanted private fields, getter methods, a tester, all due before the robotics meeting at four, and the meeting mattered because the regional was Saturday and the parts list had gone wrong.

"Wrong how?" she asked Priya, who had come in with her laptop held like a tray.

Priya sat down hard. "Stuart uploaded the full distributor catalog last night. Every bracket, every screw, everything. Two thousand entries now, and the inventory check takes forever."

Madison saved her file and pulled up the team code. There were two lookup functions, hers and Stuart's. Hers ran a binary search over a sorted list; Stuart's, older and grimmer, walked the whole list from the front. Nobody had ever noticed a difference when the list held a thousand entries, because a thousand entries had been fast enough either way. She scrolled, and Priya leaned in, chin almost on Madison's shoulder.

"Run it," Priya said.

Madison typed a tester into the main method, timing both lookups on the doubled list. Stuart's function crawled. Hers returned before the radiator clanked again. She ran it ten more times, watching the milliseconds, and the numbers held stubbornly to the same shape: one function suddenly, obviously slower, the other barely changed at all.

"It's not the machine," Madison said slowly. "It's the search. Doubling a sorted list only costs binary search one extra step. The linear one, it just does double the worst-case work."

Priya sat back. "Say that again where Stuart can hear it."

Stuart was in the corner of the lab, hood up, recalibrating a motor mount with a small screwdriver and not looking at anyone. Madison had spent two years treating him as competition, the way their coach casually ranked them, the way college applications ranked everyone, and the team's finances were the reason she'd started keeping a spreadsheet in the first place, a ledger she privately called the insolvency report because the booster money kept shrinking while the parts orders kept growing. She had a speech drafted in her head about whose function had tanked the build check. She deleted it, mostly.

"Stuart," she called. "Bring your chair."

He wheeled over, screwdriver still in hand, and Madison ran the tester again so he could watch the numbers. His function took the hit; hers took a single extra comparison, invisible in the timing.

"So mine's the problem," Stuart said. Flat, braced for it.

"Yours gets slower when the list grows. Mine doesn't, not like that." She turned the laptop toward him. "One more step per doubling. That's all binary search pays."

He read the timing output twice. "Then why did we ever write it my way?"

"Because the list used to be small enough that it didn't matter."

He was quiet, and she recognized the quiet because it was hers too, most days, the recalibration of someone who had just found out the ground was shaped differently than believed. He pulled his chair closer and opened the team repo.

From the doorway, Priya watched the two of them refactor. She had expected the blowup; she had even positioned herself near the exit for it. Instead Madison was writing the new Part class on the shared screen, declaring the fields private, and Stuart was arguing, not about blame but about naming.

"Serial number should be a String," he said. "Leading zeros."

"Fine. Then the getter returns String." She typed it. Below the class she built the tester: three Part objects, assertions on every getter, a comparison she ran against the sorted list with her search and his. All green. She added a fourth object and made a getter fail on purpose just to prove the test could fail, which Stuart called paranoid and which she called the point. Then she fixed it and the whole suite went green again, twice.

Priya checked the clock. Three fifty. "We still have to merge the catalog before the meeting."

"One thing," Madison said. She highlighted Stuart's old function. Her thumb hovered over the delete key. It was his first code on the team, from freshman year, and she knew that because everyone's first code was a small embarrassing thing they kept anyway. "Keep it in a branch? If we ever need to show the difference to the new kids."

Stuart looked at the highlight. "Commit it dead with a comment."

She typed the comment, deleted the function from the main branch, and pushed. The build check ran across the doubled list in under a second. Somewhere down the hall the four o'clock bell rang, and Priya held the door while the three of them carried the laptop and the motor mount out into the corridor, still arguing about whether serial numbers needed a checksum.

The balance said 4.90 grams, and Clara wrote the number twice, once in her notebook and once on the whiteboard beside the fume hood, as though recording it in a second place might make it more real. She was alone in the chemistry lab on a Thursday afternoon, the custodian's vacuum sighing somewhere down the hall, because she had failed the stoichiometry quiz on Tuesday and Mr. Osei had left the room open for anyone who wanted to try again on Monday. The problem was simple enough on paper: given a mass of a reactant, calculate the moles of product formed. She had the molar mass table taped inside her notebook cover, and she knew that grams divided by grams per mole gave moles, the way she knew the words to a song she'd never really listened to.

What she wanted, and could not have named until she stood there with the balance drawer open, was for the numbers to feel like something. In her grandmother's kitchen, recipes scaled by feel; you doubled a batch and you could smell when the ratio was wrong. Chemistry had told her all year that matter was counted in units too small to see, and she had obeyed, and her quiz came back with a red 54 circled at the top. Somewhere between obedience and understanding there was a gap, and she had begun to suspect it was tectonic, slow and deep and grinding, the kind of shift that only becomes visible when something at the surface cracks.

She measured out the sodium bicarbonate and set up the sealed gas tube Mr. Osei had left on the front bench with a note that read, in his blunt printing, "For the retake. Observe first." The tube held a mixture of brown and colorless gases, and beside it sat a beaker of hot water and a bezer of ice water, both from the supply sink. She wrote "observe" at the top of a fresh page, then, because she was the kind of person who liked to historicize a problem before touching it, she sketched a small timeline: equilibrium studies, she remembered from the textbook's margins, had come out of industrial chemists in the nineteenth century trying to squeeze more product out of stubborn reactions. People had wanted ammonia the way her grandmother wanted bread, and the molecules had refused to be hurried.

Before she heated anything, she made herself predict. She wrote, "If I heat the sealed tube, the reaction will speed up and the brown gas will increase because heat means energy means more of everything." Then she paused, pencil hovering, because the sentence had the shape of reasoning without its substance, and she had been guilty of exactly that on the quiz. Her lab partner Dev had a word for arguments like it. "That's sophistry," he'd said last week when she'd tried to talk her way around a wrong answer about limiting reactants, "it sounds like chemistry but it's just you being smooth." He wasn't in the room, but she could hear him anyway, and she underlined the prediction and marked it with a question mark, honest about the possibility that she was about to be wrong in public, even if the public was only her.

She lowered the sealed tube into the hot water. At first nothing, and she leaned closer, and then the brown color deepened, spread, darkened the whole tube like tea steeping. She lifted it out, plunged it into the ice water, and watched the brown fade toward pale. She did this three times, back and forth, hot and cold, and each time the color followed the temperature like an answer to a question she hadn't known how to ask. So heating pushed the mixture toward more brown gas, and cooling pushed it away. Her original prediction had the right conclusion by luck and the wrong reasoning entirely, which was somehow worse than being plainly wrong.

She sat with it, chin on her fist. The system at equilibrium had been disturbed by the heat, and it had shifted, and the direction of the shift was toward producing more brown gas, which took in heat as it formed. She turned the idea over the way she turned a conversion factor over in stoichiometry, flipping grams per mole into moles per gram. The shift went in the direction that counteracted what she had done. She had added heat; the reaction answered by absorbing it. She had taken heat away; the reaction answered by releasing it. Disturb the system and it pushed back, partly, never completely, the brown never going fully dark or fully clear. It was less like a recipe doubling and more like her grandmother adding flour when the dough was too wet, correcting without ever fully undoing the water.

Dev came in at four thirty, basketball bag over his shoulder, looking for his forgotten water bottle. He saw the two beakers and the tube still faintly warm in her hand. "Osei's demo," he said. "You did the retake prep?"

"You know this thing?" She held up the tube. "I heat it, it gets more brown. I cool it, it goes pale. And it pushes back against whatever I do to it, a little."

"That's Le Chatelier's principle," Dev said, grabbing his bottle from the far bench.

The name landed and Clara wrote it down, then wrote beneath it her own version, in her own words, in the margin where the textbook's version would never look. She looked back at her measured 4.90 grams and suddenly the molar mass table was not a table at all but a price list, grams per mole, a rate of exchange, and the reaction was a transaction that balanced its own books no matter how you jostled it. She divided 4.90 by 84.01, carried the moles through the balanced equation's ratio, and got a number of moles of product that she believed now the way she believed in flour and water. She was still not certain why the shift was only partial, still not certain what the molecules were actually doing in there, and she wrote that uncertainty at the bottom of the page with a small star beside it, a question to carry into Monday.

"Want to see it again?" she said, and without waiting for an answer she carried the tube to the hot water and held it under, watching the brown rise up through the glass like weather coming in.

Nicolas spread the two books across the kitchen table on the first hot Saturday of June, the way other people spread a hand of cards. Halloran's book said the Cold War grew out of Soviet expansion, an ideology that had to keep moving or ossify. Aldous's book said the Americans had needed markets and had drawn a line around the world to protect them. Both historians used the same dates, the same telegrams, the same conferences at Yalta and Potsdam, and they came out of the evidence pointing in opposite directions. The essay prompt, still open on his laptop, asked him to evaluate the explanations against the evidence, which assumed the evidence could adjudicate. Nicolas was starting to doubt that it could.

He had tried flipping between them, reading one chapter from Halloran, one from Aldous, and the effect was like watching two people describe the same storm from different coastlines. His mother came through for coffee, saw his face, and retreated without comment. His father, home early from the yard job, set a bag of plums on the counter and said nothing at all, which from his father was not silence but a form of attention.

The plums had come from his grandmother's old house, the one his father was finally clearing out. Nicolas went to wash his hands and found, on the counter beside the bag, a box of his grandfather's books his father had carried in, damp-cornered, smelling faintly of the garage. On top was a fat volume, The Old Regime and the Revolution, Alexis de Tocqueville, published in 1856. Nicolas knew the name only as the democracy guy, the one whose tour of America got quoted in every civics class. He opened it because he was avoiding his essay, and because his grandfather's marginalia, in soft pencil, was a kind of company.

What he found stopped him. Tocqueville, writing about the French Revolution, argued that the Revolution continued the centralization of power already begun under the French monarchy. It had not broken with the old regime so much as inherited its machinery and driven it further. Nicolas read the page twice. His grandfather had underlined one sentence and written, beside it, in a cramped hand, same engine, new drivers.

From the doorway, his sister Priya watched him for a while before he noticed her. She was fourteen and had a way of standing still that made people confess things. Their father was in the living room with the box's other books, sorting them into keep and give away, and Priya had been tracking the piles. "You're not doing your essay," she said.

"I am. Sort of." Nicolas turned the Tocqueville around so she could see the penciled line. "Grandpa underlined this."

She came closer, read it, and glanced toward the living room, where their father had paused over a book with a cracked spine and was holding it in both hands, not opening it. "He's keeping the ones with writing in them," Priya said. "The clean ones go in the box for the library." She said it lightly, but they both understood what she was reporting: their reticent father could not give away anything his own father had touched.

Nicolas looked at the book, then at his laptop, then at the book again. He was not thinking about France. He was thinking that Halloran and Aldous had both assumed rupture, that the Cold War began, that something new entered the world in 1945 or 1947, and that their disagreement was only about who launched it. Neither had spent much time on what continued, on the institutions and habits that predated the break and simply kept operating. He pulled the laptop toward him and typed a question at the top of a blank page: what did both historians miss by arguing over origins as if causality had a single door?

He worked through the evening, testing it. Halloran's Soviet expansion looked different when you noticed the tsars had sought buffer zones and warm-water ports for a century; Aldous's American markets looked different when you remembered the country had been projecting commercial power since before either war. Neither observation decided anything. It complicated both, and Nicolas wrote that honestly, that the evidence he had could not fully arbitrate between the explanations, that some of the difference between them was a difference in what counted as evidence at all. He felt the uncertainty like a splinter, and also, strangely, like a foothold.

His father came through the kitchen at eleven, on his way to bed, and stopped at the table. He looked at the open Tocqueville lying beside the laptop, at Nicolas's page of scrawled connections, and he touched the cover of the old book with two fingers, briefly, the way you'd check a child for fever.

"You can have that one," he said, and carried his coffee upstairs.

I did not care about the portfolio intensive. I want that on the record before anything else, because everyone at Camp Merrow assumed I was desperate for the emerging-artist scholarship, and I was not, or at least I was no more desperate than any reasonable person would be with tuition due in September and a father who kept saying "we'll figure it out" in the tone he uses for weather.

The assignment came from Ms. Rhee on the second day: ten works, one theme, an artist's statement by Friday. She said theme was not the same as subject. She said this three times, which made me suspect nobody in the room had understood it the first two times, myself included. My theme, by Wednesday, was still "flowers," which even I could hear was not a theme but a grocery-store aisle.

The studio was an old boathouse with the lake smell baked into the walls, and I had claimed the corner easel nearest the outlet so I could charge my phone and pretend to consult reference images. That was where Dana found me, holding her tablet with the Kahlo on it, the one with the thorn necklace. She held it out like a dare.

"Tell me what you see," she said.

"A woman who never once painted her eyebrows separately," I said, which was a dodge, and Dana knew it was a dodge, because she turned the tablet sideways as if the painting would confess at a different angle.

"The red and green," she said. "They kind of vibrate next to each other. I can't decide if it's ugly or the best thing I've ever seen."

I said something sagacious about tension, because at eighteen I had learned that the word "tension" buys you thirty seconds of sounding like you know things. But she kept looking at me, and I kept looking at the painting, and something about it refused to be summarized. Later, in the supply closet where they kept the battered colour wheels, I found the actual answer printed on cardstock: complementary colours sit opposite each other on the wheel, red across from green, and side by side they make each other look brighter. Nobody had told me this. Twelve years of art classes and a laminated wheel in a closet had waited to tell me this, which struck me as a very Camp Merrow way for the universe to operate.

I went back and dragged Dana to the closet, which sounds dramatic and was in fact four steps and a shove past the gimp shelves. I held the wheel up. "Complementary," I said. "Opposites on the wheel. That's why they do that." She looked at the card, then at me, and said, "So it's not Frida being crazy, it's just geometry," and I said, "It's both, probably," and that was the first true sentence I'd produced all week.

Here is what I am still not sure about, and I dislike being unsure, so I have turned it over the way you turn over a stone you suspect is ordinary. My mother paints watercolors of her mother's village, and her mother painted them before her, a lineage of women reproducing one particular hill with increasing softness, as if memory were something you could sand down until it stopped catching. I had spent the whole summer telling myself I was breaking from that, that my work would be hard and urban and probably ironic, and instead I had a sketchbook full of flowers from my grandmother's garden that I'd been calling studies so nobody would ask about them. I had been ossifying into an argument rather than making anything, and the argument wasn't even mine.

So Thursday night, while the other campers were at the talent show watching a boy named Elliot juggle badly and sincerely, I took my ten flower drawings and pinned them in a row, and I painted the backgrounds in flat green and the blooms in flat red, every one, no shading, until the whole row hummed like a struck fence. It was the most derivative thing I have ever done and also the only thing I have ever done that made another person say "wait, go back" when they walked past. Dana was that person. She stood in front of the row with her ice cream melting and said, "Your grandma's garden?" and I said, "My theme is inheritance, if I can figure out how to write the statement," and she said, "Write it badly, that's what statements are for."

I wrote it badly. I wrote that I came from a line of women who painted the same hill and that I was painting the same garden, and that I had recently learned that opposites placed side by side make each other brighter, and that I did not yet know whether that was a fact about colour or a fact about families, and I left the sentence sitting there at the end of the page like a door nobody had closed. Ms. Rhee read it Friday morning with her coffee halfway to her mouth, and she read it twice, and then she looked up at the row of red and green flowers and said nothing, which from her was a review.

I did not win the scholarship. I want that on the record too, because I know how these stories are supposed to end, and because on the last night Dana traded me her green hoodie for my red one, straight across, no money involved, and we wore them down to the lake where the bonfire was, sitting side by side on the dock with our sleeves touching.

Grace had cleared the furniture out of the living room by noon, pushing the sofa against the wall so the actors would have something like a stage. The community theatre had given her a one-act to direct, twenty minutes long, two characters and a bench, and she had spent two weeks deciding she had no idea how to do it. Her blocking notes filled a legal pad with arrows that pointed different directions depending on which page she consulted, and tonight was the first real rehearsal.

Danny arrived first, because Danny always arrived first; he wanted the part in the winter musical more than he wanted this one, and he treated every small role as an audition for a larger one. He read his opening line before Grace had even found her place in the script. Behind him came Priya, who had been in Grace's phonetics class junior year and could pronounce anything, which mattered because the play was full of place names Grace herself kept tripping over.

"Okay," Grace said. "So at the top you're both downstage of the bench, and when you say the thing about the letter, Danny, you cross upstage."

Danny stopped mid-motion. "Why is the back of the stage called up? It's a living room. It's flat."

Grace opened her mouth and then closed it, because she had used the words for two weeks without once asking where they came from. "Hold on." She went to the kitchen and came back with the theatre binder the artistic director had lent her, and turned past the audition forms to a page she remembered skimming, half a glossary, half a history. "Here. Upstage means away from the audience, downstage means toward it. The old stages were raked, they sloped down toward the audience, so the back of the stage really was higher. That's where the words come from."

"So we're standing on a hill that isn't there," Priya said.

"We're standing on the ghost of a hill." Grace wrote raked in the margin of her legal pad, then felt slightly ridiculous and kept it anyway.

They ran the first scene four times, and it got worse instead of better. Danny's crosses were beautiful but arrived a beat early, so that he was standing exactly where he needed to be before the line that justified going there, which made the movement mean nothing. Priya, meanwhile, kept drifting downstage toward the imaginary audience whenever her character was lying, and Grace couldn't tell whether it was an instinct she should protect or a habit she should break. She said "hold" so many times that Danny finally sat down on the bench and said, mildly, "You're going to have to let us be bad at it before we're good at it."

She knew he was right and she also knew that the artistic director was coming to the run-through on Friday, and that her whole case for being trusted with anything again rested on Friday. Her notes had been pithy all evening, or she had thought so; now she wondered whether pithy was just a pretty word for impatient. The two urges sat side by side in her like two directors sharing one script. One wanted the play exact, mapped, every cross accounted for. The other wanted to get out of the way and see what Danny and Priya did when nobody was watching.

"Let's try it your way," she said. "Once through, no holds. If something's broken we'll know by the end."

They ran it. Priya still drifted downstage when she lied, and halfway through Grace stopped seeing it as a mistake and started seeing it as a confession the character didn't know she was making. Danny's early crosses stopped mattering, because he began to soften them, arriving at his mark in the middle of a line instead of before it, and the scene breathed. The sofa against the wall became a shop. The lamp with the scarves over it became a window. When they finished, nobody spoke for a second, and Priya said, "Okay, that was actually something."

Grace marked the scene up to here in her notes, then put the pen down, because the marks she'd make next were the ones she'd have to invent. Danny gathered his bag and said he had to abscond before his mother started calling, and she let him go without giving him the note about his second monologue, which she was still saving, unsure whether it was direction or interference.

Priya stayed to help push the sofa back. "You going to keep the lying drift?" she asked.

"I don't know yet," Grace said. "Ask me Thursday." She set the lamp back on the end table, then moved it two inches toward the wall, then moved it back.

The waiting room of the Lakeshore Clinic had a fish tank in the corner, tall and green, where the plastic kelp undulated in the filter current, and Claire watched it because it was easier than watching the door. She was there for her first day of peer health training, the program Ms. Okafor had talked her into at the end of junior year. Peer educators, the brochure said, learn to explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections, then take that information back to the high school. Claire had said yes partly because it looked good on applications and partly because of what had happened to Nadia in February, which she did not like to think about but thought about anyway.

In February, Nadia had sat on Claire's bedroom floor with her knees pulled up and said, "I didn't know you could just ask for a test. I thought you had to have a reason." Nobody had ever told either of them the mechanics of any of it. Their health unit in ninth grade had been one week of diagrams and a video narrated by a man who said "responsibility" as though the word itself were a form of protection. Nadia had gone quiet for a month, then driven herself to a clinic forty minutes away so nobody would see her car in town, and Claire had sat in the parking lot with her for an hour afterward while Nadia said, over and over, that it had been fine, that it was fine, that everyone should just go.

"First shift, you observe," said Ruthie, the college student who ran the peer table in the clinic lobby. Ruthie was twenty, wore a lanyard heavy with enamel pins, and slid Claire a stack of pamphlets. "People ask you things they'd never ask a doctor. That's the whole point of you." The pamphlets were cooler than Claire expected, matte paper, one about consent with a flowchart on the back, one about contraception methods laid out like a menu, one about testing that listed what a urine sample could find and what needed a blood draw and what needed a swab. Claire read them in order, twice.

The first person who approached the table was not a teenager at all but a wiry man in his sixties who wanted to use the blood pressure machine beside the fish tank, the free one with the cuff and the digital screen. He got his reading, squinted at it, and frowned. "Two numbers," he said, holding the printout toward Claire like a complaint. "Which one's mine?"

Claire looked at the screen. There was a small placard mounted beside it, and she leaned in and read it silently first, then aloud. "It says the reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury. The top one is systolic, when the heart beats. Over the bottom one, diastolic, when the heart relaxes between beats." She traced the fraction on the printout with her finger. "So both of them are yours. Together."

"Millimeters of mercury," the man said, as if Claire had invented this personally. But he folded the slip into his shirt pocket and thanked her, and Ruthie gave Claire a look over the pamphlet rack that meant she had passed some small test Claire hadn't known she was taking.

A teenager came in at four, a girl Claire recognized distantly from the middle school, now with green streaks in her hair and her hood up despite the heat. She stood in front of the table not looking at anything. "My friend wants to know," she said, "if you ask for testing, do they call your house." Claire said no, that results came through a portal or a private call, that you could get tested without a parent, that the clinic had hours after school on Thursdays. She explained condoms, where to get them free, how to check a date. She said, when the girl asked how you know if someone actually wants to, that the flowchart made it almost too simple: you ask, and they say yes, without pressure, and they can change their mind. The girl pulled the hood down. "My friend," she said again, and took three pamphlets.

Later, shelving returns in the back room, Claire found a paper on HPV that talked about genotypes, the different types a vaccine could protect against, and she stood there holding it because it was strange and useful to think that a thing as messy and human as all this could be sorted into types, numbered, studied. In health class it had all seemed axiomatic in the worst way, rules handed down like laws of nature, when really it was closer to the blood pressure machine: two numbers at once, the beat and the rest, both true at the same time, both hers.

At closing, Ruthie asked if she'd come back Thursday. Claire thought of Nadia on the bedroom floor, of the man with his folded printout, of the girl with the hood. "I'll come back Thursday," she said. She fed the fish one pinch from the canister on the tank rim, and the water moved.

John had taken the warehouse job for one summer, to save money for a laptop before junior year, and by the second week he understood the arithmetic of the place. Eleven dollars an hour, no overtime unless the manager approved it, and shifts that ran until midnight whenever a truck came in late. His hands had hardened around the box cutter; his shoulders had learned the particular ache of lifting from the knees anyway, because his supervisor, Mrs. Okoye, kept correcting him until it was inculcated, the way she said it, until lifting the right way was as automatic as breathing.

The trouble started on a Thursday, when the ammonia-based cleaner in aisle nine made Ramon sick. Ramon was fifty-three, worked two jobs, and had been at the warehouse longer than the warehouse had been a warehouse. He sat on an upturned crate in the break room, gray-faced, waving off anyone who tried to help. "It's the fumes," he said. "They switched suppliers. That stuff is noxious, and they don't dilute it, and when I asked for gloves they said budget." John got him water from the cooler and sat down across from him, and that was where the conversation began, though John didn't know it yet.

"We should do something," said Priya, who worked the scanner station and was saving for nursing school. "Complain. All of us, together."

"We can't," said Marcus, a lanky kid who'd just started, like John. "They'll just fire everybody. That's how it works. My uncle tried something like this at his plant and they cut his hours till he quit."

"They can't just do that," Priya said. "There's a law. The big one. My mom's in a union at the hospital." She frowned, trying to pull the name out of the air, and failed, and Marcus rolled his eyes, and the conversation began to dissolve into who knew whose uncle and what had happened to whom.

That night John looked it up. He'd meant to check his pay stub against the hours he'd written in his phone, but the break room argument kept circling in his head, and so he typed the words instead: are workers allowed to organize. He found it faster than he expected. The National Labor Relations Act, signed on July 5, 1935, gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively. He read the sentence three times. Most, not all. Private-sector. He didn't understand everything it implied, but he understood the shape of it: there was a legal floor under what Priya wanted to do, and Marcus's uncle's story, whatever was true in it, wasn't the whole truth.

He printed the page at the library in the morning and brought it to the break room folded into quarters. "The National Labor Relations Act," he said, when everyone was there, even Ramon, who had come back despite the headache. "Nineteen thirty-five. July fifth. It gave most private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively." He set the paper on the table between the microwave and the vending machine. "So we're allowed. I think we're allowed."

Marcus picked it up and read it himself, lips moving slightly. "Most," he said finally. "What's the 'most' mean? What if we're not in the 'most'?"
