At seven forty the line thinned and a poll worker named Denise began unlocking the machine seals for the close, calling out the time in a voice that stayed level but carried. Charlie typed fast on her phone with her thumbs while Mr. Okafor held her clipboard steady, unasked, as if it were the most natural service in the world. She told Marcus, in the message, that the tournament case could keep his half of the argument, but her page was going to hold both halves open at once. The 1868 numbers went in exact, the way Mr. Okafor had given them, and underneath them she wrote her actual position: that she found the high bar defensible in principle and frightening in practice, and that she could not yet collapse those two judgments into one, and would not pretend to.

Marcus replied as the last voters went through: "That's not a position, that's a shrug." Charlie looked up from the screen. Mr. Okafor was at the door now, thanking Denise, and Denise was telling him she'd save him a cinnamon roll from the leftovers, and he was saying, in a voice suddenly bellicose for a man with a cane, that he would take two and she knew it perfectly well. He raised the cane in a small salute toward Charlie's table on his way out. She wrote back to Marcus one more line before the polls closed. "Then it's a shrug with footnotes," she said, and pressed send.

The folding chairs ran out before the cousins did, so Logan ended up on the piano bench in the corner of Aunt Rachel's living room, wedged between a stack of Haggadot and a bowl of pistachios. He had been to this Seder every year of his life and had never once had to do anything but eat and find the afikoman. That was the privilege, he was beginning to understand, of no longer being the youngest.

His cousin Sophie, seven, had that honor now, and she was hiding behind the ficus with a paperback Haggadah clutched to her chest like a wounded animal. When Logan brought her a plate of parsley, she looked up at him with wet eyes. "I can't do it," she whispered. "It's too many words."

"Do what?" he asked, though he already knew. He had watched his older brother, years ago, stand on a kitchen chair in this same room and recite in a voice that shook, and he had listened to his grandfather say, "The youngest asks the questions, that's how we begin." Nobody had explained it further. It was simply what happened, the way the youngest was always the one who had to ask why this night was different from all other nights.

"I have to ask the Four Questions," Sophie said. "In front of everybody. Aunt Mira already practiced with me twice and I messed it up twice." She opened the Haggadah to the marked page and turned it toward him, and there they were, printed in Hebrew above an English translation that began with the question he had heard every spring of his life: Why is this night different from all other nights?

Logan had an idea about how to learn things, formed mostly through cramming for chemistry exams: break it into pieces, then make the pieces into a rhythm. "Forget everybody," he told her. "Just do the first line for me. Quiet, just us." She swallowed and started, and her voice was so thin the words barely cleared her teeth, so he said, "Enunciate. Like you're telling a secret you actually want someone to hear." She tried again, louder, and a small astonished smile crossed her face when she finished the line without stumbling.

They worked through it in the corner for twenty minutes while the aunts argued over whether the charoset needed more wine and Uncle David told his annual story about the year he was impecunious and unemployed and someone's Passover dinner had been the best meal of his month. Sophie's brother Noah, home from his first year at college, drifted over at one point and began coaching too, but his method was all commands, tap the table on every syllable, chin up, project, and Sophie shrank with each instruction. Logan caught Noah's eye and tilted his head toward the kitchen, and Noah took the hint and went to bother the brisket instead. It occurred to Logan that there were two ways to get a kid through a performance: you could drill her like a soldier or let her discover she was capable, and he genuinely did not know which one his grandfather, who prized discipline, would call correct. Perhaps both, he thought. Perhaps it depended on the kid, which was a kind of discernment no rulebook could supply.

When Aunt Rachel dimmed the lights and lit the candles, Sophie's hand found Logan's sleeve and gripped it. The room settled. Grandpa raised his cup, and everyone leaned toward the youngest person present, who was still behind the ficus, and Sophie stepped out. Her shoes squeaked on the hardwood. She folded her hands in front of her like a news anchor, took the breath Logan had taught her to take, four counts in through the nose, and began.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?"

Her voice did not shake. It carried across the candles, across the folded chairs, all the way to the kitchen where Noah had gone, and Logan heard the pencil he'd been tapping go still. She asked about the matzah and the bitter herbs and the dipping, each question steadier than the one before, and when she finished, the whole table said the response together, a low rolling murmur Logan had never listened to properly until now. Sophie looked at him across the room and grinned, and Grandpa, wiping his eyes and pretending it was the horseradish, said, "Sophie, sweetheart, you may sit. Somebody pour this girl some grape juice."

Logan slipped her the first cup himself.

Annabelle sat on top of the climbing dome with her physics workbook wedged against her knees, because the playground was the only place her little brother would agree to spend the afternoon and the homework was due tomorrow. The problem was a soccer ball kicked at fourteen metres per second at thirty degrees above the horizontal, and for three days she had been treating the motion as one thing, one arc, the way a ball in flight looks like one thing. The textbook kept insisting it was two. Split the velocity, the margin note said in her own handwriting from Tuesday, when she had copied the phrase without believing it.

Below her, Marcus was negotiating with a four-year-old over a dump truck, so she had maybe ten minutes. She drew the kick again: a horizontal arrow, a vertical arrow, a slanted arrow between them. The horizontal part carried the ball forward at a constant rate, untouched by gravity; the vertical part rose, slowed, stopped, fell. Two stories about one ball, running side by side. She tested it on the swing set across the sand, a girl pumping her legs, and found she could not look at the swing the old way anymore.

Her phone buzzed. It was Deshawn from her lab table, and the message was a photo of his homework with the caption: check question six, I got something different. His answer and hers matched to two decimal places, but his units said newtons per coulomb and hers said volts per metre. They had been fighting about units all semester, actually, ever since he had called her method sloppy on the electric fields quiz and she had stopped sitting near him. His note under the photo said: mine has to be right, force over charge makes sense. Yours is just voltage divided by distance.

Annabelle typed back that voltage over distance made perfect sense, then deleted it, because it didn't yet, not perfectly, and she had learned something in the last hour about claiming certainty she hadn't earned. She sat with the two answers. Same number, different words. On the dome, her brother had moved on to the slide, and she watched him climb the ladder, rung by rung, each rung a separate decision about height, while the slide did all the horizontal work at once.

It occurred to her that the fight with Deshawn depended on a taxonomy she had never questioned, the idea that different units must name different quantities, that force-over-charge and voltage-over-distance belonged to separate drawers in some cabinet of physics. The ball had broken her of that once already today. The arc looked like one motion and was two; the two unit expressions looked like different quantities and might be one. She couldn't prove it from where she was sitting. All she had was the coincidence of the matching number, and coincidence was a thing Mr. Okafor warned them about, tangential evidence, he called it, evidence that touched the conclusion without supporting it.

She texted Deshawn: same number, same question, maybe same thing. He replied with a screenshot of the inside back cover of the textbook, the unit equivalence table she had never once opened, and there it was in small print, volts per metre and newtons per coulomb listed as equals. Neither of them had been wrong. That was the part that unsettled her, sitting there in the late sun while a toddler dropped sand out of a bucket in a thin, even stream, like a very small demonstration of constant flow. She had spent a week predicating her opinion of Deshawn on the assumption that one of them had to be the sloppy one, and the assumption had turned out to be the sloppy part.

She thought about telling him she was sorry, and did not type it, and then thought about how last month she would have sent something sharp instead, something about him checking his facts before he insulted her methods, and how the table in the back of the book would have let her be right and alone at the same time. Marcus fell off the bottom of the slide and looked around to see whether anyone had witnessed it. She raised a hand so he would know that she had, and that it was fine.

She finished the soccer ball problem on the walk home, holding the workbook against her hip, working the vertical half first because gravity was the part she trusted, then using the time it gave her to carry the horizontal half across. At the corner she stopped under the streetlight and sent Deshawn one more message: the ball thing and the units thing are kind of the same thing, I think. Two ways of looking that don't fight each other. Then, after a pause: I'm still not sure I'd predicate a whole grade on that. He started typing, stopped, started again. The message, when it came, was only: want to split the reading for Friday? Marcus pulled her sleeve toward the crosswalk, and she put the phone in her pocket and followed him.

The pit was louder than Mathis had expected, a turbid roar of drills and cheering that seemed to have no single source, and he stood behind Team 4021's table holding their robot's driver station like it might go off. Their first match of the day had gone badly in a small, humiliating way: the scouting app on his laptop, the one he'd written in Java over three weekends, had printed a blank line where an opponent's robot name should have been. "Team 5809, null, 62 points," the screen had said, and the scout beside him had asked if 5809 was fielding a ghost.

He hadn't known what to tell her. Between matches he sat on the floor behind the pit banner and opened the code, scrolling past the part where he parsed the schedule CSV and built each entry. He found the constructor, the one that took a team number and a score, and saw that it never set the name at all. He'd meant to fill it in later, then forgot. So where had the app gotten the idea that there was a name to print? He ran it again and watched the same line appear, null sitting there in the output like a word the program had invented.

"You look like you found something," said Priya, dropping onto the floor beside him with a granola bar. She was their programmer, a senior, and he'd been careful all season not to ask her too many questions, in case the questions calcified into a reputation.

"Why does it print null instead of crashing?" he asked. "I never set the name."

"So you left it alone," Priya said, "and Java didn't."

He tried it. He made a tiny test class with a number field, a boolean, and a String, set none of them in the constructor, and printed all three. The number came out 0, the boolean came out false, the String came out null. It wasn't an error. It was a policy. Numbers started at zero, booleans at false, object references at null, whether you touched them or not. He sat with that for a second, oddly comforted. The language had an opinion about emptiness. "I sort of assumed it would just yell at me," he said, and Priya laughed and said that was exactly what C would do, which opened a door he made a note to walk through later.

But the schedule was still wrong, and the next qualification match was in forty minutes. The real problem, he realized, was the find method. He'd written it to look up a team by stepping through the whole list from the front, comparing each entry, and with the list now sorted by team number the stepping felt clumsy, like walking down a hallway checking every door when you already knew the rooms were numbered. He'd read something once about halving. He sketched it on the back of the schedule sheet: check the middle entry; if the team number you want is smaller, throw away the top half; if it's bigger, throw away the bottom half; repeat. Each look cut the remaining possibilities in half. On a list of a hundred and twenty teams, the linear way could take a hundred and twenty comparisons, and this took, what, seven? He counted on his fingers, halving a hundred and twenty over and over until it fell to one, and got seven and a small electric feeling in his chest.

He rewrote the method in eleven minutes, and the mistake he made was an old one from his notes: computing the midpoint as low + high instead of low + (high - low) / 2, which worked fine here because the list was short, and he knew from a forum post it wouldn't on lists long enough to overflow, though he didn't fully understand overflow yet and wrote TODO beside it in pencil. When he ran it, the lookup found Team 5809 in five comparisons. The name still printed null, because that was a different bug, the one about the untouched field, and he fixed it by finally setting the name in the constructor the way he'd always meant to.

"Alliance selection's in an hour," Priya said, peering at his screen. "Is the ghost gone?"

"Gone. And the lookups are faster now, on sorted data." He started explaining it to her, the middle, the halves, why it beat checking every entry, and halfway through he noticed she wasn't the one he was really explaining it to. He was rehearsing. Their drive coach had said the judges might come by the pit and ask what each person contributed, and Mathis had contributed, for most of the season, attendance. Now he had something, and he kept talking, straightening the explanation the way you straighten a tool on a bench, until he could say it in two sentences without his voice going up at the end.

The pit announcer called their match. Priya stood and offered him a hand up, and as he took it he saw two people in polos with clipboards pause at the end of their row, looking from table to table. He closed the laptop halfway, not all the way, and pushed through the crowd toward the field.

Kate came to the library every Tuesday to escape the noise of the cafeteria, and every Tuesday she claimed the same armchair near the periodicals, where the newspapers hung from wooden rods like laundry. Today, though, her chair was occupied by Daniel from her civics class, who had spread the city paper, a national paper, and a glossy newsweekly across the table as if he were comparing suspects in a lineup.

"You're in my seat," she said.

"You're in my research." He slid the newsweekly aside without looking up. "Sorry. You can share."

She sat, because the smell of newsprint and old carpet was better than the cafeteria's fryer grease anyway, and because Daniel was tracing something with his pencil. He had drawn arrows from a story about a proposed warehouse development to the small print at the bottom of the page, then to another story, then back again. She leaned in. The arrows formed a little archipelago of circled names across three different publications, and every island was connected to the same company.

"What are you doing?"

"Homework gone sideways," Daniel said. He tapped the masthead of the city paper. "For Mr. Reyes's class I'm reading this book, Manufacturing Consent, by Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky, 1988. They argued that news gets shaped by five filters. The first one is ownership, like when a big corporation owns the outlet."

"Filters," Kate repeated. She said the word the way you repeat a foreign phrase to see if it fits your mouth.

"That's what they called them."

She remembered, suddenly, being eleven, standing in her grandmother's kitchen while the television muttered about a mine that was closing. Her grandmother, who had worked at the hospital for thirty years, said the station never told you who owned the mine, only that the miners were asking for too much. Kate had not understood then what her grandmother was implying; she had thought the news was like weather, something that simply arrived. Now, in the library's yellow light, she wondered whether she had been listening to forecasts all along, or to someone prognosticating with an interest in rain.

She pulled the city paper toward her and found the warehouse story. The development would pave over a field where the county's last community garden stood, a garden where an indigent veterans' group grew vegetables they couldn't otherwise afford. The story was careful, even kind to the veterans, but it ran on page eleven, below a half-page ad for the developer's shopping complex. She flipped to the national paper's version. Different reporter, different city, same company name in the ownership notice, same quiet placement.

"So the book says there are five of these filters," she said slowly, "and ownership is just the first. Which means there are four more we haven't even looked for."

"Which is exactly my problem." Daniel pushed his notes toward her. "I can see the strings on this one puppet. I can't tell if the whole theater works this way, or if some shows are clean. And the book is from 1988, before half these companies even existed."

Kate read down his notes, then back up, then let her eyes rest on the garden veterans' faces, small and gray in the photograph, holding tomatoes like offerings. She thought of her grandmother again, of the closed mine, of all the things a person could suspect without ever proving. Suspicion alone was a kind of laziness, she decided, but so was trusting the page because it was printed. Between the two there had to be a habit of checking, a way of reading with the ownership notice in view, the way you'd check who was selling you a car.

"We could map it," she said. "You and me. Every story about the warehouse, every outlet that runs it, who owns each one. Not because it proves anything, but because then we'd know what we're actually reading."

Daniel looked up for the first time. Outside, a shelf cart squeaked past, and somewhere a printer exhaled a page. "You'd do that?"

"I have until June." She uncapped her pen. "Start with who owns the newsweekly."

Daniel flipped to the front of the glossy magazine, ran his finger along the fine print, and stopped.

"Oh," he said quietly. "Same company as the developer."

The print of The Broken Column hung crooked on the art room wall, held up by two pins that some senior class had bent out of shape years ago. Carson sat in the second row with his notebook open to a page he had titled, then crossed out, then titled again. His problem was simple and annoying: everything he wanted to say about the painting sounded like the first three results of a search, words like "suffering" and "resilience" stacked into sentences that could have been written by anyone. He wanted to write something only he could have written, and he had until Thursday.

Beside him, Priya was already three paragraphs in, her pen moving without pauses. "You're staring at it like it owes you money," she said.

"I'm doing formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Mr. Okafor said no biography."

"So look at it."

He looked. The desert behind the figure was a warm, cracked umber, the sky a pale band, the whole background almost empty, so that nothing competed with the body at the centre. The figure stood frontally, symmetrically, cut open down the middle to show a broken stone column where her spine should be. A white surgical corset held her together, dotted with straps and buckles. And then there was the part he kept circling back to: nails pierce her face and body, a whole field of them, small and black and evenly spaced, while tears run down her cheeks. He wrote that down as an observation, not yet a claim.

What he could not write was the thing that happened when he sat with the image for longer than a minute. She looks straight at the viewer. He felt it now, in the bright room with the smell of turpentine and the radiator ticking, that discomfort of meeting painted eyes, and he tried to explain it to himself in the margins. If she looked away, or down, he would pity her. Because she doesn't, he is forced to stand where he is, in front of the damage, and be seen seeing it. The nails are directed at her body; the gaze is directed at him.

Priya leaned over. "What's 'amalgam' doing in your margin?"

"It's a note to myself. Her face is an amalgam, sort of. The tears and the nails and the direct stare all on one face at once. They don't blend." He tapped the page. "That's the composition problem. Everything vertical, everything frontal, nothing softening it."

On the wall near the window, someone's old poster of a littoral landscape, grey sea meeting grey sand, had faded almost to one tone. Carson noticed it for the first time and thought that Kahlo's desert did the opposite: the dryness made the tears louder. A little formal point, but it was his. He wrote it down.

In the critique circle on Thursday, he read his paragraph aloud, his voice steadier than he expected. He described the umber ground, the frontal symmetry, the corset as a compositional axis, and then the face. "Nails pierce her face and body, and tears run down her cheeks, yet she looks straight at the viewer," he said, and paused, because that was where his argument had to earn itself. "The discomfort isn't in the gore. It's in being watched while you look. My first draft wanted to call it brave. I don't actually know if that word belongs to a painting or to a person, and I can't get there from colour and composition alone. What I can say is that the gaze transmutes the viewer's role. You stop being an audience and become a witness, and a witness can't claim to be innocent of looking."

Mr. Okafor wrote something on his clipboard. Priya raised her hand. "But couldn't the straight look just be convention? Portraits look at you. Lots of them do."

"That's fair," Carson said. "That's the part I'm least sure of. Convention would explain the direction. It doesn't explain why the tears still work when the eyes are dry." He looked at the print again, the crooked pins, the small black nails, the face that would keep looking at whoever sat in the second row after he was gone. "I'd rather leave that open than close it with a word I can't defend."

Priya was quiet a second, then turned her notebook to a fresh page. "Say the witness thing again. Slower."

The math club met on Thursdays in Room 114, the one with the riparian view, its windows overlooking the creek that ran behind the faculty parking lot, and Grayson had claimed the desk by the sill because the light there was good for reading his notebook. He was the youngest member who had stayed after the seniors graduated, and lately he had been working alone on a problem sheet left over from the regional competition, which was this Saturday, three days away. The sheet's last question asked for the area under the curve y equals x squared between zero and three, and beside the word "area" someone had penciled a small arrow pointing to the margin, where the word "integral" waited like a taunt.

He had never computed an integral. He knew the word, knew it belonged to calculus, knew that calculus was a country he was not supposed to enter until college. Priya, a sophomore who sat across from him, kept glancing at his sheet.

"You're doing it the long way," she said. "There's a formula for that."

"I don't know the formula," Grayson said. "I know the picture, though." He drew the curve, then shaded the region beneath it with the side of his pencil. "I want this number."

Priya came around the table and studied his drawing. Her brother was a freshman at the state university, and she had a habit of carrying home phrases from his phone calls. "He talks about Riemann sums," she offered. "For area. That's the only word I remember."

That evening, after dinner, Grayson opened his mother's laptop at the kitchen table and built a spreadsheet. He divided the interval from zero to three into ten equal slices, treated each slice as a thin rectangle whose height matched the curve, multiplied width by height for each one, and summed the results. The total came out below what the shaded picture seemed to promise, because every rectangle left a curved sliver uncounted above it. So he tried again with a hundred rectangles, and the slivers shrank; then a thousand, and the total settled toward a fixed value, changing less with each doubling, like a coin coming to rest. Whatever the true area was, it lay just beyond the number on his screen, and the thinner the rectangles became, the closer the sum pressed against it.

He sat there and let himself cogitate. There were, he decided, two ways to hold the problem. One was the spreadsheet's way, practical and finite: enough rectangles gave an answer good to any tolerance you liked, and Saturday's competition only needed three decimal places. The other was something quieter, an idea he could feel the shape of without naming it: what happened to the sum as the rectangles became infinitely thin. He did not know how mathematicians made "infinitely thin" precise, and he refused to pretend he did. But he wrote both columns in his notebook, the approximate and the imagined, and drew a bracket around them, because he suspected they were the same thing seen from two banks of the same creek.

At Thursday's meeting he showed the notebook to Priya and to Marcus, a junior who had taken the competition twice. "Twenty rectangles gives me this," Grayson said, pointing. "Two hundred gives me this. The numbers keep tightening around something."

Marcus leaned in. "That's a Riemann sum," he said. "That's what it's called."

"And it never actually gets there," Grayson said. "Each one is an approximation. The rectangles get thinner forever." He tapped the bracket. "I think the area is where they're headed. I can't prove it. I can only watch it happen."

Marcus had been the club's formula man, the one who memorized identities and recited them like provenance documents for an antique, each theorem certified by author and date. He had spent ten minutes earlier explaining that competition problems were solved by knowing the right rule. Now he turned the notebook toward himself, copied Grayson's spreadsheet formula onto his own sheet, and entered a hundred thousand in the rectangle column. The laptop's fan hummed; the total appeared, matching Grayson's to four decimals. Marcus looked at it for a while, then closed his own formula sheet and slid it into his binder without commenting.

"So Saturday," Priya said, "do we write the number or the idea?"

"Both," Grayson said. "The number for the judges, the idea in the margin." Outside the window the creek ran low with October, its stones showing through, and Marcus was already asking to see the spreadsheet again, scrolling the rectangle count upward, watching the digits settle one place at a time.

The gym had been requisitioned for the drama festival three weeks before the performance, which meant Claire's one-act shared the space with folded volleyball standards and a climbing rope that hung from the ceiling like a hung jury. She had taped a rectangle on the floorboards to mark her stage, and inside it stood Priya and Marcus, holding their scripts, waiting for her to say something. Claire had wanted to direct for a year, ever since she'd watched the fall play fall apart because nobody told the actors where to go, and now she had her chance and a clipboard and a problem she hadn't expected: the play she'd chosen, which her friend Dev had written about a family argument, didn't seem to end.

"Take it from the top," she said. "Priya, you come in from the kitchen side. Marcus, you stay at the table until she says the line about the car keys."

They ran it. Priya crossed the taped line with her chin lifted, doing the elocution exercises the drama teacher had made everyone learn in September, every consonant crisp even when the words were ugly. Marcus stayed put, gripped the back of the metal folding chair, and delivered his monologue about the money. Then Priya shouted, and Marcus shouted, and then the script ran out and they both looked at Claire, breathing hard, the silence after the last line as blank as the wall behind them.

"It just stops," Dev said from the bleachers. He'd come to watch the rehearsal even though Claire hadn't asked him to. "What changed?"

"I don't know," Claire admitted. "Something's missing. It feels like the middle of something."

Dev came down off the bleachers and stood at the edge of her taped rectangle. He was disaffected about most things, school spirit, the cafeteria, the festival itself, but not about this play, and that was why his question landed so hard. "It's a whole fight," he said. "It doesn't go anywhere."

Claire looked at her clipboard, at the blocking notes she'd been making all week, arrows and X's that moved the actors around the rectangle without ever moving them through anything. She had been so focused on where people stood that she hadn't asked what the story was for. She'd been treating the play like a picture instead of a shape. The night before, unable to sleep, she had read a chapter of her brother's old theater textbook for ideas about staging, and one line had snagged in her mind. She hadn't understood why until now.

"In his Poetics, Aristotle said a well-made plot is a whole with a beginning, a middle and an end," she said, mostly to herself, then louder. "That's what's wrong. Yours has a beginning and a middle. There's no end, so nothing that happens in it matters to anything else."

Dev frowned at his own pages. "So it's not whole."

"It's not whole."

For the next hour they worked differently. Claire stopped blocking and started asking questions. What does Priya's character want by the last page? What does Marcus lose? Dev sat on the floor with a pencil and crossed things out, and twice he argued that the argument shouldn't resolve, that families don't resolve, and Claire agreed, cautiously, that an ending didn't have to mean a settlement, only that something had to change and be seen to change. What she couldn't figure out was whether the ending Dev finally wrote, where Priya puts the car keys on the table and walks out, was an ending or just a bigger stop. She said so. Dev said he didn't know either. She put a note on her clipboard to decide by Thursday.

On the day of the festival, the gym smelled like floor wax and nerves. The volleyball standards had been pushed against the wall, and folding chairs faced Claire's taped rectangle, which the janitor had half scrubbed away overnight so that the stage now had one fuzzy corner. Claire stood at the sound table with her script, and when the lights came up, Priya entered from the kitchen side exactly as blocked, and Marcus held his chair exactly as blocked, and the audience went quiet at the shouting. Priya set the keys down on the table with a small click that carried across the whole gym. She walked out through the fuzzy corner, off the tape, into the part of the floor that wasn't the play anymore, and the lights went down on Marcus alone, staring at the keys.

Afterward Dev found her by the water fountain. People were telling him his ending was the best part, and he kept saying thanks, thanks, and then he leaned close to Claire and whispered, "I cut your note. The one you gave me Thursday, about her coming back for the keys at the end. I never wrote it."

"You cut it?"

"You said you didn't know if it was an ending or a stop. So I made it a stop." He shrugged, almost smiling. "You decide. Is it?"

Claire looked back at the gym, where the janitor was already peeling up the rest of her tape.

The restaurant had pushed four tables together in the back room, and the noise of Mathis's graduating class filled it the way water fills a glass, finding every corner. His mother had booked Trattoria Rossi months ago, back when the year still presaged something orderly, and now forty-some people in caps and gowns pushed caps and gowns were actually in the kitchen, clogging a chair, and everyone was eating bread with their hands like children. Mathis sat near the middle, his diploma tube on the tablecloth like a fat crayon, and tried to locate himself inside the celebration.

His cousin Elodie, who had driven three hours and was working on her second glass of prosecco, stood up and clinked a fork against a glass. She gave a short, warm speech about Mathis being the first in their family to finish high school in America, and then, because she was a teacher and could not help herself, she turned to the room. "Look around," she said. "In our school in the ninth grade there were over three hundred of you."

Dario, two seats down, started naming names on his fingers, the way people do at funerals, involuntary andavenous for completeness. "Marcus, who moved. Ana, who had the baby. Terrell, who just stopped coming in March of sophomore year." He got to six names and slowed, frowning, working backward through yearbook memories. Nobody had asked him to do it. The table quieted around him the way a room quiets when someone drops a glass but the glass doesn't break.

"That's like a tenth of them," said Priya, who was cerebral in the way of someone who counted everything twice. "Maybe more. A tenth, an eighth, I don't know."

Mathis had actually looked this up, two weeks ago, at one in the morning, avoiding his history final. "It's not just our school," he said. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." The phrase came out of him flat and memorized, and Priya looked at him with something like respect, and Elodie nodded as if he had passed a test she hadn't announced.

"Thirteen percent," said Dario. "That's, what, in our class, of the three hundred and twelve who started ninth grade with us..." He did the arithmetic on a napkin with the restaurant's stubby pencil, tongue between his teeth, and arrived at roughly forty people, and then he looked around the back room as if expecting the forty to materialize, standing wetly by the coat rack. "Forty people," he said again, quieter.

Across the table, Dev was not eating. Dev had started ninth grade with them and had not finished, and he was here anyway because Mathis had texted him three times and then gone to his apartment and stood in the doorway until Dev agreed. Dev's want was simple and enormous: he wanted back in. He had a job at a warehouse and a plan to test for his equivalency diploma in the fall, and what he wanted from tonight, though he would never have said it this way, was verisimilitude, the feeling of still belonging to the class of people in this room, eating bread, arguing about numbers that had names and didn't.

"Congratulations," Dev said to Mathis, and it came out almost angry, and then he seemed to hear it himself and put down the bread he hadn't bitten. "Sorry. I mean it, I do."

Mathis thought about the number, thirteen out of every hundred, and about how he had always understood it as a statistic about other people, a national fact that lived in news articles, and how it was also a napkin in front of Dario with forty names that nobody had actually written down. Both things were true at once and he could not make them into one thing. He slid his diploma tube across the tablecloth to Dev. "Open it," he said.

"You'll smudge it."

"I'm not going to frame it, Dev. Open it."

Dev unscrewed the cap and slid the diploma out, holding it by the edges with his warehouse hands, and read Mathis's name in the embossed script, and then his own lips moved without sound, trying out how the same sentence would look with a different name in it, some other school's seal at the bottom. Priya, who could not stand an unfinished count, pulled the napkin toward herself and began listing the six names Dario had said, writing each one down. "Forty is a made-up number," she said, pencil moving. "These six are real. We start with these." Dev set the diploma down, careful, and leaned over to see the napkin, and asked how she spelled Ana's last name, because he remembered it differently.

Samuel had spent three weeks getting the motion passed, so when the cafeteria went trayless on Monday, he stood by the milk cooler with his clipboard and felt the morning arrange itself around him like a promise. The logic had seemed airtight at the council table: students took less when they had to carry everything by hand, schools that removed trays reported less plate waste, and their own audit, forty pounds of food scraped into bins on an ordinary Tuesday, had embarrassed everyone. He counted the first twenty students through the line. Twelve of them made a second trip.

By Wednesday the second trips had become a habit, and the habit had a shape. Kids grabbed a burger, ate it standing, then returned for fries, then for a cookie, and what they could not finish they abandoned on tables because carrying a half-eaten pastry back to a bin while balancing a drink was apparently a hardship. The custodian, Mr. Reyes, wheeled his gray bin past Samuel at the end of lunch and stopped. "Forty-six pounds today," he said. "I weighed it because I figured you'd want to know, or you'd want not to know. Which is it?" Samuel watched a girl leave a whole apple beside the napkin dispenser, unbruised, and had no answer for him.

The emergency council meeting was held in Mrs. Okafor's room, because Mrs. Okafor had the only open period and had signed the faculty approval form in the first place. She did not rescue them. She sat by the window with her coffee and let Priya defend the plan, let Marcus blame the freshman class, let the treasurer point out that the composting company had already been contracted. Then she asked one question. "Why didn't any of you see it coming?" Nobody spoke. The radiator ticked. Samuel, who had proposed the whole thing, felt the question settle somewhere under his ribs, less an accusation than an assignment.

He went to the public library that night because the school library closed at four and because he did not want anyone watching him research his own failure. In the sociology section, between thick books with cracked spines, he found the essay, and the name attached to it, Robert K. Merton, a sociologist, in a 1936 piece called "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action." He read it at a carrel under a green lamp while a man two seats over titrated, drop by careful drop, cream into his coffee with the concentration of a chemist, and Samuel thought that Merton had done the same thing to human plans, adding case after case until the mixture changed color.

"It's called the unanticipated consequences of purposive social action," Samuel told Priya the next morning, the photocopies flat on the lab bench between them. "That's actually the title." She frowned at the pages. "He lists why it happens," Samuel went on. "Ignorance. Plain error. And here's the one that stings, he says people focus on immediate interests instead of long-term ones." Priya read the last page twice. "We wanted the win by Friday," she said quietly. "The assembly, the announcement, the photo for the paper." Samuel nodded, because that was exactly it, and because nodding was easier than saying aloud that he had wanted his father to see the photo.

They built the fix over two days of skipped free periods. Second trips were fine, Priya argued, if the first trip was free and the second cost less, so no one grabbed extra defensively; Marcus added small trays, half-size, that the dish machine could handle; the treasurer, wincing, found the money by cutting the banner for spirit week. Samuel stood at the milk cooler again on Friday with his clipboard and watched Mr. Reyes weigh the bins. Thirty-one pounds. Better than forty-six, still worse than the forty they had started with, and nobody at the table that afternoon pretended otherwise. The gain had cost them the spirit week banner, the goodwill of the freshman class, and, if Samuel was honest, the clean pleasure of having been right.

The twist came at the end of the day, when Mrs. Okafor called him into the hallway. "You should know something," she said. "The principal's office asked me to sign that approval back in September. They wanted the tray savings on the dish machine for the budget. Your motion was convenient." She held his gaze. "I let it be convenient." Samuel walked out to the bus loop with the photocopies still folded in his jacket, understanding that he had been, in some autochthonous and unflattering way, part of the furniture of a decision that was never entirely his, and that Merton had not covered this part, the part where consequences were intended by someone else all along.

He found Mr. Reyes locking the kitchen door. "So is it fixed?" Mr. Reyes asked, nodding at the clipboard under Samuel's arm. "Some of it," Samuel said. "We're keeping the numbers." Mr. Reyes considered him, an epicure of long shifts evaluating a modest meal, and then held up the scale. "Then come Monday," he said, "you weigh it yourself."

Jack had one goal for third period: survive his presentation on the sources for the bombing of Hiroshima, and, if the fates allowed, beat Mara Delgado at the argument they'd been having since September. Mara read everything, cited everything, and delivered her corrections in a flat, sardonic voice that made the whole class laugh at whoever she was correcting. Usually Jack. He had spent two weekends in the library and one awkward Sunday at his grandfather's house, and now his backpack held a weapon he hadn't told anyone about.

Mr. Rowley's classroom smelled like chalk dust and radiator heat. The posters were the usual ones, Washington crossing his river, the MLK quote about arcs bending. "Today we're looking at how we know what we know," Mr. Rowley said, and sat on the front desk with his arms folded, which meant he planned to say almost nothing for fifty minutes. Jack went first, and it went badly, quickly. His sources were all from the same side, and Mara said so before he'd even finished, in the flat voice: "All Allied documents. All postwar. That's not evidence, that's an echo."

Jack unzipped the backpack. "Then try this." He set the book on the document camera, and a photograph bloomed on the whiteboard: a textbook cover, gray-green, corner softened by sixty years of hands. It was his grandfather's American history text, kept in a box in the garage. The class leaned in the way people lean toward anything that has survived longer than they have. "Published 1954," Jack said. "Same war. Watch what it says."

He read the paragraph aloud. It took four sentences to explain the decision to use the bomb, and every sentence assumed the decision had been necessary, humane, and closed. There were no Japanese voices in it. There were no questions. It ended by calling the bombing "the final act of a war America had not chosen," and Jack looked up and saw that even Mara had stopped writing.

"That can't be right," said Devon from the back. "That's the same thing our book covers." Their own textbook devoted nine pages, and the second page began with a photograph of a Japanese schoolyard and a question, printed in bold: "What did civilians know, and when?" Jack hadn't picked the old book to make this point. He'd picked it because it was the only primary thing he could get his hands on, and it had seemed, at the time, like happenstance that it disagreed so completely with the book in front of him. Now he stood there feeling the ground shift, because if two textbooks could disagree this much, one of them had to be wrong, and he had no way to tell which, and neither, he suspected, did anyone else in the room.

"My grandma has one like that," Mara said, and her voice wasn't flat anymore. "From her school in the sixties. It tells the whole Vietnam chapter differently. I found it when we were cleaning out her apartment. She got upset when she saw me reading it, so I put it back." She paused. "I keep thinking about which one she believed when she was our age, and whether she ever got told there was another version."

Mr. Rowley uncrossed his arms. "There's a word for what you two have stumbled onto," he said, and then, because he was the kind of teacher who refused to lecture, he wrote it on the board instead: historiography. "The study of how history has been written. Interpretations of the same events, changing over time." He capped the marker. "Jack, why don't you tell us what your two books disagree about. Not conclusions. Underlying things."

Jack looked at the projected page and tried to slow himself down, because he could feel the class waiting and he did not want to guess wrong in front of Mara again. "The old book doesn't ask who the sources left out," he said finally. "Ours asks that on every page. But that's not the same as ours being true. Ours might be asking better questions with still-partial evidence. The people in 1954 weren't lying. They had what they had, and they wrote from where they stood." He heard himself interpolate between the two books, filling the gap with something he couldn't fully verify, a middle account that was fairer than either and proven by neither, and he said so. "I can't tell you which version is right. I can tell you why they differ."

"So nothing's true?" Devon asked, disgusted, the way people always asked that question, as if it were a trap.

"That's not what he said," Mara said, and Jack turned to look at her, because for the first time in four years she wasn't correcting him. "He said the sources are partial and the questions keep changing. That's different."

The bell was two minutes away and nobody moved. Mr. Rowley asked, quietly, whether anyone wanted to bring in other old textbooks for a comparison wall, and five hands went up, including Mara's, and Jack realized he was still standing in front of the class holding his grandfather's book, and that he very much wanted to read the one in her grandmother's apartment. When the bell rang, Mara stopped at his desk on her way out.

"My grandma's on Sundays," she said. "Bring the book."

Tristan had claimed the carrel by the window on the second floor of the county library every Tuesday for six weeks, and he had the tracker open on his laptop again: S.214, a bill to let seventeen-year-olds preregister to vote so that the franchise would reach them automatically on their eighteenth birthdays. He had found it as a draft someone had posted online, watched it get assigned to committee, watched the committee mark it up until an amendment he hated had been stripped out, and then followed the floor debate, which a C-SPAN archive let him replay at one in the morning. The House had passed it. The Senate had passed it, minus the amendment, which meant both chambers had to vote on the same text again, and they had. Then the bill went to the president, and the tracker's status line had sat there, yellow, reading "presented," for what felt like forever.

"They still haven't signed it," Tristan said to Priya, who had the next carrel over and was ostensibly studying for the MCAT. "Eleven days now. It's dead, right? If he doesn't sign, doesn't it just die?"

Priya looked up from a flashcard about the renal system. "Why are you asking me? I know kidneys."

"You enfranchise an entire cohort of people one year early on paper and then the paper just sits there. It's infuriating." He turned the laptop toward her. "Look. Everything happened. Drafting, committee, both votes, everything, and now nothing."

Priya set down the flashcard with the particular care of someone buying time. Her own want that semester was simpler and somehow harder: a summer research position in a lab in Toronto, cosmopolitan and far from this town, and the application required a personal statement she had rewritten eleven times because she could not decide whether honesty or polish was the better artifice. "Have you actually looked up the rule," she said, "or are you just staring at the yellow box?"

He had been just staring at the yellow box. He typed. The reference desk had a copy of the Constitution in paperback, but he didn't need it; the answer was in a Senate glossary page, and he read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to contradict the yellow box. "Priya. If the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, and Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature."

"That's a sentence," Priya agreed.

"No, it's a loophole. It's the system working. It's the system working in a way nobody tells you about." He counted on his fingers, muttering, "Ten days, Sundays excepted, Congress in session." Eleven calendar days with two Sundays in them came to nine counting days. The yellow box wasn't dead. The yellow box was early. He felt slightly dizzy, the way he had when a physics teacher once showed him that the centrifugal force he'd argued about for a semester wasn't a force at all.

He called the office of his congresswoman, whose aide had answered his email about the bill a month before with a form letter so bland it had to be artifice. A different aide picked up, younger, clearly an intern. Tristan explained who he was and asked, as calmly as he could, whether the count of days excluded Sundays.

"Sundays excepted," the intern said. "Yeah. We had a whole training on it."

"And it's law even if he never signs it."

"Pocket veto's the other thing," the intern said, "that's if Congress is out. Congress is in. So it just becomes law. Honestly it happens more than people think. Was there anything else? I'm supposed to be sorting mail."

Tristan hung up and sat very still. He had spent six weeks believing that the process was a machine for killing things, that the yellow box was the system's way of shrugging. Now he understood that the silence itself could be a kind of assent, and that the machinery had more gears than the diagram in his civics textbook, and he didn't know yet whether that made him more hopeful or less. Both felt true. He decided he was allowed to hold both.

The tracker updated at 4:32 the next afternoon, while Priya was reading her personal statement aloud to the empty carrel to hear where it rang false. "Priya," Tristan said. "S.214. Law. Without a signature."

She stopped mid-sentence, looked over, and grinned at him, the first unguarded grin he'd seen from her in weeks. "You realize you now know more about this than the president apparently did." She tapped her statement on the desk. "Listen to this part, tell me if it sounds like me. And then we're going downstairs to the vending machine, because if a bill can become law by sitting quietly for ten days, Sundays excepted, I can survive one more draft."

The flyer had been taped to the lamppost outside the corner store since August, and Abigail had walked past it every morning without reading it, the way you walk past anything that has decided to be part of the sidewalk. FAST CASH, it said. NO CREDIT CHECK. She read it properly for the first time on a Tuesday in October, because Marisol was standing in front of it with her phone in her hand, thumb hovering, not moving.

"I'm two hundred short on rent," Marisol said. "My mom gets paid Friday, but rent's due Thursday. The landlord already stuck a notice on the door once."

"So ask her for it early."

"She doesn't have it early. That's the whole point of a paycheck." Marisol tapped the number on the flyer. "Fifteen per hundred. That's not bad, right? Thirty bucks to not get evicted."

Abigail did the arithmetic in her head, then did it again because the first answer annoyed her. Fifteen per hundred, for two weeks. Two weeks was one twenty-sixth of a year. Thirty dollars on two hundred, stretched across a year, was thirty multiplied twenty-six times. She said the number out loud before she fully believed it. "That's almost four hundred percent a year."

Marisol laughed, one short syllable. "Nobody keeps it for a year."

"Okay, but still." Abigail took out her own phone and searched, and there it was on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's site, plain as a bus schedule: a typical payday loan fee of fifteen dollars per hundred borrowed, for two weeks, works out to an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent. APR, the page called it, as if naming it made it friendlier.

They were late for first period by then, and Mr. Okafor made his usual remark about the bell being a hermeneutic text that certain students refused to interpret. Nobody laughed, including him. In third period, Abigail sat with her graphing calculator under the desk and ran the other direction, the one nobody put on flyers. Her grandmother had started a certificate of deposit for her when she was nine, three hundred dollars, and every statement showed the balance creeping upward, the interest earning its own interest, small and patient and going the right way. She wrote both numbers in the margin of her chemistry notes: 312.40 and 336.09, the balance now and the projected balance at twenty-two. Money sitting still and growing. Money borrowed and swelling. The same principle, pointed opposite ways, and she thought of a river that could flow in whichever direction you dug.

At lunch Marisol had already half decided. "It's one time," she said, tearing the crust off her sandwich. "I pay it back Friday and it's done."

"Except Friday you're thirty dollars poorer than you already were, and next month the same thing happens."

"You want to litigate my whole life over a loan?"

"No." Abigail pushed her tray an inch away. "I want you to do one math problem before you sign anything."

"I did the math. Thirty bucks."

"That's the fee. That's not the math." She turned the calculator toward Marisol, the screen showing 390, which she'd multiplied out on the assumption of a year, knowing full well Marisol would never hold the loan that long and feeling slightly dishonest about it, the way a frightening statistic always felt a little dishonest even when it was true. "Almost four hundred percent APR. That's what the government's own consumer bureau says it is. That's the real price of the money."

Marisol looked at the screen for a long moment. Down the table, some juniors were arguing about the volleyball roster, and the cafeteria smelled like steam and disinfectant, and Abigail had a sudden atavistic memory of being seven and watching her mother count bills at the kitchen table, whisper-numbering them, and she understood that Marisol was somewhere in that kitchen too, that they both were, and that this was why the flyer worked.

"My aunt could lend it," Marisol said finally, not looking up. "She'll make a face about it, but."

"Faces are cheaper."

Marisol snapped her phone shut and stood, and Abigail watched her walk toward the trash line with the flyer still crumpled in her fist, watched her hold it over the bin, and then, at the last second, smooth it out and put it in her back pocket instead.

Oliver had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before opening on Saturdays was even a thing he did, and now it was a thing he did. Around him the library filled with the small sounds of other people's seriousness: a page turning, a chair scraped back, the printer coughing somewhere behind biography. He had eleven books, four of them useful, and a deadline in nine days for the first real research paper of his life, the kind with an argument instead of a summary, footnotes instead of vibes. His thesis, scrawled on a napkin and then recopied onto the first page of his notebook, was that cities should not have demolished their streetcar lines in the mid-century, and that the case for doing so had rested less on evidence than on fashion. He liked the thesis. He did not yet know how to prove it.

The proving was the trouble. His history teacher had handed out a sheet titled "Chicago, MLA, or APA: Pick One and Be Consistent," and Oliver had picked Chicago because the sample page looked the most like something a person with a pipe would write. But the sheet assumed vocabulary he did not have. Bibliography. Annotated. Citation style. He had footnoted things before, sort of, in the loose way you footnote when you're afraid of being accused of stealing. He understood that ideas had owners. He had not understood that ideas had filing systems.

Priya arrived at ten with a coffee the size of a fire hydrant and dropped into the chair across from him. She was technically his writing club partner, which meant they met Thursdays in Mr. Okafor's room, but Saturdays at the library had become their own arrangement, unspoken, unaudited. She was working on a paper about the Arthur Miller hearings, which Oliver suspected was a better topic than streetcars, though he would not have said so. She leaned over his sprawl of note cards and read the napkin transcription upside down, a skill she had and he envied.

"You have an argument," she said. "That's the hard part. Mostly done."

"Mostly not done. I have to cite everything. There are rules about the order."

"There are." She flipped to his draft bibliography, a page he'd assembled the night before by listing sources in the order he'd happened to use them, the encyclopedia first because he'd started there, then the transit history, then the planning commission report he'd found at eleven at night. She tapped it. "This is in the wrong order. In Chicago, MLA and APA, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited."

Oliver looked at the page as if she'd told him it was upside down. "That seems backwards."

"It seems like a library." She shrugged, laconic about it, as though she had not just relocated his entire evening. "Think of it as a catalog. You don't shelve books by when someone last pulled them off the shelf."

He spent forty minutes reordering the page, and it was during the reordering that the trouble started. The transit history and a journal article he'd found through the library's database disagreed, sharply, about whether ridership had already been collapsing before the demolitions. He had cited both, one after the other, comfortable in their sequence, and now, forced to alphabetize them apart from each other, he could see the seam. Smethers said collapse. Volkening said sabotage, meaning the companies had run down service on purpose and then pointed at the ruins as evidence. Alphabetical order had not created the disagreement. It had only refused to let him hide it.

He sat with that for a while, chin on his fist, watching a man two tables over adjudicate something loudly with a librarian over a hold notice. At home, his father, who drove a bus for a living and had opinions about streetcars that began and ended with the word "obsolete," had already delivered his verdict on the paper over dinner. "You want culpability," his father had said, pointing a fork at him. "Somebody to blame. Write it so it's somebody's fault, and you'll get your A." Oliver had not answered, because the honest answer was that he didn't know yet whether it was somebody's fault, and saying so at the table would have started a thing.

That night he wrote to his grandfather, his mother's father, who had ridden the streetcars as a boy and who answered letters because he had never quite taken to the phone. Oliver asked him point-blank whether the cars had been dying when they went. He sealed the envelope before he could soften the question.

The reply came Thursday, in the narrow looping hand his grandfather had retained from a school system Oliver couldn't picture. "They were dying the way a neglected animal dies," the letter said. "Whether that counts as dying, you will have to decide, but do not let the men who neglected it tell you what dying looks like." Then a paragraph about a conductor named Havel who let boys ride free in rain, and a postscript: "Your mother says you are going to college. Good. Learn to distrust whoever wrote the summary."

On Saturday Oliver spread the letter beside the note cards and the reordered bibliography, Smethers under S, Volkening under V, the encyclopedia filed under its corporate name like a person with no first name. He read the two clashing passages again. His thesis still stood, but it had grown a hinge, a place where it could open onto something less satisfying: that the case against the streetcars had been an argument about evidence made by people who had arranged the evidence. He drafted a footnote that gave both sources, then a sentence in the body that gave neither of them full custody of the truth.

Priya read the paragraph over his shoulder while he pretended not to notice. "So which one is right?" she said.

"I don't know yet," Oliver said, and pulled the page back toward him, and wrote it anyway.

Lea's grandmother had left the matchbox on the kitchen table beside the panchang, the almanac open to a page of numbers arranged like a tide chart, and Lea understood this as an assignment. For eleven years she had watched her uncle circle the bonfire with the first flame while she and her cousins stood at the edge of the yard holding plates of raw grain and dried coconut. This year her grandmother had said only, "You are eighteen now," and set the matches down.

The problem was that Lea did not know whether she believed any of it. Her mother, cracking cardamom pods at the counter, had spent years calling herself a detractor of ritual in general and of fire ceremonies in particular, though she still cooked the food for them and still came outside to watch. "It's a nice bonfire," her mother liked to say. "It's a bonfire. It marks the equinox, more or less." Her grandmother never argued. She only turned the pages of the almanac with one knuckled finger, as though the argument had already been settled somewhere Lea's mother had not thought to look.

Lea had spent the afternoon trying to work out why the date changed every year, why Holi refused to sit still on a calendar the way her roommates' exams and her orientation dates did. She found it herself, in the almanac's columns: the festival fell on the full moon of the month Phalguna, which usually landed in March, and it began the night before, with the bonfire. She read the line twice, then closed the book on her thumb and went out to where her little cousin Dev was stacking the wood.

"What are we doing tonight?" Dev asked her. He was seven and liked procedure.

"It's called Holika Dahan," she said. "The bonfire part. We do it on the full moon, and the colors come tomorrow."

"Why the full moon?"

"Because that's when Phalguna ends." He accepted this the way he accepted bedtime, and went back to arranging the logs so that the biggest one leaned exactly where he wanted it.

The relatives arrived with the dusk: her uncle with his sleeves already rolled, two aunts carrying trays, a college-age cousin who parked on the street and came in through the gate texting someone the whole way. The moon came up fat and pale over the neighbor's roofline, and Lea stood looking at it longer than she meant to, transfixed by the coincidence of timing, that the fire and the moon had been scheduled to meet, that someone centuries ago had looked up and decided the two belonged together. Her mother came to stand beside her with a cup of tea.

"You don't have to," her mother said quietly.

"I know."

"It's wood and a match, Lea. Nothing happens if you do it, nothing happens if you don't."

Lea turned the matchbox over in her hands. "That's what I can't tell," she said. "Whether it counts if I'm not sure. Grandma thinks it counts more if you're sure. You think it doesn't count at all. I think it might count differently." Her mother laughed at that, a small seismic shift in her usual position, and squeezed her shoulder and said nothing further, which was its own kind of concession.

When the wood was stacked and the plates distributed, her grandmother nodded to Lea from across the yard, and Lea walked the circle her uncle had always walked, struck the match, and held it to the kindling. The flame took its time, then went up all at once, and the heat pushed everyone back a half step, and Dev cheered, and the grain was thrown into the fire in fistfuls, and the aunts began a song that Lea half remembered from other years. Her grandmother's face in the firelight was unreadable but not displeased. Her mother stood at the edge with her tea, watching, exactly as she always had, and Lea understood that this too was a way of keeping the appointment.

She could not have said, standing there with the smoke drifting sideways and the full moon climbing, whether anything had been burned away, any winter, any evil, any doubt. She only knew that the fire needed a date, and the date needed the moon, and the moon had come, and she had been the one to light it. Tomorrow there would be colors, and her white kurtа was folded on her bed waiting to be ruined, and she had promised Dev the first handful of pink.

"Closer," Dev shouted at her, dancing at the edge of the light. "You have to come closer or it won't work."

Lea went closer.

The paycheque lay on the break-room table at Halloran's Hardware for a full minute before David picked it up. He had been saving since June, and this was the first cheque with real hours on it, forty of them, two weeks of stocking shelves and hauling fertilizer bags. At the top, under gross pay, the numbers began subtracting themselves: federal income tax, Ontario income tax, something called CPP, something called EI. He did the subtraction twice on the back of a paint sample card and arrived at the same smaller number both times.

"You're staring at it like it insulted you," said Rosie, who ran the register and had worked at Halloran's since before the store expanded into the garden centre.

"Fourteen percent of it is just gone," David said. "Before I even see it."

"That's not gone, that's CPP, that's your pension someday, and EI is if you get laid off." She tapped the two income tax lines. "Those come back around in April if they took too much. You file a return, you claim deductions, tuition counts." She was already walking back toward the front, calling over her shoulder, "Ask your dad."

His father was the problem, though. In March, before any of this, David had watched him spread receipts across the kitchen table for three nights running, muttering about mileage and moving expenses, before sealing the return in an envelope with the grim finality of a man posting an indictment. When David had asked what a deduction actually was, his father had said, "Money you spent to make money, so they tax you on less of it," and then, quieter, "I'm not the person to ask. I always feel like I'm getting away with something, and I never am." That was the flashback he kept returning to, his father's hands flat on the table, the envelope, the door closing behind it.

That afternoon a customer came in wanting a refund for a wet-vac that had leaked across her basement floor, and the manager, Mr. Halloran, told her the manufacturer's warranty was her indemnity, not the store, though he would process the return as a courtesy. David rang it through while she lectured him about impermeable seals and how the advertising had promised an impermeable tank, whatever the box said. She left with her refund and he stood there holding the receipt she had refused, and on it, below the subtotal, was a single line: HST 13%.

He had been in Toronto the previous weekend with Priya, and at the restaurant she had squinted at their bill and said, "Where's the GST? And the Ontario tax? They only charged us one thing." The server, passing with a tray, had said, "Harmonized Sales Tax, one line, thirteen percent," and kept walking, and Priya had shrugged and Venmoed her half. David had pocketed the bill because he was saving receipts now, because that was the plan: keep everything, learn the system his father flinched from, walk into his first return next April knowing more than the man across the table had ever wanted to.

So after close, he sat in the break room with the rejected wet-vac receipt, his own paycheque stub, and the restaurant bill, arranging them like evidence. The cheque showed what the government took before he was paid. The receipts showed what was added when he spent, one line, thirteen percent, the same in Toronto as here. He understood, in a preliminary way, that the two systems touched each other somewhere, that the deductions his father hunted were the hinge between them, and he understood equally that he did not yet understand the hinge. He texted Priya: "Is your uncle still an accountant?" She replied with a thumbs up and "He owes me for math tutoring."

On Saturday he bought a notebook with a cover the colour of a school bus and wrote Sept 12 on the first page. He pasted nothing in yet. He copied the lines from the paycheque stub into columns, then the HST line from the restaurant bill, then a question mark where the connection should be. Priya's uncle had agreed to coffee on the twenty-third, which David had written in pen, which felt like a commitment he was not entirely prepared for. He did not know whether he would file his own return in April or end up at the kitchen table with his father, two envelopes, the same dread. Both futures seemed available to him, and he could not yet tell which one he was choosing, or whether choosing was even how it worked.

Mr. Halloran knocked on the break-room frame. "Lock up when you're done conspiring," he said, and handed David the store's copy of the wet-vac refund slip. "File that somewhere sensible. People who keep their paper sleep better."

David put it in the notebook, between the columns and the question mark, and closed the cover.

The clay was too dry by the time Leah got home, and she knew it before she touched it. The bag had sat open on the porch rail since morning, and the August heat had taken what the plastic was supposed to hold in. She worked it anyway, pressing her thumb into a ball that cracked at the edges like old paint, and decided she would wedge in water slowly, the way Dara had shown her at the studio, patient as kneading bread.

She was making a set of cups for her grandmother, who had given up her own studio three winters ago when her hands began shaking. The design was simple, five cups with a carved line spiraling from rim to base, but the clay was not the kind she had learned on. Her grandmother had left behind a shelf of materials, half-labeled, and Leah had chosen a white bag with no writing on it at all because it felt smooth, almost creamy, between her fingers.

At the studio on Tuesday she brought a test piece to fire, a small pinch bowl that had come out of her practice session better than she expected. Marcus, who ran the kilns on Thursdays, weighed the bowl in one hand and frowned.

"What clay is this?" he asked, and when she shrugged he set it apart from the row of earthenware waiting on the shelf. "Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius," he said. "Porcelain has to go between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius. It can't ride along with the rest."

Leah stared at the little bowl, suddenly aware that she had almost ruined a whole kiln load, or at least her own work, by guessing. She had assumed firing was firing, one heat for everything, the way she had assumed a year ago that her grandmother's silence about the studio meant she didn't want to talk about it at all.

She thought about that silence now, wedging the reclaimed clay at the kitchen table while the radio muttered in the corner. Her grandmother had stopped answering questions about glazes, about the wood kiln she had built with two other potters in 1988, and Leah had taken the refusal as a door closing rather than a door that was heavy. It was Dara, finally, who had set her straight, though not in words. Dara had simply kept showing up at the old woman's apartment with her obstreperous little terrier and her half-finished mugs, until one afternoon the three of them were at the table and Leah's grandmother picked up a mug, turned it over, and said the handle was set too low for a hand that knew what it was doing. It was the closest thing to praise she had given anyone in two years.

There was a letter in Leah's desk drawer that she had started and abandoned in June, before any of this. She got it out now and read it under the kitchen lamp.

"Dear Grandma," it began, in her careful cursive, "I'm sorry I didn't visit more this spring. I kept thinking you wanted the quiet, and it was easier to believe that than to drive over and find out. I've started going to the community studio on Cutter Street. Dara comes too. Last week my bowl cracked in the kiln because I rushed the drying, and instead of quitting I made another one, which I think you would appreciate, though you'd never say so. I'm trying to decide whether the cups should be porcelain or the brown earthenware. If you want to tell me what you'd do, I'll listen. If you don't, I'll figure it out myself, and I'll still bring them when they're done."

She had never sent it. It sat in the drawer like a second self, braver and more honest, and Leah had told herself she was waiting for the cups to be finished first, as if the letter needed a gift attached to be deliverable. Tonight she read it and understood that this was a lie, though a small one, the kind a person acclimates to until it stops feeling like a lie at all. She folded the paper, opened her phone, and photographed the letter instead. Then she sent the image to her grandmother with a single line beneath it: I wrote this in June. It's still true, except now I know the white clay is porcelain, so it has to go in the hotter load, and I'm glad.

The reply came while she was still pressing the spiral lines into the third cup, her fingertips ridge after ridge down the curve of the wall. Her grandmother had typed, slowly and with visible effort, "Porcelain wants 1,200 to 1,400. Your grandfather always fired it too cool because he was impatient. Don't be impatient. And don't use my old glaze book, the recipes are wrong on page nine."

Leah laughed out loud in the empty kitchen, a short sound that surprised her. She set the phone face-up on the table where she could see it, squared her shoulders over the fourth cup, and began to carve the line that spiraled down toward the base, steady, unhurried, all the way around.

Connor's father folded himself into the passenger seat with the caution of a man entering a canoe, adjusted the mirror twice, and said, "Six days until the test. Let's not waste tonight."

The car was a spartan old sedan, manual locks, no backup camera, a radio that only picked up one station out here at the edge of the suburbs. Connor had been reading the driver's manual all week, but reading was one genus of knowledge and driving, he was discovering, was another entirely. The engine started on the second try. He let the parking brake down too fast and the car lurched, and his father's hand went to the dash, though he said nothing, which was somehow worse.

They rolled down Sycamore, a street so quiet that the sprinklers seemed loud. Connor kept drifting toward the curb and correcting, drifting and correcting, a stitching motion his father finally interrupted. "You're aiming at the hood ornament. Look far ahead, where you want to go." It helped, which annoyed him, because Dev had told him the same thing two days ago at lunch, along with advice Connor had liked better: "Following distance, two seconds, that's all you need. Three is for grandmas. You leave three and everybody cuts in."

Dev had his license already, had failed once and passed the second time, and had lambasted the examiner on principle regardless. Connor had believed him, mostly because Dev said everything with total certainty and because two seconds felt like the kind of efficient, adult thing a person with places to be would do. His father, when the subject came up at the end of Sycamore, waiting to turn onto the busier avenue, said only, "National Safety Council says at least three seconds." Not a lecture, not a speech. Just the sentence, delivered while checking the intersection.

"Dev says two," Connor said, and turned. A delivery van appeared in his mirror, closer than he expected, and his stomach dropped a little.

"Dev drives a car his dad bought him with a bow on it," his father said. "Three. And you count it off a fixed object, a sign, a driveway. Watch."

They practiced it. A speed limit sign slid past and his father said "now," and Connor counted one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, one-thousand-three, and the driveway they'd chosen arrived at the count of three, roughly. His father made him do it again at a mailbox, then again at a fire hydrant, until the counting became rhythm instead of arithmetic. Then the light ahead turned yellow and the sky, which had been merely gray since four o'clock, opened up into a thin, steady rain, and the wipers scraped across a dry streak on the left side.

"Rain's a difficulty," his father said. "You add a second for each difficulty. So now what?"

Connor looked at the van ahead, at the wet sheen on the asphalt, at the brake lights blooming red and smeary through the windshield. He wanted to say that Dev would keep it at two and gun the yellow. Instead he counted to four off a manhole cover, and when traffic slowed suddenly for someone turning left, he had the space to ease off the gas instead of standing on the brake. The car behind him honked anyway, and his father said, "Let them. They're not taking your test."

They drove the loop twice more, through the rain and then out the far side of it, where the pavement was dry again and the evening light came low and orange between the houses. Connor found that he could hold three seconds now without counting out loud, that it had become something he could feel in the distance, the way he could feel the clutch point in his foot. He thought about Dev saying two, and his father saying three, and the van behind him riding his bumper as though distance were a personal insult. It occurred to him that the rule wasn't really about seconds; the seconds were just a way of pricing what the road was costing you today, rain, traffic, dusk, each one added up. He still wasn't sure where Dev's confidence came from or whether he'd ever have it, or even whether he wanted it. Two seconds was faster. Three was a bet that the world would surprise you, and tonight, at least, the world had obliged.

Back in the driveway, engine off, his father pulled the key and pocketed it before Connor could ask for another lap. "Six days," he said. "Same time tomorrow."

"Can we do the avenue again?" Connor asked. "In the rain, if it rains."
