Benjamin had claimed the dining table on Sunday afternoon because it was the only surface large enough for a laptop, a second monitor borrowed from his father's office, and a mug of tea he kept forgetting. On the screen sat the city, or a version of it: cadastral lots in pale grey, the river rendered in an unconvincing blue, and over both of these a layer he had spent the morning coloring in gradients of red. Flood risk and housing, overlaid. His presentation was due Thursday, and so far the map told him only what he had half suspected, which was that the cheap neighborhoods and the wet ones were largely the same neighborhoods.

He was seventeen and had opinions about this, most of them borrowed from a documentary and one very confident aunt. His geography teacher, Ms. Achterberg, had asked for something more careful. "Show me the data doing the arguing," she had said, which Benjamin understood to mean she wanted him to be less interesting.

The problem was the age structure layer. The city's planning department had, with what he considered excessive optimism, published a population pyramid from the last two censuses, and Ms. Achterberg wanted predictions, not descriptions. Benjamin had collated the two pyramids side by side, one from five years before the other, and noticed something odd: the bars hadn't changed size so much as moved. The fat bar that had been at the bottom, in the zero-to-four group, had thinned there and reappeared, almost as fat, one bar up, among the five-to-nines. He sat back. "It's like a wave," he said to the empty room, and felt immediately foolish, and then kept going anyway, because the wave was real. On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, and the bulge he was looking at was still near the bottom. Today's large group of babies was going to be a large group of schoolchildren soon after, which meant, if he traced it forward bar by bar, a large group arriving at the local high school in a string of Septembers he could actually count on his fingers.

His sister Priya came through with laundry balanced on one hip and stopped to look over his shoulder. "What's the red?"

"Flood risk."

"And the little squares?"

"Houses."

She was quiet for a moment, which for Priya was remarkable. "That's our square," she said, pointing. She did not sound alarmed. She sounded like someone confirming a fact she had already filed.

"You're in the orange," Benjamin said, because it was true, and because the distinction between red and orange had seemed important to him right up until he said it out loud.

Their mother was at the counter making dinner, and had been listening in the way she listened, which was ostentatiously not listening. "When I bought that house," she said to the onions, "the agent said it was a hundred-year floodplain, as if that were a warranty." She was, by temperament, mercurial about money and immutable about everything else, and Benjamin had learned to check which mood was operating before asking for anything. This appeared to be the immutable one.

He turned back to the screen and did what he probably should have done first, which was check the veracity of the flood layer against the newspaper archive. The 2011 flood, which his mother still described the way other people described wars, had stopped two streets short of their square. The 1998 flood had not stopped at all. He added both extents to the map as thin outlines, and the map became a different document, less of an argument and more of a memory. Ms. Achterberg's request came back to him: let the data argue. But the data was saying two things at once, that his mother's house had been dry for a generation and that the generation was not a guarantee, and he could not find the tool that would overlay those.

Priya had not moved. "So the babies," she said. "The ones making the wave. Where do they live?"

Benjamin brought the census layer back up and shaded the tracts with the fattest bottom bars. The shading landed, almost entirely, inside the red. He had expected this, and it still did something to his stomach, which he decided was the appropriate professional response. The school that would receive the wave in four years sat on a hill, dry as a bone, and had empty classrooms, because the district had been planning for a shrinking town. He wrote that down. Then he wrote down the thing he did not want to, which was that his own school, on the dry side of the river, was the one the wave would not reach, and that the attendance line between the two ran along a street that also happened to be the line between red and orange.

He worked until dinner, shifting transparency percentages back and forth, making the flood layer bloom and fade over the houses like weather. At the table his mother asked how the project was going, and he said it was going fine, and she looked at him for a second longer than the answer required. Priya passed him the rice without comment.

After dinner he opened the presentation file and made the title slide, and then deleted the title he had written, which was "Flood Risk and Housing," and typed a new one underneath, lower down, in smaller type, where Ms. Achterberg would find it only if she kept clicking. He left both on the slide, one above the other, and turned the transparency of the top layer down to forty percent so you could just see the second one showing through.

The launcher was Tristan's own design, a mousetrap arm with a spoon bolted to it, and the physics was supposed to be simple. He had spent the whole evening in the garage separating the ball's velocity into horizontal and vertical components, working the equations in his notebook until the arithmetic stopped fighting him. The vertical part governed how long the ball stayed in the air; the horizontal part, which nothing slowed down on paper, governed how far it went. Multiply one by the other and you got the range. His numbers said the ball should land 2.4 meters from the firing line, which was exactly where the target circle sat in the competition diagram taped above the workbench.

He set the trap, loaded the practice ball, and fired. The ball rose, described its parabola against the streetlight, and came down short. He measured, reset, fired again. Short again, by nearly the same margin each time, which was the unsettling part. If the error were random, sloppiness in the release angle, he could fix it with patience. But the error had a direction, and the direction was always backward toward the launcher.

He carried the notebook inside, where his sister Priya was folding laundry at the kitchen table. She was a sophomore in engineering and had the habit, which Tristan found both useful and irritating, of answering questions with questions.

"Everything in the equations happens in a vacuum," he said, dropping the notebook in front of her. "Nothing in the garage is a vacuum."

"What's your prediction say versus what the ball does?"

"Calculation says 2.4 meters. The ball keeps landing around 2.1."

Priya turned a sock right side out and looked at him for a long moment. "Air resistance," she said. He waited for more and she offered nothing, only slid the notebook back across the table, which was how she said figure out the rest.

From where Priya sat, the change in her brother was almost seismic. For three years he had treated her competence as an insult, refusing help with anything from bike chains to calculus. Now he stood at the counter with the notebook open, chewing the end of a pencil, actually working the problem in front of her. She could see the moment the two halves of his thinking came together: the clean world of the components, where horizontal motion ran forever, and the messy world of the garage, where something invisible leaned on the ball the whole way down. He didn't try to derive the correction. He wrote, in the margin, "real ball lands shorter than the calculation predicts," and underlined it twice.

That night he texted Marcus, whose team had built an identical launcher the year before and lost the accuracy event by four centimeters. Marcus's reply arrived as a message Tristan read on the floor of his room, screen held above his face:

"Bro we thought our release angle was wrong for a WEEK. Retried it like 40 times. Turns out the math ignores the stuff the ball actually flies through. Judges want an explanation of the gap, not just the hit. If you can say why you're short you get points for the reasoning. Tell them before they ask."

Tristan read it twice, then once more in the morning, because it had the shape of something he hadn't considered: the competition would not be won by hiding the shortfall but by naming it.

The next afternoon he dragged the target circle, the launcher, a tape measure, and his father's camcorder out to the back fence, where the grass undulated in the wind and gave him a rough sense of where each ball touched down. He fired ten shots, filmed each landing, measured each distance. The numbers didn't line up with the equations, but they lined up with each other, clustering tightly just past two meters, and that regularity was its own kind of answer. He could not write the exact correction into his notebook, and he was honest with himself about that gap. What he could do was aim the launcher a little differently, test, and test again.

On Sunday, Priya found him in the garage adjusting the launch angle by small degrees, firing, measuring, recording.

"You going to tell the judges your math is wrong?" she asked.

"I'm going to tell them my math is clean and the air is dirty," Tristan said. "And then I'm going to show them the numbers."

He set the trap, and the ball climbed into the gray sky.

Alexa had the roast out of the fridge and salted before her father came into the kitchen, still in his work clothes, still carrying the argument from last night in the set of his shoulders. The dinner was for her grandmother's birthday, and her grandmother was arriving at seven, which gave Alexa four hours, no more, no less, because a roast this size wanted three and a half in the oven and she refused to serve it late.

"You're doing it the way she does it," her father said, reading the recipe card over her shoulder. Its corners were soft with age and its handwriting was her grandmother's, a cramped, elegant script that seemed to codify every lesson the woman had ever learned about Sunday dinners into one index card. Rest until internal temperature reaches 160. Serve.

"I'm doing it exactly the way she does it," Alexa said. "That's the whole point."

He grunted and went to change, and Alexa slid the roast into the oven and set the thermometer probe through the side, the way a video had shown her, deep into the center of the meat. She had told her father she wanted to make this dinner because she wanted to prove something, though she hadn't said what, and he hadn't asked. Proving something to an intransigent man was, her mother liked to say, a hobby with poor compensation. Her mother also said everything happens for a reason, which Alexa considered a bromide, the kind of statement that closed a conversation rather than opened one.

At 4:40 the thermometer read 158, and by 5:05 it touched 160, and Alexa pulled the roast out, triumphant, and tented it in foil exactly as the card instructed, and went upstairs to change out of her flour-dusted shirt. When she came down twenty minutes later and sliced into it, the center had gone from pink to the dull brown-gray of overcooked meat, all the way to the edges, as though the roast had kept cooking on the counter while her back was turned. Which, she realized, standing there with the knife in her hand, it had.

She called Dani, whose family did competition barbecue, and got the words she needed in one sentence. "Carryover cooking," Dani said. "It keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a big roast like that can go up by several degrees while it rests." Alexa sat down on the kitchen floor with the phone against her ear and the recipe card in her lap and did the arithmetic she should have done hours ago. If it climbed that far during the rest, then her grandmother, cooking on a stove in 1974 with no probe thermometer, had been pulling hers off the heat early all along, and never knew the numbers behind what her hands had learned. The card said 160, and the card meant the finished temperature, not the pulling temperature, and there was a difference, and Alexa had followed the letter of it straight into a well-done roast.

"There's no time for another one," her father said from the doorway. He had seen the sliced meat. It was 5:35. The butcher was fifteen minutes away, closing at six, and the only roasts left would be smaller ones, and a smaller roast would cook in time but not by the card, not by any card, because the card assumed the big cut her grandmother always bought.

"Do we tell her?" Alexa asked.

Her father looked at the ruined roast for a long moment, the man who had insisted last night that some things shouldn't be modernized, that the old ways carried knowledge the new ones couldn't see. "We don't tell her," he said. "We start over. And you," and here he paused, visibly revising something in himself, "pull it early. Don't wait for the card."

They drove to the butcher with the radio off, Alexa navigating on her phone, and got the last shoulder roast, barely half the size of the first. Back in the kitchen they worked side by side, her father rough-chopping the vegetables he'd refused to touch earlier, Alexa salting the new meat, and it went into the oven at 5:55 with the probe set and a target in her head that was not the number on the card. She watched the thermometer like a hawk and, when it read several degrees below what the card demanded, she stood with her hand on the oven door and felt the full weight of trusting a number she had never trusted before.

At 6:58 she pulled it, tented it, and did not go upstairs. She stood at the counter and watched the thermometer climb through the rest, degree by degree, arriving almost exactly where her grandmother's card had said the meat should finish. When the doorbell rang, Alexa was already slicing, and the center came up rosy and correct. Her grandmother came into the kitchen still unbuttoning her coat, and her father put a plate in front of her without a word of explanation, and the old woman looked at the pink center, then at Alexa, then at the thermometer still lying beside the carving board.

"You used a probe," her grandmother said.

"I used your card too," Alexa said, and set the first slice on her grandmother's plate.

Colton had been at the Riverside Roller Rink for twenty minutes before Wren arrived, and in those twenty minutes he had laced and unlaced his skates twice, bought a soda he didn't want, and watched the same zamboni-aged banner for couples skate rotate past the ceiling four times. The rink smelled like rented leather and orange disinfectant, and the carpet, printed with cartoon wheels in colors no wheel had ever been made in, struck him as an antiquated idea of fun that somehow still worked on everybody, including him.

Wren came through the door shaking rain off her jacket, and she waved at him before he could decide whether to wave first, which felt like being handed a gift. They'd met in chemistry, where she'd argued with the teacher about significant figures and lost, gracefully. He'd asked her out by the pencil sharpener. Now they were here, renting skates, and the guy at the counter, Dez, who was Colton's friend from middle school, raised his eyebrows in a way that meant good for you and also I'm going to humiliate you later.

"Size nine," Colton said, "and, um, whatever she wears."

"Seven," Wren said, and Dez handed them over with the solemnity of a man distributing sacred objects.

They did three laps before anything went wrong. It wasn't Colton's falling, though he did fall, once, backward, in a way that made his tailbone file a formal complaint. It was Bree, from his English class, skating near the rail with her boyfriend, Kurt, a broad-shouldered junior Colton knew mostly as a name attached to a truck. What Colton noticed first wasn't Kurt's hand on Bree's arm, exactly. It was how Bree's whole body oriented around it, like a compass needle that had stopped pointing north and started pointing at him.

"He grabs her," Wren said, quietly, as they glided past. "You see that?"

Colton had seen it. He'd been trying not to see it, the way you try not to look at a dog with a limp. Now that the seeing had been spoken aloud, it was the only thing on the rink. "That's like the third time," he said. "She laughs every time."

"She laughs like it's a door closing."

They came around again. Kurt had Bree's arm again, fingers dug in white, and he was saying something into her ear, and Bree was nodding fast. Then he let go and skated backward, grinning, and she laughed, and the laugh did sound like a door, or like a window latched from outside.

Colton let himself ruminate for one full lap, which at rink speed was about forty seconds of legal deliberation. One voice said it was none of his business; Bree hadn't asked; Kurt was probably just intense; high school was full of guys who gripped too hard because nobody had ever told them hands were for holding, not clamping. Another voice, the one that sounded like his older sister, said you don't get to unsee it, and there's no version of this where you skate three more laps and then go home and feel clean. The voices were not evenly matched. What he couldn't figure out was what saying something would actually accomplish, here, under the disco lights, with the DJ announcing the wobble.

He drifted toward the skate counter instead, where Dez was wiping down blades with an old T-shirt. "Can I see your phone a sec?" Colton said. "Mines dead."

"You said that at lunch and it was at forty percent."

"It's been a hard afternoon."

Dez handed it over, watching him. Colton typed fast, read, typed again, and then turned the screen so Dez could see it, because he wanted a witness to what he'd found, in case he later decided he'd imagined it.

"Look at this," Colton said. "It's a CDC survey, 2021, the Youth Risk Behavior Survey. About one in twelve US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence."

Dez read it twice. "One in twelve." He looked out at the rink, where maybe a hundred kids were circling. "That's, like, a bunch of people on this floor right now. If they've dated."

"That's what it says." Colton gave the phone back. "I keep thinking, if it's that many, then somebody's noticing, right? Somebody's seeing what I'm seeing. And then they're deciding it's normal, or deciding it's not their business, and there's another one in twelve." He heard himself and worried he was lecturing his friend, who had not asked for a philosophy. "I don't know. I'm not even sure what I'm going to do. I just know that number makes it hard to call it a private thing between two people."

"Then don't call it anything," Dez said. "Just go be a person near it."

Wren was waiting by the water fountain, and when Colton skated over, she read his face before he'd arranged it. "You're going to say something to her," she said. Not a question.

"To her," Colton said. "Not to him. He'd just turn it into a thing about him. Her, I figured, if I can get her alone, near the bathroom or the arcade, I can just ask if she's okay. Like actually ask. Not save her. I don't think I can save anybody."

"Good," Wren said. "Because I wasn't going to stand there while you tried."

The couples skate started, an antiquated ritual, lights dimming to purple, and Kurt took Bree's hand with the gentleness of someone performing gentleness for an audience. Colton watched Bree's arm relax, then freeze, as Kurt's other hand rose toward her elbow like it was returning home. Somewhere in the rink, one in twelve was skating. Colton pushed off from the rail.

"Watch my soda," he said to Wren, and skated toward the rail where Bree would come off the floor.

The waiter at the table by the window had a way of pouring water that Charles found himself studying, the wrist turning at the exact moment the glass reached full, so that not a drop escaped. Charles was twenty minutes early for his interview at Rossi's, the Italian place on Hale Street, and he had the whole booth to himself, a laminated menu, and a phone in his pocket with three pages of notes on it.

Two nights ago his sister Maya had asked him, over the remains of a pizza, how he planned to answer the questions. "You can't just say you're responsible," she had said. "Everyone says that. They want stories." She worked in a lab and thought in structures. She told him about something a friend had used for interviews, a way of organizing a story so it didn't wander. She'd called it the STAR method, and she made him repeat the parts back to her twice before she let him leave.

The problem was that Charles had exactly one story worth telling, and it was a bad one: a group project in junior year, four people, one of whom had vanished entirely for two weeks, another who rewrote everyone's slides the night before, and a presentation that had gone sideways in front of the whole class. He had spent a long time trying to decide whether the story made him look capable or unlucky. Maya insisted it could be both. He wasn't sure he believed her, which was itself a kind of answer he couldn't put in his notes.

He tried it out now, under his breath, staring at the row of wine bottles behind the bar. Situation: a group project that went wrong, four people, a deadline. Task: pull the presentation together anyway. Action: he had taken the file back from the rewriter, called the vanished member at ten at night, rebuilt the slides with the third teammate until two in the morning. Result: they got a B-plus, and the teacher wrote a note that said the final product was stronger than the process deserved. He liked the note and hated it at the same time. The B-plus was not a triumph, and he wondered whether a story with a mediocre result was still a story you could tell.

The manager appeared at three o'clock exactly, a small woman named Deena with reading glasses pushed up into her hair. She sat down across from him without a menu, which struck Charles as a person who had done this many times and had stopped performing hospitality for the pre-interview part. "So," she said. "Why do you want to work here, of all places?"

He had prepared for this one and his prepared answer suddenly sounded like it had been monetized, every phrase calculated for return. He said it anyway, because it was true: he needed money for books in the fall, he lived four blocks away, and he liked the way the place smelled at six p.m. when the bread came out of the oven, which he had noticed through the propped door every evening walking home from school. Deena's face changed slightly at the part about the bread. She wrote something down.

Then she said, "Tell me about a time things didn't go the way you planned." And Charles understood that this was the moment his sister had been engineering for him from across a pizza box. He kept the story in order, the situation and the task first, so she would know what he'd been up against, then what he had actually done, then the result, including the B-plus and the teacher's note, delivered plainly, without apology. He watched her to see whether the shape of it was working on her the way Maya promised. She was nodding slowly, not the polite kind of nodding, the kind where the pen stops moving.

"Most kids your age tell me a story where they're the hero," she said. "Yours had other people in it. That's rarer than you'd think." She asked him about the teammate who had vanished, whether he'd stayed angry. Charles said he had, for a while, and then it had curdled into something more jaundiced, a general suspicion of group work that he was trying, without much success, to talk himself out of, because he suspected the suspicion was lazy. Deena laughed at that, a short sound, surprised out of her.

She stood and shook his hand, and told him she'd call by Friday, and Charles could not read anything definitive in her face, which he decided was probably the point of a face like that. He walked out past the table by the window, where the waiter with the perfect wrist was filling a glass for a couple who hadn't touched their menus yet, and Charles caught himself timing the turn of the pour, wondering how long it took to learn, wondering whether he'd get the chance to find out.

Hudson had failed the biology midterm on a Tuesday, and by Saturday his mother had exiled him to his uncle's farm with a textbook and a threat disguised as a vacation. The deal was simple: three hours of studying a day, and he could drive the truck into town on Sunday. He sat on the porch steps with the book open to a diagram that looked like a subway map, all loops and arrows, with the word mitochondria stamped in the middle like a brand.

"You're supposed to breathe out on the exhale, not while you're reading," his cousin Wren said, dropping onto the step beside him with a popsicle. She was fourteen and thought his misery was a form of entertainment.

"It's cellular respiration." He turned the book so she could see. "Glucose plus six O2 gives you six CO2, six H2O, and energy. Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water. That's the whole equation. I have to be able to trace it for the retake."

"Meaning what?"

He stared at the pond across the yard, where the uncle's geese were conducting their usual afternoon coup against the dock. "Meaning the sugar in my cereal this morning is turning into the carbon dioxide I'm breathing out right now. Apparently. I got that part wrong on the test."

Wren licked her popsicle and considered him with the flat generosity of someone who had never failed anything that mattered. "So when you breathe on the pond, your breakfast goes into the air?"

"Something like that." He hadn't believed it when he wrote it, either, because it had seemed too strange to be a real process and not a punishment invented by textbook companies. But the diagram was insistent. Glucose went in, got broken down in stages, and ended up in the mitochondria, where oxygen finished the job, and the cell pocketed the profit as ATP. He said as much to Wren, and she shrugged and went inside to propitiate the geese, who were screaming at her for corn.

The studying did not go well that afternoon. His notes dissolved into arrows pointing at other arrows. Every time he tried to hold the whole route in his head, glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, some part of it slid out of his grip like a wet rope. Wren watched him from the window for a while and then appeared with a folded piece of paper, which she handed over with ceremony.

"You got a letter," she said. "From the Midwest Popsicle Council. Very official."

He unfolded it. In her looping hand: Dear Hudson. The geese report you have been sitting on the porch for one hour saying 'pyruvate' to yourself. This is a bad look. Try the pond. The geese also suggest you stop calling the pond a pernicious swamp, since it is their home and they are sensitive. Signed, The Management. P.S. If you can explain where the carbon in your breath comes from, I will make you a sandwich.

He read it twice, then looked up. She was already gone, and the geese were patrolling the yard like unpaid security, so he packed the book and walked down to the water.

The pond was green at the edges and quiet in the middle, and the dock was warm from the sun. He read aloud, and the sound of his own voice over the water made the words less slippery. Glucose, C6H12O6. He wrote it in the margin of his notebook. Add six oxygens, breathe in. Out comes six carbon dioxides, six waters, and the energy the cell actually spends, ATP. He breathed onto the surface and watched the faint fog of it disappear, and for the first time the equation felt less like chemistry and more like an account of himself, of what his body was doing without asking him. The carbon in his breath had been sugar an hour ago, had been corn in the uncle's field last summer, had been sunlight before that, maybe, though that part he wasn't sure of and the book didn't say.

That was the trouble with learning it at all. He could hold two ideas at once now and they didn't fit together comfortably. One was the textbook's version, in which he was a furnace quietly converting glucose to carbon dioxide and water, molecule by molecule, every second. The other was the version in which he was still just Hudson, sitting on a dock, failing tests. He was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't know yet which idea would win, or whether they had to compete at all. Maybe it wasn't solipsism to think the second one mattered more. Maybe it was just the difference between knowing a fact and believing it. He wrote the equation out one more time, plain, with no arrows going backward, because the book was firm about the direction: C6H12O6 plus 6 O2, yielding 6 CO2 plus 6 H2O plus energy.

Wren came down at dusk with two sandwiches and the geese as an honor guard. She sat on the edge of the dock with her sneakers off and her feet in the water.

"So?" she said. "Where does the carbon in your breath come from?"

"From the glucose. Glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water. Six of each, in, six of each, out, plus the energy." He took the sandwich she held out. "It's respiration. Aerobic. That's the whole thing."

"The whole thing."

"For Monday's purposes, yes." He pointed at the water. "I breathe out, it goes there. Or into the geese. Or the corn."

Wren chewed and looked at the pond, where the surface had gone to copper under the last light. "Sandwich's yours either way," she said, and dropped a crust to the geese.

The garage smelled of cut grass and old gasoline, and the dust that came through the window slats moved so slowly it seemed to coagulate in the light before settling. Savannah sat on an overturned milk crate with her grandfather's guitar across her knees, a nylon-stringed thing with a crack along the body that made certain notes buzz like a wasp in a jar. She had been working on the same four chords for eleven days. Her fingertips had gone past sore into something numb and tender at once, like sunburn healing.

Devon came through the side door without knocking, the way he had since they were nine. He set his bike helmet on the workbench, watched her fingers stumble from C to G, and winced.

"Still on that?"

"Sixty hours down," she said. "I've been counting."

"That's the problem, though." He picked up a lug nut from a coffee can and rolled it between his palms. "You know the ten-thousand-hour rule, right? Malcolm Gladwell. He wrote that book in 2008, Outliers, the one everybody's uncle quotes. Ten thousand hours to get good at anything. My cousin read it and gave up chess over it." He tossed the lug nut back into the can. "You're starting guitar at seventeen, Sav. Do the math. That's pointless numbers of hours. You'd be thirty before you're even decent."

She let the chord ring until it died. "You finished that book?"

"I read enough of it."

Outside, past the half-open door, the creek at the back of the lot ran low for August, its riparian edge showing as a strip of cracked mud and bent sedges where the water used to be. Her grandfather had built this garage facing the water on purpose, she'd always supposed, the way he did most things on purpose.

That night she looked it up on her laptop at the kitchen table while her mother washed lettuce at the sink. Gladwell, 2008, the number ten thousand, the word outliers. She scrolled past summaries and listicles until she found the twist: the researcher whose work the book leaned on, a man named Ericsson, had said afterward that the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Not ten thousand, not any number. Quality. She read the sentence twice, then closed the laptop and sat listening to the water running over the lettuce.

The next morning she tried an experiment. Instead of playing the four chords for an hour while half listening to the radio, she gave herself fifteen minutes and one rule: every change from C to G had to be slow enough that she could watch her own fingers move and see, before it happened, exactly where they would land. She missed the change nine times out of ten at first. Then seven. By the third day of this she could do it without looking, and the surprise of it, the clean landing, made her laugh out loud alone in the garage.

Devon came by Thursday. He brought two sodas and a grievance about his summer reading, and he watched her run the changes again with the radio off.

"Your chords sound better," he admitted. "Weird. You practicing more?"

"Less, actually."

"That doesn't even make sense."

She kept playing while she explained, half because it was easier to say hard things with her hands busy. "So Gladwell's the one who made the rule famous, right? Ten thousand hours, in Outliers, 2008. But Ericsson, the guy whose research it came from, he said later it's the quality of the practice that matters more than any fixed number of hours. Not that hours mean nothing. Just that the number isn't the thing." She flubbed a change, backed up, tried it slow. "I don't know if I'm proving him right or if I just had a good week. That part I can't tell yet."

Devon drank his soda and thought about it the way he thought about most things, chewing the inside of his cheek. "So it's not a rule, it's more like a rumor about a rule."

"That's one way to put it."

"And you're still going to be bad for a long time either way."

"Probably years." She said it without flinching and found that she meant it, which was its own strange relief. Devon was, at bottom, a pragmatist; he wanted to know what a plan cost and what it paid. She understood that, and she also understood that he had mistaken the question. She wasn't trying to arrive somewhere. She wanted the thing itself, the buzz-cracked D chord and the slow landing, today, at hour sixty or sixty thousand.

Whether quality really outweighed the count, she couldn't yet say from the inside of her own sixty hours. Maybe both were true at once and the tension between them never resolved; she could hold that. She set the guitar down, and they walked out past the workbench to look at the creek, its water so shallow and clear they could count the pebbles on the bottom.

"Show me the slow thing," Devon said. "The watching your fingers thing."

She went back in, picked up the guitar, and placed his hand on the neck beside hers.

The bakery closed at six, and by five fifteen Elliot still had the vocabulary list sequestered in his back pocket, folded into quarters, where the heat of the ovens had softened it into something like cloth. He was supposed to take an online placement test that night, a test that would decide whether he started college in the regular economics section or in the remedial one, and the window to log in closed at midnight. Between now and then there were trays to wash, a register to count, and Rosa, who had opinions about everything and refused to keep them to herself.

"You're telling me," Rosa said, stacking sourdough with the efficiency of someone who had done it ten thousand times, "that if some country is better than us at making everything, better at cars, better at wheat, better at every single thing, we should still trade with them. And we come out ahead." She wiped her hands on her apron and looked at him the way she looked at underproofed dough, with pity and a little disgust. "That sounds like something a loser would say."

Elliot had thought the same thing three days ago. He had read the chapter twice on the bus and something in it kept slipping away from him, evanescent, there on the page and gone the moment he looked up at the passing storefronts. "It's called comparative advantage," he said, which was the phrase on his list, but when Rosa asked him what that actually meant, he started talking about efficiency and being the best at things, and she pounced on it immediately, because that was absolute advantage, that was the exact confusion the chapter kept warning about, and he could feel it, the idea dissolving even as he reached for it.

"Elliot," Rosa said, not unkindly, "you just told me the strong country wins and the weak country wins. Both of them can't win. That's not how anything works." She pointed at the clock. "You've got forty minutes of trays and then you're going to that test knowing less than you did at lunch."

His grandfather lived above the dry cleaner two doors down, and Elliot had arranged to eat dinner there between shifts on test nights, which was how he found himself at the little table with the plastic tablecloth at seven o'clock, still arguing, though now the argument had moved inside his own head and out through his mouth, because his grandfather had asked what was troubling him and Elliot had discovered he couldn't stop talking about it. Something better at everything, he said. Every single thing. And the book says trade helps both of them anyway, and I believe the book, I think, but I can't say why, and tonight at midnight the test closes.

His grandfather buttered a piece of bread with unnecessary care. He had run the dry cleaner for forty years and had opinions of his own, mostly about hedonism, which he blamed for the decline of everything from customer service to popular music, but he set all that aside. He asked a single question. "When they make one car," he said, "what do they give up?"

The question sat on the table between them like a coin neither had picked up. Elliot picked it up. He took the paper napkin and drew two columns, cars and wheat, and started talking about what each country gave up to make each thing, and somewhere in the middle of the napkin he stopped chewing, because the shape of it had appeared all at once, the way the design in a laminate counter appears when you tilt your head. If one country gave up less wheat to make a car, then it had to be giving up more car to make the wheat. It couldn't be less of both. The giving up, the opportunity cost, ran in opposite directions, and if it was low one way it had to be high the other, so with two goods, one country could not hold the advantage in both. Not wouldn't. Couldn't. The arithmetic of it wouldn't allow it. That was why both could gain, and he tried to say why and found he couldn't, not the deeper mechanism, not the why beneath the couldn't, and his grandfather watched him notice that gap and did not fill it for him, only refilled his water.

"The one that gives up less to make it," Elliot said slowly, "that's the one that has the comparative advantage in it. That's the word. And the other country has it in the other thing. Always. It's not a choice they make, it's just what the costs add up to." He looked at the napkin, at his own greasy pencil lines, and laughed once. "Rosa is going to say I'm still describing a loser."

Rosa had closed the bakery alone and was standing in the doorway of the dry cleaner in her coat, holding a paper bag with the day's last almond croissants, which would be stale by morning and were therefore free. She had walked over to tell him she was sorry for needling him, though she would not put it that way, and now she stood listening at the edge of the little table while he turned the napkin toward her and said, "Look, give me two minutes before you decide."

She sat down, took a croissant, and said, "Make it fast. My bus is at nine."

The foreclosure sign on the Okafor lawn had appeared overnight, orange letters on white board, and Kayla had stood at the curb that morning with her coffee going cold, reading it three times before she understood that it was aimed at people like her family, who had rented the house next door for nine years. Nobody had told them anything. The windows of the Okafor house had their blinds down in a way that suggested not absence but hiding, and when she got to the real estate office where she filed listings every afternoon for eleven dollars an hour, she was still holding the question in her teeth.

The office smelled of burnt coffee and carpet cleaner. Marcus, the agent who had adopted her as his unofficial assistant, was already at the front desk with his tie loosened, rehearsing a call. He wanted, more than anything this quarter, to close on the Delgado property, a four-bedroom with a sagging porch, because closing it would push him past his sales target and win him the corner office with an actual window. "Kayla," he said, pointing his pen at her, "tell me again why a young family would buy that house."

"Because you'd be in the listing photos with your whole head visible," she said, and he laughed too loudly, which he did whenever anyone joked, as if volume could convert a remark into wit.

She sat at the back counter with the file cabinet open. Rent checks, escrow papers, mortgage documents; the vocabulary of the office had once captivated her the way a foreign language does, all those words for money doing things she couldn't see. Now she pulled files deliberately. A mortgage, she'd slowly pieced together from the paperwork she shredded and sorted, was a loan for buying a house, usually with a down payment up front, a fraction of the price paid in cash before the loan began. Rent was different, she knew that from her mother's budget spreadsheet, money paid monthly that bought you only the month, nothing accumulating, no stake.

Her mother had said once, in the car, that renting was throwing money into the river. Then she had said nothing else for a while.

A couple came in at four, the Hansens, arguing in the low tight way people argue when they've been arguing for days. They wanted to break a lease on an apartment because Mr. Hansen's deposition had been rescheduled; he was a paralegal, and the case had moved to another county, and Kayla understood from the word alone that it meant sworn testimony given outside court, because he kept saying "under oath" like a man reminding himself. Their security deposit, one month's rent held against damage, was the thing they wanted back. Marcus explained that breaking a lease early could cost them the deposit, maybe more, and Mrs. Hansen's jaw set, and Kayla filed their paperwork feeling the unfairness of it, money held by someone else, always held by someone else.

It was Mrs. Okafor herself who came in near closing, which was the fact Kayla had been waiting for without knowing it. She stood in the doorway with a manila envelope and asked for Marcus by name, and when he wasn't back yet from the Delgado showing, she sat in the plastic chair by the window and Kayla brought her water because there was nothing else to bring.

"You're the girl from next door," Mrs. Okafor said. "With the little brother."

"Danny," Kayla said. "He's got a congenital heart thing, so everybody on our street knows him because of the ambulance bills." Mrs. Okafor smiled at that, the first movement in her face.

"Is the sign because you're selling?" Kayla asked, though she knew it wasn't.

"We stopped paying the mortgage," Mrs. Okafor said, flat, the way you hand over something heavy. "Mr. Okafor's hours got cut in March. The bank sent letters. I thought if we caught up." She turned the envelope over in her lap. "The house was collateral for the loan. You know that word? Collateral. So now the lender can foreclose. They take the house and sell it, and that's how they get their money back."

"Take it," Kayla said. "But it's your house."

"It's the bank's house until the last payment clears," Mrs. Okafor said, and laughed, briefly, a terrible small sound. "Nine years in and we still owed most of it."

Marcus came through the door then, sweating, keys already out, saying something triumphant about the Delgados wanting a second viewing. He saw Mrs. Okafor and his face did the professional thing, the arranging of features. Kayla watched him cross the room, watched him sit down across from a woman whose house would be sold to pay a debt, the same kind of sale he'd been chasing all week with his tie and his rehearsed calls. Both were true and neither canceled the other. She didn't know yet what to do with that.

"Can they make us leave?" Mrs. Okafor asked Marcus.

Marcus set his keys down slowly. "Let's look at what you've got," he said, and reached for the envelope, and Kayla pulled her chair closer to the desk, close enough to read.

Eva arrived at Marston Lanes eleven minutes early, which she decided was eight minutes too many, so she spent the surplus at the snack counter buying a drink she didn't want and then holding it like a prop. The alley smelled of rented shoes and fried food, a smell so autochthonous to bowling alleys that she suspected it had never existed anywhere else, and under the black lights her white shirt glowed in a way she hadn't planned. Marcus was due at seven. She had met him once, at a debate tournament where they'd argued opposite sides of a resolution about public transit, and afterward he'd found her to say her rebuttal was the best thing he'd heard all day, which was either flattery or the truth, and she couldn't tell which, and that not-knowing was the whole reason she'd said yes.

He showed up at 7:02 carrying his own shoes, which she took as a good sign, and they got lane fourteen and he entered their names into the scorer while she watched his hands move over the keypad. The first game was bad on both sides. She bowled a 94 and he bowled an 87, and they laughed about it, and the laughing was easier than the bowling. Between turns they sat on the molded plastic benches, and somewhere in the second game Eva noticed that they had both leaned forward on their elbows in exactly the same way, forearms on knees, chin resting on laced fingers, like two copies of the same photograph.

She straightened up quickly, then felt stupid for it.

The reason she straightened was this: over the summer, trying to fill the strange liminality between high school and everything after it, she had read a stack of psychology articles her sister left behind, and one of them she'd read twice. In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, and the people being mimicked didn't even notice it happening. She had thought at the time that it was a nice fact, the kind of thing you'd bring up at a party and then never use. Now she was using it, or it was using her, and she sat with her arms crossed instead, testing something she couldn't have named.

Marcus bowled a strike and turned around with his arms up, and she raised her arms too, and he grinned. In the third game she made a small experiment of it, casual, she hoped. When he tucked one ankle under the other ankle, she waited four seconds and did the same. When he spun the ball on the return rack, she spun hers. She watched his face for the effect and couldn't find one, which the study said was the point, that it worked below noticing, but it also meant she couldn't tell whether it was working, and that bothered her more than she expected. If he liked her more because she was copying him, was that something she had, or something she'd taken? He wasn't a lab partner. He was a boy who had remembered her last name from a name tag she'd worn once.

In the eighth frame he asked about the tournament, and she told the story of how she'd left her final speech on the bus and had to reconstruct it from memory, and he laughed so hard he had to put his drink down. Then he said, "Can I tell you something weird?" and she said yes, bracing. "I keep noticing I'm doing whatever you're doing," he said. "Like just now, you did that thing with your ankle, and then I did it. It's like you're the puppeteer and I'm not sure when it started."

Eva felt her face go hot under the black light, where she hoped the purple hid things. He was the one confessing, and she was the one blushing, because he had caught her, or half-caught her, and now she had to decide whether a partial truth was a lie. She could claim coincidence. She could laugh it off and keep the advantage. Or she could expiate the whole thing right there at lane fourteen and tell him about Chartrand and Bargh, about 1999, about liking someone more when they quietly copied your posture and gestures, all without your noticing, and admit that she had been trying it on him like a chemistry student tries a reaction, and see what he did with the information.

"I read this thing," she said. "A study. These researchers, Chartrand and Bargh, in 1999, they found that people liked a partner more when the partner mimicked their posture and gestures, and the people never noticed the mimicry." She was looking at the lane, not at him. "And when you said that, I realized I've been doing it to you for like a game and a half. On purpose. Sort of on purpose."

There was a silence long enough for the pinsetter to sweep an empty lane beside them. "So I like you because of that," Marcus said finally, "or you like me?"

"That's the part they didn't test," Eva said. "Or they tested it and I didn't read that far."

He picked up his ball and stood at the line, and instead of bowling he turned around to face her, mirroring, deliberately, the exact position of her body on the bench, one ankle tucked under the other, chin on laced fingers, exaggerated just enough to be unmistakable. "Your frame," he said, holding the pose.

She picked up her own ball and stood at the line beside him, copied his stance, and let hers go into the gutter, and he laughed, and she laughed, and neither of them moved to fix the score.

The sign on the door of Ferrand Market said CLOSED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE, and beneath it, in the manager's careful handwriting, a second sheet: THIS IS A LOCKOUT. PLEASE DO NOT ATTEMPT TO ENTER. Autumn read it twice, then checked her phone against the time, as though the numbers might reconcile themselves. Her shift started at four. It was ten past. Through the glass she could see the registers dark and Mr. Okonkwo from produce standing in the aisle with his coat already on, not shopping, not working, just standing there like furniture that had been arranged by someone in a hurry.

She found the union hall by asking Mr. Okonkwo, who came out a side door when she knocked on it. It was a low brick building three blocks over, between a dentist and a shuttered laundromat, with folding chairs in rows and a coffee urn that had clearly been running since morning. A man at a card table was copying names into a ledger. When she gave her name he paused over it, said, "New hire, September," and wrote her in anyway, in a column that had its own heading.

She had assumed, walking over, that this was a strike. That was the word from the news, the word with the picket lines and the drums. But the man at the table, whose lanyard said DENNIS, told her the workers hadn't refused to come in. "The company shut us out," he said. "They changed the locks Friday night. That's the difference, and it matters. In a strike, we'd be refusing to work. This way, they're refusing to let us." A woman beside him added, "They call it a lockout," and went back to her clipboard, as if the word itself were the whole argument.

Autumn took a chair near the back and tried to fit the pieces together the way she would a proof. Her calculus teacher called the small stepping-stone propositions lemmas: things you had to establish first before the main claim would stand. This was one of those, she thought. Who stopped the work determined what everything downstream meant: whether the stoppage was a weapon of the workers or of the employer, who was supposed to feel the pressure, whose patience was being spent. She had worked at Ferrand for six weeks, two of them in training. She was, she realized, the most junior person in the room by a margin of about nine years.

Ms. Ferreira, the assistant manager, found her there within the hour. She came in through the dentists' shared door, still wearing her lanyard, and sat down beside Autumn without being invited. "I'm not management," she said first, which was the kind of sentence that made Autumn listen harder. "I'm hourly, same as you. But they've asked me to call the part-timers, in order of hire date, and offer them the shifts. The store reopens Monday with whoever comes." She said it flatly, reading the room while pretending to read her phone. What she wanted was visible in her hands: she wanted Autumn to say yes so that Ms. Ferreira could tell the district office she had tried, so that her own name would appear on the list of people who had tried. "You'd keep your wages," she added. "Time and a half on Sunday, if it goes long."

The wages were the same wages the locked-out people in the folding chairs had. That was the thing Autumn kept circling back to. Dennis had a handout, photocopied crookedly, with the current contract language on one side and the company's proposed language on the other: the Sunday premium replaced with a flat rate, the scheduling notice cut from two weeks to one, a clause about "operational flexibility" that seemed, to Autumn's inchoate understanding of contracts, to mean that flexibility flowed entirely one direction. She read it twice. It was not about any single line. It was about who decided.

"I almost went in," she admitted later, to a woman named Priya who stocked dairy and had appointed herself in charge of the picket schedule, a grid on butcher paper so new the marker still smelled. "This morning I thought the doors were just stuck." It wasn't quite the truth, and Priya seemed to know it, because she raised one eyebrow and waited. The truth was that Autumn had stood outside for a full minute thinking about time and a half, and that standing here now felt like a way to expiate the minute, and that expiation was probably the wrong reason to do anything, the way guilt was a bad reason to vote.

The twist came at the Thursday meeting, and it arrived through Mr. Okonkwo, quiet Mr. Okonkwo of produce, who stood up when Dennis called for new business and said he had something to disclose. He had been in the building Friday night when the locks were changed. He had helped the locksmith carry his tools in, because the man had his hands full and it seemed like courtesy, and only afterward understood what he had carried them toward. He told the room this in a voice that kept dropping. Somebody near the front started to laugh, couldn't decide whether it was that kind of story, and stopped.

Autumn watched Dennis decide, in real time, what to do with a confession like that. He didn't absolve him and he didn't shame him. He wrote something in the ledger, then crossed it out, then said, "Saturday, you're on the six a.m. picket, and you're bringing the coffee." Mr. Okonkwo nodded like a man being sentenced, and half the room laughed for real this time, and Priya wrote his name at the top of the grid in letters bigger than anyone else's.

Saturday at six it was dark and very cold. Autumn held a sign she hadn't expected to hold, having assumed she would hold nothing, having assumed a lot of things that week. Ms. Ferreira drove past at six-forty, alone in her car, and slowed, and looked, and did not wave. Autumn raised her sign anyway, a small uncalibrated movement, and Mr. Okonkwo arrived with two carafes and the cups stacked inside each other wrong, so that they came apart all at once and rolled toward the curb like small white wheels, and everyone scrambled after them, laughing, before the store lights came on.

Justine had come to her grandmother's house to escape the group chat, which by Sunday evening had become a tribunal, and it half worked. The kitchen smelled of cardamom because her grandmother had decided, querulously, that nobody visited anymore unless there was cake, and so there was cake, set out on the good plate as if to propitiate some god of grandchildren. Justine sat at the counter with her phone face down and her debate binder open, rehearsing under her breath, when the doorbell rang at the exact minute Dev had said he'd come.

He came in carrying his own binder and a two-liter of ginger ale like a hostage. They were partners for the regional tournament on Saturday, and their last practice had gone badly, not because Dev was bad, but because Justine had told him so in the flattest possible way. "Your closing was weak," she'd said, and then, when he asked what she meant, she'd said, "Just, like, weak," and Shrugged, and the silence after that had lasted four days and generated the tribunal currently raging in the group chat.

They set up on the porch, two folding chairs facing the bird feeder. Dev stood to deliver his constructive speech, and Justine noticed something she'd noticed before but never named: before he began, he rolled his shoulders back, planted his feet wide, and lifted his chin like a man about to be painted into a mural.

"Wait," she said. "Before you start. What is that?"

"What is what?"

"The thing you do. The superhero thing."

He went pink. "It's a power pose. You stand like this for a couple minutes and it changes your hormones. I read about it. There was a study." He held the pose, arms slightly out, looking less like Wonder Woman and more like a scarecrow that had opinions.

Justine took out her phone, because she had learned, the hard way, that checking was cheaper than believing. She found it in three searches, and it was more complicated than Dev's version. The 2010 study had claimed power poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol. Then a larger 2015 replication had found no such hormonal effect at all, though people still reported feeling more powerful. She read it twice. "So it's real and it's not," she said slowly. "The hormones part didn't hold up. The feeling part did."

"Then it works," Dev said.

"Then it works and it doesn't," Justine said, and then stopped, because she recognized the shape of the thing she actually needed to tell him, and it was bigger than the pose.

Last month, before the quarterfinal, she had stood outside the boys' restroom and watched Dev do the pose in the mirror through the cracked door, and she had thought, at the time, that it was why he'd gone out and delivered the most wooden speech of his life. He had felt powerful, apparently, and powerful had made him stiff, had made him gesture like a windmill in a light breeze, had made him use the word "furthermore" four times. She had never said any of this. She had said "weak."

"Okay," she said. "Here's the thing, and I'm going to try to say it better than last time." She put the phone down. "Your arguments Saturday were good. Your second point about the tariff data was the best thing anyone said all round. And then you'd hit a transition and do this." She stood up and did the windmill, arms wide, chin high, and Dev laughed despite himself, a short involuntary bark. "You stand like the pose the whole time you're talking. Like you're holding a position instead of arguing one."

Dev sat down slowly, the superhero leaking out of him. "So I should stop the pose?"

"No. That's the part I'm not sure about." She found she meant it, and it was strange to say a thing she hadn't finished thinking. "The pose makes you feel something, and the feeling is real even if the science isn't, or wasn't, exactly. But the feeling is for before. In the restroom. In the mirror. Then you go out and you talk like a person, and a person isn't a statue." She hesitated. "I think. I could be wrong about the second part. The first part, the hormones, that part's settled. The rest is me."

From inside the house came the sound of the television, which her grandmother kept tuned to a channel where a populist pundit explained, at volume, that elites had ruined everything, including, this evening, breakfast cereal. The screen door creaked open and her grandmother emerged with the cake, set it between the two binders, looked at Dev, looked at Justine, and then, without comment, rolled her shoulders back, planted her feet wide, and lifted her chin at the bird feeder.

"Eighty-one years old," she said, still holding it. "I saw you two through the window. If it works for the young ones, it works for me." She held the pose a moment longer, then cut the cake, her hands steady, her expression unreadable. "I don't feel more powerful," she announced, handing Justine the first slice. "But I feel ready to argue about it."

Dev leaned over and whispered, "Is she available for Saturday?"

"She's the second speaker," Justine said, and cut him a slice too.

The pit at the regional robotics competition smelled like solder and energy drinks, and Makayla had been staring at the same twenty lines of Java for forty minutes. Their scouting app was supposed to pull match data from the volunteer table, rank the other teams, and hand a clean list to the drive team before alliance selection at two o'clock. Instead it handed them a page of nulls. Every robot showed up as "null, null, scored null points," which was less than useless, and Dev, their driver, was standing behind her with his arms crossed like the clock was her personal enemy.

"Fix it fast," he said. "I want the pick list an hour early so I can walk the pits and talk to the top three captains myself." That was Dev's whole season in one sentence: he wanted to be the one who chose, the one shaking hands, the face of the team. Makayla didn't demur out loud, but she filed the request under things that were not going to happen on her current timeline.

She read the Robot class again. She had written it two nights ago in her bedroom, following the pattern from a tutorial: private fields, a constructor, getter methods like getName and getPoints. It looked right. It compiled. She scrolled to the constructor and read it aloud under her breath: name equals name, points equals points. Somewhere behind her, a mentor from another team was telling a rookie that the team treasurer had a fiduciary duty not to spend the entry fee money on a better joystick, and Makayla heard the word without looking up.

"Can I see?" Priya pulled a folding chair over and sat down without waiting for an answer. Priya was their programmer in theory, but she mostly did the mechanical stuff now, and she watched the screen with the patient, slightly jaundiced expression of someone who had seen a lot of code fail at a lot of competitions. "The app's not crashing," she said. "So the fields exist. They're just empty."

"Then the constructor isn't running," Makayla said.

"It's running. You'd get an exception if it weren't."

Makayla put her finger on the line. "I wrote name equals name." She said it slowly, the way you repeat a word until it stops sounding like a word. The parameter was called name. The field was called name. Java had to pick one of them, and it had picked the parameter, both times, on both sides of the equals sign. The field never got anything. The constructor wasn't silently doing nothing, exactly; it was silently assigning a variable to itself, which amounted to the same emptiness. She thought of her English teacher's rule about ambiguous pronouns, how "she told her" could mean three different things depending on who was standing where. She had spent a semester learning to disambiguate sentences for readers, and here was a language that disambiguated for you, bluntly, by taking the nearest name. Except there was a way to say which one you meant.

"You need the keyword," Priya said, and tapped the screen above the line. "this dot name equals name."

Makayla typed it, this.name = name, and then this.points = points, and before she trusted it she wrote a tiny test class in another file. She made one robot, gave it the name "Ironclad" and the number 118, and printed getName. The console answered Ironclad. She made a second one with different values and printed both, and they came back distinct, each object holding its own. She sat back for a second, not triumphant, just quiet. She still wasn't certain she understood the whole rule, only that it worked here, now, in this constructor, and that two hours from now she might hit a case she hadn't imagined. That was fine. Two o'clock was more certain than the rest of it.

"Done," she said, and the pick list spilled out, ranked, real names attached to real numbers. Dev leaned in over her shoulder, reading the top three, already composing his opening line to the first captain. Priya stood and stretched and said she was going to go look at Ironclad's robot in person, because data only told you so much.

"Wait," Dev said. "Give me the list first."

"I'll print you a copy." Makayla hit print, and the page slid out warm from the printer, Ironclad at the top, and she handed it to him without deciding yet whether she would walk the pits with him or go see the robot herself.

The camp was held in the church hall two streets from Grandpa's house, so for two weeks Paige slept in the guest room under the framed photograph of Grandma and got up early to practice. She had been cast as an assistant director, which meant, as far as she could tell, that she was supposed to stand near the director, Mr. Okafor, and learn by standing. On the third morning he handed her the one-act instead. "I have to be at the middle school Tuesday and Thursday," he said. "You'll run the rehearsal. Blocking and everything."

She had directed nothing larger than a video project filmed in one take on her phone. The one-act had five characters and a scene where two of them had to cross a kitchen, open a door, and reveal a third standing on the porch, and every time the actors tried it in the hall they ended up bunched by the refrigerator like people waiting for a bus. Tessa, who played the mother, had opinions about everything and delivered them at volume. Devon, who played the son, went quiet when he was corrected and stayed quiet for ten minutes afterward.

That first night Paige sat at the kitchen table copying names onto index cards and trying to see the stage in her head, which didn't work, because her head kept the stage only when she wasn't looking directly at it. A mug sat at her elbow, left over from Grandpa's coffee, and she slid it across the table to where the refrigerator would be, then walked her fingers toward it and found the same knot of bodies forming in miniature. She was still frowning at the mug when Grandpa came in for his glass of water.

He set a handful of change on the table, leftovers from the paper, and went to bed. Paige looked at the coins for a while, then laid out a nickel for Tessa, a quarter for Devon, a penny for the girl on the porch, and the other two wherever the scene demanded. When the quarter had to reach the door before the penny appeared, the whole geometry opened up: she could see that Devon needed to arrive first and Tessa second, and that Tessa should be near the sink the whole time, not drifting. She moved the coins four more times, drawing the kitchen on a paper napkin around them, and by eleven she had the scene, or at least the scene's skeleton.

At rehearsal the next afternoon she taped an outline of the set on the floor and put the actors in their places before they could argue. Tessa objected that she was being hung out by the sink like a dish towel. "You're the one who opens the door," Paige said, and demonstrated the count herself, walking it, arriving a beat behind Devon the way the quarter had. They ran it six times. On the fourth, Devon stopped moping and started doing something with his hands in his pockets that read, even from the back row of folding chairs, like a boy deciding whether to lie.

Tessa stayed after the others left, eating crackers from the prop box. "Where'd you get the coin thing?" she asked.

Paige told her what she'd found that morning in the camp's one directing textbook, the chapter with the torn cover she'd read on the porch before Grandpa was up. "Blocking," she said, "comes from W. S. Gilbert. Him and other 19th-century directors planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor." Tessa said that was the first interesting thing anyone at the camp had said all week, which was possibly an attack on Mr. Okafor, though Paige chose not to treat it as one. Later, when Devon complained that a bellicose scene between him and Tessa had been staged too politely, with both of them angled toward the audience like presenters, Paige turned them shoulder to shoulder and let the audience watch the argument from behind, which Mr. Okafor, returning on Friday, said was the strongest choice in the whole piece.

The conflict came to a head on the day before the performance. Tessa wanted to change the door reveal; she had decided, during a peroration at Thursday's rehearsal about trusting an actor's instincts, that she should open the door herself and find the porch girl already speaking. Paige had the coin version of the scene in her pocket, worked out in Grandpa's kitchen, and she believed in it, but she could also see that Tessa's version gave the mother the discovery instead of the son, and that Devon had been quietly carrying the whole play on his indecision all week. She tried both. She ran Tessa's once and her own twice, standing in the hall with her arms crossed, watching not the actors but the space around them, the way the coins had taught her to, whether the empty air between the bodies did anything. Tessa's version was louder. Hers was lonelier. She couldn't decide on those grounds alone, so she asked Devon, in front of everyone, whose moment it was supposed to be.

He took his hands out of his pockets. "Mine," he said. "I think it's mine."

"Then we keep it," Paige said, and Tessa picked up her crackers without argument, which was its own small surprise. Paige did not tell her that she'd almost given the moment away, that the coin trick could show you where a person stood but not what a scene meant, or that she would be working that part out, she suspected, for longer than two weeks. Instead she called the scene from the top, and the actors moved, and from her folding chair she could see the paper napkin in her mind, the nickel by the sink, the quarter crossing the kitchen, the penny waiting on the porch outside the door.

The gym smelled like hot glue and printer toner, and Nolan's poster was curling at the corners because he had printed it at eleven the night before, on the family printer that was older than his sister. His table was third from the doors, between a girl growing mold on purpose and a boy who had built a robot that could not, so far, turn left. In front of Nolan sat three sealed tubes of reddish brown gas in a water bath, and next to the bath, a hot plate that had just decided it was done working for the day.

His project was about equilibrium, which he had typed at the top of the poster in a font he now regretted. The tubes held nitrogen dioxide, the gas his chemistry teacher had waved at from a distance while saying the words "don't drop these." In cold water the gas went pale; in warm water it went dark. The whole point was supposed to be that heat nudged the reaction one way or the other, and Nolan was supposed to explain why, smoothly, to a judge, in under ninety seconds. He had the hot water. He had the ice. He had, at the moment, no hot plate.

"Electricity in the gym is on a timer," the mold girl told him, not unkindly, peeling a banana. "Mr. Prasad says it's so nobody burns the school down. Very torpid of them, if you ask me." She pronounced it like a diagnosis and went back to her fungi.

Nolan carried the cold water bath to the judges' table to ask if there was a kettle anywhere in the building, and while he was gone, the trouble arrived in the form of a kid, maybe ten, with a lanyard that said OBSERVER, who had been circling the tables like a small shark. The kid stopped at the next table over, where a sophomore named Priya had a poster about hydrogen as a fuel. Priya was off arguing with the robot boy about extension cords. The kid picked up her marker and started writing on her tablecloth, which was paper, and which she had not intended as paper for other people.

Nolan came back with a kettle borrowed from the teachers' lounge and found the kid deep in arithmetic. "Two H two," the kid was muttering, "plus O two. That's two of the H-twos, so four hydrogens. And the O two has two oxygens." He counted on the paper. "Then two H two O. Two waters. Two hydrogens each, that's four. One oxygen each, that's two." He looked up at Nolan with the expression of someone who has caught the universe doing something tidy. "It's the same. Both sides."

"That's the idea," Nolan said, setting the kettle down. "Two moles of hydrogen gas, one mole of oxygen gas, two moles of water. Everything you started with shows up at the end."

"Why?"

Nolan opened his mouth and then closed it, because the honest answer was that he was seventeen hours into knowing anything about chemistry at all, and this kid was asking the kind of question that professors wrote whole books avoiding. "Because atoms don't just wander off," he said. "They keep the score even."

Priya returned, saw her tablecloth, and did not scream, which Nolan thought showed real character. "Oh, that's actually useful," she said, crouching to look at the kid's counting. "I've been trying to explain that for two weeks and you did it in marker." She looked up at Nolan. "Is your hot plate dead? I heard about your hot plate. It's the whole gym, apparently. Everyone's talking about your hot plate."

"My hot plate is not interesting enough to be gossip."

"Beguile yourself if you want," Priya said, "but your tubes are the only project in here that changes color, and right now they're all just sitting there being brown."

That was the problem, put plainly. The judges were starting on the far side of the room. He had ice and he had, now, a kettle of lukewarm teachers'-lounge water, and the demonstration needed heat, and his whole understanding of what heat did was one paragraph he had read four times without it ever quite settling into his head. He poured the kettle water into the bath anyway. It was barely warm. The tubes sat there, faintly pink, torpid as Tuesday.

The kid drifted back over, lanyard swinging. "Why do you want them hot?"

"Because I have to explain why they get darker," Nolan said. "And I mostly know that heat pushes it toward the darker stuff, and cold pushes it back, and the system kind of... leans away from whatever you do to it. You add heat, it acts like it's using the heat up. You take heat away, it acts like it's making more." He heard himself say it and stopped. "Wait. Say that again to me."

"Why?"

"No, I mean it. Ask me again why I want them hot."

The kid, game for anything, shrugged. "Why do you want them hot?"

"Because when I push on the equilibrium, it pushes back," Nolan said, and the paragraph he had read four times finally walked into the room and sat down. The system wasn't resisting him out of spite. It was doing exactly what a system with two gases on one side and one on the other could do, shifting its weight the only ways it had available. Heat was a push. Cold was a pull. The color was just the system leaning.

"Mr. Prasad says begging the judges works too," Priya offered. "He said it as a joke but he said it twice, so."

The kettle, plugged into the one live outlet behind the mold empire, began its slow climb toward a boil. Nolan stood over the bath with the kid beside him, both of them watching the pink tubes like they were waiting for something to hatch.

"If it works," the kid said, "do I get credit?"

"You get the marker," Nolan said, and lifted the kettle.

The quarry had filled with spring rain again, green-black and cold, and Morgan spread the ocean current map across the flat top of a boulder so it wouldn't blow into the water. She weighted the corners with four chunks of limestone, one of them shaped, if you squinted, like a gavel, which she thought was funny because in the fall she was supposed to be deciding between studying oceanography and studying law. Her father had offered to underwrite either degree, which he said in the tone of a man handing over something heavier than money.

The want was simple and specific: in eleven days she had to give a ten-minute presentation at a summer program's intake interview, and the assigned topic was how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. She had a folder of notes, a printed map with arrows curling like spilled hair across the Atlantic, and no speech. What she did have was Dex, who was floating on an inner tube twenty feet out, and her phone, which had one bar of signal at the very edge of the quarry.

"Come be my audience," she called.

"You come be my lifeguard," Dex called back, but he paddled in anyway, dripping, ebullient about having gone in before June, and sat shivering on the boulder while she taped the map to a sunlit slab of rock like a lecturer at the world's least convenient chalkboard.

"Okay," she said. "Warm water leaves the Gulf of Mexico, moves north along the American coast, then swings east across the Atlantic toward Europe." She traced the arrows. "So far so good."

"Very good," said Dex, who was being a generous audience because he wanted her to return the favor at his own interview, which was about a community garden and which he had not started preparing.

"But here's where I keep getting stuck." She unfolded a second printout, a latitude map, and put her finger on London. "London is at about 51.5 degrees north. Farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. More north than the whole US-Canada border line."

Dex leaned in, water running off his elbows onto the paper. "That cannot be right. Winnipeg is cold. London has, like, rain and cafes."

"Look at the line. All of it, every state, sits south of London."

He stared at the map for a long moment, lips moving slightly, and then said, "Okay, that's going in your talk. Start with that. Everyone falls off their chair."

She wrote it in the margin, and then sat down on the limestone because the problem had come into focus. If London sat that far north, its weather should look like a Canadian prairie, and it didn't, and her job was to say why, when the honest answer was that she could trace the arrows but not yet see the whole machine. The current map showed the ocean as if it were a river with a personality, single-minded and helpful, and that felt too easy, like a lawyer who only ever described one side. Her jurisprudence-minded half wanted to cross-examine the map, and her ocean-minded half wanted to trust it, and for eleven days she had let them argue instead of doing the work.

So she did what she could actually do. She spread both maps side by side on the boulder, the currents over the latitudes, and made herself look at them together, not as rivals but as witnesses to the same event. Where the warm arrow crossed toward Europe, the latitude lines ran on indifferent of it. The water went one way, the geometry another, and the talk, she realized, was the space between them: not a claim that the current was kind, only that it carried heat north and east, and that London existed inside that traffic.

She drafted a message to the program director that evening, sitting on the hood of her car above the quarry, and read it aloud to Dex before sending it.

"Dear Dr. Okafor: For my presentation I'd like to begin with the latitude of London, which surprised me, and use it to ask the question honestly rather than answer it completely.
